Do you like dark murder mysteries?  Weird visual novels with lots of distinct characters?  EXTREMELY Japanese nonsense?  This is right up your alley.
I had given up hope on seeing this game, since I do not have a Vita, and seeing it pop up on Steam was an extremely pleasant surprise.
This game has a very compelling plot that keeps you on a hook to see what on earth is going on at every point.  You are constantly suspicious of everything, while desperately needing to figure out who is lying, why, and just what exactly even happened.
The music is great, and really enhances the mood, especially during the courtroom scenes.
The game is oozing with that great style some Japanese games especially seem to have, and the anime aesthetic is well-drawn and a lot of fun.
If you dig visual novels with some great flair, and love mysteries, shell out for this one!  You'll plow through it straight through, and won't want to stop.

Year Walk is a game that haunts you when you've played it. In a good way. When you reach the credits the first time, you feel devastated and there is a hint that you can change the outcome, so you'll play it again. And it still gets to you. This little gem of an Indie game is beautiful. The puzzles are clever but not too hard. The atmosphere is hauntingly beautiful and so is the artwork. I highly recommend it to anyone who loves to get through a good story and is a Indie game lover. This game will stay with you for a good amount of time. Go play it already!

This is a really great game if you like horror games with atmosphere rather than gore. There is a bit of blood, but it serves a greater purpose. And there are a few well-done jumpscares. (I counted three that really made me jump, but I haven't seen the whole game.) The game is based off of old Swedish folklore, so there's a handy encylopedia in game if you have any questions about what you see. (It's better than going in blind!)
The puzzles are very insightful, and they require some thought. There are hints, so use them if you get stuck. Some of them require unusual means to solve. (One uses "keys" and even the game's interface to solve.) I really have to applaud the dev's creative thinking for these puzzles! Oh, and pay attention to your surroundings. Those hold the key to some of the puzzles. Especially in places you don't want to tarry too long.
The art is amazing, no lie. It's beautifully done, and the monochrome pallete sets you in a very somber mood. (There are splashes of color here and there, though)
The music is wonderful, and the song they play during the credits especially is both eerie and soothing, which ups the creepy factor by about ten. However, there is a part (In an old tree) where the music gets kind of loud, but don't mute your sound because you need it on to solve that puzzle.)
And don't forget there's a new game plus feature! That box you can't open right near your cabin at the beginning of the game? Ignore it. You can only get to it after you've already done one walk.
This is hands down one of the best indie horror games I've ever played. Go get it right now!

If you're looking for a genuinely challenging game of good, clean, puzzle-solving, and no less than roughly a dozen hours worth of play before completion, I sincerely recommend 'Toki Tori.'
In 'Toki Tori,' you play a fun-sized, flightless-jumpless bird, collecting eggs by navigating around platforms, and dodging enemies, utilizing your array of tools to your advantage. The challenge is that not all the tools are available at once, and they have a limited amount of uses, pre-set specifically per level. This knowledge provides clues to achieving your goal, placing you in a sport of trial-and-error until you find a way that works for you.
If practicing puzzles isn't your cup of tea, there isn't much I can recommend here. The game can get slow and sluggish; as more elements get added to levels, the possibilities expand, and you must keep trying similar things in various combinations until you find one that works. If you're akin to puzzle-style experimentation, you've got no problem, because the higher levels especially require tons of patience before you figure out what to do.
The art style of the game is cozily cartoonish; the physical setting and music of changes per level, which doesn't necessarily add to the gameplay, but rather to its warm and friendly vibe. A great (and my favorite) aspect in this game is the Rewind button, allowing you to carefully step back in order to do an alternative action without having to respawn. This makes learning the levels more hands-on, as you can explore a potentially incorrect move without the fear of it breaking your success so far. Furthermore, since there's no time limit, you're free to scout and plan without being pressured.
To label 'Toki Tori' as a simple kid's game (I've seen people do it) is a great injustice to the hours of gruelling, mind-mastering required to be victorious. This game makes me feel SO fulfilled and smart when I figure out how to finish a level. While I consider myself an experienced puzzle gamer, 9 hours in and I've yet to finish Normal mode, and there's still Hard and Bonus to go.
As a whole, there's not a lot of replayability here; once you've done all the modes, it's simply a nice trophy for your achievement cabinet. However, with over 80 levels, and greatly increasing difficulty, a substantial amount of commitment is required to finish the game on your own (No walkthroughs! Like a true puzzle solver!) If you like a cute, quality game that exercises your brain, I say get 'Toki Tori' and experience it for yourself.

A charming puzzle platformer with a steady difficulty curve. Playing as a cutesy chicken with a penguin waddle, you must collect all of the eggs in each level while using only a limited amount of tools, ranging from a simple platform to a freeze-ray for your enemies. The levels start out simple enough, but slowly progress into complicated head-scratchers where every move you make must be carefully planned in advance if you hope to reach every egg.
If you enjoyed games like Lemmings, you'll likely enjoy Toki Tori, especially with the added bonus of an infinite rewind.

Okay, so...
I love building games and colony type games.  I found this while browsing my fave tubers on the interwebs and decided to give this a go.  And let me tell you, even though I don't have a lot of play time itself, I found this game to be enjoyable and frustrating.
Enjoyable:
The prospect of creating colonies on different types of planets and planetoids is appealing to just about any nerd/gamer that grew up on Star Wars and Star Trek.    My first colony thrived....until I ran out of spares.
Frustrating:
The AI in this game needs tweaking.  Certain things like food consumption, sleep levels, and happiness need a secondary micro-managment filter.  Being able to set a certain percentage of your different AI types to specified jobs would be brilliant.  Case in Point:  I needed spares to repair my panels and turbines.  Were any of my 10 engineers working in the factory?  Nope.  They were standing around doing nothing even with the required items already set for the spares to be produced.
After six attempts, all of which excpet one I enjoyed, I finally made it off Mars and to Neptune.  Five attempts later, because Neptune is WAY harder than Mars if you don't set up correctly within the first 15 minutes, I am happy to say that my baser is flourishing, even with the bad AI.
I would like to see some more content added to the game, new buildings, fixtures, and new areas to colonize.  I think with the game being so new, the developers are listening and adding new content when they can.  I would definitly recommend this game to more advanced players, but it could get your kids out of your hair for several hours.

After 26 hours of play:
I have a few cities, one over 300,000 people and the game does not lag like Cities XL Platinum did on a city this size. There are videos showing that there is a large amount of lag while actively tracing out large zones. I can confirm that this does happen, but it's not even remotely game breaking. As soon as the zone is drawn out and confirmed, the lag disappears. If you did nothing but build a city using this tracing tool and traced out only zones of a size that create significant lag, you'd likely fill the map in a matter of minutes. It's not something that many people are going to do and would defeat any sense of city planning.
A second problem that people are complaining about is that the game appears to use only one core (CPU0). I have no idea why this is the case, but it simply appears to be a load-balancing issue on game startup and does not affect game play. The other cores are used, but for some reason CPU0 is favored. After the game is running, you can prevent the game from using CPU0, then allow it to use CPU0 again and from that point on it will evenly distrubute processing on all cores. Again, there is no noticeable difference in the game before or after this process.
Overall, I like this game. I don't think the simulation algorithms are as complete as SimCity4, but I haven't checked out all the mods for Platinum and there aren't enough mods in Workshop yet for XXL. From what I've read, Platinum had quite a few mods that dramatically improved gameplay and improved simulation. Perhaps with time these will be brought over into Workshop and improved. As far as graphics and being able to lay out unique city styles/shapes, it certainly is better than what SimCity4 offers.
As far as the company Focus goes, I think they did some things to earn their reputation reflected in the reviews for this game. This version of Cities is a step in the right direction, but the effort to enable multicore processing should have been made 2 years ago after they took over development from Monte Cristo. As for those giving negative reviews and outright lying in the review (especially about multicore processing and lag), they need to move on with their lives.
Overall, for someone new to the series, I recommend this game. For those that are angry over past releases, this will be the game you should have received 2 years ago.

I understand what this game is going for: an investigation sim that challenges you to identify what goes with whom, what's connected with what else, and generally hold all the facts in your head. But it's just too simplistic, too linear (their jokingly "non-linear" circular map notwithstanding), and too forgiving. The environment often provides too few cues as to where you need to click in order to find the requisite clues, and likewise the topics that will or won't prove helpful when talking to a given suspect are not necessarily intuitive. Basically, just click on every square inch of each scene until, go through every possible conversation topic with every possible person, and you'll complete the game in two hours with zero consequences. I guess that could be construed as "kid-friendly" or something, but ultimately this isn't so much a game as it is a simplistic demonstration of how investigation kind of works. And to round it all out, the voice acting is quite hit-and-miss.
I applaud the idea and the effort, and I hope these guys use it as a springboard for a more ambitious project, but for now I can't call it a worthwhile experience.

However, those levels were rather concise and their point was to traverse them as fast as  possible
and with a certain rythm.
Volgarrr is a side scrolling beat (hack) em up with a more slower pacing and wich demands more attention
to fighting and exploring and reacting to enemys direct agressively obstacles in longer levels that need
much more time to be traversed.
So considering this, the more or less complete lack of checkpoints hurts the gameplay since one gets
really tired to have to play the same level over and over again.
But the biggest problem i have with the gameplay are the controls, or more precisely when the game asks

TLDR: Close to being such a good game and yet so far away. Overall it comes across as having all the ingredients to be the the greatest city building game ever, and If they fixed some of the flaws it would be great, as it is, I just can't recommend it.
I know of the big furore over this game essentially being a poor update on a previously released title "Cities XL", but I never bought those games and cannot judge this game against it; this review will just be of the game on its own and in isolation. If anything my comparison point would be "SimCity 4", because like most people we've all just been crying out for a sequel to that game that has never happened (at least not how we wanted it, looking at you SimCity Societies).
The Good:
- You can build a city as pretty as the pictures above, it's all very zen.
- The music is quite nice and generally the onscreen notifications aren't overwhelming or irritating.
- Gameplay is fairly intuitive with nicely varied levels of difficulty, especially if you're used to the city building game format.
- The trading system is balanced meaning specialisation of a city can be done easily, you want to build a tourist paradise or an farming utopia? Knock yourself out, it's a lot of flexibility with how you play.
The Bad:
- Poor terrain modification tools, the maps look how they look and you'd better like it.
- The UI is a little bit clunky, occasionally you'll miss-click things.
- Zoom out a little bit and all the vehicles turn to weird grey/black boxes on the road. It upsets your zen greatly.
- I can build individual buildings to a style or I can basically pot-luck it with the city zoning, I can't just set a style of building? You crazy.
- Roads vs Terrain, being unable to properly terraform the landscape makes this maddening however.
- The tutorial thinks it's funny.
The Ugly:
- This game will crash on you, a lot, regularly.
- Lag. Laaaaaaaaggggggg.
Verdict:
If they got rid of the ugly, you could live with the bad, with both however you end up struggling to play the game, this then magnifies any flaws with the game. Like old Lara Crofts terrible camera angles, or resident evils weird control schemes, you fight with them for a while and then you put the game down and you just never pick it up again.

Hardcore sidescrollers used to be a dime a dozen. The classic days of old-school gaming had artificial difficulty to ensure that gamers never finished a game too fast. Recently, the trend has been to make gaming accessible so that more people actually get to the conclusion instead of simply throwing things at the players to test their mettle.
Volgarr the Viking is not that type of game. While there are certainly plenty of enemies, the game doesn't revel in being cheap. Some of the pitfalls may be unfairly placed, but the game constantly asks you to utilize your entire moveset to get the best of the environments.
While combat plays a decently big part of the experience, the game is mostly focused on the platforming. Learning how to maneuvere between projectiles and death traps will play a big part of your journey with Volgarr. That and getting hit is pretty damn deadly as you can only ever attain three hit points.
It makes for a game that starts with a near vertical cliff face for a learning curve. The first level is easily the hardest part of the game, with the second level coming in pretty close. You aren't yet acquainted with the combat or very deliberate feel of your character, so you tend to die on the simplest of things.
I wanted to smack anyone who said the game was "fair," at first. Then, as I kept playing, I realized that most of the difficulty stems from how impatient one can get. You really need to analyze what is coming at you and perform on the drop of a dime. It's not for the faint of heart, but it's definitely very rewarding.
I am still torn on how Volgarr moves. The game is fashioned after Monster Hunter or Demon's Souls in that every action has specific frames that cannot be cancelled out of. It can lead to some controller throwing fits, but learning to not repeat mistakes is the best way to overcome the obstacles in your path.
The levels are pretty well built and there is even a hidden path that leads to a harder challenge. Since I suck, I didn't proceed that way, but I'm inclined to give it a shot. Even with the design being solid, the game eventually gets easy. The final boss for Ending C is a god damned joke, which is a bit upsetting.
I also wasn't terribly fond of the music and default camera style. The game is zoomed in and it makes every 10 times harder. The graphics don't even look that great with the default style, so I'm not sure why that was chosen. If you toggle the zoom, the game becomes a little bit easier to deal with, in addition to making the sprite work shine.
While I was initially going to say skip this unless you're hardcore or dedicated, I actually think that would be doing a disservice to the game. It's well made, despite some frustrations I have with it. Most of my issues are my own, though the lessening of challenge towards the end does kind of suck.
I also don't really see myself returning to this in the future, but in the present, I'm a bit hooked. It's a really fun game and that is what matters most. It's cheap (can be cheaper on a Steam sale) and it won't be a breeze to get through. Why not give it a shot?
7.5/10

I'll preface this review by saying I've played every choice of games that has been released on steam and I have loved each and every one of them. Zombie exodus is a solid choose your own adventure game, in the same vein as all of their previous releases. However, I am sad to say that I don't recommend this game.
At first glance, the game seems to have everything I love in it. Zombie apocalpyse, variety of characters to befriend or betray, and a decent selection of starting "classes". Yet as I read through it, I became increasingly dissatisfied with the choices. Before each mission, you have the option to take a variety of weapons with you. However, I soon realized that the weapons you choose, aside from the various utility options, have absolutely no impact on the story. The shotgun, pistol, rifle, AK, etc. all lead to the same result as did the melee weapons. While the flavor text changed, the outcomes remained the same. I would have preferred it if the weapons you choose had an impact on your progression. Also the fact that you apparently have an unlimited amount of each made the trading aspect worthless, as you didn't need to consider the consequences of trading away an AK or rifle for medicine. When you got to the next mission, you'd once again have everything you traded away.
That alone wouldn't be enough for me to not recommend the story though, as the writing was solid and my favorable predisposition towards choice of games and zombie games in general kept me interested. However, the character relationships also left much to be desired. Even if someone in the group hates you (low disposition score) they would still come to your aid in discussions or battles and essentially nothing changed between low and high disposition scores. This made the relationships in the game seem meaningless. I mean, why have those stats if it doesn't change any of the outcomes?
Finally, (slight spoliers) were the ghost scenes. I am fine with suspending disbelief for the zombie apocalypse, but given that the nature of the disease was viral, it seems counterproductive towards the environment of the game to have supernatural elements in it. These scenes didn't really add anything to the story and in my opinion, weakened its narrative.
By the time I reached act V of the story, I found myself bored and unimpressed. A choose your own adventure story that is essentially without graphics (some sketches were present) and music needs a compelling narrative and meaningful choices in order to be effective. Without it, it begins to bog down. And sadly, this game did exactly that.

Disclaimer: I recieved this product for free to give it an honest review as I am friends with the developer.
Beta Runner, like it's previous game Alpha Runner, is a casual game where you have to collect the little dot thingy's (I don't know what they are called). The game is made by Lightsoutgames.
From playing 30 minutes of the game, (which is all you really need to find out what this game is all about) I've gathered a few pro's and con's about the game, just my opinion though.
- Pro's: Like the first game, it can be a little addicting to play (To the point where you would play it again, but you've got that AAA title that you have yet to play so you go play that instead). The game is the sort of game you'd smuggle onto a memory stick into a school or college and upload it onto the public drive so everyone can play it when they are bored in class.
But in all seriousness, this game is fun, but in short bursts. I doubt many would sit and play this for hours at a time (except maybe the developer), it's one of those games you'd play while you try to figure out what your going to have for lunch. Or your waiting for a phone call from a potential employer or your granny. I do recommend this game as it can be quite a time filler if your out of options or just bored. (Though isn't that the reason a lot of people play games anyway?)
The achievements are rather easy to get, so if your an achievement gremlin, you might like this game for your collection.
- Con's: I keep getting double tapped by the same enemy/object in this game and lose loads of health. The life loss cooldown should be increased, because it's REALLY annoying. The dev told me I was just bad, but I'll rally troops against his game and have this increased, I'll see to it. I doubt I'll ever get a higher score than 5 points until that is sorted. (My current score is actually 72).
Overall, the game is good for short term fun, I doubt many people buy these kinds of games to expect the same amount of hours you'd get in a game like Garry's Mod, or GTA V etc. I'd give this game a 7/10 for it's old school feel, like Paper's, Please.

This game is basically a series of boss fights. What's great is that each boss has their own personality. There's the knight in shining armor fighting for his family, the samurai wishing for nothing more than a good fight, a kindhearted girl desperately trying to save her world. Each of their attack patterns reflect their personalities as well, and they change in between their individual sequences. The knight begins with a shield, but then, as his health starts to dwindle, he abandons the shield and swings his sword recklessly, getting ever more visibly exhausted with each swing. The samurai wants a fair fight, and so eschews most long range attacks in favor of extremely hard hitting sword swings. Some like long range combat which turn it into a bullet hell, and others prefer close range combat with split second action taking the forefront, but most have a mix between the two. Best of all, none of these bosses really feel unfair. They all have patterns that can be exploited, and while some can be rage inducing none of it really felt like the game cheated. The feeling you get when beating a boss that kicked you down time and again though? Now THAT'S the good stuff.
p.s. EA, you want to see a "sense of pride and accomplishment"? Play this, and take notes.

A really fun and endearing little point & click that stands out for its narrative qualities. Unfortunately it is also very streamlined and easy, at least for anyone who has played the first game in the series and expects a bit of a sleuthing challenge.
Detective Grimoire's first appearance was several years back in a free browser game that you should go and play
if you haven't already. As a browser game it was unique, interesting, well made (for a free game) and its best selling point was that you were actually required to do some detective work: The game expected you to collect clues, solve puzzles, interrogate people with a fun little lie detecting mechanic, and actually stop, think and make some deductions on your own before you could accuse someone of the crime. It was perfectly possible to make mistakes if you didn't think things through and that was exactly what made the game really interesting.
This is sadly not the case with its crowdfunded follow-up. You are asked to sit back and enjoy an easy ride, in which yes, you are interacting with the world and the story in interesting ways, but, no, you are not asked to do any real thinking of your own. And then when you have collected all the strands and are hyped about thinking through the mystery, the game will step in and hold your hand while it reveals its secrets. To me (with my previous high expectations) it felt dumbed down, and that was a disappointment.
That said, this is a really really good, if short, point & click. It is less the answer to the mystery at its core that makes it interesting and more the charming, intriguing characters whose motivations and backstories you're watching untangle. I have a special soft spot for well written dialogue and Detective Grimoire delivers that in spades, accompanied by fantastic voice acting that makes the characters come alive. Bonus points for a dialogue system that expects you to pay attention when interviewing suspects, allowing you to become even more immersed in the game world. In fact not only the characters but the whole "Boggy's Bog" you are walking around in feels alive, thanks to some adorable art and an atmospheric soundtrack. I thoroughly enjoyed the lovingly hand-painted backdrops and all the neat animation details.
My own expectations aside, the gameplay is not bad per se. The fact that it is so streamlined may make the game feel too easy (for me), but one could claim that it also helps in allowing you to become engrossed in the game's story. Still, the puzzles are simplistic and many gameplay elements feel like a missed opportunity. For example, having a suspect screen where you can look through various facts that you have uncovered and tag them as suspicious or not suspicious but then never being allowed to use this mechanic in any meaningful way felt like a real let down. On the other hand, combining your clues into logical claims in order to open up new interrogation opportunities is a much better utilised mechanic, and thus becomes one of the most entertaining gameplay elements. All in all, there are many original ideas here, most of which were sadly not allowed to shine. So come to it expecting to interact with an interesting little mystery, but not to be a real agent of change in this world.
So there you have it. I was disappointed by this game, and yet I thoroughly enjoyed it. There is no denying its charm. It is a polished and very entertaining experience but it is also less than 3 hours long with no replayability, so gauge your preferred price tag accordingly. I experienced no technical problems, those elsewhere cited bugs seem to have been patched out. And for any achievement hunters amongst you, it is a really easy game to 100%. It gets a full thumbs up from me, it's a good little game despite its flaws and I have not regretted my purchase. But whatever you do, definitely do yourself a favour and go play it's free predecessor.

Up there you go around every hour and a half, time after time after time. You wake up usually in the mornings. And just the way that the track of your orbits go, you wake up over the Mid-East, over North Africa. As you eat breakfast you look out the window as you're going past and there's the Mediterranean area, and Greece, and Rome, and North Africa, and the Sinai, the whole area. And you realize that in one glance that what you're seeing is what was the whole history of man for years - the cradle of civilization. And you think of all that history that you can imagine, looking at that scene.
And you go around down across North Africa and out over the Indian Ocean, and look up at that great subcontinent of India pointed down toward you as you go past it. And Ceylon off to the side, Burma, Southeast Asia, out over the Philippines, and up across that monstrous Pacific Ocean, vast body of water - you've never realized how big that is before.
And you finally come up across the coast of California and look for those friendly things: Los Angeles, and Phoenix, and on across El Paso and there's Houston, there's home, and you look and sure enough there's the Astrodome. And you identify with that, you know - it's an attachment.
And down across New Orleans and then looking down to the south and there's the whole peninsula of Florida laid out. And all the hundreds of hours you spent flying across that route, down in the atmosphere, all that is friendly again. And you go out across the Atlantic Ocean and back across Africa.
And you do it again and again and again.
And that identity - that you identify with Houston, and then you identify with Los Angeles, and Phoenix and New orleans and everything. And the next thing you recognize in yourself, is you're identifying with North Africa. You look forward to that, you anticipate it. And there it is. That whole process begins to shift of what it is you identify with. When you go around it in an hour and a half you begin to recognize that your identity is with that whole thing. And that makes a change.
You look down there and you can't imagine how many borders and boundaries you crossed again and again and again. And you don't even see 'em. At that wake-up scene - the MID-EAST - you know there are hundreds of people killing each other over some imaginary line that you can't see. From where you see it, the thing is a whole, and it's so beautiful. And you wish you could take one from each side in hand and say, "Look at it from this perspective. Look at that. What's important?"
And so a little later on, your friend, again those same neighbors, another astronaut, the person next to you goes out to the Moon. And now he looks back and he sees the Earth not as something big, where he can see the beautiful details, but he sees the Earth as a small thing out there. And now that contrast between that bright blue and white Christmas tree ornament and that black sky, that infinite universe, really comes through. The size of it, the significance of it - it becomes both things, it becomes so small and so fragile, and such a precious little spot in that universe, that you can block it out with your thumb, and you realize that on that small spot, that little blue and white thing is everything that means anything to you. All of history and music and poetry and art and war and death and birth and love, tears, joy, games, all of it is on that little spot out there that you can cover with your thumb.
And you realize that that perspective . . . that you've changed, that there's something new there. That relationship is no longer what it was. And then you look back on the time when you were outside on that EVA and those few moments that you had the time because the camera malfunctioned, that you had the time to think about what was happening. And you recall staring out there at the spectacle that went before your eyes. Because now you're no longer inside something with a window looking out at a picture, but now you're out there and what you've got around your head is a goldfish bowl and there are no limits here. There are no frames, there are no boundaries. You're really out there, over it, floating, going 25,000 mph, ripping through space, a vacuum, and there's not a sound. There's a silence the depth of which you've never experienced before, and that silence contrasts so markedly with the scenery, with what you're seeing, and the speed with which you know you're going. That contrast, the mix of those two things, really comes through.
And you think about what you're experiencing and why. Do you deserve this? This fantastic experience? Have you earned this in some way? Are you separated out to be touched by God to have some special experience here that other men cannot have? You know the answer to that is No. There's nothing that you've done that deserves that, that earned that. It's not a special thing for you. You know very well at that moment, and it comes through to you so powerfully, that you're the sensing element for man.
You look down and see the surface of that globe that you've lived on all this time and you know all those people down there. They are like you, they are you, and somehow you represent them when you are up there - a sensing element, that point out on the end, and that's a humbling feeling. It's a feeling that says you have a responsibility. It's not for yourself.
The eye that doesn't see does not do justice to the body. That's why it's there, that's why you're out there. And somehow you recognize that you're a piece of this total life. You're out on that forefront and you have to bring that back, somehow. And that becomes a rather special responsibility. It tells you something about your relationship with this thing we call life. And so that's a change, that's something new.
And when you come back, there's a difference in that world now, there's a difference in that relationship between you and that planet, and you and all those other forms of life on that planet, because you've had that kind of experience. It's a difference, and it's so precious. And all through this I've used the word you because it's not me, it's not Dave Scott, it's not♥♥♥♥♥♥Gordon, Pete Conrad, John Glenn, it's you, it's us, it's we, it's life. It's had that experience. And it's not just my problem to integrate, it's not my challenge to integrate, my joy to integrate - it's yours, it's everybody's.

- New camera (just hit 'C' on the keyboard and use page up, page down / arrow keys / Ctrl button to move around)
All in all this is a great game if you want to have FUN making/designing your dream city be it modern american style city or an older looking european city or even an asian style city. Or maybe all of those on a single map. The possibilites, specially if you use mods, are endless.

Over the past week, city building fans have waited patitently for what they were hoping to be the definitive city builder since SimCity 4. Unfortunately the opinions of players has been mixed at best. So is Cities XXL better than Cities XL or worse in every way? We have heard people say this is just a re-branding of an old game, so we decided to find out for ourselves.
Cities XL first launched in 2009 and was a spiritual successor to City Life. The game offered expansive landscapes in which to build your dream city along with online capabilities (long before SimCity). However this did not live up to expectations, the online was a flop, the game suffered from poor optimization such as only using one core on multi-core systems and various memory leaks. Despite this, fans of the series have remained loyal. Despite its faults, Cities XL has offered a very fluid and flexible city building game.
When Cities XXL was announced, it was detailed to have an all new engine, more low-level micro-management and various improvements including to performance. These alone should make it a worthy upgrade or entry point for a budding city builder.
Well the first thing we questioned is the games engine. It is possible this is a new engine under the hood, but on the surface it looks very much the same engine as before. Graphically the game looks the same, albeit with a new black UI. The controls work much the same way and the menus are largely the same. So on the surface at least, the engine seems to have been tweaked rather than fully re-worked from the ground up.
Performance wise, this game is far better. Our city of 425k inhabitants is still as smooth as when we started. In Cities XL Platinum, a similar sized city we had suffered from terrible frame rates and choppiness at this point. The UI is also more responsive than before. We did encounter some minor graphical glitches, mostly that at night, streetlights would illuminate a grid beneath them. But nothing game breaking.
There are some new buildings to place in your city, like a pollution sensor and an eco-car dealer. There are not enough with too little function to add much weight behind a new game release, but welcome additions.
Talking of pollution, this has been greatly tweaked and works more the way you would expect. It makes more sense than ever before to ensure your industry is far from residential areas, where as before it was more of a case of “Does City have Heavy Pollution? Yes, City becomes polluted everywhere quickly”.
What we found most disappointing is there is not much of the low-level micro-management that was promised. What sets the Cities XL/XXL series apart from the SimCity series is the latter focuses much more on micro management and is more organic. In SimCity you say where you want residential, commercial and industrial areas, then depending on the desirability of the area would dictate what would be built there. This would not be static, you could have a luxury hi-rise apartment, but if crime in the area goes up this may become abandoned becoming an eyesore on your landscape. Cities XL/XXL cities generally remain the same, you will not find one neighborhood going from being desirable for Elites to suddenly becoming deserted.
Despite this short coming, one major addition that will help over time to make the Cities XXL the city building game we have been waiting for is the inclusion of the Steam Workshop. I really look forward to seeing the modding community making new buildings, new functions, improvements, fixes and potentially new functionality.
If you are a fan of the series, the current 50% discount off the price is very reasonable. Even not as a full game but £15 as a kind of expansion is not bad value. If you’ve never owned a game in this series and you want large sprawling cities rather than the small towns in SimCity then this is a game well worth picking up.

Year Walk was a delightfully disturbing adventure. I'd definitely recommend it to any casual gamer that enjoys point-and-click mystery games with just a hint of psychological horror. If you buy this game, however, I would absolutely urge you to figure out the puzzles on your own for the full effect. I was up all night the first time I played, writing down all the notes on my hand because I had no paper, and it was great. Sadly, it's really only replayable once or twice to get the whole plot figured out (because there is a twist at the end), and it's not hard to get all the achievements in those one or two playthroughs either. If you can look passed that, then I'm sure you will enjoy yourself as I have.
Have fun!

Year Walk is best described as a sort of stylistic adventure horror game. It's not really a hidden object game, but more focused on atmosphere and puzzles. The story of Year Walk is that you play as a man named Daniel, who lives deep in the woods. You are about to perform something known as a Year Walk, which is an old Scandinavian legend to starve before the midnight of New Years and wander into the forest and night to seek a glimpse of the future. However, there are trials, and strange beings that are said will try to apprehend you, as the very act of Year Walking breaks the two truths of our world, time and space. As you play you have to overcome these trials, explore the deep and progressively strange and unsettling woods, and over it all maybe piece together why Daniel is so concerned about the future to risk his life.
The atmosphere of the game is great. It's more unsettling, surreal, and strange than scary, but I had a constant uneasy feeling and yet fascination to events as they transpired around me. Everything dips into legends and myths from Swedish and Finnish tales, with a helpful encyclopedia if you're interested in knowing more of the origin of things around you. The whole atmosphere is backed by a fantastic soundtrack that, like the game, is appropriately off-kilter.
Year Walk strikes me as one of those games that sticks with you long after you beat it. The story isn't entirely surprising in how it plays out, but it's executed very well, and the details are a lot stranger and help make the whole situation far stranger than what actually happens. It's sort of like a classic folk-story in that what happens is somewhat predictable if you have any experience with stories of a similar kin, but that's not what makes the story interesting, it's how it's told and how everything comes to that natural conclusion. And Year Walk has a lot of depth, things to look into, and intriguing mysteries that stay in the mind long after you find out what ultimately happens.
Gameplay is pretty simplistic. You move left and right along a first-person 2D plane, and occasionally can walk forward or backward to another 2D plane. You interact with objects, and solve puzzles. The game isn't stylized like many other adventure games, with hidden item to find, as what you can and cannot do and interact with is very visible and clear, but some of the puzzles are a bit tricky. My tip is to sometimes think outside of the box. Most of the answers are often more obvious than they may seem at first, none are too challenging, but some aren't pushovers either. I also heavily suggest you keep a notebook and pen handy, it helped me a lot.
It's a game with great atmosphere, an interesting experience that'll last you about two hours, and for many I'd imagine an interesting introduction to Scandinavian myths and folklore. If you have an interest in atmospheric horror experiences, folk stories, or games with a surrealistic edge, I'd definitely give it a recommendation.

What to say about Detective Grimoire. Well, here's something: It's okay.
I first stumbled upon the game on Kongregate, some time before the sequel (this game) was announced. I remember thinking "this was really fun!". It wasn't something huge or ground-breaking, but it was a pretty cool little gem. And, to be fair, it's not trying to be grand, and I can respect that. It's not the issue I have with this game. This game is much of the same. The story is fine, the gameplay is pretty standard, but the art is definitely eyecandy.
So here's the story: You are detective Grimoire, and you've been called out to a swamp, to investigate a murder in a tourist attraction. The supposed killer is the mascot on which the attraction was built: a swamp monster. You meet a cast of colorful characters, note in your pad who is suspicious and who isn't, go over the evidence and play a silly flash game from the early 2000's until the murderer is finally caught.
So what are the good things? Well, characters and voice-acting. Both are really good, and I can't really point out many places that broke immersion (there is ONE, but we'll get to that). Their dialogue is fun and interesting, and breaking their safeguards on certain points is pretty satisfying because they keep denying or outright fighting you on the subject. The art, of course, is beautiful and colorful (much more interesting to the eye might I add, which begs the question: why are none of the triple-A companies taking advantage of more colors in their games?).
Unfortunately, there were quite a few things I disliked about this game. The little girl character is more or less there because she was in the first game (like, really, she gives you a map and pleads for you not to arrest the swamp monster). The aforementioned flash game from the early 2000's really stands out from the rest of the game style-wise (and in early 2000's flash game fashion, the sounds are really loud). The setting is almost the same as the first game. The ending is pretty weak (first gave us a psychotic freak-out, this one has mythical monsters), and the section leading up to it is so straight forward, it almost crumbles the rest of the cookie. See, whether or not you note one of your suspects as the only suspect, you will be pointed to the actual murderer so long as you take the right dialogue choices in the first part of fetching the murderer. So if you thought that wormy guy was the murderer, whoops! Looks like it was this other guy all along! The only difficult part of the game is finding all the clues and details, which really chips down in hindsight.
Then, who finally catches the murderer? What ending is this totally okay game bestowing upon us? The swamp monster. Honestly, I wasn't even angry. I was disappointed. This is a game that seems like it could be centered around our world, one that never hinted to a supernatural element (apart from the witch who turned out to be a herbalist, which I guess is witchcraft to the uninitiated), and yet here they spring an actual monster on us. I was really disappointed, because this could have been my scooby doo (there's no such thing as monsters and the whole kahoozie), and I really really REALLY wanted to like this game.
In a way, though, I want you to give it a try. It's an unrefined gem, dusty and unclear, in need to find its own place in a chunk of ore. There is potential, definitely, but I don't know if the series will continue from here on (though there are characters to grab and hold on to, and the visual style is a five-star lobster dinner to the eye), but as is, it's pretty harmless.

First thing's first: Detective Grimoire was originally created for Android, and has since been ported over to Steam. Nothing other than how the game is controlled has been altered in the Steam port, so any side-puzzles you get involve very simple drag-and-drop solutions. However in my opinion, the game itself is so strong that this lack of puzzle difficulty is
than made up for.
The standout aspect of Detective Grimoire for me is the story, which is fantastically good fun to the end. Grimoire himself is a briliant character; his humour is part cheese and part charm, with a dash of classic British dryness and a stellar voice actor to boot. But it's not just him - all the other characters have great personalities and voice actors too, and if you do end up buying the game then I strongly suggest not skipping a single bit of dialogue! Every conversation and monologue is hilariously entertaining, and a couple had me in tears from laughing so hard. Other positves I need to mention are the game's stunning, hand-drawn art style and its accompanying soundtrack, both of which are gorgeous and you can tell had great care put into them.
As for the negatives, from a personal point of view I can't list many. Detective Grimoire doesn't come with the usual roster of bugs, trial-and-error item combinations, pixel hunting and bad voice acting that I'm used to from the adventure genre - the technical aspects of the game are flawless. However if you prefer skill and difficulty in an adventure game over a good story, then Detective Grimoire will probably let you down. Little hint icons make clue-hunting fairly straightforward (although these can be turned off to make the game harder), and if you don't do well questioning a suspect you can try again as many times as you like. However, I personally had no problem with any of this as I picked up the game well aware that it was originally intended for mobile.
Detective Grimoire is a gorgeous little gem of a game which I simply cannot recommend enough, and its polished finesse and fluid storytelliing make this a must-play for any fan of the adventure game genre. The adorable art style and lack of difficulty also make it a perfect introduction to the world of point-and-click gaming for younger players. Happy sleuthing!

TL;DR AT THE END
This review assumes you uses an Xbox Gamepad like the game tells you to.
So, what is Furi? Furi is a hack-and-slash/bullet hell (which is a wierd and unique combination) romp through a beautiful world filled with colourful and interesting characters. There are no collectibles, no side quests, no standard enemies, no time limits, no random NPC's. There is only you, your weapons and the enemy.
The game starts off with you, a silent nameless warrior being freed from his jail cell by a man called "The Voice". He says to you "The Jailer is the key. Kill him and you will be free." Straight after that you fight your so called jailer and upon defeating him you realise there is more than meets the eye to that phrase. So begins your to freedom. The game does an interesting job of making you care about the world and it's characters and as you progress further through the game the characters become more developed and you start to learn more about the world. Upon beating the game, if you decide to replay it again you will understand alot of things said throughout the game that were impossible to understand on the first playthrough giving alot more detail to a world you barely knew. While all this is very interesting the game never FULLY details what's going on and leaves alot of questions. This was a bit dissapointing but it meant that the game made me care about it's world in the first place.
Furi is split into two parts: the exposition sequences and the boss battles. There are 9 bosses + 1 optional boss you need to fight to finish the game. Before/after each boss you spend time walking from one area to the next. These exposition sequences take anywhere from around 2-5 minutes each. You can move manually or you can press A to auto walk. There are no branching paths or anything, it's simply a straight path from the last arena to the next one while The Voice gives you some clues as to where you are and what the next boss will be like. First time through these exposition sequences are very interesting and give cool backstory.
So, what about the gameplay? Assuming Xbox controller is being used:
- X is your sword. You can perform up to a 4 hit combo with it, if the final hit hits it knocks the opponent down and makes them briefly invulnerable. You can hold X to charge up a strike. Releasing it causes you to dash forward and (assuming enemy is vulnerable) slash and stun the enemy allowing you to perform a powerful cinematic sequence.
- A is your dodge. It's a quick dash that can go through almost any kind of attack in the game and is going to be used ALOT. You can hold A to charge up your dash allowing it to travel a much further distance.
- B (LB in my case after changing the controls) is your parry. There's no real block button. All melee attacks can be parried and a whole bunch of projectiles can be parried back at the enemy. Hitting parry just as the opponent is about to attack stuns them and lets you perform a follow up cinematic sequence.
- Right Stick is your blaster. It shoots a constant stream of fast moving small projectiles that can cancel out other bullets and do consistent damage. Holding RT charges up a shot. You can't move while a shot is charged (you can while shooting normally). The charged shot is possibly the most powerful standard attack in the game but it isn't easy to hit.
The parry system is very lenient. Parryable attacks make a distinct chime and glow white letting you know when to parry. It's impossible to not hear this and the game is fair in this regard. Your blaster is actually super useful and you'll be holding the right stick down for a majority of the fights. There are so many tips and tricks I can give that make the game easier but it's much better to discover them yourself. But i'll give you one now: if you execute a perfect parry you don't have to do your cinematic right away. You can get a few bullets from your blaster in then do it, netting you some extra damage that may or may not be cause of you avoiding a bosses entire set of attacks.
I want to point out that this game is FAIR. Alot of hack and slash AND bullet hell games have sections where you become dumbfounded. You look the screen and go "how the hell am I supposed to avoid that? that's bull****". Furi NEVER does this. Sure, there are alot of attacks that look impossible to dodge and you'll probably die alot trying to figure out how to dodge them. However it won't take long for you to find a strategy to dodge because this game EXCELS at giving visual cues for every single attack. After time you won't need to wait to see what attack it is. You'll look at the boss and know exactly what is coming and it's up to you and your experience to dodge it. The game gives ample time to learn and adapt and as Joseph Anderson put it in his video review: "Furi wants you to beat it". It's fair, it's fun and I hate to say it but if you're constantly having a bad time then unfortunately, moreso than any other game i've ever played, you need to git gud. Furi is not impossibly hard. At the end of the story you'll get a rank which you'll probably want to improve.
Before I get onto the negatives I also want to talk about difficulty. When you beat the game you will unlock "Furier" difficulty and this is difficulty done right. Bosses will not have extra health. They will not get more phases. They will not to more damage. Furier mode simply alters many attacks in the game to make them harder to dodge, or make you use an eitrely different mechanic to avoid. For example, the first bosses final phase sees him sending out around 20 rows of bullets that you can shoot. In furier, every other row are invincible bullets so you need to stand in specific spaces and create a path for yourself. It's difficulty done right and I recommend going through the game on Furier to see the changes.
There are however some minor downfalls. In close quarters combat (after beating a phase some bosses will engage in close combat where they'll have a small number of attacks but you'll have less time to dodge) some of the "danger zone attacks" (attacks that make the arena red except for a small gap for you to stand in to dodge it) are almost impossible to dodge. Dodging is the only way to get into the safe space and in close quarters it's clumsy and hard to control. Especially on furier where the spaces are tiny, you're bound to get it. Speaking of dodge, it activates on button RELEASE not on PRESS like most games meaning you need to dodge earlier than you think you can or you're going to get hit. In some bosses after dying, it took EONS to respawn to continue. At one point I waited *2 minutes* just to stand back up. This was much more prevelant in a later boss battle.
So, what's the verdict?
PROS:
- An interesting story with unique characters
- Responsive and fun mechanics that have almost no limit
- Each boss is unique and fun to fight
- Amazing soundtrack and unique artstyle
- Hard difficulty done right
- Varied achievements
- You don't need to become a master to excel
CONS:
- Exposition sequences become tedious after the first time seeing all of them
- Achievements for speedrunning the campaign on both difficulties even though there is a dedicated speedrunning mode
- No replayability if you aren't interested in achievements/rankings
- Some attacks are undodgeable if you're in the wrong position initially because of a faulty dodge system
TL;DR An absolutely amazing game that you must play if you're interested in boss battles, unique worlds, bullet hell, rankings. It's addictive, fun and most importantly fair.
8/10

It's pretty forgiving in terms of giving you a lot of chances to figure out patterns.  Difficulty is entirely memory based, and learning the mechanics well will actually punish you a lot of times, which is frustrating.  The counter mechanic in particular is bothersome, as it doesn't do much, if any, more damage, and it limits your ability to grab some healing, so if you've got the timing down, you're generally better off to miss your timing so that you just parry.  That's my experience anyway.  Still, you're not likely to need more than one or two retries to beat a given boss.  The camera will occasionally screw you, and in between fights all the changing panoramic views tend to make it difficult to control where you're going.  There's an "auto walk" feature that will just automatically move you along, which kind of ruins any illusion that there's something to explore most of the time.  Still, it gives the feel of one of those Samurai Jack episodes that are just Jack quietly walking somewhere.
Visual style is excellent, and the story is intriguing.  I was kind of borderline on whether I was enjoying the experience or not, and one thing ruined any chance I was ever going to recommend this thing.
Before the sixth boss, you're given a chance to wander around a little forested area and explore, so I did, and there's one little extra bit you can find in doing so.  However.  Wander for more than a minute or so, and you trigger an ending.  Which is fine, you can just reload and continue, right? Nope.  You are started over from the very beginning of the game.
If you're like me, and you were already not really enjoying the actual fights all that much, it's a pretty big kick in the teeth.  It feels like some dev got a bee in his bonnet about some artistic vision and decided to punish the player for trying to do anything but stay on the absolutely linear path the game has laid out.  Or maybe it's just designed to troll, I dunno.  It makes me wish I'd just watched the game on youtube instead of buying it.  It wasn't even a very good ending, and it's made worse by the fact that it involves the character with the worst voicing in the game.
So yeah, gameplay is... eeh.  If you like twitchy controls and high difficulty, it probably won't be enough for you, and if you DON'T like those things, the bosses are just chores you have to complete to experience the story.  Visuals are great, the story is engaging, the characters are interesting, but it's not really that fun, and the arbitrary punishment just ruins it.

Furi is a unique game.
Unique in every way.
Style, gameplay, premise.
It's unlikely you ever seen anything like Furi before in your life. At least, as a whole.
Furi's style is definetely its main appeal. Designed by the same guy who designed Afro Samurai, it really takese it up to eleven by combining Afro Samurai with bright retro synth neon.
Premise is simple, but also not something you ever really encountered before:
Gameplay is the second main point after style though.
It's a unique blend of bullet hell and character action that is taken up to eleven, because the only thing you encounter is bosses, but bosses highly differ and provide several different stages of trying to kill you. It's a one big boss rush that will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ because they all are hard, and even harder when you go to Furi+ which changes their methods of killing you.
Bosses themself are also interesting from the character standpoint. You really get to know them and what are they fighting for with only a handful of lines and screentime.
Tis a truely unique game that won't ever be created again, one and only specimen that deserves to be known and appreciated.
Even if you can't handle its difficulty, at least appreciate its style and characters.

But just for that, it´s worth playing this, to experience all the phases of each boss, dying again and again, until you beat that stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥who´s being killing you for the last THREE HOURS. Stripping away the learning curve, the game is rather short, even with the DLC, which only adds two bosses (one of which I have yet to beat, screw you, Bernard), and the story, while having a huge plot twist, still is not something that blows you away in hindsight, albeit the way it is hinted at and told in general is quite good. Though you won´t be able to piece the hints together without writing them down or having already finished the game, as it will take you a long time to beat one boss to get the next piece of story.
Also, let me talk about the music. Just buy the OST. Just do it. Nuff said.
Anyways, there are two difficulties, one of which basically reduces the playtime of the playthrough by 75%. Play on the Furi/normal difficulty, it also unlocks the Furier/hard mode and the speedrun mode. The latter I´ve played through once, and I got a decent score. But that´s not important.
So, to sum it up, this game gets a big thumbs up from me. If you like hard battles against all sorts of weird bosses that trashtalk you every few seconds, then give this a go.

Year Walk can essentially be described as a classic adventure game played in first peson. You move around the forest as you go on your 'Year Walk' and slowly piece together the puzzles and obscure story. It won the iOS GOTY award last year from many publications and I can easily see why it deserves the accolades.
Year Walk is heavily based on
Swedish folklore and has an amazing art style. You will run into all kinds of creepy demons throughout your adventure. The game does have a few jump scares, but, overall, is more unsettling than scary.
I would mention that I found the atmosphere quite breathtaking. The mood is set by the oppressive musical backdrop that never distracts as you crunch your way through the snow of the forest.
The puzzles are where I really dove into the game. I assembled a full piece of paper covered with drawings, notes, and clues over the course of my travels. There is an in-game map, encyclopedia, and hint system to help you through the game and learn about the Swedish background.
The game is quite short, your first play through should take you about forty five minutes to an hour and a half depending on how quickly things click for you. Multiple play through are encouraged and, in fact, half of the story and the true ending are hidden away in subsequent play. The method of unlocking that ending and reading through the story is quite the ride.
It is unfortunate as the game has been looked over on Steam entirely. Possibly due to the stream of trash that has been coming down as part of Valve's policies lately. I hope that it gets some more attention going forward as it is a great title.

And also it is really cool to see a modern horror game that relies on a haunting atmosphere rather than cheap tricks such as constant jumpscares. I would recommend any horror fan to pick this up right now, it is definitely worth the money. All in all this is probably one of the greatest interpretations of Swedish folklore that I've ever seen.

You will die a lot, but there is no life system (unless you attempt the hard endings) so you can take what you've learned and get right back into it. Piece of advice: open the options menu, go into settings, and activate the "look ahead as toggle" option. This allows you to zoom out the screen and keep it that way until you press the zoom button again (space by default). This lets you see further ahead and have more warning from enemies.

It's Banished, but in space.
Pros.
Provides a pretty good challenge. One slight oversight even late game can kill your entire colony
Decent graphics for the price

Now for the cons and why I am feel the game isn't worth a recommendation .
Cons.
Exremely linear progression. Don't follow an exact presibed series of steps your colony will fail in the first 20 mins of play. All you do is repeat those same steps over and over as your colony grows. There isn't really more than one way to run a successful colony.
Lackluster AI that puts your colonist morale above thier need to survive. Literally they would rather starve to death than work to survive if they aren't happy, and there is a plenty of things to make them unhappy. Have an bunch of unhappy Biologists, the game's farmers, and your colony will starve to death despite having more than enough food production. The AI also has a bad habit of building one thing then walking off to do something else despite having another building to build right next to them.
Lack of content, and the only real end game is having a colony of 300.
Overall 6/10 Great Concept, but nowhere near a complete game even for an indie title. Way too linear for a sandbox city builder.

I started Hero of the Kingdom without any idea of what it was going to be about. I bought it at a good sale price, the single screenshot I saw looked nice, and I don't like to spoil myself with trailers or large numbers of screenshots going into a game. I was immediately put off, thinking that it was going to be an extremely boring hand-holding hidden object adventure. I'm not fond of hidden object games in general, and I hadn't really been expecting to play one when I started.
I wasn't actually wrong in my initial impression--Hero of the Kingdom is a really user-friendly point and click adventure with hidden object elements. The thing about this game, though, is that it is the
casual point and click adventure. The game is beautiful, the music is both relaxing and adventurous (and a true pleasure to listen to), and the sound effects feel crisp and fit just right. Tons of polish all around, and you can tell that there was a lot of love put into making this game.
Don't go in expecting to find a particularly detailed story, but what is there is enjoyable as well. Again, very simple, but it feels right. This is a game you can enjoy in small pieces, or devour all at once for a relaxing evening. Sometimes it's nice to play something simple and pleasant.
Also, the main character solving a lot of problems by being a pretty decent carpenter was oddly refreshing. It's a skill that doesn't really get a lot of serious recognition even in crafting types of games, and it's handled so reasonably and practically within the confines of the story that I couldn't help but smile at moments like finishing construction of the water mill.

This isn't a hidden object game or even a point & click with a tonne of puzzles. There is an unique "thinking" game that pops up every now and then and interrogating suspects is quite fun using the case files and evidence you slowly collect. It's a good introduction game to anyone who hasn't really played the genre before, or for a younger audience to keep amused by during a long journey.
The art direction adds to the atmosphere and a rather underrated soundtrack tops it all off. Detective Grimoire will not disappoint if you want something light and engaging; without blaster guns and impossible tasks.

If you really like puzzles, are a completionist, and are very self-motivated, then I suppose I could recommend this game to you. As for everyone else, I wouldn't bother with The Witness.
My biggest problem with the game is that I found it incredibly un-rewarding. I have never played through a game, made it to the end, and been so unengaged that I felt as if I was wasting my time by bothering to watch the ending. If this game had some semblance of a storyline to follow, like the Talos Principle did, I would think much more highly of this game.
The game is presented marvelously. The visuals and audio were really a pleasure. Interacting with the environment and puzzles all felt very impactful and responsive.
The puzzles were very well designed and the game does a good job of teaching you new mechanics without a single word. Though I would say that it does very little more than a good job at this. Getting stuck on a puzzle in this game was not at all a pleasant experience because of the lack of instruction. The puzzles force you to think outside the box, but the game gives very little guidance on how you should go about doing so. So you often get stuck on a puzzle just because you have not yet been able to guess the mechanic used in the puzzle.
Apart from the visuals and the difficulty of the puzzles, the secrets very fun to search for and find. If only there was more of a reward for doing so, I could honestly see myself coming back just to search for secrets.
All in all, if you're itching for more first person puzzles like Talos Principle and Anticamber and have already played through both, you can give The Witness a shot. Though be prepared for it to be an unrewarding experience.

Two moments really stood out for me in The Witness.
The first was in the areas where you need to use reflection of light to reveal the puzzle. On this puzzle, you could raise or lower the water to change the position of the platform for the light to strike. I kept raising and lowering the water then trying to run around the area to find the position to see the solution in the reflection. After doing this for a while, I ended up going to a video walkthrough to see how to solve it.
The second was solving the puzzle at the top of the mountain around three statues. As I walked around it, I could only see one angle to solve it. After I did that, it needed to be solved in two other ways. Each time after a surveying the puzzle from what must have been the starting position, the solution became apparent.
Those two puzzles sum up The Witness experience for me. When the puzzles work, they were quite satisfying to solve. But when they failed, they were immensely frustrating. Then as the environment starts playing a part, working out how to solve the puzzles became the bigger issues. Which environmental clues, if any, are meant to be how you solve it? And even when certain rules were established, the rules were then changed without rhyme or reason.
One of the biggest difficulties in the game is the sheer size of it. And since the game is split into areas, the kinds of puzzles found in each area are variations on a theme. This is good for internalising the rules, but solving multiple puzzles of the same kind in a row gets tedious. One area - the treehouse - was particularly egregious as each plank was made up of multiple near-identical puzzles. The feeling of grinding out solutions came a few too many times in game.
More than anything, The Witness is more clever in puzzle design than it is in puzzle execution. Some of the puzzles were incredibly impressive in their construction - the creativity and aptitude of the developers was definitely on show. This doesn't always mean a better gaming experience though. And like the beautifully-rendered world, the subtlety  can too often lead to exasperation.
So I would recommend The Witness, but do so with a caveat. It's a game that often requires patience on the part of the player, and that patience isn't justly rewarded by completion. At times it feels like a slog to get through, and the puzzles are repetitive to the point of tedium at times. But the sheer audacity of the game and some very good puzzle design make it worth playing.

Seirra's Outpost (remember that?) meets Banished. You start off with a limited amount of colonists and supplies, and have to make a self-sustaining colony. Having a nice colony attracts other colonists to land and join you, hence increasing your production capability, but also strains your resources (oxygen, food, water, beds, etc). Sucess comes at a price too... as a well functioning colony attracts criminals who invade and try to take over.
It should be mentioned that not all play-throughs are winnable. A meteorite could hit the canteen and kill your only medic, or the power could go out and your people suffocate from lack of oxygen, or a disaster (sandstorm, solar flares) could wipe out a few people left outside.
Unlike Banished [where you can walk away for 10min and the game plays itself] Planetbase requires constant attention, monitoring of all resources, and planning for your next expansion... or the inevitable disaster.

Dev attitude towards their game and their customers have turned out to be very disappointing...

My money would have been better spent elsewhere.

Short, simple, and fun enough while it lasts.  This is a very casual and relaxing game, albeit a repetitive one.  I got it for less than two dollars on sale, and to be honest, I wouldn't pay more than that.  There are a couple mechanics the game never properly explains to you, such as finding eggs, mushrooms, crates, and the like.  (You have to click on the tiny little pictures you see on the map; they don't have icons like almost everything else.)  On top of that, a game this simple could have benefited from a marginally more unique story.  I'm not saying you have to construct an epic tale, or anything, but man, you could have attempted SOME sort of a unique plot twist.  I mean, I guess there was one, kind of, but it was the sort of thing you've probably seen a million times before.
One of my biggest problems in this game was how hard it is to make money.  One of the hints I was given at some point consisted of doing tasks for people, which would have been all well and good, if it weren't for the fact that pretty much every single task required some sort of payment up front.  Occasionally, you'll get a somewhat sizable-seeming sum, but since everything is so expensive, it'll probably be gone very quickly.  Eventually, I ended up trying to gather and sell all the herbs and fish I could, but none of that stuff ever respawns, as it turns out; once you gather all the herbs and fish at all the fishing spots, it's gone forever.  So if you need that stuff later, as I did, you'll be buying them from the store.
When I say I recommend this game, bear in mind that I only recommend it if you can get it for two bucks or less.  This is one of those "I have less than five bucks left in my Steam wallet, what do I do with it?" sort of game, not the kind of thing you should go out of your way to buy.

Hero of the Kingdom is a short point-and-click adventure in a fantasy setting.  The player begins as a farmboy and goes on an adventure by essentially completing errands by interacting with various hotspots on a beautifully drawn map.  More screens are unlocked as one progresses through the story.  In addition to the main story, there are various hidden objects such as mushrooms or lost crates scattered throughout the game world.  These objects blend in well enough that they are not all immediately spotted, but if you should choose to find them all, it's by no means a pixel hunt.
Someone looking for an extremely non-challenging and casual gaming experience may enjoy this title.  In fact, I somewhat enjoyed it as something to do while watching television.
However, I am unable to recommend this game because of its incredibly short length.  I was able to 100% the game in about four hours. Most of those four hours were spent backtracking.  For instance, while fishing, you may run out of energy.  You must then backtrack to the inn to rest.  You then return to the lake to continue fishing, and you run out of bait.  You must then backtrack to purchase more bait.  And then your rod breaks.  You get the idea.
In short, Hero of the Kingdom is not all bad by any means.  It's a decent little game that looks and sounds good, even if it is simplistic.  However, the writing is not so hot.  Unless you are absolutely in love with the genre, there's almost certainly better and more fulfilling ways of spending your time.

You might be surprised to learn that this visual novel is an extremely wild rollercoster ride of twists and turns clocking at around 25 hours in length (maybe a little more, maybe a little less, depending on who you are).
Danganronpa is a fantastic little gem of a game, and while I say its a visual novel and its genre is listed as such, its so interactive that the term feels almost disingenuous to what the game is actually like. Its true that you'll spend a significant portion of your time just reading text on the screen while looking at character portraits and listening to music, but the game is so much more. A good meat of the game involves class trials, where, in a sort of Phoenix Wright fashion, you participate in lengthy debates where you find weak points in people's arguments and present evidence you found to support your claims in an attempt to determine who the killer of each case is. This is done through various different logic minigames, some taking more thinking than others, but most of them basically requiring you to aim the appropriate truth bullets (evidence you found in the case) at contradictions that people say when they say them. Its a really interesting approach to how an argument is treated, and it makes the already fun idea of debating and presenting evidence even more fun. It can especially get rather difficult at times, as sometimes discerning the correct contradiction and why is difficult. Plus people's thoughts fly around the screen while they're talking, which sometimes try to distract and/or prevent you from taking aim at a person's contradiction. Its quite interesting.
Outside of that, before trials you'll do investigating, finding clues that you'll use as evidence during these trials. And ignoring that, there are also moments of "free time" where you just spend time exploring the school and building relationships with other members of the game's colorful cast of characters.
Did I mention the characters are great? Because they are. Undoubtedly, you'll probably have a favorite character or two die, and maybe have a character or two that you loath, but surprisingly even characters you might not like you might like later on as the game progresses, because the characters DO grow and change over time, something I find very appreciatable. Its somewhat sad that this is a game about killing though; a lot of character development in a way goes to waste so to speak, as you'll just end up seeing such a character die. Still, this also means you'll care all the more when it happens, which I think strengthens this game. Which is good, because when you have a game that's as story oriented as this one, its important to have a strong cast of characters to follow and keep the story moving forward, all while throwing a few surprises in its midst, and that the game does.
The fact of the matter is is that this game has a really strong story, and its all well planned out and uses details all throughout the game even from the very start with regards the direction the story goes in. I might recommend that players pay attention to EVERYTHING that happens in the game, because it might come up later, even if you don't think it will. In that sense, the game is very well written, something that Spike Chunsoft has always been good about doing.
Disregarding all that, I think its also worth noting that the art style is both unique and appealing and the soundtrack is pretty pimpin', full of fun drumbeats and synths and even the light incorporation of vocals in some tracks as instruments of their owns (not for singing). Its fun to listen to, and helps set the mood.
All in all, this is a great title and you really should try it out if you want.
