Let me begin by saying that I ♥♥♥♥ing despise Anime Games. The entire genre is horrifically diluted with crappy arcade shooters, rpgs, and a motherload of dating sims, all of which have nothing special about them apart from what color of eyes and hair the cute little face above the massive pair of boobs has. Because of this sad reality, good Anime Games have become few and far between.
This is one of them.
Let me begin by stating that this game is not your crappy visual novel where you might as well just print out the dialouge and read it on your lunch break. Furthermore, don't let the term "dating sim" turn you off from this game. The only real elements that this game shares with a dating sim is you can choose which of your classmates you would like to spend time with to learn more about. To say that you ever "date" any of them is false, and while the game does have plenty of innuedo, no actual romance takes place among any of the characters.
The game is good. If you like Pheonix Wright, you will like this game. If you like mystery and intruige, you will like this game. If you like puzzles, you will like this game. If you're a dirty weeb, you'll probably like this game. The game is about 50% investigation, debating and solving murders, 40% storytelling and 10% of you choosing which characters you like and doing the whole "dating sim" part with them.
The characters are all wonderfully unique and you only have so much time to get to know them, but choose carefully, it can be heartbreaking to have your favorite waifu/husbando get gruesomely murdered, and even more heartbreaking for them to be the murderer themselves.
I end giving this game and the sequel my full recommendation. Don't make a huge mistake by brushing off this gem as weeb trash. Trust me, it's not.

I personally had a very good experience with this game so far. I joined casually and on a whim simply because it was a Digimon MMO, and I thought it would be interesting to give it a shot. Not only did I get attached to my Partners, but I was introduced to the ability to get nearly any Digimon that I loved from my childhood. Suddenly, I got to be my own DigiDestined and go on my own adventure through the Digital World.
While the game does get very grindy, especially later on, I can overlook that through interaction with other players and my own Guild. Nothing feels dull or too repetative (although some of the quests that require you to kill multiples of the same enemy can begin to wear down on you), and there's a slew of items to help you in battle. The translation is laughable, but I didn't find it getting in the way of any quests. On the downside though, the game does /heavily/ rely on the cash shop, and it's almost necessary to buy a new egg with real-world money. The hatching process is sheer luck and feels out of the player's favor more often than not. Again though, I am a casual player simply enjoying the game for the fact that it's letting me live one of the greatest fantasies of my childhood, and rather well at that.
The assortment of available partners can feel staggering at first. There's a pretty lengthy list of Mercenary Digimon you can have with you, and chances are, everyone has a favorite Digimon in here somewhere. Even if you're a fan of the lesser-liked Frontier (hey, I feel you there), you'll find all the main Digimon there and accounted for. Mounted on top of the actual partners themselves are the actual in-game locations.
Digimon Masters Online takes place in Season 5/Data Squad/Savers, so the starting area and main hub will look very familiar if you've seen those. However, that's not the only field based on the show-- there's places from Adventure, 02, Frontier; almost every anime incarnation is present here somehow. It's a joy to be able to level your Digimon to discover new places to go.
This game has been a very, very overwhelmingly positive experience for me. My favorite Digimon are my partners, I can visit places I never thought I could when I was young, and I can be the Tamer I've always wanted to be. If you enjoyed Digimon growing up, then I would highly recommend this game.

I can't really think much to write about, but after playing the game for more than a year, here are my thoughts:
When I start playing, Star Conflict was the only game I have in mind, enjoying many battles in PvP and PvE by destroying vast quantity of ships, spending hours and hours on the computer to play the game, somtimes those hours are just waiting for battle selection. Things was going great until i brought the first Tier 4 ship. I got rekt right at the first battle, then follow by others battle after. I realised weeks later, after rages and a bit of depression, that I was having battles with ships have much higher tiers than mine. I also realise that winning credits was getting harder and harder the higher my level is. Since my PvP skills wasn't that great and having player with way higher ship levels and spent money to upgrade all their guns and modules, I got bored of PvP battles very quickly. I know that to in order to win, I have to spent money on Galactic standard, or invest time.
Half a year after (yes, I chose time instead and it took that long), I finally have a Tier 6 ship. Also this is when I can travel out into open space to explore, to find new planets, or sectors, or whatever I can find out there, or so I thought. First sector that I arrived, I got rekt by aliens. The journey in Star Conflict is getting tougher after purchasing some Tier 7 ships. With PvE battles becoming increasingly harder to win and since no matter I won it or lose, each battle took at least 30 min to play, I change my playing style to open space grinding. But this wasn't any better, after quickly realised that my interceptors are useless against aliens and prirates, frigates was my other option. However the frigates was just barely survive alien attacks and each grinding journey to sectors took forever. More time is invested into the game for just grinding minerals and I wonder if that was worth it. When I try to hold on to the game and think that things just can't get worst, Star Conflict realeased new update which change weapon and module tiers apply to different level of ship e.g. at Tier 6 ships, I have to buy Tier 9 guns. This make upgrading ship so hard for me. A game that used to take me 30 to 45 min to play per day turns into 4 to 5 hours. At this point I want to buy Galactic standards if I want to get anywhere. but I wasn't allow to. I was trying to grind at much as possible, but the end of the summer comes and I know I had to stop. I thought this was it, I quit, no more Star Conflict, because it just simply pay-to-win.
About 3 months ago I return to the game and realised some changes have take place. Destroyers was added, with varieties of guns, modules and minerals. At first I expect nothing had change. The more I play, the more I realised how easy to the missions are and the quantities of credits that I gained. I had quickly obtain around 40,000,000 credits in just months, this much credits that I would never dream to have get me to Tier 12 ships and still going. Not sure that these are just temporary updates but this is more better than I expected. Just recently crafted a destroyer and since there is no money involve, it seem like I can success on getting everything.
I should stop now, since this review is more like my personal thoughts about Star Conflict.but I wrote this as for those who not paying any money will most likely have the same experience as I have. Honestly, if you have the passion and spending lots of time or visit the game daily to play it, I think this game is great for you (not include rages and a bit of depression xD). First of all, this is a Visual Novel.  There is no 'Action', though occasionally you will need to mix drinks.  But basically you will be reading. A lot.  I was initially put off the game by reviews from people who didn't understand that and were sad they couldn't shoot or ♥♥♥♥ things.

Most VNs have the problem of describing what the protagonist (you ) is feeling with the Jr. High technique of throwing in tons of adjectives, like 'We joyfully spent the rest of our afternoon happily, though I sorowfully sighed as I knew my hot robot little sister tragicfully was dying of nanocancer.'
Vallhalla just gives you the dialogue and you can decide for yourself what everyone is feeling.  If the author did a good job and it's an adult audience that's not a problem.
There are some cheap injokes and tropes, but if you're playing this in the first place that's probably a mild positive.
Hint 1:  USE THE KEYS. The game doesn't explain this, but after you make a few drinks, use the keyboard instead of painfully dragging ingredients with the mouse.  QWERT for the ingredients, AS for ice or aging, space for mix/blend and serve.  Eventually you'll know the drinks and can just 1-2-1-2-4
Hint 2: Don't go crazy buying everything early when it seems like there's infinite money. There will be 'random' expenses.
Hint 3: Remember what people like for better results. You've always got a recipe book, but the recipe book doesn't tell you Alma likes a Brandtini.
Hint 4: When you 'finish' the game and want more, use the + on the upper left of the title screen to open up 5 bonus chapters.

Aaaah. It started so great. And it still is so great in many ways. This title is in the middle for me, but it leans slighlty more to a no recommendation. I hope that this review can make you deside better if this is for you or not. Don't take my review as the game is no good. It is a good game, but not for me, and hence I wouldn't recommend it. Read on!
Ultimately it comes down to if you enjoy the game-mechanic or not, and if it has a satiesfying conclusion. Well, in my case, it doesn't, even if starts off well.
Look, if you like serious, die-hard, puzzle-challenges and have loads of patience, this game is for you, and I will give it a great recommendation. The puzzle mechanic is interesting and eventuelly very challenging. But I feel the game gets lost in what it tries to tell. The premise doesn't hold up, and doesn't evolve well.
The good:
Well, I loved how it started. I really enjoyed "witnessing" everything around you, finding solutions and ways to see things in a new perspecive by simply looking a little deeper around you. I truly enjoyed finding patterns in the environment. The game also looks and sounds great. It is enjoyable to walk around taking in the sites. I almost felt it could be kind of a meditation practice just walking around, observing and solving fairly easy puzzles (in the beginning) if you simply take your time and look. There is a lot of puzzles, and lots of extras even after "completing" the game.
The not so good:
Well, perhaps I don't enjoy puzzle-games as much as another. But for me, the game just becomes too hard, too fast, AND the point of the game is lost:
In the beginning a solution feels like "Oh, I got it, I see now, I understand!" and it relies on you observing around you, looking deeper.
The later puzzles do not have the same "aha" moments and evolution like the way it started so beautifully, just more complications. It almost feels like the puzzles weren't challenging enough, so "complications" were added. For example, "follow line to end", but later "follow line to end while the puzzle is blurry and spinning". That doesn't feel clever, just annoying. It is like solving a math problem while your kid is jumping on you, screaming in your ear. You still know the solution, it is just harder to do, but for other reasons, not because the problem itself is interesting.
For example, after a while (depending on how you traverse the island of course) you will start to encounter tetris symbols in the puzzles. No spoilers here, but they are not easy to solve. Because these puzzles depend on visualising the solution. And there is no clever solution or real "aha" moment here except a lot of mindbeding visualizations that take a while to solve, trust me. Sure, the easy ones are ok at first, but after a while the fun just stopped, dead. And then it got even worse.
It feels like the initial mechanics are "observe", while the later mechanics are "visualize", and here is becomes really really tricky at times, especially if you are not so good at visualizing. And I feel the game loses its premise, where the "witnessing" is now happening inside your skull more than in the actual game. You don't need the surroundings in order to solve the puzzles at later stages. You need to be really good at visualizing the solutions. Yes, not all puzzles, but the ones with tetris symbols in them, or when the puzzle itself starts to "spin out of control".
And there are so many puzzles, that you eventually tire, because each take a while to solve at later stages. Sure, if you like this, then this is a paradise of puzzles, litterally. But it is then more like doing hard sudoku (or similar) on the train. The puzzle is the only thing, not the surroundings. It doesn't matter what happens around you. What is the point of being on a beautiful island? None, and I think the game utilized this idea really well in the beginning, but not later on.
I started to look up the solutions online. For one or two puzzles, this can happen to the best of us and no big deal, but for when you start to feel you have to look all of them up... The alternative was to sit and think and vizualize which took me out of the game completely, and like the above mentioned sudoko on the train example - I'm not in the game, I'm in my own head and the immersion is lost. Alternatively I could just try a solution randomly, but that is not that much fun either after a lot of tries. I don't feel like I am learning either like in the earlier puzzles. I also though what is the point in playing this game, looking up all the answers?
Exactly.
So, I did not finish this game. But got about 15 hours out of it. I still enjoyed 75% of that time.
If you managed all by yourself to solve all these puzzles, I admire your wits AND your free time.
I loved this game for the idea of exploring your surroundings and finding solutions. I hated it for bending my mind in half while different colors flashed in front of my eyes, puzzles started rotating, and those damn tetris puzzles....
This game is a masterpiece in many ways no doubt, but a masterpiece where the message got lost and the mechanics became a pain.
If you really want to try it, wait for a sale.

1. If you are 100%ing completest, avoid this game. It will end you. I'll put it this way: if at the end of the day you won't be satisfied if you don't understand why this game is called what it is called, you won't be satisfied. It will give you a million things to do and explore--more than most sane people are going to find the time for--but it never gives you an answer. Decide before playing that you will put this down when it stops being engaging for you and you will live a happier life.
2. W/ number 1 out of the way,
is a masterpiece. It is a flawed masterpiece but a masterpiece nevertheless. You should play it. Just don't overplay it.
3. This is a combination of a puzzle game and an exploration game. You solve puzzles and solving them lets you explore more of the environment. At first, the puzzles seem to be the focus but as you progress, they become more and more incidental to the exploration.
4. One aspect of gameplay that The Witness wears on its sleeve is it doesn't hold your hand and walk you through everything. It doesn't hold your hand to the point of being obtuse. It doesn't hold  your hand to the point of being frustrating. This seems to be, at least in most cases, a specific design decision and not an accident. This is something I have to respect but you are out of your mind if you don't think its carried too far from time to time.
5. You are at first guided through a few puzzle types w/ progressive difficulty and new mechanics introduced gradually, game design 101-style. After a few sections like this, you will invariably wander into a centrally located area that seems to be meant to be sort of a culmination of everything you will learn on the on the island that serves as the game's setting. You are physically able to solve the puzzles in this area at this point but you will have no idea how. You need to go find the puzzles that teach you how to do the puzzles here.
6. This is what I mean when I say the game is obtuse and this is what I mean when I say that over time, the exploration takes precedence over the puzzle solving. Finding the puzzles that teach you how to solve other puzzles is a puzzle unto itself. The solution is neither outright given to you and you are not guided to it outside of the first few hours of gameplay. You have to explore. You earn your instructional puzzles in
, goddamnit.
7. For what it's worth, both the puzzles and the exploration hold up on their own right--well, mostly. The island is very pretty to walk around in and there are many secrets as well as sights that are simply beautiful to behold. I am not much for eye candy so thankfully the puzzles are equally good, using varied elements and generally having a solid and satisfying difficulty curve.
8. This said, I could see how some people might get a little sick of having to do a dozen very similar puzzles straight in a row over and over again. I am a maybe a masochist but I love that♥♥♥♥♥♥myself. I find myself falling into rhythm where the puzzles start to make more sense as they get progressively more complex. I almost feel as if I'm having a witty conversation w/ the game designers. "My good sir, you are making perfect sense so far but what do you say to me adding a tetromino to the mix?" I SAY I WILL SOLVE THIS ♥♥♥♥ING PUZZLE AND MUDDLE YOUR FACE W/ MINT AND SUGAR USING A SWIZZLE STICK MADE OF PURE HATRED.
9. Ok, yeah, it's easy to get carried away here. The combination of board and environmental puzzles this game offers w/ its main course of exploration is incredibly immersive and addictive. You will be seeing
style puzzles in real life while playing this. It's surreal.
10. A major flaw in this is some of the environmental puzzles require very finicky positioning of the player character to solve. In this reviewer's opinion, a well designed puzzle's solution should be easy to execute once you've figured it out. This is very often not the case w/ environmental puzzles. You will be looking at what seems like a near miss as far a potential solution and then go about looking for the actual solution only to find you were right the first time but just standing an in-game millimeter to the left of where you needed to be standing for it to work. This is not a satisfying intellectual exercise but a forced brute force approach and it's annoying beyond belief. If this is unintentional, it's bad game design. If it's intentional, it's bad game design w/ malice and forethought.
11.
doesn't have a plot but it feels like it has a story. You are not progressing anything aside from going where you chose to go but the island you're on seems to have a deep and slightly unsettling history to it that is revealed to you only gradually and even then only partially. You feel like you're on a world created by a vast and unseen intelligence and you are blindly groping your way through. Some of the more frustrating elements make sense in this context. It adds a sense of realism. Any intelligence that pops another sentient being into such a place isn't going to necessarily make everything easy for you. It's going to mess w/ you a bit.
12. As I mentioned in 1,
does overstay it's welcome a bit. It boasts five hundred puzzles and could probably get the job done w/ half that or even less. I can't say exactly why there are so many more puzzles than there needs to be--and like I said, I enjoyed the repetitious puzzle solving--but I do believe one could be forgiven for thinking that perhaps they were there to cheaply pad the game's length to justify a higher price point. Personally, I think this would be worth the full asking price even if it only took ten hours to finish but some people don't think like me.
13. The one questions I cannot really answer for myself after playing this is just exactly why I liked it so much. There are games w/ vaster and more interesting worlds to explore. There are games w/ tougher and more interesting puzzles both of the board game type and environmental type. There are definitely games with better fleshed-out stories and better developed worlds.
just seems to straddle all these things in a way nothing else has that's more effective than more traditional approaches.

Summary: A well designed and polished 2D trick platformer for oldschool sensibilities.
This game is difficulty, but its difficulty revolves mostly around learning the mechanics: movement, attack, level hazards and enemy behavior.
The controls are reminiscent of NES Castlevania: in addition to a fixed-arc jump, there's also double spears, rolling and rope climbing. (Thankfully, no stairs!)
Your offensive options consist of a sword and an infinite supply of spears, which can also be used as platforms.
During a first playthrough, you ought to be careful and approach situations slowly, but as you start mastering the game, you'll be able to flow at a satisfying pace through the levels.
Bosses are a matter of memorizing their patterns and finding the safe spots and the opportune times to strike.
There are three ending to get, each requiring more of the player, but not unfairly so.
The two additional endings raise the ante by requiring you to go through alternative stages on a limited supply of "lives," which you must earn by traversing the stages near flawlessly.
Recommended controls: gamepad with a good D-pad and at least two buttons (ideally four, for pause and view toggle)
(I played with a sideways Wiimote.)

This game tries to capture the true difficulty of classic arcade platformers. The problem is that the presentation really makes it too frustrating for all but hardcore platformer fans, as there is no real save system (you can reportedly sort of skip already beaten levels, but at a cost), no ability to control the difficulty, a tendency to put you back at the start of a level after you die, and half the levels apparently inaccessible unless you complete every level without really taking damage.
Controls are fairly tight and the graphics and music are good, although in the first couple levels I only encountered the same 5 enemy sprites, 3 of which were basically recolors of the same sprite. I also have to give kudos for a Linux port that runs well, including XBox 360 controller support (even rumble works!).
Still, this game is intentionally at the Ghosts 'n Goblins level of difficulty, with no concessions to casual players (e.g. old guys with rusty platforming skills who don't have lots of time to play). As a result, I can't recommend it to anyone who is not a huge fan of super-challenging platformers.

Avoiding repitition is something I was taught very early in game design. The human brain gets tired of the same stimulus over and over, so especially in this medium, you want to make sure you're constantly presenting the player with new concepts and ideas as time progresses. It's a matter of respecting the player's time, you see. Games like The Binding of Isaac always make you feel like you're getting something for your trouble, and the only reason Super Meat Boy gets away with being Super Meat Boy is because you respawn almost instantly, and the levels are so small to begin with. If you die, they don't make you start the whole world over. The brain trust behind this game didn't understand this.
Volgarr the Viking is the worst, and not for the reasons its creators think it is. I'm bored out of my frigging skull playing this game, because my fault or not, I'm sick of doing the exact same thing over and over. Even games like Devil May Cry manage to be tolerable because the gameplay is so deep that mastering it is the reward in itself, but Volgarr can't even manage that. It feels like nothing worthwhile is waiting for me no matter how far I get, aside from having to put up with more intentionally awful knockback and jump mechanics that make the game far less enjoyable than it should be. Surprise: design concepts abandoned by the rest of the industry over a decade ago aren't relevant in the current landscape anymore. This game was outdated before it was even released, and contrary to popular belief, that's not a good thing.

Like the first game in the series, it took me about 5 hours of gameplay to finish this game, but also like the first game, it was 5 fantastic hours of unending alien slaughter.

As with the first game, the story is pretty straight forward, but - also like the first game (seeing a trend here?) - there is one aspect of the plot that kept me asking "Why?" and "How?" and wanting to know more. It's every bit the first game's equal, and if you've played the first one, you'll probably want more, so here it is.
The weapons are mostly the same. You still have your pistol with infinite ammo, your assault rifle that can carry up to 3200 rounds, your shotgun that can carry up to 128 shells, and your flamethrower that can carry up to 1800 units of fuel; but the first game's laser rifle and ion blaster have been replaced with the Hyper Blaster (minigun) and rocket launcher, respectively. Pro-tip - make sure you have the Hyper Blaster's damage upgraded and at least 1500 rounds (maximum of 2500) for the Hyper Blaster by the time you get to the end of level 3; it's hella useful for the boss.
All in all, it's the same deal as the first game - aliens, co-op, arcade shooters, and flamethrowers. If you like at least two of those four, play this game (but play the previous game first).

I've enjoyed my time with Planetbase. At least at my purchase version, Planetbase is a stable, engaging, well-put together colony builder in the vein of Startopia, and Startopia players will immediately notice a handful of similar mechanics. Mastering the different resources and services needed for a colony with good welfare takes some time and challenges, and different equilibriums shift fast enough that the base manager always finds himself with something to do.
My critiques of the game are twofold: 1) a lack of documentation and 2) a shallow end game. The lack of documentation hampers the game in that the player is confronted with complex problems: for example, settlers in a base that is chock full of food and mess halls but still seems to be suffering from malnutrition. The solution in my case appeared to be to diversify available foods until some magic (yet still unknown to me) combination produced a healthier menu. Another problem was the creation of anti-meteor lasers: you're told that they are useful for stopping meteors from pelting your facility, but you're not told what radius they protect, making it difficult to plan coverage.
As for the shallow end game, the sole way to go from a medium sized functional base to a high scoring base appears to be either to build lots of useless monoliths or take on more and more settlers, who in turn present more of the original resource challenges. There's no new ways to tackle problems or reach a different kind of end: the tech tree is very shallow and missing obvious techs like more durable robots, improved production technologies, or improved service technologies. While I found the game very satisfying to play through to a high-pop base, the lack of different end game choices means the game has little replayibility for me.
I enjoyed Planetbase and its challenges, and I feel I got my money's worth and a bit more. But when it comes to the replay, I'm afraid I'll be going back to Startopia: while the older game is clunkier, it has more possible endings and more technological / style choices that make for a more varied gameplay.

Detective Grimoire is a well-polished point-and-click mystery adventure game, short enough to finish in a single session but packed with interesting characters, humorous dialogue, appealing cartoonish graphics, and terrific voice acting. The puzzles are simple, but the scenario was quirky enough to hold my interest for the couple of hours it took me to play through the game. I was particularly impressed by the production value of this game. It has all the little touches that make point-and-click adventures more enjoyable: map navigation to eliminate the tedium of backtracking; well-organized dossiers of the clues, suspects, and locations you've encountered; and (great for completionists) the ability to go back after you've completed the storyline to finish up your achievements. If you're looking for a fun and casual adventure, one where you don't have to worry about bugs or taking irreversible actions, give Detective Grimoire a shot.

The atmosphere seems fantastic? I went into this feeling really positive, but I was kind of flabbergasted by how egregious some of the bad qualities are.
1. The controls are pretty bad. Part of that is a gameplay gimmick that I just happen not to like. You are controlling two characters with a single input. One of them walks faster than the other. The girl walks at a steady rate. The boy either walks slower than the girl or, if you press the run key, faster than the girl. A lot of the challenge (and in my opinion incredible frustration) derives from this mechanic, as  you are guiding the characters over narrow paths that they aren't allowed to step off of or else you die and have to start over. This might not have been quite so bad if there were smooth controls, like the ability to move with a joystick, but you are limited to using WASD, making the character movement clunky and jagged, so the WASD controls (sorry PC master race) actually make things significantly worse instead of better in this case.
2. The camera angles can be antagonistic, especially when dealing with the above controls.
3. The above two gripes I probably could have had patience with for a while, but really the worst of all is that the game is just bad at communication. It doesn't tell you what you ARE supposed to do. It doesn't tell you what you're NOT supposed to do. You just start moving these characters and you don't know where you are moving them to or why. Then you will die and you won't understand why. Then you will die again with zero understanding why. It's kinda hard to win at a game that doesn't bother to tell you its objective or its rules.
If you like a game that says "die until you figure out what the point of me is" then have fun with this one, but it didn't take me long to go from optimistic to just plain annoyed.

Not bad, honestly. But while there's a lot of promise, there's also a few problems.
The Good: The building interface works -really- well. It's pretty intuitive, kinda like freeform legos. The graphics are gorgeous, flat out, especially when solar flares kick in. Ye gods. The economy is rough as hell without being impossible, meaning it's a real challenge but an achievable one.
The Bad: The interface is just plain wonky sometimes. The AI pathfinding for your little colonists is quite often pants-on-head stupid- they'll sometimes -starve to death- because isntead of getting food from a machine next to the dome they're working in, they want to go across the entire base. At endgame, that can be fatal. Security monitoring is spotty at best, and seems to be based on 'roughly when things were built.' There's no way to -force- security to watch for intruders in special areas. And, lastly, the AI can get amazingly stupid with itself. The little colonists will want to eat, sleep, watch TV (or run on the man-sized hamster wheel) more than work, so sometimes I've run into situations where the oxygen generator has been -destroyed,- and people are suffocating... and the repair man is doing pullups. The game would benefit from an 'emergency' system to force pepole to do their jobs.
Overall, though, I'd go for it. It's a fun way to waste some time.

Positives: It's certainly well done. The game is difficult and if you don't work fast you easily fail very early on in the game. The fact that you have limited suplies makes it even more difficulte and forced you to use your resources wisely. These are two things I really enjoy about the game. It's not just a click-and-drop and forces you to actually play strategically.
Another thing I love about it is the ability to build items inside various domes. This is certainly a novel concept I hadn't seen in games like this before. The falling meteors and their ability to damage your buildings is also a nice touch as well.
Negatives: There is so little time to get even the most baisic starting structures in place (Airlock, O2 Generator, Solar Panel, Water (forgot the word), and Power Storage). I enjoy that it is difficult, but at least a tiiiiny bit more time in the beginning would be nice.
When you get further into the game it's also difficult to get anyone to do anything. For instance, I needed Bioplastic, had all the people, resources, buildings, and items necessary to do it, but no one would? This gets very frustrating when you are running out of one resource or another and need to build something fast.
The buildings that you can build are also limited. The game is still technically being developed I believe, so this might change later (logging in today I did notice that the space suits on the people had changed, so I hold out hope, at least). Still, the limitation does such just a tad bit. I wash there was a little more to in terms of building items.
You do also have the ability to rotate planets and choose the LL of where you start out. I've noticed little difference in doing so, though. Another thing I wish is that this actually affected gameplay on the planet. If it does, so far I haven't noticed it. Also having the ability to scan the LL location to see the Topography would be nice. Since you cannot demolish, level, or otherwise build on the mountainous areas it is very easy to back yourself into a corner when building- especially if you are unlucky enough to have it generate a super small area that's buildable (like I have on occasion). Given this, taking even a short amount of time to look around your area to plan a strategy takes too much valuable time when starting out, so being able to scan for sufficient areas on the plant would be a nice perk to counteract that.
It's difficult and challenging for certain, but in some ways it's too challenging. Still. All in all, I am very excited to see where this game goes.
Edit February 2017: Some things I noticed in my most recent play through that I failed to mention in my intial review include Camera Controles and AI.
Concerning Camera controls, I wish there was a bit more maneuverability. You can vaguely scan around in a circle, and you can zoom out a little. But increased camera controls (like the ability to do a top down view where you view the base from the complete top) would be great.
Concerning the AI... It sucks. Point blank, it's probably one of the worst AI's I've seen in a game so far. I think the AI might have actually been better the last time I played it, but it seems to have become a bit broken since then. Or maybe I got lucky on my earlier plays? Either way, issues include 1. People standing in the middle of nowhere outside of the base for no reason until they die, 2. People refusing to fix the robots, 3. The "Prioritize" feature (which seems new, or maybe I didn't notice it last time) doesn't do much, if anything, to influence their building decisions, 4. People refusing to produce items despite having everything needed to produce them (yes, that's still an issue), and so on.
Honestly, it's been just over a year now and I haven't noticed anything much change with the game. What happened? Is it still being developed? Who knows, but I definitely hope I didn't waste $16 on what's arguably an unfinished product.

This is a great little mystery game, with a good art style and some interesting, unique ideas.  I'd recommend this for gamers preferring games that are mostly about story, but I could also see it as a good game to introduce a child into gaming, and may be appealing to fans of the adventure genre as well.  Steam reports that I got about 3 hours of entertainment from it.
As far as challenges go, it's pretty straightforward and mostly relies on discovering clues and suspects, and then interviewing suspects about those clues (and about other suspects).  For that, you're really just along for the ride as you learn more and more of the story.
Additionally, there's a clever little game mechanic that involves you choosing the correct clues/suspects and fractures of a sentence to form a conclusion that uncovers various truths.  That part emulates thinking through what you've discovered like a detective might, and feels pretty rewarding when you get it right.
Beyond that, there are a few minigame-puzzles to complete to allow you to progress to certain areas.  They're cute and fun, but really only a momentary distraction.
Overall, this won't be a title that appears to many hardcore gamers.  But the art style, storyline & mystery, and deductive reasoning puzzles will be appealing to a certain audience. But the conversation quickly diverges and both of them start to discuss how they perceive the subject of the investigation from a moral point of view. They talk about how apathy is a solution, how love takes effort, how the weight of evil deeds is incomprehensible... Meanwhile we learn about the characters themselves - Somerset's attitude is questioned by Mills when he points out, that the detective's speech about social indifference is just an excuse to justify his quitting the force.
It's a great scene really - a meaningful topic is discussed, and I mean discussed, not disregarded by posing pseudo-existential questions without answers. We learn about our protagonists' convictions and where they come from. Themes of the movie are fleshed out and the talk will heavily impact Somerset's arc.
Or a different scene - Murray's and Johansson's characters conversation at the bar in "Lost in Translation". Two people sharing stories of their lives, talking about disappointments, comparing the view of life from perspectives of different ages. No metaphysical discussion this time, only simple dialogue, small talk almost. While it's exchanging mundane experiences on the surface, there are many emotions hidden underneath, glimmers of which we can catch in small gestures, looks, unfinished sentences. All immersed in sounds of clinking glasses, night lights and solitude.
Just two people getting to know each other, finding out things they have in common and opening up to each other.
I won't say that I was expecting such moments from VA-11 HALL-A, but I was quietly hoping for them. I mean - a cyberpunk dystopia with all it's problems seen from behind the bar - a perfect setting for long in-depth conversations. And the game is basically a visual novel, so it's not like the screenplay was secondary. What could possibly go wrong? Well...
First tiny warning sign for me was Jill's wardrobe, namely a t-shirt with "sl*t" written on it. It's like a big "I don't care what anybody thinks about me" announcement, which of course means that the person cares two times as much. Going down the plot road, passing by f-bombs and curse words I've met Mr Donovan. I don't mind swearing that much. It's an occurrence common these days, so it's natural that some characters would use such vocabulary. But Mr Donovan is a whole new specimen. His filthy talk about his sexual relationships is a thing that only a bartender can listen to out of sheer sense of duty. But sometime later Betty came in. And Alma. And Mario. And Streaming-Chan. And *sigh* Dorothy...
A great illustration of my problem is the first conversation with Ingram. He starts telling me his story, he speaks about his wife and deceased child, he says that he feels empty, that he misses something crucial... And then he cuts the topic and asks Jill about her sex life. Tommy Wiseau couldn't have done that better. That's the main problem - almost every time the conversation starts getting deep and the topic becomes interesting a few obscene lines have to be thrown in. I felt like listening to a bunch of teenagers who think that being vulgar is a sign of being a grown-up.
And it's a shame, because there are intriguing stories hidden between lengthy tasteless descriptions, particularly when Ayanami Rei, I mean, Asagiri Sei enters the scene. Her story about police violence, public service and self-sacrifice is interesting and nuanced. Even on a soap opera level her relationships can tug at your heartstrings. Then again - another good allegory of the whole game - just as I'm getting into Sei's story, Dorothy comes in just to provide a pornographic depiction of her experiences. Luckily I just need to tap spacebar a couple of times to get back to Sei.
And that's how the game feels - like a porn magazine with some gripping stories hidden somewhere between pages.
Why does it have to be like this? Why almost every time I get engaged someone has to interrupt with--
Wait a second.
"VA-11 HALL-A, a booze em' up about waifus, technology, and post-dystopia life". Waifus, waifus... *typing, typing* *reading, reading* Oh... Oh. Man... Wait, wha...? With a squid...? Oh. OH.
And what's that? It takes place in the same universe as Read Only Memolgbtqwerty? I take it back. It's not that VA-11 HALL-A throws porn at me half of the time. It's actually doing its best not to throw it at me the other half of the time! The script is in reality full of restraint and tries to elevate the genre above cheap erotic thrills! I guess I've just got the wrong address and that's where the whole misunderstanding came from.
Oh well, I'm gonna close my tab in VA-11 HALL-A now. There was some good cyberpunk bar down the road, what was it again... Ah yes, Seamstresses Union. I wonder how Mr Kluwe is doing.

A very short but high quality point and click mystery. The soundtrack is terrific and the character designs are excellent. Gameplay involves individual scenes that you click on in a somewhat "hidden object" sort of way in order to collect evidence and reveal clues. Occasionally you will need to complete a very short and VERY easy mini-game to accomplish certain tasks (e.g. unlocking doors, uncovering something buried, etc). The mystery is well-written and the interfaces provided for helping you keep track of your evidence and suspicions are superb.
There are a few minor demerits:
--Voice acting, while very well performed, does not always match the sound of the voice with the character very well. For example, situations like the voice of an obviously young man who is clearly  affecting the voice of a gruff older man---and similar odd affectations on other characters, despite the excellent performances. In other words, the voice PERFORMANCES are stellar, but the voice CASTING is sorta questionable on several characters.
--Seems to be an iOS port. This is a bit of a pet peeve of mine, but it does always annoy me to play a game on the PC and get repeatedly told to "tap" on things.
--While the mystery is well-written, the characters well-designed, the dialogue superb.... the mystery is very easy to figure out. The are zero false evidence trails. There is pretty much just one evidence trail---the right one---and it makes pinpointing the culprit a piece of cake. You won't be second guessing yourself a whole lot. More astute players will figure out very quickly who the criminal is, and so the rest of the game is just checking off boxes so that you can get to the accusation phase.
--Ending sort of predictable and anti-climactic.
On average, despite being very short and a few minor demerits, it is a fun little game and will keep you well-entertained for an evening. I'd give it a solid 8/10.

Aaaah. It started so great. And it still is so great in many ways. This title is in the middle for me, but it leans slighlty more to a no recommendation. I hope that this review can make you deside better if this is for you or not. Don't take my review as the game is no good. It is a good game, but not for me, and hence I wouldn't recommend it. Read on!
Ultimately it comes down to if you enjoy the game-mechanic or not, and if it has a satiesfying conclusion. Well, in my case, it doesn't, even if starts off well.
Look, if you like serious, die-hard, puzzle-challenges and have loads of patience, this game is for you, and I will give it a great recommendation. The puzzle mechanic is interesting and eventuelly very challenging. But I feel the game gets lost in what it tries to tell. The premise doesn't hold up, and doesn't evolve well.
The good:
Well, I loved how it started. I really enjoyed "witnessing" everything around you, finding solutions and ways to see things in a new perspecive by simply looking a little deeper around you. I truly enjoyed finding patterns in the environment. The game also looks and sounds great. It is enjoyable to walk around taking in the sites. I almost felt it could be kind of a meditation practice just walking around, observing and solving fairly easy puzzles (in the beginning) if you simply take your time and look. There is a lot of puzzles, and lots of extras even after "completing" the game.
The not so good:
Well, perhaps I don't enjoy puzzle-games as much as another. But for me, the game just becomes too hard, too fast, AND the point of the game is lost:
In the beginning a solution feels like "Oh, I got it, I see now, I understand!" and it relies on you observing around you, looking deeper.
The later puzzles do not have the same "aha" moments and evolution like the way it started so beautifully, just more complications. It almost feels like the puzzles weren't challenging enough, so "complications" were added. For example, "follow line to end", but later "follow line to end while the puzzle is blurry and spinning". That doesn't feel clever, just annoying. It is like solving a math problem while your kid is jumping on you, screaming in your ear. You still know the solution, it is just harder to do, but for other reasons, not because the problem itself is interesting.
For example, after a while (depending on how you traverse the island of course) you will start to encounter tetris symbols in the puzzles. No spoilers here, but they are not easy to solve. Because these puzzles depend on visualising the solution. And there is no clever solution or real "aha" moment here except a lot of mindbeding visualizations that take a while to solve, trust me. Sure, the easy ones are ok at first, but after a while the fun just stopped, dead. And then it got even worse.
It feels like the initial mechanics are "observe", while the later mechanics are "visualize", and here is becomes really really tricky at times, especially if you are not so good at visualizing. And I feel the game loses its premise, where the "witnessing" is now happening inside your skull more than in the actual game. You don't need the surroundings in order to solve the puzzles at later stages. You need to be really good at visualizing the solutions. Yes, not all puzzles, but the ones with tetris symbols in them, or when the puzzle itself starts to "spin out of control".
And there are so many puzzles, that you eventually tire, because each take a while to solve at later stages. Sure, if you like this, then this is a paradise of puzzles, litterally. But it is then more like doing hard sudoku (or similar) on the train. The puzzle is the only thing, not the surroundings. It doesn't matter what happens around you. What is the point of being on a beautiful island? None, and I think the game utilized this idea really well in the beginning, but not later on.
I started to look up the solutions online. For one or two puzzles, this can happen to the best of us and no big deal, but for when you start to feel you have to look all of them up... The alternative was to sit and think and vizualize which took me out of the game completely, and like the above mentioned sudoko on the train example - I'm not in the game, I'm in my own head and the immersion is lost. Alternatively I could just try a solution randomly, but that is not that much fun either after a lot of tries. I don't feel like I am learning either like in the earlier puzzles. I also though what is the point in playing this game, looking up all the answers?
Exactly.
So, I did not finish this game. But got about 15 hours out of it. I still enjoyed 75% of that time.
If you managed all by yourself to solve all these puzzles, I admire your wits AND your free time.
I loved this game for the idea of exploring your surroundings and finding solutions. I hated it for bending my mind in half while different colors flashed in front of my eyes, puzzles started rotating, and those damn tetris puzzles....
This game is a masterpiece in many ways no doubt, but a masterpiece where the message got lost and the mechanics became a pain.
If you really want to try it, wait for a sale.

1. If you are 100%ing completest, avoid this game. It will end you. I'll put it this way: if at the end of the day you won't be satisfied if you don't understand why this game is called what it is called, you won't be satisfied. It will give you a million things to do and explore--more than most sane people are going to find the time for--but it never gives you an answer. Decide before playing that you will put this down when it stops being engaging for you and you will live a happier life.
2. W/ number 1 out of the way,
is a masterpiece. It is a flawed masterpiece but a masterpiece nevertheless. You should play it. Just don't overplay it.
3. This is a combination of a puzzle game and an exploration game. You solve puzzles and solving them lets you explore more of the environment. At first, the puzzles seem to be the focus but as you progress, they become more and more incidental to the exploration.
4. One aspect of gameplay that The Witness wears on its sleeve is it doesn't hold your hand and walk you through everything. It doesn't hold your hand to the point of being obtuse. It doesn't hold  your hand to the point of being frustrating. This seems to be, at least in most cases, a specific design decision and not an accident. This is something I have to respect but you are out of your mind if you don't think its carried too far from time to time.
5. You are at first guided through a few puzzle types w/ progressive difficulty and new mechanics introduced gradually, game design 101-style. After a few sections like this, you will invariably wander into a centrally located area that seems to be meant to be sort of a culmination of everything you will learn on the on the island that serves as the game's setting. You are physically able to solve the puzzles in this area at this point but you will have no idea how. You need to go find the puzzles that teach you how to do the puzzles here.
6. This is what I mean when I say the game is obtuse and this is what I mean when I say that over time, the exploration takes precedence over the puzzle solving. Finding the puzzles that teach you how to solve other puzzles is a puzzle unto itself. The solution is neither outright given to you and you are not guided to it outside of the first few hours of gameplay. You have to explore. You earn your instructional puzzles in
, goddamnit.
7. For what it's worth, both the puzzles and the exploration hold up on their own right--well, mostly. The island is very pretty to walk around in and there are many secrets as well as sights that are simply beautiful to behold. I am not much for eye candy so thankfully the puzzles are equally good, using varied elements and generally having a solid and satisfying difficulty curve.
8. This said, I could see how some people might get a little sick of having to do a dozen very similar puzzles straight in a row over and over again. I am a maybe a masochist but I love that♥♥♥♥♥♥myself. I find myself falling into rhythm where the puzzles start to make more sense as they get progressively more complex. I almost feel as if I'm having a witty conversation w/ the game designers. "My good sir, you are making perfect sense so far but what do you say to me adding a tetromino to the mix?" I SAY I WILL SOLVE THIS ♥♥♥♥ING PUZZLE AND MUDDLE YOUR FACE W/ MINT AND SUGAR USING A SWIZZLE STICK MADE OF PURE HATRED.
9. Ok, yeah, it's easy to get carried away here. The combination of board and environmental puzzles this game offers w/ its main course of exploration is incredibly immersive and addictive. You will be seeing
style puzzles in real life while playing this. It's surreal.
10. A major flaw in this is some of the environmental puzzles require very finicky positioning of the player character to solve. In this reviewer's opinion, a well designed puzzle's solution should be easy to execute once you've figured it out. This is very often not the case w/ environmental puzzles. You will be looking at what seems like a near miss as far a potential solution and then go about looking for the actual solution only to find you were right the first time but just standing an in-game millimeter to the left of where you needed to be standing for it to work. This is not a satisfying intellectual exercise but a forced brute force approach and it's annoying beyond belief. If this is unintentional, it's bad game design. If it's intentional, it's bad game design w/ malice and forethought.
11.
doesn't have a plot but it feels like it has a story. You are not progressing anything aside from going where you chose to go but the island you're on seems to have a deep and slightly unsettling history to it that is revealed to you only gradually and even then only partially. You feel like you're on a world created by a vast and unseen intelligence and you are blindly groping your way through. Some of the more frustrating elements make sense in this context. It adds a sense of realism. Any intelligence that pops another sentient being into such a place isn't going to necessarily make everything easy for you. It's going to mess w/ you a bit.
12. As I mentioned in 1,
does overstay it's welcome a bit. It boasts five hundred puzzles and could probably get the job done w/ half that or even less. I can't say exactly why there are so many more puzzles than there needs to be--and like I said, I enjoyed the repetitious puzzle solving--but I do believe one could be forgiven for thinking that perhaps they were there to cheaply pad the game's length to justify a higher price point. Personally, I think this would be worth the full asking price even if it only took ten hours to finish but some people don't think like me.
13. The one questions I cannot really answer for myself after playing this is just exactly why I liked it so much. There are games w/ vaster and more interesting worlds to explore. There are games w/ tougher and more interesting puzzles both of the board game type and environmental type. There are definitely games with better fleshed-out stories and better developed worlds.
just seems to straddle all these things in a way nothing else has that's more effective than more traditional approaches.

Bosses can be tricky, but very manageable the first time around. They telegraph their attacks clearly and you can adapt to it if you have a good feel for these kinds of games.
The level design is great because it always manages to make you use all of your tools, tricky doublejumps, spear throws and rolls. Not too many instant death pits, instead enemies will be the real threats. Enemy spawns are pretty much always the same, so memorizing them is great fun when youve gotten to the point of nearly speedrunning through levels, trying to get the best ending.
Like mentioned theres also different endings, and by running through the game once the normal way a new player would, you fight your way through the basic maps and get the, well, bad ending. But if you beat a level while not getting hit too many times you will get Warrior spirits that take you to the same themed levels, but with a much harder design. This makes for a great second playthrough attempting to get the best ending by beating all the hard maps.

The first Alien Breed was a fun twin stick top down shooter, but ultimately a repetitive stunted game. A lot of backtracking through samey environments, and a lack of variety made it somewhat of a chore to play through.
This second part addresses all of the issues, and has some decent bossbattles and enhancements to the formula. Whereas the first was pretty straightforward run'n'gun gameplay, this is like a miniature DeadSpace 2. Exciting setpieces now add some variety to the experience, that was sorely needed after the monotony of the first game.
It looks good (but not stunning), sounds great, and plays really well. If you played the first, and didn't like it, I would recommend taking a look again at this - its much improved. The third game is even better.....Part 2 & 3 are really great games after the rocky start part 1 had.
If you haven't played the first game and have somehow still come across this review - the series on the whole is well worth a look for a simple and fun shooter, with a decent challenge. Part 1 is a little dull to get through, but from then on it's a cracking ride and I thoroughly recommend it.

Part two of a trilogy, Assault delivers a competent top-down shooter experience with decent voice acting and atmosphere that reminds one strongly of the films from which the series was derived. The series increases in intensity, and I think, quality, as it progresses. Assault in particular has some of my favorite action sequences of the trilogy.

Game: Magic 2014
Summary: Difficulty out of whack, sealed deck hardly justifies cost. The rest is good.
Rating (5/10 = failure): 6.5
Multiplayer: Yes
Completion: 14
Cards: No
Cloud: Yes
Cost: 5 USD
If you played the other Magics, you know the drill. This isn't much different; just some rebalanced decks based on previous theme decks. That said, who in the world did the testing for this game?
The first few battles are pretty standard. You get to pick between a monogreen or monored deck (both of which are kind of on the weak side). Battles are a little harder than normal, but perfectly doable. And then suddenly you are pitted against a monowhite weenie deck. Those are brutal in just about all Magic editions! It's not even a special deck; it's just some random unnamed mook. Green just isn't fast enough, and red will exhaust its instants with no good permanents on the field.
Once you beat that, you get to face... another white weenie deck. Brilliant. Following that, you get an entire plane that is easy, a few moderate battles here and there, and finally some decent challenges. Suffice it to say, the difficulty is out of whack. And I've been through the entire game with each and every (non-DLC) deck. The pattern remains the same.
The campaign itself is pretty short- around 30 battles (provided you attack the other optional planeswalkers too). I would have liked about 2x more main campaign battles set at a proper difficulty curve. That would have gone a long way in enhancing the experience.
Puzzle mode still exists, but it's not part of the campaign this time around. Most of them are pretty easy too with the exception of the last one. Not much else to say about that mode.
By now you can already tell there's going to be a Magic 2015, 2016, etc. etc. So I guess the only question is what's new? Sealed deck mode! Sealed deck is the most promising feature of Magic 2014... and yet it's also the least developed.
Sealed deck plays much like it sounds. You get a handful of random cards and make a deck any way you can out of them, and pit it against another sealed deck. It's great. But there's only like, 5 battles and a few boosters, and then you're done. Wut?
How easy and fun it would have been if we were allowed to make new sealed decks over and over, and in longer campaigns? But no. Sealed decks use your username as a seed, so you'll end up with the same cards every time, and to play with more sealed decks, you must purchase DLC slots for them. Yes, you must buy slots for more sealed play which is like a 1-hour game at best.
I understand games are a business, but this is just an insulting cash grab. I understand using seeds for multiplayer games to ensure someone isn't cheating using cards they couldn't possibly get using their name. But what I'm asking for is unlimited single player sealed play. Where's the harm in that? Oh, I'm sorry, replayability is for suckers. We can't have that undermining our real card game, now, can we? Players should be grateful we even included some form of sealed play. /eye roll
Anyway, I won't include sealed play in the final rating because it's optional and grabby. The base game is fine, and fun (with a horrible difficulty curve), but without a proper sealed deck mode, there's very little this game offers compared to previous installments.
Want an incomplete buggy magic experience that requires you unlock features with mo money! Then this is for you!

Firstly, most of the base building mechanics require uneeded upgrades that`ll suck out most of resources leaving you in a rut, it will put such a heavy dent in progression that you will lose all steam going foward, you need those resources to improve your base, bulding items you need to keep your people happy and healthy, but bandits and robbers will come in and hurt your crew, requiring an early investment in the first upgrade,(which makes no sense as realisticly speaking, as you just need to fix the big gaps in your base), it wouldn`t be bad if you could just get the resources but they are limited, this is good to the setting of the game which is a war-torn city but you soon realise that these resources are so limted that even if you get a good scavenger or a good hauler(dude who can a lot of items) will leave with nothing as everything gets used to quickly.
2ndly, the morality system is so overblown! "War is Hell, even for the people caught in the middle". Johnathan gets caught by the npc, now the npc is attacking Johnathan, John kills npc, john feels sad. OH, how this could`ve worked if you just had something to counteract it. 3rdly, It`s a one tone kazoo, once you`re over it the darker tones, it becomes nothing more but a wilting playthrough after playthrough. No matter what; you going down in one way or the other! Unless you are just set to beat the thing and you find it rewarding if you do so, it`s a couple of playthrough about how this victims are surviving but are failing then it`s a clunky resource management game where you are going to be eather way, making you severly annoyed and totally angry and bitter. 4rthly, Nothing happens, NOTHING HAPPENS. You might get a npc at your door, or there is something going at this scav place, but nothing of a story happens. No character interatctions, No diplomacy between citzens unless it`s trade. No one helps you. Nothing on the military side helps or contributes anything. It`s infuriating when I`m sitting around for nothing  and then scavenge and nothing goes on or I can`t pay attention to it because I`m not trying to get the NPC killed. I was looking foward for story, there is none! Unless you count the one note kazoo of Bob never got to see his sun again. AAHH! 5thly, That`s the main mode, If that`s it why should I play custom? Why would I buy the DLC? If this it, all the mechanics always forcing you to a dead end, why bother? Why? 7thly, winter can be unplayable, the heating mechanic is so bad and so expencive that the NPC freeze to death over night with no rhyme or warning. At first glance your average gamer might dismiss Hero of the Kingdom as an oddity, a curious game with minimal feedback and graphics and could be considered a time-filler, a placeholder title to play in between longer and more involved gaming sessions. To do so would be a disservice to the gamer and to Hero of the Kingdom, as there is a lot more under the surface than what first appears, and through the course of a short story, you will become, the Hero of the Kingdom.
If you enjoy your gaming more casual, and less intense, Hero of the Kingdom definitely has a lot to offer. The game interface is simple and intuitive, and yet it is also never obtrusive. All gameplay is directed by mouse clicks. The action takes place on simple overhead maps, and your mouse clicks naturally will flow as the story and the gameplay layers on.
The complexity of Hero of the Kingdom comes in its economy and the use of selling items of value or to trade for items of usefullness. Should your character require to pass a bridge that is broken, they may need to sell unrequired items to obtain the help, rope and other necessities to move further on. You will gain skills such as fishing and hunting, with simple mouse clicks taking all guess work out of the equation. You either have the equipment to do the task, or you don't. There really is no challenge here.
This laid back notion is continued with the minimal music and sound effects. Both are equally pleasing, but ultimately forgettable. There is nothing about the game, from the gameplay, to the audio, that really stands out. It is all as inoffensive and flavorless as can be possible.
In many ways, Hero of the Kingdom feels like a slightly improved Facebook game, without the social interaction. Certainly the gameplay harkens back to that mindset, and without any kind of graphical flourish, could easily be mistaken as one. Where it succeeds is that it layers on additional systems through hunting, fishing and flower collecting, while telling a simple story about a long forgotten evil that is uniting various minion cliches in order to hunt down the good people of the kingdom.
Hero of the Kingdom is a fun diversion that requires so little of your attention and so little of the gamer that one could forget that they were actually playing a game here and not an interactive click-a-thon. There is enough gameplay here to recommend to the casual gamer but only to this subset of gamer might there be some enjoyment found.
Hero of the Kingdom is by no means a bad game, in fact, I rather enjoyed my short four hour journey. But there are a great many alternatives for your gaming dollar that demand more from the gamer, and the gamer should demand more from the creator. Hero of the Kingdom wouldn't be out of place being hosted for free on some website, perhaps with a banner ad - there just isn't enough gameplay to fully justify a purchase.
5/10.

I absolutely love this game. A mix of point and click and adventure with great story that leaves you wanting more with every newely discovered area. There's fishing, gathering and hunting to be done. This is a well paced game with a spot of what I would consider "open world" that branches off into several sidequest that tie in quite nicely with the main story.
Pro tip for beginners: When you can buy fruit from the fruit seller, make sure you spend all your available gold on fruit and backtrack to the Farmer's Wife and sell all of your fruit to her. If you do this for a while you'll be able to afford tools, food and other various items you need in the upcoming areas. One reviewer said that he barely had enough money to get to new areas but the whole point of the game is to see it from the character's perspective, he has to go between villages and barter to make a profit to continue on his journey. It's not lazy, it forces you to play the game the way it was meant to be played and not find a loophole past everything.
Update: Having completed the game a couple of days ago, I am satisfied with it's ending. All of the loose ends toward the last couple of hours of gameplay finally came together. My only grief with the game is that there wasn't enough clashing during the important end game battles, the sound effects could've been extended a bit longer to emphasize how intense and important they were.
I recommend this game for anyone looking for a casual well paced game. The point is to follow the story and be taken on the well told (albeit short journey) of a young man who's on a quest to find his Father while being unknowingly whisked into an age old battle involving the Dark Wizard.

Absolutely beautiful game with brilliant puzzles that *will* force you to stop and think. You'll often come across puzzles that you don't know the rules to, and will need to go to another part of the island and come back to solve. Are the puzzles really nothing more than the panels you see in screen shots? Yes and no. Yes, those *are* the only puzzles you will solve on your way to the end credits. But the island holds the solutions to many of the puzzles.
Just don't go into it expecting any story whatsoever.  Some of the info out there on this game makes it sound like the point is to figure out why you're on the island and what the island is about. It really...isn't. The game hints at stuff, near the very end, but 99% of the "story" is just (seemingly) random audio clips from philosophers and scientists that you'll find hidden around the island. So temper your expectations in that regard--it's just a chill puzzle-solving experience.

1. If you are 100%ing completest, avoid this game. It will end you. I'll put it this way: if at the end of the day you won't be satisfied if you don't understand why this game is called what it is called, you won't be satisfied. It will give you a million things to do and explore--more than most sane people are going to find the time for--but it never gives you an answer. Decide before playing that you will put this down when it stops being engaging for you and you will live a happier life.
2. W/ number 1 out of the way,
is a masterpiece. It is a flawed masterpiece but a masterpiece nevertheless. You should play it. Just don't overplay it.
3. This is a combination of a puzzle game and an exploration game. You solve puzzles and solving them lets you explore more of the environment. At first, the puzzles seem to be the focus but as you progress, they become more and more incidental to the exploration.
4. One aspect of gameplay that The Witness wears on its sleeve is it doesn't hold your hand and walk you through everything. It doesn't hold your hand to the point of being obtuse. It doesn't hold  your hand to the point of being frustrating. This seems to be, at least in most cases, a specific design decision and not an accident. This is something I have to respect but you are out of your mind if you don't think its carried too far from time to time.
5. You are at first guided through a few puzzle types w/ progressive difficulty and new mechanics introduced gradually, game design 101-style. After a few sections like this, you will invariably wander into a centrally located area that seems to be meant to be sort of a culmination of everything you will learn on the on the island that serves as the game's setting. You are physically able to solve the puzzles in this area at this point but you will have no idea how. You need to go find the puzzles that teach you how to do the puzzles here.
6. This is what I mean when I say the game is obtuse and this is what I mean when I say that over time, the exploration takes precedence over the puzzle solving. Finding the puzzles that teach you how to solve other puzzles is a puzzle unto itself. The solution is neither outright given to you and you are not guided to it outside of the first few hours of gameplay. You have to explore. You earn your instructional puzzles in
, goddamnit.
7. For what it's worth, both the puzzles and the exploration hold up on their own right--well, mostly. The island is very pretty to walk around in and there are many secrets as well as sights that are simply beautiful to behold. I am not much for eye candy so thankfully the puzzles are equally good, using varied elements and generally having a solid and satisfying difficulty curve.
8. This said, I could see how some people might get a little sick of having to do a dozen very similar puzzles straight in a row over and over again. I am a maybe a masochist but I love that♥♥♥♥♥♥myself. I find myself falling into rhythm where the puzzles start to make more sense as they get progressively more complex. I almost feel as if I'm having a witty conversation w/ the game designers. "My good sir, you are making perfect sense so far but what do you say to me adding a tetromino to the mix?" I SAY I WILL SOLVE THIS ♥♥♥♥ING PUZZLE AND MUDDLE YOUR FACE W/ MINT AND SUGAR USING A SWIZZLE STICK MADE OF PURE HATRED.
9. Ok, yeah, it's easy to get carried away here. The combination of board and environmental puzzles this game offers w/ its main course of exploration is incredibly immersive and addictive. You will be seeing
style puzzles in real life while playing this. It's surreal.
10. A major flaw in this is some of the environmental puzzles require very finicky positioning of the player character to solve. In this reviewer's opinion, a well designed puzzle's solution should be easy to execute once you've figured it out. This is very often not the case w/ environmental puzzles. You will be looking at what seems like a near miss as far a potential solution and then go about looking for the actual solution only to find you were right the first time but just standing an in-game millimeter to the left of where you needed to be standing for it to work. This is not a satisfying intellectual exercise but a forced brute force approach and it's annoying beyond belief. If this is unintentional, it's bad game design. If it's intentional, it's bad game design w/ malice and forethought.
11.
doesn't have a plot but it feels like it has a story. You are not progressing anything aside from going where you chose to go but the island you're on seems to have a deep and slightly unsettling history to it that is revealed to you only gradually and even then only partially. You feel like you're on a world created by a vast and unseen intelligence and you are blindly groping your way through. Some of the more frustrating elements make sense in this context. It adds a sense of realism. Any intelligence that pops another sentient being into such a place isn't going to necessarily make everything easy for you. It's going to mess w/ you a bit.
12. As I mentioned in 1,
does overstay it's welcome a bit. It boasts five hundred puzzles and could probably get the job done w/ half that or even less. I can't say exactly why there are so many more puzzles than there needs to be--and like I said, I enjoyed the repetitious puzzle solving--but I do believe one could be forgiven for thinking that perhaps they were there to cheaply pad the game's length to justify a higher price point. Personally, I think this would be worth the full asking price even if it only took ten hours to finish but some people don't think like me.
13. The one questions I cannot really answer for myself after playing this is just exactly why I liked it so much. There are games w/ vaster and more interesting worlds to explore. There are games w/ tougher and more interesting puzzles both of the board game type and environmental type. There are definitely games with better fleshed-out stories and better developed worlds.
just seems to straddle all these things in a way nothing else has that's more effective than more traditional approaches.

The Witness is one of the best games I have played. I couldn't sleep for a few nights just because I was thinking of some puzzles I couldn't solve at that moment. You start the game without any proper knowledge of its puzzles and you learn more and more as you progress in the game. I spent 23h playing The Witness and still didn't solved everything (but reached end game). Don't be afraid if you have no idea what some puzzles mean and keep exploring. There is different zones to learn basic for each type of puzzle. I will try to avoid any spoilers in review.
The game looks very nice, with the small details everywhere. Without anymore words just appreaciate the view:
All puzzles follow same path: from A to B but there is plenty of different rules and ways to solve those puzzles what makes each of them unique enough. In that 23h I used guide for 3 puzzles (yes I was stupid and tired), 2 of those puzzles was so easy that i wanted to bang my head to something because of my inability to think in that way. Third puzzle... I don't know and to this day I feel cheated by developers because i have no idea why it was solved that way (there is possibility that I will find out later in the game). Game contains more than 600 puzzles so you will spend lots of time solving everything without any help.
Sometimes puzzle games fails because of bad controls. Here you can't fail with controls and it is simple.

Game world is really nice and detailed, everything is fine but i found it a bit crowded. In the begining sometimes it is hard to determine where one zone ends and another one begins. And map layout is a bit confusing. You will spend some time figuring everything out but once you pass that stage everything is fine.
Yes there are huge learning curve in game and it comes with the layout of a map. At least once in a game you will feel lost. There will be plenty of puzzles you have no idea how to solve and no knowledge where to go to learn about those puzzles.

Despite few drawbacks of this game like learning curve it is a great game. Eventually you will reach a point where you will have knowledge of all different solving systems and even with taht knowledge you will have to sit and think for a while looking for a way to solve some puzzles. For me it was most enjoyable game at 2017 so I do recommend this game.
Caution: if you have poor puzzles solving skill be prepared for big challenge.
