Usually I really like puzzle games, even though ironically, I tend to suck at them. So given that people’s reactions to this game were so positive, I was quite anxious to see that this was part of the last Humble Monthly Bundle. Because I had a feeling that paying $40 for this game would be quite steep from what I’ve seen and heard, but at $1.50 I’ll certainly take a look.
Having now played the game I can’t really say that I enjoyed myself for the bigger part of the experience. The developer may claim that this game has over 500 puzzles, but in reality, there are maybe a dozen repeated ad nauseam. Because the central mechanic is based around line-drawing puzzles that incorporate a variety of different rules you have to follow. Some are based on blocked paths, sometimes with the addition of a symmetrical line being drawn on the board so you have to keep track of two lines simultaneously. Some require you to divide the board up as indicated by Tetris shapes or by colored rectangles and suns and all of them have different rule that sometimes get combined. So in essence there are these few rules that apply spread out over hundreds of more or less identical panels. And it gets boring after a while.
Now don’t get me wrong, the game does evoke a sense of wonder. Traversing the island, finding secret passages and making quick progress through the first couple of puzzles is interesting. But eventually, you’ll hit a roadblock. Because the rules are not properly explained at any point. You have to infer them through tutorial puzzles that are way too easy to accidentally solve or brute force your way through, that they hardly ensure you’ve actually understood the concepts they’re trying to teach you. And the fact that the island is open for exploration means that you’ll almost certainly wander into an area that uses rules from other parts of the island that you haven’t even encountered yet. Just take my word and ignore the town at the center of the island until you’ve done everything else, because you’ll be gnashing your teeth.
With this lack of direction also comes a lack of narrative. The only payoff for solving these puzzles is opening up doors to even more puzzles. Sometimes you’ll find audiologs and they’re seldom of any use. If you’re lucky, you’ll find a room containing a hexagonal pattern that can be input at a certain point in the game for some videos that ostensibly have to do with what the game is about at its core. But honestly, the game does such a terrible job of informing the player both mechanically and narratively what it wants to be about that I simply couldn’t care less about the artsy fartsy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t it’s trying to communicate.
Once you get the hang of it, the puzzles become entertaining again during the mid-game and if you keep your eyes open you’ll see environmental puzzles as well hidden literally in plain sight, right before your eyes and that revelation is really cool. However, it just drags on and on with puzzle after puzzle giving you no reward whatsoever. And the difficulty spikes between certain puzzles are insane. Sometimes you’ll be breezing through a handful of puzzles without breaking a sweat but every so often in confronts you with one that you can’t easily solve. What is are the people the game will most certainly exclude from playing it. If you have any sort of color deficiency in your vision, just skip this game altogether, there’s no way you’ll be able to beat it on your own. In the end, I enjoyed certain sections of the game, no doubt about it. But it just goes on way too long with terrible tutorials and absolutely no payoff whatsoever. Sure, it expands on the point the game has about seeing things from a different perspective, since that also what most of the game is about, but there’s no actual point being delivered, no argument made. An incredibly short crime adventure game with casual difficulty, excellent narrative, and top-notch voice-acting. It may be closer of being a Flash cartoon, but it’s a really excellent one at that.
Detective Grimoire is the sequel of a 2007 freeware Flash game under the same name (but different content), made originally for tablets (the game even asks you to “tap” with the mouse all the time).
Strictly speaking it falls under the point ‘n’ click adventure genre, but in reality it’s more of an interactive adventure cartoon with a roughly two hour run time as it offers no actual difficulty.
But it’s all inconsequential, since Detective Grimoire is a wonderful all-age murder mystery with a good plot, memorable characters, entertaining dialogues and excellent voice actors. Although the swamp setting and environmentalist messages can get a little overbearing sometimes.
As a detective story it has next to no replay value: once you wrap up the crime, this was it. Still, it’s priced similarly as a movie ticket, and it sure is a lot more entertaining than most movies you may watch.
A fun and interesting story for point and click gamers!

Short and sweet. Detective Grimoire is neither long (full playthrough with 100% achievements in about 3 hours) nor particularly difficult (some "puzzles" simply involve uncovering clues by moving objects from on top of them), but in that time it manages to be fun, endearing, and innovative. In that, it somewhat resembles an animated storybook with some opportunities for interaction.
This is just fine, as it turns out, because the story is a good one. Dialogues with your suspects are witty and upbeat, with excellent voice acting (which is fortunate, since the game rewards you for exhausting all dialogue options with all characters relating to all clues). Character animations are simple, cartoonish and expressive, and match well with the voices laid on top. The game won't challenge you greatly, but it will entertain. And with a hint at a sequel, there may be more to come with Detective Grimoire.

It's okay, not as good as I was hoping.
Volgarr the Viking is a very deliberately paced linear action-platformer. Think Castlevania 1 or 3.
The distinguishing feature of this game is that it's pretty difficult due to some unusual, unforgiving design choices. For starters, you have no horizontal air control at all, like the old Castlevanias, though you have a double jump. There is also a surprising amount of recovery after landing a jump. In addition, you die after only 1-3 hits, and getting hit causes you to lose an entire tier of power-ups.
The problem I have with the game is that it doesn't seem difficult in a particularly fun way. For example, at the very beginning you're going to die a ton just learning what you can block, enemy behavior, how to space jumps, and how to deal with enemies coming from above and below you. There's no real tutorial level to teach you the basics, which just means you're going to die a lot.
On top of that, the health system is really brutal. The game basically rewards you hugely for playing perfectly by giving you a way better weapon and better defense, but as soon as you take any 1 hit you lose that advantage. It's a weird system, because the game essentially becomes harder the less good you are the game. If you're really good and can play levels perfectly, you'll coast along with a weapon that does double damage with extra range, better blocking, and which is faster, along with the buffer health. If you're imperfect, you have to make do with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons/blocking.
On top of all that, it's a very slow game, that's very low on improvization or surprises. Everything is very predictable, and the game moves at such a deliberate pace that it's principally a memorization/timing challenge.
There are some cool moments in the levels, and the graphics have a really nice aesthetic, but it's just not a very fun game to play. It's very much a game about perfectionism, and it's just not really very fun to learn. I'm actually a big fan of the old, hard platformer castlevanias, and 2d action-platformers in general, but this game is just not a particularly good example of the genre.

If you were around for the awesome summer sale with the tickets and prizes, you probably have this game in your backlog because I think it was the only full game you could get with tickets. Obviously I've been sitting on it for years, and despite its apparent similarities to Shadowgrounds (which I love, get it) I've never given it a try. But my internet was out one particular night and I didn't have much time to play so I figured it was finally time.
Alien Breed is an isometric shooter from Team17, far better known for their excellent Worms 2, Worms Armageddon, and all the awful Worms games that came after those. This installment is the middle part of a trilogy whose story appears to be completely unimportant. Your grizzled spaceman is stuck on an exploding derelict ship that you need to either escape from, stop from exploding, or both. I got a little muddled in there because the cutscenes are voiced poorly and the in-game direction is just text.
But you really need to pay attention to all that text because the majority of the game is backtracking and flipping switches. Seriously, in the 40 minutes I played I fixed like 5 doors, three valves, flushed coolant, refilled coolant, and started three backup generators, one of which exploded and had to be repaired. Your character in Shadowgrounds is an actual mechanic and you do less busywork fixing than your hard-boiled spaceman in Alien Breed. Interaction is the new standard "Hold X for 5 seconds to fix/open/hump" which REALLY adds up in this game. In addition, half of the things you interact with trigger boring in-game cutscenes of machines moving around that add up even faster.
It's a shame too, because Alien Breed looks good for a budget shooter. It's built in Unreal3 and makes good use of the engine. The combat is good as well, but sadly not as varied as Shadowgrounds in guns or enemies. The main problem is that you start with a ridiculously effective assault rifle that can then be upgraded further, rendering most of your other weapons moot. There's a standard assortment of shotgun, flamethrower, minigun, and rocket launcher to pick up and upgrade, but outside of corner cases your AR is going to get the job done better. Plus you can pick up gear like grenades and turrets that further marginalize your other weapons. There are only a few enemy types to shoot and almost all of them are the "get up in your grillpiece" type, which only exacerbates things further because your assault rifle has a knockback effect. I really don't know what they were thinking with this thing.
There's a story mode with all the switch-flipping valve-turning annoyance I mentioned, a survival mode where you just kill huge waves of aliens, and a co-op mode which I didn't even bother looking into. I don't know if Alien Breeds 1 and 3 are better balanced in terms of weapons and switch-flipping, but 2 here just wasn't doing it for me. If you don't have Shadowgrounds it might do the trick for you, otherwise I wouldn't bother.

If you know what you are getting into with this game, I think it hits all the right notes.  It's basically a point and click adventure game, but instead of puzzles, you have resource management.  You find/collect various resources in the world and use them to create/craft/barter for other items that may not be as easy to come by.  As the story progresses (a simple story, old as time, but it moves things along), you open up new areas of the map in which to hunt, forage, and take on side quests for various NPCs.
All of the backgrounds are static, with icons representing the types of activities available - picking flowers, hunting bear, fishing, and combat animations are little more than a few 2D sprites wobbling back and forth.  But that doesn't detract from the enjoyment.  There is just enough of a "new stuff to get/see" drip, and the pacing is done well enough, that it never gets boring.  You may find a vendor selling things you don't know what to do with yet, but it won't take long until you figure it out, or the story progresses to the point where it makes sense.  There is a bit of a grind at the end of the game if you want all the achievements, but it's not a big deal.
The major story beats are advanced by having the right amount of particular resources - soldiers, healing potions, a weapon of some sort - to take on the battle or quest in front of you.  Sometimes, finding the right resources is a little troubling because the map doesn't identify where anything particular is; however, the loads are fast enough, and you backtrack enough that you get used to where the crucial stuff is anyway.
It has a demo, so I'd check that out.  It hooked me and I ended up getting all 38 achievements (most of which can easily be done by playing through it).
I had a lot of fun playing this, and the only regret is that it did not last longer. The 5 hours I spend on it, is what it took me to finish the game with 38/38 achievements.

A lot of reviews liken this game to Banished, and this is true for the most part.  However it's important to keep in mind that this is not Banished, and should be judged on its own merits.  There are some fundamental differences between the two:
In Planetbase, you cannot assign jobs to workers.  You're at the mercy of the population spread (which you can influence).
Unlike Banished, you do not have the ability to forward build (In Banished you could essentially create your entire town from the start of the game, then just pause/unpause development as needed).  Instead, you'll have to wait for buildings to be fully built and connected before you can start building components inside them.
Now, the Banished comparison aside, how does Planetbase fare on its own merits?  The short answer is: brilliantly.  Expanding your base can be a little obnoxious at times (forget upgrading or replacing rooms, most of them form integral attachments to other links so you'll be forced to expand outwards), but creating a fine balance between expansion and self-sustaining livelihood is a delicate and precise maneuvre.  Bring in some colonists to boost your productivity and watch in horror as they consume all your food and stop working, which causes a chain reaction where eventually you'll run out of parts to repair your machines, and you can only watch in horror as your base slowly falls to pieces (unlike Banished, where you can retract your buildings to reflect the population drop).  Destruction of your base through various means is a real possibility at all times, but most enjoyably, it's entirely avoidable with clever planning (save for an unlucky meteor shower early in the game).  Technology expansion comes in the form of traders who arrive at your landing pad.  These traders also offer many lifelines, such as providing food or spares when you're in decline.
The biggest advice I can give is expand slowly!  Be sure to disable colonists arriving until you've regained self-sufficiency.
The AI can be somewhat useless at times, but I have not run into any situations where the AI has been at fault for issues with the base; moreso they fall under minor inconveniences where a stray meteor might hit because nobody's manning the telescope, etc.  Generally, these are not game-ending scenarios.
On the surface, Planetbase is simple at its core.  You juggle resources to expand your base and survive.  At its more intricate levels, any lapse in attention can bring about Apocalypse for your unsuspecting colonists.  I would love to see an 'evacuation' option for when the end is nigh, so you can watch them flee the base instead of starving to death or dying of oxygen deprivation.
Pros
Off-world building experience.
Nice visuals.
A genuine possibility of mass extinction with any lapse of judgement.
Very little time spent 'waiting for resources'.  There's always something you can be doing.
Traders can save a struggling base.
Cons
Can't pre-design your base.
Can't replace or upgrade most inefficient or obsolete buildings.
Can't disable single components in a room; you'll need to disable them instead.
Can't pause building production to save it for later (the best you can do is prioritise other buildings).
Overall, this is the colony/building game I've been waiting a long time for.  Easily a 9.5/10

The Witness is a puzzle game within an open world environment. Don’t be fooled into thinking you get an open world RPG or anything. The island is divided in areas that contain a different set of puzzles with a goal to achieve at the end of each section. The game lets you roam around the map almost freely, but some areas require a better knowledge of the rules of the puzzles before you tackle them.
Now the puzzles are clever and well thought out, but there are SO MANY!!! I had solved over 500 by the time I was just too tired to keep going, which is where this game’s biggest hurdle is. It’s just so big that you get physically tired of using your brain. Aside from the easy puzzles (the ones on the screens) you’ve also got secret environment puzzles. It’s just too much to handle. I clocked up over a dozen hours in this game and I’ve still got at least 10% of the game left to do, and those are the remaining secret puzzles and the hardest puzzles in the game. My brain just can’t process them anymore.
With all said and done, I loved this game. It was enjoyable from start to finish, but I do wish there was more to the ending than there was.

In short: looks nice, but has really bad controlls, cheap tricks in the overall badly designed levels, dumb enemies and one of the worst saving/checkpoints implementations I have ever seen.
The game looks realy nice, but that's all I kinda liked. The game is tough, but the difficulty does not come from the complexity of the levels or any impossible enemy. No, the levels are fairly simple by design and the enemies are slow and dumb. So, where's the problem. The problem is in the controlls. For example, you cannot change the direction of your jump and that is your biggest enemy, They made some things right in this game, but left many others (I presume intentionally) broken. On top of that they designed the levels to benefit exactly from your impediments which is extremely cheap.
And the worst thing - the dealbreaker - is the save system, or the lack of one such. The game consists of 5 levels (a sixth level and some bonus/secret stuff is also there, but this is the main thing). Each level is split in two parts and has a boss fight at the end. Listen closely! Whenever you die you resurect at the beginning of the part of the level you died in. The second part includes the boss as well. So, given that the bosses are based on patterns (at least those I saw before I abandoned the game) you will need to die at least a few times so you know what to do. Each time you die you must go through the whole second part of the level! You accidently jumped at the wrong direction and cannot turn back mid-jump? Back at the beginning! This accumulates a lot of game time for nothing and this precious game time can be spent in other, more awarding games.
Sadly, I don't recommend this game to anyone except some REALLY hardcore overachieving complitionists. For God's sake, the game has GUI timers for fast runs, as if the game is famous for the skill you can gain...

Horrible design choice ruins this gem of a game for me. It highly relies on learning from your own mistakes but not in a fair way. You will die at every new trap and will have to restart your whole tedious run again. As i remember, Ghosts'n Goblins had more frequent checkpoints and better lives system, which made it more friendly for practice and highly adaptable, depending on your skill in genre. In Volgar there's more "puzzling" approach to every obstacle, which you have to memorize after. Its pretty nice but done wrong, intentionally killing you no matter how good you are.
mechanics is what made this game great for me, interesting spear platforming system, rolling, shield blocking, a bit clunky but adaptable jumping and etc. Really easy to get into but hard to master. I wouldn't mind level editor for this, as i see really huge potential for custom levels here.
So, intentionally unpolished doesn't mean it's still not unpolished. I would like if they added easier mode, so players could adapt to game faster, and only then try their best on 1-life run. I think this is the only fair way, as i got bored pretty quickly from getting to the first boss on my first try without any hits and constantly dying from him, only to start from the beginning. I can take the challenge, but not when it has this tedious feel to it. For Switchcars, the main question a future game buyer may ask is "Can I wait?" Obviously, it's not because the game is unpolished and far from good standards, or because there is unreleased content that was promised by the developer which wasn't delivered. Essentially, what you the buyer needs to know is whether or not you can live with two types of gameplay as of the moment of writing, or wait for a better chance down the line where the game may (or may not) have more to offer for you.
The gameplay concept is a basic one at first glance, but there is meat to it. Just don't expect massive lists of controls; you enter vehicles, you exit vehicles, you install and use powerups, and move. That's about it. The reason why this works so well is because there isn't a single run you will make that feels the same as a previous one. The vehicle variety is enough to distinguish countless eras and classes of vehicles, the powerups add plenty of possible variations to said vehicle variety. Want to see if you can move a gun turret? That's possible. Do you think a train would work better with a rocket thruster? Have at it. Finding these combinations of vehicles and powerups is a part of what makes this game fun, the rest being made of the adrenaline which comes from running away from aliens with a limited time frame.
Needless to say, this game isn't without its issues. The main one is that while there are two types of game modes, there aren't fleshed out yet; the Run and Hardcore modes are only different in difficulty and session length, and the Free Run mode still lacks the flexibility of a proper sandbox mode. This means that if you play the game for long periods of time, you may get bored easily if you are looking for mode variety and not things to do within said modes. And if you dislike grid-based games, you are not going to like this one, because the grid-based movement is key to how the game is played. But as I said before, no one knows what will be done to this game in terms of future additions. Things like Steam Achievements have been teased, so they are a plausible possibility, and other things like resolution support are available, albeit in Beta format.
For me, this game never gets boring because of the powerups and the vehicle variety which is currently offered. But if you love to have countless game modes and hunt for achivements, the game doesn't quite offer that just yet. If you love fresh concepts and pixel game hommages, give this one a go, certainly... But be prepared to fight some mean green aliens!

Good city/colony builder.  If you've played "Banished"(also good), then you pretty much played this...but in space.  Take care of your colonists needs while they go about doing there work. You can also build or buy robots that can do some of the work freeing up your workers and engineers for other projects.  Balance is key as in most games of this type.  Supply and demand.  After you get going you can accept tourists who pay for services provided.
Before you think "sweet!  I'm buying it!", here are a few cons do keep in mind
Dumb workers.  Pathfinding and job priority being the biggest.  Robots!  Build lots of robots to alliviate this.
Disasters.  Not a big con, makes it more challanging and brings a lot of "Oh Crap" moments.  Mostly though, it's more of a "Why the heck did we pick THIS planet to colonize?!?!
I haven't seen a way to build two airlocks to connect two colony modules.  Meaning two seperate sections.  You can have 15 off your base if you wanted but I want to have a seperate base on the other side of a valley that I can't build in for space reasons.
Only three planets to colonize with different enviroments and disasters.  Wish there was more is all.
I'm a fan of "Banished", city builders, and almost anything sci-fi, so I might be bias.  If you fit that same bill I think this game is a good buy.  No enemies, just the elements.  Just the way I like it.
I hope this helps you.  Enjoy!

On the flip side, that is only a con if that is what you are expecting and looking for in this game IMO, Planetbase is only $20 and it should provide you with twice that in hours of fun, what it lacks in depth it makes up for in catchy graphics, base building, trading, helping travelers etc with enough freedom of how you build things to keep you on your toes from start until self efficiency (another reason why I say arcade over Sim, it feels a bit more action orientated to me).
Until you play a bit you might find starting out a little challenging, one suggestion that stood out for me with this game was "take it slow", it's to easy in this game to try and build (and/or process) too many things at the same time dividing up resources and taking everything longer to build/process and a LOT of times (especially at the start), time is key if you are losing power or water or waiting for spares. Try to focus on what you need "now" and just think of the next thing once you have all/most of the the resources for whatever you are currently doing.
Also, make sure you create the means to make metal before you use all the metal you start with or, well, game ova!

Coming from Cities XL 2012 to this, gameplay wise, its almost exactly the same game.
Its got the same UI, just recoloured from blue to black (although it does look a little more tidy).
Resources are still all the same as well as all the categories of buildings such as heavy industry.
I have noticed a few new features and buildings in the game such as being able to edit how many plots the game places in the square building zones when building and choosing if the game places plots on one side or both sides of the road with the linear zoning tool. New buildings include things like the pollution sensors and electric car dealership just to name a few.
Now whether these new features and buildings were in Cities XL Platinum, I have no idea. I never played Platinum or have seen any gameplay of it.
The graphics look slightly better in this than Cities XL 2012 but its really not by much. I'm not sure if its me but the colours look a bit more vibrant in XXL though.
Performance is much better in this than XL 2012. Focus Interactive have finally figured out that multicore computers are a real thing. In Cities XL 2012 there would be a noticeable drop in performance once your city hit around 50k population and would gradually get even worse as the population grew. In Cities XXL however, I have a city with 600k people and although there is a bit of a loss in perfomance it is no way near as bad as XL 2012 and still perfectly playable.
For a new player to the Cities XL/XXL this game would probably be an 8.5/10. For a player who has owned previous Cities XL games its a 5/10 at best.
So basically if you're new to the Cities XL/XXL franchise. Get this.
If you've owned previous Cities XL games and are willing to pay for some really minor new features and multicore support then get this but maybe wait for a sale.
If the performance of previous Cities XL games doesn't bother you then don't get this
I'm gonna vote yes to this game simply because of the fact that you can now build massive cities and still get a playable frame rate which in previous titles was almost impossible.
TL;DR
The performance is a lot better. The are some very minor new features. Other than that its pretty much the same as previous Cities XL games.

Since the demise of the original developer, Focus has had the tendency to ride it like a cash cow. It has neglected the franchise like an abusive parent witholding affection from its secretly adopted middle child.
CitiesXXL is the latest annual crayon drawing posted on the refrigerator from the intern at Focus. Its release was preceded by an intentionally anemic campaign consisting of decent stills and an admittedly well-done video of the city they made for their marketing coordinator. Thinking about it now, it probably took that intern longer to build that city than the entire update to the poor shattered dreams of Monte Cristo's original code.
It's been made clear why the publisher was so quiet leading up to its release as the expressed promise of a new game would have been somewhat misleading. CitiesXXL is sort of a new game...
..but it's more of an update.
I wouldn't call it a patch because that would imply a fix. My experience so far has been that it runs a bit slower than XL Platinum. It uses the same maps, and the same textures on some buildings which clearly spell "CitiesXL". Ironically, this seems to be the only thing spelled correctly. The updated metro-esque menus are poorly QC'd and have flagrant visual bugs on the surface. It feels like I'm beta testing.
While I would love to be completely on one side of the black and white vitriol I find in the forums, I find myself kind of liking this update. The flaws haven't so far been game-breaking, and I really like the Steam integration. Mods are now incredibly simple to install and they have improved my experience. There is greater control of the camera, an updated soundtrack, and an Expert mode which is a wonderful addition.  I still don't like the classism that plagues the heart of the series, but I understand how it works and Expert mode helps dull that edge quite a bit.
Attention to some of these details but not others has left me confused. Why are the controls so strange? I know it's European, but I would love to use WASD instead of arrow keys and edge tripping. Why can't I edit these controls? Why can't I edit mouse sensitivity? I should be able to upgrade roads in place-- especially when I meticulously curved that one to fit that ridge. Ugh.
This isn't a bad game. Yes, it is an obvious cash-grab that should have been an update or DLC. Yes, Focus is deceitful and disgraceful. It is, however, an update to a pretty fun game. Casual CitiesXL Platinum gamers will be disappointed. This would likely be worth the purchase for avid players and new players who just can't wait for Cities:Skylines.

Oh, detective Grimoire. I played this game with my boyfriend last night and we both often found ourselves smiling at the game: It has a lovely style of art, and very, very charming characters. The voice acting is great, the dialogues are great, and the protagonist is a charming, slightly sarcastic, definitly cool character.
The gameplay had some refreshing mechanics to it in my opinion, letting you form thoughts that you probably already figured in your head. That really allowed you to stay on top of things and for once incooperate what you thought into the game - something most detective games don't do. You sit there thinking you figured it all out, but you can never tell anyone, well, this game tries to change that up a little.
The puzzles were all quite easy, and the story itself is not hard to understand for any adult. So if you are looking for a challenging game, this will probably not be for you. It is also relatively short, with a playtime of maybe two hours, and whilst it is entertaining for that duration it will probably not have any replay value for some time.
I would gladly hand this game to a child, because the puzzles and the story will be absolutely appropriate for them. The art style and characters would simply charm them, and I remember playing games like this in my past and loving them with all my heart, because to me they were still mysterious and unpredictable when I was still a child.
For adults? Not challenging, nothing too iconic - if you are someone who enjoys games aiming at a younger audience, this game is great. If you want something more adult and complex, I would not recommend this game.
Overall I really enjoyed it for its playful and childlike charm. If you ever got 5 quid to spend, I think this is a good purchase.

Bored of weird stories in puzzle games like Talos Principle and Portal? Want a Myst-esque experience but felt the "story" was non-essential? Do you just want difficult puzzles with various mechanics that will tax your brain? DO YOU LIKE DRAWING LINES?
The Witness is an open-world puzzle game where you, the Player, enter an island that is littered with grid panels that are individual puzzles (most of the time). These puzzles begin at the disc shape and end at a curved point and the objective is to draw a line from the disc to the end. As simple as this sounds, the game makes this challenging by adding rules to the grids which you must follow carefully otherwise you will fail. Some of these rules are you must separate the black and white squares, you must draw the line over all the hexagons etc. Meanwhile there is also something strange about the island which you may or may not notice (you mostly will, it's in your face half the time).
There is a story... kind of. If you're expecting a linear narrative that goes from A to B then it's not here. In fact the only narrative you get is from narrations of quotes from various famous intellectuals that are strewn about the world in the fashion of audio logs. These really don't mean anything and most of what's happening will have to be pieced together. I'll say right now, there's no logic in what's happening so don't look for it. You're not there for a reason (not really) and what's told to you (or shown) doesn't matter to what you do. For all intents and purposes, you are on an island and there are puzzles so go solve them.
There's barely any music in the entire game. The ambient sounds are very well recorded and play well into the game and are sometimes integrated into the puzzles. But my one criticism in this department (barebones as it is) is there's no volume adjustment AT ALL in the game. At times, especially in confined spaces the ambient sounds are way too loud and it gets close to becoming a horror game despite there being NOTHING to be afraid of.
This game is EXCEEDINGLY beautiful. This is a pretty big open island with various themed areas that tie in to the type of puzzles in that area. Areas have been carefully crafted with many weird and interesting details that make you wonder what more is littered around. The textures are stylized and I feel the visual will most certainly hold up in a few years' time.
As I mentioned earlier, the gameplay is almost entirely the player tracing lines across grids placed at various locations, each with some rule that bends the nature of the puzzle. The puzzles are mostly fair with certain tutorial-esque sequential panels laid out at various locations that teach you a single mechanic which you will then use in other grids. Some grids will activate certain elements in the world such as gates or other grid panels which you will then use to move forward. I would say a good 95% of the puzzles are fair with few of them requiring you go out of the way to look for a clue around you as some of them use the environment extensively. There are definitely the occasional completely ridiculous and unfair puzzles but in the hundreds panels I've solved, there are maybe 10 that are just unfair. Towards the end there are some panels that made me motion-sick and some that gave me a headache which I'd rather just weren't in the game. One frustrated me so much physically that I didn't bother figuring it out and just looked it up because I felt weird and if I were an epileptic, I'd have a seizure. In most matters regarding the puzzles, the game is highly polished almost to a straight sheen. You cannot move where the game doesn't want you to and there is ONE method to solve each of the puzzles though there may be multiple actual solutions.
My biggest gripe with the game is there is some sense of the game not respecting your time. There is no fast travel and the game requires you move across this island numerous times especially since you may come across a puzzle whose solution is not obvious because you haven't learned to solve it yet. There are also MANY moving platforms that move SO GODDAMN SLOWLY. Sometimes they move slowly for a reason but it's still hard to justify especially when the movement of the platform is  tied to a puzzle in itself meaning you have to "re-solve" the puzzle to move it.
This is a fantastic puzzle game that requires you use your wits to solve. One issue is that there's no real sense of satisfaction of solving many of these puzzles aside from the satisfaction of solving it itself. If you're the kind of guy that solves Sudoku puzzles for fun, you may LOVE this game. If you like puzzle games in general, I recommend you check it out. At $40, this is quite steep (the asking price is because the devs spent almost 6 years crafting it and feel that's fair) so I'd recommend it at 25-50% off. At $30, it's fair and at $20 it's worth every penny.

I gave this game "The Even Better Than I Excpected" award on the 2017 Steam awards and here is why:
Furi is all about combat against bosses, and almost nothing else. It is an experience stripped to it's essentials as there are no levels to traverse, or puzzles to solve, or sidequests to do. You get all of your tools right from the start: your gun, your sword, your dodge, your parry and so on. You don't upgrade these abilities, you don't learn new ones, you don't get any new weapons. From the very first moment of the game you have all of your tools to defeat every challenge the game will throw at you.
For a game this focused it's extremely important to get the core right and I am happy to say this game's core - Furi's combat system - is one of the most enjoyable ones I've encountered in my years of playing video games. The controls are great. Some things like the fact that your dodge will activate on button release rather than button press might feel strange at first, but I got used to it very quickly and came to understand why it works the way it does.
Each boss tests your skills of pattern recognition, execution of your abilities, your reflexes. The game is challenging all throughout, and there is a ton of variety between each boss. The bossfights are long and have multiple phases. You will mostly likely need to fight most bosses multiple times before you finally defeat them, but once you do you will have the satisfaction of knowing you have mastered the fight. This feeling is one of the best that a game can give you, in my opinion. That said, the game isn't overly punishing and it does give you enough breathing room on many areas. You will enter each fight with three lives. If you lose a life the phase you are currently on will reset, if you lose all three you will need to start the fight over from the beginning. If you manage to beat a phase, you will get one of your lives back (up to the maximum of 3). What this means is that you will enter each new phase with at least 2 lives, so you will always have a second chance to defeat each new phase before being forced to restart the fight. This way the game will never blindside you with a new mechanic. On top of this Furi is extremely consistent with it's visual cues, which give you more of a chance of knowing how to respond when you see a new phase or attack from a boss.
There are things to criticize but not many. The absolutely worst thing about the game are the walking sections between bosses. These are effectively unskippable cutscenes. The speedrun mode takes these out, luckily but playing through the game normally there is no way to skip them or speed them up. While the exposition, world building and atmosphere of these sections could be at times nice change of pace to the frantic gameplay of the boss battles, forcing the player to go through them was absolutely the wrong decision. The other criticism I would have for the game is that while the content that is there is great, there's not quite enough of it, even accounting for the changeups of the Furier difficulty. The DLC boss The Flame is a good addition to the roster (and I would recommend it if you are thinking of buying this game) but I think it should've been included in the game to make it feel like a complete experience, and even then I would argue that it's still a little lacking. Then again as far as criticisms go "the content is great I just wish there was more of it" is a pretty good one to get. There are a few minor flaws that barely make a dent in the experience, like after losing a life Rider sometimes takes his sweet time getting up.
Additionally, it has one of the best soundtracks from any game I played. All the songs are bangers and amp up as you progress through the phases of the bosses you are fighting, it's great. While I griped about the walking sections earlier, I cannot deny that they are often very nicely framed and the environments are often very nice to look at. Each boss has a unique visual design, the fact that The Game Bakers got Takashi Okazaki to do the character designs truly paid off.
All in all, I would call Furi one of my favourite games and it gets a glowing recommendation from me.

Before I begin the review, I'd like to say that I got this game for free during the 2011 Steam summer event, where you could pick various pixel items aswell as this game. This game is best described as Starship Troopers and Dead Space having a baby.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
You're a combat engineer named Conrad sent to a large spaceship to discover what has happened to it. You are greeted by waves upon waves of different aliens, skinless cadavers of the former personal aswell as the ongoing destruction of the ship and the alien infestation inside of it.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A over the top shooter, you aim and turn Conrad by moving your mouse around the edges of the screen. Few times did I try where the aiming would be unprecise because of this.
There is quite a selective amount of weapons to find and use. You start with a pistol and eventually can get a shotgun, assault rifle, rocket launcher aswell as a minigun. The aliens are quite different themselves, both appearance wise and abilities to fight you with. A few honourable mentions would be the time slowing alien, aswell as an alien that can lift up some kind of shield to block your bullets, but won't be able to move. Another alien can heal the rest. The other aliens are more simpler, like a long ranged alien. The rest are simple meatshields and can easily be taken down. There are also alien pods around the game which spawn small child aliens and when they attack you, they implode, rendering them not a massive threat, only in large numbers.
You can also find and buy healthkits, grenades, body armor, turrets you can place around the game at "powerpoints". You use X to switch between your items, and right click to hold down the useable item.
As mentioned, you eventually come to saveable stations where you can also buy items, ammo and upgrades for your weapons, aswell as the items. Throughout the spaceship you can explore, finding credits and items.
The interaction system isn't the best. When opening doors a bar will appear over Conrad showing the progress untill you have activated the item. If you stop, the progress will reset. This forces you to redo it should an alien or more appear suddenly, coming for you. This counts for everything. Checking a dead body for loot, checking lockers etc. There are even spots where you must do this for atleast ten seconds, while risking being attacked from behind.
The aliens rarely appear running around, instead, they -always- come up from the floor, leaving a hole. It also makes a sound, one you will hear atleast one thousand times, as they can be heard breaking up from the floors ahead of you. The spaceship clearly has a massive ventilation system around it or there's alot of space below the floor boards.
This games uses cutscenes alot, especially during entering through a scanning room, waiting for a walkspace bridge to turn around and link with the one youre on and even when going up or down an elevator. Which is horrendious, as you don't have much to look at, leaving you waiting and wasting a few seconds of your life on something so pointless.
Some places in the game you can't turn your camera, leaving you forced to use your minimap and see when aliens approach, though this only occurs two or three times.
There are only two boss battles in this game, first one is relatively good and slightly challenging. The second on the other hand is overused. Without revealing too much spoilers, it forces you in a camera angle to fight off the boss and extra aliens, but happens atleast three times, the very same cut scenes and boss tactics, aswell as how the boss attacks you. It's one of the worst boss battles I've ever encountered and is defently among my top 10 worst.
There is in all, 5 chapters, where each one takes almost an hour and a half. Overall only giving you around 6-7 hours of campaign storymode.
There are other modes aswell though, you are able to replay the chapters again, and there is a survival mode where you can play with a friend. But trying to find other players through the matchmaking seems impossible as the game is abandoned long time ago when it comes to multiplayer. Your best bet is asking around on the forums.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The graphics for this game isn't bad, atleast for a game that came out in 2010.
The game world is detailed and has alot of objects cluttered around a destroyed spaceship. The alien infestation appears on the ground and walls and you will encounter lairs of alien pods, the rooms fully covered in alien nastiness. A neat detail is that you can see the outside of the spaceship, aswell as the engines at some parts of the game. The aliens look great graphics wise, though one of them looks more comical than scary, being able to stretch its mouth wide.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The story is your usual sci-fi horror with aliens killing off humans. Only difference here is, that you only encounter one other person, who's from what I gathered, an android or such.
The story does have a small hinting buildup, but that's where it also stops with the goodness.
During each chapter start and end, you are shown cutscenes in a comic styled manner with background voice acting.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
It's not worth the 8,99 or so price tag, and I'm sure it costed more back in 2010. Though I did get this for free. But for 4,99, it's worth it. This game isn't for any gamer though. You really have to like over the top shooters and the overall theme this game has.
The game tries very hard to be scary, but fails to achieve this. There are a few nice small surprises, but they are very, very few. One good example was entering a changing room, and searchng a locker, only to have an alien come out of the ground behind me and attack. Other than that, the game lacks surprises. The game does have a few interesting rooms, like a boxing ring with spectator seats.
At the last chapter, the game overuses an annoying laughter, without spoiling too much, which only serves as destroying the game's horror atmosphere. The only other person you encounter has one of the worst walking animations I've seen, and leaves you cringing. Makes you feel the devs at Team17 rushed this particular part.

Man, been a good while since I wrote a review...
I decided to try this out since its theme is pretty similar to Alien Swarm (a very old L4D-like top-down co-op shooter that I actually liked and played repetitively to 100% achievement despite its lack of content). And yes, I realize that I'm writing this review after playing only the story mode on Rookie difficulty. But that's the point here: after a playthrough, it just doesn't have the same "kick" in Alien Swarm that makes me want to play it again or even try the co-op.
The story is okay; it kind of drags on after a while but that's understandable for a dark alien-based theme (and that the entire time MIA never speaks outside of between-chapter cinematics didn't help either). I suppose there isn't much to talk about on this anyway when you make the storyline split into three games.
The thing that gets me most is the gameplay... it's overall very clunky. The laser sight never felt right on with where the cursor is currently aiming. Then at certain points of the game the camera angle decides to root itself, at which point your aim gets even more screwed than it is already. Weapons/items aren't too clear-cut on their comparative usefulness; I simply just choose whichever weapon has the most ammo at the time being. I seldom used items either, but that's probably because I was at Rookie difficulty. Oh, and the aliens are really bad at being threatening (aside from the scratch damage in Rookie difficulty, that is); they spend like five minutes screaming at you before trying to attack. Their relatives in Alien Swarm would've just ram into your face right off the bat.
Then there's the level design. I get it that we're exploring a ghost ship, but at least a map that plots itself out wherever you have been through would be much helpful. Just navigating around is really confusing let alone trying to scavenge all those lockers and human corpses with space bars. Oh yeah, also the space bar... part of the culprit of making AB2:A a repetitive A-to-B-repeat game.
My score would be a 5~6/10. It's not too terrible per se, but it's rather bland compared to Alien Swarm which has better flow and is much more fast-paced. I suspect that the other two games of the trilogy are just as much.

I recommend this game on the condition that the dev team continues with the updates.  This is a fun little base builder sim.  The biggest thing I've noticed with being sucessful in the game is managing not only the supply level of your base but it's accessability as well.  If your colonists have to go all the way across the base to get supplies, eat food, or get sleep then you're losing out on their productivity.  It does get repetative though once you've unlocked everything.  The occasional intruded raid or meteor strike are the only real threats.  More diverse accidents and some new buildings would go a long way for replay value.  Also steam workshop support would be amazing.
EDIT: I've changed my review to a negative based on what I percieve to be little to no real progress in the development of the game.  All I've seen are some added challenges and some slightly different threats that don't really require much effort to beat.  I bought and recommended this game based ont he hope that development would continue and new mechanics would be added.  I seem to have been wrong.  The most glaring opportunity for this game is the lack of modding.  Drop some modding tools on your community that make it easy to add/change/remove some of the gameplay mechanics and jsut watch what people do.  Incorporate the most popular ideas into your game and keep on going.  For now this game is just way to easy and lacks any realy depth.
1) I'm tired of the same attackers every. single. time.  Give me the opportunity to upgrade my security force and give them bigger and badder threats to fight off.
2) Give me some sort of blueprint tool where I can plan a base expansion to make sure everything is arranged the way I want it before I let my guys build it.  I'm so tired of planning large expansions only to find out one of my buildings won't connect because it's placement is off by 2 degrees.
3) Let me design the tunnel layout instead of the simplistic point to point we have right now.  It was good early in development but it's time to upgrade.  I want T-junctions, 4-ways, 90 degree turns.  It'll help tremendously with base layout and design.
4) Expand the manufacturing cap options.  I want to set a cap on veggies, medical plants, plastic, ore, and everything else.
5) Storage.  I should be able to set limits on the ammount of individual items stored in a specific storage dome.  I'm tired of the storage dome next to my metal plant being filled up with veggies because the veggie production is ramped up.  Yes I know I could aim for perfect balance in my production/consumtion ratios but I prefer to overbuild in preparation for my next expansion.  Hey if you did this it would take care of the manufacturing caps from point 4 too.  I could have storage bubbles all over my base with a few of this and a few of that or a few everything.  It would be amazing!
6) Colonists.  I saw this point in another review (one of your devs shot it down actually) and I agreed with it.  Let me disable certain colonist types arriving.  I don't always go for a certain percentage of colonists.  Sometimes I just have a specific number in mind.
7) Which makes another good point.  Instead of percentages, let me choose either a percentage OR a specific number.  I setup a ring of structures around several landing pads.  I place 2-4 airlocks inside the circle with the pads and I put guard posts adjacent to the air locks.  Anyone coming into my base is immediately faced with armed guards.  I don't need a certain percentage of guards.  I want the number of desks I've placed x2.  If I could set that specific number on guard colonists coming in, I'd be able to leave colonists ships active 24/7 and not have to worry about forgetting them and having 100 guards roaming my base because of percentages.  In my mind it would work so that if I select the specific number option for guards, the percetage option would redistribute evenly among the remaining colonist types.  I also don't need to worry about adjusting my percentages as my base grows because my guard force never needs to grow once I setup my starport.
8) Mod tols, mod tools, mod tools, mod tools.  I can not stress it enough.  Do whatever it takes to grow your modding community.  They'll literally help you develop your game while you still get all the money for sales.  In this day and age it's insane to release something like this and not make a serious effort to grow a modding community.
That's just a few of the things that I as a customer, word of mouth advertising opportunity, reviewer, and hopeful future fan would like to see in the game.
PS.  How you continue to delop and support Planetbase going forward will determine my response to any plan for a sequel or a different game from you.  Will I be super excited and pre-order or will I wait it out until the game does or doesn't become worth buying?  It's up to you.

"This game is best played getting comfortable" a text box says when staring a new game. And that is the truth of this game. Above all else, it is comfy. I just want to sit in it with something to drink as I play into the late night.
VA-11 Hall-A calls itself a "Cyberpunk Bartender Action"-game. And in truth, there is a lot of bartending and action. Or people getting some action, anyways. And it's cyberpunk without a doubt. A good blend of retrofuturistic cyberpunk and more contemporary ideas, all swirled into the most delicious Cobalt Velvet.
While it's basically a bartender-driven (hah!) visual novel, it feels more much like one of those adventure games you'd find on old japanese computers and consoles. If words like PC Engine, PC-9801, X68000 or FM Towns gets you going, all the more reason to check out this game.
While there isn't that much gameplay in VA-11 Hall-A, what is there does a good job of being immersive. Blend drinks after customers orders (or not, up to you) and check your feeds and shop while home, all while everything is dripping of this cozy dystopian cyberpunk future. Sure, the city where the story takes place, Glitch City, is a mismanaged hellhole but at the very least it's atmospheric and true to the theme.
Speaking of atmosphere, the soundtrack is fantastic. While not as retro as the graphics on a technical level - I mean, it's still retro, just not chip tunes or anything, it's spot on a thematic level.
All of this comes together for a fascinating experience with a story to tell. So by all means, get yourself some beverage and get comfortable. It's time to mix drinks and change lives...after all, Every Day is Night.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the incredibly addictive casual indie game, Flobe. Flobe was released on Steam Januray 23, 2016 by Developers Skinny Jean Death Studios & Porcelain Labs and Publisher Forever Humble PDX.
(NOTE: This game was reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Cheap, pretty and insanely addictive. Also, less than a buck. 5/5
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
Flobe. It is pronounced just as it looks. Flobe. Flobe is a casual little strategy-type indie arcade game with a puzzle feel to it. Essentially you are a blue "bar" that can move all around the screen, change sizes, flip around, etc. With this blue bar, you need to catch these little blue guys flying down the screen. Seems simple enough, but there are other colors. Catching another color will end the game, making you start over. Missing one of your own "collectibles" to catch, however does NOT kill you. It only makes the game harder from that point forward by forcing your bar to become one size larger, which can become a pain quite quickly. You need all the mobility you can get in the game! Keep collecting though, and not missing any, and your score multiplier increases. Once you hit 15X, the game exands itself and now you find yourself chasing 2 colors. IT ramps up quickly! The first thing you notice, is that it is very pretty.Very visually appealing. It has both fantastic graphics, and great sound too. The controls are very responsive and slick. Just make sure to use a controller, as the game was definitely designed with that in mind. The gameplay is so addicting. It is your basic arcade game in that your motivation is to keep increasing your top score. Trust me, you've never had enough. This may be the indie-casual-arcadey type version of "One More Turn".
5/5 for my tastes. It is under a dollar, beautifully presented, easy to pick up and difficult to master. Go give it a shot, and when you do I want you to keep one thing in mind too.....the kid the coded this fantastic game is a mere 14 years old...if this is what we get while he's 14, we have a bright gaming future ahead! Keep an eye on this Forever Humble PDX studio..
Happy Gaming!

This is a continuation of, and mechanially identical to, Alien Breed: Impact, as such please refer to my previous review of that game:
This game is somewhat more well done in the ways that its predecessor was not: The levels have more variation, there are earlier and more boss encounters, there is more storytelling, both through ingame logs (such was entirely absent in ABI) and in the comic interludes, which also seems to have recieved more attention to detail than in ABI, And there has been a few weapon switches, which is of little effect, but noie nevertheless; the "ion spike" was n't that impressive anyway.
Another gripe that I was reminded of since playing the predecessor is that, yes, there are small "secrets" in the games, however, they don't actually DO anything, apart from giving you an achivement if you find the lot of them, a thing that would only matter to achivement hunters, but not the least to those who expect things to actually do things or reward you for your exploration. (The "secrets" are actually visible, marked by rotating blue signs, which usually makes it fairly straightforward to track them down, hence why i put them in citation marks).
Assuming you already own, and have played AB: I, have familiarized yourself sufficiently with the control system, and aren't too put off the straight-lined level layouts plus isometric perspective (plus the rest of the minor gripes with ABI), I'd RECOMMEND that you get this game (extension to ABI). It's of course a no-brainer considering that the first game was lacking in story and entirely lacking a conclusion, NECESSITATING that you get this to get any sort of closure.
If AB:I was not to your tastes, this extension/successor will do little for you, in which case you should consider this a NOT RECOMMENDED.

Boss rush games have always appealed to me, as it makes the player learn, and overcome seemingly insurmountable opponents and obstacles that have taunted them for so long. Furi excels at this model, with tight controls, fluid combat, distinct visuals, a sinister plot, great replayablility with it's different difficulties and speedrun modes, and probably one of the greatest videogame soundtracks in recent history to back it up, this game is well worth its price. This game destroyed me on my first playthrough, and after defeating the final boss, I jumped right into the hard difficulty, only to be crushed by the tutorial boss. New phases and attacks keep the player alert and active, and a lack of unskippable cutscenes means that retrying the same damn boss you've been fighting for the past hour doesn't grow tedious. The character design is fantastic, with all twelve bosses having their own unique style and battfield that makes them even more memorable. While the graphics may not be stunning, they're pretty in their own right that makes them enjoyable to watch. I can't think of much else to say, but yeah, this was a great game, I mean the time I've spent in it shows how much replayablity there is.

The game has lovely graphics and animation (but if you know SFB you expected that), quality voice acting and is obviously made with love and care. The characters are interesting and charismatic, not your run-of-the-mill lifeless cookie-cutter supporting characters. The conversation options might not be all that hilarious but they should at least make you smile. The mystery itself is not obvious at all from the beginning, there's some complexity to it, the writing is pretty decent. All good up to this point.
The main reason I advise you not to purchase this game is simple: the difficulty is next to none, it is almost an insult to our collective intelligence. 'Almost' because at least at the ending you have to consider a few pieces of evidence at the same time to find the culprit, aside from that the game poses no challenge whatsoever. The puzzles are so easy they seem aimed to very young children - except they couldn't possibly be able to consider so many pieces of info as you are supposed to at the end - plus there are some violent themes and graphic grizzly sounds (nothing visual though) so it is definitely not a game that should be aimed at little kids either. I am unsure what the target audience of this game is, to be honest, and that's my biggest bone to pick with it. There are hardly any puzzles anyway, and you'll spend most of the time talking to the same characters over and over and presenting the same clues and profiles - hint: they won't have anything to say about them 80% of the time - so on top of the non-existant difficulty, it can get extremely repetitive despite its short duration.
I really, really wanted to love this game because I've been an SFB fan for way longer than I care to admit, and when I could finally pick up Detective Grimoire I expected something much more well-rounded. I am disappointed as you have gathered already from my review. There's too much hype about this game, and I'm sure there are many more SFB fans like me around here, back from early Newgrounds days, who mean well and are trying to support who they know are very talented guys. But getting the hype about this game up is doing no good to anyone, this game is seriously flawed and I hope they will do some serious work in these weak points if they plan to release a sequel. You can do WAY BETTER and we KNOW IT.
In conscience, I cannot recommend this game to anyone who isn't very young (but not a kid!), very inexperienced with adventure games and looking for a beginner's experience that poses near no challenge, or someone who is looking for a VERY casual game experience.

This game is wonderful. From its animated characters, background art and its music; this game is worth playing.

Still, you can find the influence of the Wright games in the interrogation sequences(questioning, presenting evidence/profiles, cross-examination) but its the inclusion of the puzzles(though I must admit, the puzzles are very easy to solve, I just love more challenge to my puzzles and this game has none of it. But its not a bad thing mind you, its pacing is designed for easy puzzles to get the story moving.) that make it a mystery/detective game.
The narrative is very impressive; This seriously gave me some Call of Cthulu vibes. Although, it is kind of lacking in the character development. Can't say anymore since I don't want to spoil a cool story (you'll just have to buy the game and play it for yourself)
This game stands on its own and in no way a clone of anything else aside from its influences. I am slightly disappointed since I expected the puzzles to be more challenging, most of the time you could just show every single piece of evidence, really its just a diligent point-and-click. I really wish that the developers would hurry the next game since I feel that this has the potential to be a great episodic game.

Toki Tori is -- on the surface -- an adorable little puzzler that serves as a nice break in between other games. Actually, that's precisely what Toki Tori is, but don't let its appearance fool you. Even on the normal levels, expect brain-busting puzzles that'll give you fits on occasion. Some of the hard and bonus stages will really challenge you.
Aside from touchy controls, the game plays fair. When you fail, it's because you -- yeah, you -- failed. Trial and error is the key to solving Toki Tori, and you'll feel proud of yourself upon completion. Actually, now that I recall, there are a handful of stages that do require a bit of timing, but not too many.
Anyhow, until you solve the puzzle, expect many moments of second-guessing, self-doubt, self-loathing, and cries of "I'm not bright enough for this game."
In other words, congratulations to the developers for creating a game that makes me feel both smart and dumb.

If you're looking at Planetbase, chances are you're a fan of city builder survival games, too. Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria, Stonehearth, and others are probably games you've tried and enjoyed. Me too, but it was the nastolgia for Sierra Entertainment's Outpost, released in 1994, that initially sparked my interest. Planetbase promised to scratch that itch for survival on a remote hostile planet, where a breakdown in logistics wasn't just a nuisance, but a death sentence for your colony as vital systems shut down one after another, your colonists choking on the cold vacuum of space.
Planetbase delivered on that promise.
A fantastic addition to the library of any city-building survival enthusiast who enjoys some roguelike elements. Planetbase isn't just your typical survival builder in space, with gnomes or dwarves replaced by spacesuit wearing colonists. Instead, Madruga Works has created a space colony theme that looks, feels, and plays like you're trying to get a fledgeling colony off the ground on an atmospherically hostile planet.

"This game is best played getting comfortable" a text box says when staring a new game. And that is the truth of this game. Above all else, it is comfy. I just want to sit in it with something to drink as I play into the late night.
VA-11 Hall-A calls itself a "Cyberpunk Bartender Action"-game. And in truth, there is a lot of bartending and action. Or people getting some action, anyways. And it's cyberpunk without a doubt. A good blend of retrofuturistic cyberpunk and more contemporary ideas, all swirled into the most delicious Cobalt Velvet.
While it's basically a bartender-driven (hah!) visual novel, it feels more much like one of those adventure games you'd find on old japanese computers and consoles. If words like PC Engine, PC-9801, X68000 or FM Towns gets you going, all the more reason to check out this game.
While there isn't that much gameplay in VA-11 Hall-A, what is there does a good job of being immersive. Blend drinks after customers orders (or not, up to you) and check your feeds and shop while home, all while everything is dripping of this cozy dystopian cyberpunk future. Sure, the city where the story takes place, Glitch City, is a mismanaged hellhole but at the very least it's atmospheric and true to the theme.
Speaking of atmosphere, the soundtrack is fantastic. While not as retro as the graphics on a technical level - I mean, it's still retro, just not chip tunes or anything, it's spot on a thematic level.
All of this comes together for a fascinating experience with a story to tell. So by all means, get yourself some beverage and get comfortable. It's time to mix drinks and change lives...after all, Every Day is Night.

So, the gameplay in VA-11 Hall-A is comprised primarily of mixing drinks. Like, that's mostly it. Talk with the customer a bit, take note of their drink, mix the drink, serve it, then chat away until the next drink. Hell, most of the time the drink isn't even something you really have to think about, the ingredients for each drink are literally given to you from the get-go.
I'll be damned if it isn't engaging however. Like
(get used to many comparisons), it takes a rather simple and tedious task and finds a way to make it engaging for both the story and for the player. While Papers, Please slowly ramped up the difficulty to show the increasing paranoia of Arstotzka and, well, to engage the player in the spot the mistake gameplay, VA-11's gameplay never gets any more "difficult", but the characters are often requesting "the usual" or making you guess what they want, which lets you know how a character behaves and has the player infer on what they know.
The gameplay is directly tied to the storytelling too; as is in the Steam Store description,
Maybe a customer's depressed as hell, perhaps slip some extra booze in their drink to loosen them up a bit, maybe tell their story? Or grow closer to someone by understanding their taste? Seriously, as simple and repetitive the gameplay is, tying it into the story like this is brilliant.
The other major bit of gameplay is also very much like the major bit of gameplay in Papers, Please: managing finances. Maybe buy a thing so you won't get distracted at work, or save up a boatload of money to just barely scrape by your rent payment, or buy some tunes for the bar. Simplistic, and shows what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the world really is.
It's a visual novel, so this is the clear main focus. VA-11 is about the life of Jill, a bartender at the VA-11 Hall-A bar (which is a mouthful, so everyone calls it Valhalla), and her interactions with the various colourful characters that live in Glitch City, namely the bar's regulars and her coworkers.
First things first, the world. A cyberpunk corporately owned ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, what do you expect? The way characters bring up the events surrounding them is...certainly not how most would discuss them with a friend, however it's still rather engaging and eye opening, drawing influence from the exaggerated 80's cyberpunk and our own rather ♥♥♥♥ed up time period. It also clearly doesn't take itself too seriously, drawing a lot of influence from pop culture, which is always fun. Especially the newspapers and not-♥♥♥♥♥/reddit that's on Jill's phone.
Then, there's the characters, the main driving force of this game. VA11 is a story about the people of a cyberpunk dystopia; broken, depressed, and not in control of their lives, slowly learning about how they ended up at VA11. I love these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Despite the situation, there is a faint glimmer of hope that they discuss with you over a nice round of booze. Each of the characters are somehow, inexplicably linked in one way or another, and they are all so damned interesting, relatable and fun to "talk" with that it's impossible to hate them.
Aaand, the story itself. I err, I actually don't know what to say about this. It's great, don't get me wrong, but I really don't know how to approach this. Since the "main" story is driven mostly the interactions of characters, there isn't much to talk about that I haven't just said.
Resembling the graphics you would see on an old PC-98 adventure game combined with an anime look, what's not to love? Some of the characters are a bit inconsistent in the quality, but they all look great. Each of the characters has a distinct look and feel, and a lot of care has clearly been placed in crafting these characters & their designs to correspond with their personalities and their role in this world.
Okay, I have a bit of a hard on for music made with synthesizers, but c'mon! This soundtrack is amazing! The cyberpunk genre is a perfect match for synthwave, and here it's no exception. Garoad did an amazing job with balancing the 80's synth of cyberpunk with the calm jazz that would play at a trashy bar.
It's a ♥♥♥♥ing cyberpunk Papers, Please.
There's also a part-timer dog wearing a hawaiian shirt and sunglasses.
Soo, I'm not the biggest fan of visual novels. I've never really been interested in them (primarily being a gameplay first ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) and none have really caught my attention. I've seen some works based on them, yeah, but not much else. A friend recommended this to me on a whim, and I just went "Eh, ♥♥♥♥ it." What a great decision that was, though. I insantly fell in love with the characters, setting, simplistic gameplay, basically everything about this game. VA-11 Hall-A is without a doubt, one of the most cleverly written games I have ever played and I would easily recommend it to anyone else.

As someone who has played MTG for more than a decade now, I would have to say that MTG Duels of the planeswalkers is like buying a core set...an amazing value for the first time but a total waste of money moving forward. If you are new to the MTG scene or have not played in years, then yes, for 10 bucks you will have a whale of a time with this game. If you have bought the 2012 or 2013 edition though, don't bother unless you really want the new decks. I have no idea why but MTG has decided to make each year of the DOTP separate, it's a lot like one of those sports franchises that only change the players, except in this case you change decks so WTF? It's bad enough you can't build your own decks, now you have to own separate editions as well. Why can't all these decks be DLC attached to the 2012 edition? There hasn't been any fundamental change, even the so-called "sealed mode" is just a gimmick and could've been sold as an expansion so to be honest releasing a new version every year is just forcing everyone to keep buying the new edition at full price, something which is ok for a first timer but a total rip off for someone who already bought an earlier edition.  You can definitely make the argument that $10 is ok for a new edition, but the fact that you can't use your previous decks unless you keep the previous version is really limiting and keeps fragmenting the customer base with every edition they put out, unless you keep the games  installed in which case you'd have like 10 different DOTP games in your pc by 2022 or whatever.
Just look at all the useless "DLC" on offer for this game, it is clear they are more interested in gouging out as much $$$ as they can without any regard for the game quality. IMHO if you want real value for money you are better off playing HearthStone or waiting for Hex, whatever amounts of money you invest into those games will be retained unlike this POS crap you need to keep buying every year.
