The Witness sets out to capture the sense of wonder and discovery through a simple act of seeing patterns and lines in things and solving puzzles around this simple concept. And at it's best, it is really exciting to be discovering solutions, finding patterns and seeing how many creative things can be done with a simple concept. Even without any story or real motivation, apart from this sense of discovery.
And then the game decides to be "challenging", by gradually becoming tedious, annoying, frustrating, unbearable and at times outright sickening. It thinks of a nice (but potentially difficult for more tone-death people) idea of using sound as a hint for a solution. And then discards the idea almost immediatelly. But at the same time ponders around a ridiculously tiring idea of "find the exact pixel perfect and timed solution in a room" for about 30 puzzles. It thinks of a nice concept of using the shape you draw as the solution, to use it very few times in a game and instead - have some epilepsy inducing puzzles that will make your eyes bleed.
It's all about this idea of seeing shapes and symbols in your surroundings, but so many of these shapes are easy to notice, but a real b*tch to actually complete just because they tend to be pixel perfect. And because despite clear physical presense, your playable avatar cannot move their head slightly to the side or up or down.
It has a "challenge" area that is just timed random puzzle stuff and the "challenge" being that not only this is timed, but the puzzels are actually random, to the point where they are not necesserily completable. And it "rewards" you for "completing" the game by reseting your progress and dumping you back at the start (the saves are not deleted). As if forgetting that vast majority of the stuff it asks of you has one or extremely limited solution possibility so there's absolutely no fun at all in replaying it again (since you're not discovering anything anymore).
The Witness is such a sad huge waste of amazing potential, with it's fantastic concept, amazing looks and tight art design. But implemented in such a way that it all just falls apart rather quickly. And I'd say that at least there's nothing that mixes the magic of exploration, wonder and puzzles better, except there is. Called Antichamber and available for quite a while.
I am glad I experienced The Witness. And I do not plan to revisit it ever again.

Let me start off by saying that The Witness is a very different type of game. It doesn't hold your hand or guide you through any parts of the game. It respects you as a smart person, and expects you to be able to take care of yourself. When starting the game, you're placed down in a room with the only way out being doors with puzzle panels. These puzzle panels are what make up the entire game, getting progressively harder and requiring more thought as you go. While at heart this is still a puzzle game, the fact that it is shouldn't make shy away. The experience given by The Witness is truely phenominal, and I have only scratched the surface. The gameplay consists of roaming the open world, solving puzzles, and connecting beams of light to the top of a mountain. While simple in concept, these puzzles become quite challenging and extemely rewarding. After being stuck on a puzzle, taking a break, and then coming back to it only to find that the solution was right before your eyes is rewarding in a way that no game has ever made me experience. The game makes you feel stupid at times but then boosts you right up to feeling like a genius. The one thing that I cannot stress enough is
By this I don't mean looking up the answer to a few puzzles if you really do get stuck, but in most cases, even this is unnecessary. The game doesn't require that you solve each puzzle to win. If you do end up getting stuck on an area of the map, walk away, explore the island a bit, then either go back and give it another shot or just start in another area, one that may be easier for you. Personally, I find this game to be perfectly made. The game is also surprisingly easy to run considering how good it looks. Every shot looks beautiful and is perfect for screenshotting. The world gives you plenty of freedom without feeling linear, something I have never experienced in a puzzle game. Even if you don't like puzzle games, pick this up and you won't regret it, I know I didn't. I look forward to continuing my amazing experience with this game and recommend for you to do yourself a favor in picking up this game. The Witness is a 10/10 game and a true gem.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Switchcars
Update Version: Update #7
Disclosure: The game copy was bought by the reviewer.
It has been almost two years since I found myself behind the wheel of a vehicle and the allure of driving is still a distant feeling. It never mattered what type of vehicle it was as long as I could feel the fresh breeze against my face and the tranquility of driving along a deserted highway. Unfortunately for the protagonist in Altfuture's Switchcars, he does not have time to observe the scenery. Every second counts in the race to 2055 and he has to use whatever vehicle he can get his hands on to reach it. Does the simple, but hard to master gameplay help this game set a new record or does it slow down enough to miss the finish line?
Driving against the flow of time and the creatures that look a lot like langoliers is unique for a genre usually trapped in a dungeon setting. The visuals, however, are the same retro Super Nintendo graphics that have been trending as of late. This is a considerable negative most of the time, but the developer has taken the time to give each biosphere the right amount of detail to make them really stand out. Most of the vehicles found in the game also have a defining look which I thought would be hard to pull off in such a limited, pixelated style. Upgrades also change  the look of the car with new tires, frame attachments and paint jobs. It fits strangely enough and allows everything to stand out amidst the total chaos of constantly switching from vehicle to vehicle at top speeds (against incoming traffic).
The main focus of this game is combat though, more specifically the fight to stay out of combat. The only way to do so is by rushing through the ten stages during each run and reach the safe zone using your grappling hook while on foot and avoid incoming clutter such as houses and incoming vehicles. You have a wide range to use that each have a strength or weakness to traits such as speed and armor/ resistance or terrain (treads work better in desert, trains on tracks). With nine lanes (six ground mixed with land and sea, three air) and an ever changing biosphere, using the right vehicle is always a concern, so thankfully you can have a reserve of three to constantly switch to on the fly. This is where the mastery comes into play and while it can be more luck based than skill, identifying and utilizing specific upgrades to compensate for weakness can be enough to overcome this factor. Once the clock reaches zero, the giant whale-like worms enter the picture and will not stop trying to squish you until you manage to get to the next stage. Time is always counting down, so keep driving to the right and adapt to the environment.
Unfortunately, this one trick pony can get extremely repetitive quickly and grind more on the nerves of the player than the gears of the vehicles. It can be very addicting in the beginning, but after a couple of hours this addictive high slowly wears off and the fight to reach the end starts to feel like a grind. More vehicles unlock, starting dates get closer to 2055, more lanes open up, but it is still the same game from the very beginning. There is no real complexity or improvement. Others might never run off the high created from the start, but in the end the game never evolves or offers anything other than what is introduced initially.
Some other issues are still relevant with the game, but it is important to mention a lot of general bugs were already dealt with. What remains are some resolution errors that create a black screen display while in full screen and start up issues. Crashes do occur as well, but not as frequent before. Screen tearing can happen (most likely due to the speed of which environments are passing by). Frame rate drops did pop up in place of the screen tearing as well. Just something to keep in mind.
The game is in no way a negative experience and presents a unique idea into a overused genre. Endless runners and rogue likes are too numerous to address properly and generally fall flat on entry. What some of these other games tend to do, however, is evolve over the course of the playtime in order to overcome the challenges. This adventure is trapped on the same rail from start to finish. It is a shame to say this when the game has such a quirky premise, but at the current point this game just is not worth a recommendation. Hopefully there might be some more variation added in the future, but until then this one trick pony is better off staying in the stables.
Pros
- Very clever premise
- Detailed pixelated visuals with a catchy soundtrack
- Can become very addicting...
Cons
- ...but loses it's initial flare quickly
- Gameplay never evolves and seen what it offers in first couple of minutes
- Crashes, black screens, start up errors

I'm unhappy that I even got this for free. I think I would pay to have this removed from my library because of how frustrating and anti-climactic this game is.

Knowing that it's an update/sequel to an early 90s series, I'm inclined to forgive it somewhat for its repetitious gameplay, heavy backtracking, trite dialogue and plot, and bland characterization. The voice-acting leaves much to be desired. Monster closets are its stock in trade, though I'll admit to yelping at some cheap jump scares.
The isometric camera is fine, and the camera only becomes frustrating for the moments in which the designers decide that this inexplicable angle is most appropriate, and you're stuck with it until you progress to the next area. As in, the camera pans to face you head-on as you move down a corridor -- you can't see any enemies more than two feet ahead of you, and if you happen to spot some behind you, you have to spin around and take them out, anyway. There's an irritating boss fight with a fixed camera, making it more challenging than it ought to be.
That said, it is a graphically beautiful game, and the set and sound design are well-done. The shots you get of the area surrounding the ship (the planet in the distance, debris burning up, or thrusters firing) are lovely and detailed, and while the alien sounds are (like the monsters themselves) repetitive, they are evocative, and the other environmental cues are thoughtfully done.
If you enjoy the grind, or end up with this in your library and want to knock one out of your backlog, here's my advice: keep your expectations low, play for short sessions, and just power through it.

The game can be challenging, and even downright frusterating at times, particularly when you're trying to fight a death loop from a resource shortage.  Unhappy colonists won't grow food to save themselves from starvation, for example.  My experience is limited, but so far a certain amount of luck seems to play a role in the success or failure of a colony in the very early game.
I had just reached the self sufficient state in my last attempt when a meteor crashed through the roof of my sleeping quarters and wiped everyone out.
There are some balance issues as well; it seems to take a lot longer to build robots than their actual lifespan ingame, so I'm not seeing a real good return on the investment there.  I've also had several instances of colonists dying at airlock entrances due to how they only allow one person or robot to enter or exit at a time.  Granted, an airlock can only allow one direction of travel at a time, but that doesn't necessarily mean that it should be restricted to only one person going in that direction, unless it was an extremely small airlock.
I've found through much experimentation on the desert planet that a base at 60s and 60w yields a nice big open area to build on, which I would recommend you try out for your first colony.

So Ive seen some negative feedback on Planetbase and thought I would write a review , and give this a bit of a boost , because I enjoyed this game , and feel that for whats advertised that its not as bad as others make out.
First , those of you saying its too hard need to realize your being challenged. If you find bugs with AI pathing and decision , try altering your colony layout, and tweak incomming personel to the task at hand. Ive beaten the first 2 stages pretty much and have had short term success on the class M planet , so I know its possible to succeed , just hard. And thats what I like in these games : challenge.
I have seen pathing bugs including AI not picking up well from saved games , not building critical structures before other planned ones (which I note the developer is working on in the current iteration) and ridiculous traffic decisions among personel when faced with a bottle neck in airlocks ; remedied by having more than one airlock where more people need to use the facility. I also note in the aforementoined case that having an airlock open to the opposite side of the base can help in central junctures.
These problems can all be cured by a little dillegence in AI prioitization and pathing , and it seems the developer is working on it , so give him that chance.
If the current bugs are addressed , I would give it a  6/10 , and as I see direct engagement and work towards that end that seems to be working , I feel confident in that rating. Now that said , as I would rate something at 5/10 as worth playing , this isnt a stellar endorsement , but confidence that others can be entertained in the title as advertised.
Now as for those saying this game lacks depth , I say : "Your right, but wait and give the developer time to add this before you make a final assessment." If your expecting a finished game , hold onto your cash for now , but if you want it as is , which is ALPHA and under construction , you can be entertained.
Im hoping and expecting to see more depth added. I feel this game has all the potential to garner a huge following if its fleshed out a bit. Im reminded of "Outpost 2" , where you could design the colony ship and pick from different planets. I remember "Light of Altair" where you could look out from your rock and see in the sky other closeby planets in the solar system , the stars closeby and backgroud gas clouds. Im reminded of EVE where the sceenery reflects the locality in gas cloud formations and local stars. Admittedly turning this into an MMO game like EVE from its present state would be like building a pyramid in ancient Egypt , but I would love to see the dev able to grow this product into something even close to it.
Back to something more realistic , I would think adding a local star map and letting the player choose his destination and design the launch vehicle wouldnt be too much of a stretch.. add a half dozen more planet classes and then according to star class have the planets a bit randomized/procedurally generated.
Maybe reward player success with more cash to build a better ship and take more stuff. Add other buildings like reactors you could set up (would last say 5x as long as other power gen but then needs advanced spares , fuel processing , tech and lab to research many of the components etc) add resource 'radiologicals'.
You could add a bulldozer , big tracked driller to go with the drill bots , make people choose where to drill and hit viens of metal that give more metal / radiologicals / gold / other minerals. Add underground habitations , schools , malls , hospitals , better residential areas shielded from solar flares and add radiation to those staying on surface on planet classes without magnetic fields to shield them and atmopheres. Add terraforming so you can add or thicken the atmosphere and after weeks of playing your colonists can take the space suits off for good. You could design and upgrade your own trade ships , load them with the food and goods you make and sell them to other computer players and humans in a persistant galaxy. Lets face it , theres billions of stars in the milky way - you could accomodate all the players there. Even have competition sending out hostile saboteurs , theives , spies to other places.
Theres so much potential here it would be a shame not to acknowledge that though theres work to be done , this is a work in progress AND IS ADVERTISED AS SUCH.
If you buy a game in the process of construction , you have to expect it to be unfinished. I for one acknowledge that and support the developer in his effort. If that effort is abandoned too soon , thats on him down the road , but Ive given my money to try it here and earnestly hope the effort is continued. Ill say if your also going into your purchase with eyes open and realistic expectations , and your a fan of colony sims , that I think you will be reasonably entertained for a time.
Good luck to the dev,  and Ill be watching !

After logging almost 30 hours, and maxing out the achievements on the first planet, I felt I could offer some insight into the game.
Pros:
The first world was challenging enough to require strategy, which I appreciate. You can't just go crazy with your construction and expect your colony to survive.
The level of complexity is appropriate for a casual gamer. This isn't CIV 5 or any of those other massive world building games, so don't expect it to be.
Base design is important, particularly considering your connections can be damaged by asteroids. This requires you to plan out your base using the finite amount of space you have to build.
Cons:
The AI still needs work. I've watched people in my colony die of hunger while standing IN the canteen with food readily available in the dispenser. You have absolutely no control over individual people, so you can't correct this strange behavior for them. You just have to give them the outlets they need and hope they eventually take advantage of them.
Power-Outages seem unusually devastating to a base, particularly if they're very short. Despite having huge surpluses of food and plenty of water in reserve, one 3 minute power outage suddenly makes EVERYONE both hungry and thirsty, and the mad rush that ensues once the lights come back on can easily kill 10 - 20% of your colonists. I had to watch several times as a brief outage killed almost a quarter of my population, despite the fact that they were perfectly fine only moments ago.
There's a frustrating logic to how the buildings can be connected to each other. Sometimes you think the building should fit, but it won't. If you aren't careful, you can use up all of your free space and not have enough room.
Finally, the relative simplicity of the building structures limits gameplay pretty significantly once you get everything up and running. Sure you need to get bigger in order to hit the achievements, but that just means building bigger versions of the same buildings. The next two worlds offer unique challenges in the form of different natural disasters, or crippling how you generate power, but offers no change in the fundamentals of gameplay. You simply do exactly the same thing, they just make it more difficult to do.
Overall I give it a thumbs up. My rule is if I get an hour of gameplay for every dollar I spend, the game was worth it. I clearly enjoyed the game enough for it to hit this benchmark, so it gets my stamp of approval. Just don't go into it thinking it's more than it is, or you'll be disappointed.

Planetbase is annother space-colony sim. What does it bring to the table? Pretty graphics, mainly. Also, it is a "complete game" (It's sad that I have to use those quotes). OK, so let me be clear in that it's a good game. Now, I have yet to see the pirates, but there is only three glaring weaknesses in this game (or three that I'll go into).
1. No pause button, other than the menu.
Now, in reality, there is no pause button in our day to day lives. But neither is there speed up. I get the idea of the challenge of not pauseing to see the lay of the land, or a head start on build orders, but let the player decide if they want that challenge.
2. The initial supply of reasources.
Sure, you might have enough for the bare necesities, maybe, if you think a dark first night is fun due to lack of wind. To me there are a set of major buildings that need to be built. O2 generator, followed by airlock, solar and wind generators, and a capasitor of at least medium, waterpump, cantine, bio-dome, mine, and factory. Oh, and all the conectors, and the facilities inside. That is litterally all the metal and bioplastic for something even reasonably longterm. Not to mention you'll need dorms, for sleep (which is funny that that is a low priority to the mine), storage so nothing goes bad, and medic bay and lab. But i guess they expect you to build the smallest ones, which wouldn't be bad, if not for the fact that after a bit of conga line of buildings, everything is structually vital to the base. But oh, well.
3. The manufactoring tree
Now, "things take time, el presidente" to produce, I understand. But if you can build a dome in under an hour, you sure as heck can turn ore into metal in less time! This goes somewhat with above, but it's especially annoying when the people operating the thing come over and take an hour to do it, and do only 10%. The Plant heairerarchy works fine, but not the building reasources. And while all that's going on, you're using up all the food, and then your bots need repairing, and the windmills outside, but, "Uh oh", you're out of scraps. Enjoy the darkness, and pay 250 credits for a stinking carrier bot.
Minus the things up above, this game could barley be better. It's beautiful, the developers seem active to a fully released game, and when things look up in it, it is up... until I will enevitably reach pirates, and it all goes up in smokes.
(P.S. to developers: Seriously, you don't need that many medpacks, you need more metal. My God do you need the metal.)

Star Conflict has done most things well. This game has:
-A pretty good soundtrack(it's more situational than memorable, but that's not necessarily a bad thing)
-Smooth, easy-to-use controls
-Creative maps
-Great visuals that run incredibly well even on integrated graphics
-A TON of ships and upgrades(the upgrade tree is similar to "World of Tanks")
However, one thing is preventing me from being able to enjoying this game fully, or even be able to give a proper rating. I downloaded this game with great wishes to pla pvp primarily. Little did I know that in order to decrease waiting times, players get thrown into battle against the AI(remember, this is in pvp, not pve or skirmish). This is a great idea in concept, but within the 6.6 hours I've played at the time of this review, I've only played REAL pvp in two matches. Not only have I won every battle against the AI, the fact that I'm not getting to do pvp is preventing me from completing certain achievements, which I WANT to complete so I can move on and complete more to get more in-game credits. The fact that I have started matches with 6 players against 6 bots makes this even more of a frustration since I have fought many battles with just 2 players and 2 bots. Why can't the matches just be 3v3 instead of 6 players vs. 6 bots?
I give star conflict a 4/5 only because of the "pvp issue" and a UI that can sometimes get on my nerves due to a lack of information. If anyone has played and liked "Metalstorm"(I know it's at least been on iOS) then I highly suggest downloading Star Conflict. It's basically a Sci-Fi metalstorm with the upgrade tree from World of Tanks.

It's very beneficial and eye-opening for me, as a fortunate Singaporean player who played this game for about 20 odd hours. At first I cannot imagine how life would be like if there's a civil war happening like that. Now I have briefly understand but cannot fully comprehend what life is like during a war like that, since I did not experience that before.
This game let me learned two main things:
1. Humans are all sinful: No biblical reference here, I'm just saying that we, as humans, have desires to get what we want. Whether is it through stealing, looting from random pile of trash, or even trade with the church, hospital and even at the military outpost. Trading seems fair, looting looks okay as well, but the capability of stealing from various homes let me realised that we are just as disgusting as the soldiers and the rebels. Stealing may seemed to be a bad-but-minor thing, but this is fueled by something within humans, which is called desire, or greed.
2. Humans are made to have a relationship with one another:  Whether is it Emilia and Roman trying to talk things out with a kid (and did not really help), or Katia trying to trade with the trader, we all are capable of communicating with one another and help each other. Helping our neighbors from gunshots, collapsed buildings, or even providing medication, is something that is hard to do, but it's pretty much fulfilling as I put my neighbors' needs above anyone else.
I still haven't encounter the militia in front of my doorstep, but I hope I can make a wise choice, whether is it for me, or for my neighbors. This game is awesome. Words cannot describe how depressed after I get from all the feels and aesthetics I get from this game, but numbers can: 10/10.

If you want a good challenge them I would recommend this game. Otherwise you're probably going to play for about an hour and then give up on it. I just feel like a game should be more rewarding than this. At least Ghosts N Goblins had cool spells you could unleash when you manage to grab a full set of powerups. Volgarr only manages to give you a triple damage spear with the first power up, and the final power up? A double damage sword. Not sure why the sword would end up being weaker than a powered up spear, but alright.
Another mechanic that's frustrating is the inclusion of all these nice golden items, gems, etc.. But, Sonic the Hedgehog fashion, you lose about 75% of your treasure when you die. I have no idea if you can use your gold to urchase upgrades between levels, but I very much doubt it. It just seems like a pointless and not-very-rewarding mechanic to me.
Another point of confusion is the checkpoints. On the first level you're given one after a very easy area. Then you're given one halfway through the level. You want one before the boss? Nah. Forget about it. There is, of course, a door that closes before you reach the boss. This seems like a mechanic borrowed from the Mega Man series, but makes no sense to have it here without a boss checkpoint. It would have made more sense if extra lives were involved, but instead you have unlimited continues and VERY few checkpoints. I would have preferred an Extra Lives system, having to restart an entire level when you run out of them, and more checkpoints.
It's not all bad though. The combat mechanics and the art style (aside from a few out-of-place goofy looking enemies, like the smiley 'Joker' snakes in Level 1)  are both mostly very cool. It's too bad most players won't get to see all the art the game has to offer.

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a PC port of a PSP game released in 2010. It's a visual novel mystery adventure game, similar to the Ace Attorney series. However in my honest opinion, this game is the poor man's version of the Ace Attorney (AA) series.
The game is about 15 teenagers, trapped in school where their only means of escaping is to murder other teenagers trapped under the watchful gaze of Monokuma, a derange psychopath remote controlling a mechanical bear. It's up to the main character, Makoto Naegi, to find out the murderer when a murder happens, discover the mysteries of the school and escape.
The characters are very colourful and well diverse (except for the main character who is self-aware to be completely average and have absolutely no special traits or talents whatsoever). Thankfully the supporting casts are not as boring but since this is a murder mystery game, players might not have the chance to fully know some of the characters. In fact, there's literally only 3 characters including the MC that are fully capable of running an investigation. The others are basically dead weight. Some are more likable than others but most are completely useless. Even worse, one of the characters who survived the whole game is a comic relief who brings absolutely nothing to the game other than making stupid and bad jokes. I assure you, the jokes are not funny and it honestly makes me question the devs decision to keep the character alive.
Gameplay, as I mentioned before, are similar to the AA series, only not as polished. There's an element of dating sim in the game but sadly underdeveloped. I appreciate the first person mode but it honestly doesn't do much to add to the game. The murder mysteries are inferior compared to the AA series and the clues are either too obvious or too vague. Nothing is more frustrating than not knowing what exactly the game really wants.
The ending sucks, too. The games tried so hard to give a fulfilling ending with it's plot twists and all but I found it to fall short. Honestly it kinda makes me a bit depressed in the end.
One thing people should know about this game is that there's little to none replay value. Once you've beaten it, that's it. Unless you like reading mountains of texts and re-solving the same murder, you probably won't replay this.
Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a good game, so I'm giving it a thumbs up. However compared to the AA series, this game is clearly not as good.
RECOMMENDED: For anyone who enjoys the AA series, visual novel games or solving mysteries.
NOT RECOMMENDED: For those who doesn't enjoy anime-styled visual novel games.

The Witness sets out to capture the sense of wonder and discovery through a simple act of seeing patterns and lines in things and solving puzzles around this simple concept. And at it's best, it is really exciting to be discovering solutions, finding patterns and seeing how many creative things can be done with a simple concept. Even without any story or real motivation, apart from this sense of discovery.
And then the game decides to be "challenging", by gradually becoming tedious, annoying, frustrating, unbearable and at times outright sickening. It thinks of a nice (but potentially difficult for more tone-death people) idea of using sound as a hint for a solution. And then discards the idea almost immediatelly. But at the same time ponders around a ridiculously tiring idea of "find the exact pixel perfect and timed solution in a room" for about 30 puzzles. It thinks of a nice concept of using the shape you draw as the solution, to use it very few times in a game and instead - have some epilepsy inducing puzzles that will make your eyes bleed.
It's all about this idea of seeing shapes and symbols in your surroundings, but so many of these shapes are easy to notice, but a real b*tch to actually complete just because they tend to be pixel perfect. And because despite clear physical presense, your playable avatar cannot move their head slightly to the side or up or down.
It has a "challenge" area that is just timed random puzzle stuff and the "challenge" being that not only this is timed, but the puzzels are actually random, to the point where they are not necesserily completable. And it "rewards" you for "completing" the game by reseting your progress and dumping you back at the start (the saves are not deleted). As if forgetting that vast majority of the stuff it asks of you has one or extremely limited solution possibility so there's absolutely no fun at all in replaying it again (since you're not discovering anything anymore).
The Witness is such a sad huge waste of amazing potential, with it's fantastic concept, amazing looks and tight art design. But implemented in such a way that it all just falls apart rather quickly. And I'd say that at least there's nothing that mixes the magic of exploration, wonder and puzzles better, except there is. Called Antichamber and available for quite a while.
I am glad I experienced The Witness. And I do not plan to revisit it ever again.

Let me start off by saying that The Witness is a very different type of game. It doesn't hold your hand or guide you through any parts of the game. It respects you as a smart person, and expects you to be able to take care of yourself. When starting the game, you're placed down in a room with the only way out being doors with puzzle panels. These puzzle panels are what make up the entire game, getting progressively harder and requiring more thought as you go. While at heart this is still a puzzle game, the fact that it is shouldn't make shy away. The experience given by The Witness is truely phenominal, and I have only scratched the surface. The gameplay consists of roaming the open world, solving puzzles, and connecting beams of light to the top of a mountain. While simple in concept, these puzzles become quite challenging and extemely rewarding. After being stuck on a puzzle, taking a break, and then coming back to it only to find that the solution was right before your eyes is rewarding in a way that no game has ever made me experience. The game makes you feel stupid at times but then boosts you right up to feeling like a genius. The one thing that I cannot stress enough is
By this I don't mean looking up the answer to a few puzzles if you really do get stuck, but in most cases, even this is unnecessary. The game doesn't require that you solve each puzzle to win. If you do end up getting stuck on an area of the map, walk away, explore the island a bit, then either go back and give it another shot or just start in another area, one that may be easier for you. Personally, I find this game to be perfectly made. The game is also surprisingly easy to run considering how good it looks. Every shot looks beautiful and is perfect for screenshotting. The world gives you plenty of freedom without feeling linear, something I have never experienced in a puzzle game. Even if you don't like puzzle games, pick this up and you won't regret it, I know I didn't. I look forward to continuing my amazing experience with this game and recommend for you to do yourself a favor in picking up this game. The Witness is a 10/10 game and a true gem.
If you like puzzle games, this game is for you.

This is a tough one. I personally had a great time for 95% of this game - many of the puzzles are extremely clever and the island is just so beautifully crafted and rendered. Other reviews are wrong on one point - the puzzles are consistent to their rule set; I completed the game without looking up any solutions and never had an issue figuring out any of the "tricks" after putting some effort in. I agree with everyone who has lauded the game's ability to teach and combine concepts by only showing and never telling.
However, would I *recommend* it? If you're a fan of puzzle games like me, then yes, I think you'll have a good time. But the pleasure of this game doesn't really go beyond the pat on the back you can give yourself for solving some tough logic puzzles. While the environment does play an ingenious role in many puzzles, I can't help but feel it missed some opportunities. The coolest part of the game (no spoilers) is relegated to a tedious game of "I Spy" that has no real reward or consequence.
My criticism here is the same as with Braid - though doubly so this time. The slight nods to some kind of underlying story or profundity come off as disconnected pretentiousness. Come for the puzzles, stay for the puzzles - there's no story here outside of the developer felating himself like a freshman in philosophy 101.
And the puzzles were fun. It was genuinely thrilling to unlock the next door or find a new area of the island. But behind those gates were always just more line puzzles.
For me, the game only barely outstayed its welcome. By the final area, I had had enough of The Witness's line puzzles for one lifetime. But the time I did spend, I personally enjoyed very much.
One of the most challenging games I've ever played and also one of the most rewarding.

Alien Breed is an isometric sci-fi shooter where you independently control the direction your character aims and moves. You maneuver through a series of 5 stages in each episode, collecting weapons and items, and shooting aliens as they appear while you move from objective to objective provided on your mini-map.
It is difficult to write a separate review for each Episode, as they all largely play the same - you move from point A to point B to pick up access code C to open door D to get to point E to get access code F to.....you get the picture. Lots of backtracking through same-looking corridors, fighting similar looking enemies which pop out of the floor and walls.
It's fun, but only moderately so - I would NOT recommend playing through a single episode in one sitting, let alone all three episodes. The gameplay is repetitive and it's the sort of thing you'll want to put down for a while between sessions (I'd actually say on the level of months between episodes) so it doesn't get stale.
Glad I got this steaming load of a game for free because I would've contacted Steam Support for a refund had I wasted the asking price for it.

A very good basebuilder, not many citybuilders in space at the momet, so it's a nice variation on good titles like Banished or those more historical titles like Civcity & co.
It has all the classic ingredients:
_start small and grow bigger
_keep people happy and healthy
_attract more people
_reach some important milestones of growth
_get annoyed by the elements and external disturbances
_trade
_manage your resources and people
_unlocking more/better buildings
My favorite highlight in this game of that type is also no surprise: the atmospheric scenery of an exoplanet comparable to Mars, the moon or some gas planet.
EDIT: (I waited a few days before adding these notes)
Yet it lacks some features that are an essential part of most citybuilders:
_Replayability: the means to try to build your base a different way you did the others are not sufficiently present. You can restart a map and you'll have a different landscape, but you'll still have to use the same buildings to fill each need of your base, the same techs, the same people... I restarted a map on another planet, and except the feeling of a different atmosphere which needs a bit of tweaking of my energy production facilities, I didn't really feel a challenge to it. So I guess most players could get fed up after 20-40 hours of playthrough, which for a city/basebuilder is really not so long.
Other petty annoyances:
_Storage management: because not everything should go to a random pile around my base
_Historical stats: how did I evolve ? You only have stats of the last past 8 days or so to plan for immediate shortcomings, but how did I do in the long term ? I even have no idea of the amount of spent in-game days.
_grid placement of base structures: I'm an interplanetary civilisation but I can't put my buildings on a straight line ??
With that said, the pricing makes it really worth it anyway.

The player assumes the role of being a colony administrator; it his your job to establish a fully functional colony on another world.
This task is all but easy though; you will face a variety of problems such as power shortages, lack of food, meteor showers, sandstorms and even hostile takeovers from intruders.
All in all Planetbase is indeed a very enjoyable game, make no mistake however as it is far from being easy. Your first colonies will almost guaranteed be failures, over time you will learn from your mistakes and create the perfect colony.
So far I have very few complaints, which is the lack of a "easy mode" (for filthy casuals), the lack of vehicles (inter-colony transportation when?) and the sometimes goofy AI which have the rare tendency to ignore prioritized orders, alongside with the fact that there's no way of directly ordering the colonists.
And while the game is unforgiving, the cute graphics, loveable art style and cheesy soundtrack completes the experience.
After all, who doesn't want to listen to a cheesy soundtrack while building up your galactic emp-err, colony. All in all it's a fun game which I recommend to anyone who liked Banished or to the person who just wants a tough challenge.

What a brilliant game.  Failure is frustrating early on because the consequences usually lead to the demise of everyone in the base, but success is very rewarding because the game forces you to pay attention to what is going on.  I personally had several failed colonies before I finally got a handle on things.
This game is very different and enjoyable to play.  It does require some forward planning and resource management is essential.  Once you get through the initial start up, things ease up slightly and so long as your power, oxygen, water and food supplies stay at tolerable levels, your colony is pretty much set.  As soon as you get the meteorite defence lasers deployed, you don’t even need to worry about huge rocks falling from space.  A bigger effect from sandstorms might add a little flare to things.  The regular attacks from ships attempting to take control of your base keeps things interesting though.
There is certainly plenty of scope here for additions.  Waste management, filtration for o2, terraforming, and environmental control to name a few things.  I have noticed no bugs so far in Planetbase
I sincerely hope the developers stick with the game to further refine and add to what is shaping up to be something quite unique and entertaining.

This is a neat little base building game. I picked it up a few days ago and have quite enjoyed my time with it so far.
There are a few issues but none that I have encountered that hurt my experience too badly.
The colonist AI could be tweaked a bit more but it seems like the Devs are working diligently on this.
- In 1.0.5 I had 10 or so colonists starve to death because they would not stop taking items to a trading ship long enough to eat (I had back to back ships where I attempted to offload tons of items). It was kind of funny since the path they had to take was only a few modules and they had to walk through a canteen  filled to the brim with food.
I have only loaded a few maps on planet 1, but I seem to end up surrounded by hills and mountains most of the time which severely limits the area that can be built on.
- Luckily I found a few tricks that help mitigate this. You can use pads, mines, and connections to flatten terrain and cut paths through some hills to get to other flat areas. Placing a mine on the other side of a hill and connecting it to an exterior module will place a 'path' that flattens out the hill in that spot. Repeating this can lead to extensive landscape adjustment.
In one of my first games my colony ended up dieing out. My only starting engineer was unlucky enough to be crushed by a meteor and my construction bot broke down before I could build a Landing Pad so I was left with no ability to build new structures and was not yet at a self sufficient stage.
There is a lot of room for expansion in this game as new modules and hazards can probably be added relatively easily.
tl;dr  A fun base building space game to pass the time. Recommended.

YOU CAN PRESS A TO WALK AUTOMATICALLY DURING CUTSCENES.
I have no idea why that isn't actually indicated to you in the game, but hopefully that will spare you the irritation I felt for the first few cutscenes trying to navigate the world with a constantly changing camera.
Anyway, Furi is a fast-paced boss rush game - the first of its kind I've played, and I kind of like the style. I can't imagine any platforming that they could have put in between the bosses that would make the game more enjoyable, and they get to focus all their design energy on just a few enemies instead of generating a bunch of mooks that you cut through without thinking.
That focus on design really shows - the game looks and sounds gorgeous. The story's pretty good, also, the mystery of it kept me engaged throughout.
It's not flawless - I got very frustrated during the fight with The Edge. All the fights have unskippable cutscenes (a sin to begin with) when you get knocked down that last 5 or 10 seconds, which is normally fine because the phases last a few minutes - but The Edge can kill you in 5 seconds if you get a bad run, so you'll spend as much time watching your character slowly picking himself up as you will fighting. And when you get knocked down - I think just in this one fight -
you have to move the stick to trigger the cutscene, which feels unnatural. He also has unpredictable combos (well, not wholly - he has a few different combos that he uses but you can't tell which one he's doing until partway through, and if you're prepared to react to the wrong one you're almost certainly just taking those hits),
Furthermore it's hard to enjoy this game casually - normal difficulty is still pretty tough, and asks a lot from you in terms of reflexes and knowing when to dodge and when to parry. If you don't have several hours to devote at a time so you can get in the groove, I can imagine getting tired of it pretty quickly, and the game is pretty condescending towards people wanting to play on easy; the main menu's "easy" description pretty much says "this is for babies who cannot gitgud".
Despite those things, though, I would recommend picking this up - I wouldn't blame you for waiting for a sale though.

Steam recommended this game on release day so I checked out the videos and it looked interesting.  Over the course of the next week I watched a few let's plays which looked better and better, and saw how active the dev is with answering questions - you can see the guy's passion for this game, and he alludes to some really cool future features.
Realizing this is early access, I am having a TON of fun with this game.  After splattering my head a number of times during the first hour, I find the game is pretty easy to learn.  Once you understand the controls it's a matter of experimenting with the mechanics to optimize your game play, but I feel like mastering this game still takes long enough to keep you coming back.
The first few games I played I either died immediately (either splattering my head on a car/bus/plane/house, or jumping out of a car and getting run over on a racetrack) but after ~5 hours of playing I can regularly get to stage 7/8.  The unlocking system is really cool as the more challenging terrains only unlock once you get past a certain stage - the first time I was in the space stage it was pretty nuts, and the alien world where you can spawn 4 aliens if you don't have a car are hilarious.
Even death can be funny as most games don't last more than 10 minutes, which I think makes this a rogue-like for people who don't normally like perma death.  You also have a graphical tally of all the cars you've used that run which is really fun to watch for some reason.  Each car you enter gets entered into a database which for completionists like me is great - with over 1000 cars I'm at 400 so far and loving it!
One of the best things about this game though, is of course the cars!  You can store 3 cars to be swapped between at any time, and can always ditch a saved car for a new one.  The variety is staggering, and the small details in the pixel art is amazing (drive through a muddy level and your vehicle will get mud on it, that will slowly clean off as your drive away).  One of my early games I drove through a battlefield and got 3 different tanks, which I used to get stage 7, swapping when running out of fuel and blasting everything out of my way, including killing 6 or so aliens - very satisfying!
When not in a car, you have the ability to run around on foot with a permanent grappling hook which you can use to catapult yourself forward dodging the object as you approach, drag yourself closer to a vehicle to hop into it (several initial runs will be lost when learning how to enter the car as you as speeding towards it).  Most of the time you'll only be in the "on foot" stage for a split second as the swap cars.
Scattered throughout the levels are powerups which range from cosmetic to amazing.  Repair all/ refuel all are fairly common (and highly useful), but there is something very satisfying with turning a battleship armed with rockets into an offroad vehicle, arm a sports car with a tank's cannon.  Because each object has a mass of their own, the lighter vehicles smash into pieces when hitting a heavy object/vehicle, but the big heavy vehicles can plow through almost anything.  The battleship mentioned above eventually was given nitrous (replacing the rockets - doh!) and smashed through EVERYTHING it ran into.  One of my first wow moments was finding and entering a stationary WW2 cannon, storing it for use when aliens showed up and swapping to it to blast them to pieces, eventually adding a fuel engine powerup so I can drive it.
To sum it up, this game is very very promising for early access.  There are some quirks to work out, but the game ran bug-free for me and was highly enjoyable.  Also if you don't always have time for longer gaming sessions, this is a great game to load up for a few runs.
Very excited to see what new updates have in store!

My biggest concern with getting this game was it looked like a simple puzzle phone app (which I like, but just for a few minutes on the phone) with an unnecessary 3d perspective to basically choose different levels (which would be tedious). At first that's what the game feels like. However, before that wears out it's welcome, you start to see a point to the 3d perspective. It becomes not just a way to get from puzzle to puzzle, but the puzzles become integrated in the 3d perspective experience.
I wasn't looking to get a deep meaning from a puzzle game, but it seems some reviewers are. There is meaning to the game, but it's light. As I think it should be. The meaning is abstract, about about the perspective experience, which is what the puzzles are about also, so it's well integrated. The absract nature means even the meaning could be considered open to interpretation, and what is interpretation if not perspective. But so far into my gameplay, that's it. I don't expect it to get any deeper than that. And I don't feel the game is trying to be super deep, but it's deep enough. If you go in thinking this is a deep meaningful experience, yeah, you'd be dissapointed. If you go in thinking the delevopers are trying to hard to be artistic, yeah, you could be dissapointed again. But if you go in thinking the game has some meaning sprinkled about in a way that compliments the play experience in a moderate way, then you'll be pleasantly satisfied. And I think that's all the developers are trying to do. Sometimes (in any medium, not just games) if you take in an artistic experience (like viewing a painting), you will be dissapointed with the same outlooks that could make you dissapointed in this. And satisfied with the same outlook that would make you satisfied with this. So it's up to your perspective if you think the games trying to hard. I'm fortunate enough to think it's trying just hard enough.
Finally (this could be percieved as a slight spoiler as it is a general clue for when you get stuck, so feel free to stop reading), the game does a good job at teaching you how to solve the puzzles without throwing it in your face. You still have to look for it. There are rows of puzzles that start simple and introduce a new concept. If you get stuck on something you've never seen before, take that as a clue that you are jumping ahead. Come back to it once you've found the learning row(s) for that type of puzzle. You do get to a point pretty quickly where you are expected to know a lot of the puzzle types. So just contine exploring, you'll figure it out. I enjoy that part of the puzzle is knowing when to stop and do a puzzle, and when to move along and come back later. I enjoy that the "tutorial" are scattered through the game, and somewhat of a minor puzzle to figure out the best way to let the game teach you. The teaching is very subtle, but guided in a good way where they respect your intelligence. This is a risky way to do things, but I think it works here.

If you DO already have a Cities XL game - skip to the second section below - or tl;dr - it's a rip-off patch for a game you already own.
So, if you don't already own a Cities XL game, then this game offers a lot of fun and creativity, and is arguably THE best city-creator on the PC scene at the time of writing.  Unless a new offering improves on the genre, then this is the title you want, even though it's not perfect.
o You can zone areas and let the game choose properties
o You can select property designs and styles yourself instead of zoning (with the community made mod in Workshop)
o The maps are huge and varied
o Granular choice of industry (you choose types of industry, farming and commerce)
o There is a rudimentary trading system
o A blueprint system as now used by Simcity 2013 for advanced developments
o Very mod-friendly with thousands of compatible mods for the Cities XL franchise
o Full cheat system so you can choose the constraints with which to play
o No dynamic population (unlike Simcity - no births, deaths, people who move in or out at will)
o No fires, crime or disasters
o Little choice of mass transit (nothing has been implemented properly since XL days)
o A buggy interface
If you had performance issues with prior Cities XL titles, then this upgrade might be for you.  Otherwise, there is very little new on offer for Platinum owners and XL owners are justifiably angry about being charged for what amounts to be a performance patch (hence the swamp of negative reviews).  Even with my 'nice' hat on, I think FHI should only have charged a minor-DLC amount, not advertised it as an all-new game.
So what do you get?  There is a new 'sky' feature where you can select a pre-designed sky effect.  This is static (doesn't bring any weather effects) but does add a prettier ambience to your cities.  Right now there are around 6 to choose from (not many) but new versions have started to appear in the Steam Workshop.
All the primary buildings are exactly the same as before.  There are something like 8 new buildings added by this new version ('green' buildings for the climate-friendly builders) and a small number of additional maps, but no other content.  The advertised multiple international and period architectural styles are purely a category list which sorts the existing buildings (nothing extra).
Lighting appears to be a little improved, but old bugs remain (tree bugs, box vehicles etc).  The good news is that the mods that fixed these problems in the other games work here too - but that's not really surprising because the game is essentially the same as before.  The majority of custom content  mods from XLNations and other sites are compatible but I recommend you try a tiny few at a time because quite a few won't work at all.
In short, unless you experienced terrible performance in Platinum/XL, this is a greatly overpriced, superfluous 'upgrade' that you probably don't need.  Wait until it's around £5 or so then buy it for the prettier sky - but that's all.

Pros:
- Aesthetically pleasing.
- You must foresee problems, else it is probably too late.
- Gratifying to grow your colony and use new technologies.
- Entertaining for the 10 hours I played.
- There is a variety of challenges for the colony to overcome, including weather, power, water, food, sleep, and more.
- You have to experiment to understand what you need and how much of it. For example, should you build more solar panels, wind turbines, or power collectors?
- No micromanagement. The colonists satisfy their own needs and put themselves to work. You can indicate certain tasks as priority however, and you also choose what professions new colonists need to have.
- Simple and mostly intuitive controls, though the menus are somewhat confusing to navigate and difficult to find despite being few of them.
Cons:
- The game is more difficult when your colony is small, and becomes easy when your colony is large.
- You will have already used all the buildings and technologies long before you achieve some goals such as population 300 (which is a tiresome goal to achieve).
- There is a maximum building count which prevents you from spanning the entire map.
- Intruders do not make sense. They come to your colony and their only objective is to shoot innocent people until they themselves get shot.
- Trading can severely harm your colony or even destroy it. This is because one colonist carries one good to the ship (carrier bots help if you have them), and during that time they are not fulfilling their duties or personal needs. If you are trading away several dozen goods then this occupies many colonists for a long time. To me this is a con because trading is an integral part of the game and it has a nonsensical consequence – why wouldn't colonists task themselves appropriately?.
- In a large colony for some reason the AI stopped refilling food and drink machines despite hundreds of food being available. This resulted in everyone dying of starvation. After a recent patch I reloaded the game and this did not recur, so perhaps it is fixed.
- Personally I find no reason to play again after reaching population 300, though there are achievement-like challenges.
Conclusion:
I recommend this game if a 5 to 10 hour experience suits you. The game offers challenge as you learn the ropes and progress towards a large colony.

This game is commonly compared to Shadow Of the Collousus, for being a game composed entirelly of bosses, but really the similarites end there. This game is a genre bending action game, with elements of bullet hell, and fighting games, and its damn fun, even if the dodge button can be a little wonky.

The summary:
This game is very fun, though the difficulty can be frustrating at times and it is not particularlary long. Nonetheless, I would absolutely recommend getting this game if a reasonably challenging bossfighter/occasional bullet hell game sounds like the sort of game you would enjoy.
The real review:
Furi, in case it wasn't already obvious, is a game about fighting bosses. 10 of them, to be exact, plus two more in the misleadingly-named One More Fight DLC (which is also worth buying if you enjoy the main game). These fights usually follow a broadly similar pattern: first you run around, dodging or parrying the boss's attacks and hitting them when you get the chance. Then, when the boss goes down you move into a melee fight in which your movement is restricted to a small circle and again you have to avoid a series of attacks before getting an opening to attack. Defeat this and the boss loses a life, gets back up, and moves into the next phase, of which there are 3-6. Fail, and you lose one of your three lives, which regenerate at a rate of one per defeated phase.
The combat here controls fairly smoothly and almost always feels fair - the challenge comes in knowing the pattern of the bosses' attacks and mastering the timing to avoid or parry them. You have a faily limited repertoire of skills with which you fight: to avoid attacks you can run, parry, or use a short ranged teleport, while you fight back with a sword and gun. This limited set of options is kept exciting, however, by the wide variety of boss movesets and I certainly never felt the game got repetitive. Between fights, there are slightly drawn-out walking sequences in which the game's story is told.
As for the length of the game, it is probably fairly variable, but it took me around 6 hours to beat the main game + DLC on the normal difficulty, and closer to 8 to do it again on hard mode (which is well worth playing through since it changes up many of the bosses' attacks and tends to make everything much more challenging and bullet hellish). After that, there is little left to do but replay fights in order to get a better ranking, which may be fun for some people but is not for me. For the price, this is a decent amount of content, but not spectacular.
Overall, though, this is a game that is well worth buying, and any frustration is easily cancelled out by the satisfaction of mastering the bosses' patterns and defeating them, especially when they make it difficult for you to do so.
Oh, and the soundtrack. The soundtrack is great too, and suits the game well. Honestly, if you have made it this far into my review then concept of the game clearly doesn't bore you, so you should probably just buy it - it's really good.

I wrote an Evaluation Essay for this game for my Enlgish Class, and decided why not post it here? I had to cut out the Indroduction and the Story sections due to the character limit. But I pretty much said that the story is great for a short action game.
Visuals and Presentation
The visuals of this game were one of the first draws for me. The world is rendered with a well-executed cel-shaded art style. The colors of this game jump out at you and are accented by the lighting effects that come from machines and projectiles. The character designs were created by the man behind Afro Samurai’s characters. The art direction is inspired by Eastern culture, featuring Samurai-like armors and Japanese flora. Each Jailer gets their own stage to match their character, which allows for a wide variety of unique set pieces. During battles, it is always clear what is happening thanks to the high fidelity and impressive camera that always has the right zoom and angle to keep track of any danger. In the final phases of each boss, the screen is usually saturated in projectiles and waves attacks, yet you never lose sight of your character or get blind-sided by an unseen attack. The large amount of these special FX can sometimes cause stuttering for consoles and low-end PCs, so there is a video option for either “High Quality” or “High Performance”. If you can’t tolerate the framerate drops, you won’t be sacrificing much by choosing “High Performance”, as the game still looks very pretty. This game has no pre-rendered cutscenes, they are all live-rendered, which is evident by the physics that can often be wonky with the protagonist’s hair. This, combined with the fact that the transition is just you walking down a “hallway” while the mystery man stands in a static pose to talk to you, makes it clear that this was a budget choice. Though, extra work was put in to make all of these “hallways” gorgeous and interact with your character as you walk through them. Each jailer has a large amount of animations for each phase of their battles, and they are all very smooth.
Music and Sound
Furi’s soundtrack is a collaboration of many talented electro musicians. Each jailer has their own lead-up and theme that perfectly captures their personality in audio form. The music captures the essence of each intense, blood-pumping battle. Even more impressively, each phase of the boss fights has a different phase for the songs too. I downloaded the whole soundtrack before even finishing this evaluation! The sound design is not bad, but not amazing. Most enemy attacks have a clear sound cue to help you know what’s coming next, which is good for this kind of game, but some sounds are very limp and quiet. The voice acting, on the other hand, is very impressive for a game of this size. The mystery man has a smooth yet slightly malicious timbre, making you want to hear what he has to say while having you wonder is you can trust him. Each jailer becomes fully realized as a character thanks to the on-point performances of all of their voice actors. The sound mixing in this game is masterfully handled. All sounds and music in this game are loud, yet not of them overpower the each other. Even the voices are heard crisp and clear when either the jailer or mystery man speaks, even during the most intense moments.
The Gameplay
Great visuals and audio are nice, but the ultimate deciding factor to get this game is how the gameplay stacks up. Furi is a boss-rush style game, you must defeat the 10 jailers to set yourself free. Furi was structured this way to put all emphasis on intense one-on-one battles against a powerful foe. You and the jailer’s health bar and lives are displayed on the screen, and each life of the jailer is a different phase of attack patterns. There are two parts to most phases: A projectile-heavy shooting and attacking part, and a close-combat swordplay part. During the projectile part, the game has both sword and twin-stick shooter controls. Close-combat is just as it sounds, you must dodge and parry the jailer’s attacks until you see an opportunity to attack with your sword. During the final phase of the fights, the jailer throws on onslaught of projectiles that you must dodge and counter to a level reminiscent of bullet-hell style games. When you lose a life, the phase you’re on restarts, if you lose them all, the entire battle restarts. Furi has a heavy reliance on fast reflexes and pattern memorization, so simply having two means of defense, a dodge and parry, helps you focus on just reactions. There is always a sound and visual cue for attacks you can parry, and most projectiles can be deflected back at to the jailer. The action in the game never stops and it is a great amount of fun. Even if you lose, you’ll naturally get through each phase faster and faster as you learn the jailer’s attack patterns and dominate them. It can be very satisfying to time a perfect parry or dodge and attack successfully with a very small window of reaction, so in what regards does this game struggle to impress?
The Issues
In a game that requires such split-second reactions, it is almost required that you use a wired controller, to reduce input latency. The game also doesn’t teach you everything you can do in the tutorial fight, you have to go through menus to find all the things your character is able to do. There are some boss fights where the patterns can be completely random, turning what should be progression of skill into a coin flip of when to react. There are even times where the positioning of your character, relative to the size and angle of the enemy attack, are 100% unavoidable, leaving you feeling cheated. There’s even a fight where the jailer can one-shot kill you if you don’t hide behind a wall in time, but sometimes it would go off without warning or chance to avoid it. In a game where any mistake can cause you to restart a 10-minute fight, you can see how this could lead to controller-smashing levels of frustration. The largest flaw I encountered though, was the execution of your dodge. It happens upon release, rather than press of the button. This can render any split-second reaction useless because of the bit of extra time it takes for your finger to come off of the button to dodge. My other issue is that the dodge feels a bit too strict to be consistent and satisfying. There are times where you’re dodge is either slightly too short or slightly over-shot, and it makes me wonder if this game had enough focus testing to fine-tune the dodge to be consistent. For me, many deaths came from a dodge that wasn’t perfect enough for the game’s standards, and upon watching people who have S-ranked the game, they only took hits from bad dodges.
The Verdict
Furi is an engaging experience in all regards. It challenges you from the very first fight to the final blow of the last boss. If anything, the music and visuals with defiantly leave a lasting impression on anyone who plays this game. Despite the hurtles that made this game harder than it should be, I still managed to complete this game at its base difficulty, which is considered a great achievement on its own. You can tell a lot of love went into making this game with how much work is put into small things like transitions and even the features given to you to master the game. When you beat the game, a harder difficulty called “Furier” is unlocked, and rather than you taking more damage or giving the boss more health, the attacks and patterns are completely remixed to be more challenging and some jailers are even given NEW attack animations for a fresh challenge. At a base price of $25, the amount of production put into this game for the size of its development team is more than worth the money. While I can’t promise there won’t be times of unjust frustration in this game, I can say that it is an experience you won’t regret diving into.

First impression of a bit of the first level - review to be taken with a grain of salt.
I'm not saying no to this because 'oh it's too hard!' I'm saying no to tihs game because the controls on the first level are lacking. The 3 hit system? Totally fine with it. What I'm not fine with is my character being swarmed by unlimited spawning enemies. That isn't good game design, so I don't get where the praise is coming from. On top of this, you cannot nudge your character when they double jump. There is a section with spikes where you have to push it just right, or have a previous thing to absorb the spike damage. I got it right once, but honestly not liking how the controls feel.
Good call back to the old platformer days, but fails to meet modern standards in terms of combat. Might be up the alleyway of those who enjoyed it though. I just feel the game is making it unecessarily janky on purpose.

Some people complain about the fixed jumping.  Don't listen to them.  The implementation of the "Double Jump" makes the mechanic very flexible and versatile.  You can initiate a double jump at any point in the arc, and in any direction, giving the player ample control.  It all feels very natural and intuitive.
Although some weak enemies respawn at a few set locations in each level, the majority of the enemies are completely predictable, appearing in the same locations and behaving the same way every time.  This makes the game feel more like a puzzle-platformer to me.  "Solving" levels requires figuring out what sequence of jumps, spears, and sword attacks to use, and remembering the enemy placement and patterns.  Some reflexes and good timing are required, but learning the levels is the most important thing.
If you get stuck, keep persevering and experimenting with different approaches.  Eventually you'll discover a viable strategy!  I recommend NOT watching a walkthrough or guide before solving the levels for yourself, since that's where most of the satisfaction comes from.  After you've beaten a level, then you can watch other people's solutions to help streamline your play.

There's a much bigger world out there outside of the bar you work in, and just being able to influence the outside world through your drinks is a lovely achievement in itself. I just want to say....Valhalla is amazing, and I'm hungrily devouring what it's offering me, taking the time to throughly savour it before moving on.
Depending on how it ends, it could very well end up in my top 10, and that's no simple feat. Top 5 if it tops my expectations.

Newcomers may find this game more enjoyable than Magic veterans, and the new feature of adding a sealed deck is both one of the best and worst things this game has to offer.
As a long time player of MTG, this game is about 85% accurate on it's interpretations of the rules and game play. It has improved on previous versions, but it is particularly annoying to know that a card works one way and DotP seems unaware of this fact.
New players won't notice this, and the 2014 version certain makes the UI a little more responsive, making it less likely for you to miss an opportune trigger.
Deck building is a generous description of what really happens. each deck is, in essense a 90 card deck, and you unlock a good number of those cards throughout the playing of the game - or you can pay to unlock them. The final deck is no powerhouse, but when compared to the relatively terrible decks you are started with, it's a rewarding experience to take those powered up decks against previous opponents against whom you may have struggled and crush them mercilessly.
The sealed deck element is both brilliant and remarkably dumb at the same time. You can do sealed 2 times before you must buy more slots. This little money grab makes the experience highly frustrating. You can not delete the boring, or bad, pool of cards you once had. It was the most fun I had in the game, and the one reason I never went back after finishing them. If I wanted to pay money to draft, I would actually go draft online or in person and walk away with cards I can use for other things.
Nothing is overly challenging in this game, and with any level of decent magic skill, you will outplay your opponents easily. they are predictable, easily trapped and setting up blowouts can make even the unfair matches seem relatively easy.
Overall, however, the casual magic player will enjoy this game, and deal with the limitations and weaknesses. All in all, it was a positive experience and I recommend it.

I like how it presents all this bare-numbers nerdy♥♥♥♥♥♥with a bare-bones doofy fantasy story. I like the online play, which I'm sure is going to be devouring most of my life very shortly. But: I dug Magic before that. I played it as a kid, and I'm pretty sure I like this particular, online, Steam game because of the lingering, salty taste of preteen tears.
Magic, like Dungeons and Dragons, is such a niche hobby, and now such an old niche hobby, that it either appeals to you or it doesn't. If you brushed past a hobby shop, saw full, adult grown-ups arguing over why that one cardstock spell shouldn't have killed that one cardstock goblin, then this isn't going to be your thing. But if you already suspect that it might be your thing, or it was once but then you grew up and sold your cards and paid rent with the net, then, well, this is Magic.
Don't worry. I'll be around to tap all your swamps with my fat blue deck. We're in this together. We were always doomed.

Danganronpa is a great visual novel about hope and despair. The game is pretty much SAW plus Ace Attorney but with high school students. Great idea? I know right. Did I mention there is a crap ton of neon pink blood from the 80's? Anyhow, this game is a rollercoaster of a story in my opinion. Loved every bit of it and how to tries to look innocent but is also incrediably dark. After all, kids murdering other kids isn't done alot in fiction anymore.
Danganronpa's art style is made to look like that of a pop-up book most of the time which constrasts greatly to the dark contents of this read. Many scenes show the characters as cutouts and each scene comes to life with what looks to be cardboard props. Plus all the characters have parts of their body such as hairs or clothing which have small patterns in them to look like those cut out from fabric. Its cute, calming, and feels you with hope in the dire situation.
The story is best gone into blind as with many mystery games. After all, it ruins the suprise twists the game might throw at you. After all, figuring out who it is in Ace Attorney or L.A. Noire by being spoiled isn't nearly as fun as solving the case by logic. I will say this though, many interesting and quirky characters. You have biker dude, karate chick, swimmer girl, rich ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the dorky shut-in who writes romance stories, adorable programmer, and more. These may sound like cliched but each character has a deeper story to devel into and aren't as stereotyped as one might think. Okay maybe a few.
Next is the gameplay which is mainly point and click. Nothing much to say other then a neat feature that allows you to see all the possible items that can be clicked which helps in cluttered and crowded crime scenes. That's about it.
The soundtrack. Oh my ♥♥♥♥ing god it causes ear-gasms and I love each track. Some of the the best music this side of Mystery Games.
While this sums up why I love the game, there is one big problem. Porting issues. The PC version is an port from the PS VITA version which had to be ported from Japan. The game was ported like 2 times. From what I've heard, there are many issues such as graphical issues and even some game-breaking bugs such as saves being deleted.. Luckily, I've only encountered some issues pretaining to frame-rate and odd graphical issues. They should be patched soon as not even VITA had this many issues.
Overall, Danganronpa is a cute and sinister game about murder mystery involving young high schoolers. The soundtrack is absolutely perfect. Story is fun and entertaining. Characters are pretty good.
