My biggest concern with getting this game was it looked like a simple puzzle phone app (which I like, but just for a few minutes on the phone) with an unnecessary 3d perspective to basically choose different levels (which would be tedious). At first that's what the game feels like. However, before that wears out it's welcome, you start to see a point to the 3d perspective. It becomes not just a way to get from puzzle to puzzle, but the puzzles become integrated in the 3d perspective experience.
I wasn't looking to get a deep meaning from a puzzle game, but it seems some reviewers are. There is meaning to the game, but it's light. As I think it should be. The meaning is abstract, about about the perspective experience, which is what the puzzles are about also, so it's well integrated. The absract nature means even the meaning could be considered open to interpretation, and what is interpretation if not perspective. But so far into my gameplay, that's it. I don't expect it to get any deeper than that. And I don't feel the game is trying to be super deep, but it's deep enough. If you go in thinking this is a deep meaningful experience, yeah, you'd be dissapointed. If you go in thinking the delevopers are trying to hard to be artistic, yeah, you could be dissapointed again. But if you go in thinking the game has some meaning sprinkled about in a way that compliments the play experience in a moderate way, then you'll be pleasantly satisfied. And I think that's all the developers are trying to do. Sometimes (in any medium, not just games) if you take in an artistic experience (like viewing a painting), you will be dissapointed with the same outlooks that could make you dissapointed in this. And satisfied with the same outlook that would make you satisfied with this. So it's up to your perspective if you think the games trying to hard. I'm fortunate enough to think it's trying just hard enough.
Finally (this could be percieved as a slight spoiler as it is a general clue for when you get stuck, so feel free to stop reading), the game does a good job at teaching you how to solve the puzzles without throwing it in your face. You still have to look for it. There are rows of puzzles that start simple and introduce a new concept. If you get stuck on something you've never seen before, take that as a clue that you are jumping ahead. Come back to it once you've found the learning row(s) for that type of puzzle. You do get to a point pretty quickly where you are expected to know a lot of the puzzle types. So just contine exploring, you'll figure it out. I enjoy that part of the puzzle is knowing when to stop and do a puzzle, and when to move along and come back later. I enjoy that the "tutorial" are scattered through the game, and somewhat of a minor puzzle to figure out the best way to let the game teach you. The teaching is very subtle, but guided in a good way where they respect your intelligence. This is a risky way to do things, but I think it works here.
I can't say if I'll be able to solve the game entirely on my own, but it's a good experience so far. I took a risk because the developer has a good reputation. Even if I stopped playing now, I'd say the experience has been worth it.

I enjoy challenging games, especially when they look as pretty as Volgarr. The only problem I have with challenging games in this instance is the very nature of the challenge: trial and error. This is by no means old school platforming, merely a modern take on platforming where fun is replaced with frustration and called a challenge. For an old school game, I have played it about as much as I need to in order to assess what I love and and hate about it.
I love the graphics and the sound, which are top notch, old school throwbacks. The graphics are detailed and thoroughly eye-opening, especially when you're swinging around the fire sword. The sounds that compliment it are simple, catchy tunes with very little in the way of complexity, again allowing you into the world of Volgarr easily and without much trying.
What I hate about this game is the absurd view the developers have of what makes a game challenging. Forcing a player back to the beginning of the level, then making them get back to where they died, travel an extra few feet and die to something else they couldn't possibly anticipate, is frankly insulting. I lost my cool with the first level because the enemies that spawned did so differently from death to death, making my learning of the level impossible. When I finally did get through a difficult wave of enemies and pratfalls, I was faced with an arrow trap that just shot me in the face without me even having time to move out of the way. I dislike games that do away with fun and Volgarr certainly did for me.
For those of you who have the tolerance to sit through death after death, this is a game for you (especially for dark souls players), but if you enjoy a really good platformer, buy some of the mega drive classics and fusion games like risk of rain to get the best out of your money. Volgarr would have been superb if it was anything like the classics it was trying so hard to emulate. Ghouls and ghosts for the new generation? Absolutely no doubt...

Old school arcade style hardcore game with good and fair game design.
This game gets a lot of hate because it doesn't follow modern game design. But what most people don't realize is that most of their complains are part of the design. Which means it won't appeal to a lot of people.
Volgarr has some game design decisions that I feel is unappreciated. This video
explains a good example of their design, specifically, how to introduce enemies which the player sees for the first time.
Here are some common complaints about the game:
*Checkpoints*: Yes, the checkpoints are real far apart. But the designers are trying to push for an arcade experience where you get better the more you play the game. If you have less frequent checkpoints, the levels will more memorable since you'll be playing it more. Also, the design of the power-up system means that the checkpoint cannot be near the boss. Here is the dev's statement on check points:
.
*Jump arc*: People say the jumping is stiff. But the entire game is built around that. Think of the original Castlevania games. The character has an uncontrollable jump arc but you can still reach the platforms. The same can be said about Volgarr. If you see a pit, you can simply jump over it. No need to double jump.
*It feels that you have to play perfectly*: Not true at all. When I started playing, I felt this way but as I progress, I noticed small tricks that I can use. For example, the shield can be used to block a lot of attacks including those intimidating ones used by tougher enemies]. Once I figured that out, I was able to progress through the stages way faster by just using that item since most enemies have a delay after attacking. The game didn't teach me that but it was something that I noticed later. And when I decided to experiment, I felt the game rewarded me for my lateral thinking.
This game rewards patience and methodological play. Which is why most gamers don't this game a second chance. It takes many playthroughs to see the brilliance of the game. The people who stick with it to the end will have the most rewarding feeling of accomplishment. They will feel that they've earned it.
Sadly, this game isn't for everyone. If you're the kind of person who gets frustrated at repeating a level over and over again until completion, this isn't for you. The game's core design is that this is an arcade game meant to be played over and over again so you'll gain the skill needed to complete the game.
Tl;dr: give the game a chance. You'll get frustrated, but that's part of the design. Because nothing beats the feeling of you overcoming the game's obstacle is throwing at you.

First, it only allows for two of the most unreliable energy sources ever conceived (wind and solar). The summary:
This game is very fun, though the difficulty can be frustrating at times and it is not particularlary long. Nonetheless, I would absolutely recommend getting this game if a reasonably challenging bossfighter/occasional bullet hell game sounds like the sort of game you would enjoy.
The real review:
Furi, in case it wasn't already obvious, is a game about fighting bosses. 10 of them, to be exact, plus two more in the misleadingly-named One More Fight DLC (which is also worth buying if you enjoy the main game). These fights usually follow a broadly similar pattern: first you run around, dodging or parrying the boss's attacks and hitting them when you get the chance. Then, when the boss goes down you move into a melee fight in which your movement is restricted to a small circle and again you have to avoid a series of attacks before getting an opening to attack. Defeat this and the boss loses a life, gets back up, and moves into the next phase, of which there are 3-6. Fail, and you lose one of your three lives, which regenerate at a rate of one per defeated phase.
The combat here controls fairly smoothly and almost always feels fair - the challenge comes in knowing the pattern of the bosses' attacks and mastering the timing to avoid or parry them. You have a faily limited repertoire of skills with which you fight: to avoid attacks you can run, parry, or use a short ranged teleport, while you fight back with a sword and gun. This limited set of options is kept exciting, however, by the wide variety of boss movesets and I certainly never felt the game got repetitive. Between fights, there are slightly drawn-out walking sequences in which the game's story is told.
As for the length of the game, it is probably fairly variable, but it took me around 6 hours to beat the main game + DLC on the normal difficulty, and closer to 8 to do it again on hard mode (which is well worth playing through since it changes up many of the bosses' attacks and tends to make everything much more challenging and bullet hellish). After that, there is little left to do but replay fights in order to get a better ranking, which may be fun for some people but is not for me. For the price, this is a decent amount of content, but not spectacular.
Overall, though, this is a game that is well worth buying, and any frustration is easily cancelled out by the satisfaction of mastering the bosses' patterns and defeating them, especially when they make it difficult for you to do so.
Oh, and the soundtrack. The soundtrack is great too, and suits the game well. Honestly, if you have made it this far into my review then concept of the game clearly doesn't bore you, so you should probably just buy it - it's really good.

I wrote an Evaluation Essay for this game for my Enlgish Class, and decided why not post it here? I had to cut out the Indroduction and the Story sections due to the character limit. But I pretty much said that the story is great for a short action game.
Visuals and Presentation
The visuals of this game were one of the first draws for me. The world is rendered with a well-executed cel-shaded art style. The colors of this game jump out at you and are accented by the lighting effects that come from machines and projectiles. The character designs were created by the man behind Afro Samurai’s characters. The art direction is inspired by Eastern culture, featuring Samurai-like armors and Japanese flora. Each Jailer gets their own stage to match their character, which allows for a wide variety of unique set pieces. During battles, it is always clear what is happening thanks to the high fidelity and impressive camera that always has the right zoom and angle to keep track of any danger. In the final phases of each boss, the screen is usually saturated in projectiles and waves attacks, yet you never lose sight of your character or get blind-sided by an unseen attack. The large amount of these special FX can sometimes cause stuttering for consoles and low-end PCs, so there is a video option for either “High Quality” or “High Performance”. If you can’t tolerate the framerate drops, you won’t be sacrificing much by choosing “High Performance”, as the game still looks very pretty. This game has no pre-rendered cutscenes, they are all live-rendered, which is evident by the physics that can often be wonky with the protagonist’s hair. This, combined with the fact that the transition is just you walking down a “hallway” while the mystery man stands in a static pose to talk to you, makes it clear that this was a budget choice. Though, extra work was put in to make all of these “hallways” gorgeous and interact with your character as you walk through them. Each jailer has a large amount of animations for each phase of their battles, and they are all very smooth.
Music and Sound
Furi’s soundtrack is a collaboration of many talented electro musicians. Each jailer has their own lead-up and theme that perfectly captures their personality in audio form. The music captures the essence of each intense, blood-pumping battle. Even more impressively, each phase of the boss fights has a different phase for the songs too. I downloaded the whole soundtrack before even finishing this evaluation! The sound design is not bad, but not amazing. Most enemy attacks have a clear sound cue to help you know what’s coming next, which is good for this kind of game, but some sounds are very limp and quiet. The voice acting, on the other hand, is very impressive for a game of this size. The mystery man has a smooth yet slightly malicious timbre, making you want to hear what he has to say while having you wonder is you can trust him. Each jailer becomes fully realized as a character thanks to the on-point performances of all of their voice actors. The sound mixing in this game is masterfully handled. All sounds and music in this game are loud, yet not of them overpower the each other. Even the voices are heard crisp and clear when either the jailer or mystery man speaks, even during the most intense moments.
The Gameplay
Great visuals and audio are nice, but the ultimate deciding factor to get this game is how the gameplay stacks up. Furi is a boss-rush style game, you must defeat the 10 jailers to set yourself free. Furi was structured this way to put all emphasis on intense one-on-one battles against a powerful foe. You and the jailer’s health bar and lives are displayed on the screen, and each life of the jailer is a different phase of attack patterns. There are two parts to most phases: A projectile-heavy shooting and attacking part, and a close-combat swordplay part. During the projectile part, the game has both sword and twin-stick shooter controls. Close-combat is just as it sounds, you must dodge and parry the jailer’s attacks until you see an opportunity to attack with your sword. During the final phase of the fights, the jailer throws on onslaught of projectiles that you must dodge and counter to a level reminiscent of bullet-hell style games. When you lose a life, the phase you’re on restarts, if you lose them all, the entire battle restarts. Furi has a heavy reliance on fast reflexes and pattern memorization, so simply having two means of defense, a dodge and parry, helps you focus on just reactions. There is always a sound and visual cue for attacks you can parry, and most projectiles can be deflected back at to the jailer. The action in the game never stops and it is a great amount of fun. Even if you lose, you’ll naturally get through each phase faster and faster as you learn the jailer’s attack patterns and dominate them. It can be very satisfying to time a perfect parry or dodge and attack successfully with a very small window of reaction, so in what regards does this game struggle to impress?
The Issues
In a game that requires such split-second reactions, it is almost required that you use a wired controller, to reduce input latency. The game also doesn’t teach you everything you can do in the tutorial fight, you have to go through menus to find all the things your character is able to do. There are some boss fights where the patterns can be completely random, turning what should be progression of skill into a coin flip of when to react. There are even times where the positioning of your character, relative to the size and angle of the enemy attack, are 100% unavoidable, leaving you feeling cheated. There’s even a fight where the jailer can one-shot kill you if you don’t hide behind a wall in time, but sometimes it would go off without warning or chance to avoid it. In a game where any mistake can cause you to restart a 10-minute fight, you can see how this could lead to controller-smashing levels of frustration. The largest flaw I encountered though, was the execution of your dodge. It happens upon release, rather than press of the button. This can render any split-second reaction useless because of the bit of extra time it takes for your finger to come off of the button to dodge. My other issue is that the dodge feels a bit too strict to be consistent and satisfying. There are times where you’re dodge is either slightly too short or slightly over-shot, and it makes me wonder if this game had enough focus testing to fine-tune the dodge to be consistent. For me, many deaths came from a dodge that wasn’t perfect enough for the game’s standards, and upon watching people who have S-ranked the game, they only took hits from bad dodges.
The Verdict
Furi is an engaging experience in all regards. It challenges you from the very first fight to the final blow of the last boss. If anything, the music and visuals with defiantly leave a lasting impression on anyone who plays this game. Despite the hurtles that made this game harder than it should be, I still managed to complete this game at its base difficulty, which is considered a great achievement on its own. You can tell a lot of love went into making this game with how much work is put into small things like transitions and even the features given to you to master the game. When you beat the game, a harder difficulty called “Furier” is unlocked, and rather than you taking more damage or giving the boss more health, the attacks and patterns are completely remixed to be more challenging and some jailers are even given NEW attack animations for a fresh challenge. At a base price of $25, the amount of production put into this game for the size of its development team is more than worth the money. While I can’t promise there won’t be times of unjust frustration in this game, I can say that it is an experience you won’t regret diving into.

Half an hour was perfectly enough of this garbage! I cannot emphasize the importance of quality management so that games such as this will not live to see another day! But first things first.
Atomy's "story" is about a guy who is suddenly gunned down in a pub. Miraculously he survives - if having a skeleton body can be called survival, that is. The bartender then proposes that he wash away all his sins. We are then on to a destructive path which means elminating everybody in our sight (and for some reason this all occurs in the Wild West).
If you check the trailer video on Steam you see how the display is divided up into two parts - it appears that the game's top-down view is mandatory and only by holding the right mouse button can we switch to the FPS perspective. This is pretty annoying - not only do you have to keep it pressed constantly but the right click is not available for the zoom function.
Thank God we have the spacebar for that! Reload, by the way, is non-existant so pressing R shows how many bullets we have in our belt. This adds another section to the screen - it is pretty dumb looking at a picture divided up into 3 different parts (adding a bullet counter - so-called HUD - would have sufficed, dear developer!).
Then of course we have the issue of the English translation. I really do not understand how come you cannot have a close friend speaking the language fluently. Do you really, blindly, believe in a translation provided by Google Translator or another site? Just how much time does it take to ask a friend to do a proofreading?
While under the trailer we hear music the game has no such thing. Only our shots emit a noise but that's it. Also, the game is locked to 30 FPS and switching to FPS view can often decrease it to 20. All this thanks to a probably custom-made Unity package. Then we have other things to mention: missing settings menu, inability to quit (hitting escape does not do anything), enemies killing you by one-hit shots (I did remember picking up armor and something called "second chance" to no avail).
This game is a disaster. I think Atomy meant to have been Anatomy but a typo was made. And to think this game received awards and that there are features such as "procedurally generated world" (Really? Every item / building / enemy is at the same place after a restart) is a shame.

Candice DeBébé's Incredibly Trick Lifestyle is a video game. Yes, it looks atrocious. Yes, it sometimes sounds atrocious. Yes, the characters and writing aren't entirely great either. And yet, this game oozes charm from every fake tanned pore.
I mean honestly this to me is a peak bit of bedroom indie games. This isn't some shovelware title like you'd expect; there's actual effort put into this game. Every line is fully voice acted, the game is fully soundtracked with original tunes complete with vocals, at least half of the models were created by the dev themselves. Honestly, if you can look past the corny and occasionally badly written dialogue, this game is a fantastic little romp and well worth playing. It's a wonderful little reminder to stop taking things so seriously and to have a laugh every now and then.
That's not to say there isn't negatives to this game, though. As previously mentioned, the graphics aren't the prettiest thing this side of indie games but that's to be expected, and it adds a lot to the experience. But for actual problems this game has? Well, I'd say its biggest offense is not having a run button. It wouldn't be as much of a problem if the levels weren't so long and maze-like and the game didn't gleefully push backtracking on you partly as a joke. The meta/4th wall breaking humour in this game definitely damages it a bit and it's rather bluntly written which doesn't entirely work too well imo, but is passable at best. The camera controls are a bit awkward, the menu is only accessible through pressing enter (?!) and the cursor doesnt get locked into the game itself either. But again - all of this stuff adds to the overall charm of the game. It's adorably terrible in its own special way, and 100% worth your time.

While this game features a form of gameplay, and I’m very glad that it does; the mixing of drinks can be a bit repetitive at times. No wonder some people say that you should play it in sessions and take breaks, just like the protagonist. The problem is the fixed number of recipes at your disposal and the way the system works, you have the initial 24 drinks but that’s it really, no new ones will be introduced during your playthrough which is a missed opportunity. A double-click option would’ve been nice to add the ingredients directly instead of dragging every single one of them. Checkpoints are often very far apart from each other which can result in frustration since you have to possibly play huge chunks of the game again, if you fu-ck up or want to do something differently.

I’m truly glad to have the bartending as a way of interacting with the characters in the game, without this feature, the game wouldn’t be half as engaging as it is right now. Mixing drinks together is fun and thankfully doesn’t require a crazy tutorial or anything like that. Simply mix together the ingredients based on the recipes and you're done with the exceptions of big drinks and a few others. Manage Jill’s home between days to spent your hard-earned cash for silly stuff or save up to pay the rent. You even get tiny bits of lore in her smartphone and the ability to save/load, which can also be done during work-breaks.

What I think is the most important part is the need to satisfy the customers taste through mixing alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks together from scratch. You are often asked to guess the right drink for the right customer, luckily the game has a built-in list of 24 available recipes to help you with that. Some clients require you to be quick, remember their favourite drinks or even guess the right one that could trigger new events and story bits. This is the main way to influence the game's progression and the ending that you will get, so be sure to try something different then the game is telling you. Just pay attention to your customer and what they order, it might not always be what they really want or need! A character is depressed and orders something sweet? Add some alcohol to let him forget about their troubles thanks to optional recipes where you can add as much of it as you want.

VA-11 Hall-A’s story revolves around the everyday life of bartender Jill and her customers as well as her boss and co-worker Gillian and many others. A diverse cast of characters who are relatable, believable and interesting in one way or another and have their own problems and worries in life that you can be a part of. Even though you don't have any choices during the conversations itself, the discussions are still pretty engaging and well presented making you crave for more.

The visuals are reminiscent of old Japanese adventure games for the PC-98, the first visual novels one could say. Everything is more detailed though and gives this a very modern look and feel. Good looking characters also make sure that you are interested in finding out more about them and exactly why they chose your bar of all places.

Fitting, satisfying style of music fitting a cyberpunk city so incredibly well and don’t ask me why but some songs even reminded me of games of my childhood like Zone of the Enders, Final Fantasy VII, Breath of Fire III and countless others. The soundtrack is certainly one of the bigger contributors to VA-11 Hall-A’s success.


VA-11 Hall-A is an incredible 10-20 hour adventure that is without a doubt one of the best Visual Novels currently available on Steam. This game is an amazing and mature experience and I’m glad that I finally got around to playing it, and do hope a sequel is in the works!

I recommend it to anyone who is interested in Visual Novels with lots of text. Fans of the cyberpunk will also find great value in this beautiful game.

Valhalla is a visual novel game where you step into the shoes of Jill. She's a bartender at the eponymous Valhalla and you stick with her over the course of 3 weeks. In those 3 weeks you meet a variety of other characters who both flesh out the cyberpunk world that the game takes place in and tell their own stories of past relationships, experiences, adventures and troubles. In addition to this, between shifts at the bar you manage Jill's life in a very simplistic management sim and you are able to read the daily news paper and a parody ♥♥♥♥♥ style message board, which help to add additional detail and context to the world of the game. This culminates in a more well fleshed out cyberpunk world than that which Deus Ex: Human Revolution built in the 28 hours I spent playing it.
The thing that I liked so much about the game was that Jill is the first video game character I've really connected with. I'm a little doubtful that everyone else in the world would enjoy Valhalla as much as I did because my ability to relate and understand the emotions that Jill experiences throughout the game's overarching story are the reason why Valhalla had such an impact for me. I left the game genuinely caring about the characters within it and that is...well frankly that's not really a thing I have happen very often for me.
This is a game I really enjoyed for the writing within it. If what I've described above has caught your interest then consider giving valhalla a try.

So, I guess words fail me on this one. This game isn't fun... it's necessary. Although technically the puzzles progressively become harder, that's not the point. They progressively become more profound, and I'm surprised at how inspiring and thought provoking this puzzle game is. Excellently selected quotes from famous thinkers are sprinkled sparingly throughout the game to draw attention to the fact that there is art to be discovered in the puzzles - brilliance to be uncovered within yourself.
Unlike games like "the graveyard," which try way too hard to appear like art within the form of a game, this game truly is art. It is effortless, subtle. The game barely notices that you're there. You get exactly one instruction the whole time, and that's just the button to press to interact. The rest of the game is experienced through your own personal pursuit.
If you desire introspection, if you want a slow and satisfying stroll through your mind, if every other game is starting to blur into one mess of combat and acquisition... the Witness is for you.

The Witness is a game, where you solve puzzles of varying forms on a mysterious island. This review won't contain any spoilers, however if you want to go into the game completely blind, I'll advise you to skip to the conclusion.
First and foremost The Witness is a puzzle game. You solve puzzles by drawing a line from A to B in various ways. Since there is no tutorial the puzzles difficulty ranges from very easy to very hard. Even though the premise sounds pretty simple the game gets really creative with it, so you rarely get bored doing the puzzles.
Overall I would say that the puzzles are created very fairly. Once you figured out how a certain puzzle mechanic works, only very seldom there are ones, where the developers want to take you on a journey of thought that you can't quite follow.
You only interact with the world by walking and drawing lines, which I prefer to other adventure games where you have gameplay mechanics such as items and dialogue, which sometimes lead to very questionable puzzles. The only thing that limits you in The Witness is your own knowledge or the lack thereof and much of the game is about advancing your knowledge and perception to solve problems you could not solve before.
The way that the puzzles are presented in the world is quite remarkable. The island itself with its clean graphics looks very beautiful. The island is what elevates this game from being a simple phone/tablet game to being a full fledged "gaming-experience".
Pretty much from the start you have the whole island accessible, meaning you have to explore it in order to advance in the game. There is no given linear order on how to do things, you have to figure out yourself. Obviously this can be a double-edged sword, since on the one hand you have a great sense of exploration in the game and more significant AHA-moments, when you return to puzzles you couldn't previously solve. On the other hand however it requires you to be patient, observant and it can lead to frustration, when you don't know whether it is you or the game holding you back from solving a puzzle.
I won't say much about the story to avoid spoilers. If you know Jonathan Blow, you know that he can be very pretentious about some of his ideas and that the inherent strength of his games lies in the gameplay itself, not so much in the story.
If you like puzzle games or solving puzzles, by all means, get this game. However, don't get this game if you are "in for the experience" or the story. Puzzling is a very huge part of the game and if you don't enjoy that you probably won't enjoy the game. This game wasn't built to appeal to everyone.
I would say the price point for the game is quite high. The price on release should have been something in the 20-25€ range. I myself got it through the humble monthly (12$) and would say that, even if it turns out, that the other games in this bundle are useless, it is still well worth the money.

Draw lines on squares! Wander around a pretty island, and find more places to draw lines on squares! I never thought I would have so much fun drawing lines on squares, but this game proved that it was far cleverer than I am over and over and over again. I'm glad that you can get to the end without actually completing all of the puzzles, as I gave up on a few. I'm still not sure whether there was meant to be a story, and the graphics optimization seems a bit dodgy (I had to play on low everything, and still got more dropped frames than in some other games that are subjectively better-looking; maybe my hardware is just showing its age), but the puzzles are top-notch and that's what we're here for. The Witness never wastes your time repeating an idea that you've already mastered; each puzzle brings something new and builds on what you've already learned. I'm amazed by the variety of puzzles that can be built from a simple set of constraints. Some were easy and some were brutally hard, but most hit the sweet spot of just hard enough that it's immensely rewarding when you reason your way to the solution.

New to Cities? This game is for you. Stop reading the thumbs down reviews. they really aren't helpful….period. If you're looking at it, it's most likely because you are looking for a more original city building simulation game. Its simple mechanics allow you to focus more on the city building while easily managing economic efficiency.
Once you spend the first 30 minutes going thru the tutorial *i recommend* your basicly ready to lay out something quickly and effectively. Starting is very simple and allows you to focus on the design and layout. While later slowly introducing elements that open up more economic strategy. City utilities are managed on a simpler and more macro size scale. You can create trade routes between two cities to share resources, *yet to explore it more* and so on.
Basicly its enjoyable.
Now for quality. This game has no more bugs than an average AAA title does that releases for “your console of choice” or any other system. I personally have not run into anything. I have a 2014 edition of the razer “blade pro” playing on full settings at 3k. I have not experienced any lag or slowdown. I average about 60 fps and dips down to about 45 fps while exploring on ground level. So im sure anyone with a mid core gaming desktop or consumer laptop should be able to run this ok. I have also managed to run it on low settings on a surface pro 3 i5 variant. Runs around 20fps, so hopefully that gives you a benchmark range of what to expect.
Well what's with all Bad hype behind Cities XXL?
Lets be real, what more do you want to see from this particular series? A future space theme skinned game that really gets no improvement in gameplay and just adds more bugs?

They added steam workshop content to the game and which is like the developers giving us the tools to build whatever you want. So for the hardcore citie player you have nothing to complain about. If we give it a chance to grow it has the chance to become basically whatever we want.

Switchcars is a time traveling rouge-like runner game where you use any means necessary to reach year 2055.  The catch is, you have to do this all while avoding a giant green alien caterpillar that moves with the gracefulness of a potato and trying not to splatter yourself on cars and rocks along the way.
This game has no mouse support but it has no need for it.  It uses "classic arcade and arrow key" control scheme
.  In the game you will use three keys to "capture" and control cars that you can switch to on command and are interchangable for any other vehicle you find
.  Oh, and did I mention that your character has a freaking grapling hook?!
The graphics in this game are really well drawn pixel graphics but the best part is the content.  The game has over a thousand different vehicles each with seperate speed, mass, abilities, and other attributes.  There are also many different lane types (road, water, lava, etc.), each with different attributes that affect vehicles, you, and the giant alien d*ck chasing you
.  There are also powerups that you find on the ground that do anything from adding propulsion systems (tracks, rockets, etc.) to pimping out your vehicle.
The author released it in Alpha on Steam Early Access with a couple bugs here and there, but a little over a week after they released a fix for some of the bugs.  This is how Early Access was meant to be, no abandonware here.
Over all, this game is very much worth the cheap price and has a ton of replayability.

Plot of the Counting Kingdom: You are a little boy tasked with saving the kingdom from monsters using magic spells (increasingly complex addition problems). At the end, you are rewarded with a giant cake, which you share with the monsters, because you are a sweet boy, although in such case I hope you have not actually been murdering the monsters with your math acumen.
Gameplay wise, Counting Kingdom is a turn-based tower defense game. Each monster has a number. You have various “spells” at your disposal, small-to-large numbers that you must add up the monsters to equal. A handful of potions allow you to tweak monster numbers or “cheat” by exploding or freezing a line of combatants. And since spell numbers don’t always match monster numbers, if you can’t apply the right “spells” right off, the monster horde increases next turn, and so forth.
I don’t think the game will ever pose a significant challenge to an adult of average math skills, but the sums, and the hordes, still get large enough to require thinking and strategy. And it’s a great help for kids transitioning to big-number addition (look! a big number is just smaller numbers added together. You don’t have to add all the numbers on screen up at once. You can make 10 out of these numbers, and 11 out of these numbers, and bam! 21!).
Anyhoo. The Counting Kingdom is an appealingly designed, easy to learn, trickier to master math game.

I find it hard to decide whether to recommend this game or not, honestly.  I picked it up when it was on sale for $5 because I saw it on Extra Credits.  I figured it was a math game, and I like math, so it should be a fun little diversion.  It was, but that's where the problem comes in.  I beat the game in less than an hour.
In terms of mechanics The Counting Kingdom is quite sound-everything works together, complexity and difficulty are added in nicely as the game progresses.  It all feels a bit same-y though.  The difficulty I also found to be a bit low until the wizard was introduced: then it had the wrong kind of difficulty, and I lost 2 towers on the final level (the only tower losses I took through the entire game) due to the wizard hitting a doubling tile and not drawing any ways to make 30.
I wish you could cast spells greater than 30.  That would have added a lot.
The game could have stood to be a bit longer, but I'm sure I'll get further playtime out of it with speedrun attempts.
Even after writing the above I'm still not sure whether to recommend: it was a fun hour, but it's hard to suggest $5, let alone 10 for an hour of gameplay.  I'd suggest picking this game up if you see it 75% off or more, but I can't justify recommending it for much less than that in its current state.

So, without a doubt, this is one of my favourite games - and most importantly, one of my favourite cool-down games. I think the track "Wisdom of Rage" really nails the game's expectations on the head.
The big reason that a lot of people think that this game is hard is because it's not asking you for flurries of button-mashing combat. If you've done meditation in the past, Furi is a great exercise in just those skills:
Step back. Take a deep breath and ground yourself. Observe your opponent and your environment. Dodge and counter when your opponent asks for your♥♥♥♥♥on a platter. And when they tire, pound into them mercilessly with all your fury... er.... Furi.
What really brings the game home for me, besides the gameplay, is the art direction and the characters. Admittedly, they're mostly archetypes, and one-liners - but each boss brings something to the table regarding your (The Stranger's) past and origins. Their powers, personalities and subversions of what you've learned after each boss fight.... It's something you need to experience for yourself, and it's well worth the price of admission.
TL;DR - Amazing gameplay, and amazing characters, just don't run in guns-a-blazing.

More of a visual novel/story-focused game. Each day you serve drinks according to the customer's desire (and sometimes you have to figure out what they want) and mix the ingredients yourself according to the in-game recipe guide. Everything is relaxed, there are no time limits to rush you and you can restart the drink without penalty. However, this gameplay is really just fluff that you do while you read the conversations going on that reveal more about characters and the world. You're not especially a protagonist/changing force in this world, you mostly just hear stories about things that are going on or have happened in the past. For me, it was really more about learning about and revealing the mysteries of the world and characters than any actual over-arching plot.
The story is pretty railroaded; there are very limited choices in what you can do to see alternate dialogue. There are no dialogue options where you choose what to say, it's just what you serve that can sometimes change the dialogue or ending. It's fine enough for a single playthrough and there are plenty of guides that let you know what you need to do. There are plenty of save slots so you can always go to a certain day to serve a different drink and see that dialogue. Endings are just based on if you pay your bills on time and how well you serve your customers.
Also, you may find the story lacking if you desire a clean-cut plot with everything resolved. Not everything is explained fully and you're free to draw your own conclusions about certain happenings (like:
).
On a side note, it can become tiring using the mouse to create drinks. I was hoping that right-clicking or at least double-clicking would add the ingredients automatically, but no such luck. However, I learned too late (after I beat the game) that there are keyboard shortcuts that make it a lot easier to play.
On another side note, the achievements are pretty straight-forward and you get most if you spend the time grinding cash to unlock all the extras. However, there's a bullet hell minigame that is painfully long and reminded me of why I avoid playing them. If you don't have the reactions/aren't masoschistic enough to have fun repeating long sections over and over again. I'm thankful that there's a steam guide that shows how to skip most of the enemy waves. I was at the point of giving up when I took a look at the guide section for help.

is an absolute marvel of a game.
This game, almost does not even deserve the title of a game, I believe a more proper term for this would be an "experience".
The game's plot is AAA level, rivaling the works of Shakespeare, Stephen King, and the mysteriously anonymous author of the famous fan work,
. Now, I don't want to spoil the story for any potential buyers or art enthusiasts, but I will brush over the first hour or so, as to give you a benchmark of sorts, so you can understand the true potential.
You play as Candice DeBébé herself, a noble hero and a magic ♥♥♥♥♥. You go out to get a tan, and an appropriately named "TanVan". It is then realized that the TanVan is out of an essential material for the tanning process, and you are asked to enter a forest to get more. Now, you may be wondering why you would find materials you would need for a tan in a forest, and it is perfectly right to think so. But, what happens is the characters acknowledge the outlandishness of such a task, something not many serious stories are willing to do. But what separates the boys from the men of story telling, is that despite the fourth wall being broken, full immersion is kept. At no point at all during my hours of playtime was I pulled away from the plot, and I struggled to even bring myself to stop playing to write this review. But, I cannot go deeper into the plot line, as you will be very much able to discover what Candice DeBébé has in store for you.
It runs on the Unity engine, and despite the engine's tropes of having a "look" it manages to overcome that and create an art style of it's own, an art style I don't believe has even ever been done before. It's a crisp and vivid art style, popping with colors, bump-maps, and above all, personality. Everything in the game is very smoothly animated, and the models are very detailed, yet minimal- showing only what you need to see and nothing extra. Many lesser games attempt to pull this off, but very few are successful. Candice DeBébé is an artistic masterpiece of design and execution. I especially love the depth of field effect the game has, I feel it is a subtle reminder that no matter how big the story is, we do live in a small world after all.
The gameplay is fantastic fun, and kept me excited and on the edge of my seat whenever I was in either a tense moment of risk during a boss fight, or casually fighting a grunt such as a beetle or a sexy ghost. the gameplay is deceivingly simple, and although it may seem that you just click in the direction you want to shoot at, it's more complex than that. You see, the pellets you shoot at them are actually influenced by physics, and can be moved around on your own just by walking into them. This extraordinarily unique gameplay mechanic raises the skill ceiling to nearly unreachable levels, as there's no telling what ways this can be manipulated to your advantage. Any foe who shoots pellets back at you, also has their pellets affected by physics. This means that with your own pellets, you can both attack and defend yourself. When I came to realize this, I was blown away. This raises the skill ceiling, that was already incredibly high, to nearly infinite levels that even gods could not reach. I encourage you to try
's Incredibly Trick Gameplay.
The soundtrack is godly, with twenty-four original tracks, most of if not all of them containing original lyrics sung by Candice DeBébé herself. I found this to add a deeper sense of emotion, and when I was listening to the "Lady Garden" song, I was nearly brought to tears. It's a song of love, with a hint of homosexuality. I believe the homosexual underlying tone of the lyrics add a depth of emotion I couldn't even fathom a game could bring to me. I feel that this song is Candice's love song, a song that shows that love is truly love, even through anything that fights it. If this alone won't bring you to your knees crying, It's accompanied by a masterful piano track, that adds so much more emotion to this song. And this is just one song of twenty-four, and I can leave you to experience it on your own.
In every single department, from every angle and all perspectives, I give this game a perfect
(Tan out of Ten).
This game is a must-buy for anyone that dares call themselves a gamer. Because if you've never played
, you haven't played a game yet. If you don't have the money, even for this game's incredibly humble pricepoint, I recommend you earn it as soon as possible by any means possible, even if it means holding off your daily spray tan for a week or so. What's a week of work? A month? For Candice DeBébé, it's nothing at all. It's worth it.

The detective is back after a hiatus. This game is a sequel to an identically titled flash game. It expands and improves on the tested formula by adding additional layers of detail to the evidence, voice acting, high quality animations and heaps of polish. The user interface in particular is very well designed, making it easy to do anything you want to do.
The story is simple, perhaps a tad too simple in that many developments are only loosly related to the actual crime.
The game has a few minigames, but they are all very easy. They do break things up a little, but they are nothing worth bragging about. The game also has short quizes at times to ensure that the player is following along with the logic. This helps to reinforce the ideas and ensures that players don't miss critical points.
The character design is strong and clear, there is no risk of mixing up the characters. The characters aren't obvious stereotypes, but they don't have a lot of depth. There may be a layer or two to find, but nothing tought provoking here.
The voice acting is well done, both from an audio quality aspect and from a casting aspect. The audio is well timed to the character animations and you genuinly belive that the characters are speaking.
Those looking for inventory puzzles have to look elsewhere, this game is not about rubbing everything on everything else, this is about pure investigating.
The game isn't very long, only a couple of hours. While there are many other games in the same price range that offers a lot more of play time, this game offers new content for its entirerty. It's worth the money. It's neither over- nor under-priced, it is just right.
Fans of the original should obviously play this. There is no requirement to play the first game, even if it is free, the story is self contained and barely makes any references to the previous game. Newcomers will like this game if they like mystery stories with a detective who investigates a situation and makes a conclusion in the end. It is not a difficult mystery to solve once all the facts are gathered, you play this for the experience getting there, not for clever puzzles or a challenging mystery. Give it a shot if you simply want to experience a story.

The Witness is a game, where you solve puzzles of varying forms on a mysterious island. This review won't contain any spoilers, however if you want to go into the game completely blind, I'll advise you to skip to the conclusion.
First and foremost The Witness is a puzzle game. You solve puzzles by drawing a line from A to B in various ways. Since there is no tutorial the puzzles difficulty ranges from very easy to very hard. Even though the premise sounds pretty simple the game gets really creative with it, so you rarely get bored doing the puzzles.
Overall I would say that the puzzles are created very fairly. Once you figured out how a certain puzzle mechanic works, only very seldom there are ones, where the developers want to take you on a journey of thought that you can't quite follow.
You only interact with the world by walking and drawing lines, which I prefer to other adventure games where you have gameplay mechanics such as items and dialogue, which sometimes lead to very questionable puzzles. The only thing that limits you in The Witness is your own knowledge or the lack thereof and much of the game is about advancing your knowledge and perception to solve problems you could not solve before.
The way that the puzzles are presented in the world is quite remarkable. The island itself with its clean graphics looks very beautiful. The island is what elevates this game from being a simple phone/tablet game to being a full fledged "gaming-experience".
Pretty much from the start you have the whole island accessible, meaning you have to explore it in order to advance in the game. There is no given linear order on how to do things, you have to figure out yourself. Obviously this can be a double-edged sword, since on the one hand you have a great sense of exploration in the game and more significant AHA-moments, when you return to puzzles you couldn't previously solve. On the other hand however it requires you to be patient, observant and it can lead to frustration, when you don't know whether it is you or the game holding you back from solving a puzzle.
I won't say much about the story to avoid spoilers. If you know Jonathan Blow, you know that he can be very pretentious about some of his ideas and that the inherent strength of his games lies in the gameplay itself, not so much in the story.
If you like puzzle games or solving puzzles, by all means, get this game. However, don't get this game if you are "in for the experience" or the story. Puzzling is a very huge part of the game and if you don't enjoy that you probably won't enjoy the game. This game wasn't built to appeal to everyone.
I would say the price point for the game is quite high. The price on release should have been something in the 20-25€ range. I myself got it through the humble monthly (12$) and would say that, even if it turns out, that the other games in this bundle are useless, it is still well worth the money.

Draw lines on squares! Wander around a pretty island, and find more places to draw lines on squares! I never thought I would have so much fun drawing lines on squares, but this game proved that it was far cleverer than I am over and over and over again. I'm glad that you can get to the end without actually completing all of the puzzles, as I gave up on a few. I'm still not sure whether there was meant to be a story, and the graphics optimization seems a bit dodgy (I had to play on low everything, and still got more dropped frames than in some other games that are subjectively better-looking; maybe my hardware is just showing its age), but the puzzles are top-notch and that's what we're here for. The Witness never wastes your time repeating an idea that you've already mastered; each puzzle brings something new and builds on what you've already learned. I'm amazed by the variety of puzzles that can be built from a simple set of constraints. Some were easy and some were brutally hard, but most hit the sweet spot of just hard enough that it's immensely rewarding when you reason your way to the solution.

Danganronpa is a visual novel style game which basically puts the mechanics of the Pheonix Wright games into Saw movie.  While it is certainly flawed, if the basic concept intrigues or excites you, this game will deliver the fundamentals you want.
Est play time, 20 hours
You are trapped in a school with other students, and the only way to escape is to kill someone without getting caught. If you are found guilty in the ensuing class trial, the master mind kills you. If the class trial gets it wrong, everyone but the killer dies, and the killer goes free.  Overtime, the group struggles both to stay alive as individuals, escape as a group and figure out the overarching mysteries surrounding this school and their imprisonment.
Each chapter will have 4 basic componenets:
A barely interactive cutscene sets the stage for the chapter and advances the story.
Free Time, in which you attempt to woo students with gifts in order to learn skills from them and more about them.
Investigation: A body has been discovered, you must explore to find hints and interview other students.
Class Trial: You must use the clues to deduce the killer through a series of minigames, including spot the contradiction and a rhythm game to deal with irrational students.
Danganronpa has two great strengths: the cast and the mysteries.  Everyone (except the protagonist) is colorful, and generally bounce of eachother in interesting ways that change over the course of the story.  The murder mysteries can generally be relied upon to be more than meets the eye, and each one fits in with the emotional mood of the story at the time.  The General Mysteries over-arch through the plot nicely.  Both types of mysteries manage to construct a sidewinding path that you must take to deduce them while remaining simple enough in execution to not be unbelievable, to an extent.
Unfortunately, while the fundamentals of this game are good, there are faults even here.  The writing occasionally takes a nose dive, and the prolouge and epilouge are almost painful to sit through.  The Class trial minigames grow tiresome, as once youve solved the whole mystery, you wont see why youre stopped because you cant hit some spinning dialogue text in time.
Furthermore, this game is the patron saint of petty annoyances.  The vending machine in which you can only buy a random present one at a time, the habit of teleporting you back to your room only to ask you to go out again, the lack of an inter-floor teleport late in the game, and other minor issues stop this game from being as immersive as it could be.
Conclusion: A solid 7/10, this game keeps you coming back with its excellent narrative and setting, despite its several minor failings.
This game is sorta like if you combined Ace Attorney with the movie "Saw."

The game so nice I bought it thrice, on three different platforms, with a sequel and a spinoff to boot.
Edit: This game is probably one of my favorite games that I've played in recent years. A friend introduced me to the series years ago and now having played through the game multiple times on PSP and Vita I developed a strong liking to the characters and the story that was developing over multiple games. That being said this games story can be slightly predictable and can sometimes fall into obvious mystery clichés that could deter some from continuing onward with your school life. I urge you to stick with it as this game gets deeper as the story goes on and does a few original things that I haven't seen done in other mystery style games or books. The characters are the driving force of this game though and they all have interesting quirks to go along with them. Most players will probably find themselves liking some characters and disliking some others for varying reasons although I believe that each character is extremely well written and have their own unique characteristics that make the interactions between them fun.
Next we have the gameplay which revolves around three distinct sections. Free time allows you to interact with characters and give them gifts much like in a dating sim. Each time you interact with them during this period and give them a gift that they like, they will tell you more about themselves. If you do this enough with any one character you get a skill to help you during the class trials. Next comes the investigation mode in whioch you search the school for clues in order to solve the mystery of whodunit and piece together the mystery of the school and its inhabitants. Finally we have the class trials in which you do several puzzles that lead to the eventual solution to the case. Most of the puzzles  are fairly simple so you may want to play on a harder difficulty from the beginning in order to get a more challenging experience although it does get a bit more challenging in the later trials.
TLDR: I would highly recommend this game but be sure to not have it spoiled for you before you play it and be ready for a healthy dose of reading.

However, this is not the case. The game decides what happens no matter who you decide to get close to (gifting, unlocking special dialogue etc). For some people that's not going to matter since everyone has their own preferences when it comes to which characters they like, but in my case I'm at a point in the game where all the characters I cared about are no longer around; leaving nothing but characters that I'm not interested in. AT ALL.
Now even this would be fine, but in that case I'd like there to be an option to attempt getting out asap because as said, I'm really not interested in conversing with the remaining characters so that would just make it painful to continue playing the game until the end. Unfortunately, such an option is not available either.
So, if you're like me and think "Ah it has a VN tag and there's choices that you can make", be warned: They don't make the impact that you'd want them to make on the story. If this is not a problem for you then by all means, follow the positive reviews instead.

A few days ago I came into some money. Like any responsible person I spent that money on steam. I bought 3 games, two of which I returned, the third I've been playing every day since i bought it.
Switchcars is the third game. It drew me in with it's art style and 'gimmick'. Said gimmick is switching vehicles at breakneck speed to adapt to your current terrain which changes every few seconds or so. Your goal is to travel from 1950 to 2055. Simple no? You'll be going much faster than 88 miles per hour though. The game gives you over 1000 vehicles to achieve this goal. Ranging from a rocket so fast that I just crashed it into an asteroid to...a shopping cart with no engine.
Said shopping cart can be given an engine though through 1 of 41 powerups you find on your journey. Things like drills and rocket thrusters can adorn your vehicle as you hurtle forward through time. Of course you can't get to 2055 in one tricked out shopping cart.
You have three vehicle slots which you can store vehicles in for a rainy day. A good variety of vehicles is necessary. Sure three supersonic planes sounds good and fast but they don't have that much fuel and are about as useful as...well a shopping cart when that fuel runs. Three solar powered race cars might be smarter but they wont be very good in an underground cave...full of lava. The three slots add a lot of on the spot thinking to the game which helps make the experiance engaging.
I do have a few gripes. It is very easy to feel cheated when your last car brakes down on a rocky field where nothing drives and a space worm is doing a full body tapdance on you. It can also be easy to lose track of what you've driven before which makes completion a bit trickier. However the dev is very active in the forums addressing suggestions and problems quickly and politely.
I personally reccomend Switchcars for one of those games you play for an hour or so every day. I would say to atleast wait for one major update to fix some of the bigger problems like resouloution and audio control but other than that I liked it. So go on, its a bit of fun for a relatively cheap price.

A couple days ago, the people over at the Humble Bundle finally dropped their monthly bundle. There were a few standout games that caught my eye but i will be honest, Switchcars was not one of those games. However, once I decided to load up this ‘vehicular rogue-like’ game, I was pleasantly surprised. It was like finding that elusive piece of pizza that had been sitting at the back of the fridge for days, sure I was hesitant to try it at first, but after going for it, I was glad I did.
‘Switchcars’ was developed by Slobodan Stevic, originally a 3d artist who worked on several games in the industry including, but not limited to, Space Engineers and Infinity: Battlescape. This experience is immediately evident as Switchcars boasts some impressive graphical details. The pixel art is distinct and colorful and your vehicle can get coated in mud and slime. The alien worm antagonist stands out vividly, with its bright green exterior and its hulking frame. One nitpick would be that the resolution seems to be currently locked at 1200×800, and as a result this leads to black bars on the screen when using a high resolution monitor.
What is the goal of Switchcars? It is simple, you need to travel from the 1950s to the 2050s whilst at the same time trying to avoid becoming dinner for a tenacious and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Alien worm. To achieve this, you have to constantly switch between vehicles. The game also features 9 different lanes. This may seem straightforward until you realize that the terrain also changes at set intervals during each stage. That car that you just had? Yeah it is in the river now. That is a nice train you have there, shame you are now on the road. This leads to some  intense and nail biting moments where you have to think on your feet and also have a contingency plan in place. You are able to save vehicles in 3 different slots but each vehicle can get damaged and depending on the vehicle type, will need fuel. There are 40 different power ups scattered across the 10 stages, some of these can upgrade your cars to get special abilities, like a helium balloon that allows you to take your car into the air, or a nifty turret that will destroy anything that was unlucky enough to be in your path.
The game isn’t limited to just vehicular play. You can also roam around on foot and traverse the area with the help of a special grappling hook, although you have utilize this tool attentively or you may find yourself as road kill for the oncoming traffic. It was at these moments that I feel like a 2-bit Rico Rodriguez, grappling from car-to-car, furiously trying to get to the ‘safe zones’ at the end of each stage.
The game has a variety of different vehicles to fool around with. Currently there are 1,047 different vehicles you can utilize in your bid to escape the aforementioned hungry alien worm. There are also 101 different types of terrains, this leads to the need for constant micro-managing of your 3 slots as you need to ensure that you have the different types of vehicle, be it a plane or a bike or even a train, to survive the game’s ever changing terrain. I have yet to master these tools and ascend to stage 10,but unlike Sisyphus, the rock shall one day stay atop the mountain and I will reach stage 10!
It must also be noted that the game does have a few problems. Apart from the resolution issue, there is also no way to turn down the game’s sound. Only an option to turn on or off. Although I am sure the developer is aware and working on this. The game can also get quite repetitive once you have mastered the initial mechanics. This can get frustrating for players looking for more depth in the game. However, as the game is still in early access, the developer still has time to address these issues. Currently it is very fun is bite-sized chunks.
Overall, just like in the game, there is still a long road for the developer to traverse. So far, the charm and fun that can be had from these short ‘runs’ through the game have been well worth my time. This game has only been released in early access on steam so I am sure there will be future updates that address some of the issues and improve upon the game play. So far it has been a fun and chaotic romp through the game’s stages. One day I shall reach the space craft in 2050!

Pros
Excellent throwback to old-school arena FPS
The developers of Toxikk are extremely passionate about the game, and it shows in the gameplay.
The weapons are varied and satisfying to use, the movement is extremely fluid, and the game looks excellent.
The gameplay is similar to the oldschool greats, such as UT99 and UT2004, but Toxikk has enough of its own to set itself apart, instead of being a carbon copy that feeds on nostalgia.
thermoplasticsKeith Dean
Polished and optimized
Despite being in early access (written on the 23rd of August, 2016), Toxikk is extremely polished and well optimized.
The core gameplay feels like a finished product, and even on an average-spec laptop, Toxikk runs with a smooth framerate.
Keith Dean
Developers that care
Toxikk has a development team that genuinely cares about the product. You can feel the developer's passion throughout the gameplay.
Not only has this delivered an excellent product so far, but it means there is a far more optimistic outlook for the future of the game.
BryanKeith Dean
Free demo alongside full release
When Toxikk is released (9/9/2016), a free demo will be released alongside it.
This way, you can see if Toxikk is the right game for you without committing to a purchase right away.
This demo will allow you to play on official servers on a limited amount of maps.
The full version will have leaderboards, all maps, achievements, character customization and custom content (maps, weapons etc)
Cons
Low playerbase (for now)
This is a frequent complaint from newcomers.
As of now, Toxikk has a very low playerbase.
However, this is due to the developers intentionally doing zero advertising since it was released on Steam in Early Access.
Once the game is closer to its release day (9/9/2016), the developers will shift their focus to marketing to build the playerbase.
Keith Dean
Future is uncertain
Due to early access, and a current lack of players, the future success of Toxikk is uncertain.
It may do well, and gain a sizable playerbase, it may gain a small group of dedicated players, or it may flop.
If you are unsure whether or not it will be a success, wait for the full release to play the free demo.

Currently in early access
Early Access is not a popular concept for everybody.
It has happened all too frequently where an Early Access game has had development dropped midway through the process, leaving unhappy customers with an unfinished game.
However, Toxikk has received solid, consistent support, and its release date has been announced.

I'll preface this with this: I really want to recommend this game but I just can't in good concience as-is.
The miserable lag compensation (stemming from wild rubber banding and poor hit detection) and reliance on a central server for hosting while playing on a healthy 5Mbit network connection with nothing else running keeps me from recommending this game, especially to anyone in the Western US. Which is a shame because the mechanics and graphics are polished to a reflective sheen. Movement is remarkably responsive and feels good, which rather surprised me because for some unknown reason most Unreal Engine games feel floaty and unsatisfying to move around in.
The graphics are beautiful when they are not a suffering from a bloom overdose and even on a low end RX 460 the framerate stays at a steady 60+FPS. Not much for me to talk about here though as I don't care much about visuals, being the kind of person who still happily plays Sonic Adventure and honestly doesn't care that it looks terrible even compared to Fallout: New Vegas.
The gun combat has a good weight to it, with the weapons giving a felt kick with each shot and realistically jerking the bullet pattern upwards and inconsistantly out wide being a feature I didn't know I wanted until it felt like I had it. But the weapons themselves are lacking in balance, with the Plasma Caster being utterly useless when the Assault Rifle and Pistol do the same damage per hit but have a higher DPS and are hitscan, making even the Sniper Rifle look pathetic despite it's 70 damage body shoots. The rest of the gear is a cavalcade of bog standard shooter weaponry that behaves the way it has since the dawn of shooters, a M1+W flamethrower, a spammy rocket launcher, and a "overpowered" shotgun.
But again, none of that really matters when there is no way to properly "track" a opponent as you are stuck teleporting around the battlefield with every alternate step. Even whilst walking in a perfectly straight line you will uncomfortably jerk forward every so often. Finally, hitting your enemy is difficult bordering on impossible when your opponent may or may not be occupying the same space on the server as they are on your screen.

The difficulty level is set just right too.  You will die repeateatedly - very repeatedly - but you'll always know it's your own fault, and with a little practice everything is achievable. If you're still not sure, go check it out on YouTube.  If it looks like it appeals to you, you'll love it.

More of a visual novel/story-focused game. Each day you serve drinks according to the customer's desire (and sometimes you have to figure out what they want) and mix the ingredients yourself according to the in-game recipe guide. Everything is relaxed, there are no time limits to rush you and you can restart the drink without penalty. However, this gameplay is really just fluff that you do while you read the conversations going on that reveal more about characters and the world. You're not especially a protagonist/changing force in this world, you mostly just hear stories about things that are going on or have happened in the past. For me, it was really more about learning about and revealing the mysteries of the world and characters than any actual over-arching plot.
The story is pretty railroaded; there are very limited choices in what you can do to see alternate dialogue. There are no dialogue options where you choose what to say, it's just what you serve that can sometimes change the dialogue or ending. It's fine enough for a single playthrough and there are plenty of guides that let you know what you need to do. There are plenty of save slots so you can always go to a certain day to serve a different drink and see that dialogue. Endings are just based on if you pay your bills on time and how well you serve your customers.
Also, you may find the story lacking if you desire a clean-cut plot with everything resolved. Not everything is explained fully and you're free to draw your own conclusions about certain happenings (like:
).
On a side note, it can become tiring using the mouse to create drinks. I was hoping that right-clicking or at least double-clicking would add the ingredients automatically, but no such luck. However, I learned too late (after I beat the game) that there are keyboard shortcuts that make it a lot easier to play.
On another side note, the achievements are pretty straight-forward and you get most if you spend the time grinding cash to unlock all the extras. However, there's a bullet hell minigame that is painfully long and reminded me of why I avoid playing them. If you don't have the reactions/aren't masoschistic enough to have fun repeating long sections over and over again. I'm thankful that there's a steam guide that shows how to skip most of the enemy waves. I was at the point of giving up when I took a look at the guide section for help.
Worth a look if you like game stories that deal with social issues in a cyberpunk future like 2064: ROM (whose characters make cameos in easter eggs).

I'm not going to write a long drawn out review.  Simply put, Furi is a beautifully stylized sword/blaster based dueling game.
If you love a challenge then this is the game for you.  Each boss feels like a full level, so you're not missing out on content.  They all have unique styles, abilities, and sass.  While outsiders may assume that games like this are very scripted in terms of strategy, there are actually many ways you can take down a boss.  The soundtrack is a great synthwave backdrop that makes the action more intense.  Art = gorgeous.
Basically, if you enjoy getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked to great graphics, and a killer soundtrack then this game is for you.
There are difficulty levels, but only ableist pansies start on easy.  If the ableist pansies take offense to that statement well then they have proven my point for me. :)

Furi is... frantic.  It's fast-paced muscle memory in reaction to certain visual or audio cues, mixed with precise timing requirements and bullet dodging.  There are only boss fights here, the stages in between encounters aren't peppered at all with minions of any kind.  They are brief intermissions, pure opportunities to catch a breath and to stop and smell the roses while a softcore Donnie Darko speaks to you in verse.  Though you can move yourself, these in-between walkways were meant to be watched rather than manipulated, featuring graphical designs that take cues from 64k computer demos from the mid 2000's.
Furi is a hard game.  Well, at least it should be hard, if you play on the recommended difficulty setting.  I started on the Furi level, then after learning the ropes (meaning I died a lot) I moved down to easy and then cruised right through the main campaign.  There are other game modes, but to unlock them you have to complete the "normal" scenario, where death will be a close companion many a time before victory.
The gameplay in Furi is overall rather simple.  The tight controls are well refined and make it so you can take full advantage of how nimble the protagonist is.  That's all well and good, but there is still just as much probability to get things right as there is to get it wrong, and it calls for small celebration every time a ring of fire is dodged without taking damage.  The enemies themselves are all variations to a theme so you'll be making only minor adjustments to your strategy for each fight.  There are a couple standout moments, but that's it.  Just a couple.
For the bottom line, Furi is a method to a madness kind of game.  If it accomplishes anything, it's making you aware of how much input lag your setup has.  I put a total of about 5 hours into it and have absolutely no desire to unlock any of the extra content.  More of the same, but more difficult?  mehh, I'll pass.  The main drawback is how the experience so easily breaks down to learning the strategy for boss A, then learn what small things to change for boss B and so on and so forth.
In conclusion, Furi is an easily skipped game, especially for the steep asking price of $20.  I got 5 hours out of it and have no plans to bloat that figure.  For $5 it would definitely get my recommendation, but anything higher is a no-way-Jose situation.

A middling port of a great game.
Pros:
+ Story is engaging and tense.
+ Memorable characters.
+ More exploration than the average visual novel.
+ "Objection" logic is cleaner and easier to follow than in other courtroom games.
+ Fantastic psycho-pop art style.
Cons:
- Poorly-ported/confusing control scheme.
- All achievements currently broken on Mac, some achievements just broken, period.
- Crashes enough to be annoying.
- Rhythm minigame never feels intuitive.
- $30 is a lot for a port of a 2010 PSP game.
The only thing that's really holding this game back is the aforementioned control scheme. The buttons used include F1, F2, esc, tab, q, w, e, r, a, s, d, left shift, x, space, enter, arrow keys, left click, mouse wheel, right click... It's just a visual novel.  You shouldn't need that many buttons. Additionally, it's the truly bizarre combinations of those buttons that make the control scheme so counter-intuitive -- for example, the aforementioned rhythm game uses right-click, left-click, q, tab, and space. Most buttons for this game seem to have been decided by throwing darts at a picture of a keyboard.
All that said, though, I very much enjoyed this game and strongly recommend it for anyone who's into visual novels.
