FYI I beat this game in about 8 hours on the normal mode (it's called something besides just normal mode but I can't remember what it is). Ok, so let me start out by saying I think this game did a lot of things right. The health system is cool, 3 lives vs. an opponent with 3-5 lives. Kill the opponent, your health is restored and you regain a lost life. Die, both you and your opponent regain all your health and their phase resets. Lose all lives, start back to the beginning of the fight. Successful parries restore health. I liked how there was the normal sword attack, charge attack with sword, normal gun attack, and charge gun attack and also perfect parries doing extra damage is cool. Even your dodging ability can be charged up for better range, just so many rewards available for playing well. The soundtrack is really good, very techno. The art style is really cool too. There was only one fight where I thought the choice of colors could've been better because it was hard to tell what the enemy was doing. All gameplay being boss fights is cool. After beating the game you unlock a harder difficulty which apparently not only makes all the bosses harder, but gives them extra attack variety too, so kudos for that. I also liked how you had to judge when it was ok to attack, and for being smart and charging attacks at the right time you were rewarded by doing a lot more damage and mastering phases of a fight allows you to breeze through to the part you died to before pretty quickly. I ended up getting an achievement for beating a boss in 5 minutes after several tries, which felt really nice.
What was not so great? Most of the gameplay concepts are introduced at the first boss, which is nice but also you kinda know what to expect for all future fights, and it seemed like they were running out of ideas for 2 of the 10ish bosses.
I hated certain parts that had places where you could fall and get hurt. Sometimes I would accidentally dodge into one of these places and get punished for something you don't have the best control over. Sometimes I would get hit which would knock me into a pit and take damage for the pit too, which was especially annoying during the bullet hell segments. Even though the art style was simple, I ran into lots of times where I dropped from 60fps to 30ish, and I could never really tell why because the game's graphics didn't seem like they were super complicated when it happened.
In short, a very enjoyable experience that I'd reccomend to anyone looking for a challenge, just keep in mind it loses variety and gets more repetitie towards the end, but that may be remedied in the harder mode.

Danganronpa is a fantastic game. That's about all there is to say. The plot of this game is gripping and paced excellently. Each character you meet is well written with their own quirks and personality traits, and you care about all of them. This is what makes the game so tense; you don't know which of your friends is going to die next. One day you could be talking to them in the laundry room and the next moment you find their body at the scene of some horrible murder. It's a grim experience, made even more so by the presence of Monokuma's insanity.
The gameplay itself is logic based, requiring you to listen to what each character has to say and work out the events of the crime. The mechanics whilst in the "class trial" sections of the game can be a little clunky at times, but it's still a highly satisfying experience. Finding that contradiction you've been struggling on for a little while fills you with a great sense of pride and the tension of what's going to happen next makes these segments highly enjoyable.
The sound design of the game is what I have the highest praise for. I've been listening to playlists of it's soundtrack since the game came out and every time Monokuma's damn theme hits I can't help but grin a little bit and sing along. Each piece of music is very well implemented and fitting for the moment, and the voice work is believable and well delivered.
This game is an experience, a pretty damn fun one at that, and if you enjoy cute anime girls getting murdered in brutal fashion, it should be right up your street.

On all accounts The Witness exceeds as a puzzle game; in a visually satisfying and perfectly challenging way it presents puzzles for the player to solve. I want to rant and rave about all the puzzles I solved, I want to convene with others and pick their brains over the challenging ones, I want to describe in vast detail the great variety of challenges The Witness presents. I wish there were more to add but there is no story, there is no soundtrack, there is no combat, there is no antagonist, there are no upgrades, there is nothing except line puzzles. Been playing this game since it came out on my Ouya.  (RIP, Ouya.  You were a great little system.)  I finally took the plugne and forked out the money to buy it a second time for Steam, since we enjoyed it so much on the Ouya.  Did not disappoint and the amount of stuff that we gained access too was well worth the extra investment.  I look forward to where this game is going and can't wait to try out the upcoming Unity 5 version.  If you want a game where you can just run around, have fun, and not really have a 'goal' in mind, then this one works well.

A) The ranking system is absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥
1. You get rankups for gaining exp, which you get for doing literally everything, including completing solo missions against bots (which are insanely good at higher levels, but cannot complete mission objectives for♥♥♥♥♥♥ and there is no way to make them cooperate either).
2. Getting a rankup matches you against tougher players (even though you were just playing against bots).
3. Those tougher players then proceed to completely wipe the floor with you. Great.
B) Advanced movement system is crap.
1. You have a kind of dash functionality by pressing shift while moving or double-tapping WASD keys, but it has a weird delay in between. If you double-tap, then it is not that noticeable, but if you shift-WASD, then it becomes glaringly obvious and annoying as ♥♥♥♥, because you can't chain it immediately, and there is no cooldown bar anywhere as far as I noticed.
2. There is a double-jump functionality, but unlike another game that implemented it right, Shootmania Storm, this game's second jump only has a very short time window to be activated. You press jump once, then you have about half a second or you cannot double-jump anymore. Again, annoying.
3. Wall-jumping is extremely unintuitive. In Shootmania Storm this was IMO done right - to jump off a wall, you run into it and press jump while moving TOWARDS the wall (if wall on left, hold A + jump). In a tighter space you could chain this indefinitely, provided you have the skill. In this game, however, for some dumb reason you have to LOOK AND MOVE AWAY from the wall to jump off it! But the big problem with this is that this game has strafing, meaning if you hold A/D midair, you bend your trajectory, which makes wall-jumping almost impossible since you have to jump towards a wall, time the absolutely perfect 1ms time window when you're touching the wall (assuming you want to jump to the same height across a hole in the ground; wait any longer and you lose the height), then look away, hold the opposite direction key (if wall on left, hold D), AND tap DASH, not jump. If that isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, I don't know what is. It's an extremely useless game mechanic as-is, since only the absolutely hardcore players are going to use it with such a low chance of success.
Also, the wall jump essentially jumps horizontally, barely upwards at all, so cannot be used to scale walls. Shootmania Storm was so much more fun in this regard.
The new Quake is so much more enjoyable in both regards.
The flamethrower is OP in close encounters, has an insane range, and obscures the view for everyone.
The rocket launcher, in turn, has very weak AOE damage - direct hit does 100 damage, while a hit right below the feet/right next to the player does only about 30. One would imagine that the damage would decrease based on range, but there is a huge drop between a direct hit and the tiniest miss.
The good parts:
nice visuals,
decent guns (but maybe a bit too many of them, like there's essentially 2 machine guns, except one does more damage to machines, and the BFG seems kind of unnecessary),
decent game modes (but for some reason, they've renamed all the well known names, i.e. deathmatch = bloodlust, team deathmatch = squad assault, capture the flag = cell capture)
but that's not enough to outweigh the negatives for me.
If I could just somehow derank to play with normal people and not quake veterans, that would be nice.

In this exciting detective adventure game filled with twists and turns, by SFB Games, you will find yourself playing the role of Detective Grimoire. Your job is to take on the mysterious death of Remington, the owner of a swamp amusement park in the far reaches of a swamp. The odd thing is that the apparent killer is the infamous Boggy, a creature so unique that it hasn't been seen in 60 years, and yet came out of hiding to kill the man that created a park about the creature itself.
Graphically I loved the look of the game, the characters all had a very different look to them, and the different sections of the "park" definitely went with the vibe of what was going on in the scene. All the screens are static back drops, and some of them have characters that will appear somewhere in the foreground. There was just something about the character design that just draws a person in, I can't tell if it was the way that they were drawn, or if it is the use of colors, but whatever it is, it works for the game. I also really liked the HUD layout of the game, you definitely new where you were in the game, in terms of progress, as well as where you stood with the different characters that you would be interviewing as you try to track down the killer.
One of the biggest things that I have found makes or breaks the game is the voices and sounds of the game. This particular game nailed it. Along with the look of the characters I could feel the voices breath life into them. Each was very unique and each made me believe that those voices belonged to those characters. I also really appreciated the humorous dialogue that was thrown in from time to time to keep things a little lighter in the game.
The controls are really simple, this is another point and click game. So as long as you feel confident left clicking with a mouse, you'll do just fine.
Alright so lets get down to it, as I stated before you will be playing the role of Detective Grimoire. You have been asked to consult in this truly bizarre death which everyone is claiming was done by an almost mythical creature that has not been seen in 60 years. It is your job to interview everyone on the island and try to uncover all the truths, lies, and obstacles that get in your way. My only problem with the game was that the overall length wasn't all that long, but there was something about this game that I didn't really care. I enjoyed it for what it was, and that was a great story, with a great cast of characters, and surprises spread throughout. I also enjoy the interrogation mechanic that was in the game. There was always a chance that some new bit of information or perhaps an actual clue could get more information out of the different individuals spread out across this very unique theme park.
Now I'd like to go more into some of the twists and turns, but that would be a terrible thing to give away for anyone out there wanting to play the game, and I think most will want to play this game. So if you like point and click mysteries with colorful casts, and a very mysterious murder, this is the game for you. You can beat the game in under 2 hours, that's the only thing that I want to warn you about, but outside of that I think most will greatly enjoy the time they spend playing this game. This game gets an 8.8 out of 10.

I really liked this game. The plot is captivating, the dialogues are fun and the characters are memorable. I must admit the game is not hard, you can finish it in about 2 hours, but I'm sure you will not regret spending your time on it. 5/5 for me!

I reccommend this game, but
.  This is a game designed in the style of arcade cabinets and the first few generations of home console games.  It's full of pattern memorization, precise timing, obscure mechanics you need to work out for yourself, and repetition.   I found myself dredging up skills I learned from classic NES games, training muscle memory into my fingers to get past each section.  The one major change from games of that era is infinite lives: No longer do you only have 10, or 3, or even just 1 try to learn and beat an area before you have to start over.  Instead, it breaks it down into well-paced but brutal sections, and death sends you back to the beginning of the section.  (Quitting, however, sends you back to the very beginning, although I'm told there's a warp system).
All in all, I suggest picking this up, if you're prepared to find yourself immersed in a
game, something that's exceedingly rare these days.
'nuff said. Man up and play this awesome old school game!

The second part of the Alien Breed series, this is my first A.B game i played since i don't own part 1. When playing you can slightly feel that is was made with the twin-sticks controller in mind, on most occasions you won't have a hard time with the keyboard/mouse controls but as soon as a enemy is close too you it can be rather difficult to turn around and shoot.
The game exists out of a one-player: Story-mode, Free-play-mode and survival mode. Story mode is self explaining, Free-play-mode is a replay-mode and survival is a wave based survival mode. multiplayer consists out of a Coop assault mode, the story-mode but then coop, and the Coop survival mode.
The game:
Starting the single player for the first time gives a you small recap of what happened in Alien Breed 1, the cut-scene has the old comic book style and what probably is the first thing to notice is the high quality of the dialogs. The background resembles that of a terminal screen and fits the overall look of the game, the green really suits the game as a whole. In-game notification are also green and appear on your HUD as text, depending on the area you are in this can cause a little bit of difficulty to read the text. The graphics look really good, you can see that the dev's took the time to make the levels as in the big amount of details. The music and sound effects fit perfectly in the whole atmosphere of the game, the cries of the aliens are also really good. Objectives in the main campaign are mainly going from A to B and activating a switch to proceed in the level.
Verdict:
I personally didn't like the campaign mode so i mainly played the survival mode instead, this could be because i actually don't really like top down shooters. it's also worth mentioning that the on-line match making is pretty much deserted but besides that the graphics are really good and and with a twin-stick controller you will probably get the most out of this game. Although top-down-shooters aren't really my type of game i still rate it a 7/10.

Switchcars is a vehicular rogue-like that feels a bit like a not-so-endless runner game. You begin as early as the 1950s (by default you start in the 80s), your goal is to drive your way to the 2050s while running away from what is best described as a giant, green killer whale. After three hours of playing what are generally five minute runs, I’m nowhere near beating the game but I’m also nowhere near giving up. Switchcars is pretty simple, because of this, you’re either going to like the game or hate it.
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developer.
The idea of being a tiny little human running away from a giant alien is a daunting one. Thankfully, Switchcars gives you just enough help to make this task possible, even if it is incredibly difficult. For the most part, you won’t even find yourself dead at the hands of the alien, you’ll find yourself splattered on one end of a high speed train or car. That’s what Switchcars really comes down to, switching between different vehicles.
You can store up to three vehicles (that includes whatever you’re using) so providing you’re able to keep three good vehicles on you and you don’t crash too often then it’s actually quite easy to stay far enough ahead of the alien to reach safe zones (placed at the end of each one of ten stages a run consists of) with ease. Sadly that only happens in an ideal world, one filled with vehicles that are all super awesome.
The game currently has one thousand vehicles in it spread out across the years, many of them with names. Ranging from tractors to racing cars, paragliders to jets and canoes to submarines. Of course, not all of these vehicles are as fast as a race car, or as armoured as a tank and so you’ll often have to make do with something slower or weaker. These are the really challenging parts of the game, the parts where you’ll need to quickly switch between vehicles in order to keep going and stay ahead of the alien.
Every vehicle has a fuel and health bar and some vehicles also have abilities. Fuel is obviously drained by simply using the vehicle but there are refuelling points along the way, as well as repair points. The health bar of a vehicle is drained by, you guessed it, damaging the vehicle which happens when you crash into something or drive into lava, that kind of thing. For the most part, a vehicle’s ability is just a horn (or siren for emergency vehicles), it’s the more specialised vehicles that have the ‘cool’ abilities, like fighter jets with missile launchers or submarines with the ability to go underwater. Offensive abilities can be used to blow up obstacles in your path and even kill the alien chasing you (not sure what effect that has on a run since I haven’t pulled this off yet.)
Speaking of paths, Switchcars has nine different lanes for you to drive, fly, or swim through. Six of these lanes are ground lanes, ranging from grassland to water canals to train tracks and the other three are for airborne vehicles. Airborne vehicles can travel along ground lanes too but generally there’s more traffic, and therefore more to crash into, down there. There are a hell of a lot of different lane types and most of the vehicles are only suited to one or two different types of lane so you’ll need to change up your vehicle roster accordingly when you enter a new area with new lanes.
Now, though it does sound like it’s all about the vehicles, you’re actually able to get around on foot rather well thanks to a grappling hook. It’s pretty effective at pulling you towards stationary objects and speeding you up but it’s most effective when you pull yourself towards something going incredibly fast, such as a race car. Not only will you be able to catch up to a vehicle you otherwise wouldn’t have been able to, it’ll also pull you through the level a helluva lot quicker than you would have been going, even if you were in the vehicle you’re after.
Before I move on to the negatives, I’ll quickly mention powerups, of which there are forty in the game. The powerups are dotted throughout the levels and range from machine gun turret attachments to helium balloons that’ll let you fly even the largest of cars. As long as the powerups don’t conflict, i.e. you can’t use two ability powerups, you can use as many of them as you want and there doesn’t seem to be a limit to how many you can carry.
Although I have been enjoying the game thus far, it certainly has its negatives, one more important than the rest. You basically see all the game has to offer in the first two minutes of gameplay. Sure, the addictive nature of the game has been enough to keep me playing for just over three hours but in its current state will I go back and play more? Probably not. There are basic unlocks, like new lanes and later starting years, but there’s nothing that changes what is already a very simple game. There’s just not enough here to keep the game interesting for more than a couple of hours. You can see from some of the forum discussions that the lack of complexity means some people just don’t enjoy the game full stop. That may be the case for you as well, all I can say to that end is that I have enjoyed it but I do understand why others have not. It’s worth remembering that Switchcars has only just released in Early Access, so there’s every chance that it’ll be improved to a point where there is enough complexity to keep it interesting for longer but this review is about the game’s current state, not what it may become.
I do have a couple of other issues with the game. The first, and hopefully soon to be fixed (this’ll be updated accordingly) is the complete lack of resolution support, Switchcars only runs in 1280x800 (16:10) which means anyone with a higher resolution monitor will have big black bars at the top and bottom of the screen as well as the game being slightly stretched out. The second technical issue I have is the complete lack of options, you have a control configuration menu, a fullscreen toggle, a music toggle and a camera shake option. That’s it. Taking the resolution support issue into consideration, the least I would have expected is a music and sound effect slider rather than just a toggle for music. Lastly, I did come across a few parts in a number of runs where there are no vehicles and nothing that you can use to pull yourself along with the grappling hook. This can be avoided by keeping a couple of backup vehicles of course but those may well run out of fuel or breakdown, especially as some terrain types damage vehicles (or the player if you’re on foot). I didn’t have this happen to me too many times but, as some people have said in the forums, these parts really slow the game down and I found myself losing the run either during these sections or shortly after.
Switchcars may be too simplistic for some but for others it’ll be an entertaining and addictive experience, perhaps not for long enough to warrant a full price purchase though. If you think the game, even with its lack of complexity, is something you’ll enjoy then go for it, if not hold off for a sale or wait for it to get further along the development process to see if anything changes.

This game is so GOOD!
Characters are three-dimensional, endearing, and incredibly funny. As a bartender, the protagonist's story takes a backseat to listening to the struggles of your customers in a cyberpunk dystopia. The varied clientele and their changing moods as events unfold lead to a variety of heavy, deep, hilarious or just plain weird conversations.
The bartending gameplay reinforces the story by making you pay attention: Remembering a person's favorite drink or that they always like their drinks doubled in size impacts dialog, the endings you can get, and how much of that sweet cash money you can make.
...and you're going to want that money, since it is spent on paying bills to get the best endings and to buy useless apartment clutter that helps the protagonist focus at work.
The game is also highly polished. Menus are slick, the pixelart is gorgeous, characters animate expressively, and there is even enough extra content in NG+ to justify a second playthrough.
I consider this a must-play for fans of quality visual novels. Strong gameplay elements through the game's bartending system also make it an approachable starting point for gamers who like story-heavy games and are curious about trying a visual novel.

VA-11 HALL-A is a game that isn't meant for a majority of the gaming community. There are no tactics, strategy, and skill involved in this game at all. Instead, what VA-11 HALL-A offers is a narrative that allows you to delve inside the mind of a humble bartender in a dystopian world where the fruit of the game lies in its masterful storytelling, atmosphere building, and character development.
The heart of the game lies in its atmosphere building and characters. Set in a technologically-advanced dystopian world in which androids (or Lilim as they are addressed) are considered members of society, big corporations rife with corruption control the city, and talking Shiba Inu dogs, VA-11 HALL-A offers an outlook in a future where technology and capitalism outrun humanity. Most of the "action" is set in a quaint bar named VA-11 HALL-A operated by 2 bartenders and their boss. The meat of the game lies in the conversations between bartender Jill Stingray, the main character of the game and a distraught bisexual, with her absurd, yet charming clients and her co-workers. The dialogue mainly consists of topics such as the nature of sexuality, the boons and banes of technology, business, and an insight into various lifestyles. The characters in the game are all given unique traits and quirks that shape them into lovable and near-realistic beings trying to get by in the world with character development that is as natural as it needs to be. Aside from dialogue, characters are revealed through their drink choices, with each drink possessing attributes such as "Spicy", "Cute", or even "Manly". These drinks help define and continuously shape the characters in the game and acts as the sole determinant for the dialogue options the player will encounter. Surprisingly, I was able to strongly resonate with the main character despite being straight, male, and free of any vices.
This game is a perfect fit for those seeking a softer, quieter game. VA-11 HALL-A is meant to be played with only a mouse on one hand and perhaps a snack in the other, and optionally with a good sound system for immersion. The gameplay is not groundbreaking, and uses most basic elements found in common visual novels. There are different types of endings, but overall the choices don't matter as much as I would have thought; furthermore, there is no skip text function which is quite frustrating if you're trying out different dialogue options. Aside from clicking textboxes, players have to make drinks according to the specifications of the client. There is neither an imposed time limit nor penalty for screwing up a drink (unless served to the client), and the formula for each drink is located all in a database that appears only when needed. There is a segment before every work session that is set in Jill's apartment in which players have access to her phone and can use news and forum apps where netizens discuss current events and share opinions on various things. At home, players are also given the chance to manage the money Jill makes from bartending and use it to spend on rent and items to decorate her house which keeps her focused in her work.
Aesthetically, the game is sound. The anime pixel art imbued with a modern flair is a homage to the old-school Japanese games created decades ago and served as a primary source of inspiration for the game's developers. Sukeban Games made excellent use of color with a muted background palette to set the cool and quiet atmosphere, and a more impactful, vibrant palette for character designs to place greater emphasis on the people Jill encounters throughout the game. The excellent soundtrack composed solely by Garoad, is not heavy on beats nor has a fast rhythm, but rather is meant to calm and soothe the player and accompany them as they progress throughout the game set in a quaint, little bar. Players can, in fact, choose which songs to play during the bartending sessions thanks to the jukebox feature (though can be quite frustrating to use) to set the mood for the player.
In terms of performance, pretty much any computer produced in the Windows 7 era can run this game. If you really do care, it's capped at around 25~30 FPS, and it doesn't need to be any greater than that considering there are no dynamic visual effects. This 2D game will not eat up your GPU resources.
TLDR: It's a quiet game that achieves greatness in its simplicity as a visual novel and offers a realistic take on modern life with its excellent dialogue. A must-buy for those seeking simple games with a heart rather than groundbreaking gameplay, or visual novels fanatics in general looking for something different. This game deserves my recommendation and a 9.5/10 rating.

Hero of the Kingdom is a point and click adventure mixed with a resource manager. You travel through different overview screens, visiting villages, mountains, forests and so on. On your way, you pick up items either by clicking (said "Search those 5 pixels"-moments) or by buying/trading/questing at NPCs. The more you progress, the more resources you have. For example you need Energy to fight (a boar or wolf costs X energy), which you replenish by sleeping. You can sleep when you pay gold at inns or in the wild, if you have enough food on you (different camping sites ask for different kinds of food). You can also carry items, which hold longer (Weapons and tools, though they might break sometimes)
Sadly, the system is kinda broken after a while for those, who notice how to milk endless gold out of the resource cycle. Maybe a patch would help here?
The artwork is pretty good, I expect the designer to give us a full course of his abilities in the future. Everything looks very detailed and alive and every screen carries a different kind of atmosphere with it The background music is nothing outstanding, but it doesnt kill the atmosphere either. "Generic" comes to my mind here.
Still, seeing as this is an endless orgy of clicking and searching I can not recommend it at its current price of 6 Euro. Maybe some mini-games and riddles would have helped to add simply MORE CONTENT to this game. In the end I just played it to gather all achievments, having absolutely no interest for an ending (and there is only one. Why not make different endings, depending on how you choose to solve quests and stuff? A simple BAD Ending would even give more depth...)

I enjoyed this game immensely. I'll break things down as follows:
As far as the story goes, the game does a very good job of not making it too obvious (in most cases) who the next victim/culprit will be, or what the final act will entail. While not quite a masterpiece, the story is still fairly intriguing and full of mystery/twists/reveals. The cast is overall enjoyable with good voice acting. Fans of the Zero Escape series should enjoy this.
And for the gameplay, fans of the Phoenix Wright series will be right at home. The mysteries aren't quite as difficult to solve, and many things are made easier, but the overall flow is almost exactly the same (investigation followed by a trial) and it works out pretty well. I especially enjoyed the "final argument' segments where you have to put together a comic ordering the panels correctly to summarize how the murder was committed. there are some gimmicky reaction based elements that I found troublesome, but they didn't hinder my overall enjoyment.
There's also a gameplay element similar to Persona's "social link" mechanic, where you can spend time with other students. While it serves for a nice change of pace, it's largely irrelevant (it unlocks skills for trials that are marginally useful) and also skippable if you're not into that sort of thing.
Anyone that's a fan of a good story/mystery-based video game (or a fan of the Zero Escape / Phoenix Wright series) should enjoy Danganronpa. I can't wait until the sequel hits steam!

Ridiculously addictive!
It's all about staying organized and maintaining a buffer.
Everything is snappy, graphical/navigation glitches are non-existant, and of course it's absolutely beautiful!
Also, when you want to know about something before you build it, there is plenty of info in-game.
Also, I like to be able to play a game slowly, and Planetbase allows that - you can't do anything with the game paused, but 1x speed is slow enough to really analyze the colony.  I think the game is meant to be played with a combination of high and low speed, and it does get a bit tedious if you only ever play at 1x because things really do happen VERY slowly.
I hate to list off cons, but there are a few:
My biggest issue with Planetbase is the layout system - there is no grid, which in itself isn't a problem - it gives the game an organic feel - but frequently you encounter gaps where things
fit, but don't, or you take out one dome and try to put in another that is the same size and it won't fit.  There is also a whole lot of slowly roving your mouse around until the template turns green, meaning you can place a structure.  This can be very frustrating.
The AI does have a logic to it (I suppose it would, wouldn't it..?), and once you start to figure out how it behaves the game gets to be a whole lot more playable.  That said, there is definitely some fine-tuning to do, particularly when it comes to distance-based prioritization (an engineer will do one of two queued jobs and then return to the airlock because an engineer on the other side of the base is queued for the other job, for instance), although I haven't encountered any major issues with pathfinding.  I'd like to say the issues are just a part of the challenge, but in many cases it's a matter of foregoing a completely logical course of action because you know the AI won't get it, or you're forced to micromanage one action at a time rather than queue a series of actions.
Still.  I've played for 49.4 hours at this point, so I can hardly say I don't enjoy the game.  In fact, I'm probably going to go back and play some more right now.

TL; DR: Excellent, very enjoyable, "build-a-colony-up" genre game set in space on uninhabited planets; Well worth the purchase.  Excellent, excellent, job by an unknown (to this reviewer) publisher, Madruga Works.
------------------
Longer Review:
Graphics -
Pros: It is a very good looking, clean game with good usage of flares, reflections, shadows, light and dark during night and day.
Cons: After a while all of the bubble-domes start getting repetitive, although, I have not yet build the Farm Dome so we'll see.
Sound -
Pros: For a build-up-a-colony game, the most you hope for is background sounds and a repetitive soundtrack that doesn't distract, but provides ambiance to the setting of the game.  Madruga Works did just that.
Cons: None.
Build Types:
Pros: Despite the all-bubble dome look, there is a good selection of build types, build-additions, etc. to make your colony unique.  Additionally, there are several types of colonist (humans & robots) which you can attract and perform various jobs.
Build Action:
Pros: The actual building up of domes and structures is pretty good.  You assign a task and the various members of society add that to their to-do list.  Materials are assembled, and the assigned task is built once things are in place.  Buildings are linked to one another for power/water/etc. and you assemble a mesh network of domes for the society.  It's a generally good system, and I would like to see it get even better.
Changes I hope get made:
1.  Actual placement of buildings is still a bit clunky in that there is a larger-than-should-be required distance between domes.  I would like to see this get reduced to 0 in some cases, such that you could adjoin two domes edge to edge.  This change would greatly enhance the game IMO.  Yes, sometimes you want a corridor, other times though, you dont.
2.  There is still a builder-gets-stuck-inside-what-it's-building error.  IE - If I build 4 buildings and connect them into a square, there is a chance the builder will get stuck inside and I'll have to demo/rebuild.
3.  I would like to see a large indoor water feature, eg Aquaculturing fish and clams.
That's all, overall it's a very good game that could make a leap to best in class if they can do a bit more differentiation and add more fluid design.
My colony right now:
Good job, Madruga Works, good job.

One of the most "pure" puzzle-platformers that I've played, sometimes to a fault.  You are tossed into a level with a set of tools and a set amount of times to use them, and then asked to navigate to find all of your eggs.  The majority of the levels are short enough to not be too frustrating, but some of the later, longer levels have an absurd amount of steps to complete in order to finish them.  The difference between this and other games is the complete lack of hand-holding in a level.  When a new tool is introduced you will learn how to use it in a sort of tutorial level, and after that you're on your own for figuring out how to use the tool in future levels.  For me the issue is that there are a HUGE amount of variables when it comes to playing through each level; where, when, and how to use each tool will make a big effect on the outcome.  And it can be quite easy to get stuck, though thankfully the included ability to rewind time after getting stuck or dying is a huge relief and necessity.  Most of the normal levels I had a lot of fun with, but sometimes they get exhaustively long and I would have to look up hints online in order to not be too overwhelmed.  It's a game that requires a lot of experimentation in order to succeed, but when you do it's very satisfying, and thankfully most levels have multiple ways to solve them.

Well, to start with, I have played all CXL there is, from the very first one to this - very last one. And I will have to say that this is however worth the money for once. I am actually impressed by the small things I have been annoyed by in earlier iterations of this franchise. Let me sumarize briefly what elements they've improved, and what is not changed about the game.
This is my list of things I have considered annoying for the past few games, and the status of their current state.
While they've improved plenty, there are also many issues here. Some are even newly introduced and others are adopted from back in the previous versions.
If you place long stretches of roads, it becomes laggy when you lay new roads intersecting these roads. It stutters a lot but is not unplayable. They should fix this very soon.
Broadcasting can introduce some lagg as well, Especially when you try to zone large districts.
If you a large amount of cities, it can have a slight effect on the trade menu.
I have already experienced savegame corruption and crashes from loading saves. To avoid this, do not use workshop yet. And do not download the community pack yet. There are issues which have deleted my savegames  (or they just disapeard from the load menu). And when I load pre-workshopped saves the game just crashes. This is a must solve as soon as possible..

If experienced more instabillities, the game is very laggy when deploying new Metro Systems or other routes for public transport. Once you lay more than 10 stations of metro, and have a few lines running allready, you will start get lags and other issues like problems to move about, long waits while calculations are done.
Another point here is that it seems they have downtweaked the amount of people using the metro and bus systems, making it harder to maintain traffic flow and forcing you to be really smart when planning ahead for a new metro system. This can of course just be my imagination, but I feel that I need to be more careful now than in previous games.
OmniCorp trading is just the same as before.

It's worth mentioning a few of the things new to this game in terms of content. Here are a few things i've come across so far:
It looks to me as if they have tweaked the plopping of farming zones, it is easier to make irregular shaped farms around corners and along the boundries of the areas where farms can be plopped.
Terrain responds better to changes done by development. For example, you will notice that laying out all types of zones in slopes and uneven terrain is easier and you experience less problems with road issues (Where roads cannot be constructed.) This is done by finding alternative paths for them in a more smooth way. I like it this way, makes more sense.
If you construct tubes with max amount of stations, they will just disappear after a while, leaving only the stations behind and potentionally crushing your infrastructure. This has to be fixed at some stage very soon!
All in all, the game is a fresh breeze of cold air on a hot summer day.. Still there are a few issues here and there, surely these will be fixed in later patches for THIS game and not for future COMPLETE rewrites of the engine.
For the
folks out there, many of the problematic traffic, population and polution issues are solved. And I can confirm that it runs on all my cores and has so far not burned up all my memory (at a stable 2.2GB RAM) I'd buy it.

An odd visual novel where Jill's your name and bartending is your game, in all senses of the word. Your role in the game is more of a conversational one where peculiar characters walk into the bar and you just talk to them. It's pretty simple. It taps into one of the very few positives that arise from public facing jobs, in that you get to hear odd and crazy stories and learn about people's interesting lives. It cuts out the areas where the customers smell like they've not washed for their entire lives or the verbal harassment (well most of it) but you can't win all battles, eh?
The characters you interact with are wonderful, unique and interesting. One day you'll be talking to a sex robot about how she deals with more violent customers, the next you'll be talking to an actual brain in the jar about sentience and AIs, in between it hitting on you, and then maybe next a dog in sunglasses and a Hawaiian shirt will be talking to you. While it may sound crazy at times, it's fun and interesting. Philosophies are exchanged between customers and yourself and lives are learned about and stories are witnessed.
I came to really like a lot of the regulars you deal with and kept on going, one day after the next, slowly burning the midnight oil, purely because I wanted to find out what may have happened to one of them during a terrorism attack.
The setting is that of a crime riddled dystopian city, Glitch City, where corruption and cyber crime run rampant, but it's less about that and more on the characters within this setting, you still learn about the city, but only through word of mouth as you, Jill, live a rather secluded life of drinking beer in your flat or working in the bar.
The gameplay element is loose at best. Occassionaly the patrons of the bar will ask for a drink and you mix it for them, a simple situation of finding the drink in the book and just putting enough of each coloured chemical in. This is probably the biggest area the game lacks in purely just because of the few times the game gives you a few curve balls, where it may test you on what characters had been talking about. It's not that these were bad, but that they were so few. A lot of the time the patrons will just ask for a drink by name, plain and simple, which is fine, but a little boring. There were a few times when someone asked for something based on the death of a bartender's best friend and it was something that had been mentioned prior in the story and I got such a buzz from remembering that. Otherwise it's just one guy who asks purposefully obtuse requests which aren't fun either, although still pretty hard to fail, apparently.
You don't exactly need a guide for the game as it's simple enough to follow and fulfill requests correctly.
A wonderful soundtrack that goes along side the game as well as character portraits that are wonderfully detailed and gorgeous to look at there's not a lot to hate about the game, in my opinion. It's a wonderful game to sit back and relax to maybe after a long day of living in the real world. Grab a drink, and just quietly click through people's lives and maybe you too will feel genuinely tense at times as you learn of characters being in danger.

VA-11 HALL-A's pixel art is beautiful. The dark/neon cyberpunk color palette fits perfectly with the game's theme and setting. You can either choose to play with the flat, plain art, or to turn on "scanlines" (just rows of alternating darkened pixels). It's a minor thing on paper, but it really adds to the mood of the game (I personally played with the scanlines on all the time).
You're more than likely to find at least one of the characters likeable. The cast is incredibly diverse in race, sexuality, gender, etc., in a way that doesn't seem forced or awkward at all (except maybe in a few small instances, but even then that might be just me), and would probably only upset the worst "anti-SJW" types. The sprites are all very well designed, and while some characters look like they fit the art style of the game a little less, it's never enough to be a real bother.
The game is styled like a visual novel; primarily dialogue, but it diverges from the common formula by throwing in the bartending aspect and a few other gameplay twists along the way. To discuss a few of the gameplay features:
The soundtrack, is probably one of my favorites in any game so far. There's a mix of fast and slow songs available on the jukebox, and they've all got a cool cyberpunk-futuristic vibe, but they've all got distinct enough "moods" that the song playing in the background can have a noticeable bearing on the feeling of a scene.
Last but not least, replay value. There's a sort of New Game+, where you keep you items/money. It sort of feels like it might be hassle to go through all the days again, so I haven't done it, but there is some value in playing through again. Though few, there are a few moments in the game that can affect the "cut scene" you see at the very end. In addition, some customers give you a choice in drink, and some drinks give you choice in alcohol level, which results in variations in dialogue. Unless you're very invested in the game, it's unlikely you'll want to go through and see all the possibilities.
All in-all, I'd give it a
, definitely recommend to anyone who likes a good story and has ~8 hours to kill. The prologue and "Anna" demo are small, but very interesting/fun additions. I had only very minor gripes (the lack of real explanation on the consequences of your actions and how the shop works, and I wish the jukebox had a "save playlist" function), but otherwise I really enjoyed everything about the game.
P.S. This game is a bit deeper gameplay-wise than you might think. Don't be afraid to try doing things differently, maybe even "wrong".

This is a game that would be describable as "lovably janky" if that jank wasn't "a lack of handy UI features and wild inconsistency". Some dungeons are massive (and I do mean MASSIVE) mazes, but there's no minimap there, because as far as I can tell, the minimap is actually just a top-down screenshot of the map itself, and the level is too large for it. Candice Debebe's Incredibly Trick Lifestyle is a quirky game with a weird plot, even weirder characters, and a soundtrack that has to be heard to be believed. It's a game that at first glance looks like a poorly made rushed project that was hastily put on Steam to try to make a quick buck, but it actually had a lot of work put into it, despite it's shoddy appearance. It's a silly yet charming game, and if you're into silly joke games like I am, I say you should check it out. A few words of advice though on some improvements that could be made:
1. Add a run function so Candice can move a bit faster.
2. Add a map for Digital Hex or at least make it a bit easier to navigate. That was probably one of the most tedious parts that i came across and can be off putting since it's pretty early in the game.
3. Invest in a pop shield for your microphone.
4. There's a "bug" where you can use the boat to climb over the guard and get on the Lusty Mermaid before completing the necessary steps which should probably be fixed.
5. The price is a bit high to be honest, and I would definitely recommend the game 100% if it was at a lower price, but I'm not sure how much power the creator has over setting the price.
Overall, although it may look like Steam shovelware at first glance, the game is much more than that. It's not just an asset flip. It has original models, an original plot, and a soundtrack that although the singing may be not top notch, the music itself is actually well composed and the pianist definitely knows their way around a piano. Is it stupid? Yes. Should it be on Steam? Probably not. But for all its ridiculousness its amusing and you can't help but have at least a little bit of respect for the developer putting the amount of effort they did into this wacky RPG. I recommend this game if you are into silly joke games as this one has a lot of charm.

I really wanted to give this game a good review. I love the visual style and the games has a lot of potential. Here are the problems:
1a.  Colonist AI needs A LOT of work. There gets to be a point where the colonists get depressed and only get out of bed long enough to hit up the canteen or the bar, then go back to bed. Which is fine until all your Biologists start doing it at the same time and your entire colony starves to death. (Maybe I shouldn't keep naming my colony Miranda!?)
1b.  Producing to 99%. Colonists will work a project (i.e. refining ore, creating vitromeat, building spares, etc.) until it's nearly complete and move onto something else. And very potentially (read: commonly) never come back to it.
1c. The sceenic route. The coloists will take the longest path possible every time, Airlocks abound and they take the one furthest from the module they need to get to or exterior worksite they are destined for.
2. Random event generator needs a little work. It random, really random, annoyingly random. Which is fine for a simulator, but a city builder/strategy game should have a little bit more consistancy.
3. Only one "stragey". There is only one successfuly build path out of the initial game, there after it's a game of ratios which is where the entertainment ends. Moreover if you play the tutorial you're given the stategy, so really you're just clicking through the motions.
Things I recommend as quick fixes to outright issues:
1. Automate refinery projects. Require a Biologist/Engineer to start them but remove the need for their continued oversight.
2. Instantainous trade. Colonists occasionally starve to death while a trading ship full of food waits for their payment to be delivered by a bot/colonist taking the long way round the planet! Sometimes, it's even the colonist carrying the payment that dies. >.<
Given some more work this game could be amazing. Just not right now. I look forward to playing updates!

If Ghouls and Ghosts and Actraiser had a baby, and they had a twisted uncle called Donkey Kong Country, then that's where Volgarr came from.
A new game done in the style of old, it really is quite a gem. Simplistic as can be in terms of gameplay, though that is not to say that learning how to control Volgarr is not an obstacle with a nice skill ceiling. Some may consider his controls rather rigid, but if you learn how to use him, he's fluid and most importantly, much like Ghouls and Ghosts, very fair. Remember guys, sometimes you have to jump back a bit before you jump forward to get to where you want to go -- little ghouls and ghosts tip for those not used to this jumping system.
From a level design perspective, I personally quite enjoy both paths of the game. However, I think overall the Valkyrie path has superior level design. The crystal path suffers a bit from too many enemies and not enough platforming, but, that may be your thing. Enemies are in and of themselves obstacles, but the game is at it's best when you have to manage both at the same time. So learn to Volgarr well and experience the bliss of the Valkyrie path.
The soundtrack is pretty good, but not good enough to warrant listening to it beyond your 50th hour of playing -- though I think most won't play it that much, so you're fine!
From a replayability perspective, the game doesn't offer much variety once you complete both paths. There are no alternative ways to play, so, once you've beat it, you can either stop there, or grit your teeth and become the best Volgarr player you can be. As a speedgame, Volgarr is simple, but very skillful and both a joy to play and to watch. It may not look particularly "fast", but, trust me, there's always time to save. So if speedrunning is your thing, by all means pick it up and grace the leaderboard -- please, I seriously wish more people ran this game.

PlanetBase is a pretty good game where you basically build structures to expand your colony in a planet (which is unlocked after reaching their respective milestones). The first planet is a Mars type planet, which is also where the tutorial is so you can learn the basics. It plays like a city building type game, as well as Banished, so it's building the essential structures (Bio-domes, processing plants, factories, solar panels, etc) to survive. Fail to do so, your colony will fail quickly.
I do have a few gripes about the game though. One is that it's easy to lose your colony because the AI just gives up if they have needs that are not met and they end up dying. Another gripe is that you can't maximize space because all the buildings have to have a certain amount of space around them, sometimes leaving big gaps in-between that could be utilized. A final one is that once all the human colonists die, that's it. Robots apparently don't count toward the population and maintain the essential buildings for the next ship of colonists to arrive.
Apart from those cons, there are lots of positive. One is obviously it's set in space! Another is that you could play this until you meet your milestones or when you get tired. A final one is that you get to select where on the planet you want to land your first (second, third, etc) colonists, so you don't have to sit and suffer through the same location over and over again. This is also a pro because it enhances replayability, letting you challenge yourself in different areas. However, the weather happens to be exactly the same depending on the planet.
Overall, it's a fun game that you'll spend hours on!

Magic 2014 is by no means a perfect game. It has the occasional game breaking glitch, and has a terrible dlc system in the form of sealed play slots.
On the other hand, i'm hard pressed to think of anything else that Magic 2014 fails to accomplish.
The game is beautiful, and it has near endless replay value. 21 decks exist in the game, although about half need to be bought as dlc (buy during a sale if you decide you like the game enough to do so!). Each deck has a radically different play style from the others, providing the basis for a solid multiplayer meta where decks tier differently and each have their various strengths and weaknesses (except Avacyn's Glory. that deck is broken as hell).
The game's campaign is good fun to play through, and is very well paced. For a novice MTG player, it provides him with a good understanding of the game, gradually increasing in difficulty and complexity as it goes along. For the veteran MTG player, it's good fun in the sense that he gets to relive cards from across the history of magic, find out about card combinations he never thought of, and more. Just a warning: the balance of the tutorial boss battle is rather off, and you may end up having to retry it over and over. If this is your first DOTP game, like was the case with me, remember that you can edit your deck in the main menu to make this battle easier!
Multiplayer has some issues where some people complain of connection difficulties. From my experience, connection issues do not occur when you go through the custom game menu or host your own game, whereas the quick game option is a headache to connect to. Occasionally games will hang halfway through - i suspect this happens when the host disconnects or lags out. There's no good fix for that and it has ruined a fair share of games for me. Very annoying when it happens, but otherwise multiplayer plays well enough to provide great fun. The community is very much alive, and you may end up remembering quite a few names that you see around often.
There's real value for money in this game, especially if bought for sale like i did. It's definitely a better buy then paper Magic, anyway, where a good Standard deck could cost you $400 USD. Pick it up, have fun, and avoid Sealed Play like the plague.
Certainly not as complex as actual tabletop magic, but it is a good stand in.

NEW VERSION... BUT SEVERELY LACKING THE 'NEW'
As soon as I heard that a fresh new Cities XL game was on the horizon, I had really big hopes that this would finally be a new start for the series, a proper major upgrade from Cities XL that maintained the best bits of the series whilst introducing significant improvements in gameplay, customisation and capabilities. This is a game that had to be MORE that Cities XL was and, given the title's new X, one would assume this to be the case. But, alas, two hours in and I find myself disappointed.
Like with previous annual 'new releases' it feels that Focus have merely taken the same old game, given it 2015's lick of paint and sent it on its merry way. Underneath it all, this game feels exactly the same as the previous three incarnations and offers very little in the way of new. Don't get me wrong, it's not a 'bad' game. As city-builders go, Cities XL (or XXL) is a very different take compared to others in the genre, and where it excels in some areas of micro-management, it's lacking in others. But ultimately, if you are looking for an evolution from the previous versions of the game, XXL just does not cut it.
Focus are crying "wolf" with this latest offering, and had I known Cities XXL would be an almost identical carbon copy of Cities XL, I would have stuck with the Platinum version and invested the money in alternative new takes on the city-building genre, such as 'Cities: Skylines'. Whilst Focus' rivals, Maxis, may have their critics and problems with their latest SimCity offering, they've atleast made the effort to evolve the series, even if it is with varying degrees of success. And while the latest SimCity has been an education for Maxis, Focus have yet to demonstrate that evolution is in their nature.

Apperently this game had development costs. I'm not entirely sure what they were, because 90% of the game is identical to Cities 2012. When I played the tutorial and realised it was *exactly* the same as before, horrible character graphics and all, I stopped and went "No one else can make this mistake."
As many people have pointed out, support for various graphics or processor options does not constitute a new game, nor does slightly increasing the number of buildings.
Cities 2012 wasn't even that good a city builder, or one that gives you any level of connection to what you've built. The reason why I purchased this was down to it being marketed elseware as an "anti-SimCity" with much more space to build and better options overall. And it probably is better than the release version of SimCity. But that was several years ago, and things have changed in that game that make it much more engaging and less restrictive. This on the other hand feels like a £15-£30 cash grab.
I am going to play more of this, and try to establish if anything of note has actually changed and if not I will edit this review accordingly to point these things out. But don't buy this game, buy Anno, buy SimCity, buy a casual city building game on your tablet but do not buy this game until other users have established whether or not this is just Cities 2012 with a slightly cleaner interface and less horrible music.
EDIT: It does feel faster, having played it for a couple of hours. But it looks nearly *identical* to Cities 2012, a now three year old title. The interface is better and the music is better. Nothing else is different.
I would go so far as to call this a con. I do not say that lightly and I don't want to sound overly dramatic, but it does feel as though Focus Interactive have promised a new car and just tuned the old one and sold it back to me at full price.

Switchcars is the game that every infinite runner style game should strive for. The game looks initially simple, with a grapple hook player running on a field with the ability to instantly enter any vehicle and switch between 3 at a whim to take advantage of the different terrains on the map. The game randomly generates the course of terrain types and it's up to you to grab the most efficient vehicle for the track ahead. However, you slowly begin to peel back layers in the game that you weren't expecting. The game's timer doesn't simply end the game if you fail to reach it, it unleashes a chaotic worm beast that tries to kill you. If you grapple onto an object, it'll sling you towards it at breakneck speed (quite literally) and you must dodge or enter the object you grappled on to. Ambulances heal you while you drive, every vehicle uses fuel differently, there's powerups to change the vehicle's fuel source and terrain specility or add weapons. Sporting a rogue-lite system of unlocking new vehicles and tracks as you play, I highly recommend this game to any fan of rogue-lite games and those who enjoy the "perfect run" style games.

Danganronpa is an incredibly stylistic visual novel with a morbid atmosphere where you play as Makoto Naegi with 14 other students, trapped together, in a prestigious private school known as "Hope's Peak Academy". The only way to escape however, is to kill.
But wait just one second, there's fine-print, isn't there? T_T
In order to escape or "graduate", nobody must know who is the real killer, by placing the blame on someone else, only then, may the blackened one can truly escape from the despair that is Hope's Peak Academy.
In a classic "whodunnit" game, you're tasked to find clues & evidence leading to the true murderer followed by a showdown in a class trial, piercing through statements & contradictions for the execution judgement. If you get it right, the killer gets punished. If you get it wrong, the real killer walks away and everyone else gets punished i.e. dead.
It's a dialogue-heavy game with some engaging gameplay mechanics that'll leave you hooked for more. You just have to try out Danganronpa. It may deter you if you knew there's no multiple-routes in this game which is expected for most visual novel. Hell, if you have no love for visual novels, you might not enjoy this game.

It starts as a simple point & click RPG, if there even is such a thing, and becomes progressively complex, fun, and in some spots even brilliant. Unfortunately, the story is very short, and grinding around for stuff to do kinda gets repetitive, for that, you can progress through the game however you want. Hunt, gather, fish, and craft potions, trade them around, or sell them for money, complete small quest and you're done. It's true that it could have been more, it even looks like it could have been more. The map screen is large and it unlocks as you visit each area for the first time. However, I initially though it's going to be completely uncovered, but it's not. Still, if you're not using the helpful quick travel and instead try to backtrack area by area, you might get confused at first. The graphics are pretty, there is no animation, but it still looks great and nostalgic. The soundtrack is okay, I guess, although I wish it wasn't just that one song the entire time, accompanied by sounds of cows, goats, dogs, birds, bears, wolves, and other "ambients" over and over again. But you can turn the volume down whenever you wish, fortunately. If more than anything, this game made me nostalgic and opened an appetite for older RPGs. Thanks to this game, I am now craving for Nox.
That being said, I recommend this game.

Returning player, used to play before in 2014-ish, returned due to destroyer update (as I liked frigate gameplay, sadly now impossible to play)

As enjoyable as before ? No
Basically this game is a arena based game
PVP sets you in a arena with different objectives ranging for plantings bombs to team death matchs and capture points, you get unlimited respawn but in recon where the designed commander has to be alive to allow respawn
PVE sets you in a different arena, sometime with 3 different section (allowing you to respawn after each section) or a 1 block mission like fire support (no respawn), objectifs are usually destroy designed targets/capture points/kill boss
Open space is explained in the rest of the review
-Looks good
-Ship handling is decent
-3 faction to choose from with the only big game changer being the Long Range Frigate (LRF) for the Empire and Jericho as the ship capability are quite the same otherise for the same ship classes
-Open space mod (more like linked arena maps, because its litteraly the PVP maps with bots & loot linked via portals most of the time)
-Ship design is very caracteristic of a faction
-Can run on potato PC
-The game lore evolves with updates (some old map station in open space are now turned into wreck field)
-Other stuff I didn't mentioned because I'm too lazy to remember them
-New tiering / unlock system (January 2016) :
For War Thunder players, its the same here minus the BR thing
For non War Thunder players : you have 5 tiers, to go the next tier you need to unlock every ship of the previous tier, so if your like 1 gameplay style your forced to play all the other one too if you want to unlock the next ship of your favourite class
-Remember what I said about the LRF?
Forget Jericho for 90% of the time
-Fire a manually guided torpedo travelling at ~500m per sec
-AOE effect
-Possible to detonate it at any moment
-Create a radiation cloud dealing medium amount of damage for 6 second
-Don't require a direct line of sight
-Reload every 15 sec
-Easy to dodge
Guardian frigtate : module destroying any type of guided missile
Flares : all ships can carry it and it reload rather fast, disable torpedo steering controls
Small ships : outrun your torpedo speed
-Enter a sniper mod when activated, fire a projectile travelling at ~3km per sec
-Weapon can't be fired directly after activation
-Reload in 2.5 sec
-Has +2km more range than a Jericho torpedo
-Afterburn damage dealing 25% of you shot damage 0.5 sec later
-Require a direct line of sight
-Deal more damage than a Jericho torpedo
-Hard to dodge
-Solid cover
-Small ships : hard to aim
-Engineer shield wall wich nearly no one ever use
Due to the huge firerate / projectile speed and countermeasure gap, torpedoes falls flat into the utteraly useless section

Guardian basically play the same role as their name, they guard allies with powerfull defensives modules, and act as meat shield so they got one of the best HP & shield stats, its good defence is countered by bad offensive capacity (mind that a figher is outgunning you)
Destroyers get 3x their HP & shields stats, they are more bullet spongy (is that even a word?) than the ship with this specefic role in mind with the icing on top being actually able to kick asses and move faster
The only viable firgate are engineers because you will always need a healer and the Empire LRF because of reasons stated earlier

I knew roughly, what I was getting into, before I bought the game.
I thought "this could be fun". Solving puzzles. Taking in the beautiful environment.
....
Well, I guess not.
It's really exactly as tedious as it seemed at first glance.
Which wouldn't be that bad, except the game doesn't communicate AT ALL what you're supposed to do.
....
Sometimes you see an entirely new and strange puzzle and the game just expects you to guess that surely you'll be taught how to solve it in another location via little tutorial puzzles - so that you can just continue onwards for now. While on other instances the game expects you to, though you have NO CLUE AT ALL that the puzzle is even possible for you to solve at that moment, somehow just FEEL that there are clues hidden around you.
...
I really tried hard to like this game, but I just kept feeling completely confused of what was expected of me,
of what I should solve and of what I should be able to solve in the first place.
Where should I go? What knowledge was I expected to already possess?
...
...
Another example, which frustrated me immensely, was the final switch below the desert.
So I solved all the tedious reflection-based puzzles, and some door opens, and there is a simple switch again.
I press it, rumbling starts and I instinctively go back a few steps to see, if my surroundings change in some way.
At which point it turns out the area around the switch was an elevator, which now lifts itself out of view, -
WITHOU ME ON BOARD. I couldn't believe it.
This should have been a moment of relief und pride, some sense of accomplishment at least -
I beat the whole damn level ! - But no, I just stood there below the earth, trying desperately
to get that freaking elevator back down, which of cause didn't work.
So in the end I walked all the way up again through all the puzzle rooms I just solved an felt IMMENSELY frustrated.
This game lacks any kind of reward, or feeling of accomplishment even. You literally solve hundreds of boring puzzles like a little monkey, without gaining anything. The beautiful nature is there from the beginning, nothing to gain here. New abilities, or quicker movement or leveling up or WHATEVER ELSE - nope, nothing to gaing here.
Just quotations of long dead people, which often feel more like the game is lecturing you, then anything else.
I really hoped, this game wouldn't make playing it SO DAMN HARD.
Maybe I even try playing a little on, later.
But for now I really REALLY need anything with even the slightest bit of fun.
Best way i can describe this game is it's like somebody dropped a lot of puzzles from a tablet game into a walking sim.

Games with puzzles which are not just trivial are few and far between. The Witness presents a mental workout that I really appreciated.
However, the game lacks any kind of story, narrative, action or meaning and all you get for your efforts is the satisfaction of having figured out the puzzle and some insufferably smug philosphical readings which are completely unrelated to the game.
The island is pretty, but following a path for what feels like ages to find that it only goes to a nice view or a spot where the scenery lines up into a picture wears very thin, very fast.

A great introduction to the card game, Magic the Gathering. 2014 DotP is a great way for anyone interested in this very popular and very fun card game. Duels of the Planeswalkers is a format in Magic that limits the cards you can use to give you an introduction of sorts into how the game works. Still a great game for Magic verterns as well with things like sealed and the multiplayer leader boards.

Alright, here's the thing: If you're a seasoned vet of the Magic card game, this may not be for you.  The simplicity and lack of real deck-building could be a real turn-off.  Unless you participate in Sealed Play (which has a laughably short campaign and limits you to only about 100 cards by the time its done), you are shoe-horned into using themed decks within the game that you must unlock.  There is no way to collect massive amounts of cards and create your own custom deck.
That being said, Magic 2014 is a real solid way to be introduced to the card game, and I think that's what WoTC is going for here.  It explains the rules of the game rather well, introduces you to the strategy surrounding the game, and gives you some pre-constructed decks to whet your teeth on.  In all honesty, what they want you to do is get so interested in the game that you feel compelled to go out and buy the cards in real life... which is what happened to me.
If you like card games !! :D

As with the previous game, the cards and decks included are not all necessarily legal. I doubt there's enough legal cards to make this many decks, but I would've liked it if there at least some.
Overall a strong game pick for the price. Tons of hours (and grinding, you have to play and win with a deck 30 times to unlock all it's locked cards, for EACH deck), but it's rewarding to see how you continually improve and develop strategies.

Candice DeBébé's Incredibly Trick Lifestyle is essentially a joke/parody action RPG that follows an extremely chavvy women on a quest to retrieve the fake tan van that was stolen from her own town (Think Ali G). The graphics are bad, the story is bad, gameplay is also pretty bad but still I enjoyed my time playing this.
As a brit I can relate to the jokes and songs found in the game that are all very tongue in cheek. I feel a lot of this humour would be totally lost on other nationalities so if you aren’t British or in some way very knowledgeable of British culture this may be a total no no especially when it comes to the games soundtrack.
Along the way you gain items, fight bosses and go through a number of different worlds and levels in an ultra-light action RPG game. The game is bad… in most ways but (and you are probably going to just have to take my word on this) it is oddly fun to play and I found myself continuing even though my usual common sense indicator told me the game wasn’t any good.
At £3.99 or your regional equivalent there are better games out there but for the price of a pint in London, a magazine or a coffee you will find a gag game that will make you chuckle and offer at least something.
This game really isn’t for everyone and most will probably not “get it” but Candice DeBébé's Incredibly Trick Lifestyle is a massive tongue in cheek game that for those of you who will get the references is a giggle worth undertaking.

On the surface, this game is just a big bunch of stereotypes put together. However, this turns out to be one of its biggest strengths. The game strikes a good balance between rolling with the tropes and subverting them, constantly leading you into an 'obvious' conclusion and then pulling the rug from underneath you. Then, as soon as you start accounting for this, the game once again switches gears to keep you guessing. I encountered quite a few unexpected plot twists during my first playthrough of the PSP fan translation a few years back, which was a pleasant surprise given the predictable nature of most video game stories.
While the story is still pretty fun even if you do know what's going to happen, if you are currently unspoiled, I suggest you try and keep it that way. Stay away from forums, don't look online for fan art and for God's sake
(I managed to spoil myself by reading the tracklist during my first playthrough).
In terms of replayability, I consider the game to be worth at least two playthroughs: there is a lot of clever foreshadowing that you will simply not get on your first playthrough hidden throughout the game and focussing your gift-giving and free time activities on different characters will reward you with additional backstory for them. As such, I'd say the current asking price is very fair, even for a six-year old port.
Aside from buying the game based on its merits, if you are at all interested in seeing similar games get ported from Sony's ill-fated handhelds to Steam, buying Dangan Ronpa is a good signal to companies like Spike Chunsoft that there is, in fact, a market for them. It's unfortunate for Sony, but thanks to Spike Chunsoft, I won't have to consider buying a Vita (TV) anymore to play the second installment of this series and I sincerly hope that other hidden gems will eventually make their way to Steam as well.

Then, why I do not recommend this game?
Because of it's gameplay. And not because it's difficult, that's not the point. The problem here is the "fake" difficulty.
The ONLY reason to play this game for more than 30 mins it's not the story (there is none), it's not the graphics or the music: it's the gameplay. It's not difficult because the game has good AI, or because enemies are unpredictable.
It's difficult because we're not used to this kind of games, and after dying 20 times and reaching the second checkpoint full geared you realize that it's not challenging, it's boring, plain and simple.
If you like to memorize patterns and play for hours without really any kind of motivation except to complete a game so you can tell your friends "hey, u know what? I finished volgarr the viking, i'm such a pro player", then this game is for you.
If you're looking for a game with a story, with good IA, or with a real challenge that goes beyond dying and repeating the same thing over and over, then this is not for you.

Overview: Retro Style 2D action Platformer
The Good:
+ The developers intentions were to create a retro 2D action game and in many regards succeeded wonderfully. This game is easy to learn but hard to master.
+ Great controls
+ The game is hard only because it requires memorization of the level and enemy patterns to succeed at the game.  With only 6 levels each only taking around 10 minutes to complete...IF you know what you're doing. If you are playing for your first time then expect each level to take roughly over an hour to complete.
+ Only one checkpoint per level. (This is an old school 2d action game after all!)
+ The game has a normal path and a hard path to complete. You can only unlock the hard path by successfully collecting treasure chests throughout the level without getting hit.
+Three different endings depending on which path you took.
+ Great sound and music
The Bad:
- Warning! may cause stress, frustration, and other bad feelings.
Conclusion
A game like this is difficult to review in modern times because the developers intention was to create a game a few decades earlier.  This game borrows heavily from Ghosts n' Goblins.  It was "refreshing" to play an old school game, it makes you realize just how much easier games have come.

One of the most innovative, challenging, and rewarding puzzle games I've ever played.
This game does not hold your hand in the least. It can be frustrating sometimes, but the experience is ultimately rewarding, as it gives you chance to decide where to go and what to do, and lets you toy with puzzles as much as you like without interupting you with tutorials. If one puzzle type stumps you, move to a new area. You have to beat a certain number of areas to win the game, but you don't have to beat all of them, so you can pick and choose which areas are worth finishing to some extent (I really wish I knew this before getting to the end of the game).
Each puzzle type is a new twist on the same puzzle format, so everything feels fresh yet related. This makes it easy to combine puzzle types, which makes the late game very interesting. The whole game feels liek a huge connected island with small sections that are completely their own thing yet part of the bigger picture. It works wonderfully.
I don't want to spoil anything to specific. I just want to say that the puzzles are extremely creative and I I found myself gitty to try and solve each problem I found. The more you play, the more you begin to understand the game, and the more fun you having solving it. It's an elegantly designed experience that is a must-try for any puzzle fans.
Very relaxing but also challenges your brain, very fun if you enjoy puzzle games. Even has a touch of undelying story/mystery to it.
