Detailed review ahead.
10/10 Classic arena fps gameplay.  If you liked Unreal Tournament, or are a previous Quake player looking for a different style, this game is great either way.
10/10 Graphics.  They are really well optimized, which is all I really look for, and quite pretty, as an added bonus, and the particles don't kill your GPU as other games might.
7/10 Sound.  The design is really well, and it sounds good, but sometimes it's hard to pinpoint exactly where things are, although this might just be my sound driver.
7/10 Customization.  I've yet to expirement with too much of the HUD, and crosshair changes are kinda confusing at first, but the mouse and keybind settings are where it's at.  You have your bread-and-butter keybinds, you can use any wasd or esdf set up you want, however the mouse settings lack a bit.  You can't set up real mouse acceleration curves, at least to my knowledge, but you can set up acceleration damping.
10/10 Resource allocation.  For myself, it runs at around 1.7 GB of RAM, and takes up 33% of an i7-6700 3.4 GHz processor, and load times are ridiculously fast on a 512 GB SSD, and on a 2TB HDD.  At maximum settings, takes up around 43% of my Nvidia GTX 1070.
10/10 Weapons and Hitreg.  All weapons work just as they should, rocket and other projectile speeds are predictable and great, sniper and headshot registration is amazing, and the alt fires they have work really well, aside from the rocket launcher.
8/10 Movement.  Air control is lacking, but to be expected, and you do have SOME control of where you end up, just not as much as CPMA or Team Fortress 2 or something.  Dashing has a decent cooldown, but sometimes your input gets eaten.  Walljumps and double jumps work smoothly and fluidly, jump height is fantastic for each and every map.  The only movement thing that CAN be wonky, and it's mostly because of the dash timing is the slope jumps. movespeed is fast but not blazing, and you can reliably hit targets once you get muscle memory for aim down. crouch speed is good, not too fast, not too slow.
7/10 Vehicles and Combating them.  The vehicles I can personally say I'm not a fan of, I definitely prefer ground combat, although the modes where you fight them can be extremely fun, taking down a rather large mech with pure firepower feels pretty nice, although they respawn rather fast.
8/ 10 Ground abilities in misc. gamemodes.  You have a stealth ability, the ability to feign death, and a jetpack.  I've not much experience with the jetpack, but feigning death can be useful when timed correctly, especially because you can't tell how much health somebody when they are damaged.  The stealth is ok, makes a relatively loud noise and lasts a very short amount of time, but can be used to get away from a chasing enemy if they don't have headphones.
9/10 Skill factor.  Aiming and movement go hand in hand in this game, you stop you die.  Weapons like the plasma rifle are used for suppression, hitscan used for chasing and securing kills, and they are all great at what they are meant to do.  The only thing that barely limits this is the aforementioned hurt sounds not changing based on HP left, but this is a small factor in the grand scheme of the game.
9/10 HUD and Vitals.  The hud is really good, crosshairs are visible, ammo is easy to see, health is easy to see, the only reason this is a 9/10 is the armor display is rather small.
10/10 Maps and design.  Powerful items are out of the way, health is well distributed, be it a team gamemode or 1v1, armor is strong, so it isn't in the middle of maps usually, and is a rare pickup.  Weapons are plentiful and in appropriate locations for their use.  Maps are pretty and movement through them is fluid and precise, with no sticky geometry in most places.  Visibility is really good, and picking out targets is a breeze.  Chokepoints at flag captures and capture objectives are nice, and health pickups aren't readily available at them all the time, so taking an objective isn't a completely one sided fight.  Respawn timers are frequent enough to be available when you need them, but not so short as so someone on a rampage can continue indefinitely.  The map selection is decent, and there is even the classic DooM 2 Map 7, AKA Dead Simple.
All around a great AFPS, if you are a fan, play this game, and I personally bought the full game to help support some pretty cool devs.  The game is exactly as it is marketed, with a modern twist.  I really like this game, and it's free, so why not give it a try?

Personally, I'm not a huge fan of visual novels, but found myself captivated and enthralled by it, and, despite already knowing the outcome to each case, it was still enjoyable nonetheless to compile the evidence to each trial. So, people who have watched the anime and are uncertain as to whether they should invest money here, take heed: if you liked the anime, this game is not a dissapointment.
That being said, that are some minor things that are offputting. The sprites, mostly in cutscenes, appeared with white edges around them, which detracted away from the overall theme of the setting. Furthuremore, the controls during the trial could've been better optomized to make it feel smoother and whatnot - I found myself repeatedly playing through certain scenes because of controls alone. Despite these, however - I don't think these glitches took away from what really drives this story: the story itself.
All in all, if you're a fan of mystery, this game's anime series, visual novels, or just good story-telling in general, this is worth a playthrough.

Slightly lukewarm recommendation for this one, as I am torn on how I feel about it. On the one hand, I really like the cyberpunk/technoir aesthetic of this game as well as the retro graphics and synth music. It also features callbacks to classic Kojima adventure games like Snatcher and Policenauts. The title of the game is also a fairly unsubtle reference to the Tactical Espionage Action of Metal Gear Solid, but don't be fooled: there is very little 'action' in this game.
If you like Visual Novels and have no problem with minimal gameplay then you will probably enjoy this. The gameplay basically consists of following a recipe book on how to mix drinks and then serving them to the various patrons of VA-11 Hall-A.
In between shifts at the bar you can spend your money on trinkets and merchandise for your apartment, the only caveat being that you need to make sure that you save enough money to pay rent, internet costs and electricity. You also need to be mindful to purchase specific items in order to retain 'focus', but failing to do this just requires you to pay slightly more attention than usual when taking orders for drinks. In other words, the gameplay lacks depth.
It is possible to get a game over if you do your job badly enough, but generally speaking it's not going to be a taxing game even for videogame illiterates or newbies.
**Avoid the next paragraph if you want to avoid minor spoilers**
-----
One aspect of this game that annoyed me perhaps a bit more than it should have was the appearance of a fictional character created by the reviewer Jim Sterling in-universe as a real character in the game. There's a good chance that many people won't even realise this, but if you do you might be like me and find it distracting and more than a little immersion-breaking to see a joke character appear more or less as Sterling himself would write him in a game that otherwise feels like its own thing (ignoring the names pilfered from Kojima's stuff). It makes me wonder if there are other cameos like that but which I'm not aware of outside of the game, which could explain why a lot of the patrons lack depth and come across as nothing more than stereotypes.
----
It's not going to win any major awards for its storytelling either, but if you're looking for a fairly comfy experience and enjoy VN's, you could basically view this game as a decent VN which is occasionally interrupted by a somewhat tiresome drink mixing mechanic. I have a lot more fondness for this game than this review might indicate, but that's mostly because it's a fairly niche combination of themes and elements I happen to enjoy personally. I wanted to try and give a more objective look at the game for people who don't happen to be me!

VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action is a mouthful of a name for a mouthful of a game. Set in the titular VA-11 Hall-A, AKA Valhalla, in the futuristic dystopian cyberpunk Glitch City, you play as Jill, a poor bartender who works in a run-down bar.
You know that NPC bartender you wander in and talk to in games?
Yeah, that’s who you’re playing as.
Valhalla is less of a game and more of a visual novel; the only “gamish” aspect of it is mixing drinks for patrons. This is really nothing more than following directions 90%+ of the time; rarely, they will give you something you need to think about (usually “the usual”, requiring you to remember what your patrons liked the last time, but sometimes they’ll try to be tricky and ask you for something specific – cold and sweet (so some sweet-tasting drink with ice in it), or even for something more obscure based off of something someone said previously).
Alas, this is the limit of the game’s interactivity. While there are a handful of times you can give someone another drink and get a different reaction out of them, mostly you are just following orders and clicking through what amounts to a visual novel.
And this would be fine if it was actually a good visual novel. Unfortunately, it isn’t.
The game has a cast of characters, and the characters actually do have character. Gil, Jill’s coworker, is a man with a mysterious past which is played for laughs, as your boss Dana is constantly trying to figure out what the deal with him is, while simultaneously Jill worries over him a bit. Dana herself is a boisterous bit of comedy relief herself, but she has a good head on her shoulders and is a good person, albeit one who also relies on the “mysterious past” gag a bit. Jill herself is a kind of sad girl at times, but she has a particular sense of humor (she finds the Bad Touch drink amusing, and she enjoys puns) and she certainly plays off of and teases other people a bit, even while she is grumpy at other times – and a bit more troubled than she lets on by her own past (which takes a bit to come up). Jill also definitely has a crush on her boss, which lends a slight tilt towards some of their interactions.
The patrons also have character – there’s Dorothy, the Lilim (android – or I suppose gynoid, seeing as she’s female) sex worker. She is a complete pervert, but is just so cheerful about it that she really is the high point of the game, grossing out Jill with her stories while simultaneously amusing her and showing just how much she cares. Dorothy genuinely cares about Jill, and Jill cares about Dorothy as well. Alma is another patron who shows up a lot, a female hacker who just got out of a bad relationship and who is another friend of Jill’s. As the game goes on, you meet a lot of other people, some of them fairly forgettable, others who stick out just for their weirdness (and rely too much on it for their characterization), others who just show up and leave without leaving much of an impact on the player, and one, a kindly White Knight (basically a paramedic/rescue worker) named Sei who you end up worrying about after some bad stuff goes down, along with her catgirl friend Stella.
The biggest problem with this is that while some of the characters actually do build up some emotional bonds with the player, it ultimately doesn’t feel like it goes much of anywhere. Around a third of the way through the game, something bad happens to Sei, and the characters worry about them… but ultimately, while the plot seems like it is going to be some big thing, it doesn’t go anywhere. There’s a hacker called White_Rabbit who is involved with that whole thing, but they seem to just kind of fade out of the plot, and you never actually interact with them in person, just read news stories about them in the paper. Alma complains about White_Rabbit towards the beginning, and then as it fades from prominence she starts talking about other things. A plot about Jill’s ex-girlfriend comes up, leaves, comes back, then leaves again before returning at the very end of the game, and is the closest thing there is to a main plot – but it only really involves a couple characters.
And this is really where the game fails. There just isn’t a point to it. There’s no overarching plot tying it all together. A glitch girl who keeps showing up seems like she might be related to the whole thing, but the subplot doesn’t ultimately go anywhere interesting, and I never really ended up caring about her beyond “Why is she important?” There’s no real payoff with Jill’s feelings towards her boss, nor Dorothy’s feelings towards Jill. You never find out what the real deal was with Gil or Jill’s boss.
In the end, there’s nothing that ties the lives of the characters together beyond brief interactions, and in the end, there’s not some way that this all gets tied together into any sort of coherent story. Even the plot that the bar is going to shut down at some point in the indefinite future gets no payoff.
The whole thing just sort of ends, and there was never really any point to it all. You just mixed drinks and talked to people.
A story needs a plot. But Valhalla lacks a real sense of rising action, let alone a proper climax, and there just isn’t enough of a coherent plot for you to feel a real sense of resolution. The game aspect of it is far too lightweight to be entertaining for any real period of time, and at time feels like more of a nuisance than anything, as there’s little sense of actually doing anything meaningful there beyond busywork.
In the end, this is something which feels pointless. It has characters and a setting, but it fails to tell a coherent story with them. There were so many hints of it all having some sort of point in the first week of the game, but then it doesn’t really go anywhere and it all just fizzles out.
I can’t recommend this; it isn’t awful, but it just feels like it is kind of empty, like I spent my time on it but didn’t get much back out of it.

I love physics games. I was a huge fan of them on iOS, playing games like Amazing Alex and Stair Dismount. Inside the Gear adds another layer to the genre, with a slight amount of story and some great mechanics.
Inside the Gear is very hard. An hour into the game, and I was only up to the third level, out of the twenty-five available. Trial and error are your best bets for success, and trying to roll the small wheel onto the platform was a challenge that was sometimes completed by a mere fluke. Once that level is finished though, you are presented with something even more complex, testing you to your limits even further. Although these are very complex at times, I never felt like I was achieving anything, and it sometimes began to become a drag playing through basically the same space, just with different objects.
The shapes used as transport for the "wheel" are basic, from passive and hostile planes, to cubes and triangular prisms. Everything is presented in a 3D platforming perspective, and portrays itself in a whimsical mechanism known as "the Gear", an old contraption of noise and steam.  Sparks would often fly up from the ground, spraying into the space. The Gear's colour palette are mostly oranges and reds, with a few yellows and pinks dabbled with here and there. They keep the game feeling warm and inviting, but at the same time, all the levels' backgrounds looked similar in aesthetics, so I never felt like I was progressing to a new area, despite the game's increasingly difficult level design.
Inside the Gear's menu is also something that could use a bit of sprucing up. There are no graphics options, so playing with a slower PC is difficult when you can't change the settings. There was an informative help option, but there was nothing to help you in the inevitable position where you were stuck on a certain stage.
The wonderful sound in Inside the Gear is definitely mentionable. The background movements of gears and cogs turning and whirring parts gave it a general feeling that you are actually inside a "living" thing, and your interaction with it manipulates it in some way. My only problem was that in the menu, the same sounds were repeated and got slightly irritating when navigating through it.
Inside the Gear is a game that lives up to its title, delivering some very challenging puzzles that will test your ability. It is worth noting its soundtrack, which is simple but well-fitting, and the great animation used to set the scene for what is otherwise a game that will keep you interested for a short time, but after can become a grind to play through.

(+) The graphics are simple, but atmospheric and relatively consistent. I can't think of any other positive aspect.
(.) The sound is ok, but nothing to remember.
(-) The levels don't have much of a learning curve.
(-) The controls are unintuitive and not changeable.
(-) There is only little visual feedback. No real HUD, no real markers of which object you are controlling and which are controllable except for a small movement when you cycle through them.
(-) Even the simplistic menu is lacking the most basic things. The selected menu entry is only slightly larger than the rest. This should be covered in UI Design 101.
(-) No options at all.
There is a demo, so if you are still interested, try that out first.

wow. just wow, man.
the witness throws you into a mysterious island full of gorgeous scenery and incredible challenges. the puzzles all follow the same "maze" theme, and become increasingly more difficult as you progress and learn new rules.
I am not a photography guy, and I rarely take screenshots. but as I was playing I was really compelled to capture more and more beautiful landscapes, and before I knew it I had a whole photo album's worth. visually, the game is stunning.
in fact, the whole environment, down to the subtle ambient sounds, is excellently built. there's not really any music, but the environmental noises are still complementary to not only the game, but also certain puzzles (chirp CHIRP chirp).
you know how in a metroidvania style game, you'll come up against a wall that you can't seem to break down, so you go another way and explore until you find a rocket launcher, then come back and continue your original trail?
the witness does the same thing. but instead of rocket launchers and double jumps, you learn new rules that allow you to progress through more advanced puzzles. what I find so incredible is that, though the first time you encounter a new puzzle rule, you probably won't be able to solve it, but once you find the "tutorial" area for that rule, the game does such an amazing job teaching it to you without any vocal guidance whatever.
that's not to say that as soon as you know the rules you'll be able to complete a given puzzle! I recommend busting out the graph paper and a couple of colored pens/pencils. you will absolutely need to make notes and/or redraw some puzzles to figure them out. one of my favorite things about having played through the game is now I have some really cool looking sketches and notes showing my progress.
I do have two negative points: firstly, that the game /does/ sometimes become a little "too much," and after hammering at a puzzle for 25 minutes, I got a bit frustrated. my advice is to not be afraid to step back and do something else for a little while. the solution might come to you when you don't expect it :)
secondly, this game is definitely about the journey, not the destination. I didn't have any expectations for the ending, but was hoping for a bit more. this has not stopped me from doing a second playthrough, however :)
overall, this is an excellent game. if you enjoy games like myst, or logic games like sudoku, you will be in heaven. if you enjoy just the idea of those games, but never really took the leap to actually play them, this is a great game for you.
of course, if you don't like puzzle games, if you're looking for a platformer, or if you are expecting a great arcing plot, then do look elsewhere; this is not your bag :)

A tremendous amount of work was put into this game.  Technically and creatively, it succeeds.  There is a nice variety of spatial, environmental and audio/visual puzzles.
Unfortunately, I feel that some of the puzzles elements were introduced too quickly.  Many of the puzzles are incredibly difficult.  Compare to Portal, which I felt was completely "fair" in that all its solutions were logical in hindsight.  In The Witness, solutions can involve items that are easy to overlook.  The player is often put into a situation where it is unclear if the puzzle is just broken, if the solution involves puzzle elements that were missed, or if they just aren't smart enough to figure it out.
I think the game wasn't playtested with a general audience.  The frustration level would have been clear to the designer.  It looks to be created for an audience of very skilled, patient puzzle solvers, who are very good at visualizing spatial problems.  It looks like I am not a member of this audience, because I was frustrated early and often.
I am still giving this a thumbs up, with the caveat that I think the game is unsolvable without help for 99.9% of players.  I admire the vision of the designer to create a game that really pushes the boundary of the genre, even though I ultimately found the difficulty to limit the fun I had with the game.

[This review targeted to those new to Magic] Magic is a turn-based strategy game with well defined rules and unlimited variation in strategic gameplay.  It is a modern day chess analogue, offering quick games (<20m) with a myriad of potential outcomes.  There are colour combos, deck variations, deck size and synergy, and a tremendous amount of variables to control that keep this game appealing from newbie to veteran.
This 3rd implementation of the Magic game offers new, well thought out decks, sealed play (random decks), multiplayer options (though I'm not happy with timing issues for mp rounds).  Magic is a visceral visual treat, drawing upon the deep and stunning art assets from the past two decades.
The game UI is the best yet, with the exception of a poorly placed "Skip Attack" button which will frustrate you when playing fast.  The AI is very well thought out, however, the fixed encounter decks are repetitive and tiresome, especially when "card mining" (Planeswalker battles are random though).
My only real gripe is the in-game promotions.  Be careful or you may find yourself buying DLC inadvertantly.  I've paid for the game, so what's with all the ads for Magic?  Paying to unlock a deck, offering foils you can only get through payments, and providing achievements that can only be accessed by buying DLC is a disappointing aspect to a "A" title.

I picked up Planetbase a while back and it was worth every penny. It's challenging, beautiful and most importantly, a lot of fun. While it doesn't have the depth you'll see in other cit games like Banished, it holds its own and provides us with a great experience.

UPDATE - As of March 24 2016
Planetbase has been polished a lot just recently and the changes have made a subtle but definite improvement. All of the things I complained about in the original review have been attended to, particularly with regard to the AI. The colonists and droids now behave in a predictable and sensible fashion, and I have not seen any strange behaviour, such as colonists walking across the colony just to get a drink, droids getting lost, etc.
On the whole, gameplay feels "smoother" and more like finished game.
The game does definitely have an initial "hump" you have to get past, but apart from landing in a really bad place to build and choosing bad locations for your starting structures, it's unlikely that your colony won't survive. After that development progresses in "waves" - you can't just add a desirable structure at any time, as planning for power, water, food and particularly spare parts is vital. Morale is a very important consideration, too. However once you learn the correct way to proceed it is unlikely you'll fail.  After this point I must admit the game can get a bit "samey". I don't mind this too much as I enjoy just starting a new colony and taking it as far as I can in an alotted time.  However some sort of more complex long-term goal would not be a bad addition to the game.
Armed intruders still bug me. They work much better than they used to, but they seem like a wasted possibility. All they ever do is enter the base and shoot people - it's just a very simplistic annoyance. It would be nice if they might sometimes sneak in and out and steal things, or do something other than randomly kill colonists.
Disease is also something that could be introduced as a problem for the colonies to face, and it would be really cool if the immediate vicinity of the base could be explored in some simple manner. I'm not sure how this might work, but it feels like it could be an interesting addition.
Also it would be really, really nice if a "junction" similar to the pad but for inhabited structures, could be built. This would make building a more pleasing base structure possible. You can achieve the same thing by building a small storage dome, but a cheaper option that just joins the connecting tunnels would be great.
It would also be nice if structures could be upgraded to the next size, but due to the way the structures are placed this is probably not possible. It is annoying also that you cannot delete a structure in the middle of a chain of structurse - only at the ends.
As it stands now I'd say a definite 7 / 10 at least.
If some sort of long-term goal or benefits/new challenges on subsequent planet types could be added that would take it up to 8 / 10, no problem.
UPDATE- As of February 3rd, with 8 hours more gameplay.
The updates have been good and have addressed some issues, but there are still issues with the colonist AI that I think might be unfixable without a major rewrite. eg The colonists just don't behave sensibly sometimes - walking right across the colony to find a meal when one is available nearby.
Apart from this relatively major issue the game is solid and enjoyable.  I'd recommend it for the atmosphere and overall gameplay, but beware that the AI is glitchy, and it can be glitchy enough to wreck your game. Save often!
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
So far with about 15 hours in the game I'm enjoying it a lot.
Issues at the moment include:
* some bugs in the AI that allow colonists and bots to wander endlessly sometimes instead of carrying out a goal,
* glitches that allow colonists to wander past a canteen with food and starve to death before they reach a different canteen.
* security guards are slow to respond to threats, and the colonists behave in silly ways around invaders - sometimes just ignoring them, sometimes attacking and being killed by the dozen.
I believe all of these are known bugs and are being addressed.  Other than that the game feels solid and well balanced and has the required addictive quality.
Some more options and complexity for the colony would be good, as would the option of micro-managing either production or colonist's actions.  Also it would be nice if invading characters did something besides just killing people - stealing stocks or sabotage, for example.
The game has a great potential and if the developers follow up the bug fixes with more content, and greater long-term game objectives it could become a very popular game.  The space setting and overall look of the colonies is very pleasing.

Don't be misled. PlanetBase is NOT a simple city-builder in space. PlanetBase mixes resource management, city-building, and raw survival into a game that's as frustrating as it is rewarding. Small mistakes, or inattention can lead to a cascade colony collapse that devastates your budding colony. But, everything that happens in the game is firmly YOUR fault. PlanetBase creates the feeling of intensity, exploration, and raw survival that would accompany new settlers on a new planet. The developer, MadrugaWorks, is busy taking feedback and producing patches making the game more fun/exciting every day. Combined with impressive graphics, fun design, and clever gameplay, Planetbase is a game you will easily sink hours into.

If your looking for a retro style game then this is the one for you. Volgarr the Viking is an awesome game that takes you back to the NES and SNES days. One thing that might turn you off on the game is the difficulty, this game is by all means simply HARD!
Great Pickup for your Library

The first thing that catches your attention is the old-school feel.  The player controls a Viking that must fight his way through an army of monsters.  By the way that the game looks and plays, it has a style similar to Taito’s Rastan, a classic from 1987.
One thing that makes traveling through the levels more interesting is that your weapons are for more than just combat.  For ranged combat, you have a spear to attack from a safe distance.  However, it is also useful for navigation.  If there is a wall that is too tall to jump over, throwing a powered-up spear will cause it to stick to the wall acting as a ledge.  By making the weapons multifaceted, it makes for some well-designed platforming.
Of course, the combat is the real draw of the game.  With the simple and tight controls, fighting is as easy as it was back in the 8-bit days.  As for the fighting, the action is as varied as the environments.  In one stages, you are dodging spears while sliding down slopes.  In another, you are fending off mermen while riding on a raft.  With the action constantly changing, it makes you want to continue progressing throughout the game.
One problem about this progressing is that it is too generous with progressing.  If your character dies, you lose half your treasure and return to the latest checkpoint.  Otherwise, the game does not hurt you.  With unlimited lives and saved progress, it makes finishing too easy.  Having either is good, but having both takes away from the old-school feeling that the game was going for.  In order to make the game play like it should, the player should stick to a lives cap.  Otherwise, it is possible to finish in a single day.
Even though the combat is good, the enemies, while interesting, are not as deep as the combat.  The stages have its own enemies to make each location visually interesting.  The problem with this is that there are only a few enemy types in each stage.  In most cases, it is only a palette swap to turn the same enemy into a new one.  Once you see the first enemy, expect to see it repeat constantly until reaching the boss.  This might have been acceptable in the 80s and 90s, but nowadays, more variety is expected.

When a store page uses words like "old school hard" or "brutal difficulty", I can see the appeal. Völgarr the Viking is hard in the same way that early entries in the Castlevania series are hard. Yes, it's not something that just anyone can pick up, play, and enjoy. No, this is not necessarily a good thing, but some players need that extra bit of a triumphant feeling in completing a level.
One thing that's clear from the very outset is that this is in no way one of those modern games that so many grognards accuse of excessive handholding. No, you're thrown right into the world from the beginning, with no direction but the innate instinct to go right. Be sure to check out the game's manual, too, as it explains a few helpful concepts that the game's (intentionally) meager tutorial might not make explicitly clear. Be sure to check it out, also, for the fact that it's a loving recreation of the kinds of manuals one finds packaged with (better) retro cartridge games, although black and white would have lent that extra sense of nostalgia.
The graphics are old-school only in the sense that there's a (relatively) limited color palette and movement occurs in only two dimensions, as you slash and spear your way through seemingly endless ranks of palette-swapped enemies of varying strength and ability. There's clearly a lot of love on display in the general and specific "feel" of it all.
Völgarr the Viking is absolutely not for everyone, and it never intends to be, but if you're of the kind who enjoys approaching combat as just as much of a puzzle in rhythm and positioning as the rest of the level, it might just be the game for you.

VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action is a mouthful of a name for a mouthful of a game. Set in the titular VA-11 Hall-A, AKA Valhalla, in the futuristic dystopian cyberpunk Glitch City, you play as Jill, a poor bartender who works in a run-down bar.
You know that NPC bartender you wander in and talk to in games?
Yeah, that’s who you’re playing as.
Valhalla is less of a game and more of a visual novel; the only “gamish” aspect of it is mixing drinks for patrons. This is really nothing more than following directions 90%+ of the time; rarely, they will give you something you need to think about (usually “the usual”, requiring you to remember what your patrons liked the last time, but sometimes they’ll try to be tricky and ask you for something specific – cold and sweet (so some sweet-tasting drink with ice in it), or even for something more obscure based off of something someone said previously).
Alas, this is the limit of the game’s interactivity. While there are a handful of times you can give someone another drink and get a different reaction out of them, mostly you are just following orders and clicking through what amounts to a visual novel.
And this would be fine if it was actually a good visual novel. Unfortunately, it isn’t.
The game has a cast of characters, and the characters actually do have character. Gil, Jill’s coworker, is a man with a mysterious past which is played for laughs, as your boss Dana is constantly trying to figure out what the deal with him is, while simultaneously Jill worries over him a bit. Dana herself is a boisterous bit of comedy relief herself, but she has a good head on her shoulders and is a good person, albeit one who also relies on the “mysterious past” gag a bit. Jill herself is a kind of sad girl at times, but she has a particular sense of humor (she finds the Bad Touch drink amusing, and she enjoys puns) and she certainly plays off of and teases other people a bit, even while she is grumpy at other times – and a bit more troubled than she lets on by her own past (which takes a bit to come up). Jill also definitely has a crush on her boss, which lends a slight tilt towards some of their interactions.
The patrons also have character – there’s Dorothy, the Lilim (android – or I suppose gynoid, seeing as she’s female) sex worker. She is a complete pervert, but is just so cheerful about it that she really is the high point of the game, grossing out Jill with her stories while simultaneously amusing her and showing just how much she cares. Dorothy genuinely cares about Jill, and Jill cares about Dorothy as well. Alma is another patron who shows up a lot, a female hacker who just got out of a bad relationship and who is another friend of Jill’s. As the game goes on, you meet a lot of other people, some of them fairly forgettable, others who stick out just for their weirdness (and rely too much on it for their characterization), others who just show up and leave without leaving much of an impact on the player, and one, a kindly White Knight (basically a paramedic/rescue worker) named Sei who you end up worrying about after some bad stuff goes down, along with her catgirl friend Stella.
The biggest problem with this is that while some of the characters actually do build up some emotional bonds with the player, it ultimately doesn’t feel like it goes much of anywhere. Around a third of the way through the game, something bad happens to Sei, and the characters worry about them… but ultimately, while the plot seems like it is going to be some big thing, it doesn’t go anywhere. There’s a hacker called White_Rabbit who is involved with that whole thing, but they seem to just kind of fade out of the plot, and you never actually interact with them in person, just read news stories about them in the paper. Alma complains about White_Rabbit towards the beginning, and then as it fades from prominence she starts talking about other things. A plot about Jill’s ex-girlfriend comes up, leaves, comes back, then leaves again before returning at the very end of the game, and is the closest thing there is to a main plot – but it only really involves a couple characters.
And this is really where the game fails. There just isn’t a point to it. There’s no overarching plot tying it all together. A glitch girl who keeps showing up seems like she might be related to the whole thing, but the subplot doesn’t ultimately go anywhere interesting, and I never really ended up caring about her beyond “Why is she important?” There’s no real payoff with Jill’s feelings towards her boss, nor Dorothy’s feelings towards Jill. You never find out what the real deal was with Gil or Jill’s boss.
In the end, there’s nothing that ties the lives of the characters together beyond brief interactions, and in the end, there’s not some way that this all gets tied together into any sort of coherent story. Even the plot that the bar is going to shut down at some point in the indefinite future gets no payoff.
The whole thing just sort of ends, and there was never really any point to it all. You just mixed drinks and talked to people.
A story needs a plot. But Valhalla lacks a real sense of rising action, let alone a proper climax, and there just isn’t enough of a coherent plot for you to feel a real sense of resolution. The game aspect of it is far too lightweight to be entertaining for any real period of time, and at time feels like more of a nuisance than anything, as there’s little sense of actually doing anything meaningful there beyond busywork.
In the end, this is something which feels pointless. It has characters and a setting, but it fails to tell a coherent story with them. There were so many hints of it all having some sort of point in the first week of the game, but then it doesn’t really go anywhere and it all just fizzles out.
I can’t recommend this; it isn’t awful, but it just feels like it is kind of empty, like I spent my time on it but didn’t get much back out of it.

wow. just wow, man.
the witness throws you into a mysterious island full of gorgeous scenery and incredible challenges. the puzzles all follow the same "maze" theme, and become increasingly more difficult as you progress and learn new rules.
I am not a photography guy, and I rarely take screenshots. but as I was playing I was really compelled to capture more and more beautiful landscapes, and before I knew it I had a whole photo album's worth. visually, the game is stunning.
in fact, the whole environment, down to the subtle ambient sounds, is excellently built. there's not really any music, but the environmental noises are still complementary to not only the game, but also certain puzzles (chirp CHIRP chirp).
you know how in a metroidvania style game, you'll come up against a wall that you can't seem to break down, so you go another way and explore until you find a rocket launcher, then come back and continue your original trail?
the witness does the same thing. but instead of rocket launchers and double jumps, you learn new rules that allow you to progress through more advanced puzzles. what I find so incredible is that, though the first time you encounter a new puzzle rule, you probably won't be able to solve it, but once you find the "tutorial" area for that rule, the game does such an amazing job teaching it to you without any vocal guidance whatever.
that's not to say that as soon as you know the rules you'll be able to complete a given puzzle! I recommend busting out the graph paper and a couple of colored pens/pencils. you will absolutely need to make notes and/or redraw some puzzles to figure them out. one of my favorite things about having played through the game is now I have some really cool looking sketches and notes showing my progress.
I do have two negative points: firstly, that the game /does/ sometimes become a little "too much," and after hammering at a puzzle for 25 minutes, I got a bit frustrated. my advice is to not be afraid to step back and do something else for a little while. the solution might come to you when you don't expect it :)
secondly, this game is definitely about the journey, not the destination. I didn't have any expectations for the ending, but was hoping for a bit more. this has not stopped me from doing a second playthrough, however :)
overall, this is an excellent game. if you enjoy games like myst, or logic games like sudoku, you will be in heaven. if you enjoy just the idea of those games, but never really took the leap to actually play them, this is a great game for you.
of course, if you don't like puzzle games, if you're looking for a platformer, or if you are expecting a great arcing plot, then do look elsewhere; this is not your bag :)

A tremendous amount of work was put into this game.  Technically and creatively, it succeeds.  There is a nice variety of spatial, environmental and audio/visual puzzles.
Unfortunately, I feel that some of the puzzles elements were introduced too quickly.  Many of the puzzles are incredibly difficult.  Compare to Portal, which I felt was completely "fair" in that all its solutions were logical in hindsight.  In The Witness, solutions can involve items that are easy to overlook.  The player is often put into a situation where it is unclear if the puzzle is just broken, if the solution involves puzzle elements that were missed, or if they just aren't smart enough to figure it out.
I think the game wasn't playtested with a general audience.  The frustration level would have been clear to the designer.  It looks to be created for an audience of very skilled, patient puzzle solvers, who are very good at visualizing spatial problems.  It looks like I am not a member of this audience, because I was frustrated early and often.
I am still giving this a thumbs up, with the caveat that I think the game is unsolvable without help for 99.9% of players.  I admire the vision of the designer to create a game that really pushes the boundary of the genre, even though I ultimately found the difficulty to limit the fun I had with the game.

Inside the Gear is pretty interesting physics puzzle game with a deceivingly simple objective - activate the pressure plate on the platform by using the round object. Making the object touch the platform is not as easy as it sounds and will require your creativity and patience.
There are no options whatsoever, but I don't really feel that I'm missing something - there is no music, just the ambient sound and the occasional rolling sound of your gear, so I don't need the adjustable sound sliders, the keys are listed in the help screen and are not remapable, but work just fine and I didn't feel the need to change them. Now don't get me wrong, having those options would definitely be good, but the game gets away nicely without them.
Now, as good as the keyboard controls are, I would love to see some mouse support implemented in the game, as that will clearly make the control of the objects more intuitive.
Once you complete a puzzle, you move onto the next one, out of a total of 25. Most of them will require you to fine tune your available object's position and angle, and I would just love the option to save my original and unorthodox solution, so I can easily show it to a friend, without wasting a couple minutes, trying to emulate it.
With the ambient sounds and the slowly moving gears in the background, surrounded by mist or in some kind of liquid, I could agree, that the game is atmospheric and I don't think, that the lack of music is that noticeable.
Overall, I think the game delivers quite enjoyable experience for all puzzle fans, but might be quite strange / irritating for players new to the genre or lacking the patience to complete the puzzles, because it's one thing to understand what you're supposed to do, and another, to actually carefully position the objects and succeed. The price tag, the steam trading cards and the fact that I love puzzles, make this an easy recommendation!

Inside the gear is a unique physics puzzle game, you are inside a big rusted old machine. You have to get a little wheel onto a platform, to do this you will use various intractable objects such as cubes,planks and planks that defy gravity. Sounds easy? NO. I am not ashamed to say I didn't do the level 1 on my first try but once I got a feel for how the game works it wasn't to hard.
The game includes 25 levels all with different puzzles that will make you think, you might have to make a seesaw and launch the wheel over to the platform or maybe drop the cube to push the wheel. If you studied mechanics then that should give you a leg up on the competition but don't worry its not required. If getting something wrong annoys you and then just give up then you probably won't get very far with this game.
The game doesn't have music it has mechanical sounds to really get you to feel like you are inside a machine(everyone's dream come true, I'm sure). The game is 3D but you can only interact in 2D fortunately but you can sometimes have spinning cubes and wheels rotating and landing on their sides.
As for the looks of the game the machine is old so things are a bit rusted in there so if you don't like the colour orange your out of luck, there are some other colours though so don't worry. The game looks like an old machine as it should with big moving gears and floating platforms.
Obviously this game isn't for everyone, if you do not like puzzles then you probably won't like a physics puzzle game. The game can annoy you but also make you think and completing a hard level can make you give yourself a pat on the back or if you are really stuck I am sure some people will do walkthroughs/guides.
The game has no tutorial so you are just thrown straight into the puzzles there is no holding your hand here, to find the controls just look under help which the game tells you to do.
to summarize I believe the game is well made as I haven't encountered any bugs or glitches, depending on your skill level the game could take you several hours or if you have know what you are doing it could take you just 1.
The game is fun if you enjoy puzzles and obviously not fun if you do not, for the price it is easily worth it to pick up. I give this 8/10 clearly a well made puzzle game with a high enough difficulty to keep people thinking.

I just finished Hero of the Kingdom (2.5 hours, give or take). It's a very unique game. Basically you're presented a top-down isometric screen that looks a little bit like Age of Empires 2 or HoMM3 or something. You click through text prompts on the screen in a sort of combination text adventure and hidden object game. You become a hero of your kingdom by moving through screens and helping people out. Maybe someone lost their son, so you hidden object find him. Nothing is difficult, it'll just be like you see a patch of mushrooms, and you click it so you get mushrooms added to your inventory. Or you are on your boat and click a barrel underwater to salvage it. So not really hidden object, more like click-to-acquire. Maybe a farmer needs someone to go to town to sell his flour, so you get flour, click to switch screens to the town, and sell the flour to a merchant. Your inventory has dozens of different types of commodities that you manage, flowers, eggs, swords, handymen, antlers, pearls, etc. Across the world various merchants buy and sell various commodities. There's no actual difficulty in that it seems like it's impossible to make a bad transaction. If you just keep buying and selling stuff and foraging and fishing and hunting you'll eventually get enough of what you need or enough money to buy what you need. I really can't compare it to any other game I've ever played. I had a fun time playing through it. I guess I wasn't really playing. Just kind of clicking everywhere.
I also laughed every time I'd go into some big climactic battle and my guy would be like "We scored a crushing victory over the Dark Goblins. Oh and all of my soldiers died. We will miss them." and then -10 soldiers in my inventory. Hahaha. Made them feel very disposable.
One flaw: The game autosaves and when you beat the game it erases your saves, meaning that if you want to get all the achievements you should do so BEFORE fighting the last boss (the last boss is clearly marked and identified).

You can perform actions such as fighting, collecting crafting materials, trading with merchants, and hunting for hidden loot. But there's something about the game's simplicity and steady stream of medal unlocks that's strangely appealing. Worth giving a try, especially if you bought it as part of a certain indie bundle...

Very nice, very casual point&click adventure RPG, Hero of the Kingdom tells a familiar story of a farmboy turned hero.
The wannabe hero begins his journey when bandits burn his family farm down. He gets to do all sorts of jobs from woodcutting to burning to healing wounded people. Gameplay is simple: clicking a marker will give you a short written description (no voice-over here) of your character's thoughts, what you can (and therefore should) do and what you need to accomplish that. You need many kinds of resources in the form of food, vitality, gold and tools.
While the gameplay is a casual adventure, you also have to manage the said resources. You'll gain vitality by resting, which requires food that is acquired by foraging or hunting, which in part require tools and skills. Many parts of this chain could have been removed to smooth the gameplay: with them, however, it is an adventure RPG game, not just a barely visual novel.
There are also many details in the areas that turn out to be significant later on. Some of them are "hidden", though, meaning that you just have to click them to see if they react: stuff like collectable mushrooms and lootable barrels form this category.
The narration is casual and easygoing, containing little to no fancy words. In effect, it would be quite suitable to be played with young children who can't read yet, assuming English proficiency. Like so, the story is rather traditional with the evil dark wizards and all. It's still nice enough to keep in its grip for the while it lasts.
Full completion would have lasted about 4 hours, but I went for all the achievements. This added about an hour to the playtime because I just couldn't find several last mushrooms and hidden caches. While challenging, I was irritated to check the same areas ten times just to find those last missing items. Anyway, this is amended, as I really enjoyed the leisure style.
Replay value, IMO, is meager though. Once played through completely, there isn't much more to accomplish. That said, it is rather alright an experience for its price.

is a slightly unusual mix of point-and-click adventure and rpg. It looks like an old-school isometric rpg, but there is no character to control - instead all actions are performed by clicking on object like in a point&click title. The basic rpg premise is still here (slight spoilers!) - an ordinary boy on a quest to find his father turns into a hero that saves the land from dire evil. Yeah, like no one expected that, spoilers over. The boy learns skills during the adventure - hunting, herbalism, etc - in order to get closer to his goal. As if the mix wasn't unusual enough the game adds in some Hiden Object elements - there are treasures and extra items hidden around in the bushes, rivers, barrels.
Visually the game has nothing to be shy of, it's a simple but well drawn style. Map elements are clearly distinguishible and even the hidden items are fairly easy to spot with a little practice. It's overall easy on the eye even for longer sessions. The audio is pleasant enough too, can't say much in detail about it personally but at least it feels right. Sadly, there is very little, if any, voice acting and that might diminish the enjoyment for some players - while lots of detailed text and dialogues can be enrich the world it might also bore the player.
Personally I find the mix pretty entertaining, then again I enjoy casual games so take what I say with a grain of salt. Nevertheless, the story moves at a good enough pace to keep boredom away and it's easy to enjoy this in bite-sized portions if so desired. Time-wise the game takes around 5 hours for a relaxed playthrough, dipping to maybe 3-3.5 for a speedy run and climbing to approx 8 for a single 100% run. At L5 that is pretty good value for anyone who likes a more casual adventure.
tl;dr: At £5 it's a good mix of point&click, adventure, and casual gameplay.

If you've never played Magic before, this is the place to start. Duels serves as an excellent teaching tool, and it's also a lot of fun. I've played through every scrap of it on the iPad, and I'm now starting over on Steam since the iPad version has some pretty crippling bugs in it as of late.
Just beware - once you get into this, you're more than likely going to start building real decks, getting your friends into the game, and possibly spend lots of time at your local game shop. Not that that's a bad thing ;)

On one hand, the deck designs, possible card combos, and some of the actual cards themselves are really fun in this version of Duels, but it feels like the AI has not caught up to some of the more intricate Magic mechanics in this year's offering - there are a lot of cases where the AI seems to make what you might call "rookie mistakes" dealing with some of the more complicated cards.
The game itself is fun (it's Magic, so of course it's fun), but the various game modes are not as good as in the previous game in the series. Your only real game styles are regular and Sealed, and the Sealed is very limited in that (without buying additional content) you only get one card pool to play with, meaning that the Sealed campaign has approaching zero replay value, since you get the same cards every time. There's no Arch Enemy, Planechase, or any other fun variants this time around.
On the positive side, the campaign mode feels a lot more like an actual campaign mode now, rather than just a series of unrelated games. They have added a little bit of story, put in some narration, and made the "final boss" fight a lot more entertaining than in the previous games in the series. For example, there is no "tinker a Mox into Darksteel Colossus on turn 1" like in the original game.
I'd say this game is a good fit if you are either a very new Magic player (what the game was really designed for), or you just liked the first two games in the series and ran out of stuff to do in them. That said, if you're just looking for a Magic game to play, I'd probably go with the 2013 version above this one.

While it doesn't compare to paper magic, Duels 2014 is another great experience for entering into the wide universe that is Magic the Gathering. With the introduction of sealed mode, you get a sense for what its like to actually construct a deck from a pile of cards and make tough decisions on what to include and what to cut from your deck. All in all, its an enriched experience that does a good job of mirroring paper magic.
Its hard to enjoy this game by itself as someone that loves the deckbuilding aspect of paper magic, and the competitive side. Without true deck customization from the get-go, this game is a tough sell for the hardcore Magic crowd. With that being said, there are plenty of third party mods to enable you the ability to create your own decks and utilize the deep cardpool found within the game.
Some of the legacy issues that this series suffers from is the AI. If you aren't playing online, you are playing against an AI that stacks their deck (encounters), or comes up with the perfect draw on a situational basis (actual Planeswalker opponents). On the highest difficulty, it does make the game a little difficult to play and enjoy knowing that you are at a disadvantage right off the bat, but knowing that the AI is still very much beatable, and the fact that they walk into obvious traps even on the highest difficulty means that the game rewards you for playing smart, and punishes you for misplaying.
This game certainly isn't for every magic fan out there, but if you want to have a gateway to learning magic the correct way, Duels has, and will be, the best way to learn the basics and build upon the basics. 8/10

Having played through it and completed all the in game achievements and the steam achievements (The Hardest of which is the Express Outpost, 100 colonists in 30 days) I can say that I do recommend this game.
It's a pretty and fairly chilled (most of the time) base builder, strategy, survival game. It has issues like most games when first released, but the developer does seem to be working through and fixing them at a fast rate. Initial problems with general AI are improving, and a lot of the bugs that were there at launch are disappearing. Although I do keep coming across the food bug where upon my colonists just stop loading the meal makers after a long play session, which in turn causes everyone to starve to death even though I have huge stockpiles of meat and veggies. A quick save and reload resolves that one though.
Why do I recommend it?  Because I've done everything the game currently has to offer, and yet I still want to play it more.  It's challenging mainly at two main points while playing; in the initial base build to get core rooms done before you run out of resources, and when you are trying to build as fast as possible to grow quickly, stretching your resources to breaking point without getting everyone killed, and there are a lot of ways to kill your colonists.
To be honest about the only thing that's really negative about the game there just isn't quite enough content, or replay value. Only 3 starting planets are available when they could probably have 100’s more. There aren’t any aliens or hostile creatures you have to cope with, or events/disasters that take place outside of the occasional human intruder, solar flare, and blizzard/sandstorm. Also as the French would say it lacks a certain "je ne sais quoi" which if you play it you'll see what I mean, it's like the game is missing some of the charm or humour you'd get from other games like "The Settlers" and at times the game just feels outright brutal when a meteor hits your massive bio dome full of biologists because your workers decided to take a 2 minute tea break from the laser defence system.  But that’s possibly a balancing issue that the developers will address. They could improve it a lot buy adding more interesting buildings for you to expand your colony with so that your colonists can do something other than just try to survive. If they opened the game up for modding I’m sure that’s one of the top things that modders would add along with new locations.
Ultimately you'll get your money's worth if you purchase the game and try to complete the steam achievements, but not much else, which for a game of this type is a little disappointing. It's like the developers have built a core game, and released it with the thought to make some money while they make the real version as a sequel which has all the bells and whistles, which in today's games market is understandable if not entirely wanted. Still it’s a decent game that’ll be keeping an eye on to see if it becomes a great game.

Hard to say much about Danganronpa without spoiling it, but it's a hell of a time. The characters and aesthetic might be a little off-putting to non-anime fans, but they're much more entertaining than you'd think, and are complimented by a well-written, self-aware plot that will keep you guessing. The gameplay has a little more meat to it than most visual novels, and plays like a bizarre mashup of Phoenix Wright, Persona 4, DDR and an arcade-style rail shooter. Yep, it's weird. There's also a pretty trippy soundtrack and a unique graphical style that give Danganronpa its own look and feel.
This PC port is also really well-made, and plays great with both KB+M and controller. I put 20 hours into the original Vita version, and with this great port, I think it's safe to say that I'll be taking another semester at Hope's Peak Academy.
The game is great, plot and characters are super interesting, highly recommend it. Hopefully, Danganronpa 2 and Another Episode come to Steam as well!

Farcry 4 is an open world survival game with lots of similarities with its predecessor, Farcry 3. The game has a beautiful map and a mediocre storyline. Along the story missions, you will find yourself captive, high (literaly and figurativly), heroic and an errand boy. The game has a multiplayer coop system where you can join ohters game and play campaign missions or capture outposts together.
Inventory:
- There are sidearm guns enables you to shoot while driving a car or sliding from a sipline. SMG, Assault rifles, sniper rifles, LMG and launchers like a rocket launcher. The aresenal is pretty enough for any kind of stealthy or explosive action. You can carry 4 different weapons of 4 types. Oh and there is a bow.
- There is a looting system in the game. You can loot corpses of enemies or friends and there are loot crates that will reward you with money and sellable objects.
- There is a crafting mechanism in the game. you will see flowers and collect leaves to craft different styringes. A health syrige will give you health, overdose syringe will make you faster, hunting syringe will enable you to see enemies and animals behing walls or even a mountain. In Farcry 3, the hunting syringe was just making animals visible. All the items are stored in your loot bag and you can upgrade your loot bag and other bags like explosives or ammo etc. with animal skins. Yes, you will be able skin animals. You can also sell them in market. Some animals will reward you with a bait, rather than a skin. A bait is a piece of meat that you can use to attract wild animals. You will have molotovs, grenades and C4 explosives too.
Map:
- The game is placed on a beautiful landscape (i guess somewhere near himalayas). There are gorgeous views to enjoy, mountains to climb. You will have a graple hook to traverse some parts of the map. This is a bit of an identity crises in my opinion, cuz i think Farcry is a survival game more than an exploration game. And i think there should have been less mountains and more waters or plains.
- But there is a nice addition for traveling in the game. You will be able to use a glider or buy a wingsuit to glide from the top of a mountain from the beginning of the game. And there is a buzzer, a mini helicopter thing, that will literaly carry you anywhere within the borders of the map. It is too good to have, i was worried that it the game might take away that useful thing from me :) There is another improvement of the vehicular transportaion. You can drive cars in the island or just set a destination point on the map and press shift to activate auto-driver. You will be able enjoy your surroundings, shoot your gun with ease or go to bathroom :D while the car is following the road. This mechanism is not that smart though, it may crash into other vehicles on the road, but it is definitely a useful feature.
- You have to explore the map and conquer radio towers, which are being used for propoganda. You will need to capture outposts, small enemy bases. Basically you are freeing the island from bad guys.
- The map has plenty of land and spots to discover. There are collectibles, propoganda posters, loot crates and karma wheels to spin.
- There are side activities like helping people who are being attacked by wild animals, excorting a cargo truck, avenging someones death or mastering the outpost with stealth. There is an arena where you will have to fight your way to survive. The endless mode of the arena will test your endurence :)
- There are fortresses other than outposts but you can just assume they are heavily guarded outposts with walls. It is a more challenging outpost in other words.
Gameplay:
- There is a heavy stealth emphasis in the game. But usualy in these kinds of games, the stealh mechanism sucks. Enemies are either blind or have powers like superman :D If you snipe someone even with a silencer, a nearby enemy may be able to pinpoint your exact location even he is looking another direction. There is a silent takedown element, where you get close to an enemy and press F, and there are skills to upgrade this ability. For example you can takedown an enemy and throw his knife to a nearby enemy to get a second kill.
- There are animals on the map, so you will frequently have problems with wild ones. Sometimes they get tempted and attack you, sometimes they get scared and run away. I honestly did not understand some animals behavior. There is a skill to enable you to ride an elephant. I have never used it but you can charge the elephant and get a seriously destructive power. It is probably hella fun.
- There are lots of cheap deaths. An ally crushed me with his car, i killed an enemy driver on the road and somehow the truck steered towards me and crushed me, i have crashed into a tree while gliding with wingsuit and died, a rhino got angry and cornered me and killed me with its horn, i have missed the timing of graple hook and fell down from the cliff....
- There are skills to gain in the game. Some will require som campaign missions to be completed. This is ok but some skills dictates you to do some activities on the map. This is another identity crisis in my opinion. Why would i have to do cargo activities to get a skill? A skill is a useful thing and will be useful in missions and game progress. This way, the developers forced you to spend time with side activities on the map. This is a no go for me. This game is a survival game, not exploration.
- You will need health syringes in the game. If you collect 2 green flower leaves, a syringe will automatically be crafted. This is a small but very useful feature. The green leaf will not occupy apace in the inventory for no reason and you do not have to worry about crafting a syringe in the middle of a gun fight.
- You have a camera to pin the enemies without the survival syringe. There are couple of different enemies. Ordinary lunitics, guys with rifles, snipers and heavy gunners. There is a special type called hunters. They can disappear from the pinned view and they can call wild animals on you with a freakin whistle. Take them out first. The enemy will have a pattern so you should take you time to investigate and kill them silently while capturing outposts.
- I have never played multiplayer but i know you can play coop misssions with different people and you can jump on someones mission too. I do not know if there is a deathmatch or team deathmatch mode :D I think farcry is a solitary game. Multiplayer can be realy fun with friends if you can coordinate.
Story:
- The story begins with you visiting an island to scatter you mothers ashes to fulfill her will. As you might guess, you will be captured and run away and liberate the island and murder your way to the top of the food chain. The story will have 2 different possible ways and you will have to chose a side. They say this changes the ending but i do not think it would be a whole different ending.
- Campaign missions will get you weird places and situations. My favorite 2 missions are the one where they throw you into the arena to fight you way out, and the one where you invade the chemical factory. Some missions will purely be based on some weapons or graple hook.
Visuals and Audio:
- You will visit himalayas and feel like a snow leopard or something :D The visual quality is above average in this games time. Audio, especially the gun fight, is amazing. You can hear animals foot steps with a headphone and it is exciting. The optimization could have been better, i could play with 1080P very high but saw frame drops in some places.
Overall, Farcry 4 is definitely a receommended game by me, just like Farcry 3. If you think this game is expensive, go for Farcry 3. It is pretty similar. Survival, exploration, lots of gun fight, beautiful visuals and lots of activities. Even with this long review, i have probably missed something :D

After only 3 hours of gameplay (and counting- I'm not throwing in the towel just yet), I've beaten Level 1 a few times, and I've quit two different ways:  clicking the X, and selecting the Quit Game option. Neither one saved my progress, so next time I'd go to play, I'd have to start at Level 1. What am I doing wrong here? I understand Volgarr is supposed to be difficult (which it is), but shouldn't I be able to see just HOW difficult it is by being able to get past the first 2 levels? I mean, how about some mid-level checkpoints? And how about a world map where I can pick and choose levels that I've already beaten (should that ever happen), and not some bland, "follow the yellow brick road" system.
And what all cool upgrades for Volgarr lie beyond Level 2? I looked it up. Additional weapons? Nope. More armor? Nope. Wielding the Fire Sword for more than 5 seconds before getting hit and losing it? Hopefully. Furthermore, why does getting hit while wielding said Fire Sword also cause me to also lose my helmet? That's TWO pieces of equipment lost from ONE hit! The upgrade/armor/health system reflects that of Super Mario Bros., but Volgarr's first two levels aren't nearly supplied with as many treasure chests (where upgrades are found) as Mario's first two levels were with question mark blocks, and some of Mario's blocks had stars.
Also, when you slaughter enemies they will sometimes drop treasure, which is used for leaderboards. That's cool, but I find it hard to focus on killing every single Lizardman, hoping they drop treasure, just to top the leaderboards when I'm trying to survive until the next treasure chest. Perhaps with all this treasure to collect, a Sonic-type health system would've made sense.
However, the controls are simple, the graphics are nice and accurately reflect the retro aethestic of its SNES counterparts, and the triumphant battle themes remind me of the good old days of splurging quarters on Gauntlet Legends.
I REALLY wanted to like this game, and [adult swim] is an entertainment brand I trust. The trailers make Volgarr look like a fun challenge, not a frustrating chore. Until some issues are addressed, I cannot fully recommend this game.
TL;DR:  Gee, I can't wait to get to Level 3.

This is a casual Resource Management game.
I mean casual by both slow-paced and easy to beat.
The Good :
- Simple, Relaxing gameplay.
- Resource Management. It's one of my loved genre, but there isn't much games focused on that.
- More and more things interactable on maps as you progress.
- Lots of bonus loots hidden everywhere, for extra coins.
- Map interface allowing you to travel anywhere you've been. It's helpful as you'll be travelling everywhere.
The Bad :
- Remember, this is NO RPG or STRATEGY. All about handling resources and clicking tiny hidden things.
- One playthrough's enough for all achievement. 3 hours for me to get them all.
- Management gets too easy once you found out a way to make money.
- You never know when you don't need tools anymore(Resource nodes will decay in one or two gathers, and are limited. But don't worry that you can BUY resources from NPCs)
- Interaction effects. I'd really love to skip them.
- Bulk purchase option needed. It's tiresome to click hundred times when shopping.
6/10, Well worth the price, but not too great. And they're making the sequel so I'd like to play it as well.

Loved the game! The best part is that this game is one of a few that provide entertainment & stimulation for the intellect while not being too taxing for those with physical limitations.  The characteristics I most appreciated in the Hero of the Kingdom game is that it was story-driven yet you have free choice of direction and resolution.  The pace is slow (by that I mean there is no "need for speed" or required talent in manual dexterity & yet the game never lags and manages to remain mutable enough to keep it fresh, with minimal manual interactions.  The achievements are challenging yet still realistically acheivable.  The game is adequate in length & not over-long.  The only things I would add to my wish list for the sequel would be a few more dashes of wit & whimsy (along with additional humorous dialog throughout & perhaps an Easter Egg or two). All-in-all it was a great game & I send my thanks & congratulations (on the Greenlight for the sequel) to Lonely Troops.  I'm really looking forward to the next one!

Built For Beginners.
I'll start with the cons: You don't have any freedom of deck design. You play the decks available in game with the option to add or subtract cards from a preset list for that deck. It's not a good game for learning about deck building.
Why I recommend it: This is an excellent tool for learning the game mechanics. The pace is nice and slow, and the visuals make things very simple. The game won't allow you to make an illegal move, so as a new player it's an excellent way to learn what to do and when; it even goes as far as to show you which cards you CAN play at any given stage. It breaks down the steps and phases of a turn very clearly, so again, you can learn how the game works. Another, and probably one of my favorite features in the Digital MTG series is that whenever an ability is triggered, the game will slowly and visually show you exactly which cards are involved, with the option to enlarge the card and read the ability.
It's a lot of small things that help learn to play the game that you probably wouldn't get with a human player, regardless of their patince. They just don't want to wait while you read every single card 2 or 3 times and trace with a finger everything that's going on.
I recommend this game 100% for new players or people who are interested in starting out. It's cheaper than buying a pre-made deck in stores and comes with the advantage of masterfully teaching you how to play, without being so all encompassing as to eliminate your reason to play the 'real' game.

Disclaimer: I don't own any of the DLCs
This was my first official exposure to the trading card game (other than a few casual duels with friends using borrowed decks).  After playing through the main and sealed deck campaigns, I've developed a much better understanding of MtG and had a lot of fun with the variety of decks I unlocked.  There are many things I like about M2014, but a few aspects that I disagree with.
The interface is very intuitive and easy to use.  As a beginner, I found the "More Info" button to be very useful in explaining various game mechanics like Devour, Undying and First Strike.  Soundtrack is excellent and gets you pumped for the duel.
The main campaign was fun, but I didn't like how the "encounters" (non-boss duels) were scripted so that the AI basically plays the same cards each time you duel against it (ahem, Sewers.  goddamn Sewers).  It was exciting to unlock a new deck at the end of each chapter, and though the plot was pretty basic it added a nice bit of flavour to each duel.  However, the final battle was disappointing to say the least.
Sealed mode (where you get a bunch of random cards from boosters and build a deck from them) was fun in theory but M2014 put on a bunch of unnecessary restrictions.  The sealed campaign is short and allows you to unlock some more additional boosters, but other than that you're stuck with the cards you have.  You can only make up to two decks in sealed - any more and you'll have to buy additional slots.  Because of the limited number of cards you get for each deck (and the fact that you can't exchange cards between decks), I found myself stuck playing decks of the colours for which I had the best cards.  I wish they'd had a mode where you could just build a deck from any of the cards that you collected (including the unlockable decks), without any restrictions.
Multiplayer with friends, of course, is always nice.  I've also had matchmade games with strangers, and those turned out alright too.  Two-headed giant (2v2) mode was super hectic fun.  In order to be somewhat more unique, you can customize your player avatar and title, and those are unlocked by doing certain deeds in the game (like achievements, but the objectives are different).
Challenges are either easy or tricky puzzles, and the tricky ones helped me understand the mechanics of Magic a little better.
Verdict: This is a decent Magic game, and you'll definitely get more out of it if you're a beginner.  The replay value wasn't as great as I expected, and experienced players can probably skip this one unless it's on sale. Either way, you may want to wait for a sale to pick this up.  I'm looking forward to seeing how M2015 will turn out.

I found the Witness to be one of the most intriguing puzzle games I've ever played.
I'm the type of player that enjoys the journey as much as the destination so the process of learning how each new puzzle mechanic worked was immensely satisfying for me. Some reviews I've watched have said the game should have been a straightforward puzzle game on a tablet or phone because the exploration doesn't offer anything, and I completely disagree. One of my favorite segments in the game involved walking through a series of mazes and trying to pay attention to any sort of clue I could find in order to discover how each maze related to the panel at its end. Exploration is key to the enjoyment of this game, and offers a welcome break from a tough puzzle you just can't solve.
Overall, I think this is an exceptional game for the small audience it was designed for. If you're like me, where the process of discovery is something you enjoy, then you should check this game out. However, if you're looking for action or a compelling, clear storyline, look elsewhere.
Also, if the $40 price tag scares you off, check out a game called English Country Tune. It has similar elements of figuring out abstract puzzles on your own and is much cheaper. If you like that one, chances are you'll enjoy The Witness as well.

This game is a pile of hipster bull♥♥♥♥♥♥ Had i spent 42$ on it, as steam seems to want me to in Canada, I would've been immensley disappointed. That said, it came with Humble Monthly so I guess the indie games/other games i get at the end of the month will make up for it.
I beat it, spent a fair amount of time with a guide online, and really what I can say from that time is that it's kind of a mess. It's not fun - I like puzzle games, but this doesn't really work along those tropes. Generally speaking, the game sets up rules for how to do things, and that's great and all, but those rules tend to fall apart as the game progresses.
No to it, not that there has to be one, but anyone imposing a narrative on it is really just jerkin' their gherkin to justify their enjoyment of the game.
