Yeah, I got stuck on a puzzle because I wasn't standing exactly equidistant between a door and a puzzle while being 3.2 metres from a tree, with my back to the sun and my face inclined 87 degrees from the horizon. That said, it was because I was checking out the pretty surroundings.

Some absolutely brilliant line-based puzzles placed around a pretty nice looking island.
The way the game gradually teaches you each of the puzzle mechanics seperately, then works to slowly combine them with one another to form more complex puzzles is fantastically done. If you pay attention through each puzzle, look at the environment around you, and take 30 seconds to sit and think it over carefully, you'll be able to solve most of them without hints even if you're only modestly skilled at puzzle games like me.
If I had one gripe, it's that the puzzles involving tetris pieces were significantly less fun than any of the other puzzle types, sometimes to the point where I felt more like I was trying to solve a math problem than solve a video game puzzle (to the point that I often just looked up solutions for the late-game ones), but this may very well be my personal puzzle taste rather than those puzzles being definitively not as good as the others.
Also there's basically no story so don't go in expecting anything like lore about the island beyond a few very ambiguous audio logs and some old philosophical quotes. There's also the requisite super-pretentious "SO INTELLECTUAL" indie hipster lesson you're meant to take away from the game (which I won't bother sharing unless one of you -really- wants to know because I think it's just plain silly), but it really doesn't mess with the gameplay experience at all if you just pretend it's not there.

I feel like I've played long enough to give up on this without risking missing "the moment" where it all clicks and it suddenly becomes an unforgettable experience.
After the first few hours of learning and conquering puzzles and exploring the vicinity of the starting area, you'll start to encounter new puzzle types - however this is where cracks begin to appear.
Some puzzles simply do not convey the idea behind them well enough. It's much too easy to accidentally stumble upon a puzzles solution without actually LEARNING how it works, and in doing so robbing yourself of the knowledge required to proceed in successive puzzles. Also, each area will have a point where a rule is altered slightly to mix things up a little, however if you were already grappling with a puzzle you didn’t understand in the first place this will hardly be a welcome change. To top it all off, getting some puzzles wrong will ‘lock’ them until the preceding puzzle is completed again (the puzzle doesn’t change, you just have to repeat the process again), which is done to prevent ‘brute forcing’ puzzles. The irony being that if the difficulty escalation and new mechanics had been introduced properly in the first place, this would never be a risk, and so all it does is penalise players who weren’t taught what to do properly in the first place. In the end, all you have left is a failure and frustration loop which drowns out any jubilation earned through progressing with hard work and ingenuity, and replaces it with contempt and loathing.
The world looks gorgeous, driven from a first person perspective, but unlike Portal and others there is no story here. The world is a series of miniature biomes with little purpose other than to hold more puzzles. Once you exhaust all the puzzles in an area, you move on to another one and begin the process again.
The Witness, at least for me, is simply not a rewarding experience. If nothing else, the joy should be derived from the act of solving puzzles itself, but the frustrations mentioned above make that impossible for me.

Well, to be honest, living in the same place forever might not bother some people , but all the hopes and dreams (There's no True Pacifist route right here, sorry) get flushed by maybe the most unexpected villain in a story: A talking plush Bear with a certain taste of 'Despair and Bloodlust';
Anyway, your casual life in this school-trap is to search (for an eventual escape?) and act with people...Yep, there's a relationship system like Persona but less complicated
and with an reward for it when you decide to interact withyour fellows : skills.
What is those you might say, it's  a supplement help in the second part of the game: The Class Trials
Depending on what difficulty you are, the harder you decide to take('Kind' to 'Mean'), well, the harder you got.
But what are exactly those Class Trials? Let's say there's a murder with all a mystery besides it, you, the MC of the story decides(and try his best) to find clues, then, when enough clues are found( It's automatic, you can't fail at searching the evidences), the trial starts(Oh boy!). No worry out there, a secretly placed narrator will help you through the procedure (I don't remember who much time he comes to help you, though. And I'ven't finished the game at this moment but, y' know)Through Non Stop Debates, Hangman's Gambits , Closing Argument and Bullet Time Battle, you'll see through the light of truth and so, the murderer...
If you don't manage to catch the 'fiend' by not being logic at all/By being a slow-pow, this guy will leave the school,seems cool? Well, maybe not for you, you are sentenced to death and not a normal death: A spectacular death (Afterall, the students are Ultimates;so the punishment). On other hand, if you caught the culprit after breaking him down to a final proof/exposure, you are spared for this moment...But not the murderer, duh.
In three words: Good old memories.
And again, thanks for the devs to bring for all the fan of DGR that remake, seriously, thank you.
(I would really hope the same think for DGR II ;and if possible, Persona3/4 Golden, but meh,not the same company after all)

I played through this awhile ago on another platform, buying again here because I really want to support this and other NIS titles getting into more people's hands.
The game is very similar to the Ace Attorney series in that you'll follow a structure of "lull period > murder > investigation > trial", but it's a much darker setting where an average joe and various eccentric upperclassmen are locked up in a private academy, with the only way out being to kill another student and get away with the crime. All the while goaded on by a malevolent cartoon bear.
It's a hybrid between visual novel and adventure game, with a cast of absurd characters who you actually get pretty attached to over time, ratcheting up the tension of wondering who's going to off who next. Whereas the court sections in Ace Attorney are fairly static affairs of "present evidence here", in Danganronpa they're comprised of these ridiculous minigames, like firing your evidence at opposing statements in an on-rails shooter, or playing a rhythm game to out-argue your opponent. It's nuts, and it's awesome.
Masafumi Takada's soundtrack is a real gem too, it's an absolutely fantastic blend between the creeping dread pervading the grim atmosphere and high-energy electro beats during the court sections. Though unfortunately the soundtrack on Steam doesn't seem to contain all the tracks of the game, rather a few extended mixes of scattered tracks.
Definitely one of my personal favorite games, had me hooked the whole way through.

Let's get one thing out of the way first: Detective Grimoire is not the bonafide Professor Layton clone some may have been hoping for. Though it shares a few similarities, and even references the top hat wearing puzzle solver at one point, where Layton focuses heavily on brain teasers and riddles Grimoire is a pure detective game; something akin to an elaborate game of Clue crossed with an adventure game. While I could see developer SFB Games losing some people at this point, Detective Grimoire is actually all the better off for straying away from Nintendo's franchise and carving its own original, highly enjoyable path for itself.
Set in a swamp located in the middle of nowhere, populated by suspicious individuals, and potentially home to a mysterious and brutal creature, a murder takes place. With little to go on, the police turn to Detective Grimoire (whose first name I never did find out), who arrives at the scene of the crime and begins to get to work putting the pieces together of just what occurred the night before.
And this is where you come in. When I said this was a pure detective game, I meant it quite fully, as the entire game is broken down to finding clues, questioning suspects, and gathering evidence to eventually track down the culprit. As a result, the actual gameplay is rather simple, and usually involves little more than asking suspect A about clue B to get clue C, and repeat this until you've exhausted what you can get out of who you're questioning.
It's a bit dull on paper, yes, but what kept me engaged throughout the 3 or so hour story was the brilliant writing, lively character, and dry humor and wit of Grimoire. There is a huge amount of personality in every character, every line of dialog delivered with some truly fantastic voice work leading you one step closer to the final reveal, and the vibrant and wonderfully animated art is just the character on top. The plot itself likely couldn't hold its own among most other whodunits, but the way everything is presented more than makes up for the occasionally straightforward narrative and kept me entertained and guessing right up to the very end.
Perhaps some will miss the puzzles or elaborate plot of other detective games, but I for one found Detective Grimoire's offbeat style, basic but enjoyable sleuthing, and buckets of personality one of the more uniquely enjoyable games I've played all year. It doesn't try to do a whole lot, but focuses its energy where it counts and makes my only real disappointment being there is not more of it. Thankfully, if what is hinted at after the credits becomes a reality we'll be seeing more of this detective soon, and that's definitely something to look forward to.

To start off with, everyone looking at this game should know that it is 95% visual novel, which means it is almost entirely composed of simply reading. If this isn't your jam, this game is not for you.
To everyone else, I can heartily recommend VA-11 Hall-A. A memorable cast, good writing, vibrant art and jammin' music makes for a great little cyberpunk romp where, as a bartender, you listen to the stories of your patrons while simultaneously getting them totally sh*t-faced.
Now for a few nit-picks. First, the game is relatively short; at a moderate pace your first playthrough will probably be between 10-12 hours, and with only an extra few hours you can 100% it with all achievements included. While I would have preferred a longer experience to fill out the multitude of character stories going on, the $15 price tag gives it a bit of leniency in this regard.
Another aspect that has some room for improvement is the actual gameplay component; every so often you will be tasked with using a set of controls on the right side of the screen to make drinks for your customers based on their order, or what you *think* they want. While it works well enough, and complements the storytelling well, it becomes fairly tedious as the game progresses. After the tutorial at the beginning, the recipe list and steps to make each drink stay exactly the same throughout the whole game; soon you will know the recipes by heart, and are simply forced to go through the motions to progress the story. I wish they had thrown some curveballs in this regard, maybe add some new drink recipes or change the drink making process somewhat due to certain occurances. Not a huge deal, just something to keep in mind.
Lastly, and this is more just my personal taste in literature, but I feel that Vallhalla's writing props itself a bit too much on lewd humor and sexual undertones. While sexuality is definitely present as a major theme, it feels a bit forced, as if most characters only have sex on the brain. I still enjoy the writing in Valhalla overall, but this is something that stood out to me as a bit of a narritive crutch.
tl;dr
While not perfect and relatively short, VA-11 Hall-A is a very enjoyable Cyberpunk visual novel that fans of the genre should absolutely check out.

Toki Tori is a puzzle game with very simple controls.  Using only the mouse to point and click directions to your avatar, and using the tools provided in limited supply, you need to navigate your avatar to each egg in the level. The first few levels warm you up to the control scheme and tools, but it gets really tricky really fast.  The normal levels aren't all that hard, but the hard levels had me wracking my brain for a bit of time, looking for any tiny loophole; anything to exploit.  The game goes from fun to maddeningly frustrating, but not in a hurry to punish.  If you love simple puzzle platformers, you definitely should give this a shot.  If you are looking for an action platformer, this is definitely not what you are looking for.

I would not recommend the game in the current state. I do not know if developers are going to fix what I consider shortcomings, and if they are not, then I'm not recommending the game altogether.
When you start a new game for the first time you are presented with 3 difficulty choices. Two of them are locked at this stage, so you only can choose the easiest. (Very minor gripe: why the heck to give a choice when there is no choice?)
When you are playing the game there are 10 "milestones", certain conditions during the game that are used to measure your progress. They could be "reach 500 power" or "reach 100 colonists" or sopmething else. In my first and only game (that took 17 hours across three sessions) I got 9/10. The last one "reach 300 colonists" was not possible for me to achieve because I ran out of space for colony buildings, and here is my problem number 1.
When you start a new game, you "choose" a pinpoint on the planet where you land. The interface for choosing it is abysmal	. You cannot rotate the planet with keyboard and you cannot zoom in or out. Mouse speed when rotating is about of a dying snail. I honestly cannot understand why they included this game element, it's awkward and pointless. In zoomed out state you do not see what landscape is like so you are just choosing at random. And here is where the real problem starts. I happened to land in a relatively small area surrounded by mountains from 3 sides, and the 4th side was the edge of the map (which is also bizarre, because I mean they just allowed me to rotate the freaking planet, I know that it's a sphere and I know that it does not have an edge). When I started the game I did not realize that there would not be enough space for me to fully develop, and that the game gives you a zilch ways of crossing the mountains. The "edge" is also not obvious. At a certain point you can no longer build in that direction, no line in the sand, perfectly level surface, it just does not let you place a building as if you are trying to place it on to  another building or on a mountain. Frustrated, you are trying again and again, until you realize that you are not supposed to build on the other side of an invisible wall. Anyway, after 17 hours of play it is a surprise that you cannot actually finish the level.
That was problem number 1. Note, that the game is probably meant to be open ended, so I'm not sure if it would properly "finish" even if I got 10/10. So how they say, the pleasure is the journey, not the destination. (Edit: the game does not have a win condition. You have a hard limit of 200 buildings and 500 colonists)
Here is problem number 2. Some sim games give you an info panels about your minions (in this case colonists) and this one is no different. What is different from some of the games I played before, is that the info panel usually have a button to find the minion or to follow it. Not in this game. You click a colonist, you look at the panel and when you are done this colonist already wondered away and with a big base you cannot find her any longer, because she looks exactly like anyone else. By the way if the person departs (visitor) the info panel does not reflect this and displays the last known data. Now, you might be thinking, but do you actually *need* to look at the colonist information? I'll be honest with you I wondered the same. You see, I'd be happy if the game was built so that this information is of no use and can be totally hidden. I'd also be happy if it was there and easy to use. But currently if you'd like to investigate why your colonists are dying for no obvious reason you really can't. First of all, "a colonist has died" notification when clicked does NOT show you the colonists or her info pane. It just jumps somewhere on the map. Presumably, this is the place where the colonist died. There is no body or any indication of what happened though. So you reload a recent save if you were lucky to have one, and you are trying to find that person that is going to die. But since the game does not have a colonists list, or colonists search, you cannot really find this person, no way. If by some crazy accident you managed to find her and select her and look at her info panel... well I did not manage that.
Here is problem number 3. As game flows you get event notifications in the bottom left corner. You left click to follow them, you right click to dismiss them. If you are not fast enough they are gone. If these where landing permissions and you missed it, well sucks to be you, you just lost these coins you otherwise could have earned, better luck next time. If there was two similar events about different objects the game group them up and excludes any specific information. So if two building were completed or two people died, you won't be informed what these building where or what theses people died from. Why is there no log, that one could browse at leisure? Btw, sometimes but not always, even if just *one* person dies the game does not tell you why. "Well he died. Whatever."
So the above sums up to the following. I wish I did not need the log, I wish I did not need to track individual colonists, but I do. And here is why. When my colony was developed with about 100 colonists and 30 bots, I had all my production lines up. I did not have absence of any particular resource. In particular, there was enough food. Still a colonists died "from starvation". Then another one, then another. Soon there was enough dead that there was not enough people to for the hydroponics, so the food supply plummeted and everyone died because now there was really no food. This happens, and the game gives you no way to find out what went wrong. You are simply left in the dark. This leads me on to...
Problem number 4. This game does not support any corrective actions. If you ran out of an important resource (any important resource) there is no way to recover. (If you have plenty of other resources and lucky timing a trader flies by you might be able to salvage the situation, but from my about a dozen reloads it did not happen once). The only thing you can do is to reload your previous save and make sure that this resource does not run out. I'm not sure, maybe it's a genre staple? If it is I do not like it, I feel that there should be an in-game way to correct a mistake without the need to reload.
Problem number 5. There seems to be a limited number of save slots and the saves are called save1, save2 and save3. I'm serious, that's what they are called and you cannot change these. (I understand that this is probably so that they can port to a mobile device easily, but it's just an explanation, not a good excuse)
Problem number 6. So remember I told you that there is no way to find out what happened when something goes wrong? Well what the game wants you to do is to use built in resource graphs to figure out what dynamic led up to the current situation. The only problem is that there are bazillion of different resources and a single graphs screen. You have an icon per resource that you switch on an off to show the line on the graph or not. This is so bloody inconvenient. Because they did not have enough colours, half of the colours are the same so you cannot tell on the graph one line from another, and there is no legend. Also certain types of resources mean something to some people like me in combinations. So for example I want often to see raw ore and metal produced from it. And then I want to see starch and bioplastic produced from it, and also vegetables, because they same as start come out from the hydroponic pods. And in order to switch from one view from another I need to unclick all the old resources one by one and then click all the new ones one by one, what a nuisance!
This game could be good. Currently it is not. The worst thing, that most of the problems are only noticeable only when you are well in the game, and not immediately.

For those who already know and enjoy the franchise, Cities XXL is a must,  the 50% discount is a fair deal for Cities XL owners. The multi-core support is the most important feature of this release along with Steam Workshop integration for custom content.
If you never played Cities XL, this could become your favourite city builder.
The new UI though is not very different, looks better than the old one, at least it looks more stylish for today standards.  The new filter allows you to filter buildings by Architectural style, period, geographic location, etc. That's quite useful considering the game has tons of buildings and many more are constatly created by the modding community.
The game overall feels and looks the same but the improvements are noticeable, the new skybox that allows you to select different environments (cloudy days, beautiful sunsets, etc) makes the cities look more alive and realistic.  The shadows were improved and the texture filtering is better (no blurry textures).
There are some new buildings like freight airport, a new sport marina, bike rental, and many more including new transport related buildings like Park and Ride. Industries now can be upgraded to more eco-friendly versions.  There are no new residential buildings, though.
The game's still not perfect, but still quiet enjoyable and no other game offers the graphic detail or the map sizes of CXXL.
If you didn't like the previous versions, move along. It's likely you ain't gonna like this one either.

I found the Witness to be one of the most intriguing puzzle games I've ever played.
I'm the type of player that enjoys the journey as much as the destination so the process of learning how each new puzzle mechanic worked was immensely satisfying for me. Some reviews I've watched have said the game should have been a straightforward puzzle game on a tablet or phone because the exploration doesn't offer anything, and I completely disagree. One of my favorite segments in the game involved walking through a series of mazes and trying to pay attention to any sort of clue I could find in order to discover how each maze related to the panel at its end. Exploration is key to the enjoyment of this game, and offers a welcome break from a tough puzzle you just can't solve.
Overall, I think this is an exceptional game for the small audience it was designed for. If you're like me, where the process of discovery is something you enjoy, then you should check this game out. However, if you're looking for action or a compelling, clear storyline, look elsewhere.
Also, if the $40 price tag scares you off, check out a game called English Country Tune. It has similar elements of figuring out abstract puzzles on your own and is much cheaper. If you like that one, chances are you'll enjoy The Witness as well.

Some absolutely brilliant line-based puzzles placed around a pretty nice looking island.
The way the game gradually teaches you each of the puzzle mechanics seperately, then works to slowly combine them with one another to form more complex puzzles is fantastically done. If you pay attention through each puzzle, look at the environment around you, and take 30 seconds to sit and think it over carefully, you'll be able to solve most of them without hints even if you're only modestly skilled at puzzle games like me.
If I had one gripe, it's that the puzzles involving tetris pieces were significantly less fun than any of the other puzzle types, sometimes to the point where I felt more like I was trying to solve a math problem than solve a video game puzzle (to the point that I often just looked up solutions for the late-game ones), but this may very well be my personal puzzle taste rather than those puzzles being definitively not as good as the others.
Also there's basically no story so don't go in expecting anything like lore about the island beyond a few very ambiguous audio logs and some old philosophical quotes. There's also the requisite super-pretentious "SO INTELLECTUAL" indie hipster lesson you're meant to take away from the game (which I won't bother sharing unless one of you -really- wants to know because I think it's just plain silly), but it really doesn't mess with the gameplay experience at all if you just pretend it's not there.

Some puzzles simply do not convey the idea behind them well enough. It's much too easy to accidentally stumble upon a puzzles solution without actually LEARNING how it works, and in doing so robbing yourself of the knowledge required to proceed in successive puzzles. Also, each area will have a point where a rule is altered slightly to mix things up a little, however if you were already grappling with a puzzle you didn’t understand in the first place this will hardly be a welcome change. To top it all off, getting some puzzles wrong will ‘lock’ them until the preceding puzzle is completed again (the puzzle doesn’t change, you just have to repeat the process again), which is done to prevent ‘brute forcing’ puzzles. The irony being that if the difficulty escalation and new mechanics had been introduced properly in the first place, this would never be a risk, and so all it does is penalise players who weren’t taught what to do properly in the first place. In the end, all you have left is a failure and frustration loop which drowns out any jubilation earned through progressing with hard work and ingenuity, and replaces it with contempt and loathing.
The world looks gorgeous, driven from a first person perspective, but unlike Portal and others there is no story here. The world is a series of miniature biomes with little purpose other than to hold more puzzles. Once you exhaust all the puzzles in an area, you move on to another one and begin the process again.
The Witness, at least for me, is simply not a rewarding experience. If nothing else, the joy should be derived from the act of solving puzzles itself, but the frustrations mentioned above make that impossible for me.

Tenho andado pelos reviews da página do jogo, e não encontrei nenhum ainda comentado em português sobre o mesmo. Então... vamos ao trabalho.
Muitos devem ter conhecido o jogo na adaptação em anime que aconteceu em 2013, alias, foi um belo anime naquela season. Outros podem ter conhecido ainda na época do PSP, ou depois pelo port para o PSVita. O importante é, o jogo se manteve sempre no alto, considerado um dos melhores
do console. E hoje [18/02/2016], é lançado um port para os computadores via steam. Foi uma longa jornada até chegar a esse ponto.
Você assume o papel de Makoto Naegi, um garoto que se auto-intitula
, e se joga numa aventura obscura, misteriosa, onde nem tudo é o que parece dentro de uma escola. E tudo isso piora com a chegada de um ser misterioso (que por sinal é bem divertido, se não fosse
), colocando um peso na atmosfera do jogo. Seu papel é sobreviver e proteger aqueles que você gosta. Como uma visual novel, você vai passar muito tempo conversando, lendo e andando pela escola, e criando *laços* com os personagens, até que se prove o contrário.
Como toda Visual Novel, você vai ler, e ler MUITO. > se você não tem conhecimento médio, ou pelo menos básico de inglês, além dos famosos slangs que aparecem bastante durante o jogo, você terá alguns probleminhas de entendimento <, os personagens tem personalidades diferentes, e a reação de cada um em seus diálogos faz com que o jogo tenha uma imersão profunda. Além da parte de visual novel, temos a parte de gameplay (que são diversos puzzles, minigames) durante cada capítulo, que entram em conjunto com a exploração e investigação do jogo.
Geralmente eu tenho medo de responder essa pergunta... mas... SIM! O port é excelente. Foi bem trabalhado, 1080p / 60 fps / dual audio / sem slowmotion / nenhum crash.
Não tive *e espero não ter* nenhum problema com o jogo.
Então se sua dúvida é se o port é bom, a resposta é:
.
Se você está disposto a viajar em uma acid trip, com personagens caricatos e bem trabalhados, em uma história de ~terror~, com um clima de suspense em cada minuto. Esse com toda certeza é o jogo que você está procurando.

There's little to no randomness or luck to the game. Every single time you get hit it's your own fault, and if you manage to overcome a situation without getting hit, it's all thanks to you: the player.
As you progress farther and farther in the game the areas you already cleared before become a breeze and you can easily jump, roll and slash through hordes of enemies that you used to have trouble with. I never felt a situation or enemy was particularly unfair. Got hit by an arrow? Duck faster next time! Fell into a pit? Time your jumps better! Like I explained before, the hazards in every world won't change, your skill will. Greatly.
If anyone who reads this is having a hard time completing the game, or heck, even the first world. I'll tell them: Keep going! it is definitely worth it.

Detective Grimoire is a very neat little game created by duo brothers, Tom and Adam Vian, both collectively known as SFB Games, or, The Super Flash Bros. Grimoire is the second in the series, the original being available on the Newgrounds website, although the game doesn't hold many throwbacks to that game, aside from one remark, so it isn't ultimately necessary to play in order to enjoy this game, although  still whole heartedly recommended.
Detective Grimoire details the story of the titular character's attempts to solve the mystery of the death of an attraction within an unusual place, and his main suspect is the tourist attraction's prominent star - Boggy, a creature that nobody has seen in decades. The Detective has been called to this murky bog in order to solve this mystery. While finding his misplaced hat, preferably.
First thing first - there is no doubt that Detective Grimoire is an excellent game, and with the price I spent on it, I was pretty satisfied. However, the issue I mainly had for this  game was the puzzles, and the overall difficulty is a bit lacking. The puzzles that arised were very simplistic, and the game never really presented much of a challenge. Aside from that, I really did enjoy everything else. Unraveling the mystery of the swamp was very irritating, and the presentation of the bog was excellent, both in terms of art and sound. The humour in the game was also very amusing, and I must admit, I did find myself having a bit of a childish giggle at Grimoire's thought puzzle sections.
Detective Grimoire is definitely something people should check out, and, as a huge fan of SFB Games, I look forward to what they produce next!

This game has a lot going for it, but also some glaring faults.  You're a silent (so far) captured guy who is trying to fight his way off an elevated set of floating island "jails".  You don't know why you're there, and you have a man in a bunny head providing exposition and direction.  Gameplay is a boss-rush twin-stick shooter with melee fighting elements, including a parry system (will get to this later).
Pros:
- Nice art style
- Great soundtrack
- Generally fun gameplay.
Cons:
- The time between fights is ridiculous.  You have to walk (slowly) to the next boss while the bunny-head man delivers vague context to your situation.  It's simply not fun, or that interesting, to be honest.  Everything so far is "the next boss has been locked up for a long time, they do/do not deserve their fate, they are/are not insane now".  No clues on how the fight is going to be, no real background, no reason why you have to fight them and just can't go on your merry way (yet).
- Parry system is busted and/or too hard for me to deal with.  Maybe I should just get good.  I've logged hundreds (if not thousands) of hours in the Dark Souls series and the Batman games, so I think I should be able to handle this alright, and for the melee combat, I can, it's fine.  But the projectile parry apparently requires pixel-perfect timing and positioning - and the "almost, but not quite, top-down" view of certain parts of fights makes that almost impossible unless you're straight on. You also can't entirely control where dodges are going to leave you (you go different lengths depending on how long you hold the button down), making the positioning even more difficult
-  The fights take an eternity.  Maybe that's a good thing.  But if you defeat a phase of a boss, you get full life, and they gets an "energy tank" (a la Metroid) taken away.  However, if you lose an energy tank/die, they not only get full life, but they restart the previous phase of the fight.  If you're not the parry-master, these fights are going to take upwards of 10 min or more to complete.  I'd enjoy the game a lot more if they just gave you 3 knockdowns and didnt' reset the phases of the fight.
Overall: It's fun despite its flaws.  It's a frustrating and difficult, but some people like that (myself included).  I could see this being a popular game to speedrun.  7.5/10

While the game isn't too original of a concept (It's essentially one of those ant farm style colony management games) its story and message are actually rather powerful. Essentially, it's a war game that takes a new point of view on war. Rather than playing as the soldiers and fighting the battles mentioned throughout your session, you play as a group of civilians. Lost, homeless, and broken with only the most basic of survival necessities. It's a rather eye opening experience on how games tend to take on the topic of war. While Battlefield, Call of Duty, and all those other FPS titles tend to glorify it, making the explosions big and the action constant, This War of Mine takes a much more human approach. You start with two or three 'survivors' of the war (Depending on who you choose to play with, you can have up to four) and start out with a bare minimum supply of food and medicine.
You would typically spend the first day clearing out debris, opening doors, and finding anything you can within your 'base' while you get your bearings. The first night would typically start with relatively safe areas to scavenge for supplies and, if you're really lucky, may even have someone to trade with. Anyway, every night you spend scavenging has a chance to bring long lasting damage to your crew's moral. If you decide to rob someone, kill another person (Even in self defense) or decide to let two civilians fight it out, resulting in the death of an innocent person, your crew will regret that decision for a long while. This regret, if left unchecked, can eventually turn into depression which can, eventually, end in suicide. The suicide will then make your crew even sadder, and so on and so forth. As a mechanic, however, sadness actually lowers the productivity of your survivors, as they lose motivation.
As for story, most of it is rather up front and basic. You're in a city under seige and you're trying to survive until a cease fire is called so that civilians can evacuate. If you read notes, graffiti, and your characters' bios (Which update at certain intervals) you can find out more about the game's plot and the life your characters had before and during the war. You'll find abandoned notes from other civilians about how snipers had just killed their best friend while scavenging, or how a school had to go under lockdown due to rising tensions in the neighborhood. Your characters will also comment on each area you enter upon their initial arrival, giving a little bit of context as to what the area used to be like.
A few flaws I've noticed, though, is that combat is a bit confusing to newer players, at least in my experience. You start nightly scavenging runs in 'scavenge' mode. A mode that doesn't let you fight until you enter 'combat' mode by clicking your weapon's icon on the side of your screen. I believe you're then supposed to click who you wish to attack, but I haven't been able to do so succesfully since most combat has been largely in the enemy's favour. Another small flaw, in the case of gameplay, is that some items are able to stack while others, which would be able to stack within reason, cannot do so in a reasonable manner or at all. For instance, you can have two planks of wood per inventory slot, but, you can't carry more than four units of 'parts' per slot despite them being a good bit smaller than a plank of wood. While this is obviously meant to make gameplay more difficult and force players to prioritize certain supplies over others, it's a bit annoying that you have to make an annoyingly large amount of trips to pick up items that, really, should be able to fit in your inventory based on the game's logic.
The game is definitely a challenge early on and supplies tend to be rather rare throughout the entire game but, and there's always a but, it gets kind of easy in the later game if you plan properly. If you prioritize barricading and weapons, you'll be almost immune to raids and you'll be able to kind of brute force your way through hostile areas, assuming you're able to bring a gun and plenty of ammo (Which are both relatively hard to obtain early on). If you plan well ahead of time, you'll also be able to get through the winter section of the game with ease, assuming nothing goes wrong. Essentially, the game can be a cake walk for experienced players which kind of takes away the fun after a while. Newer players, however, may really enjoy the challenge of this game for a while. The decisions you have to make, and the time frame to make them in, may ultimately spell your doom if you make a choice before you're prepared for its consequences.
Overall, a solid game with a powerful message. I'd suggest it to anyone who wants a new take on war in video games.

Toki Tori is an eggcellent and hard-as-eggs puzzle game. Do not be fooled by its cutesy look, for underneath it lies very solid gameplay and clever level design.
The goal of each level is to collect all eggs using a limited number of items available at your disposal. Some levels have enemies you need to circumvent, but usually the main problem becomes planning your way through the level and finding the right order in which to collect all the eggs. Toki Tori has this peculiar puzzle game quality that often makes you think “this level is impossible, the game must be bugged!” in frustration and despair until you finally stumble upon the unexpected solution and marvel at how you couldn't think of it earlier.
Despite its appearance, the game is NOT a platformer. Toki Tori has no inertia and can neither jump nor dash. All characters and objects in the game are always “snapped” to a large grid, which saves you from that awful mentality of trying to find a pixel-perfect location for a block to place. After having learned the game mechanics, you’ll soon find yourself able to plan your way throughout the entire level without any prior experimentation. The game does, however, feature a convenient time rewind function that lets you try your idea and, if you see it fail, rewind it back.
If you’re unsure, I dare you to try the demo and see if you can resist Toki Tori's cuteness and wit.

Well, where do I begin? With the fact that this game is an amazing re-creation of vintage FPS games? How about pointing out the great in-game design of the playing field? I'll just keep it simple.
This game is simply amazing. The graphics are awesome, the movement is fun, and the idea is timeless. I was browsing through the free-to-play FPS games to kill some time while I got my old copy of Quake 3 Arena set up again and thats when I came across this game. If I'm just being honest, this is pretty much a knockoff of Q3A, but it's dissimilar enough that I really don't mind as it's still a very fun game to play. Mind you, I've only been playing the free version which, unfortunately, only comes with one playable map. However, that one map has got me hooked. I think that the developers did an amazing job with re-creation, and took great care in crafting the playing field. The gameplay is highly immersive, and will keep you playing for hours (if you're into this kind of game). The movement mechanics are pretty fun, too, and make it a very fast-paced game, just like Quake.
The BIGGEST problem I can see is that there is a very, very small payer-base for this game. It's unfortunate, too. I would have guessed that more people would be into this kind of game as well, but I guess times change and people's gaming priorities will as well. If you do come across this review, though, and you've gotten this far.. Please give it a shot? It really is worth the free download at the VERY least. As for myself, considering buying the full download, I'll most definitely reconsider if I start noticing a larger player-base. For now I'm perfectly content with the free version.

An addictive, space themed resource management game. It's not a city builder and it's not a realistic simulator. The goal is to build a base and shape it to achieve a good flow of resources.
Planetbase is good for a few weeks of entertainment. You'll probably like it if you enjoyed similar games such as Banished, Prison Architect, or Clockwork Empires. This type of game has a shelf life, because once you figure it out it's over.
If you want to build a big base and not worry about fiddling around with it to make it work this might not be for you. Tossing buildings down with little thought is recipe for disaster. It's far less forgiving than SimCity. The game ends if you make a bad decision.
It takes patience to design a base that doesn't implode when it gets to big. Once a base starts a death spiral it can be quite hard to recover. The fun of the game is discovering how to construct a stable base.

Far Cry 4 is Ubisoft's fourth installment in the "core" Far Cry franchise, set in the fictional Kyrat the game follows Ajay Galle's (son of Golden Path founder Mohan Galle) trip to Kyrat in order to spread his mother's ashes but ends up coming face-to-face with Kyrat dictator Pagan Min. Ajay ends up meeting Sabal, leader of the Golden Path resistence group. Ajay joins The Golden Path and begins to weaken the army forces of Kyrat.
Far Cry 4's story is a gripping and deep plot flowing seamlessly over the 15-20 hour campaign. The charecters you meet have a deep past and motives behind every action. The game has great replay value because of the "Balance of Power" missions which allows the player to choose if they want to follow Sabal or Amita, this can lead to many play throughs trying different combinations of these missions, although from what I understand the games ending will always end up the same. But I do appreciate giving players the freedom to influence part of the game's campaign.
The game, for me, is mainly domainated with positives and great experiences with the game. Although there are a few things that I cannot get past. The first is UPlay (like I say in every Ubisoft game review that I write). The second are the odd limitations placed upon the player. The one that really damages the experience for me is only being able to carry 90 rounds for a gun. This commonly leads to issues in combat where there are many enemies, which you will experience a lot, and you'll have to solely rely on takedowns to collect more ammo of enemies. At least the small weapon range in this game works in the player's favour for this. I still got quite frustrated with it and it just doesn't make sense to have that limit. The main problem I have with this game are the set of missions based around the sub "Shaning-La" plot which you are part of the main campaign missions without providing any benefit to the story. Every time one of these missions came along I dreaded it. Not because the gameplay in these missions were bad. But because I didn't see a benefit to the story. There is no tie-in what so ever to the main Golden Path story line and I wish these were just side missions. The game is also hindered with an amazingly small weapon selection for a first-person-shooter, but I feel the FPS aspect of this game was majorly overlooked and rushed in favour of the open-world aspect which was great but shouldn't have taken such a big dominence over the FPS aspect which still plays a major role. Finally my issue with the game being very unbalanced. I found that as the game goes on you'll end up entering unbalanced areas of the game leading to a sometimes frustrating and un-enjoyable combat experience at points in the game. Although when you finally do complete those parts you feel such a big sense of achievement.
In conclusion, Ubisoft's Far Cry 4 has a perfect blend of action with Golden Path missions, adventure with the vast open world of Kyrst and a great story in the end creating an amazing game despite my issues with it. For $30 (at the time of writing the review) you can't do wrong with it and I would recommend it highly.

Cons:  Don't expect a lengthy game!  I beat it twice in under 10 hours for all the achievements.  The entire game only encompasses a small group of tiles, so not much exploring.  The harvesting can be tedious when combined with the constant need to rest and exchange for supplies. At the moment, I really cannot reccomend Amazing Frog?. Although there are some interesting mechanics and worthwhile gameplay, it has yet to capitalize on itself. They've definitely made an interesting sandbox, and Swindon appears to be teeming with life at first glance, but after logging 4 hours, I had to get a refund. I've had this game on my wishlist for 2 years and have neever seen it on sale, but I decided to give it a go anyway, figuring it couldn't be the worst $16 I'd ever spend.
I really can't say that it's worth buying at the moment, unfortunately. There just isn't anything fun to do, after exploring the world. Picking up trash is suprisingly fun, but because you can only pick up one thing at a time, the movement is so slow, and trash receptacles are so spaced apart, it gets boring quickly. Searching for skins is fun, but the movement feels so broken and never does what I ask of it, it's almost unbearable. I understand the point of the movement is to be goofy and funny, but when a joke gets in the way of core mechanics that should be reliable, it's hard to take the game seriously.
This review isn't very in-depth, but the takeaway here is that it's just not worth a $15 price tag, plus tax for a digital toy with no goals, no functionality, and is likely to never see the light of full release. If it was a $7.50 game, I absolutely would have recommended the game, for the 4 hours of play and laughs it provided; $16 with no vision of a full release and no sales is just unacceptable, in my eyes.

I really want to like this game, it's got some awesome parts. But the AI is just way too dumb, when you've got a full food stock and empty meal areas and colonists die because they wait too long get a meal that's not a planning flaw that's a game mechanic fail. Please patch this AI soon.

EDIT NOTE: The devs are taking the AI problems seriously, and are patching it for the better with each update, as well as adding new elements that make managing your workers mutch easier.
With this in mind, it is obvious that the developers are dedicated to this game. As support to its development, I have revised my opinion and now think that it is worth its price.
TL;DR: Grate fun game that is coming to being near perfect as the developers fix all the AI.
Pros: Fun to play, with something to do at all stages.
It is a simple but in depth planning game where what you decide to do will have a ripple effect on everything else. As you build you have to keep in mind distance of travel, and make sure that there is enough utility spaced out to meat the needs of your colonists no matter where they are stationed. (one canteen at the end of your base will be a recipe for disaster).
You will be finding your self checking graphs as a predictor of whether or not you can afford more colonists, and also to make changes before things go bad. (the more storage you have, the better of a buffer you will have to detect a production problem.)
You also have to balance your work force, to make sure that all production will go smooth no matter what. Biologists and Engineers will be your main life blood. But you can't forget medics and guards, and workers when your starting. (robots will replace worker duty's down the line).
Cons: The AI
I once had 3 canteens with 2 meal makers in each, and 2 colonists dyed of starvation even though I had a food stock pile of over 200 meat and 200 veg.
I set up a guards station at the entrance of my base where visitors come in, in order to get intruders before they attacked unarmed colonists. But all the guards did was just blindly watch the CCTV and did nothing, while 3 guards and some unarmed colonists was running from across the base thinking they was going to Chuck Norris the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them. All 7 guards in their seats just watched the bloodshed going on behind them on the monitors...
lazy people! It is not uncommon to find non of your production being tended to, wile your colonists just stand around in the halls idle. this means that you will need more colonists then you would think to man the equipment half of the time. (note: this does not include going for food, beer, lesher or bed. They will have full stats and just stand there... In the hall... For 2 minutes.
summary: It is a fun game, and if you like games like banished, you will enjoy it. I would recommend playing it, and the AI wose are a small hiccup that you can get around if you build your base right.

10 X 16 X 2 = 320 "Ore"

25 X 2 = 50 Hours for 1 "Plates"

That's means that in order to get 2 Structures you have to play every second of every day (WITH PREMIUM) for two months in order to complete 1 of 6 parts that you need to build a destroyer. This is FAR different than the '50 a day" drop rates one of the developers stated.

Now that I'm a working adult, I rarely have the energy or time to play games. Even the most engaging epics (Xenoblade Chronicles, Skyrim, etc) can only hold my attention for a few hours, MAX, before I need to do something else. Maybe it's because they don't feel as rewarding any more, or the stories just aren't as engaging as they used to be, but I know that I peeled off the "hardcore" label from my gamer card long ago.
I tell you this anecdote because I just spent nearly 10 straight hours playing Volgarr, and didn't even realize it.
This game is a pungent distillation of everything that I loved and hated about video games in the 80's and 90's. Back then, memory was at a premium, so in order to make a game feel like it was worth the $50 price tag, developers make them hard as nails in order to extend the play time you would need to devote in order to complete the game. This meant hours upon hours of committing each level, every enemy and all the boss patterns to muscle memory, and knowing how to react in each situation. It was an arduous process, but when you finally mastered a level and beat the boss, you felt like you had accomplished something. I realized, upon completing Volgarr, that this is what I had been missing from most modern games, where victory is all but ensured.
Volgarr is hard. Words like brutal and unforgiving don't really do it justice. Its smartly hard. I had quite a bit of trouble with the game, and actually gave it up for almost a year after I got stuck on stage 2. When I finally picked it back up this weekend, I approached it as a puzzle game; each encounter, every enemy's placement and movement, was done with care - all I had to do was find the pattern and "solve" the puzzle with Volgarr's moveset. This made every advancement feel like a real victory, and this game is one of the first in a long time to elicit actual cheers of joy when I completed a stage for the first time.
Volgarr never felt cheap, exploitative, or unfair. I died hundreds of times, repeating stages over and over, but it never made me angry or frustrated, only determined. Determined because every playthrough got me a little bit further: into the next room, understanding a new monster's attack pattern, or solving a new section of platforming. Every death had an "aha!" moment attached to it. If I died at a section I had played through before, it was 100% my fault. Overall randomness is low, so it is extremely rare that a strategy you succeeded with once will fail the next time.
I could wax poetic telling you about how good the controls feel, or the quality of graphics and music, but there are lots of other reviews for that. I simply wish to convey how satisfying this game is to play, and how accomplished I felt (and hopefully, you will too) when I beat each and every stage. I experienced a range of emotions, from trepidation, anger, fear and elation, something that few modern games can achieve, even with their grandiose storytelling and advanced visual presentation.
I'm not going to assign a number value to my review, because I think that trying to quantify any gaming experience is fairly pointless. Games aren't commodities with certain valuable characteristics, like a vacuum cleaner or toaster oven. Ultimately, what each person gets out of a game really depends on what they expect, what they like from an interactive experience, and how the game meets those needs. Games, in this regard, are like art, and you can't rate art, you can only relate how it makes you feel.
Volgarr challenged me, it made me feel young again, and it gave me a sense of accomplishment.

Ignore the Steam played hours I have played a lot of this game on Vita and played enough to see how the PC port holds up.
This game is very similar to the Phonix Write Ace Attorney series of games, it is very much a visual novel with point and click detective parts and the trials are a mix of several different things but the main thing being using the right clues at the right times. It is very heavy on the text talking and so expect to read a lot in it. The dective parts are simplistic check every searchable spot you can find and talk to everyone. The real enjoyment of the game comes down to the case trials which are interesting to play and have very interesting outcomes. If you enjoyed Phonix Write games you will find this right up your alley, if you hate visual novels with how much of that there is you may have a hard time getting to the trials before giving up because it is very visual novel heavy, heck it took almost 30 minutes to skip through all the intro dialog as quickly as possible for me to see the PC port status.
With that said now for the port quality, I would say its passable but not great. The graphics look like taking the Vita version and just blowing them up to fit your moniter, they don't look any higher rez then the Vitas version, but it does atleast stay at a constant 60FPS even for the cutsceens. The keys are not rebindable (atleast not in game, maybe you can in a ini file, but in game definitly not), and while the mouse works for a fair chunk of the gameplay there is zero mouse support in menus which is my biggest gripe with this port, its bad enough not having rebindable keys in a PC port, but having no mouse support in menus is a big turn off.
Despite its poor PC port, I would still say that this is an enjoyable enough of a game to be worth the money and would actually like to see some PC loving for this game so maybe one day the publisher of the Pheonix Write games see there is an interest in that style of games on PC as well because while I love those games its just so hard for me to play games on my handhelds for long periods of time.
I hope that the devs add in some PC features into the game, like the two complaints I had, but for the price the game is good, and the soundtrack is decent. If anything I would say maybe wait and see if the devs add in the features that should be standard for PC like rebindable keys before buying to try to enforce better porting standards, but other then that I would definitly say this game is good and would like to see more of this type of games like Phoenix Wright/Apollo Justice, and the second Danganrompa game on PC.

Hero of the Kingdom is a pretty solid adventure/very light RPG hybrid. It's a bit odd to describe it, as the game wants to seem like an adventure but it comes out as something fairly unique. You start as a simple farm lad trying to find where your father went off to after bandits ransacked your farm, and end up being, as the title says, the hero of the entire kingdom.
To achieve this end result, you must click, and click, and click! This can be from anything as simple as delivering a letter from clickable person to clickable person #2 to defeating various armies of villainous foes by gathering troops and supplies. There's also objects in the background that, when clicked upon, give various items relating to what they are. These can be very helpful for trading for what you need or selling to get extra gold, though none of them are necessary typically and are just there to make the game last longer.
Speaking of length, it took me 3.3 hours to beat the game, including all my clicking of the extra objects (of which I got about 95%). I was somewhat annoyed to find that I couldn't go back and clean up the last few objects I needed once I had beaten it, but this will only affect you if you're a completionist or achievement hunter. If you are, just be wary of that.
The story is very basic of course, even just basing it on the summary I gave, but it's a quaint little adventure-sorta game. At $7 (and cheaper on sales presumably), this is a nice choice for an interesting game to check out.

Things I liked about this game:
*
. I liked the cartoonish style. It was simple and nice. It conveyed very basic body language (well, facial actually) in a humorous way. The atmosphere is very well achieved.
*
. The scripts were rather humorous, dynamic and very well acted. I liked the different choices in dialog, even though they don't always affect the outcome of the interrogation (but sometimes they do). Little objection:
*

My favourite game of 2016. Furi knows exactly what it's trying to give you in terms of gameplay and an experience, and is delivers to an impressive degree on every front.
The game itself is fast and fluid, with a challenging difficulty curve that feels deeply satisfying to master.
The visuals perfectly mesh with the aesthetic of the game's setting, and lend every encounter a sense of style and flair.
The music is quite possibly my favourite of any game I've played, with each boss having a memorable and unique song that matches each stage of the fight - there are a few tracks that are merely average instead of excellent, but it's overall a joy to listen to.
What's more, this is the first game from Game Bakers, which means they're just getting started. With a first entry this strong, I'm looking forward to what they're going to produce in the future.
And the price is the icing on the cake. £15 is perfect for the amount of time the average player will put into this game, and for those who enjoy speedrunning or are willing to try the Furier difficulty, is absolutely impressive value.
This game is very highly recommended, provided you're comfortable with a challenging boss rush game.

Alright, Amazing Frog, lets go. Note, I'll be re-writing this review when the Unity 5 version is out.
Graphics - To be honest, the graphics in this game aren't great. Most things around the map have a low-poly model and a low res texture making some entire buildings look like nothing more than a colored cube. This is to be expected however, the game was originally built for the OUYA, which doesn't have the highest capacity, and the game is now being remade for the PC. Some buildings have been turned high quality, such as the swindon town planning office or the Frog Court. The lighting is kind of bland, objects dont react to light the way real ones should, and I'm pretty sure most of the lighting in the game is pre-baked. 6/10
Gameplay - What the game lacks in visuals, it makes up for in content. Theres a lot to do in swindon alone. Rescue cats, do a Time Trial, lock up robbers, collect costumes, etc. Outside of swindon theres a giant island with cool stuff to find here and there. Theres a blimp up in some mountains, and a beach with some sharks and cool boats. In the sewers, you can explore all the tunnels, fighting or running away from zombies, trying to find the legendary giant toilet, or trying to unlock a strange mysterious vault, which surely leads to something amazing... And if you ever get sick of Swindon, take a trip to the moon! Fill the rocket outside the warehouse with gas, and blast off! 9/10
The Community - This game has a really nice community of people who play it. Theres forums where you can ask questions if you need help with the game, or a discord if you just wanna chat with some fellow players. My only complaint about the community is that theres always one guy who asks if theres gonna be online multiplayer. The answer is yes, and I swear, no matter how many times anyone answers this question someones always gonna ask it again. I think I may or may not have been one of these people, I don't think I was, but I may have been. 9/10.
Overall - 8.5/10
Side note: the game won't be optimized to f0.3.0, so a lot of computers will lag horribly when playing this game... make sure you have a good computer

I'm particularly ensnared by this game, despite how many attempts it took me to get to the second planet. There's a lot more depth to particular aspects of it than I first expected (the sheer number of different meals that can be produced, for example).
There is one thing that is really getting to me, however. There isn't a way to change priorities once construction blueprints are laid down. Resources will be allocated to new construction before spare parts for repairs, even if the room to create the repair parts is at a heightened priority. For someone like me who will place down multiple rooms at once and then lose because the workers mindlessly build while the energy infrastructure falls apart elsewhere, this is killing me. I was hoping for something more like Dwarf Fortress, where you could set individual workers priorities and have a dedicated repair engineer, dedicated machinist, dedicated builder, instead I have to recycle structures halfway through resource gathering because there's no other way to stop for more pressing work.
Also, the fact that specialists will carry materials (a worker's main job) but won't do anything else outside their field is something that makes losing painfully slow. My first few attempts I didn't realize this, and sat there for a good 20 minutes at 4x speed as my base slowly fell into disrepair as biologists kept everyone fed, but no engineers meant no repairs, and no medics meant no healing. I sat through it hoping adjusting priorities would get the work done, but instead they mindlessly went about their normal tasks until they asphyxiated. After I figured it out of course I was able to recognize the point of no return and restart, but it's just another lack of AI that is making me consider reinstalling Dwarf Fortress...
Despite this I'm continuing to play hoping future updates make up for it.

Magic 2014, like the other Duels of the Planeswalkers titles, is good for two things.
The first is trying out Magic: The Gathering if you have never tried it and you're curious. You can easily learn the rules at your pace and see some examples of particular strategies. If you like it, you can consider starting with the actual card game, which will give you the freedom this game lacks.
The second thing you might use this game for is if you already are a Magic player and want the chance to try out some thematic decks. This way you can save yourself a lot of time and money.
Magic 2014 simply isn't the best game in the series for either.
The first Duels of the Planeswalkers is your best choice if you want to try out Magic, as it is much more beginner-friendly than this one.
Magic 2013 is, on the other hand, the best choice if you want to try out some fun decks, not only beacuse it had the Archenemy mode.
In conclusion, Magic 2014 is not bad, but perhaps not the best choice if you want to buy a Duels of the Planeswalker game.

I'm only a few hours in and I can smell the P2W a mile away.
It seems there's an upgrade discrepancy. Upgrading takes time and resources or you can put in $$$ and get it done immediately. Thusly, a game with a fun layout turns into "mom and dad's credit card" slugfest. Another (personally at least) issue is the fact that the game quite literally shows you where to shoot to damage individuals. There's no guessing game as to where you need to place your cursor to lead onto targets. Kind of spoils the entire fun really and basically assures that no matter what kind of engagement both sides will be taking losses (unless your motor skills are just slightly better than a spider monkey's and can't follow a small circle's general direction). This also makes it feel like there's little to no maneuvers that one can do to try and mitigate damage....
Which brings us to the next problem. Upgrading gives ships health. So not only do you have more damage you also have more health. And since previously stated it is very difficult to mitigate damage (besides trying to play peek-a-boo with a floating celestial body) it makes it almost nearly mandatory to keep on your person a health kit unless you're just that type of "team player" that enjoys the skills that make each ship unique. Thus, every battle feels sort of spam spam spam instead of taking each tactical role and applying it.
Then again, it might be better in the later stages/levels but honestly I'm just not "wow'd" enough past the paygrind to try and get there.
Don't get me wrong, it's a good game just to pick up every now and then and shoot some AI ships or shoot some player ships go pew pew. But I am already seeing a pattern with how much ingame currency you get vs how much gets chewd up by the game's Uncle Sam: the Repair Bill.
It's like War Thunder, but better.

I easily recommend this game for my friends who enjoy games which are a little different yet delightful.

First the most important: this game cannot really be considered as a "game", it is more of a paid patch to older Cities XL versions with many of the bugs STILL present. No surprise, that owners of older versions of Cities XL get a discount - In fact they are just buying the same game again (as I did -_- ).
If you already own one of the previous Cities XL titles, please don't make the same mistake I did: please do not buy this "game". The game is 99% identical to older ones, only the interface is now black instead of blue and the performance is slightly better. Normally, one should expect this type of change in an update instead of a new release.
If you are interested in how this game works and what it offers, I propose you may watch some gameplay videos on youtube, as they might tell you more than I could describe in a text here on Steam. However, I'll try with just a few words:
You start with one of different pre-defined maps, lay out roads, build a town hall and then start zoning residential, industrial and commercial areas. The game offers quite a few nice ideas: residential zoning is separated into different "wealth" categories. The different types of residents are required to operate different types of industry, offices or other workplaces. There are also different density options with higher density offering larger and higher buildings. The "trading" inside the city is calculated using "tokens". Heavy industry needs tokens of unskilled workers and generated heavy industry while manufacturing industry may convert this into manufactured goods which may then be used in commercial areas. If a city is in need of tokens of a certain type, or may have a surplus, tokens may be traded with other cities. However, this trading system is heavily bugged since the first version of Cities XL and was not fixed until today. Of course there is also power, water, pollution, leisure, police, healthcare, fire, etc... However, the simulation is only based on statistics, there is no "real" simulation of vehicles, inhabitants or anything like this.
If you look for an alternative in the City-Building genre Cities (X)XL might be the right game for you if you can withstand bugs. However, you might want to take a look at one of the (almost) identical older versions of Cities XL for a cheaper price ;)
And again: please think twice before buying this "update" if you own a previous game of the franchise.

Furi is insanely cool. It's just different really.
Furi is literally just Final Fantasy style boss fights, in that everyone has like 6 forms that you have to beat until they're truly defeated. Each form consists of one stage where you fight in the whole arena top down. There is usually a lot more shooting going on in this stage. Then when you damage the boss enough, you drop into close combat. Every boss is different and actually really challenging. It'll take you a few tries to beat any boss most likely.
One thing about Furi that I think is the key to it being great is that the timing for interations such as parrying and dodging are so precise, that even if you know what an enemies abilities are, you have to be focused on the game because you know you have 3 sweeping attacks to dodge and only a .1 sec window to do it on each of them. This makes you really get into the game, and also gives you one of the greatest feeling I've ever had in a game. It's challenging, but occasionally you do well, and you really do feel like a f***ing super saiyan when you're blinking across the battlefield, shooting, slashing, and parrying all perfectly. It feels amazing.
Also the music is pretty dope.

tl;dr France's apology for all the half-baked♥♥♥♥♥♥David Cage has put out since 1997. The animation does look a bit jank, given the low budget, but everything else is near-perfect. Astounding action game, ♥♥♥♥ing buy it.
-Gameplay-
Four simple moves (slash, gun, dodge, parry) make for a surprisingly in-depth combat system, built by character action aficionados for character action aficionados, meaning you can CANCEL ANYTHING INTO ANYTHING. The game itself can be completed with a basic grasp of those mechanics, but the skill ceiling and purpose-built speedrun strats are all there, and make the game look gorgeous when played in the right hands.
"Excellence is not an art, it's an habit."
-Structure-
So, this game alternates hi-octane, masterfully designed boss fights and...well...remember those bits in Samurai Jack where Jack slowly walks through those sick ambient backdrops? Yeah, that. The boss fight are 9 (+1 DLC) in total, but last from roughly one hour (your first 5 attempts) to 20 minutes (the near-perfect run you pull off after that one hour of attempts), so in terms of the first playthough's longevity you've got nothing to worry about, with -at least- 8 hours of gameplay, pretty standard length for a character action game.
-Visuals & Sound-
Ok, i'll be fair here: as stated above, the animations do look janky at times, that's french animation in general for ya. If you pay attention to that stuff, it might irk you more then a couple times, so be advised.
Everything else though, from character and enviroment design to OST it's just pure bliss: character art from Takashi Okazaki (Mr. Afro Samurai) and a neon soaked yet kinda pounding synthwave OST by Kn1ght, Danger, Waveshaper, Lorn, Scattle and Carpenter Brut make for a sick ♥♥♥♥ing mix.
So yeah, if you like character action games, synthwave and getting your♥♥♥♥♥♥PUSHED IN, this is the game for you, so go, buy it, GIT GUD and don't forget to have fun.
Also yeah, learn how to parry by the time you reach boss 7, or you're in for some serious damage. He's a Vergil type, 'nuff said.

Detective Grimoire is a good game, it also is a bad game... It is a engaging game, it is a boring game. Yet what does that mean?
The game involves you questioning subjects and looking around crime scenes for clues. You can question subjects about one of four topics, ask them about another character, or about an object in an inventory. Get enough clues and you get a special interrogation section with a character that plays out like a memory game, if you can remember the details, you will recieve an extra clue. Get even more clues after that and you will play a matching game that allows you to also recieve an additional clue. All to discover the solution to the mystery. Forgot details? Don't worry every single clue is written down for your convenience. There are even a few puzzles like trying to open a door available as well, but these are trivial.
On the possitive aspects Detective Grimoire is a creative game with bright vibrant characters with voice acting and animation that instantly brings them to life in a way few games ever achieve. The world is quite fleshed out and mildly interesting as well as a tourist attraction in a swamp feels like a place that really could exist. The game is very intuitive and discovering who the criminal is stems naturally from the clues given to the extent where you could solve the case in your head without the need for sudden reveals.
The negative aspect of the game can be summed up as busy work. There is an old saying that in adventure games when you get stuck you need to use everything on everything else. Detective Grimoire is a game based around using everything on everything else and unfortunately in some cases it is what you genuinely need to do. You will sometimes find yourself bringing up every item and suspect to every single character... Now you might think to yourself "But divulging that I am onto the criminal might scare them away or put me in danger." Not so in Detective Grimoire, you can bring up all the evidence you need to catch the criminal to the criminal and they won't even bat an eye. Essentially making this feel like a large game of "busy work" instead of a full blown detective game. It is also a bit on the short side.
Difficulty wise the game is easy. Hints are on by default, essentially it will give you solutions, and even with them off occasionally the hints they give in the game should entirely give the puzzle away. There is no game overs and the game even has a system to tell you when you missed something. If you think Telltale point and clicks are too hard, this game is for you.
This game confuses me because on paper I should dislike the game because it is incredibly easy and ultimately requires no real problem solving... Yet I actually like the game because of its atmosphere, voice acting, and world building as well as the characters that inhabit it. It helps that it is priced quite fairly.
I give this a 8/10
By the by, those 3 hours on record? I beat the game in that time, and probably could have done it faster.

Ok so I want to love this game I really do and its overall not a bad game I had fun playing it but in the end this game has little replay value and I'll go over each stage of the game and explain why it fails for me personally.
EARLY GAME
The early game is great, you have to really think about how to position your building and managing the starting resources that you get. You start getting your first colonist and start processing resouces while trying to not run out of food or power reserves. Overall a challenging but great early game.
MID GAME
The mid game is  awesome by far the best part. You start expanding out and ramping up production, increasing your population and getting more technologies. You start getting visitors and you get invaded for the first time and you start getting transmissions from ships and building lazers its awesome there is so much to do in the mid game.
LATE GAME
This is where the game falls apart for me. Once you get past the mid game and have built most of the buildings there is nothing new its just repeat the same set of buildings that you already have, its just about getting more population. Now if this was the only problem I would say its a good game just a weak late game but that's not the only late game problem
Dealing with late game storage is really annoying. Build too many plants and suddenly all of your storage is full  with starch and food with no good way of getting rid of it. I explain below why trading it all away screwed me over.
The AI was already not great but in the late game when your base is huge the AI becomes infuriating to deal with.
Example one : I had too many resouces and decided to trade away 200 bioplastic at once to a trader. BAD IDEA. It took my colonists so long to get in and out of the base that 60+ colonists died due to starvation. WTF. Maybe my base design sucked but the AI should priorities their lives over their current action.
Example two:  Too many colonists enter a room and the oxygen gets all used up you would think the AI would make them leave so they dont die but no they just stay and die :/
Different planets dont really do much except increase the early game difficulty. Map size is also limited, its really large but its not like you can build across the whole planet.
Trading and visitors are basically useless in the late game you so many resources and money from visitors that trading ships are only good for getting technologies and vistors have no value at all.
Also took over 3 hours to finally get a trading ship with the last technology I needed to finish the get all technologies milestone WTF I actually thought that the game was bugged at one point I spent hours just dismissing trading shipping and adding on starports to get more trading ships.
FINAL THOUGHTS
Overall it reminds me alot of banished, its fun to play through it once but after that there isn't much left to do thats new. Early and mid game are amazing I had a ton of fun playing these and if you are ok with this then go for it. Late game combined with a poor AI kinda ruined it for me but at 20 bucks I definitely got my moneys worth I just probably wouldn't recommend it to someone in its current state. That being said it has a ton of potential and I hope it continues to improve. Thanks :)

Is this game worth putting a lot of hours into it? NO, this is why I don't recommend it.
