Planetbase is a good game.  It does have its share of flaws, and it's by no means perfect nor is it something that I think everyone would enjoy.  The AI is probably its most glaring weakness: your colonists are incompetent and their bots are about the same.  Colonists frequently starve themselves simply due to other colonists having actions queued from the other side of the base, or because they're waiting in line to deliver goods to a trade ship, or because they've ignored the fact that they're dying of thirst since they have a construction task at the opposite end of your base from the nearest water fountain.
While the AI does leave an awful lot to be desired, games that take a relatively realistic approach to planetary colonisation and resource management are a very rare breed, and despite a couple missteps I still think it's a fun, challenging game with an awful lot on offer if you're a fan of base building.
Go nuts with this one, it's pretty rad.

Hmm where to begin.  I guess I'll start by saying this game is good to a point.  Here are a few things I like and don't like about Planetbase:
Pros:
1. Addictively fun
2. Simple to learn
3. Interesting mechanics, such as having to manage power through day/night cycles with solar panels and wind turbines
Good variety of buildings with decent interior building options
Cons:
1. Incredibly stupid AI
2. Poor prioritization options
3. No options to power down bots.  This was a big deal to me in the beginning since sandstorms wreck the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them, and you can't stop them from getting destroyed in a storm when they have an action queued.  Especially so when you don't start with engineers who are the only other able bodies who can build things.
4. And this is really the biggest problem with the game in my opinion, but RNG will always ♥♥♥♥ you.  You will get hit with a meteor near the beginning on a major building with over half your guys inside, and they will all die.  Maybe you'll build wind turbines to generate power during the night only to find the wind hardly ever blows.  Or maybe you'll run out of spares which are needed to repair your solar panels/wind turbines and be powerless to stop everything from dying.  With the amount of resources you need to build things, spares included, and the slow rate your workers generate these resources it will happen more than a few times.
All in all the cons are more of a problem for me than the pros so I'm gonna say this game still needs more work.  Don't buy this game unless you prefer to rip your hair out playing perfectly only to watch everything die anyway.  This is definitely the Dark Souls of city building games even though it won't be your fault if you lose.

This War of Mine scores on both sides of the spectrum. It's an honest depiction of the horrors of war as seen from the perspectives of innocent but affected bystanders. It's also a good survival game relying on tactics and resource management. The first aspect alone makes at least one playthrough worthwhile just for the experience.
It's entirely possible to survive without ever resorting to violence. As the days go by, it's getting harder and harder to scavenge for usable items though. The game's difficulty depends on the number of people in a group and a little bit on what predispositions, strengths and vices they have. Areas with cautious or hostile people, nightly raids on the shelter and cold temperatures with snowfall pose additional problems to the already heavy situation. Hardship and loss are to be expected and there's almost no way around it.
The gameplay revolves around a rudimentary crafting system, scavenging for resources at night and tending to the inhabitant's needs by day. The mechanics are reasonable and well balanced, so long as there are no bugs that may lead to inexplicable circumstances. It's troublesome encountering even minor bugs as they can easily spoil a run, but at least they're rare and the autosave function reliably solves any problems.
The overall aesthetic bears a ruined vibe with rough pencil lines, realistic and unadorned animations and gritty, cold and almost monochrome colours. Real life portraits give the character's stories a face that promotes empathy and provides a more personal form of involvement for the player. On a mechanical level, there are characters with traits that are more advantageous to the group, at least in this situation, than other characters. The portraits, however, show the people behind the sprites seen on screen and ideally suggest equal importance as human beings.
There are only a few but good ambient music tracks. Especially the acoustic guitar tracks, which are played by the characters after repairing a guitar ingame, add immensely to the atmosphere similar to the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games. The guitar is supposed to brighten the mood of the inhabitants but really, it's there to offer respite for the player.
Without a doubt This War of Mine is a valuable and ever relevant display of how war impacts the civilian population and more precisely the fate of an individual. All the while still being an enjoyable game with flawed but essentially solid survival mechanics.
Incredible replay value. Definitely worth the price.

Gorgeous world, and a masterclass in Game Design.
However, this game is not for the faint of heart, and the difficulty level of some of the puzzles was excruciating, as even understanding their specific rules was a herculean challenge in itself.
In essence, if you accept from the get-go that you will most likely never be able to completely finish this game, and play only for as long as you are enjoying yourself, this will be a treat.

Absolutely would recommend, but this isn't a game for everyone (and that shouldn't be taken as a challenge).
This is the puzzle game's puzzle game.  There's no story to speak of and no hand holding.  The Witness teaches you by having you observe and do.  It will never explain to you what you're supposed to do.  And yet, you will know what it asks of you.
The Witness is challenging in a way I haven't seen in puzzle games in a very long time.  I took a lot of screenshots to save myself time backtracking, my modern version of taking notes like I used to do playing games growing up.  For those that have found a lot of popular puzzle games fun yet lacking any real challenge, The Witness will inevitably stump you somewhere through your playthrough.  You'll figure it out eventually, but you won't be able to just smash through everything it throws at you.
The game is infused with a philosophy, possibly even described as a conversation.  It's hidden throughout the game, but the times when you find those hidden gems are incredibly fulfilling.  Those pieces, like the entire game itself - from the puzzles to the island - are all selected with much care to how everything in this game fits together.
The Witness really is a masterpiece of a puzzle game.

Tested out this port and it plays fine. This is my review from the Vita version.
So do you like the Zero Escape series? How about the Persona series? Or how about the Ace Attorney series? Ever wondered what would happen if someone combined them together? It would be DanganRonpa, yo!
The story was simply incredible. It was full of twists and unexpected moments. You play as one character who is trapped in some weird school and must work with a cast of characters to escape. I won't get into details but there are also trials where you must win to survive. The main plot was simply riveting from beginning to end. What really grabbed me was how much risk it took with its characters and setting. You just never seem to know what will happen next. The game plays around with your expectations all the time. Even when I figured out who the suspect was or how someone was murdered, the game would throw in multiple curve balls to screw with you. It was a lot of fun and kept me entertained. I never got bored with any part of the game. I was sucked into its crazy world. Some of the things that happened was incredibly morbid and disturbing. It definitely made me felt uneasy at times. There is a lot of dark humor that some people will enjoy. When the game wanted to be funny, it was funny. When it wanted to creep you out, it was pretty darn creepy. So good.
The characters were incredibly diverse and fun. They took your typical archetypes and totally messed around with them. I was continually surprised at how well developed and written they were. Most of them weren't what you'd expect from how they looked. Although, there was one stereotypical geek/otaku/nerd fat guy who encompassed all the negative sides of that trope. At least he wasn't dumb, sorta. But anyways, I really liked most of the cast. Most of them were very smart and very clever. In fact, some of them are even smarter than your character which was refreshing. I need to point out that it was very bold of NIS America for them to keep the original Japanese names. They could have gone the other way and made up English names but they didn't. I liked that.
The dialogue between the characters were very well written. I have to give NIS America HUGE props for the localization. I was super duper impressed! The dialogue was extremely natural and flowed really well. It felt like how people would speak in real life if they were put in these situations. Even the jokes were super well written. The lewd jokes in particular were funny as hell. I'm not sure who was in charge of them but they were biting and insanely well timed. Hell, even the cursing felt right for whoever was saying it in their situations. I laughed out loud quite often. I also liked the multiple references to other games and other forms of pop culture. Some are quite subtle while others blatantly mention specific product brands and/or names of real world people. It's a bit jarring when that happens but they don't date the game or make it feel awkward. If it weren't for the strong translation, I don't think I would've liked the game as much as I did. So once again, kudos to NISA for a job well done.
The visuals are absolutely stunning all around. Both the 2D and 3D art are super colorful and sharp. The 2D character art in particular is gorgeous. The character designs themselves are very attractive and well defined. There are several art styles that pop up but they're all beautifully illustrated. The character sprites don't have actual animations like with the Ace Attorney series but they are well drawn and very expressive. The event art (the painted scenes) is stunning and the occasional pixel art is cute as hell. The 3D parts of the school are also beautiful and very detailed. The FMV scenes are a mix of 2D/3D and really interesting. I really love the look of this game.
I also want to point out the gore in this game. The blood has been colored pink for some reason. I assume they were done to stylize the murder scenes or make it less gorey for anyone squeamish about blood in general. Personally, I think it took away some of the horror of the crime scenes. I wish there was a toggle for it. Just a minor gripe.
The audio was equally outstanding as the art. I loved all the music in this game. The trials in particular had several tracks which pumped me up. Great soundtrack all around. I also need to point out the English dub. IT WAS AWESOME. Yea, I'm not even exaggerating, it's just that good. The voices felt shaky at first when I started the game but they only got better and better as the game progressed. I didn't really fall in love until the first trial where it was fully voiced and you could really admire their performances. Everyone matched their roles and they did a great job making all these characters come to life. They read their lines with gusto. If it weren't for them, I wouldn't have liked the characters as much as I did. I became a fan of several voice actors simply because of this game. There was one character that totally floored me with their performance in particular. I won't spoil who though. *grin* Once again, great job NIS America.
Overall, DanganRonpa exceeded my expectations even with all the hype from its fans. I loved every minute of it and was compelled to keep playing all the way to the end. Great writing, great story, great characters and great VO with fantastic art and music. It's a complete package and anyone who's into games like the Zero Escape and Ace Attorney series MUST play this. LOVED IT

Old players: Don't buy it, unless you play it every day, then you'll have bought it anyway.
New Players:  I would characterize this game as more of a City Editor instead of more of a city sim in the manner of the old SimCitys. Tl;dr: An excellent bullet hell/hack ‘n’ slash hybrid with lightning-fast combat and a stylish presentation. Has some shortcomings, but is absolutely worth your time if you’re into: speedy and tough-but-fair gameplay, anime action series and/or artsy neon visuals and pumping synth music. Might not be your thing if you’re looking for a lengthy game, substantial narrative or are unwilling to invest the time and effort to “git gud.”
It’s rare for me to find myself so engaged in an action game these days. Among all the games I’ve played over the years, I’d say that Furi is second only to higher-level Smash Bros. Melee in terms of speed, precision and satisfying sense of movement. It’s hard to match the rush that accompanies those times when you’re dialed in and executing your cyborg ninja dance flawlessly. The energy of the combat has that impossibly fast and punchy quality that makes the best anime action series so enjoyable to watch.
Some may be put off by the relatively short length of the game, but I found it to be about right. Didn’t overstay its welcome but was still enough of a journey to be satisfying. I think it’s the kind of game you’ll probably want to play in shorter bursts anyway; a boss or two per session was enough for me. My first run clocked in at around six hours. You can expect to double that or more if you end up liking it enough to play through again on hard and conquer the DLC. This is the good kind of hard mode that isn’t just some lame damage/health stat tweaks; most enemies have their speed and attack patterns re-worked significantly.
I do have some minor complaints. You have to be willing to bear with a wildly fluctuating difficulty curve and forgive the occasional “that was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t” moment. The couple of fights that focus almost exclusively on either the hack ‘n’ slash or bullet hell gameplay were not nearly as enjoyable as the rest. I think it’s the unique combination of the two styles that really shines here.
On the whole, though, I had a blast with Furi. I don’t imagine I’ll find an action game to rival it for a long time. This one just hit all of the right notes for me. The narrative elements weren't extensive but I liked what was there. Plus dat music tho; I love how it was dynamic with the gameplay and fit the mood of each fight so well. Discovered some new artists from this score, which is always nice. Hope my ramblings gave you a better idea on if this game is up your alley.
One final note: If you’re looking to scratch a similar gaming itch, Hyper Light Drifter is another great game I’d recommend checking out. The combat is similar, although not as fleshed-out since the game focuses a little more on Zelda-esque exploration and item/power acquisition. Rad art style and soundtrack on display there too. Have a look!

text:
Volgarr tries to take the gameplay style of older games, but forgets to take the mechanics. Enemies out-pace your swing, and animations are painfully long stun-locks, so you'll frequently be losing health/abilities to animations. If they were consistent, it wouldn't be so bad, but a spear thrown in air is near instant, while a ground spear takes many times longer and locks you into the animation.
As enemies are often above and below you, you might be inclined to attack them - except jumping takes time and will lock your direction, and while you may swing your sword, it attacks forward, not in at any incline, so every jumping guy will get priority for hitting you. As the shield only sometimes is effective (shield direction doesn't change either), a few pixels make the difference between blocking a jumping guy, and getting hit by them. In any case, if you are decently far into a level and lose your shield, it is far more practical just to immediately die and start over, because random control weirdness will kill you. A note on sword-mechanics is you hold your sword straight up, and when you swing, it doesn't go through your front, so if an enemy is up-right you can't hit it, but you can if it is above or in front. At the same time, sometimes when you're done throwing a spear, if you press the sword attack key, you will instead throw another spear, which introduces some of that animation locking when you're not expecting it.
In some vein it tries to take fixed-jumping mechanics, but then your second jump can influence your direction. Inconsistently, as in the first level, jumping against a certain wall can easily launch you over a smalll edge on the second jump straight into spikes.
The "look ahead feature" is just a zoom out, and overall it feels like the game had good controls at one point (including a wider view), then to stand out, they threw in fixed-travel-distance spears, leaderboards/time trial, and animation locks to ramp up difficulty, instead of just letting the game be fun without having to memorize every level or be crippled as soon as you start getting hit.
Make no mistake, this IS a trial-by-death game, except the death part is painfully long-winded and perfectionist marred by poor controls. Sonic, Kirby, Little Nemo, even Castlevania 1, any of their mechanics would have made this game far more tolerable.

Short Review:
A nice investigation "point & click" game with high quality voice acting behind it and very detail animations, with a very unique style that reminds of Professor Layton, Zelda Windwaker, and old-style cartoons of the 50s. If anything, the game lacks depth and it's rather too short, and the final part of the game is very disappointing since it does everything for you.
Worth a check, considering the low price point.
Long Review:
Detective Grimoire is technically the second game of the series, with the first being released as a free flash game on their site (which is still pretty good in my opinion! Give it a check!). However, with this game they did a HUGE leap of quality, adding a ton of stuff that the original game didn't have, such as voice acting (A LOT of voice acting) better animation, different art style and more complex puzzles (but not as complex as they should be really).
Initially released for portables such as iPads and what not, I was anticipating this game for a long time, as I loved the original DG for being quite interesting, and the character is actually very likeable and very funny; what we have here is basically a port that didn't suffer from it and still maintains its core mechanics, such as the "theory-maker" thingie.
If anything, the resolution cannot be changed, and the volume is at max by default: little nitpicks, so nothing to worry about.
The game itself is splendidly made: dialogues are fun to follow and don't drag too much, as they flow very fast and I rarely skipped the dialogues, since they were very interesting and very funny (especially Grimoire: he really tells a lot of stupid things. Oh, and they made the hat joke again!). The puzzles are ok, but just too easy to follow: the real challenge at times is the Theory-making part, since at times you'll put the wrong statement...but at the same time, it's a lot of fun to mess up those, making him say the dumbest thing ever. The game is fluid and has also animated cutscenes as well, and the characters are...okay, for the most part.
However, there are some issues in my opinion: for one, the story is good, but the last part is a joke: you do nothing at all when you catch the culprit, and that's a huge disappointment considering that the first game, a flash game, had a far more complicated part where you EVEN have to guess who did it. In here, he picks it up for you.
The game is also too easy: you really can't fail anything at all, and as soon as you get your clues you can just spam them to the suspects and see their reaction...and Grimoire even tells you "when it's time to go". They also gave you the possibility to see if something is suspect or not on a culprit, but it's completely useless and serves no purpose: it's just there for letting you  check your progress to catch the culprit. And let's face it, you'll guess who it is pretty soon.
I honestly hoped the game to be more intriguing: the art is amazing and the game is very fun, but the story behind is disappointing and lacks to be intriguing, which is a huge problem for me.
Still, I do recommend this game, because it's always good to have nice adventure games and the game is still VERY well done.
Avoid it if you don't care about investigation, reading, or point and click adventures in general.

The first thing you may notice about Tap Adventure: Time Travel is the graphics. Whether it’s the character design or the different environments that you end up going to, everything is all very well drawn. It’s genuinely pleasing to look at, especially for a clicker game. Unfortunately, I think this is the only strong point about this game.
Things start out as any other clicker game; you’ll be able to hire a few mercenaries and get through a few hundred levels before you’ll have to time loop. You will have to repeat this process hundreds of times of course, getting a little further each time. You’ll earn more gold, runestones, keys, and manacoins, unlock more artefacts and heroes, and so on and so forth. It’s a typical clicker game.
While I think it’s entirely possible to really enjoy this game in the beginning, things really start to drag on the further though the game you get. 98% of the achievements can be earned in three to four months. The last two achievements take an additional three to four months. If you’re looking to complete this game, it’s going to take you a good 3,000 hours of play time. I’d say the number one problem with this game is that it gets way too repetitive, even for a clicker game. It doesn’t take long to see what this game has to offer, and then it just shows it to you over and over again. I found myself just wishing I were done with it more often than I was enjoying it.
During your first few time loops as you’re still getting used to the game, you may notice that someone just said something in chat. Someone just said something in chat? What? There’s an in-game chat in this clicker game? Yes, there is. This is something I’ve never seen in a clicker game before, and in many ways it was a refreshing idea. Clicker games aren’t exactly known for taking up too much of your mental acuity, so chatting with others can be a nice distraction while you sit back and let your heroes grind a few hundred levels out. This is a really nice addition and I would love to see more clicker games implement this feature.
Yes, the in-game chat feature WAS a really good idea, in the beginning. I remember having lively discussions with groups of people when the game was new. The problem is that over time the player base has shrunk considerably and now it’s difficult to have a conversation with anyone, let alone a lively one. Today the chat consists mainly of people posting their friend codes in the hopes that a few other people will use them, or the odd person asking a question about how the game works. Add to that the fact that many people just leave the game running in the background, and it can seem dead most of the time nowadays. If they didn’t separate the chat into two separate rooms, maybe it would help things a little. It’s sad to see the most unique feature about this game, the one setting it apart from other clicker games, is just a novelty at this point.
There are a number of different things that you can buy with real world money in this game; some good and some worthless. The slot machine coins and all of the DLC packs are too expensive, and everything you get from them can be earned for free after enough play time. The four extra heroes and the fourth master are worth considering. The four extra heroes cannot be unlocked for free at this time, and they very well could speed up your progress. The fourth master can be purchased for one month using real world money, or temporarily unlocked for one time loop using the in-game currency of gems. Gems are very rarely earned so you won’t be able to unlock him often, but the good news is that he isn’t necessary. It’s possible to unlock every achievement in the game without paying real money.
Overall, Tap Adventure: Time Travel has some great art style and a unique (albeit dead) chat feature, but the game play is tediously, agonizingly repetitive, and the achievements are not distributed evenly.
If you’re looking for a clicker game with deeper game play and management, or one with an active and friendly community, Clicker Heroes and Realm Grinder are both great alternatives.

Toki Tori is a bright, cheerful puzzle-platformer where you lead Toki Tori – a bright yellow chicken with the power to teleport between a variety of environments via wormholes while collecting some erratically misplaced eggs in standard avian-puzzle-platformer style. It’s an entertaining addition to your Steam library, but falls just short of becoming a shining example of the puzzle genre.
You lead Toki Tori through a myriad of environments – forests, a castle and some sewers, primarily – and it is quickly apparent that visually and thematically Toki Tori is pitch-perfect. Toki and the roaming enemies in each level have fantastically clean and crisp animations and the overall aesthetic of each world fits the bright and bubbly theme the exuberant loading screen promises from the outset.
Toki Tori oozes ‘Suitable For All Ages’ from nearly every pore, with high energy music and cutesy consequences for spinning on the spot too much or dying where you fall off the screen Mario style. Toki Tori can also rewind time to a moment he was less stuck – or indeed less dead – and this further lends to the light-hearted atmosphere that ‘everything will be all right!’, in a world where nothing can really go wrong or, at least, not for too long.
The gameplay itself is also very tight and clear. Toki scurries to follow your mouse-clicks in comical fashion, and every one of his handy tools –  including summonable platforms, a small range teleporter and a freeze ray, among others – have great visuals and sound; the ‘thud’ of placing a bridge piece is immensely satisfying for all sorts of reasons.
Where Toki Tori falls short is in the level design. To complete a single level Toki Tori has to collect every egg on the map but this all-or-nothing completion mechanic is marred by a lack of creative level design. Toki’s supply of tools is limited strictly to finding the designers’ solution, as opposed to the player creating their own. This need to discover the correct path, not create one, treads the very fine line between ‘challenging puzzle’ and ‘impossible rage-quit’, more often than not requiring a walkthrough to continue.
The game does give you a useful Wildcard which you can play to skip a level (and by going back to complete the level, earning the Wildcard back), but this doesn’t really mitigate the problem at the heart of Toki Tori: if you cannot find the path the creators designed, this game has no more content for you. Given that many puzzles are incredibly convoluted, in a way almost certainly not suitable for all ages, this complete lack of progression becomes highly frustrating very quickly.
Overall Toki Tori is a fun, bright and exuberant puzzle-platformer that does many great things well but unless you are a die-hard puzzler, expect to never see the finish. Or be prepared to cheat and use walkthroughs – a lot of walkthroughs. The first 20 or so levels are absolutely excellent, but the shortcoming in level design is just too large an issue to ignore.

By far, the best puzzle game I've ever played. Every area forces you to have a mental lapse. It starts simple, but becomes incredibly complicated as time goes on.

Right from the start, it's clear how much time and effort the developers spent trying to make their seemingly limitless supply of maze puzzles feel fresh and exciting with each new iteration. It's clear how much time was spent trying to create a gradual ramp up towards the elusive "eureka moment". That moment when you've been struggling with a puzzle for 10, 15, or 30 minutes, and all of the sudden you say "OHHHHH!" and you solve it in 3 seconds. I imagine that if the developers of The Witness ever watched me play this game, they'd be incredibly disappointed.
My problem with this game isn't that I never got the eureka moment. It's that every time I got it, my "Ohhhhh..." was quickly followed by "that's stupid" or "so what?"
This game is plagued by a constant feeling of "so what?"-ness. The Witness has no plot. The Witness has no characters. The Witness has nothing to discover that doesn't already exist in your own imagination. You'll wander from puzzle to puzzle, erroniously believing that the next puzzle will reward you with some new revelation, or at least a general feeling of "Oh, wow!" But the harsh truth of The Witness is that the "eureka moment" is the games only reward. The only reward it has to offer is that you did it. You solved a puzzle. And no one had to hold your hand to do it. You did it all on your own. Gold star.
For some people, this will be enough. But for me it certainly wasn't. I was constantly looking for something to sink my teeth into; A story that I could pick up the threads of, even if it was only a hint. I desperately needed a reward beyond my own sense of satisfaction. But sadly all I found was a tape recording with a quote from Albert Einstein. And after several hours of guiding lines from point A to point B, I was quite over this game.
To be honest, it really is quite a shame, as the puzzles are occasionally fiendishly clever. But they simply aren't strong enough to carry this game on their own merits. The game just lacks real substance. And for all its avant-garde pretension, it ends up feeling incredibly hollow.

"You wake up, alone, on a strange island full of puzzles that will challenge and surprise you.

They got the alone on a strange island part right.  The problem is, the puzzles are on these incongruous pads littered all over the landscape.  You draw a colored line from the round start pad to the exit.  Now draw it while separating these colored dots from those colored dots, or while covering dots on the path.  Or something else.  There's literally nothing to explain any of this to you - you figure it out by trial and error.
Some of the pads are pretty self-explantory.  Others you sit there scratching your head and wondering what on earth you're intended to do.  Once you've figured one type of pad out, you'll easily plow through others of the same type... but that won't be any help at all with the weird unmarked hexagon pad that you were scratching your head about.  Now I enjoy a good puzzle as much as most people, but somehow I'm not getting my jollies when I'm drawing lines on pads to get power to more pads so I can draw lines on them - it's just dull.
In the two hours I spent as of this review, I've wandered around a few different areas and completed one.  My reward for this completion was a laser pointing way off into the distance.  What does the laser do?  Why does this island have hundreds of panels devoted to drawing lines, simply to power it and presumably other lasers?  Maybe you'll get some sort of plot exposition at the end of the game, but you certainly won't for the rest of it.  You're alone on a strange island, deal with it.

This game is brutal; tough as nails, but its not a cheap kind of difficulty. There are patters and clear signs that can be avoided with enough skill and practice. There had been multile times where I would rage quit and close the game, but I would always come back and try many more times until I finally cracked it and moved on to the next boss. Tl;dr: An excellent bullet hell/hack ‘n’ slash hybrid with lightning-fast combat and a stylish presentation. Has some shortcomings, but is absolutely worth your time if you’re into: speedy and tough-but-fair gameplay, anime action series and/or artsy neon visuals and pumping synth music. Might not be your thing if you’re looking for a lengthy game, substantial narrative or are unwilling to invest the time and effort to “git gud.”
It’s rare for me to find myself so engaged in an action game these days. Among all the games I’ve played over the years, I’d say that Furi is second only to higher-level Smash Bros. Melee in terms of speed, precision and satisfying sense of movement. It’s hard to match the rush that accompanies those times when you’re dialed in and executing your cyborg ninja dance flawlessly. The energy of the combat has that impossibly fast and punchy quality that makes the best anime action series so enjoyable to watch.
Some may be put off by the relatively short length of the game, but I found it to be about right. Didn’t overstay its welcome but was still enough of a journey to be satisfying. I think it’s the kind of game you’ll probably want to play in shorter bursts anyway; a boss or two per session was enough for me. My first run clocked in at around six hours. You can expect to double that or more if you end up liking it enough to play through again on hard and conquer the DLC. This is the good kind of hard mode that isn’t just some lame damage/health stat tweaks; most enemies have their speed and attack patterns re-worked significantly.
I do have some minor complaints. You have to be willing to bear with a wildly fluctuating difficulty curve and forgive the occasional “that was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t” moment. The couple of fights that focus almost exclusively on either the hack ‘n’ slash or bullet hell gameplay were not nearly as enjoyable as the rest. I think it’s the unique combination of the two styles that really shines here.
On the whole, though, I had a blast with Furi. I don’t imagine I’ll find an action game to rival it for a long time. This one just hit all of the right notes for me. The narrative elements weren't extensive but I liked what was there. Plus dat music tho; I love how it was dynamic with the gameplay and fit the mood of each fight so well. Discovered some new artists from this score, which is always nice. Hope my ramblings gave you a better idea on if this game is up your alley.
One final note: If you’re looking to scratch a similar gaming itch, Hyper Light Drifter is another great game I’d recommend checking out. The combat is similar, although not as fleshed-out since the game focuses a little more on Zelda-esque exploration and item/power acquisition. Rad art style and soundtrack on display there too. Have a look!

This was my first bullet hell game experience, and I am incredibly glad I started with this game. This game absolutely nails the concept of personal progression, so that I always felt like I was getting better, even as the game continually beat me down over and over again. Each boss has a unique personality and reflective moveset; they all bring new elements into play that constantly refresh the game and pushed my reactionary capabilities further. The worldbuilding in this game has made many phenominal wallpapers, and the soundtrack is so solid that I believe it is capable of standing alone, even as it adds to the game it was made for.
But what I was most impressed with was how the entire thing is shown to the player. I was thrown into a violent world and told to fight. That is all I had. I was the guy breaking free, fighting in a world that makes no sense but at the same time amazed me. Throughout vast and foreign worlds, my character and my oddball companion were the only constants. Yet, despite having complete control of a character with no voice lines, I grew to realize how little this game was about me, the player. Although there is a predominant plot twist, it is paired with a gradual change as the player finds hints about the past of the character they inhabit, and the stories of those around him. By the end, the abstractions that make up the playable world feel relatable, and the "people" feel more human than anything else.
All this adds up to a game with unequalled replay value. The in-fight mechanics have an infinitely high skill ceiling, that always pushes me to improve. The various worlds in the game jump out and provide amazing explorability that I have hardly ever seen in any game, much less a game with set plot progression; the cinematics and choice camera angels of the game are incredible. The characters are thoroughly fleshed out, and able to tell their story and the protagonists with a handful of lines that never waste a word. The plot is steady, yet revealed for you to figure out through glimpses in words and phrases. I honestly don't think I'll ever complete this game, but I'm damn sure gonna love trying.

You are Volgarr the Viking in a 2D sword swinging platformer set in a gorgeous old school fantasy world and this world is designed to murder and brutalize you. Almost every step is a challenge with death waiting around every corner. The game lives and thrives off of an old school feel and an incredible challenge that only the hardcore will be able to tackle. If you want a challenge, this game is for you. Vulgarr will also climb chains and vines, jump over arrows far quicker than you, ride boats, slide down slopes and jump over spikes. The enemies are big, detailed and deadly. There is a lot of enemy variety and you'll face off against waves of lizard men, giant snakes, spore spitting plants, giant spiders that wait for you to come to them before they spring into action, zombies that split in half if you attack their lower half causing the top half to tumble forward, shielded skeletons that will jump and downthrust at you and so much more. These enemies are probably the best designed enemies I've seen in years. Almost all of the enemies and areas are a homage to games like Rastan, Castlevania and Zelda 2.
The controls are simple and could have been done with an original Nintendo controller, but there is some depth, left and right to move, down to duck, attack with a sword, and jump (double jump that works as a screw attack). You can roll under things by holding down and the jump button. You can duck attack, jump and down thrust to break through floor tiles and enemies. You can also throw a spear by pressing up. The spear is not only a long range weapon, but a way to create platforms. You can also hold up to charge the spear and throw it across the screen to impale several enemies at once.
As Vulgarr you are slow and deliberate like the original Castlevania. You need to time attacks, and know where to stand in certain situations. You will need to kill or be killed rather than dodge enemies. Most enemies can be dispatched with a single swing of your viking sword, but Vulgarr is just as fragile as most of the enemies. One hit will result in death. You can break open treasure chests to find upgrades, first the wooden shield, then the helmet & iron shield, then the flame sword. All of these upgrades that allow you to take an extra hit that will lose a piece of armor. So if you have a flame sword and get hit, you will not only lose the flame sword but your helmet. When you have the shield, you can block attacks by not attacking. Then it becomes a case of knowing when not to attack. However, wooden shields break after taking so much damage. There are other secret power ups that you will find by breaking through walls and floors ala Castlevania.
The game is painfully difficult with long challenges between check points. At least the game offers unlimited lives. There are tricky jumps that rely on knowing where to throw your spears. Finding where to stand might result in playing the same level over and over countless times. Doing the exact same thing over and over with no real deviation to what you just did your previous life. Eventually, you will remember what to do, where to stand for specific enemies and you'll get better like all murderous old school games.
This game has a lot going for it, but because this is a painfully challenging game, I can't recommend it to players. But judging from the downvotes. I'm wrong and people love difficult games.

A true masterpiece. If you love platformers, you should get Volgarr ASAP. One of the best level design and gameplay in platformers I've ever played, no matter the era. Right there with all the 8- and 16-bit classics.

Toki Tori is a 2D puzzle platformer, with more of the focus on the puzzle side of things. In each level, the player has access to a specific number of tools, each of which may or may not have limited uses, and needs to use them in order to get all the eggs in the level. Additionally, there is a "rewind time" feature which is more so you can redo levels after you've messed them up in lieu of redoing every step.  It has very clean and vibrant graphics, and ultimately does accomplish what it set out to do.
That being said, I chose not to recommend this game because, at its root level, it seems to have failed in what I find most important in games: I didn't find it particularly fun. The first few stages of each world, the levels are interesting and introduce new mechanics in a myriad of fun ways, but as you progress to the later levels in each world, they become hard for the sake of being hard - not challenging, which proves to be fun as you overcome them, but something more difficult than that to where the game ceases to be fun and ends up being a chore.
There are some people who will enjoy this game throughout because they like that sort of difficulty. There are others who will pick it up, play the first few levels and be satisfied. But I think for most people, the game taken as a whole will just not be that entertaining.

This is going to be my third review for the game since I purchased it a little of over a year ago.  I went from disliking it when I first purchased, to being satisfied, to once again feeling as though there is just something...missing.  But I am getting ahead of myself here, so let's talk about what Planetbase is (or at least, is trying to be) and how it's features hold up now that the game has had its 1.2.1 patch.  (and don't worry, there is a TL;DR at the bottom)
Planetbase is a game about landing on a barren alien world (such as Mars or Hoth) with a handful of skilled specialists and establishing a colony.  It has often been compared to Banished (another game about building a colony out of a handful of survivors) due to the similar mechanics.  In both games you choose where to build new structures, and what to produce etc but beyond that you have next to no control over the colonists themselves, acting as little more of an advisor than an all seeing overlord.  For some (including myself I might add) this is part of the fun as it involves more long terming planning that a game like let's say, Rimworld.  This kind of a game is however very reliant on its AI, which sadly in this case is a few biodomes short of a colony.  Often your planning simply revolves around trying to keep your colonists from killing THELSELVES as their pathfinding and priority's seem to be a bit out of wack.  For instance, colonists have been known to travel to the edge of the colony for a resource which could have already been right next to them.  For Instance:
I had an Engineer go to fix a solar panel at the north end of my base.  He picks up a spare part and walks out to the panel.  He then decides he is too hungry to work, and drops the spare part next to the panel and comes inside.  Engineer #2 decides to fix the solar panel next, and walks the south end of my colony to grab a spare part only to walk all the way to the north end to fix a solar panel when there was already a spare part right next to it.  On top of that, there was a second solar panel n the south end he could have fixed instead.  Finally, to make matters even worse, the second Engineers decided to leave the base from the south airlock, rather than the north airlock...during a sandstorm.  Meaning Engie #2 took unneeded damage walking the extra distance outside.
Now in order to fix problems like this from happening there is a priority system.  Unfortunately however it consists of a simply toggle between "low" and "high" priority.  There is no ability to pause the construction of something, or lower its priority beyond normal.  This means that lets say I have a couple of projects running at the same time, some at Normal and some at High.  It is completely down to fate which high priority project is completed first, or which normal is.  To make matters worse, buildings take further priority over item production (which includes things like food, or construction materials i might add) so even if I have a room producing spare parts (needed to vital maintenance) at high priority, and a bedroom constructing at normal priority your colonists will still consider the bedroom more important that the parts and waste your resources on that instead.  And wasting resources is a critically important thing not to do in Planetbase as you need a constant supply of everything or you risk total and immediate that is very difficult to stop, once again due to the lack of a priority system.  This game is in desperate need of adequate priority tools, including a pause construction ability.
Beyond your own colonists the only other "real" danger is power.  For some reason the developers of Planetbase choose to limit your power generation to just Solar and Wind power, which are both incredibly unreliable due to the extreme fluctuation on their outputs.  ).  I would not even care so much about this is if there was any kind of late game solution to this, but there just isn't.  No geothermal, or Nuclear reactors.  Just bigger Solar and Wind generators.
Besides that the game suffers from a real lack of late game content.  There are no raids (like you might find in Rimworld), even though you have armed guards and giant meteor defence lasers.  ust a couple of armed stowaways every now and then.  There are no vehicles, like moon rovers.  everyone is always just on foot.  There is literally no reason to explore or have your colonists even go outside anymore once you get robots.  Every single building in the game you can technically build after the first 30 seconds of game play assuming you have the resources.  There are no real epic late game structures, just more domes.  Every single game basically plays out the same, as the different planets only slightly change how much solar/wind to use.  Each and every time you create a new colony you will end up creating the same generic colony, with the same all purpose buildings.  Even the monumental buildings, such as the obelisk or the Pyramid just feel bland since they just sit there not doing anything.  There is nothing you can build to be the centerpiece of your colony, nothing to make it special or different from everyone else's.  You cannot even "specialise" your colony.  When I say every colony is the same I mean it.  There are no mechanics or structures in the game to make a tourism based settlement, or a mining colony, or a science outpost or anything beyond a generic base.

And then finally there are the little things such as:
-You cannot rotate buildings
-You cannot place buildings on top of boxes (which colonists leave everywhere so buckle up)
-You cannot order food processors to make certain meals or recipes, So instead of waiting until it has the ingredients necessary to make lets say a hamburger, it will use the ingrediants as soon as its gets them to make simple meals (which are much worse)
-No pause function.
-The building system is finicky, and you cannot make things such as tunnels, or overhead bridges.  Water is also impassable, and you cannot even build water extractors on lakes so they are just another means of artificial difficulty.
*Anyway, as promised, the TL;DR*
PROS
-Nice aesthetic
-Good Graphics/visuals
-Good UI
-Excellet amount of little details, such as tv's or Security cameras
-Good Animations
CONS
-Debatable AI and Pathfinding
-Bad priority system
-Lack of a pause feature
-Poorly explained features
-Lack of specialization
-Finicky building system
-Severe lack of end game content

When I bought this game I had never played Magic: The Gathering (MTG). As a fan of trading card games I had to give it a shot. The game has a perfect entry level and an excellent tutorial on how to actually play Magic. When the tutorial is done you start by playing the campaign, which has some really cool challenges and opponents. What I really like about this game is the fact that it runs really smooth, the card animations have a nice flow and some cards have cool effects. Another positive thing is the music, great, ambient background music that does'nt bother you while you're playing or thinking about your moves.
The multiplayer mode is quite fun, you can play 1v1, 1v1v1v1 or the so called "Two Headed Giant" mode which is a 2v2 game. You can even play 2v2 with a friend against 2 CPUs (and their difficulty can be adjusted so it can be quite challenging as well).
The game does not have create-your-own-deck function. however. You start with a basic deck and unlock some more decks to play with. And to play the sealed mode more than twice you have to buy new slots which kinda sucks.
All with all the game is a really cool for either beginners or advanced magic players, and if you like trading card games this is a worthy addition to your game collection.

This was my first bullet hell game experience, and I am incredibly glad I started with this game. This game absolutely nails the concept of personal progression, so that I always felt like I was getting better, even as the game continually beat me down over and over again. Each boss has a unique personality and reflective moveset; they all bring new elements into play that constantly refresh the game and pushed my reactionary capabilities further. The worldbuilding in this game has made many phenominal wallpapers, and the soundtrack is so solid that I believe it is capable of standing alone, even as it adds to the game it was made for.
But what I was most impressed with was how the entire thing is shown to the player. I was thrown into a violent world and told to fight. That is all I had. I was the guy breaking free, fighting in a world that makes no sense but at the same time amazed me. Throughout vast and foreign worlds, my character and my oddball companion were the only constants. Yet, despite having complete control of a character with no voice lines, I grew to realize how little this game was about me, the player. Although there is a predominant plot twist, it is paired with a gradual change as the player finds hints about the past of the character they inhabit, and the stories of those around him. By the end, the abstractions that make up the playable world feel relatable, and the "people" feel more human than anything else.
All this adds up to a game with unequalled replay value. The in-fight mechanics have an infinitely high skill ceiling, that always pushes me to improve. The various worlds in the game jump out and provide amazing explorability that I have hardly ever seen in any game, much less a game with set plot progression; the cinematics and choice camera angels of the game are incredible. The characters are thoroughly fleshed out, and able to tell their story and the protagonists with a handful of lines that never waste a word. The plot is steady, yet revealed for you to figure out through glimpses in words and phrases. I honestly don't think I'll ever complete this game, but I'm damn sure gonna love trying.

If you had said to me that a game with the tagline "Cyberpunk Bartending Action" could be remotely enthralling then I would look at you with disbelief. How could a game about a seemingly mundane job be any sort of fun even with the Dystopian setting?
Well it turns out, very much so! In fact, taking on said mundane job is actually what makes this refreshing from a lot of other Cyberpunk ficiton and games. Events are happening around you that you have no control over, so all you can do is pull up a pew and listen to what the colourful cast of characters in this game have to say about themselves, what they think about the world etc.
It's a masterclass of worldbuilding because of this, and one that manages to do it with just two main locales, home and work! It even manages to do this despite the fact that there are no dialogue options (or at least at the time of playing), which is something that would usually be a death sentence for a game like this, but in all honesty it actually doesn't matter as the characters have interesting things to say regardless.
That's not to say the gameplay is a slouch either, whilst on the surface it seems simple the game ramps up pretty quick, some requests customers make are straightforward, but some of them make requests in fashions ranging from vague to downright cryptic (but not in the usual negative connotation of the word). It means you have to pay attention not only to what customers are ordering on the night, but also any information that would've cropped up several nights before, as well as using deduction skills on the spot. It's a remarkably fresh approach to this sort of thing.
All in all I highly reccomend this game for someone who is immersed in the Cyberpunk genre, but wants something a little different out of it. Happy drinking!

Genre: Retro 2D 16-bit Platformer
Sub-genre: Hardcore Platformer
Presentation: 10/10 - Each pixel is beautifully rendered and lovingly placed to burn a hole directly through your skull with enduring love.
Gameplay: 10/10 - With simplistic yet unforgiving controls, this game will have you high fiving your best friend one minute, and smashing your face into your desk for sweet release the next.
*Keyboard and mouse compatible, as well as Gamepad compatible.
Sound: 10/10- With a soundtrack that feels like it was ripped right out of the 90's, it fits right in sync with the mind-numbing sound effects that will have your ears bleeding from extreme brutality.
Replay Value 10/10: What exactly is "Replay Value"? If it's in the sense of playing the game over again, then I can tell you I am almost 100% positive once you complete this game fully you will never want to play it again, unless to show someone else or submit yourself to more torture. That being said, you are going to put so many hours into this game that it justifies the $12 price tag ten times over. You are going to die so many times that technically you can consider that your "replay value". If you beat the game and feel like it's not hard enough for you, then you can go back through the first level and not die. At all. Do not die, get to the end of the level, and defeat the boss. In one sweep. You will then exit off of the stage and be taken to a seperate set of levels that are called the "Path of the Valkyrie". These levels are much more challenging and give you all of the migraines you crave. Enjoy!
Review Summary:
Never have I played a game for four hours straight to still be on the first level.
I am on the fourth level now and I have put 23 hours into this game.
It teaches you how to play by spanking you like a little school girl.
You will yell. You will cry. You will never laugh. You will step by step memorize enemy locations, level traps and upgrades to the point of madness...and then you'll continue to the next level and do it all over again.
There is one checkpoint in between each level, splitting them into two for each world. There are six worlds in total, making it twelve levels total. If you do not make it to the checkpoint then you will start at the very beginning upon death.There is a boss fight at the end of each world.
You have two weapons the entire game: a sword and a spear. Use these to navigate and decimate your way through each uniquely designed world. There are upgrades. If you can manage not to take any damage, each upgrade you get builds on top of the last one. It starts with a wooden shield, next upgrade is a metal shield and you can charge your spear throw. After that comes a viking helmet, then a flame sword. Only once you have claimed all of these upgrades can you truly claim you are still only mediocre at this game. There is also a bonus item you can find called Mjolnir, that gives you temporary invulnerability.
BEWARE: This game instills hope just as fast as it takes it from you.
If that's not your cup of tea, then you are a sissy.
Fun? Extremely. Metal? Of course. Beatable? Only if you are a true viking.

The gameplay offers a bit more options than many other clicker games and therefor stays fresh a few more hours. So much for the upsides.

It is an average attempt, several steps below the also free top competition in clicker games. Playing it won't hurt you, but won't be worth your time either. The hours, you're spending here, can be better spent on some other game. Maybe there will be a reason to change my mind in further development.

For a game that looks a bit like it's made with Paint(tm),
is a simple, decent platformer with distinct levels.
As Merv, a walking blue sphere, your task is to collect all collectables in the level and find exit.
What immediately strikes as odd is the unorthodox double-jumping. Merv can double-jump in the air once but only when he's at his peak. To make matters worse, jump height cannot be altered.
While awkward, the decision does have meaningful consequences, as the jump mechanic restricts the available routes and requires timing the jumps precisely to e.g. avoid certain spikes or enemies.
Curious jumps I can live with. But Merv also has trouble jumping on angled surfaces, and they are a plenty in
. If the ground is ever tilted, Merv kind of walks on his toes and has cumbersomely unresponsive jumps, presumably because he isn't truly standing but actually falling. This is by far the worst quality of the game.
Twelve (12) levels begin with a few really easy ones but by the end they have evolved into death traps, amplified by the annoying jumping scheme.
There are couple kinds of enemies and numerous traps, both static and moving ones. Some collectables are in obnoxious places, so you have to retain a good awareness of the movement capabilities of Merv.
Finding your way can sometimes resemble a puzzle, as not all routes work, and sometimes pushing a rock to a suitable place will open the way.
Overall, levels are reasonably branching and challenging, even if ultimately linear. There's at most a minute until the next check point, and most levels last a few minutes to complete if you don't die too much. As a nice detail the visuals vary vastly from level to level, from forests to caverns. There's no real story despite the scenery.
Settings are really simple, with only adjusting for sound and music volume. I couldn't find resolution options or whether you can play in a window too. Music is freeware stuff but the lighthearted tunes are oddly fitting nevertheless.
Though the length was estimated at 2-4 hours in the forums, I played it through in mere hour, without retrying for par times. You can skip levels if you beat levels fast.
I did enjoy myself though, despite raging at the clumsy controls - there is some clever level design here. However, considering the unpolished jump problems, uninspiring graphics and the short length, this is frankly at most a $1 game if that. Thus, take my recommendation with that consideration in mind.

Does anyone here remember the PC game Lemmings? Well if you don't, let me explain. You'd get a constant flow of cute little pixely critters, often upwards of 50 of them, and you'd have to guide them to an exit by designating a few of them special skills like digging of floating or exploding. In the end you had to rescue only a set number of Lemmings, and as a result you often had room for error that let you experiment a little at finding a unique solution and have a hilarious mini-panic when you accidentally lead half of them off a cliff.
Toki Tori reminds me of this game that I have a lot of nostalgia for because it brings to mind the more challenging levels where you'd only have one lemming, and there really only was one solution that didn't involve the cathartic 'nuke all' button. By about a fourth of the way through this game, the levels take a turn towards complexity so baffling that you will have no room for error and no ability to predict what tools you might need to save for later.
Don't get me wrong, the game is cute and entertaining, but it is far too shallow. Frustration with the invariably complicated one and only solutions lead me to use a walkthrough for most of the second half of the game. Each time I'd wonder aloud "How was I supposed to figure that one out?". I later found out that there is an (undocumented I think?) feature allowing you to zoom out enough to more carefully study the level and predict what you'll need. That would have helped a little earlier, but I still probably would have resorted to drawing out the level and spending 30 minutes working out the solution on paper. Maybe Toki Tori 2 has improved on the difficulty curve, or on the general boredom that results from the uninspiring puzzle design. I wouldn't know as I'm not willing to risk the amount of money it costs.
Two Tribes has made better. EDGE is a personal favorite of mine. But Toki Tori is just a bit too unforgiving and tedious for me to enjoy it, and as such I cannot recommend it.

Far Cry 4: a game that is in essence a love note to its parents, Far Cry 3 and the Map density of Far Cry 2.
What FC3 did and did right was build a huge world, that cast a trustfund baby into a journey to becoming the bloody faced hero of an island nation ripped apart by drugs and violence. 3 builds a star-studded cast of evil and clever characters, of which any player would love getting to meet and love getting to kill. But the reason 3 had such a star studded villainous cast was because you never knew when they would appear. Popping up around a random corner on the journey to be just insane enough to keep you roped in all the way to the conclusion.
FC4 is a good game all and all, but the story, cast, and the world itself doesn’t hold up to its parents. The main point at the pitch meeting was “what if we had a slightly more restrained villain but instead of making him come in every once in awhile we made him call you every 8 minutes to make sure you don’t forget him? Oh and the drug missions, we need to make that basically the only interesting thing the player does so lets hammer a fun one off into the ground with annoying repetition to where they become so dull and mainstream that the rest of the game loses its punch.”
If you haven’t played it, FC3 is a superior title. if you have, FC4 is good not better. If you want more of the same but slightly more stale buy it.

Best puzzle game i've ever played.
Pros:
[+] Nice visuals
[+] No music, just nature sounds. Makes the whole experience so very relaxing
[+] No pressure whatsoever.
[+] Open area with many puzzles that introduce different rules but still use the same mechanic that is introduced in the beginning. if you stumble upon something you don't know how to solve you can just go the other way and solve something else until you figure out that specific rules you didn't understand before.
[+] No plot. I'd say is a pro, even though many people consider it to be a huge con. There are some collectibles and other stuff that makes you think there is something happening, but in reality it's just a puzzle game. Don't expect interesting ending or deep messages. You can on the other hand expect some cool secret stuff.
[+] Incredible depth of the puzzles. The gameplay consists of you "finding a route on special tablets". It may sound boring, but each different zone introduces new rules that define the puzzle. There are sound puzzles, color puzzles, tetris-block based puzzles and many many more. Not only that but rules get combined and harder.
[+] Vast ammount of secrets. As you gradually proceed through the game you begin to understand that there's something else besides simple puzzles. Not to spoil everything but there's a huge amount of secret puzzles, secret places and such and such. You just have to know where to look. And where to look from.
[+] Everytime you boot up the game you continue from the point you left the game at.
Cons:
[-] No plot. If you're into puzzle games for plot then you should probably skip it.
[-] It's not rewarding. You don't get a candy for solving all the puzzles in the area, you don't get rewarded for different actions. There are some specific things that will trigger secret scenes but that's pretty much it. The puzzles are their own reward.
[-] Some puzzles include sound and color which might be challenging for tone-deaf and color-blind people.
[-] Other puzzles you might find to be extremely difficult. I never felt frustrated with the game because if i found myself lost i usually checked a guide or something, just to keep the experience flowing and relaxed. Some other people might have problems with that and stay stuck at some particular puzzle, which might result in some frustration.
I can't recommend this game enough for all the puzzle-genre fans but i've read lots of reviews where people felt lost due to the ending and misleading nature of the game, that occasionally makes you think there is a story, a point behind all that. Citing words of infamous Sean Murray "Don't go in looking for that kind of experience. It's not that kind of a game".

So I have no idea how anyone plays this game alone, but my friend and I play it together both solving the puzzles, having fun, and taking in the view it's really great if you play it that way.  If you play alone, I'd imagine you'll need to take a pencil, there's a lot of drawing out of the puzzles necessary.

This is a mixed review - I recommend The Witness with caveats. I haven't beaten it and probably won't return to it, but the time I've spent playing has been magical.
Pros:
Cons:

It is truly an enjoyable game, the equivalent of having many tablet/mobile puzzle games in one open-world, which at times, is dependent to that environment. It requires you to think in perspective, to pay attention, to learn, to evolve...to think. Sometimes if you can't figure something out, you'll just try some trial&error, if you consider yourself weak, you'll just ask someone or check a tutorial for help.
The level design is truly nice, the ambient sounds are soothing, everything is really calming (until you get annoyed by a puzzle, of course). Probably the lack of voice acting is a good thing, but the level limitations are sometimes confusing/annoying...I mean, what must one do if someone wants to jump off a cliff?! In rest, pretty much everything else is intuitive. Armed with a sharp mind, patience and time, one can truly enjoy this game.

The Witness is a gorgeous, exquisitely-detailed game. If you like exploring a peaceful and colorful island, if you like being challenged with geometric puzzles that test your logic and observational skills, if you like the satisfaction of spending time on some of the puzzles and eventually having the satisfaction of figuring them out, then this is right up your alley. Most of the game is non-linear, in that if a puzzle is blocking your progress in one area then there are plenty of other areas to work on until you have an epiphany.
The game has a first-person perspective; all you ever see of yourself is your shadow. There are no other people around (aside from many beautifully-posed clay statues). You're free to explore the island at your own pace. There are some doors beside computer monitors that display mazes and symbols. Figure out the patterns and solve the mazes to open the doors and get access to more of the island. Sometimes, scenery nearby will help show you the correct path to choose through the maze. It's a lot like a modern-day Myst. No weapons, no jumping, no dying, no health bar, no inventory, no automap, no music, no words; just puzzles to solve and an island to explore.
Everything about the game feels handcrafted; it even uses its own custom-built graphics engine. There are many locations where, if you stand in just the right place, the scenery will line up just right so that you know it was intended.
The endgame is The Witness's only drawback. Suddenly it becomes very much like Portal (without the homocidal AI), and the puzzles become much more difficult not because they're more challenging but because the game makes them harder to see. And I found the game's actual end disappointing because it left so many questions unanswered (like, what's the point of all the obelisks?).
Still, it's a journey I recommend, though you may want to have a hint guide nearby to avoid getting stuck for days trying to figure out what a puzzle is looking for.

The rest of the game is identical to previous versions of Duels of the Planeswalkers, and the controls are just as clumsy and poorly designed as they've always been. The only thing this product is valuable for is to walk newbies through the basic mechanics of the game so they can start off playing kitchen table Magic with friends. If you already play Magic, avoid this like the plague and just get Magic Online for your digital MTG fix.

This game is very simple to play. There are a few structures to build, and a few componants to build in some structures. You manage only a handful of critical resources and a few sort of bonus ones, like coins or guns that make things easier but can be done without. So on the face of things, it's very simple to play, and as simple games are, easy to get bored with... but there is a catch, it really doesn't get boring at all. For all it's simplicity, as you expand your base and move from survival to thriving, the dynamics start to shift slightly. It becomes a game of balancing critical resources with less vital type resources that you can't grow or maintain a huge colony without having. Can you survive without a massive stockpile of spare parts? Of course you can... But survival is a handful of colonists in a handful of structures, not 300 colonists, countless visitors, robots, and a sprawling city's worth of buildings and support structures. The real fun begins when you get to that point. When you have to start asking yourself questions like, "How do I FEED this many people?" or "How do I expand my power grid without getting in the way of future buildings?" Then there are the colonists themselves. " How many Engineers do I need? Or Guards?" This game is simple to learn, but the fun is in the details.

Space city-builder? Check! Good graphics/environments? Check!
This game is a solid example of the city-builder genre. After a few patches, I feel comfortable in recommending this game to folks who enjoy the genre. The logistics of building a colony on a new planet, and keeping your citizens breathing, fed, hydrated, entertained, and happy while building your colony towards new milestones present a fun and interesting challenge.
Base building reminds me somewhat of Evil Genius, in that it is an optimization problem. You'll spend most of your time laying out different modules essential to the survival and productivity of your colony. The maps will vary based on which part of the planet you land; the planet map is consistent, but each set of latitude/longitude will provide you with a different experience.
As the game advances, the logistics of maintaining a base require more efficiency and increasing threats; you will have to face down invaders who mean to kill your colonists, and have to keep ahead of the food/meal/O2 curve.
All in all, I recommend this game. It's not overly complicated, but it still has some depth.

if you ever wondered what happened to the freak baby of hotline miami and shadow of the colossus after its parents were murdered by suda51, you finally have your answer. overall, this game is a lot of fun, but a lot of the things that make it enjoyable are the same things that really hold it back from true greatness.
+ beautiful aesthetic and stage design bring the world to life.
+ great soundtrack will help you fight through your frustrations.
+ risks and rewards are usually well-balanced (see below). do you want to chance the charged sword and leave yourself open to attack, or is a quick combo the better option? can you tough out an assault in order to gain back some health?
+ each character is varied, ensuring that no two boss fights are totally similar - personal favorite: the edge.
+ because you don't level up or get anything new, every fight is challenging in its own way and so winning is highly satisfying because of the skills you as a player develop along the way.
- sometimes the bosses are very cheap in their execution, which makes them more of a chore.
- the miniscule amount of health you can regain during a fight makes for some frequent frustration during particularly brutal combat scenarios.
- the overall plot is weightless. because of this, the ~big~ ~reveal~ lacks impact and the story mode's unskippable cutscenes really pull the wind out of your sails the second time through.
- has some weird technical issues, like sometimes not recognizing the controller, that occur frequently.
obligatory numerical rating: 7.5/10

Danganronpa is one AMAZING anime/visual novel game and it is the best I have played in this genre. It's amongst my favorite games ever and is hella sweet to see it on Steam and PC port is excellent :). I already played it on PSVita before but had to buy again.
In the story you play as Makoto Naegi, who gets a lucky chance to join Hope's Peak Academy, a school for talented people. Once he enters there, well he quickly notices that the place is pretty different than what he thought... Danganronpa has very likeable and funny characters xD. The cast will notice quite soon to be part of a crazy and dark game of survival. This game of despair is lead by a mysterious nasty and funny bear called Monokuma, who btw is one of the BEST villains ever haha :D! The only way to survive out of there is to kill another student, without others finding out that who did it.
The soundtrack is really awesome with many cool songs. During the game, there is fps-freeroam in certain areas around the school and you can have conversations with the other characters a lot, to get to know them better.
One of the highlights of the journey, are definitely moments called Class Trials. It's when you have to find out the murderer with the others, blaming and arguing against each other in intense word battles. Trying to find out the guilty one is never easy and I love this about DR. You have to search for clues and complete puzzles to clear them and the Trials can last for a long time. The game keeps you guessing and addicted to the end.
A very nice bonus is that there is also the option to choose between English and Japanese voice acting, personally I looooove the Japanese VA it's WONDERFUL :D.
This journey will make you laugh, feel sad, surprised and care about the fantastic, crazy characters.
Everyone should definitely play this and Danganronpa 2 if can, because I think Danganronpa 3 releases this year and because Monokuma is beary awesome :).

"But I watched the anime, I don't need to play this, right?"
Let-
Let me stop you right there.
The anime is trash*, plain and simple, but this... this is another matter entirely.
Danganronpa answers the age old question of "What happens if you let a mechanical bear with a despair fetish capture a bunch of highschool students with extreme proficiency in one field and force them to kill each other?"
The answer, of course, is one of the most incredible visual novel experiences I've ever had. Danganronpa takes everything up to 11, shows you what it would look like if you went to 12, and then skips straight to 15. Everything about it is enthralling and horrifying all at once. I lost a lot of sleep thinking about this game.
Do yourself a favor and just sit down and play it straight through. Don't read anything else about it. Don't risk ruining the experience for yourself, because hot damn is it an experience. Everything after like the first 30 minutes is a game changing spoiler.
I can come up with about 11037 more reasons why this game is great, but I'll spare you my ramblings. Just... just play it.
*This is called comedic hyperbole. Please read my edits.
EDIT 1: In response to some of the comments on this review, let me expand my discussion on the anime a bit. The anime is a direct adaption of only the most essential elements of the plot of the original PSP game. The result is next to nothing as far as character development, and the suspense and thrill of solving the crimes is completely eliminated by the investigation/courtroom montages that sort of just... exposit, with little of interest otherwise. I have absolutely nothing against the adaption as its own work or even against anime in general. It's just that when compared to the extremely detailed characterization every single character gets in the game and the satisfaction of actually having to solve all the crimes yourself, the anime falls flat.
In short, the anime is definitely not a substitute for actually playing the game. I hope this helps!
EDIT 2: Well... yes, if you've watched the anime you'll have the plot spoiled for you. However, like I said, you still only know the gist of how each crime happened. You still have to actually do all the legwork to prove it, which is still a lot of fun in and of itself. At least I think so. Plus, there character events and bonus scenes that can't be seen by just watching the anime. So if you have any attatchment to the characters, then yes, I do think there is value in playing the game. If you just wanted the plot, well... you got it.

Toki Tori is a puzzle game by
, released in January 2010. You play the game as a chick by the name of Toki Tori, who is on a quest to collect all the eggs in the world. The game is divided into five worlds, who are also divided into several levels. To proceed into the next level, the player has to collect all the eggs in one level. By proceeding through the game, the player unlocks different tools, which he needs in order to reach certain eggs, but every level has a limited amount of tool uses and this is where the tricky part comes in.
If you are familiar with puzzle games, the game will probably not be very challenging and if you aren't, it's still very easy in the beginning, but gets very hard in the end. The levels are monotone and once you get the hang of one level, you can project that procedure to other levels.
The game gets quite hard in the end and the monotony that I was talking about is compensated by the different worlds in the game, which all have very different themes and different tools. The atmosphere is happy and joyful in the first world, but soon turns darker and more dangerous as more enemies and traps appear. The game features adorable colorful comic graphics and a cheering and catchy music.
Toki Tori is overall a lovely game if you want to pass the time or if you just want a casual game that cheers you up. It's great for people who don't want a serious game and it's a must-have for every puzzle game lover.
