This little bird first saw the light of day back in 2001 on the good old Game Boy Color, but it manages to remain entertaining and relevant to this date thanks to HD versions, remakes and the fact that you can get it on almost any possible platform including the PC. So, what makes it fun to play 13 years later? Maybe it's the fact that it looks cute and childish and somehow reminds us of a time when games were made for fun and this is certainly an easy to learn, hard to master kind of game because it looks simple at first, but you'll often find yourself looking for the answer somewhere else as you'll get stuck more often than you'd think. The story is simple and just like in Angry Birds you are supposed to rescue your lost brothers, which come in the form of eggs, and not actual birds, but you'll have to go through quite a lot to achieve that. The menu is simple and intuitive and choosing what level you want to play once you unlocked the hard and bonus levels is easy to do, so you won't find yourself navigating the menus in order to find something because all you need is always one click away.
The gameplay in Toki Tori is as simple as it gets as you can move left/right/up/down using the mouse to point the next place you want your little bird to go and use items in order to pass a certain obstacle or defeat your enemies such as worms, ghosts or porcupines; such items include a freeze gun, a vacuum, instant rocks or the ability to teleport or create bridges. The PC version also has a option to rewind, so in case you screw up you can always go back a couple of seconds and try again which will reduce your frustration because sometimes you might press the wrong button and use an item instead of another or make a wrong step near the end and playing the whole level again would drive you mad. The only thing missing was the ability to jump as I always tried to jump thinking that it would make the whole puzzle easier to solve, only to remember that I can't do that, but either way it's not so bad because you don't really need to as the items and abilities are more than enough.
This game looks good as it has a nice pallet of colours and it has that childish look that will make you nostalgic as it is one of those games that will age very well in the purest Nintendo style. Each stage has its own theme so when you will find yourself in the sewers the level design will make it feel like unique and different from the previous stages and the little details like the mud interacting with Toki's feet are going to display the level of attention this game got from the developers and it really shows that they wanted to deliver a better experience with this release and not make it look like just another HD remake.
Toki Tori sounds just as good as it looks as the sound manages to deliver the same thing: a childish experience that will stay with you for a long time, and while it repeats the same music over and over again in the menu it never feels overused and during the actual levels the sound manages to deliver the same experience the design does and this helps the player's immersion. The sound effects are also okay, nothing will take you out of this magical world where a chick fights ghosts and worms.
The PC version comes with some exclusive levels and the ability to rewind, but the real win comes with the level editor which allows you to create your own unique adventures and challenges for the little bird and thanks to Steam you are able to share them with your friends. The Steam Achievements are also a nice incentive to make you play again certain levels and thanks to all that I managed to spend more time in Toki Tori than in some big triple A games out there.
Toki Tori is a cheap and fun game and no matter if you're getting at full price or grabbing your copy during the next sale, Toki Tori is need to buy because it will take you by surprise regarding how much you will enjoy it no matter if you like that type of games or not and even if you go in to play just a level you will end up spending hours in it and for such a small price it's clearly a bargain.

Best puzzle game i've ever played.
Pros:
[+] Nice visuals
[+] No music, just nature sounds. Makes the whole experience so very relaxing
[+] No pressure whatsoever.
[+] Open area with many puzzles that introduce different rules but still use the same mechanic that is introduced in the beginning. if you stumble upon something you don't know how to solve you can just go the other way and solve something else until you figure out that specific rules you didn't understand before.
[+] No plot. I'd say is a pro, even though many people consider it to be a huge con. There are some collectibles and other stuff that makes you think there is something happening, but in reality it's just a puzzle game. Don't expect interesting ending or deep messages. You can on the other hand expect some cool secret stuff.
[+] Incredible depth of the puzzles. The gameplay consists of you "finding a route on special tablets". It may sound boring, but each different zone introduces new rules that define the puzzle. There are sound puzzles, color puzzles, tetris-block based puzzles and many many more. Not only that but rules get combined and harder.
[+] Vast ammount of secrets. As you gradually proceed through the game you begin to understand that there's something else besides simple puzzles. Not to spoil everything but there's a huge amount of secret puzzles, secret places and such and such. You just have to know where to look. And where to look from.
[+] Everytime you boot up the game you continue from the point you left the game at.
Cons:
[-] No plot. If you're into puzzle games for plot then you should probably skip it.
[-] It's not rewarding. You don't get a candy for solving all the puzzles in the area, you don't get rewarded for different actions. There are some specific things that will trigger secret scenes but that's pretty much it. The puzzles are their own reward.
[-] Some puzzles include sound and color which might be challenging for tone-deaf and color-blind people.
[-] Other puzzles you might find to be extremely difficult. I never felt frustrated with the game because if i found myself lost i usually checked a guide or something, just to keep the experience flowing and relaxed. Some other people might have problems with that and stay stuck at some particular puzzle, which might result in some frustration.
I can't recommend this game enough for all the puzzle-genre fans but i've read lots of reviews where people felt lost due to the ending and misleading nature of the game, that occasionally makes you think there is a story, a point behind all that. Citing words of infamous Sean Murray "Don't go in looking for that kind of experience. It's not that kind of a game".

So I have no idea how anyone plays this game alone, but my friend and I play it together both solving the puzzles, having fun, and taking in the view it's really great if you play it that way.  If you play alone, I'd imagine you'll need to take a pencil, there's a lot of drawing out of the puzzles necessary.

This game has been a wild ride.
I bought it the day it came out after watching beta youtubers play it, I thought I had to have it, I love these kind of simulation games. Right out of the gate I felt like I knew what I was doing. I felt intelligent and up to date with how to work this system, but what I didn't know was just how fragile the game really is. My first desert colony crashed and burned when I began to stress the ai (100+ people). I wanted to blame the ai, and how the game is formatted and designed. But after the rage had subsided I began to take a different look at it.
The ai needs work, the developers know that, but this game isn't broken. Just very fragile. The amount of micromanagement required to survive is absolutely stress inducing. As I feel it should. Your every move has a consequence on your end game and I never realized that, right down to the type of colony lay out, structure type, size, and where you put components. Every little action has a profound impact on your journey, and a lot of people don't realize that. They try to bruteforce the game, break it and then blame the ai. But this game requires a lot of finesse and patience, and I adore that it was developed that way. I bruteforced my desert colony, placing stuff willy nilly everywhere and not paying attention to my micromanagement and I asphyxiated 175 people. But after watching youtubers like Negark handle game mechanics, I sailed through both F and M all 10 milestones in one shot.
Looking back, my view of this game has changed a lot. I thought of it as a more layed back style game where you wouldn't have to worry about what kind of food you were growing to assure no one would starve, or worry about how you should distribute workers to gather metal ore during a power crisis while juggling processors and factory components. But indeed every move you make should be well thought out and calculated, like a game of chess.
Would I recommend this? yes and no. I think this game appeals to more methodical people, the kind of people who like to sit and plan out what they're going to do while under stress. For those who just want to bruteforce everything, this game isn't for you. I've loved playing this and I really hope the developers add more mechanics, more planets, and continue to enhance the ai. Thanks Planetbase for a blast!

[This is before the 1.0.6 patch; I'm definitely going to give it another go and I have high hopes.  Previous review below.]
This is not the game it appears to be.
It looks like a Banished/Cities-type simulation, but the NPC's astonishingly narrow AI makes it more of a puzzle-solver of a game.  For example, nobody but Medics can use medical kits; if your workers are injured and you have no Medics or a landing area, you might as well just restart.  Too much functionality is limited to a specific class, and losing any of them is a gamebreaker.  They are every bit as single-minded and single-functioned as the robots they work alongside.  They aren't people; they're logical constructs to solve the equation that is the base.
It's imperative that you use your starting resources very carefully, because your base will have to be in perfect sync to start creating your own supplies (and you'll need to do that fast, before you run out of spares).  Odds are you'll need to recycle a ton of things when circumstances (low power, low water, lack of resources) back you into a corner, and that's if you can get out of it at all.
I took a chance on this after reading Kotaku's enthusiastic write-up, and I regret that.  It has great potential, but the narrow-minded AI breaks not only immersion but a sense of enjoyment.  I don't know that a patch will solve what makes this game so unlike expectations -- and typically disappointing.  I have a very faint spark of hope, but until then, don't come into this expecting Banished-levels of flexibility and depth.  It's just not there.

...and then they got greedy. The shift wasn't even terribly subtle. They annihilated the balance, and the only fix was to pay more. I kept hoping for a patch-fix that, of course, never came. In the end, they proved my every concern to be true. They just took a bit longer than usual to reach the inevitable point of screwing up a Good Thing™.
What a waste.

Below is my response to the following comment from Gaijin: "Hello. We never anihilated balance and never ecouraged anyone to pay for anything. Star Conflict is a free game, where every pilot can do and earn anything without any payment. Premium license gives you advantages in faster rank progression, but not in battles."
The same geriatric excuse trundled out by every game that goes P2W? Yikes. Sure, a free pilot is structured within the same progression as a premium player. However, by the time they reach the same point as the premium pilots they're playing against (because matchmaking went out the window too), the universe will have have terminated entirely through heat-death. Where a player's two choices of keeping up are either "pay through the nose" or "quit your job and play the game full-time", your game is pay-to-win. The attempt to downplay the correlation between battle advantage and faster rank progression is just weak.
See, there used to be a reasonable middle ground. Players who could pay for a bit here and there. There was enough progression without paying that it was feasible to play normally for the most part, then just buy some GS & a license every so often. You got your money out of us - heck, I even picked up a premium ship. The problem was, you distanced those two sides of things so much that it was no longer a remotely workable option. Crafting became a pipe-dream and progression without GS slowed to a pained hobble. It was either "shell out the big bucks" or "go home". So congrats on turning away paying customers too I guess?
Oh, and you "never encouraged anyone to pay for anything"? Do you know what normal people call that? A "lie". It's called a lie.

While I have no hours on the PC  yet, I have played it on the Vita. This game is good to put it shortly. I will rank it on Gameplay, Story, Graphics, and Sound.
Story: You are Makoto Naegi, a normal/average boy who got accepted into Hopes Peak Academy with the title of Super High School Luckster. You enter the academy and suddenly your vision goes black. you wake up in a classroom and meet the other students. During the confusion, a Black and White Bear arrives, calling itself Monokuma. The bear then tells the students that the only way to leave is to kill another classmate witout getting caught. While the format and basis for the plot feels very "edgy" it works well. the writers work these students into this out of this world experience very well. Combine that with the trials, which are very intresting and keep you engaged. It overall a good story, and highlight of the game.
Gameplay: The gameplay is a combination of a visual novel and mystery game. You interact and hang out with students to learn more about them, and then the mystery  you search for clues in the school to find the murderer. Trials are almost half of the game, and this where you put all of your evidence to the test in finding out who the killer is. these segment can be at least an hour to two hours at some points. During the trials are minigames that i wont go into detail with, such as nonstop debates and panic talk. The gameplay is okay. It controls well, but not perfectly which can lead to mistakes that are not your own. the gameplay can also drag on for a while, as the game itself does.
Visuals: Danganronpa takes things in an artstyle pleasing to the eye, with many character designs either fitting the character, look good, or both. the enviroments are a bit dark at certian points which can be bothersome. However, the most different change is the "Pink Blood" in which everyone has pink blood instead of red. It is really dumb and an excuse to make it so that teens could play it, which is very idiotic.
Sound: Voice Acting, especially in english, can feel very dull at points. While some have good performance, others feel like they put no effort into it, which is heart breaking. The OST is okay, with some good tracks, bad tracks, but mostly average tracks that may or may not fit the situation. This is easily the weakest part of the game.
Overall Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a good game, with fantasic visuals and story, with okay gameplay and sound. I'd reccomend you get at a sale if you can, $30 is a bit too much.

SPOILER FREE REVIEW -- [I have beaten this on Vita]
Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a deceptive, mystery-driven variety adventure title with visual novel, horror and romance elements. Sounds like a mouthful? But this game manages to split these elements proportionally to make them enjoyable and add fuel to the evolving, amazing, storyline that will haunt you for years to come.
Originally a PSP title, with multiple ports for years to come, the PC version is more akin to a straight-up port than a HD remake. Which is fine, and understandable, because it isn't the games' aesthetics which make it one of the best adventure games I've ever played; but its story, characters and setting.
Again, spoiler-free, but you play as Makoto Naegi, an average high school boy finding himself trapped in a mysterious building one day with other students; aptly nicknamed given their personality and fashion. Not long in, there's been a murder and you are put in charge with finding out who murdered said person, by learning about the other characters, finding clues and going into a trial with them ala Ace Attorney. Speaking of - I feel Danganronpa is a strong franchise which can be compared to the Ace Attorney series as there are identical gameplay elements and quirky design choices.
Moving on though, general gameplay consists of room-to-room movement, talking to characters in visual novel-esque, with their beautifully drawn portraits to keep you distracted from the text. During the trials, there are well-placed, reasonable and sensical QTEs that tie-in with how both the story and gameplay present themselves up until that point. Your quick fingers, your own intuition and feelings for the characters will make you feel confident, or weasel out of wanting to press those button propmpts.
Anyway, for me personally, one of the best portions of the game is its atmosphere: its forboding, compelling, repressive and tense building was mostly on my part because of the direction the game goes. It... isn't your typical raincoat detective story, there's nicely used humour, a strange but loveable villain which is introduced early, whacky, bizarre, creative yet at the same time, reverse-stereotypical characters. But what did it for me... was the way the game progresses, what happens when each new day passes... what your consequence is for not finding the murderer quick enough. All the dread, mystery and tension is added as layers of fear, heh. At one point, I felt legitamately frightened to continue, but I did anyway knowing what would happen next was going to blow my mind.
I can't say enough good things about this game, BUY IT. BUY IT NOW. It will be one of the best adventure games you'll play, there is something for everybody in this game, big and small. This game is a masterpiece.

It's a game that draws you into its world of crazy characters and pepto bismol blood and then makes you sad every time a character you dislike dies.
Dangan Ronpa is a Visual Novel game with more gameplay than you'd normally see from a visual novel. Each chapter is composed of 3 parts. You have your 'Normal School Days' your 'Abnormal School Days' and your 'Class Trials'. The first part is always more of a storytelling part. You walk around the school and watch/participate in predetermined events and sometimes you get free time to "hangout" with whichever character you want where you'll learn more about them and maybe unlock a cool ability. If you've read the actual game description it won't surprise you that at some point one of the students ends up dead. That is what triggers 'Abnormal School Days'. This part is mostly an investigation and also where the more gameplay elements start to peek its head out. Now you need to search around the school (specifically places pertaining to the incident) and find all of the evidence you can as well as a few testimonies. You can't really fail this part as the third part of the game won't trigger until you have all the evidence, but running around finding the pieces to the crime and trying to solve it as you go is always pretty cool. Then once you have all the pieces it is the 'Class Trial' part triggers where you get to set abilities (which are things you might have gathered through your free time events with other characters) and then you play a few different minigames to try and solve the case. You'll shoot people's wrong claims with bullets and then solve a few other word puzzles. Eventually you'll find the killer (or get a game over and have to try the class trial again) and that's the best part of the game. Their execution. The moment that you watch something super crazy pertaining to their character's title, come up and kill them...and then you feel bad because if you're like me your favorite character always dies first.
You do have to go back and do free time events after passing the game to 100% it because obviously the killed person and the killer in chapter one aren't going to be around long enough to finish both of their paths and you probably won't finish any character's story unless you happen to start with one of the ones who die closer to end game or survive until the end. But it's easy enough to get their free time events without replaying the whole game.
I'd definitely recommend this game to anybody who likes mystery, story based, visual novel, or darker games. Anybody who knows me will know I've been recommending this game since the fan translation came out and I even chose to get a PS Vita over a 3DS just for these games.
As a bit of history about this game, it was originally released in Japan in 2010. A few years later some guy played it and thought it was "the best thing since sliced bread" or at least thought it was good enough that he was willing to translate the whole game for us as if it was a movie script. He put the screenshot of their face to the left, what they said to the right. Translated the whole game for the western audience. Dangan Ronpa got a pretty big cult following and soon after got an anime (don't watch it follows the story plotline but very bare boned and 100% spoilers) and then an English translation.
Which it deserved. And the Steam port, which it really deserved (because seriously most people weren't going to buy a PS Vita just for Dangan Ronpa).
This game is the reason I really enjoy visual novels, a very interesting story, with some pretty fun blood and gore, it was easy to get attached to the characters even though they were all based on some over the top stereotypes. The gameplay was fun, the story was what really held me in.

This is definitely one of the best puzzle games I've played in a while. Everything comes together in a nice, neat little package. Unlike puzzlers like Portal 2 and all those stacking and matching games, which give you one core mechanic to work the whole game off of, this game gives you a variety of items and puzzle elements which must be used in order to complete the game. Most of the time they have a limited number of uses so the puzzles are about knowing what items to use, where to use them and when to use them so you can gather the many eggs located in each stage.
The story is pretty thin, but this isn't the kind of game you play for the story anyways, the point is to solve cleverly designed puzzles. Not to mention each world has not only 12 regular stages, but also hard mode stages and bonus levels (which you need to join the Toki Tori steam group to play), and a load of achievements, so there's plenty of bank for your buck.
There's also a level editor, which isn't hard to use, but I haven't sunk enough time into it nor do I really care to (mostly due to my inability to design half-decent puzzles) to figure it out completely.
A great buy, and I'd recommend it to any puzzle enthusiast.

The Duels of the Planewwalkers games have always had problems with land draw, but this particular version carried that to the most absurd maximum. Play a hand with 1 land and be thankful if you draw 1 land in 5 turns. Play a hand with 5 lands and expect to draw land pretty much every turn. This exacerbates the luck factor, making the opening hand much more important than it should be if actual probabilities were used in the card draw. The previous versions, although not given the ability to adjust the land ratio, plays much better even with this problem due to the balance and design of the decks.

I bought this game as a treat for myself because I haven't touched MTG in a VERY long time. But it is very clear to me from the outset that this is a game that relies entirely on luck. Yes, the campaign gameplay is more or less balanced, but unless you are willing to grind away at duel after duel like you've got nothing better to do you get stuck with what is essentially an out of the box preconstructed deck versus an out of the box preconstructed deck, so there is no skill involved in building a deck and even less (than usual) involved in using it. This goes doubly-so for the sealed campaign. Granted, your selection is completely random and you have to build a deck from that, but then you're limited to more or less basic strategies without--what's that called?-- Luck, again yes. Add to this the fact that you have to buy extra sealed slots (you can't reset them) AND the fact that there is over fifty dollars worth of DLC for this game and you see what the strategy is here: first taste is free, the next one costs you a child.
Also: What the heck is with premium foils? Uh. Hello? This is a computer game! Who gives a rat's rear-end about foils and who on earth is gullible enough to pay money for digital foil cards? If you really want to spend a small fortune on MTG, just go to your local gaming store and buy some actual cards.

A game that needs a "Neutral" or "Mixed" rating, between "Recommended" and "Not Recommended". I'm voting "Not Recommended" purely because this game already has overwhelmingly positive reviews, merely as a counterbalance.
The Good:
- Remember the first time you played Portal? Remember that brain-opening moment when the concept of a "portal" finally clicked, and changed from an unfamiliar and abstract concept to a tool as natural as WASD? "The Witness" has that moment, over and over and
again. To put it another way, this is an adventure game where you collect keys and combine inventory items to open locks - except the "keys" are abstract concepts expressed in symbolic language, the "locks" are puzzles (with varying degrees of literalness), and your "inventory" is your brain. Puzzles that look incomprehensible at first will become merely baffling and tricky a few minutes later, and then suddenly near-trivial with a bit more experience.
- Adequately describing how
this game is would trigger Steam's profanity filter. It's one thing to look at screenshots and video footage of the game, and another to freely walk around inside an impressionist painting made three-dimensional.
The Bad:
- If you've played Braid, you may remember a "puzzle" involving waiting for
- real-time, not game-time - for a cloud to move across the screen, to collect one of the stars needed to reach the game's "true" ending. Well, that style of "challenging puzzle" is back, and in greater numbers. Many of them are "optional", but there are still times where you'll need to backtrack and circle around a very long way to get over a very short distance, or repeatedly cross a mechanical bridge that takes almost a full minute to pass over a mere six-foot gap - unless you're on the wrong side, in which case, get ready for some cardio. I have a callus on my pinky now from running everywhere - in retrospect, I should have just wedged the "Shift" key down with a toothpick. In this game's description, the phrase "This game...treats your time as precious" is used, and it's
- Without referring to guides, there's a very good chance that you'll reach the "boring ending", and entirely miss out on about a third of the full game, which contains actual clues as to what's going on as well as giving you the key to the "true ending". However, because the gameplay is so concept-based, reading those guides runs the risk of spoiling chunks of the game , depending on where you happen to glance on the page. Also, the "boring ending" gives the impression of
and starting over, which might be rage-inducing until you discover that you can still reload earlier quicksaves (which you may
have interacted with up until that point).
The Meh:
- The game seems to want to either communicate or trigger some deep insights into consciousness, spirituality, the process of science, escapism, and the relation between gamers and gaming as a medium. At times, this gradual unfolding of deeper mysteries turns into a tedious slog to get to the next good bit, which may or may not be all that good. However, the "good bits" do exist. Eventually. Your Mileage May Vary.

fresh-baked artisanal bread, fragrant and toothsome, garnished with a tomato rose so intricately carved that it's practically non-Euclidean. And a big ol' slimy hunk of Spam.

This review contains some spoilerfree knowledge that I would have liked to have had before playing the game.
The Witness is all about Curiousity. Exploration. Contemplation. It is not a fast game, and it is not a game that you will be able to play in one sitting. Not least because it does not take you by the hand.
While in many other games the exploration aspect is mostly about studying your environment (think of large open world games), and pherhaps adapting to new enemies (of which The Witness has none - it is an entirely action-free puzzle game), The Witness only appears to work in that way at the very beginning. After a while, you will begin to realize that this game takes exploration to a much more fundamental level. Namely, into the game mechanics themselves. The Witness will ask you to learn new things right until the very end.
From a game design perspective, one of the greatest achievements of The Witness in my opinion is the way the player is taught new mechanics. While you might be frustated at times, after a while you will learn when to walk away from a puzzle (in order to return later) and how to solve even complicated logic puzzles (by questioning all your assumptions from different perspectives, by writing things down, and by drawing the puzzle on a sheet of paper and walking through different possible solutions). All in all, I was able to solve all puzzles without hints (except the "environment puzzles", which you don't need for the "core" game). But it took at least 20-30 hours. And that's just the ingame time, without the outgame subconscious processing. ;-)
If you liked The Talos Principle (not talking about the very though DLC), chances are you're gonna enjoy The Witness as well. Both games require logic and have a philosophical undertone. However, while much of The Talos Principle's complexity comes from its 3D world (such as placing parts in the right spot and knowing what can go where), The Witness is much more about changing your perspective on the problem itself.
// TLDR:
This is a game that plays with your mind. If you enjoy playing with your mind as well, get it! ;-)
Addition:
It should be noted, that the game has a strong religious undertone. Which at times can be a little bit too much.
It's a puzzle where you have to find the rule of the puzzle itself.

It is without a doubt the finest Level design in the history of games. They have depth and thought in them that can make you laugh with delight when you unlock some element of it's construstion. The areas you walk through are lush serene and tangentally related to the core game. The puzzle screens.
It leverages one puzzle mechanic over and over and over again adding variations, some fun and inventive but eventually so many variations that you will struggle to remember their interactions. It clearly expects you to play the game with a pad and pencil. Remembering the mechanics of the puzzles in a game unto it's self. The problem is the puzzles have a finite set of variations. Roughly half are related to the circumstance of their placement. the other half are grinding experaments in mathamathecial make work. The only solution to give your brain a rest is not to walk away to another puzzle but rather to stop playing the game. Which is sad considering how glorious the enviroment is.
What leads me to not recomending the game is the painfull utter and total lack of a satisfying story. It's spreads hidden audio recornings about Zen and Space and Human perception about the place. All of them quotations, all read by actors who dont match the origional writers who are credited a the end of the stories. No charicter in any of them. I dont consider telling you that a spoiler. It's not possible to spoil this game except by looking at a completed puzzle screen. Even then you need context of the near by screns to work out how a alter screen is a spoiler.
The game simple has no story of any level. Anyone who says it does would probably mistake a mix tape for an oprea. They my have intended one may have woven one in there unding other peoples words but on completion what's there all comes across as rather painfully self indulgent. Like a film about making films and how awesome people who make films are.
TLDR: Expect a very slight self indulgent thin story with no ending. One puzzle twisted over and over and over again. Play with a pad and pencil. If your tired of the core puzzle take a break from the game. There isint enough variation in the game to stop it from becoming frustraiting.

I will say that I didn't know much about The Witness before playing, and I did this somewhat intentionally. It did something I have never seen done in a game in that it's almost anti-linear. I guess you could describe that as open-world, but even most of the open-world games I've played had a clear path you were supposed to take (especially those that don't give you access to the entire map from the beginning). The Witness silently encourages you to explore your surroundings. I would look around my immediate area and complete line puzzles until I would get to one I coldn't solve in a reasonable amount of time. Once here, I would walk away and find a new area to work on. The Witness is interesting in that you almost were required to do this, as some areas are unfinishable until you have learned certain puzzle mechanics from other areas.
Since I didn't have any prior knowledge on The Witness, I was definitely disappointed to learn that this game is 95% solving line/grid puzzles. If that isn't what you are into then I do not recommend this game at all. As I progressed through the various types of line puzzles, I thought they were cleverly designed and made in a way so that each type felt new in a way. This kept me from getting too bored. What I did not appreciate was the difficulty. After finishing the 'tutorial' area for a new puzzle type, I would feel a sense of accomplishment that I figured out something new. Then I would face the inevitable "oh wait, maybe my initial assumptions about these puzzles were wrong" feeling, and I would go back and figure out my mistake. Once I got past that though, I was frequently met with the same frustration. I would have a line puzzle in front of me, I would know how to go about solving it, but I just couldn't find the right path to do so. It's similar to how I feel while playing a lot of point and click adventures. I have a platform thats too tall to climb up to, I have a rope, now how do I proceed?!
The Witness is absolutely beautiful, and it upsets me that there is no badge for this game. I would have loved to see the backgrounds that could have been made. Every different 'puzzle area' had it's own look and feel to it, and I loved the beginning of the game when I was simply exploring everything.
There is basically no story in this game at all, and anyone who says otherwise is lying. You can make up a story in your head, but what this game presents to you is too vague to give you anything concrete. This is my main problem with The Witness. Nothing about it felt fun. I would enjoy the lovely colors around me, but eventually I'd have to trudge around to find out where the puzzles were. After solving a puzzle, I'd feel satisfied but then the next one would be waiting for me and that satisfication quickly disappeared. I'd find audio recordings where the voices would just read a quote from a noteworthy person from history and some artwork drawn by who knows.
I marched on despite all this. I did the majority of the puzzles without much help, and I got to the mountain. Once I got there though, all shame went out the window. I just wanted to get to the end of the game, and once again the game throws me more line puzzles. And for what? Is this some kind of challenge to see if I was paying attention to the hundreds of other puzzles I solved before? Am I supposed to struggle through them and eventually feel smart and good about myself that I did it? I don't find that rewarding. I will say that I'm glad I didn't waste the time going through the mountain puzzles given what the ending was like.
There are no jump scares, although the whole time playing I felt like something was watching me. Kind of creepy.

So, this is the first ever review I have written for any game on Steam. There is a reason for that. Here is that reason:
For a game to be equal parts captivating, challenging, intuitive and refreshing, a developer needs to put in a serious shift. Such was the case with The Witness. Isolated on an island filled with maze-like puzzles, the player is left to their own devices, with nobody there to assist or talk to them, no form of out-and-out tutorial, and a whole lot to explore.
The way The Witness teaches you about the basic rules the game is built upon (solve puzzles by tracing a line across a grid, starting at a circle and ending in a semi-circle "exit"), and then goes on to introduce a plethora of extra elements one has to familiarize themselves with to progress through each distinct area of the island is beautifully innovative. Instead of giving you an explanation of what to do, it simply...lets you do it. This paves the way to one of the game's central themes: the joy of epiphany and discovery. There are no direct clues. The player relies on their own intuition, capacity to challenge their own knowledge and view of what they have previously learned, ability to read their environment (I will get back to this in a second), all to slowly work out what each new symbol or environment represents, and how it fits in with the ones encountered in other areas.
Areas. There are about a dozen very distinct landscapes gracing the island. From desert ruins, orchards, and swamps to a quarry, a windmill, and a cliffside bunker, The Witness has loads of exciting, visually stimulating areas to explore, in virtually any order, each with a unique twist to the common maze-grid concept serving as obstacles on the way to that area's laser. The lasers, once activated, aim towards the islands central mountain, paving the way to the endgame once 7 out of the 11 lasers are activated. Activating all 11 allows access to an optional "post-game" challenge, which I have yet to beat (because it is hard, don't judge).
Riddling all of those areas are puzzles hidden throughout the environment that mimick the familiar concept of circle-to-semicircle-lines. With a keen eye, and a habit of stopping every now and then to become aware of one's surroundings, the player will soon become able to spot these seemingly everywhere, from small lines in the sand, to the entire exterior hull of a sunken ship. These environmental puzzles are by far my personal highlight in an already astonishing game, that often left me breathless, and always left me scratching my head, staring at a seemingly unsolveable puzzle only to jolt up, trace a line across a grid, and exclaim my excitement aloud, much to the annoyance of my roommate.
10/10. This game is a legitimate work of art. Masterpieces do not come along all that often, so do yourself a favor and grab this as soon as your wallet permits it.

Did you enjoy games like Ghosts 'n Goblins, Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts, or the NES/SNES Castlevania games?
. Don't know what they were about? Read on.
If you're looking for a game that will hold your hand or provide a lot of guidance, then don't buy this game. Save for showing you the controls at the start and showing a few hints, you have to figure out everything for yourself. The checkpoints are spaced out quite a bit, especially compared to most modern games. Don't expect checkpoints right before the bosses.
On the other hand, the levels are short, so once you get the hang of them, getting back to the boss won't take much of your time. Breezing through a level that made you grunt and curse like a viking initially is a clear indication of real progress, not just haphazardly making it to the next checkpoint.
You're expected to find safe routes through the environment, and solid tactics for defeating your enemies.
At the start of each world you'll encounter a new set of enemies, and you'll often see new ones in the second part of the world as well. While some enemies are very similar in appearance (not
palette swaps, though), their moves and properties will differ. The bosses vary greatly in appearance and attack patterns.
The levels must be attempted in a linear order, though you can choose a harder version of the next world after defeating a boss, provided you're able to loot enough chests without getting hit. You can sometimes choose more difficult paths within levels, which often lead to chests or secrets.
There aren't any blind leaps of faith, provided you use the "look ahead" button, though it comes close at times. You can spot hazards by carefully observing the level.
The levels have distinc looks and the hazards change as well.
If you think a 2D action platformer which will punish you for your mistakes sounds like fun, then buy this game.

I had a good childhood.  My parents were pretty lenient, I was allowed pretty free reign on what I did growing up.  It was pretty sweet.   The reason I decided to bore you with this little anecdote mind you...is because one of the few times I remember getting banned from my Super Nintendo for a week was due to Super Ghouls and Ghosts.   That game was hard as hell and instigated fits of anger on a regular basis.  Controllers were broken, swears were shouted loudly, and about the time the controller bounced off the screen of the TV as I screamed "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!", it was all over.
Despite all that?  I still loved it.
Enter Volgarr the Viking.  That little love song to Ghouls & Ghosts was written, because Volgarr is a love song written to Ghouls & Ghosts.  The game feels straight out of the Super Nintendo long box.  The challenges are unrelenting and difficult from the very beginning.  Yet, there's a lot of nostalgia and enjoyment packed in here that leads you to keep hitting retry and going back over the same deaths time and time again.  Veterans of Volgarr the Viking will say that the game is easy and comes down to memorization.  Sure, it does come down to memorization.  That memorization comes from a drive to perfect the game and push through to the end that leads to you eventually become a master of the game.  Just like its predecessor, Super Ghouls and Ghosts.  (Important note:  No, I haven't mastered yet.  By god, I will though, just to spite this game!)
And yes, the loud swearing still happens with Volgarr.  Not the controller breaking though.   I mean, I'm an old man now; I'm above throwing and breaking controllers.  Not from any kind of evolved self-control mind you, simply because I know what it costs to replace those things!  That and the dirty looks I get from my wife when I start teaching our kid colorful ways to insult my PC.

This game is just on the cusp of being 10/10.
The controls are tight, the combat incredibly satisfying, the human bosses are balanced incredibly well and all have their own unique feel, and the story of the jailers, the Stranger, and the spooky bunny man is wonderfully intriguing.
Warning, spoilers ahead:
Then you beat the game, the credits roll, and you walk around a bit and find the secret final boss. And boy lemme tell you, this boss is garbage on all accounts other than the music.
At this point, the mystery of the Stranger is revealed: You're Rider, some random clone of an alien AI's clone army, sent down to the planet to determine if it was suitible for assimilation. You're immortal because you're an alien, I guess? And everything you get near dies and decays because uh, I guess that's you assimilating it or something?
Half the draw of the game's story was how mysterious it was. Why was the Stranger immortal, why is he here on maybe-Earth, why does the ground around him crumble away? It was all great to wonder about, but it never -needed- to be answered. The focus was always on the Stranger just wanting to be free, coupled with the dark implications of what would happen to the world if he was. The only reason these plot points existed was to act as a justification for him to be imprisoned. We didn't need to know -why- he was immortal, or -why- he fell from the sky one day, we just needed to know that it'd be -very bad- for the planet if he was allowed to walk around as he pleased, but that he was willing to do whatever he had to to be free. This last 10th of the game pulls a complete and total 180­° on these themes and just turns it into generic "Robot gets emotions then rebels against his masters" schlock, and it totally destroys the atmosphere the game had going for it the entire time.
Also the fight itself is just bad. The entire rest of the game was one-on-one melee fights where you had a gun for dealing chip damage as you dodged attacks, but the focus was always the melee combat (Some bosses did shoot at you quite a bit, but your own controls remained the same in said fights and your goal was always still to get up and smack them around). Then this boss just completely takes that away and turns it into a generic bullet hell with clunky controls (doesn't even matter whether you're on M/KB or gamepad, they're♥♥♥♥♥♥either way). It even gets rid of the one-on-one aspect for 4/5ths of the fight by giving the boss a set of drones who all have their own attacks and seperate health bars. To top it off, your power attack, a giant laser beam, which you -have- to use at certain points as the boss's bullets cancel out your own, has so much bloom that you're completely unable to see the bullets it's overlapping, so expect plenty of cheap hits because you literally couldn't see them coming.
My recommendation: Play the game up to the credits,♥♥♥♥♥♥around in the final area until you find Bunnyman, then close the game without ever going to the tower. Then, imagine to yourself that the game had a choice point where the Stranger either walks off into the distance, the ground decaying as he does, or he decides to go back up into the Jail because he decides for himself to stay there, free but making the sacrifice of not expressing that freedom so that the world can be safe. If you do that, then the game's 10/10.

I am not sure what I could add or take away from some of the reviews here. This War of Mine is a survival-themed strategy game where the player controls a group of civilian survivors in a makeshift shelter in the besieged, war-torn fictional city of Pogoren, Graznavia. The main goal of the game is to survive the war with the tools and materials the player can gather with the characters they control. Most of the characters under the player's control have no military background or any kind of survival experience, and will require constant intervention by the player to stay alive. That simple. It had different effects on the entire family when we tried it.
PROS
•	A: if you love survival games and teaching your kids the reality of war in a game without blood and gore. Then War of Mine may just be a great try to you
•	B: It can be very addicting and has a day to day satisfaction in accomplishing tasks development.
•	C: Clear, clean and straight forward. There is a total of 12 playable character that can be played.
•	D: This game has been out three years, so not much to add except my family’s response. It is dark and musty in its presentation that fits its theme.
•	E: Daughter, loved it to a point. She enjoyed the stories. Son, enjoyed the strategic day to day tactics. The game has meaning which many games do not. It does not insult your intelligence and children can learn some lessons in its gameplay. Realism does not mean disgusting gameplay.
CONS
•	Though the lack of save at any time hurts, especially when a bad tactic can lead to death can frustrate many. Especially the young, since my daughter was upset that she had to stop only the morning of a day.
•	My son’s biggest issue was too much mouse control during confrontations that hurt actual tactic times. The lack of Controller support hurts the speed of switching between tactics. That may frustrate players. Mouse is fine, but clunky in maneuvering in player tactics.
•	My wife and I felt too much repetition and not enough tactical or gameplay choices. The Upgrade unit system does force you to plan specifically and just drags out the day to day gameplay of War of mine.
•	Lack of Backpack upgrading can frustrate even the best planned raids. Game should not count defensive or offensive weaponry or equipment. They should have been more literal in this translation. For example, Helmet or Vest if you’re wearing it should not take up a pack slot or gun and ammunition. We understood a shovel or other units taking up space. The bad allocation design of storage can frustrate players unnecessarily. Pick one, be realistic or not. Their choice a con.
•	The game does not go beyond the initial game template. This game also is hurt by the flat development of its presentation. Better graphics, engine and presentations. For example, first person view or effects hurt its overall gameplay. It lacked depth.
OVERALL: War of mine is not going to change the world in gaming. It has some great plusses and minuses and will keep you occupied, but in the end, you’re not sure why you bothered. Surviving cannot just be the result of all the work you do in a game. I give it a positive review because for the most part all of us enjoyed the overall presentation of a game that tried something different. We rewarded the passion of the developers here. I would preview the game in VIDEO in the discussion section A nice game to try on sale. It does have an expansion, but does not offer much more than a different story perspective from survivors. The game is easy to execute and play and there are online wonderful tutorials to help. My advice to the developers is go beyond the initial idea. Adding more choices and better tactics to a survival game will enhance gameplay and give players reasons to come back.
My final score: 2.5 out of 5. Despite the three years being out, a good first attempt.

Know what you're getting.  This is not a fully fleshed out RTS, by any stretch.  It's not exactly a building game, either.  It's essentially a management game.  And it can be a fun and challenging one, if you approach it from that angle.  Here's what I've learned:
Anything you build can be un-built without penalty, infinitely, all it takes is time and man- (or bot-) power.  So for instance, your colonists can sleep in beds made from the machines they were working on a few minutes ago.  Later, you may want to deconstruct large sections of your base and rebuild it elsewhere.  Don't let the relatively low number of upgrade options fool you, base design is a major aspect of the game and the possibilities are endless.
You cannot directly control units.  Get over it. It's a management game, but not micro-management.  Pay attention, learn how the AI prioritizes tasks, and your colony will succeed.  Colonists basically only do their jobs during their "spare" time.  So if there's something to be moved or built, they will do that first.  Stop giving them things to do!  That's what bots are for.
Look at the game for what it is and I think it's an enjoyable one.

This is a masterwork of interactive fiction. It took me about fifteen hours to beat it, with only a handful of hints. (mostly because I'd missed a piece of description somewhere, and didn't feel like wandering around examining *everything* again.) There were only one or two 'ye can not get ye flask' moments; the nuances of how the players attention was directed was, for the most part, very well done.
The 'repeat anything' mechanic is, frankly, amazing, and the sort of feature an entire IF parser could be built around. The world is exceedingly well-realized, and the puzzles are brilliantly designed.
All in all, this was a unique and interesting experience, that I'll look back on fondly... as a puzzle game.
My biggest problem with this is, in fact, the 'fiction' part of 'interactive fiction'. The story was... eeeeehhhh. I dunno. Maybe I'm weird for wanting something like 'closure' and/or 'denouement' in my narratives, or thinking that trying to tell a story through dribs and drabs of half-connected hints is a bit frustrating for the reader. Suffice to say, this story felt more than a little pointless, and rather was a rather large let-down for me upon reaching the end. Maybe I wouldn't have been so dissapointed if the rest of the game hadn't been so great...? I dunno.
If you like puzzles, (and since that's most of the game, I do recommend it for that,) play this for sure. If you like fuzzy 'bring-your-own-interpretation' litfic, you might even enjoy the story. But if you're expecting a narrative that's as concretely tangible as the atmosphere, execution, and puzzles... you may find yourself dissapointed.

If you like puzzle-driven Interactive Fiction and a magic system that clearly has internal logic which you learn as you play, you will love this game.
There is mystery, you will learn, and you will definitely solve many tough puzzles.
One of the greatest UI features is that if you already know how to solve a puzzle and have to repeat it, which will come up, the game remembers the solution you last used and will do all the steps for you if you say what you want to do. A simple example: there is a locked door to the east and you dropped the key in another room. You say "go east". The game navigates you to the room where you dropped the key, picks up the key, navigates you back to your current room, unlocks the door, opens the door, and goes through the door. But only if the game knows your character knows all the steps required.
[Hours on record do not reflect complete playthrough when I bought the game directly; purchased on Steam too because the original price was so low and I thought the developer deserved more.]

One word of warning if you're considering buying this for the Sealed Deck mode - don't.
To get the negative stuff out of the way first, the sealed deck mode is a cheeky attempt by the developers to eat your wallet - you only get two deck slots in which to build decks and take them through a campaign, and while building decks and unlocking boosters is INCREDIBLY fun, if you get an awful deck to start with, you're pretty much never going to win.
And you can't delete decks, so you're stuck or you have to buy a new deck slot. It's a paltry sum of £1.59, but you should at least be able to delete the decks you've already made, rather than being strong-armed into spending more money.
Sealed Mode's cons aside, this is a great game. It helped to ease me into Magic as a hobby, and allows me to play the game in spite of having no human opponents to play against. The AI is admittedly unrealisticly lucky, but that often adds to the challenge. Add to that the replay value of unlocking more cards, the expansion and deck DLCs (I haven't bought any new decks yet, but the expansion is absolutely worth it - it's a shorter campaign, to be sure, but a very fun one!) and you have a great experience with a LOT of replay value.
Pity about Sealed mode, though.

Furi is cyberpunk Shadow of the Colossus.
In fact, a good chunk of Furi's aspects are shared with SotC. Slow and steady walk times taking in scenery between bosses, intimidating openings for each boss, specific movesets and patterns analyzed and weaknesses exploited(sometimes environmental).
This is the end of the similarities.
Furi is it's own game, combining a well fleshed out bullet hell system and a swordplay duel aspect that is never dull. Certain bosses you fight entirely in bullet hell(The Star), and others are entirely in a duel(The Edge). Each boss is entirely unique, with very little to no overlapping similarities between them. Every single boss serves as both challenge and plot development, a masterful storytelling that completely melds gameplay and narration, similar to Dark Souls' form of plot description.
Of course, no game is without some vice. Some of the bosses(The Burst, The Line) have excessively hard mechanics and an extremely steep curve in difficulty compared to their predecessors. The learning curve is more like a graph of stocks than a steady increase. Some mechanics are just a bit too intense for some of the easier bosses(final phase of The Scale) and come out of nowhere. Inconsistency is Furi's greatest problem.
Otherwise, this game has a stellar soundtrack, great visuals, utterly unique gameplay, and a decent plot. One of the best games of 2016, and it still holds up today.

The game teases a lot of events going on in the outside world, but instead of utilizing its decent world-building it flips into a story about mourning your deceased lesbian ex-lover halfway through... Yeah.
You could excuse this odd direction of the story by saying that the game is all about the character interactions and not about a grand plot; After all, its a bartender-simulator, not a JRPG. It may be a matter of taste, but I was getting tired of memes and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes towards the end.
The game's ending also disappoints and leaves a lot of plot-points unresolved, ending on a sudden, unsatisfying note. Its possible that the other endings provide a more satisfying ending, but I highly doubt it and at this point I won't bother playing through it a second time.
Its not a terrible game, I got some genuine enjoyment out of it, but with the jarring second half of the game I can't help but slightly regret my purchase. At best I'd wait for a discount. Watched a guy starve to death with food in his hands in the hallway, followed by another habitant picking up his meal and walking off to the canteen with it. - 10/10.
Make no mistake, Planetbase is BRUTAL. This game will make you watch each of your habitants slowly starve/suffocate/burn to death because of a mistake YOU made 12-24 hours ago.
Didn't build enough Solar or Wind generators the day before? - You didn't really LIKE Jimmy, right?
Not enough Biologists to cultivate your crops? - I hope the 10% you eventually lose are in non-vital roles.
For those complaining about Planetbase being too "simple" or "not complicated enough for $20", I'm of the opinion that the is right in the sweet spot of Base/Survival Management - Simple enough to learn the basics quickly, but also not so complex that its entirely your fault when you fail.
I have 20+ hours in the game, and my current (7th) colony has about 120 Habitants and 25 Robots...after 120+ Days. (THE PREVIOUS COLONIES ALL DIED) - (HOW IS THERE AN ACHIEVEMENT IN THIS GAME TO REACH 250 HABITANTS IN 60 DAYS).
This game is not for those who want to be rewarded constantly for their efforts and told how great a player they are. It's for players who want a hardcore survival simulator, have the game slap them in the face for their mistakes, and ask for another.
All that being said, here's a few tips for new players:
1. Get used to your colonists dying. It's going to happen. A LOT. I once had a meteor land right on the landing ship as soon as I started, killing 3 of them. It's not an issue with AI, it's an issue with YOU thinking you can save all of them. Hostile groups infiltrating your base are almost guaranteed to kill at least 1 colonist per intruder.
2. Get your resource generation going ASAP. The key is becoming self-sufficient as soon as possible, and never taking your eye off the amount you produce/consume in each category. The game is a constant balancing act. If you build too many structures, you won't have enough colonists to maintain/work each item, and will produce less overall, if anything.
3. TURN OFF THE COLONIST LANDING PERMISSION FROM TIME TO TIME. I cannot stress this enough. The game will keep adding colonists to your colony before you are truly ready for them. It's not a bug, it's a feature. YOU are in charge of the base, and the game will CONSTANTLY challenge you on this.
4. Never get comfortable. The day you lower your guard is the night the wind doesn't blow hard enough, your colony runs out of power before morning, and people are starving to death in the hallways.
5. Build a good number of airlocks throughout your base. Airlocks only allow one person/robot to pass through at a time, and colonists will line up as they need to go outside (This happens a lot when trade ships land, as your colonists will HAND DELIVER cargo to the ship from your storage). You need additional airlocks near the landing/trade pads to accomodate this traffic, and airlocks in general throughout the base to efficiently reach repair sites, mines, etc. I suspect complaints about pathing are due to this.
6. BASE LAYOUT IS CRITICAL. External structures cannot efficiently intermesh with Internal structures, because of oxygen. Furthermore, learn which structures interact frequently with the others. For example, placing your Storage/Canteen/Biodome close to each other will assist in your colonists harvesting crops and staying fed. Likewise, keeping your Mines/Airlocks/Reprocessing/Factories in close proximity will assist in processing raw materials into spares, metals, and other usable materials. Failing to maintain an efficient base layout will ultimately cripple you in late game, in my opinion.
Overall, I'm thoroughly enjoying the difficulty of the game, and I'm glad there's no way around it. You either become knowledgable and overcome, or you lose. 20+ hours and I'm not even done with the first planet of three.
Lastly, allow me to make the following comparison, for those who have played the early SimCity games - When you play Planetbase, you are effectively playing a game with the complexity of the original SimCity. If Planetbase were as complex as say, SimCity 2000, no colonist would survive.
Now that you know what you're getting yourselves into. Good Luck!

This is an old-school text adventure. You type commands (GO NORTH, GET COIN, UNLOCK OAK DOOR WITH RUSTY KEY) and the game carries them out. It includes a tutorial for brand-new players. I cannot speak to the tutorial as I haven't played it; been too busy diving in.
The plot: you're an ensign on His Majesty's Marcher (an alchemical starship) The Unanswerable Retort. Something has gone horribly wrong, and it appears to be up to you to figure out how to put it right.
The prose is first-rate. "You smell copal incense, machine oil, rosemary, alcohol, and blood. Creaking, bending steel beams... no, that's not an odor. Why did you think the bulkheads were crumpling in on you? What would that even smell like?"
The puzzles make you think, in interesting ways. You start out with a basic alchemy recipe; tweaking it slightly is sufficient to get you past the first locked door, where you find a few more ingredients and recipes. So you tweak, and devise, and wrack your brain to figure out how exactly to do Thing X when all you have is a formula for Procedure Y which is sort of similar but not really, and what makes a "lunar influence" anyway? Plenty of "a-ha!" moments, where the structure falls into place.
And the plot ... oh, the plot. Or maybe plots, because what *did* go wrong on the Retort, anyway, and what's with the strange possibly-alien possibly-lifeforms that you maybe keep meeting?
Highly recommended.

I just say that I've bought this game for PC from the game developer last year, for IOS some months ago and now  for STEAM.

Hey, it's an old-school text adventure game, like from 1977! But it's also from an alternate universe where we actually spent the intervening forty years refining text adventures as a medium!
Because it turns out we kind of did. Our universe is a big place.
(Note: I actually played through this in its initial pre-Steam release, so much of this review is based on that edition. This Steam release adds a lot of the quality-of-life features that the iOS release had, and they are very welcome indeed.)
In one sense, the setup is pretty "normal" for an adventure game. You are a novice (so the player will learn as the character does) who is stranded (giving an obvious motivation and win condition) on an abandoned (no complicated social interactions to model or interfere with) magical (lots of neat ways to influence the world) environment.
In the other, the magic system here is alchemy, and the ritual system is extremely rich and complex. It also turns out to be a lot more fun to actually type out RECITE CATEGORICAL IMPERATIVE and INVOKE SIMPLE SEALING WORD and such rather than just pushing a button to make it happen.
Well, once. The rituals are all neat, but once you've proven you know how to do something, the game has an extremely sophisticated AI that will allow repeating a goal, a command like PERFORM KITTEN DUPLICATOR SYNTHESIS or GO TO BRASS COIN will execute all the intermediary steps for you. This is a game where your options grow as your knowledge does, and after you, the player, have decided on a plan, you may end up uttering a command that turns into over a thousand sub-commands. That frees you up to work on the puzzles themselves.
And those puzzles are quite meaty. It took me a couple pages of notes and a week of evenings to fully solve the game, and even revisiting it a year and a half later my memory has become hazy enough that a replay hasn't been entirely trivial. That said, this edition does seem to be a bit clearer about a few bits that I remember getting stuck on last year.
There's a fair number of text games on Steam now, but there's never really been anything quite like this.
This game is hard, but fair. REALLY hard. Mostly fair.

A text adventure for real puzzle-lovers. This is a game that's all about mastering something huge and complex. Sophisticated automation of multi-step tasks helps you manage the complexity, but that just allows it to become even more complex. The alchemy here is a little reminiscent of the ritual magic in King's Quest III, but gives a stronger sense of being a system, with recipes that support substitutions.
I originally played the iOS version, but the Steam version has the same content, with a somewhat improved UI. (Finally I can keep the Alchemy Journal open in a separate window while typing in commands!)

Hadean Lands is an excellent modern text adventure / Interactive Fiction game. The puzzles are unique and satisfying, with a good level of difficulty. You'll need to combine the things you find in very interesting ways with rituals and formulas. The game's memory system, allowing you to repeat a series of commands all at once is crucial and an excellent innovation.
All together, Hadean Lands is what IF should be -- the experience of both reading a book and adventuring inside it at the same time.
I played Hadean Lands previously outside of steam. The new packaged verison includes a Game menu that has a built-in map, list of your formulas + rituals, and the IF Reference card, all of which are very useful for new and old players alike!

character cards that grant heal on all of your monster cards at the end of each battle.
Defense is handled differently too where in cards must be placed in the front row but you can't just opt
for that placement initially meaning other actions have to allow that opportunity or the card has a specifc instruction
to be placed in the front line upon entry.

The phenominally small $1 asking price is fair enough but if you're swamped in card/board games already

Game: Toki Tori
Genre: Puzzle
Developer: Two Tribes
System: Steam (PC)
Total Score: 76/100
Value Score: 7.6/10
• Story: 3/10
o Toki Tori's storyline involves a little chick by the name of Toki Tori who must rescue his brothers and sisters after they were swept away to a dark castle. After he hatches from his eggshell he goes on a journey to save them.
• Characters: 7/10
o You have Toki Tori who pretty much has a nice personality for a character of a game that doesnt seem like it has much, his cute and hilarious appearances and actions will put you in high spirits even in times of frustration when trying to solve the puzzles in the game. Along with that you have the enemies in the game which vary depending on the stages and offers a variety which has no clones at all which is nice.
• GamePlay: 10/10
o Toki Tori's gameplay involves mainly in a puzzle genre with some platforming abilities such as jumping and moving around in a 2D stage. You will get access to all sorts of abilities and items which can do anything ranging from teleporting, freezing enemies, providing you cover or a path to a certain area which you couldnt do before. There are also different obstacles and enemies which will be in your way which you can pass through using various methods. Your goal in the game is to collect all of the eggs in the level. By collecting all the eggs completely you will go to the next stage within the level which offers a whole different layout with new obstacles and enemy placement. You will be limited to certain items with certain amounts as well. There will be times when you make a mistake and you can undo this by rewinding or even forwarding if you undo a rewind - this is very useful as you will tend to make more mistakes as you progress through the game as the puzzles and layouts get more complex.
• Graphics: 8/10
o The visuals have improved quite well from the GBC version of the game, the game is in HD and the animations are quite nicely done. The environment and levels are well designed as well. Visuals are spot on in terms of quality however there will be times where you might see a glitch but the chances of that happening are pretty slim. Although the visuals are nicely done the backgrounds however could of had more work on it - the obstacles and the objects which you interact with were the ones which were mostly focused on.
• Sound: 8/10
o Toki Tori's sound effects go well with all the events in the game from walking, jumping and attacking a enemy. The sound effects are nicely done although there can be at times when the game may and can be seem to be too quiet.
• Music: 7/10
o The music is quite well done in Toki Tori, each set of stages have their own theme music, you have the main theme song and the credits. Although its OST isnt as huge as other games - it has a pretty decent variation of different types of songs.
• Length: 5/10
o Toki Tori's main fault is possibly its length, the main storyline will take you no more than 3 hours if you know exactly what you are doing, there will be at some points where you may get stuck and may take you some time in the game however if you are looking for a long term experience - it might not be the best option for you unless you do the extra stages and re-do the main storyline in the harder difficulty.
• Replay Value: 10/10
o The game includes a whole new difficulty setting for the main storyline along with some new additional custom stages and a campaign which spins off from Portal 2. The bonus levels and the extra difficulty makes up for the replay department for Toki Tori and is heavily recommended.
• Player Value: 8/10
o Toki Tori is a short and sweet game for those who love puzzles and a bright colored atmospheric game. The game's puzzles will leave you thinking on how to progress and the colorful themes in the design and music will keep you on your way as you try to solve through the puzzles in the game. The game comes with about 4 worlds with a set number of stages and the PC version includes additional bonus levels and a rewind/forward button feature which allows you to undo mistakes.

This is a genuinely fun, no-frills attached arena shooter. It knows what it wants to do, and it does it well, and it does it for -free-. Now usually, free to play is a dirty phrase that attracts all sorts of skepticism: microtransactions, DLC, hats, pay to win, etc... This game doesn't do any of that. The paywall only excludes character customization (again, no hats or DLC, just stuff you unlock through XP from playing) and access to hosting your own games. Otherwise, you pretty much get the whole of it.
PROS:
+ Free
+ No BS FPS action reminiscent of the early Quake arena shooters, complete with lots of jumping and hauling tons of weapons
+Solid graphics and a fun cyberpunk'esque soundtrack, like a legit soundtrack that plays ingame- I cannot think of the last time I had that in an online competitive shooter
+Weapons and controls suit a wide variety of playstyles
+ If you want to 'upgrade' to the complete game, it's 15$. 15. No incremental payments, no dlcs, just one time payment of 15$ to support the devs. The game's already finished, and there's no dancing around any hidden shekelmancy. I'd say it was easily worth the 15, but....
CONS:
-Nobody friggin plays the game. Seriously. That is the only real issue to an otherwise well rounded, fun title. I've played with more bots then I have people, and that's just depressing.
Final thoughts:
If you're getting sick of Overwatch's BS and you just want to blow some people up, this is a wonderful alternative. You're probably just gonna want to get a couple friends on board first, and being F2P, that (hopefully) shouldn't be an issue.
In a day and age where Steam is bloated with tons of indie titles that are just asset flipping scams, half baked kickstarters and unabashed Minecraft clones, this is a pure little gem that just wants to give you the blistering action that was PC online gaming before it all became about chest high walls and waiting for the red jam to get off your screen.
It's F2P and I absolutely reccomend it for that price. I'd even reccomend just paying the 15$ for the full, where it not for the game's sparce population.
Overall a great game especially if you can get it when its having a discount.

TOXIKK was a great game.  It had that classic FPS fast paced action, excellent weapon variety, good maps, relatively intelligent AI, and a decent multiplayer.  Only one problem:  when you read the above statement that, "The Free Edition of TOXIKK is more than a demo: It features the core experience, has no competitive disadvantages versus the Full Game, and lets you play TOXIKK for as long and often as you like.", they lied about the "as often as you like" part.  Immediately after I passed 3 hours combined solo bot play and multiplayer, and once I had logged out, the next time I tried to play everything was paywalled off.  Initially I was perplexed and thought my gamefile must be corrupted, but after I reinstalled the problem was still there.
This is disappointing because I was intitially pleased with their paywall system.  Full access to all weapons, two great maps (both on multiplayer and in solo play), and the only thing taken out was character customization.
Before anyone accuses me of trying to free ride, I had no qualms about buying the game.  I was hyped to buy, but I wanted to get a good amount of play in before I paid, since they offer the free, UNLIMITED Demo.  3 hours, however, isn't enough for me.  You can tell I'm not exactly the pre-order type of guy.
In conclusion, this is a great game, and I still recommend the full version, but I am very disappointed with the demo.  I would have been fine if it had been advertised as a 3 hour demo, but lying about an UNLIMITED demo is skeezy and dishonest.
P.S.
Dear REAKKTOR Studios,
Please come clean in the future about your demos.  This game is technically proficient, the gameplay is enjoyable and envokes memories of old FPSs, and the mods are especially fun.  But lying isn't, so please be honest.

Obviously poor performance is not a good start (and
while playing it).
Sadly, that's not my biggest gripe with this game. It may be confusing that anyone could complain after 13+ hours of playing, but this game is such a grind. Not in the tradition sense of the word where you're doing mindless work to improve your character, but rather it's a grind of 2D line puzzles.
70% of the puzzles in this game could be placed in a flash game and they would play the same. Being in a 3D world surrounded by potentially interesting things is pointless if you're fixated on a 8x8 square screen! The times when the game forced you to take in your surrounds to solve the puzzles were amazing, but that stopped happening towards the end game.
Unlike other FPS puzzle games (Portal 2, Talos Principle, Quantum Conundrum, Q.U.B.E.) this game has no real story. The world is completely lifeless, and there's no in-game soundtrack. I played the game honestly for the first 8+ hours, not looking up solutions online, but holy crap... this game wouldn't end.
After the 8 hour mark I stopped having fun. I didn't care because the game hadn't presented me with any reason to care (other than the fact that I paid good money for it).
Getting to the final section I was presented with a door which had a randomly generated puzzle.
That's fine, I knew the rules of the game by then, but the puzzles had to be solved in a short amount of time or they would be reset. That's just cruel and obnoxious. This game was hostile towards fun and appeared to be doing everything it could to not be played.
Maybe I'm bad at puzzle games (I doubt it, since I have played others and loved them) or maybe this is for the "true puzzle fans" out there searching for a hard core challenge.
If that's you I hope you enjoy this. I was able to for a while, but in the end, the fun was lost before the game was over.
But the ending left me sour and I will gladly be uninstalling this never to play it again.

For an old game from my youth, this has definitely brought back good memories.
Pro's:
+ The combat is still a fun, turn-based strategy fight.
+ The economy is well put together.
+ The newspapers from the loading screen are cheeky quips about history.
+ There is a combat simulator, that allows you to test out the battlefield mechanics!
Con's:
- Unit management has come a long way, and sadly it can be a chore to move units between generals and colony inventories.
- There isn't a way to put a unit to sleep, which can make it hard to manage which ones you still want "exploring"
- Late-Game, it takes a little effort to manage excessive trades in each city to keep the resource stock-pile managable
- All players turns are resolved at the same time, which can make chasing enemy units tedious.
- There isn't an easy way to switch between towns, and on larger maps can make it a chore to check the production of each town you control.
Tips:
* The War College, keep money flowing into that to keep your troops combat capable.
* If you're producting too much, build as many docks as possible to increase the number of trades a town can contract.
* If you're done with the level 1 explorer or ship, just disband it.  By the time you've explored the map, you can either make Level 4 units or don't require their assistance.
* Naval combat is strong, if you're going to send an invasion fleet, split the units up into 2-4 ships to ensure greater success when attacking another island.
Yes, its a 20 year old game.  But I would highly recommend it, its simple and complex in all the right ways.
