It's an old game (1996) with poor graphics but great gameplay. You establish and manage colonies, there's a good combat minigame, and a huge amount of depth.
You start with explorers and a small army to explorer the new world. A few turns later your colonist arrives and you find a place for a colony. You gradually develop it and later start other colonies.
Your mothercountry asks for increasing amounts of tax over time, so you will eventually want to declare independence and fight off it's armies.
You can fight other European settlers or the natives for land to start other colonies. You can also trade with them instead. Interestingly, you can play as a native tribe and try to federate other native settlements.
I love it as you can set the number of turns to be unlimited and just play as an open-ended sandbox game. It has good replayability as it has a random map generator. Also, each country has individual bonuses and you can also pick skills too.
Eg I am currently playing as Holland who earn interest on their gold (I cannot remember their other bonuses) and one of the skills I picked was the "missionary" skill, so my relationship with nearby natives increases over time. (They wiped out the first army to find them but are now friendly).
The PDF manual is included in the "Local files" for the game, and shows the countries' bonuses. The in-game explanation of these bonuses is non-existent as this game was released back in the era when gamers read manuals. There's also a detailed guide online by "SMcInerney" which is easy to google and worth a read.
The two main game features are:
1) Colony development.
A bit like the Anno series. You place buildings down, you accumulate resources, upgrade the colony and it's buildings from levels 1 to 4.
There's a large element of micromanagement as you plan what resources you will need. However,  there are only 5 resources so it's not too bad. (wood, metal, food, goods and gold). You generally harvest the first 3, make the 4th, and earn the 5th by trading.
Each colony can be totally self-sufficient but you'll generally want to specialise them a bit to take advantage of nearby terrain bonuses.
Terrain gives bonuses to the production of buildings within colonies, and you can specialise colonies for more bonuses (to food, wood or metal). You can trade resources between colonies but you don't need to load it onto a ship like Colonisation. You just create the trade, and they arrive a turn or more turns later.
A colony's population is a number, eg 100. It grows by a fixed % each turn and you can build churches to attract more. Buildings have labour requirements, and units have a pop cost too.
It's very satisfying to gradually grow your colonies. You won't have many so you won't drown in micromanagement hell. Eg in my current game I have just 2, and I'll eventually declare independence with just these once they're fully developed. Then I'll see whether to continue to expand/fight or restart as another country.
2) Combat
Once you build a fort in cities, you can recruit armies. These cost population and resources. Upgrading your colonies allows better armies (they have more hitpoints),
Armies are led by leaders, who gain experience over time. This is spent on allowing them to control more units, increases the number of units who can attack each turn, movement speed, etc.
The combat minigame is really well thought out. This is unique as combat in other turn-based games gets too tedious with large armies, or too simplified where you give high-level orders and watch cinematics.
You make meaningful choices about positioning and movement, as you get strong flanking bonuses and can also win by reaching the enemy flag. You also make meaningful choices about which units to attack with, as you have a limited number of attacks per turn (based on the army leader's abilities). Even with large armies, the constraints of the minigame mean that combat is never overwhelming.
Combat occurs when armies attack each other but you also get natives raiding your colonies.
Other features:
- research = spend gold to get various bonuses
- map has "nodes" that give bonuses to buildings within a certain radius, IF you control it. So there's a reason to station armies around your colonies, not just within it.
- maintenance of armies: number of units is capped, based on number of forts and their level of upgrade. These buildings take up space and labour in your colonies so there's a trade-off between large armies and your economy.
- you get militia units when defending your colonies but each hit they take will reduce your population
Technical note:
This is the Deluxe Edition, which is has the patches on the original game up to v1.12. So don't think it's version 1.0 with no patches.
In case you're wondering whether an old game like this would work on modern PCs, don't worry. This release on steam works fine. No crashes or bugs.
Alt-tabbing causes issues, as the resolution of the screen switches back to your normal resolution, which means instead of being full-screen, the game now only takes up a fraction of it (eg 10-20%). You can press alt-enter to make it full screen again (thanks Jack).

This is a quick but not dirty game.
To get the bad things out of the way first, there is not a crazy amount of story, and there are a few graphical issues during cutscenes and other parts of the game. I don't wish to undermine the art-style here, however, because that bit is very nice. I feel like the devs focused as much effort as they could into the gameplay and its mechanics, and understood that these other elements were of low priority. I agree with this notion.
This game is literally boss-fights paired with walking to the next boss-fight. In addition, there are no powerups, no level system, and no equipment; there is only health and the abilities available at the start of the game. This makes progression completely based on the player, and their ability to play this game, which each boss does an excellent job of forcing out of the player.
Probably a minority opinion here, but I heavily appreciated the parts where you just walked to the next fight. It was a couple of minutes of just scenery, but it gave me the break I needed between fights. There is an auto-walk button, which was a life-saver.
Difficulty was perfect as well. It was right inbetween auto-piloting and rage-inducing, and constantly pushed for improvement. Moderately experienced gamers will have a blast, as long as you use a controller.

Sombre, Depressing, Engrossing.
Few games capture what it might be like to survive in a warzone. Many similar games fall into the trap of zombie apocalypse at the expense of exploring the human drive to simply survive. Thankfully this device has been eschewed making it a unique and more poignant experience.
Artfully bleak and depressing; this game presents a unique blend of character personality, crafting mechanics and intuitive controls. With a story told via radio and a cast of characters you control, and in the warzone itself. Each day is a battle, each victory hollow and each play through, addicting.
Overall Score: 4.25/5

Wow.
The mood and atmosphere of this game simply is quite overwhelming.
Set in the fictional location of Pogoren, Graznavia, a group of survivors are trying to live through the rage and damage war can cause, battling hunger, illness, and bandits in order to pull through. In order to gain resources they must scavenge many locations or trade with the occasional traveling trader.
This is arguably the most grim and bleek game I have ever played. Instead of living the "glory" of war being on the frontline going 10 and 1 for kills, this game has a riveting change of perspective. Living as survivors, dealing with wounds, having to build improvements to shelter, among many other things make this game truly haunting.
The atmosphere, sound design, and graphic design make this game just plain depressing. Dark colors, the sounds of war in the background, and very somber music play almost all the time. Also this game may test your humanity as there are some rather appalling decisions that must be made in certain parts of the game that can affect the survivor's morale.
The characterization isn't super heavy, but you truly get the sense that these are just people. Sad, worried and scared they may not see the next morning, whatever they are thinking you will see very well.
The point-and-click gameplay may sound a little lacking, but the scavenging mechanic is pretty interesting, and it truly feels like a stealthy-type game having to avoid threats and potential killers.
Overall, this is a truly difficult and riveting game to play. It feels like the end is near after supplies start to dwindle and medication is lacking, and at that point you feel like giving up. I have to force myself to finish a game before restarting in order to get full effect and practice of this game. Nonetheless, I would recommend giving this game a try so long as you are willing to get a feeling of unease when playing it.

Volgarr the Viking is fun to play, and it controls pretty well.
But just like Jörmungandr can grasp his own tail in an endless loop, so too will you be trying to make progress in this game.
I believe our modern gaming age is trying to capitalize on what they like to call "NES Hard".  In other words, a lot of people crushed their skulls in some sort of mechanical accident, and seem to remember every single classic game as being brutally difficult.  I know for a fact, being 34 years old, that not every game was this way.  There were quite a few games that offered health, lives, powerups, passwords, and continues to help you progress.  Even when you barely made it through a tough boss fight, you still felt like you were progressing.
Volgarr the Viking is a well made game that doesn't capitalize on being cheap.  All the enemies are static for the most part, so you can learn the patterns after a while.  If you keep messing up, it's your fault.  Just change the way you look at things, and you will progress.  There are powerups to give you shields, an extra piece of armor, or even a flaming sword.  You just have to get powerups(chests) consecutively to get the full set.  First pickup is always a shield, unless you already have one.  So if you lose your shield, your next powerup will be another shield to replace it.  If you still have a shield when you get the next powerup, you get a better one, and a better spear.  Keep that pattern going of not getting hit(easier said than done), and you get better and better stuff.  Without this gear, you are literally one hit, one kill.  Pretty flimsy for a Viking badass.  :D

As a beginner Magic player and long time table top gamer, this game immediately grabbed my attention. While I wasn't too big into Magic before playing this game; the game did however make it easier for me to understand Magic much better than I did before. However, the actual game itself suffers from a short campaign and a shorter sealed campaign; as well as a low number of opponents to play against in custom play.
First the good stuff, while the campaign is too short for a seasoned magic player; a beginner should find the campaign as a 4 hour tutorial on the basics of the game. The sealed campaign is also a good way for beginners to apply what they've learned to create a deck with a strategy all their own.
But unfortunately the main game only uses cards from the 2014 Core set and there is a limit in the sealed campaign that keeps you from creating more decks. You could buy those slots, but it's more beneficial to just get into the actual trading card game.
The experience is enjoyable, but too pricey. I recommend picking this game up if you’re a beginner or a seasoned player with very few people to play with. I also recommend picking this game up when it’s on sale.

Granted it's an improvement from not having it at all, but as much as I'd love sealed deck play, I don't play it because it's just not what it should be compared to the decks pre-built. Now to the bugs - the game freezes mid game as if you're waiting on someone to make a choice, but it never will go through, until everyone leaves and restarts the match. That happens about 40% of the time. The other times you aren't able to play instant cards when you try to. These bugs not only happen to me, but my friends that I play with as well. 2013 was put together much better IMO. Also, 2013 seemed to be on a more level playing field. All in all, I would say don't waste your money. I keep going back to 2013. This game needs fixing badly.

Turns out that they give you two slots to build a deck from randomized card draws, and once you have drawn all your cards, that's it: the slot is locked. Here's the catch: It's a money grab, because they charge $1.99 for every extra slot, and they know they can do this because they lock those slots down and don't let you reset them.
That's fine for multiplayer, but there should be a single-player option where you can reset your Sealed Deck. As it is, you play through the Sealed Campaign twice and you're done. Then it's back to using pre-fab decks that come with the game. Avoid this one if you are looking to customize your own deck.

Planetbase is pretty much Banished in space.  While I agree that the AI needs a bit of work, the game is still playable and fun in my opinion.  Having put almost forty hours into it, I think thats a fair conclusion to make, but the game is not without its flaws which I will list in addition to the positives as well:
+ Good graphics design which runs pretty smoothly.
+ Intuitive controls and a nice tutorial for everything that isn't.
+ Seems to be a good balance of difficulty and fun (at least for me).
+ Plenty to micromanage but without being overwhelmed
+ A small bit of progression as it takes milestones to unlock the other two planets which adds a sense of achievement and a reason to do well.
- AI needs some work, because if just one of their needs isn't met, they refuse to work which is annoying.
- Prioritization needs to be improved/implemented, as many of my workers will distribute materials in an order that I wish I could control and rearrange when needed.
- Power always seems to be an issue and I wish power storage units would drain just a bit slower
- The morale system just flat out needs to be removed in my opinion, as they start getting depressed for stupid reasons such as overpopulation despite an abundance of resources and living space.
- Lastly, the guards should be better at fighting intruders.  My base gets raided regularly and it annoys me that for every intruder that enters the base, just as many guards are going to die and will have to be replaced.  Not to mention that people get depressed when the guards die so everyone always has some stupid reason to be sad, which again is why that whole morale system needs to be done away with.
Overall the game is good in my honest opinion despite the work it needs.  I wouldn't have put so many hours into so far if I thought otherwise, but if you haven't purchased this yet and are still skeptical then wait for a sale.  If the issues that I listed get addressed and fixed, then this will get two thumbs up from me.

Game concept is rather fun, and seemingly challenging. But not the kind of challenge you can win thus far, it's the kind of challange that tests your mind and willingness to stay calm whilst watching every attempt you make at holding down a stable ecosystem fail and ultimately lead to seeing every single one of your collonists die off.
I have many things to point out about this game which I will list to you potential buyers;
1.) At the start you have to sit through at least 20 seconds of watching your ship land and crew get out. No way of skipping this and it happens every time you start a new world (which is a lot.) Get's rather annoying.
2.) You start off with enough resources to build the innitial 4-5 building you need as the bare minimum to have your AI survive, after this you must recycle the craft your people arrived in which allows you to then build the other 3-4 buildings you then need to keep the food/ resource supply stable for the 7 people you start with. Why I am mentioning this is because it doesn't allow you to build the base how you want. There is a line set that you have to follow and if you don't, your AI will either die or run out of resources to do anything which gets rather dull.
3.) Now, you have come from Earth and yet you only get 2 sources of power, Solar or Wind. Now, Mars has never known for it's lovely breezes and at night there is no sun. This gets rather frustrating if there is no wind at night, the sun is down and your base drains the power storage to 0. All your buildings lose power, and your AI all die because the oxygen gen has no power. So right there you have to start again, this time you put more time and resources into more power supply for the night. But that means you have less for food, or other important supplies so you fail again and your AI die because you din't feed them well enough or something stupid.
4.) Bunks. I just played a game where all my engineers decided to go to bed at the same time... Then an astroid hit the bunk room and killed them all. This means nothing else can be built or repaired. I watched as my other AI stood around and eventually died from lack of sleep as no one had the skills to repair the bunk room. So I had to start a new world, again. Also, people will sleep whenever. If they get tired half way into the day because they carried some leaves from the bio dome to the vending machine, they will go sleep and their job that they are supposed to do doesn't get done.
5.) Your base is made from Potatoes. No really! Starch from potatoes. Plastic from starch. Base from plastic. What the F**L!?
6.) Colonists arrive in ships from Earth (I'm guessing)... Yet they bring no supplies to help your base. Bit selfish if you ask me.
7.) Trade ships offer you♥♥♥♥♥♥in return for diamonds. You think trade will save you? You better be willing to part with everything you have in payment.
8.) AI arrive at refinery machine... 5 minutes later decide they earned some sleep. Metal/ Plastic doesn't get made until next day.
9.) Everyone seems to break their bones all the time, and medicine repairs the broken bones. Medicine devized from leaves you grow in your biodome... on mars! Why are not funding this?
10.) If you don't have a control center, people will wander out into huge sandstorms. Because they cannot think for themselves that it is a bad idea. They require a yellow alarm to show them outside is wrong, inside is right. Storm very bad.
11.) Guns seem to be a factor. Though god only knows what for, since I can't even get the factory working properly before all my AI die of something or other. But I still want to know why violence is part of a seemingly peaceful mars base game?
12.) Some spawn locations on new worlds have just enough space to build 1 thing then no space to build anything else. I have had this a few times. So it's over before it begins.
Overall it seems like an Alpha game testing phase. Not a full release. Definately needs a huge AI/ UI overhaul before it is actually fun to play.

Nice little card game, learning how to play is easy with the tutorial, after that you can practice with the AI or join any game online. There is also an in-game card browser for you to learn about each card, and you can mark the cards individually as underpowered or overpowered, which will presumably give feedback to the developer to balance the cards.
The design and variety of the cards, however, are rather mediocre, but the developer seems to be committed to improve the game. There is no deck-building. You start off with 1 hero (either human, undead, elf, or orc), each comes with its own minion cards. Each turn begins by picking a number of minion cards, scroll cards, and mana points. The minion cards are mostly played to attack the enemy minion cards or enemy hero, although some are played defensively. Scroll cards are cards that have a variety of effects either on self or the enemy, eg. "+ATK" or "damage enemy". Playing both types of cards require mana points. Win the game by killing the enemy hero. Good mix of strategy to plan which cards to play and luck getting good cards to win the game.

I can look past bad art. Dream Quest's art is roughly this terrible, but I played at least a hundred hours of it, because its deck building roguelike gameplay was great. But Pick a Hero is just BAD. It's just a cheap clone of Hearthstone, or rather just the Discover mechanic. Real card drafting is fun - trying to pick the best cards from a random selection to add to your deck is tense, nerdy fun. (When's the digital version of Seven Wonders going to come out?!) But that's not what this is. Each turn you're presented with a selection of three cards to pick from to add to your hand. You have no idea what's coming next. It sounds really random because it is.
The interface is also AWFUL, especially how you have to activate a special mode to see what the text on cards mean. There are also major glitches, such as the way that all the cards disappear from the gallery if you Alt-Tab away.
Maybe buy this now if you want it as a conversation piece after Blizzard sues it off of Steam?

Good:
1. Love the mana system, compared to other tabletop card games such as MTG. There is a constant supply of mana and it is up to the player to decide if it is worth gathering. In other words, you can forgo drawing a card (you can draw two per turn) in exchange for adding one point of mana to your pool, permanently.
2. The cards appear to be well balanced and, for the most part, fun and interesting with multiple uses.
3. Game is short and sweet with just enough decision making to make it engaging. I love the fast-paced games. Most of my games last about 5 minutes.
4. The game has a built-in ratings system for player feedback. You can let the creators know if a card is over or under powered as well as if it is boring. I love the forsight put in by the developer.
5. Art work is good and fits with the style of the game. Sound effects are also complimentary.
6. The heros you have to choose from, while not numerous, have a distinct abilities that, I feel, change the game significantly. Players can level up (if you draw the card for it), further powering their starting  abilities (do more damange, spawn more powerful minions, etc.).
The bad:
1. Not a big enough user base. It is nearly impossible to find a match. Also, given the general lack of players, it is difficult to find a challenging partner.
2. While some human opponents are challenging, the CPU is most definitely not. I have never lost to the computer in overr 30 games.
Overall:
Fun game, well worth the money. However, it is waaaay too easy playing the CPU. Also, given the lack of a user base, human players are typically not very challenging either.

Ok, here I can't speak for everyone 'cos there's lots of language options for the client (you can choose from English, Italian, Turkish, French, Chinese, Greek.. ok, there's 12 languages total xD) but for what concerns Italian well, it's clearly machine-translated; even though the game of course is intuitive and doesn't need many words and menus, they're all wrong. So, if on one site it's an awesome game for learning new words and new languages in a funny and light-hearted way, in my opinion you'd better start by going in the properties of the game and choose English as the Client language, 'cos really there's not a single sentence in Italian that's written in a proper way xD
Apart from this, of course, the core of the game -are- the languages themselves and so you can start it windowed (I suggest windowed mode and low resolution, it'll run even faster and it's best enjoyed on a medium-sized window in my opinion) and you'll be pointed to the main choices of the game: on the left side you'll have to choose the language of your game (currently you can play and learn English, Russian, French, Italian and Turkish) and on the right side there's a rectangular box in which a "theme" can be chosen.
This section is a little bit twisted in my opinion, 'cos there's no text and you've got to rely only on an image: there's an image of weather conditions (so your words will be about weather), vegetables, fruits, animals, vehicles and such, but sometimes since there are only four or five elements in the rectangle the theme can be a little bit confusing. Nothing that affects in any way the game itself of course, since it's super fast and you can whenever you feel like go back to the menu and choose another theme.
You can also add some more time on the left side if you want, but it's just a small help :) Basically it makes you choose from +30 to +2 the number of additional seconds you'll get when you complete a word! Don't go for +2, trust me :P
Then, the core of the game consists of an image - and the graphics are great, very easy to understand and to detect - and scrambled words under it, everything superimposed of a minimal background. On the right upper side there's a clock - your timer - and with your mouse you'll have to re-arrange the letters in order to form the word matching the image. Of course you'll start with 3 letters and then move on with the rounds.
The game's all here, but it's great to me and it really makes you think about your English lexic knowledge and learn other languages' most common words!
For what concerns the machine-translation, it's not a big problem when it comes to the game itself: I played it for about an hour in Italian and I haven't found many mistakes, even because you're guessing single and precise word that don't need human work to be translated!
I'm quite a little bit "angry" for what concerns the game page and similar stuff, since they offer an extensive explanation if you go through a non-English Steam client but.. it's completely wrong, everything.. for sure, nothing has been checked by native speakers since errors are quite big and compromise also the comprehension of the game hub page. Verbs are completely wrong, and even to me it's quite difficult to get everything in what's supposed to be my native tongue, apart from my academical degrees in fields dealing also with the Italian languages, like history and such. So I think it's better to keep everything in English and leave the languages you want to learn for the objects in game only.
So, back to the game, what you see in the users' screenshots and in the store hub it's what you'll get - lots of simple, cartoonish images and lots of scrambled words to put together!
Before finishing my review I'd like just to add something else: the game came out (at least here on Steam) just two or three months ago and I saw some posts in the discussion page that were rightly asking to someone (zero answers so far) if the game has planned to add other languages, 'cos as I said before you get only Italian, English, French, Turkish and Russian for what concerns in-game play, but the hub store talks about 12 languages that so far are only available for the client and nothing else.
So, I don't know if more languages will be added in the future for the game itself, but if they will be they'll be added in the same manner that Italian, French and so on have been added, so it will be awesome :) The pictures are always the same ones (there's a lot of them though, so you can learn lots of words xD) and only the language changes, so if they'll add say, Spanish or Chinese in the future, the system will be the same for sure - pictures, and under them words to put in their proper way.
In the end, if you like word games and if you wanna learn or improve your knowledge of one of these five languages, this game is really recommended and I hope they'll add new languages in the future, even though to me English and French are more than enough being definitely not born for learning foreign languages ahahah :)

I find this is quite an educative game.
I expect its more geared towards younger audiences.
Its very helpful to associate a word with the corresponding picture :)
You are given a timer which extends every time you solve a word puzzle. Theres a timer configuration which can range from a beginner level(+30sec) to a chess solving expert(+2sec).
There are soooooooooo many words to unscramble, for many different themes which you can pick from. I think the difficulty rises along with the progress. At least the number of letters does.
There are many achievements as well. Many of them unlock right after you solve a puzzle. With over 300 achievements, it seems this is quite easy to unlock them after playing a number of times in a casual manner, a few minutes at a time. I already have 100 of them unlocked in this short time i played the game. :)
The achievements come with cyrilic and normal alphabetical letters and numbers, which might come in handy to show off in your personal profile :D
In a personal note however...
I did struggle with quite a lot of words. But then again, i'm not very good at solving words or at guessing games xDD
Sometimes its not easy for me to guess the word. It may be because i'm not familiar with the word, or it is so scrambled that i can't make up what it is(my brain cant process it xD). Sometimes its because the picture is also not very helpful in solving the riddle. In any case there is some decent difficulty factor there, which riddler/puzzle solvers should love :)
There is also some work for improvement in my opinion:
Sometimes you guess a word out of the blue without fulling realizing what you guessed, since theres a new word coming right after you solve a puzzle.
It would be nice to have some options in the game, so that you can see what word was solved before you move on to the next one(preferably for kids). Or just move on after you solved a puzzle, so you don't lose time.
Also would be nice to resume the game after you close it, so you don't have to replay all over again from the start. I think this is what would benefit the game the most.
Also it could be enhanced by having profiles, so that each person could have his own progress.  I grow tired after playing the game after a few min at a time.
In another line of thought, the developer could perhaps even make a steam workshop to add a library for words, which could be shared. Not that it needs it. I know its just a simple game. It does have a lot of words and themes to pick already so i don't expect it to ever happen :p
Other remarks i had, which won't influence you in purchasing this game:
The word "Bee" came spelled just right and i had to swich one of the E's with the other E xD
One of the words i struggled with was "ohmtre" which had a picture of a water container recipient. I tried using a word unscrambler website to see what it was, but nothing came up. So i don't know what word i was trying to solve(and i can't think or be bothered to test all the combinations to find it out). Because of this i was stuck in this word puzzle, so it would be nice to have some type of help, like a solving agent in the game, or an option to skip the word with a timer penalty.
Theres an option at the start that you can pick which language you want to play with. There's English, Russian, French, Italian and Turkish. So that's good :)

This game has upsides and downsides. Overall I cannot recommend it and here is why:
The graphics are really neat, I love them and the artist was probably the person with the highest enthusiasnm producing a good game. The sound can get a bit annoying after a while but that is not new for clicker games - after all a clicker is supposed to run for hours at a time and is usually low production cost.
The gameplay is mediocre at best. A clicker lives of numbers and the numbers are off here as far as I can tell.
The UI is horribly designed for a clicker. The UI would work on a software piece like word or photoshop where everything needs to be spread out and seperated, for a clicker however you never have the things at hand that you need. It has fancy buttons and the font is really nice - but apart from its good looks it makes a point of being slow and weird.
Currency:
Gold - obviously the "main" currency here. You get it from enemies and you spent it on hero upgrades
Hero skill points - whenever a hero levels up you get points for that allowing to put into some skills
Chests - every level has a boss and every 5th boss drops a chest - which can be opened with a chest. It contains equipment for your heroes and hero upgrade which means skill points
Keys - to open chests they have to be bought with
Green Gems - You buy them from the shop or get a handfull from achievements - not enough tho trust me. There is a heavy pay us to play mechanic in place. you cannot play to farm these
Blue Gems - yeah they do stuff. dont know.
Purple Gems - they do other stuff
Research stuff - just unlocked this I dont even care any more
In the end you have a game that looks really neat, has a convoluted interface, a basic and not well planned out gameplay mechanic behind it and it points you towards the shop whenever it can. The real money shop. Yes it is free to play but there is no point in spending your time (or money) in this game when there are others that fix the same need so much better.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Man, Adult Swim Games sure have been publishing some pretty great titles. I think this one is top of the pile, though. The fact that this game doesn't have a Wikipedia page as of the time of writing is a great injustice to just how good this game is. In fact, a friend of mine named this game his Game of the Year for 2013. After playing through the game myself, I can certainly see why he'd say this. One phrase he used to describe this game is "a 2D Dark Souls." While the best phrase to describe this game is a "newer Ghouls 'n' Ghosts game;" in fact the studio's vision for this game, that can conjure up negative ideas about the game's design and how it handles difficulty. For now, just think of it as a 2D Dark Souls.
After some retrospection, I found that my first playthrough of this game was auspiciously similar to my first playthrough of Dark Souls. In both games, I was never too sure of the control scheme at first, but once I got used to it (and in this case, stopped using the analog stick in favor of the D-Pad (no seriously, the D-Pad on any controller beats the analog stick for this game)), I found that the control scheme worked perfectly for the game. Combat, much like Dark Souls, is very accurate and weighty. Likewise, this game has some excellent hitboxes; in fact, sometimes a bit too excellent. That's not a criticism, though; just know that you can get beaned in the head with an arrow even if your shield is extended, since your shield doesn't cover your head.
Another comparison to Dark Souls is the fact that this game does the most vital thing in a difficult video game (in my opinion), and that's signaling. You can do whatever you want to enhance the challenge of a level, as long as there's proper signaling. Again, the comparison between this and Dark Souls arises; both games were excellent at signaling, meaning that there were never any cheap deaths. Stages are surmountable without any memorization necessary, although if you're kinda dumb like me when it comes to video games, some memorization may be necessary. Plus, this game does that magical thing where you just get better at stages. That's a true sign of a well designed challenge level; where you can come back later on and find it easier without needing memorization. Overall, this game is a masterpiece in challenge level and level design.
In fact, my only real gripe is how this game handles bosses. Each stage is broken up into two halves - much like Ghouls 'n' Ghosts - with a boss at the end of the second half. This is a thing that I've thought about for a while now, and I think it may just be an unfortunate necessity due to how the game handles health (you get bits of armor and weapon upgrades from chests throughout the level and lose them if you're hit; again, pretty much exactly like Ghouls 'n' Ghosts). Either that, or it may be a bit more rigid conformity to the Ghouls 'n' Ghosts design ethos. The bosses themselves are fairly easy and incredibly patternated, so once you get the pattern down, you should have no problems with the bosses. This may just be me injecting my personal design sensibilties, but I feel like the bosses could've been a lot better if there was a checkpoint beforehand (along with making the bosses harder overall, of course).
Again, though; this isn't too big of an issue, but it is one that I thought could've been handled in a bit different (and in my opinion better, but you've figured that out already) manner. Nevertheless, I can definitely see why this was my friend's Game of the Year for 2013. While I can't necessarily make a statement about 2013 with regards to games, since I just started PC gaming in October 2013, if it had came out this year, it would most certainly be Game of the Year for 2014 for me. Yes, that means beating out Dark Souls II. 10/10.
Story: Literally the only story you get is a credits scroll at the end. Not even gonna rate.
Graphics: Man, there's some pretty great looking art in this game. The graphics feel like an "HD Genesis/Mega Drive game," which once again fits perfectly with the Ghouls 'n' Ghosts inspiration. All of the enemy designs are great, there's detail practically oozing out of every pixel laid down, and it still looks great at 1080p. My only gripe with enemy designs are the bosses of level 2 and level 5. They're literally reskins of enemies in the area. All the other bosses are unique designs, but boss 2 and 5 are somewhat disappointing. That's not too big of a deal, though; the core enemy design is great anyways. Of course the game runs well, so there's no worry about not being able to run it. Even though it windows at a relatively low resolution, it fullscreens to match your resolution of choice without a hassle. 5/5.
Sound: I've found that I like a lot of brass and percussion in my orchestration. This game... delivers a LOT of brass and percussion. This makes sense, of course; we're a viking, after all. We don't want a panflute chronicling our journey; no, we want big, bombastic horns, tubas, timpanis... the whole nine yards. Suffice to say, the music in this game is good. Really good. So good that I grabbed the OST literal minutes after I completed the game. There's no voiceacting in this game, so I don't really need to worry about that. I think it's pretty obvious that a 5/5 is in order for this game's sound department.
Overall scores are 10/0/5/5; cumulative score of 10/10. Yeah, this is Game of the Year material. You should probably buy this game before a viking busts down your door and impales you with a flaming spear of awesomeness.

"Rise, Warrior!" They don't make many games like this anymore, and that's a shame. Volgarr the Viking is a masterful throwback to hardcore arcade-style design philosophy. Volgarr's presentation lovingly harkens back to the machismo and high fantasy of 1980s popular culture icons like Conan the Barbarian and He-Man. But its throwback design is not merely skin-deep. The creators of this game have taken the best design elements from classic action games like Rastan and Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts, added their own elements, and infused them with a modern touch. The result is a fluid, deep game that is extremely challenging and, in turn, consistently rewarding.
Volgarr has a few simple attack and movement mechanics that are easy to understand but take careful skill and situational awareness to implement effectively. The enviroments in this game are not random and they are not cheap. They are intricately designed set-pieces created to challenge you, to teach you how to adapt to changing environments and various enemies. Your skills with Volgarr's simple but powerful moveset will be tested, but each obstacle you face is molding you into becoming the ultimate viking warrior. Going from being at the mercy of common lizardmen to dispatching with hordes of enemies and giant monsters with style and ease is an incredibly satisfying process.
If you are fan of classic arcade-style action games or if you are interested in a true hardcore challenge, buy this game as soon as you can.

TL;DR
Learn to mix drinks in a quiet bar in a post-dystopian era.
Pros
Cons
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
You mix drinks for customers. The type of drink you make for them determines how they react and what they tell you. Some customers will be easy where they’ll tell you what drink they want, and others won’t be as easy. You’ll have to start memorizing who orders what drink as the game progresses.
The main character has something from her past that she's trying to suppress, but it somehow ends up at her workplace and she has to face it head-on. VA-11 Hall-A (the name of the bar) always seems to attract the most fascinating people.
The main character, Jill, is one of two bartenders at the bar. Her catchphrase is, "Time to mix drinks and change lives." She's a really quiet girl that has a huge crush on her boss, but if you get her drunk, she'll reveal a lot more. Her boss, Dana, has a mechanical arm and is well known around the area, but Jill could never figure out why. Gil, the other bartender, is seen going in and out of the story and it seems as if his mind is always somewhere else.
Pixelated, futuristic, anime-ish. It draws a lot of influence from PC-98 games, which were based on 16 and 32 bit.
The game is fairly short, however, to get all the achievements, it'll require a few play throughs.

Obviously poor performance is not a good start (and
while playing it).
Sadly, that's not my biggest gripe with this game. It may be confusing that anyone could complain after 13+ hours of playing, but this game is such a grind. Not in the tradition sense of the word where you're doing mindless work to improve your character, but rather it's a grind of 2D line puzzles.
70% of the puzzles in this game could be placed in a flash game and they would play the same. Being in a 3D world surrounded by potentially interesting things is pointless if you're fixated on a 8x8 square screen! The times when the game forced you to take in your surrounds to solve the puzzles were amazing, but that stopped happening towards the end game.
Unlike other FPS puzzle games (Portal 2, Talos Principle, Quantum Conundrum, Q.U.B.E.) this game has no real story. The world is completely lifeless, and there's no in-game soundtrack. I played the game honestly for the first 8+ hours, not looking up solutions online, but holy crap... this game wouldn't end.
After the 8 hour mark I stopped having fun. I didn't care because the game hadn't presented me with any reason to care (other than the fact that I paid good money for it).
Getting to the final section I was presented with a door which had a randomly generated puzzle.
That's fine, I knew the rules of the game by then, but the puzzles had to be solved in a short amount of time or they would be reset. That's just cruel and obnoxious. This game was hostile towards fun and appeared to be doing everything it could to not be played.
Maybe I'm bad at puzzle games (I doubt it, since I have played others and loved them) or maybe this is for the "true puzzle fans" out there searching for a hard core challenge.
If that's you I hope you enjoy this. I was able to for a while, but in the end, the fun was lost before the game was over.
But the ending left me sour and I will gladly be uninstalling this never to play it again.

I loved this game on the 360 when it came out.  When I saw this game on Steam, I was like "$2.50 is a great deal for this game!"
The minigames are a lot less tolerable than I remember them.  The minigames in this game really just do not stand up on their own.  I went through them with a friend and the experience was just awful.  I'd never play this over something like Towerfall or Lethal League in local multiplayer.
The single-player portion is serviceable.  The game doesn't have a core gameplay loop that makes the game work.  Rather, it shuffles you between all sorts of different activities:  talking to guests, playing minigames, and building coasters.  The voice acting is entertaining, but some of the plot is weird as an adult.  Some NPC journalists get bribed during the story to give a bad review of your park (you have to bribe them back to get them to write an "honest review"), and it's weird seeing journalistic integrity treated so haphazardly.
Should you buy this game?  If you're nostalgic for it, the game is dirt cheap.  If you have no nostalgia for the game, skip it.

Thrillville: Off The Rails is fantastic sequal that improves upon everything that made the first game fun, The changes from the first game are as follows:
-There are new WHOA! Coaster pieces and crashing coasters.
-There are new games such as Coastertron and Robo K.O. along with sequels to existing games such as Sparkle Island 2.
-You can see your friends and love interests on a special list which lets you warp to them and they come to whatever park you are in.
-Certain games might give you a prize if you score high enough 4 or 5 stars which you can give to people to become friends or love interests faster.
-You now have a HQ, where you can edit your character, save your game, view cut scenes, view your trophies, and more.
Like the first game, you are once again dropped into the manager position at a newly opened theme park and given a tutorial on how the games mission system works. This is the exact same as the first game, with all mission categories following suit and teaching you everything from the interaction with your park guests to building rides to building game stalls and playing them. The only thing missing is an ability to skip the tutorial entirely, which makes starting a new game annoying sometimes, but the tutorial doesn't take long to finish thankfully.
Once you've completed all parts of the tutorial, you are given 'free reign' over the current theme park and may approach available missions as you please. This is the point where the game really starts.
There are 5 major parks in the game, each with 3 themed areas. all 3 areas contain 'build spots' where stalls and games can be placed. There will also be 2 spots for building coasters in each area as well.
The variety of games/stalls/coasters that can be placed/edited/built is quite amazing and can successfully distract you for very long periods of time, especially when playing the mini-games.
mini games are part of the games and stalls, with most games actually being playable as there own mini-game with high score egging you on to get the best scores possible in each. The playable mini-games range in genre from beat em ups to racing and boxing, each offering its own unique flare.
My personal bias on this game is rather high considering I played this game a lot when I was younger, but bias aside, I honestly think this game is worth a try for its unique style and addictive gameplay

There's three problems with this game:
1. It's lifeless
2. It's boring
3. There's no god damn point.
1.It's lifeless.
There are bugs and there are maybe balancing issues and maybe broken game mechanics, but none of that really matters when Planetbase can't make you believe that you're managing people on an alien world instead of a group of fish-eyed imitations of real human beings.
What you're really managing is a colony of pod people. In this reality, the Body Snatchers took over the Earth sometime in the 70's, had no need for warfare, so they were colonizing Mars by Fall 2015.
They don't need to interact with each other, they don't need to♥♥♥♥♥♥or ♥♥♥♥, which means they don't need to shower, which means they can't reproduce. But they also don't need to pray or laugh or dance or grieve. They're hardly indistinguishable from the robots that help with some of the manual labor.
It wouldn't take much to fix this. Some dancing and disco lights in the bar. Some chatter in the hallways instead of colonists' status reading "idle" as they stare blankly the walls. A love suite, where two, three, four colonists could unwind a bit. An amalgamated church a la Futurama where colonists could get space-married and then drive off in a Mars rover with some cans tied to the back of it. A toilet for pooping. You know, things that people do.
2. It's boring.
And this sort of goes hand in hand with the lifelessness of it. When you're managing your colony of pod people there's a stunning lack of emotion, which means a lack of excitement, or sadness, or anger. Sure, you might curse under your breath when your first two colonies collapse because you're still getting the hang of things, but once you do get a base working smoothly, there’s really nothing left to do.
Meteor impacts, sandstorms, space pirates. It doesn't matter, this game remains stubbornly boring. Meteor impacts on facilities are rare, and when they do happen, they only briefly incapacitate the single room they hit. Even if colonists die in an impact, they're quickly replaced and it simply means more food and oxygen for everyone else until the next delivery of pod people arrives.
Space pirates don't make any sense. I don't know where they come from, because they don’t seem to have a ship so much as they simply appear suddenly in your base. I don't' know what their motives are, because it's not supplies or credits. They seem to just want to kill everyone in sight. If that's their plan, good luck. Because these are pod people baby, and pod people don't know fear. Even when completely unarmed they'll swarm a space pirate until his gun runs out of ammo. It's extremely effective too. You'll lose four or five colonists, but because there's no need for a graveyard or a funeral service, the bodies'll evaporate and things get back to the regular hum drum of LIVING IN SPACE pretty quickly.
Planets don't have unique minerals or attributes, so there's nothing you can offer the occasional space-faring trader that he really needs or wants. There's no unobtanium to be obtained, the planets are all completely lifeless, so no alien bison to farm, no scientific research to be done and sold to some Galactic Space Association. You have nothing to offer that can't be gotten any god damn place else in the universe.
There's no reason to be on the planet. There's no reason you should just shut off the oxygen supply and watch your fakey-faux-people all suffocate. There's no god damn point.
3. There's no god damn point.
There is no winning scenario for this game. There are achievements to be unlocked, sure, but there's no satisfying conclusion to work towards. There are no other colonies on the planet, so you aren't trying to become the most self-sufficient.
There is nothing to explore on the planet, so you are trying to reach a destination, nor can you, because vehicle production is not possible. So no rover expedition to send your colonists on. No exploring a nearby space jockey ship.
There's no tech tree to unlock so it's not as if you can eventually produce a terraforming superstructure to ultimately make the planet habitable.
The only thing you can do is eventually unlock enough achievements to let you go on to the next planet. Which begs the question, why the hell isn’t the point to eventually build another colony ship? Why doesn’t winning one level on a planet mean building the ship that you start the next level?
It’s almost as if Planetbase wants you to chose your own winning scenario. So I’ve named my colony New Jamestown and once I’ve reached 300 colonists, I’m going to shut off all the oxygen.

Well, many referred to this as banished in space, and while that's true, the nostalgia for me was from another game (era...) called Outpost. The buildings and some of the interactionned brought back fond memories.
Overall I like the game and it's mechanics, There are a few things I would change/add (detailed below), but overall the game in interesting.
There have been a few comments already about content and the initial hurdles followed by what some have referred to as boredom. This could easily be tweaked and in fact a game difficulty level could be added. That being said, I feel too many games go overboard on the constant break and fix. There is such a thing as building and stocking, not everything has to go bad every instant.
On the suggestion front;
More control should be available at all levels. In fact, a colonist "scheduler" could be an interesting adjustment to the challenge of the game.
Each internal structure should be controllable individually. Giving priority should not be done just for a whole surface, but to individual machines.
Colonists and bots should have more self preservation reflexes.
Adding a queue to the work performed by colonists and bots would also be a great enhancement, in fact this mirco managment might present a fun challenge to the game.
Terrain work would also be a nice addition, so removing obstacles, fetching surface resourrces, etc..
Abother possibiolity would be mountain and subterrain construction.
One thing I found to limited was actual research and developpment, instead of just being bought, reaserch could be a fun challenge as well.
Adding space based systems and multiple colonies per planet is another venu that could be explored, as is multi-planet colonies and interrelated economies..
DLCs or addons could also be a nice way to take this game further.
A customisable quick access bar would be very nice.
So, overall positive. Nice design, great attention to detail, nice interface. Looking forward to more from these folks :)

Many games these days attest to having "NES hard" difficulty, but only a few truly understand what that means. Volgarr the Viking is one of those precious gems. It finds its difficulty, not in cheap deaths or overpowered enemies, but by giving you a variety of ways to deal with challenges and leaving it up to you to decide which course of action will lead to success, and leaving it in your hands to execute it flawlessly.
Every step towards the end introduces a new challenge, combining existing traps and enemies in a new way, forcing you to rethink your new strategy on the fly or die trying. It is not unfair, however, and introduces any new traps or enemies well in advance on their own, before blending them with any other traps or foes.
The secrets are superb, especially Thor's blessing, which (as far as I've seen) requires the unwavering courage to climb down to the very edge of a vine to strike at a hidden wall, or down-thrust your sword into a flower that spews deadly spores straight into your face.
This game is certainly no slouch. It will break you, but if you have the strength to persevere, you will rise from your own ashes and pay this game back every blow it has dealt you.

Every enemy you encounter has a specific way of being defeated that will often require you to have a solid grasp of the fighting and platforming mechanics.

VA-11 Hall-A is a game about serving drinks and talking to clients in a bar. Most people assume it's a puzzle that focuses on the serving drinks part, but the core element of this game is the story (the 'talking' part). You get to learn about the world and the people through basic conversations, but with exceptional bartending skillz, you may alter the fate of some characters and get the different endings.
It is
a visual novel, and a clever one at that, which instead of dialogue choice, you get a
choice via the drinks that you serve. For a small game, it offers quite a large cast, with each characters having diverse background and story to tell. It's definitely the main charm of this game, as the story itself is pretty much character-driven. The writing isn't perfect, with some minor gripes but overall it's pretty good. There is no wasted lines. Each character is given a unique personality by the way they talk and react to certain topics. The running gags are nice too, I guess. These are the things that make you really invested in the characters, which makes the story very enjoyable.
The aesthetics in this game is also really nice. Character sprites each use unique color pallete that is easy on the eyes as well as dithered shading for an added retro feeling. User interface gets its own aesthetics point for making use of different picture/dialogue layout to match different situation. The blatant reference to a certain OS shutdown sequence was an especially pleasant and nostalgic surprise for me. Oh, and don't forget about the music. It's totally a 10/10 worth getting the OST and listening outside of the game.

It's a shame this game is called 'The Witness', rather than more simply 'The Maze'. The Witness is a puzzle game interrupted by a 3D environment. The puzzles themselves are about as stimulating and satisfying as completing a sudoku, but instead of you completing said puzzles in a newspaper you found during your lunch break, or in a puzzle book you bought to pass the time while you're on the train, you're sitting at your computer struggling to be completely engrossed in the game. Unlike the lunch break or the train scenario, both of which eventually end and you get on with your life, The Witness rewards you for completing each puzzle by giving you even more puzzles.
I've invested a small amount of time in this game, but after playing for 3 hours, I don't feel any more as clued in to the narrative as when I started. Many have compared the open world part of this game to Myst, but after playing Myst for 3 hours, that world made more sense to me than The Witness's world does now. I really want to learn more about the open world, but the game isn't giving me any clarity. Evidently, this clarity is not a reward for completing any of the puzzles and I don't have any reason to believe any amount of additional playing will add any depth to the world. I had found 2 different audio logs, but neither gave any explanation of where I was or what was happening.
I think this game will go down in history as gaming’s 2001: A Space Odyssey. The cultured public will love it, but for me, it’s just a monumental waste of time.

The Witness is such an eye-candy with its vibrant colors and rich contrast.
There are no words or inventory windows or anything of that sort in this game. 10/10 immersion.
Drawing lines -  that's pretty much the only thing you can do. But with the many different mechanics and environmental puzzles, it never gets boring; though occasionally some puzzles might be hair-pullingly frustrating.
What I love the most about The Witness is that despite how difficult some puzzles may seem, after a few tries and maybe a couple restarts with a fresh mind, there's always that moment when you go "oh ♥♥♥♥ how did I miss / not think of that". It is definitely possible to go through the entire game in a reasonable amount of time without looking up any walkthroughs .
Also, you won't need pen and paper for most of the pieces, though I'm not sure about the secret area. Throughout the main story, there were only about three puzzles that require you to take note of portions of them (maybe even less, I do have awful short term memory).
All in all, amazing game, would recommend it to be played over a nice sunny afternoon in a dark room with a trash can handy for lost hair.

tl:dr this game has all the core technical features of a great eSport - high skill cap, strong team-based gameplay, and just fun to play/watch - but with literally EVERYTHING else going against it nowadays:
1) impossible to actually practice with people and improve
2) impossible to coordinate any sort of strategy in hot-join matches
3) extremely low quality forums, full of complaining and no strategic discussion whatsoever
4) new patches focus on adding more grind rather than dealing with core gameplay problems
long version:
I'd say I'm an above-average player, have a 1.32 win/loss ratio from 1600 PvP games, all from solo queuing and mostly t3-t5. Recently I feel like I've hit a giant brick wall with this game. Here's what I see of this game: it's a very high skill-cap and rewarding game which almost deliberately makes it impossible for you to improve your own gameplay. Ironic, isn't it? Let me explain.
Typically in team games it's hard to see whether you lost because you misplayed or because your teammates failed. This problem happens in MOBA's like DotA a lot. However, those games have a nice replay system where you can actually go back and analyze what you did wrong to improve as a player.
Star Conflict has nothing like that. Every loss just feels one-sided, frustrating, and not constructive at all. I don't mind losing if I can take something away from it, see what I did wrong, etc. but I can't here.
There are often times during a game where I'm not quite sure what I need to do in order to turn the tide of a game. Unfortunately there's no way for me to actually post a replay on a forum, ask for advice, get better, etc. as I used to do with any other competitive game. One, because there is no replay system, and two, because the official forums for this game seem to be inhabited by 10-year olds. The quality of posts on the official forum is downright disgusting; people start arguing with each other on every possible thread and drown out any constructive conversation.
So maybe one solution is to play with people to improve right? Well, not really... that brings us to:
Team play. How to?
Dreadnought battles between corporations are actually a lot of fun. However you can only do one battle once per day realistically (the game limits you to 3, but for most people 2 of those are during work/sleep hours), so it's really hard to actually get better at the game by playing these.
Most of the hotjoin matches you play, everyone else speaks Russian. You can't talk to them, and they can't talk to you. It gets boring/frustrating really fast watching your team throw the game and not even being able to coordinate any sort of strategy with them. And guess what, you can't actually hotjoin matches with a friend unless you sync and get lucky or are content with waiting 20 minutes between games, and you can't hotjoin matches with more than one other person period. Apparently this is a actually a feature of the game.
There's this mythical game mode called Leagues where you can play with large pre-formed teams using end-game ships. My corporation supposedly has a team for this but I think they are able to play a grand total of two games a season. There's also t3 tournaments which used to be good I think, but with the addition of destroyers, the few that I've played have consisted entirely of: Mexican standoff until one minute before time runs out, then rush in and try to grab kills in the last minute. Oh and they're also Sunday-only.
This review is from the perspective of someone who likes playing challenging games and wants to improve and outplay other people. This game feels like it should be an appropriate game, and the sad part is I think it used to be, but it really isn't anymore.

Pretty fun! If you're addicted to clickers (which I am) and time wasters (which I am) this is another good addition.  Repetitive backgrounds (of course) but a lot more diverse than others, and the fantasy & guild heroes theme is actually utulized unlike most clicker games! Very Free, just expect to leave it running a LONG LONG Time. If that's not your thing? This is not your game.  If you're looking for a total time soak with easy to play in the background of work? PERFECT!
Edit 7/13: Updating to add a ton of TL;DR basic tips
The game doesn't hold your hand, it assumes you're smart enough to figure out the basics of a pretty simple game.  But I hate watching people flounder, so REALLY BASICS! NOT for people already "experts" in the game, it'll bore you to tears:
Each hero has 5 item slots for power ups, the gold from monsters is used for this.  Every ten levels or so, the bosses can drop things like 1) chests 2) runes 3) uhhh... blue money >>; Yeah I don't really know what it's called. You need keys to open the chests, but ! You *get* keys by sending your autoclick faerie on quests OR by time looping (which of course, unwinds all your gold spent on level ups and heroes!) The chests have free perma-items for heroes at completely random. You start off with only 2 items per hero: basic health and demage, these are expanded to heightened health and damage + boots which will give that hero a damage bonus specifically for the map they're "experts in" ie: Thief does best in graveyards, priest does best in city etc.
Runes give you items for your magic fae/OVERALL EVERYONE and this sticks through all timeloops and more runes = leveling up those items.  You do this with the 3rd master (click master tab ofc) and you can get free runes (purple square things) in chests too.
Blue money you can exchange for items. Each item requires a key to use (again, you only get keys by quests or timelooping). Summon friend = go to the forums, click a thread with everyone's code and put in two. Switch them around until you find active friends and then love them forever.  It only lasts 24 hours, but it's a cheap (25 blue money) item aside from the key.  Passage books skip 10 levels, so they're best saving for when you timeloop, have keys, and don't have the time/patience to go the slower route! Garaga-something gives you double gold, so always use that ONLY after coming back from being AFK for ages and collecting all your quest/afk money. (failed quests = bonus gold money)  And way better on MUCH higher levels ofc. Wizard's Notes are the BEST and most expensive (100 blue money /CRAI!) but they automatically complete your wizard quest no matter how much time was left (so don't use it for 3 min. quests stupid self yeah I DID THAT A LOT lol) and double the chance of success rate for that and 3 other quests.  Bangin! TOTALLY worth the key, SOMETIMES worth the blue money if you have a lot or are like me and as quest obsessed as clicker obsessed :\
There are 3 masters. The chest & key master, the exchange master, the rune master, and a BONUS master whom you have to buy with 50 gems (green things you get for completely achievements and quests and being stupidly lucky.  Or you can buy with IRL money.  I mean I haven't, but you can if you have more money than time and no patience.) This will give you a mimic.  The mimic is an automatic chest that fights on your side. You can employ extra imps with blue money and set them to work on making things to power up your mimic/chest. Things like: extra items. Extra DPS (damage per second u nub) Extra HP (who doesn't love HP amirite?) all of which is immensely handy.  YOU WILL **NEED** THESE MUCH MUCH LATER IN THE GAME.  If the mimic is killed in a boss fight, that's it, no more plussing it up. You have to pay 10 more blue money to enchant another, get a new chest (which means additional key to open >:T) and while that's almost certainly worth it; it will NOT be worth it on your first two or three timeloops.  You want to get to the 250/300 level range MINIMUM imo.
You can't timeloop until you reach level 100. This is not a fast game. You will not reach level 100 in the first hour unless you are insane or did something wrong.  And not all the cheating autoclickers in the world can help you with that, because the game's mechanics prevent it. :P At lv. 500 your bonus for timelooping doubles. THIS IS TOTALLY WORTH THE EXTRA DAY OF BOREDOM YOU MIGHT HAVE TO SPEND TO WAIT. SERIOUSLY. So many keys. So many runes! So very good!  You can't afford to get all the heroes before your first timeloop. If you've ever played other clicker games, you know this is standard.  This is PROBABLY NOT a good "baby's first clicker," because it definitely DOES assume you know all these things already.
SKILLS: As you buff your heroes with items, they get skill points.  Sort of like Masteries in League of Legends.  I always go with the Hunter/Ranger's Item grabs, and the Thief's Shakedown (more gold :V) but ymmv. DO try to get enough stuff to buff and heal your dudes though.  This is part of the "All the autoclickers in the world can't help you cheat" because it's not a damage only system, it's combining the guild and RPG elements in a way I PERSONALLY ADORE, but if you aren't into those games? SKIP THIS.
Lastly: Gems & rings. You can get 500 gems REALLY quickly early on (first week) by fast completing achievements and using wizard's notes and such, but TRY TO SAVE THEM.  100 gems will give you 100 special gold for the governors slot machine's, but I blew mine so fast there XD Slot machines will get you every time.  It's better to wait for the runes & key machines if you are determined to play the slots at all. (the key machine has little keys in it, the rune machine is purple, the chest machine has a chest in front, and the gold machine is obvs. loud and blaring)  Eventually as you get to the higher levels of the game, you will actually start exchanging 10 chests for blue money.  Because the more you buff your dudes, the better your odds of chests, and DO NOT BOTHER OPENING THE UNBOOSTED CHESTS. They're NOT worth the keys. Boosted chests ARE. (they remain boosted for a few minutes when you first get them, but if you're afk, just collect the chests for blue money, it's worth it.) And don't use the special gold for regular gold slot machines, sooooo not worth it. 100 gems = 100 slot machine gold. REALLY only the runestones and key machines are worth it imo, but ymmv.
RINGS: Each ring (goes in your main fae's pockets where the other items like wizards notes and♥♥♥♥♥♥are; then open your jewlery box ofc) is per a hero. You are not always guaranteed to get the same heroes, even if you buffed up say the conqueror a bajillion times, you might get the defender ring and then the defender instead. (same hero spot: #1, different skills and items) THIS IS OKAY.  STOP PANICKING. (specifically to those who did/do/are on the boards and reviews) Variety is what keeps us from getting bored ffs. After 3 failed playthroughs, I finally managed to beat This War of Mine.
10/10 learned the horrors of war, and that peace is something that must be protected at all costs.

A game that's different to most others in the best possible way. Making you think with decisions that could benefit or cripple you in time.
The game has balance, and for me, that is it's strength.
Even though This War only gives you just a few options to customise how you want to start, it doesn't give you so little to choose that each new game feels like a total repeat of the last one. To help, selected DLC will give you more choice of characters and/or stories.
Using characters to their individual strengths is important. But a big part of the gameplay requires you to manage basic resources, ensuring they are replenished as quickly as they are consumed. In addition to this, you will need to gather items to help construct equipment which will potentially make life slightly better in some way. The main challenge, whilst doing these things, comes not only in the limited amount of things you can carry whilst scavenging or looting, but also keeping an eye on the time, or you could struggle even more.
Your characters will also feel the morale pressures of the decisions you make. This is most evident if your character takes another persons life or steals from others needing these items as much as you do.
Overall, This War of Mine is fairly slow in pace and will not be one for people craving explosive action, but it delivers a thinking persons game through its unique characters, atmosphere and varied amount of in-game choices that decide how your characters will survive the hells of war.

TOXIKK is a bouncy, fun arena shooter that reminds of Quake Arena or Unreal Tournament. Fast-paced action, punchy weapons, generous gore are all featured in this game.
Unfortunately, TOXIKK does not seem to feature a consistent playerbase. After completing a quick tutorial on movement free players can only select the 'quick join' option, which has again and again dumped me into a match playing with bots. While fragging bots can be fun, as a free player I have no way to set how difficult these bots are - so far, I've experienced 'standing still facing a wall' and 'oh my god why do they have such good aim' from the bots.
Eventually my patience was rewarded and after about half an hour I matched with another free player in a mode called Arch Rivals, which is a 1v1 deathmatch. It was painfully clear that my opponent hadn't tried the tutorial - while I jumped and dashed around he slogged his way through the map on foot, and after I killed him twice he quit, and it was back to the bots.
The next time I squared off against an actual player I only spent 15 minutes playing against bots, and again we squared off in Arch Rivals. This player, however, was a different caliber. As I frantically tried to gun him down he blasted me again and again, a seemingly unkillable bulwark of blazing guns. "Get the powerups" he explained after exploding me into giblets with a shotgun.
Powerups? Those weren't in the tutorial. Still, I had been collecting small bonuses to my health and shields, giving me small, cumulative bonuses of +5, but against my adversary it didn't seem to make a difference. Was I missing something? I asked my tormentor, and after incinerating me with a flamethrower he paused to explain further. "Not the little ones. You need to get the big ones. They're hard to reach." With that he proceeded to kick my♥♥♥♥♥for the next five minutes before the match ended.
I decided that I would dedicate my next match to looking for these powerups so that I might offer a smidgeon of a challenge to the next good player I faced. TOXIKK, however, had different plans for me and instead stuck me in a match where the bots and I all had instagib laserguns with no powerups in sight. After losing to the bots I was matched against the same noobcrushing player, with the same game mode and map. "Find the powerups yet?" He asked me. That was the only thing either of us said as he slaughtered me with ease for ten minutes.
With such a minimal tutorial, a tiny playerbase and a bar set high by experienced players, TOXIKK has not been an enjoyable game for me.
Edit: After being told that this game has a bigger playerbase on Friday nights, I figured I would give it another shot. I quick joined a game that had three other players, a high point in my experience with TOXIKK. After playing the last half of a match with these swell fellows, they voted for a cool looking map and I was promptly booted back to the main menu. The next two matches after that were, unsurprisingly at this point, populated entirely by bots and myself.

The true concept of PLANETBASE is not just about building a colony on some distant planet. You will NOT be able to accurately predict the behaviour of most of your colonists and even though you will be supplying them with the means of satisfying their needs, they will occasionally send themselves off to sleep or eat just when you desperately need them to manufacture materials or build something etc. This is part of the game's appeal, as it makes the colonists more human with minds of their own who won't blindly follow orders just because they are in a computer game.
Some of your colonists will refuse to work at all and then you will spend valuable time trying to fix the issue. There is always a reason, usually to do with bad planning on your part. If you can't fix it quickly enough the penalty can be brutal. . . . death of some, or even all of your colony. This is my kind of game!
You, as their manager, will have to work around their frailties to ensure they have the best chance of surviving and expanding in a hostile and risky environment ie. meteorites, sandstorms, solar flares, asphyxiation, starvation and general stress from trying to survive on an inhospitable planet.
Your colony will grow organically as everything is linked to each other and I don't just mean the physical links between the buildings. It's a fine balance. The game is more complex than first meets the eye and there is alot going on here. If you don't plan ahead, your colonists will die. Have I said this was my kind of game yet?
The game loads well, decent graphics and buttery smooth gameplay on my mid-range PC. Oh! and the devs are really on the ball and are amazingly quick to put out tweaks etc.
If you buy this game, allow me to give one hint. . . . do not run out of food!  Your colony will die surprisingly quickly.

Developer feedback is disappointing, instead of talking about adding new features to the current game, the respond in terms of "we might add that in planetbase 2".

With the current price tag of 20 euro... unacceptable.
Wait for the game to go on sale sub 10 euro.
Verdict : Still a rough diamond that needs some serious improvements beyond the basic gameplay.
