The Witness is a beautifully crafted puzzle game. Simply put, that is what it is, and if you play this game hoping for something other than that, you may find yourself disappointed. There is little to no story, no suspenseful plot, no explanation behind why people everywhere are statues... just you and the island full of puzzles.
That is not to say the game is disappointing at all! If solving puzzles is your jam, if you enjoy immersing yourself in a world to uncover its secrets, if those moments of "A-ha!" epiphany excite you, then this game is absolutely for you. The world is constructed with absolutely no instructions or tutorials anywhere. You intuit and explore your surroundings to learn what you need. Eventually, you will piece together the pieces of knowledge necessary to progress, and the carefully constructed moments of epiphany are truly wonderful. Over and over again, you will find the lens through which you see the world of The Witness change radically, and that brings with it even more discoveries. For me, that is what this game was about: experiencing the process of learning and epiphany, and witnessing the transformation of how I saw the island.
While completely "100%ing" the game requires some work I find incredibly tedious, or simply cannot solve on my own, "completing" the game itself was completely reasonable and I solved it without internet help in less than 20 hours. If you are easily frustrated by puzzles or if you are expecting more mystery, story, or plot, you will not find it here. If you love puzzles for the sake of puzzles, and the experience of learning and picking things apart for yourself, then this game is for you. It is hands down one of the best puzzle games I have ever played, packing so many different ideas and layers into a singular puzzle mechanic. As cheesy as it may sound, witnessing The Witness is truly an experience worth paying for. (I got it on sale though!)

For such an innocence looking game, Toki Tori is cruelly challenging. Yes, I like playing puzzle games, but Toki Tori’s sense of challenge just goes from mild to infuriating hard. I really do like everything Toki Tori has to offer, and despite looking like an incredibly easy kiddie game it turns into one of the hardest challenging puzzle games around, and that alone is impressive. It really is a hidden gem amongst puzzle games, and one that would challenge anybody that thinks they’re clever.
The game is simple enough; Toki Tori needs to collect all the eggs in order to proceed to the next level. Toki can use a number of gadgets to get all these eggs, but usually there is a limited amount of uses on each item. These gadgets tend to range from simply building a ladder to arming an ice bazooka. The main objective is then to find a way to optimize all your items so you can collect all the eggs, and in lies the sneaky cleverness of Toki Tori. Toki Tori has a tricky twist on how you might simply try to get one egg only to not have enough resources to get the next one. More often than not, Toki Tori’s tricks you enough that it can really be trying on any player, and even with the ability to skip a level in a world it gets to the point of aggravation. Toki Tori can just spike in difficult so easily that in one moment you are getting puzzles done left and right, then in the next you don’t even know how to string two eggs together. You could spend an hour on just one puzzle and still not solve it. The game can often get stuck in your head just wondering how you can make it work, only to realize that you were completely doing the wrong approach. And all this could really just be avoid if the game gave you some clue on how to get the eggs. Whether the hint be which order to get the eggs or how to just get one of the eggs, any kind of hint system would have made such a hard puzzle game become a bit more bearable. But don’t let the games hard difficulty fool you that it has nothing else to offer, because after you solve all the regular puzzles harder puzzles are unlocked. Making Toki Tori last far longer with even more challenging puzzles then the ones in the main game. So needless to say, Toki Tori will have you scratching your head for quite some time. But for what it’s worth, it’s quite a wonderful mountain of a game to conquer, even if it looks and plays cute music while you’re doing it.
Final Thoughts:
Toki Tori is really a surprising gem of a game, and one that holds the phrase, “don’t judge a book by its cover” quite well. Although it may look cute, this game can be quite cruel with nearly each puzzle requiring all your resources of weaponry and tools, leaving little room for error, meaning this game will challenge anyone’s wit when it comes to solving puzzles.

Shigeru Miyamoto, the creator of Super Mario, Zelda, Donkey Kong, etc., says the first thing about the design of a game should be the sense of accomplishment. That satisfaction when you overcome an obstacle and noticed you've become better for it.
Furi absolutely nails that feeling in the first 10 minutes of gameplay. If you're making a game exclusively about boss fights with an unforgiving combat system, you have to make sure there are patterns in the enemies' movements, quirks and strategies they use, so that we as players can learn them, choose the best direction to take on them, so that we can feel we've defeated the enemy, not just with our character's powers and weapons, but also with our own skill. That's what The Game Bakers have done.
And it's not just the satisfaction of winning a battle that's at play here. The feeling of progress, when you notice you're actively becoming better at the game, which is so present in games like Super Meat Boy and Dark Souls, is so very noticeable in this masterpiece of a game. Sometimes, when your three lives end at the very last phase of a boss, you will notice that progression within a single fight, because the frustration of losing when you're so close to victory is quickly dismantled by the fact you can now deal with their earlier phases with so much more ease, now that you've been through all they can do.
None of the bosses you find here can be taken lightly when you first face them. They will all keep you on your toes, forcing you to master the controls and have quick reflexes. No boss here is made difficult simply by being damage sponges. You either pick up skill or you lose. It's that simple. They also did an amazing job with making each boss not only feel but also look unique, which is reflected by the environment you fight them in. Each fight is complemented so well by the scenario, the soundtrack (I can't even begin to talk about how great this soundtrack is), the personality and style of each opponent. It's an overall solid 10 in atmosphere.
If you are into the challenging and hardcore genre of gaming, please pick up this game. Hey, even if you aren't so into that genre, it's still worth picking it up, simply as an experience. I'll be looking forward very anxiously to any other title these guys might release in the future.

I'm torn on this game. I love the aethetic; the music, visuals, and combination of gameplay genres makes for an amazing style. I just find the combat has too many subtle flaws that add up.
Raw attacks rarely land, so you end up relying on shooting and parrying, the latter especially in close combat phases. Parrying is always signaled by a white flash and sound effect, but there aren't clear animations accompanying the attacks, so you can't tell if they are in the middle of a combo, meaning you might just get a single hit or be dodged, or a finisher, so you can do the full combo. There are subtle stance changes after the attack, but it is too little visual feedback to pick up on until you have gone through enough trial and error to recognize them quickly enough to get a combo. A clear animation with distinct windups would have been both more helpful and more engaging than memorizing a parry timing. The timing also is slightly inconsistent. While most attacks have a fairly consistent slight delay before the parry, there are some exceptions which makes the attacks feel cheap.
The game handles death in a unique way; on success you restore a lifebar, but on game-over you have to do the whole thing again. I like this, as you can't cheese your way through a boss, but it does get repetitive for the longer fights, and when you add in that there are often things you simply can't anticipate until you have seen it before, it feels like a grind of just getting a little further each time and knowing when to whiff punish. It does feel good when you weave in and out of patterns that gave you trouble before, or nail a series of parries in a row, but I feel like there is too much reliance on trial and error.
Furi is definitely a game that gets better as you improve as a player, but until you know all the patterns it just felt like a grind for me. I wish your skill as a player and control over your character grew more than knowing what to do during each phase of a boss fight, or just testing if you have the parry timing(s) down, which are essentially quick qte's when you think about it. I do really like that they included Furier mode though, for those who want to master it, and that there is a speedrun mode (I think speedrunners who are used to repeating things to perfection would dig the game). I tend to enjoy both quick action games and bullet hells, so I should love this game, but it just felt like too much trial and error for me. If you're still interested I'd say wait for a sale at least.

Probably the Tony Hawk: Underground of the theme park simulators, since this game has a plot (although pretty simple and somewhat disappointingly short) and it follows a single character that you can make. Thrillville: Off The Rails is a pretty casual game, so if you're looking for a realistic park sim, I'd suggest Planet Coaster, by the same developers.
My personal favorite part of the game is the minigames. There's the classics like mini-golf or pool and the throwbacks like Event Horizon (similar to Gradius) and Luftwaffe 109 (similar to 1942.) The coaster building part is pretty good, too (similar to Planet Coaster.) Thrillville's coasters have a unique part to them: Whoa! pieces. They can be anything from a ring of fire to a stunt jump. Either way, it's probably a safety violation.
It's worth pointing out that the game doesn't go as into depth as Planet Coaster or RCT, and there isn't nearly as much creativity. All the parks have a set path and places you can put things, so each park can hold two coasters/race tracks, and there's three spots for things like rides, games, or stalls, each of which could hold maybe three or four. You'll probably be fine with the space, though, since the missions won't require too many of anything.
Recommended if you don't have the creativity or patience for Planet Coaster or RCT, or if you want something a little different. Also recommended for the nostalgia.

Thrillville: Off the Rails is nice spinoff of the Roller Coaster Tycoon games. There are 4 major things I will talk about and compare to Rollercoaster Tycoon. The 4 things are the parks, building rollercoasters and other stuff, minigames, and the story.
The parks is the only thing I can say that I don't like about this game. Unlike RCT, TV (which stands for Thrillville) will not you edit paths, out of bounds scenery, move the floor up or down, or let you buy extra land. The only thing you can remove are some of the animatronics in the empty build areas, but you have to place something down that takes up their space. If you want to build a roller coaster, you have to go to a coaster area, and build on there. That means that their are a limited amount of coaster slots so if you build 6 (less or more depending on the park) then you can't make any more. The things I do like are the out of bounds stuff happening in the background. Stuff like bikers doing long jumps, a monster truck running over cars, and a stunt man jumping into a trampoline and just a few things that can happen in the park area. But yeah the parks are ok at best.
Building roller coasters is fun in this game. Not only do you have the freedom to put whatever you want wherever you want as long as it applies to some rules, but you can also place down some special parts like a jump, an upward spin, or suddening falling slowly and randomly. Almost each coaster has it's own special ability, so one might have the jump, but a different one might have a spin. You can also not finish the coaster and people will eject from the carts and fall down with parachutes. This dose mean that the fun of death parks is lost in games like RCT however. Building stuff like stalls and mini game buildings are simple but easy. but just move it, rotated if needed, and just place it down. The minigame buildings have different models for what they represent, Like an arcade one looks like an arcade, but the trampolining looks like trampolines and not an arcade. However other stalls don't have as much differences from each other.
Minigames are not present in the RCT games. The minigames are good for most of them. they have a variety of shooters, fighters, racers, and more. Very enjoyable, challenging old-school game. retro 16 (or 32) bit graphics. tight controls (though not perfect) and an addicting level of difficulty.
My one qualm is that with the game's design, and thats THAT YOU CAN'T SAVE. Spend an hour getting past just the first level? Quit after spending a half hour on level 2? Well, bad news, because you'll have to start straight from the beginning with no saves or continues if you choose to quit the game (which any normal human will do, at some point or another).
That's right, its just like an arcade game-- which is clearly the style this game succeeds at emulating-- no saves or continues once you stop playing. You get checkpoints, 1 per level, whilst you play, but once you quit that's it.
I love the game, I really do, and I was lucky enough to get it on sale for less than $5.00, but I can't help but feel a little ripped off due to this single element of the game.
That being said, some will thrive from the old-school challenge, experiencing deja' vu from the 80's-90's arcade era-- knowing that it's all or nothing. Once you stop playing or run out of quarters, you'll have to try again next time right from the start.
For its challenge, controls, retro appeal, and sheer enjoyability, this game deserves an 8/10. The no-saves feature holds this challenging Castlevania-style game back from being a fully-fledged game. Again, some will really love that, but in these days where time is a constraint for most, its a nuissance.

I initially gave this game a positive review for the following reasons:
1) Nice soundtrack
2) Gorgeous scenery (albeit, even if sometimes pixelated and appears to have a low resolution)
3) I like surreal / abstract games and especially walking simulators
4) Took some amazing screenshots which I still enjoy looking at
However, I left my positive review after one playthrough, and since then, I've had several more playthroughs...
Upon playing it several more times, I've noticed many flaws. Many, many flaws.
1) The invisible walls of doom are EVERYWHERE, to an absurd degree. You WILL run into an invisible wall almost every few steps. I understand that these road-blocks are in place for a reason, but, the exploration aspect of this game is so severely limited due to constantly running into invisible barriers - moreso than in most other games that utilize them.
2) The one and only achievement appears to only be unlockable by using Steam Achievement Manager. Some of you may argue that it's stupid to collect achievements, but, some of us like doing it as a hobby. In my case, I genuinely thought that the achievement was on a level (I was thinking on the second level because it's like a labyrinth, with a lot of areas to explore) and I spent 10 playthroughs looking for it. Not just for the achievement, but, because I thought that maybe I overlooked something crucial in the game. If I couldn't find the achievement, what if I missed a secret level? Or something important? So, this caused me to re-play the game in search of something... that was never even there, and requires SAM to unlock, it appears.
3) I came to the realization that the game is only 10 minutes long or so, and, once I got over the initial glamor of the game, which had lots of sparkly visuals, I realized that... there isn't much to do.
There isn't much to explore, the exploration aspect is VERY limited due to invisible walls everywhere, as I said, and the level quality is extremely inconsistent. Some levels look very polished and clean, while others have extremely pixelated backdrops and bad quality JPEG looking backgrounds. Some levels also appear to be so unrefined. In the level with the giant staircase, for example, so many textures looked so raw and unpolished.
Overall, this was a frustrating experience, especially the more I played it.

Lego Harry Potter 1-4 is still my favorite Lego game. Keep in mind that I haven't gotten sick of Lego games yet. I don't know why. I should be, right? That's what game reviewers keep telling me. "It's been done all before," they say. "They're all the same game," they say. And of course, they're right: they all suffer from the same hard crashes and bugs. But colorful puzzle platformers held together by snapping, clinking bricks, featuring IPs with great music, characters, and stories...? I can't get enough. Sue me.
This was the game that provided players with the first (and one of the best) "microcosmic hub worlds" in the Lego game series. In this case, Hogwarts castle and its surroundings. You get to explore a version of the entire castle, complete with its own puzzles, collectibles, and secret rooms, but the main levels accessed within this castle take you into larger, more detailed linear levels, each with their own puzzles and secrets.
All of this is accompanied by the great musical score from the movies (the John Williams score from the first two movies especially). I can't overemphasize how much the music adds to the experience of playing the game.
As with all other games, a second player can jump in or out of the game at will, or you can play it solo.
IMPORTANT NOTE ABOUT REFLECTIONS / ENHANCED GRAPHICS: the PC version has a strange quirk. By default, Enhanced Graphics (including shiny reflections on characters' hair) are permanently disabled, even when you turn them on from the graphics menu. You have to modify the game's "pcconfig.txt" file, which is in one of the game folders (its exact location changes depending on your OS). You might want to do a search, but I'm pretty sure you have to change the "IgnoreVendorPresets" variable from from "0" to "1", then save the file, then restart the game, making sure enhanced graphics are turned on. The opening Traveler's Tales sequence should have reflective textures, so you'll know right away if it worked.

This game is great.
You're dropped on an island with no context or any dialogue, and it stays that way throughout. I fell in love with this game because they left the story telling up to you, with you having to not only figure out all the puzzles on the island, but what's happened there in the past. I've played through a fair chunk of it (I'm guessing around 80%) and I still want to go back in and keep finding all the mysteries. This is a particularly big thing for me, since I rarely finish games these days because I get bored of them too quickly.
The puzzles vary in difficulty ranging from relatively easy, to down-right hard, and often I found myself trying to actually figure out what the rules to the puzzles were; which was a great feeling when you finally figured it out. It's a genius idea for gameplay, because you do get those moments of frustration, but they're always outweighed by the satisfaction of figuring out the fundamental rules of a puzzle set, and then being able to apply it to all the subsequent puzzles.
The design of this game is also breathtakingly beautiful. The time and effort of all the modelling, texturing, ambience really shows, and it helps to just absorb you into the game, where hours just disappear. I love how a large portion of the game is based around context, and in playing it, you gain understanding of why it's named "The Witness". Even the decision to only use WASD and the mouse for controls, and not have any other way to interact with things was a great choice.
It's a beautiful, emotive experience, which I'll be recommending to all my friends. So glad I got this game, it'll go down as one of my all-time favourites.

The Witness is a first-person puzzle adventure game set on a vibrantly realized island sprawling with vegetation and dilapidated architecture. Your time will be spent exploring a myriad of fully realized miniature biomes and various man-made locales as you solve increasingly difficult puzzles.
The graphics are hyper stylized and visually appealing to the eyes; the sound design and general audio is superb, but is confined to ambience; the controls are exceptionally minimalistic; and the puzzles range from somewhat challenging to absolutely frustratingly difficult.
There is very little in actual story elements to be found here, but various audio logs do scatter the landscape; much of which is out-of-context quotes or readings from promising historical figures, but tends to raise more questions than answers. In a similar style to that of the in-game readings, allow me to summarize my experience of The Witness by quoting Ecclesiastes 1:18 from the American Standard Version of the Bible: "For in much wisdom is much grief; and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow."
Ultimately, The Witness is an incredibly difficult pizzle game that requires patience, tackling problems from various perspectives, and critical thinking skills. When stumped, take a relaxing stroll through an autumn-colored forest, or poke around a bit in an abandoned quarry to pass the time. This is not a game for everyone, but for those who find pleasure in completing challenging puzzles or ever-increasing difficulty, this is a game for you.

Solving a hard puzzle in The Witness will make you feel like a genius.

I've put 60+ hours into the NON-STEAM version, the downloadable version from Reiza's website, but decided to immigrate to Steam instead because it's significantly easier to deal with updates, and there's no need to ask for new activation keys if you change the hardware or OS. In other words, getting the game on Steam is much more convenient.
Anyway, this game offers something you simply can't get in any other game, and that's no exaggeration. How many other truck racing simulation games have you seen out there ? I actually can't think of any.
You get driving physics that is technical and challenging, which is no surprise since it's based on the ISI engine. If you have played Reiza's other games you'll notice that the feel of the game is quite similar when it comes to physics.
Sure, the game could be prettier, but a proper PC sim should focus on physics rather than glitter. This game does that; it's a sim game, so you need to practise, practise and practise.
There are multiple controller options, which you can fully map and customize. It plays really well with a regular gamepad. However some kind of wheel control will make it smoother to steer. For example if you use a steering wheel or a gamepad with a mini-wheel attached.
You also have several Assists- and Difficulty options, so anyone can play this game and be wowed by these powerful machines.
The game has real-life tracks and real-life truck brands. If you haven't played Reiza's Stock Car games you'll experience a whole bunch tracks that you won't see in any other racing sim. This is another unique characteristic of a Reiza game.
To sum up: if you like sim racing games and/or truck driving games (hello ETS and ATS !) you should give this a go.

This game is a bit like Dark Souls except stripped down to the most basic components: the boss fights. It has all the important elements: parrying, dodging, hitting dudes with your sword. It's set in this really stylish neon futuristic ninja world, very cool. The mixture is spiced up a bit with the "bullet hell" component: while fighting you can use your pistol, and the boss will also shoot projectiles, sometimes the camera zooms out and it feels more like a twin-stick shooter. I don't like bullet hell games and I was a little wary, but I was surprised to find myself enjoying it: it works nicely and adds just enough complexity so that each fight feels like a full brain massage.
Between boss fights the game strangely turns into a walking simulator as you calmly navigate to the next area, giving you time to contemplate your certain doom. It's peculiar, the game is mostly ridiculously intense fights punctuated by artful moments of philosophical serenity as the narrator unfolds the story. Did I mention the soundtrack? Possibly the finest game soundtrack ever composed.
Furi comes with two difficulty settings: ultra-hard and impossible. If you like a challenge you'll soon find yourself completely hooked on it. I've been playing it for over a year and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface. Leaderboards, speedrunning tools and stats are built into the game, and controls/mechanics are so finely-tuned that you feel like you're a four-armed cheetah operating a nuclear reactor. It's one of the most satifying gaming experiences available. And if you can beat this thing on the hardest setting then you officially have wizard powers and from that day forward people will find you much more attractive and cool.

Volgarr the Viking is one of the very best action/platformers ever made so go buy it now.
Still reading instead of adding it to your cart? okay perhaps a bit more convincing is needed for some reason. I agree with those who say it's a bit reductive to compare games to fusions of other well known titles, but here it's perfectly applicable as Volgarr is what you'd get by combining Ghosts & Goblins with FromSoftware's Souls series. The Ghosts & Goblins influence is felt immediately not just by the slower, more deliberate pacing, but also by the nonrefundable jump arc, once you jump you're committed to it with only a double jump to save you from a poorly timed one. At the same time Volgarr conjures the spirirt of the souls series by teaching gamers through death and punishing failure as it's primary tool and while countless games have done the same thing years before any souls game existed Volgarr mirrors the souls games emphasis on combat and environment awareness. Learning each enemy's attack and movement pattern while avoiding stage hazards is the core of the game so if you rush your way through it without being as patient and methodical as the game wants you to be then "you're gonna have a bad time". That being said if you accept the fact that you will die a lot and manage to not throw your controller or keyboard through your monitor, then eventually some of Volgarr's badassery will transfer to you with that percentage growing as you master the mechanics and start feeling the flow of the game. Each chest adds an extra piece of armor to your arsenal depending on what you already have equipped while getting hit knocks off a piece so don't get hit if you want to keep your gear. No one is scared of a naked viking...my apologies to the naked viking communities of the world , but c'mon you know a flaming sword and metal shield can't ever hurt...well at least not you!
If you're sick of the AAA, casual friendly, hand holding of modern games that think you're incapable of coloring inside the lines then pick up Volgarr the Viking and be reminded that some games still respect your reflexes and intelligence as a gamer.

This game reminds me of Ghosts n Goblins. It is very challenging. It isn't a bad game by any means. In fact, it is very well designed action platformer;  it is just very challenging. I only recommend this game, if you want a very challenging but good game. If you are looking for a game you can breeze through, stay far, far away from this game.
To give you an idea of how hard this game is,  I can't believe I've been playing this game for over an hour, and I still haven't beaten the first level. I have never played a game, aside from the original Ghosts n Goblins, where I haven't beaten the first level within an hour. And I bet you it will take several more hours before I finally get good enough to beat the first level.
This game is very challenging for the following reasons.
First of all, it only takes two hits to get killed in this game. You can increase your hit points to three hits with an armor upgrade (so you can get hit no more than two times), but that's about it. By default, you better not get more than once, or you are dead.
The levels are long, and full of hazards and enemies that can kill you. The checkpoints are few and far between, so you have to last for a very long time without getting hit. Lastly, many of the enemies and hazard are VERY cheap, and there is no way you can avoid them  on your first encounter. Sometimes enemies and hazard can appear out of no where and kill you before you can even react. This can be especially frustrating when you made considerable progress, and then you are sent back to a checkpoint, losing five or more minutes of progress in the process. The only way you can avoid these hazards is to first get killed , know in advance that the hazard is coming, and then avoid it.
Also, you have to beat an entire world/level before you can save, and the worlds in this game are very large. If only you can save your progress and start from each sub-section of each world. That would be nice. But no, this game requires you to beat a very long and difficult level in just one-sitting, so you better have good endurance.
Basically, the only way you can make ANY progress in this game is to play the levels over and over again until you can reach the end in one sitting.  You need perfect precision to avoid getting hit in this game. In other words, you need VERY GOOD hand-eye coordination, and LOTS of trial and error before you can beat this game. You need to memorize the entire level, where each hazard and enemy is, and play almost perfectly (get hit no more than once) to reach each few-and-far-between checkpoint and beat each level.
Luckily, this game gives you unlimited continues. You can continue from the same checkpoint as many times as you want. Thank god that's the case, because you will die many times until you reach the next few and far between checkpoint. If you had limited continues, this game would go from very challenging to downright frustrating and near impossible.
Control-wise, this game is very responsive and accurate. The only downside is that, like in Ghosts n Goblins, your character cannot change his direction in mid jump, so you need to be very precise in the timing and positioning of your jumping; otherwise, you will get hit and DIE.
Overall, this is a well-designed, albeit very challenging, action platformer. It remains me alot of Ghosts n Goblins, because of its stiff jumping mechanics, challenging level design, two-hit deaths, and medieval/fantasy setting in the format of an action platformer.

As much as I enjoy this game, I cannot recommend its purchase.
A very interesting and beautiful looking game that has a lot of potential. I really enjoy the challenge of starting the colony and growing it ever larger.
The biggest downfall is the faulty AI - it is a game breaker. Colonists will avoid doing any work, preferring rather to stand (idle) in connecting tubes and alternating between sleeping and eating/relaxing. External structures will go unbuilt even when they are required to be built. Food will not be managed, even though stavation is rampant ... the list goes on. At one stage I saw a group of colonists waiting to exit the Airlock, hopefully to construct a dome, but rather they immediately turned around and went back into the habitat, having performed nothing at all of the jobs outside - like carry supplies to the Storage Dome - everyone can carry things!
After having played for over 2 hours, there are glaring issues with the game. I suggest the following improvement, beyond just fixing colonist AI:
- Use three levels of priority (Medium/High/Critical) for ALL managment AND construction tasks (even those constructions within a dome, e.g. the Water Fountain).
* Critical: only one task of each category Engineer/Medical/Biologist, at a time can/should be allowed to have Critical priority, ensuring the AI takes *immediate* notice, even if the colonist assigned to the task is starving/sleepy, etc. However, priority of the assigned colonist goes to free/idle colonists first. Those colonists that are already assigned a task are not to be considered for a priority task, unless all colonists of the same category are busy. Maybe decreasing the resulting Condition rating of the object being managed/constructed, based on the colonist's status (Normal (100% Condition)/Yellow (85%)/Orange (50%)/Red (25%)).
* High: based on the required task, a specialist colonists will be promptly assigned, before he/she takes on more menial &/or personal tasks. Again, the resulting Condition rating could be affected by the working colonist's status, as above.
* Medium: colonists will get to the task when there is nothing better to do, or have a higher priority task waiting for which they are specialised.
At the moment priority cannot be set to a higher level for the construction of buildings and this is essential within a multitasked and multi-skilled environment. While it is possible to set a specific dome to have increased priority, certain tasks within that dome also need to have their own priority rating, even if they have their status icons showing. For instance, taking care of high-maintenance plants.

The Witness is a lovely world, filled with puzzles and, presumably, some sort of mystery or story to solve, but after almost four hours, I just can't be bothered.
Every puzzle builds on the last, but figuring out exactly how the mechanics of those changes work can be a lot of trial and error, as there is no tutorial or instruction anywhere to indicate how some mechanics work. You feel insanely clever when you figure it out, but if you can't, it can be a bit immersion breaking, as some puzzles that are so obtuse that you have to resort to a wiki. For me, that's either a sign that you designed the puzzles badly or you expect all of your audience to be on your wavelength.
I enjoyed the first few sets of puzzles, but when you get to the point that you're either writing stuff down or taking screenshots (it's not cheating, btw, PrintScrn takes in-game shots), it just becomes tedious.
I would also have liked more variety in the puzzle styles, as another reviewer said. If you really enjoy solving maze puzzles with all sorts of logical roadblocks layered on top, you'll think Christmas has come early.
The openness of some areas makes finding the next logical evolution of the puzzle a chore. Take a wrong turn, take the boat somewhere out of the way and you're fairly and squarely in walking sim territory, slowly lolloping your way to the next set of puzzles.
I really want to like the game, but, truthfully, I think I'm genuinely either too stupid or too impatient to play this game, with a high likelihood of both being the case! If you like to spend hours wandering in a beautiful world, solving mazes and have a very logical mind, then I highly recommend this game. It's just not for me.

This game is great.
You're dropped on an island with no context or any dialogue, and it stays that way throughout. I fell in love with this game because they left the story telling up to you, with you having to not only figure out all the puzzles on the island, but what's happened there in the past. I've played through a fair chunk of it (I'm guessing around 80%) and I still want to go back in and keep finding all the mysteries. This is a particularly big thing for me, since I rarely finish games these days because I get bored of them too quickly.
The puzzles vary in difficulty ranging from relatively easy, to down-right hard, and often I found myself trying to actually figure out what the rules to the puzzles were; which was a great feeling when you finally figured it out. It's a genius idea for gameplay, because you do get those moments of frustration, but they're always outweighed by the satisfaction of figuring out the fundamental rules of a puzzle set, and then being able to apply it to all the subsequent puzzles.
The design of this game is also breathtakingly beautiful. The time and effort of all the modelling, texturing, ambience really shows, and it helps to just absorb you into the game, where hours just disappear. I love how a large portion of the game is based around context, and in playing it, you gain understanding of why it's named "The Witness". Even the decision to only use WASD and the mouse for controls, and not have any other way to interact with things was a great choice.
It's a beautiful, emotive experience, which I'll be recommending to all my friends. So glad I got this game, it'll go down as one of my all-time favourites.

The first thing most people would expect after watching the trailer of Furi is a third-person action games similar to the likes of Ninja Gaiden Black, DMC, and Bayonetta, centered around mastering a deep combat system and getting high ranks by being flashy. Yet Furi is a boss rush game whose moveset is downright basic, has no ranking outside of not getting hit/knocked-out and speedkilling bosses, and has no zillion encounters to test your skills in. Rather, the game that could be compared the most to Furi would be Treasure Co.'s Alien Soldier for the Sega Genesis, a similar boss rush game which pits you against 26 bosses and features several mechanics used in Furi (parry to regain health, bullet canceling, dashing), and Treasure is even listed in the special thanks section of Furi's credits.
While your moveset may be incredibly simple, as you will be mostly shooting, slashing with one combo, dashing and parrying, all of which chargeable except the parry, Furi's strongest aspect is definitely how it can make the most out of these limited moves through its incredibly varied bosses. On top of the audio-visual presentation and the wildly differing personalities of the bosses, each boss also brings its own gimmick to the table, so no two bosses feel the same. This isn't a case of having an incredibly deep combat system and never being challenged enough to use it to its fullest extent, but a case of simple gameplay being utilized to its fullest through incredibly varied encounter design. Furi isn't the best twin-stick shooter, nor is it the best hack 'n slash, but it combines all these elements to provide an incredibly varied boss rush experience, and a damn good one at that. On top of that, the boss fights in Furi have some excellent pacing and build-up, making the fight feel like an actual fight with its ups and downs, as each fight ends with a final desperate attack you must survive until the boss stops being invincible. It's worth playing because of its variety alone, as none can say Furi feels samey.
One of Furi's biggest draws is the many speedrunning strategies for speedkilling bosses, which is a core focus of the game. Many phases of the boss fights are designed in such a way that the boss initiates a more difficult attack during the later part of his current phase while turning invincible, which you can skip by simply dealing more damage as quickly as possible and moving on to the melee phase of the current phase. With proper zoning, you can control the position of bosses in such a way that you can dash behind them when they perform a directed bullet hell attack as you effortlessly keep shooting the boss in the back while he's too busy spamming bullets in another direction you're completely safe from. Bullets can be parried back, so you can effectively keep shooting at the boss while parrying back the occassional bullet. You can also keep shooting while parrying attacks in general. During melee phases your ability to shoot is replaced with the ability to boost, which temporarily locks you in place as you boost yourself and boosts your next attack to (usually) deal so much damage that it depletes one-third of the boss's HP, but the boost effect is lost when you get hit.
On top of that, there's several other neat little tricks within the basic moveset. Charged shots can be used to interrupt attacks since bosses usually dodge charged shots when they aren't in an vulnerable position. Half-charged attacks and shots can be used to optimize your DPS. If you land a perfect parry, you can shoot the boss for a little while as he's stunned before performing a Punish attack. When you have to strike the boss to initiate the melee phase, you can strike him with the fourth and last hit of your only combo to knock him down and give you some time to boost your attack. You can charge attacks while dashing. And there's many boss-specific speedkill strategies as well.
An unfortunate consequence is that some phases of boss fights feel like they're not designed around shooting while parrying, which will become your dominant strategy. You can literally sit in a corner and keep shooting at the boss while parrying any incoming attacks until the boss dies, like in The Scale Phase 2, 4 and 5, and The Burst Phase 4, 5. Having speedkill strategies is nice, but it shouldn't trivialize the challenge completely.
While Furi may be difficult, it's easy to learn as long as you play aggressively. You don't have to wait until the boss' combo ends before you can attack, you can also try and attack him halfway through his combo to save you some time. Shooting the boss is always an option, and over time you don't need to learn bosses through trial and error since the telegraphing used for attacks is mostly identical across all bosses. The timing for parry attacks is always the same, bullets are clearly destructible and indestructible, you always have to dash through wave attacks, and so on. But it's the little variation in these basic attacks which can give a lot of personality to each boss. However, it might be difficult to come to terms with the controls.
Most people will feel like there's a input delay when dashing, but in reality that's because you only dash when you
the dash button, the reason being to accomodate the charging function for dashing by holding the button down. It's still a nonsensical decision to tie an important function such as dashing you want to use on reflex and delay it by making it an on-release function, leading to situations where even though you did respond to an attack by pressing the dash button, it didn't count because you didn't release it on time, which is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. While most wave attacks are slow, for fast attacks like the blue waves The Song ♥♥♥♥♥ out it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The implementation of the controls isn't as perfect as it should be either. It's hard to gauge whether you're actually aiming at the boss while shooting normally over long-ranges, and some attacks require dashing in a precise direction which is better executed using the right stick used for aiming and shooting, rather than the left stick which has you move while charging your dash. This also poses a problem where if you are using both sticks at the same time and dash, which input it uses for the direction of the dash can be seemingly random, as I can shoot forwards but I want to dash to the left, yet the game interprets it as dashing forward since I held my right stick forwards. This could have been simply solved by having seperate inputs for charged dashes and normal dashes which activate on-press, or simply ditching the need for a charged dash.
The story of the game excels at feeling like a personal journey, though this is done in part through unskippable walking segments, despite the presence of skippable cutscenes. People can say they tolerate it, but nobody will tell you it's necessary for the game, as it will likely do more harm than good to people's opinion of the game. They're about a few minutes long doing nothing but holding forwards, though an auto-walk button exists. It's there because the developers wanted to give weight to the story, but people wanted a boss rush game, not Gone Home.
Overall, Furi is a nice stylish boss rush game with excellent music and presentation on top of a lot of varied boss fights. The dialogue is still quite quotable and the story is still interesting, despite the forced implementation. The controls may not be as perfect as they have to be, but at least the game is somewhat built around it, there are already people who have speedrun the game without taking a single hit. It's challenging, but not impossible.

In 'Furi' you enter the role of an unnamed male suffering an uncommon complex reffered to as a 'furry'. Dealing with the cruel prejudice society places on this peculiar niche, you as the player must navigate through a variety of terrain and enemies to reach a satisfying conclusion and crush the status quo. 'Furi' masterfully uses all its assets to enrich its environments and boss battles with deep and meaningful symbolism, pushing the message in a deeper level without cramming it down your throat. To conclude, 'Furi' has changed the way in which i view these 'furries' making me empathise with them on a much more deeper level. 10/10 would cry again.
P.S. Furi is actually a wonderful game with deep and rewarding gameplay accompanied by a solid soundtrack which is really intuned with the environment and character design. I would recommend this game for anyone who has enjoyed previous titles such as: 'Dark Souls', 'Hyper Light Drifter', and 'Nier'. While I will admit this game is a unique beast it draws a lot of similarities to the previously mentioned titles.

What makes a game great? Difficulty? No. Progression and a sense of overcoming ever increasing challenges? Yes. Perhaps the developer wasn't trying to make a great game, perhaps he was, but bottom line, it's a BAD game.
It's not hard to make a bad game. Consider this; let's take Diablo II, a game heralded as best of its genre even after all these years, could I screw that up? Easily, by tweaking something as simple as drop rates, or damage etc. Just look at Diablo III for proof.
Thankfully, the PC game is a forgiving medium, look at what Aarkalash did, they made their easy mode easy. Volgarr has no different modes, and thus is such a niche game as to be inaccessible to the market. Folks that grew up playing games like Rastan (and still do) would find this offering a waste of time. Rastan is better. Why would I play Volgaar?
Maybe buy this game for 50 cents. Maybe.

This game is not a fun game. Its a boring hard grind from start to finnish. The game tries its hardest to kill you in cheap ways, miss time a jump - dead, swing your weapon at the wrong time - dead, use the downward attack (doesnt work 25% of the time) - dead. Start from the beggining of the level and redo it all without any mistakes. If you get hit once on the way to the boss you may aswel restart. It tries to be hard for the sake of being hard which doesnt lead to an enjoyable experience.
The game pads its length out by making you redo the levels everytime you die, this made sense back when we were all playing megadrive games and you couldnt save progress but this is 2014 and we have moved on from this artificial style of difficuilty. While the majority of games these days are far to easy and hold your hand through everything this game goes the exact opposite way and too far in that direction. Its hard because you have to remmember the location of every enemy and their attack pattern and the exact way to deal with that enemy in that location, the game is basically one long session of memorising trivial details and then carrying out those movements precisely each time.
The game has a certain charm to its style and it can be satisfying when you finnaly defeat that boss you were stuck on. There is pretty much no story, your a viking, go forward and hit things, you pick up gear to take more hits and do more damage, get hit and you lose that gear. It tries to be somewhat of a 2d darksouls, but that game betters it in every concievable way, the game is hard to better portray its story not for the sake of being hard, the combat system far superior etc.
Its a hark back to old style games which is fun for 30 minutes and then you remmember why you dont still play those games.

The island is big. You will run around a lot. That makes the game long. Not that it has a huge amount of content, just the fact that you'll run around. You can't jump. So you have to run around some more even though the area you want to go is right in front of you, but it's a meter too low. So run. Run run run.
Nothing in the island means anything to me. There is no meaning. Why am I here? I don't care. Why do I do these puzzles? I don't know. They don't do anything. There is no feeling of purpose.
And immersive? No. It's just a colorful island. Since I don't have a purpose or a goal I can't be immersed.
Then there's the videos and audio files. I don't care about them either. They don't relate to anything in the game. They seem to be there so people will spend even more time in the game, without actually accomplishing anything.
I like puzzles. Just not the same puzzle 500 times without accomplishing anything or feeling like I am doing something worthwhile.
I'll still finish it. And hate it. And have no idea how some people have spend over 50 hours in this game when it clearly doesn't deserve it.
If you find this on sale for $5 it might be ok. More than that... No.

Unbelievably good game. The challenge of every puzzle is, despite frustration, extremely rewarding. The setting and atmosphere of the island are also unbeatable. Yes yes yes.
It starts very slowly. Admittedly I didn't play for long, but I got bored. It's part walking simulator, part puzzler. Nice graphics. Not much else going for it.

Can't say I'd recommend it. Really poorly designed. Puzzles are thrown all over with next to no organization. You're going to run into puzzles you haven't been taught to solve yet randomly, and you'll end up having to leave areas half completed until you find the one bit of information you need to solve it.
Credit where it's due, there's some really nifty secrets and interesting puzzles. Sometimes it's totally ordinary, sometimes you have to use sound to complete the puzzle, and sometimes there's hidden puzzles hidden in bricks and flowers. But the lack of direction really kills it. Running into dead ends isn't fun, challenging, or rewarding, it's just frustrating. If there was any indication as to where you should next, it would be way better, I might even recommend it. But the fact that there's absolutely no guidance and you'd have no idea how to complete some areas until you've learned what to do in other areas is really bad.
Basically, almost good, no direction, gets really boring before you can figure out what you're supposed to do next.

(TL;DR: no music, great visuals, TONS of varied puzzles and hidden stuff to find, with an optional plot that you will or will not get into. If you're in it for the puzzles, you should be okay.)
A beautiful, huge island to explore at length, and a MASSIVE amount of puzzles to solve on the way. That's the way it starts. The game system is easy to understand, the puzzles themselves start easy enough until you get further into the island and realize how devious they get.
Let's be clear: The Witness requires a lot of walking around, and to that effect, the beautiful visuals and scattered hidden soundclips help. I read a review mentioning brute-forcing puzzles with unknown mechanics in frustration. They're doing it wrong. Every puzzle type has its own dedicated area, and this is the beauty of the game: The Witness
, and it does so very naturally. You'll come across a new area and find a new puzzle type, a very simple one. Then a slightly tougher one. And so on until you get to the difficult one that will ensure you figured out how that specific type of puzzle works. And when you have, many other areas will open to you. It's an
gratifying feeling to get in a puzzle game.
Granted, some puzzle types are harder to figure out than others, some areas have their own logic based on the environment. This is what's keeping things interesting. You can also largely bypass some of the toughest puzzles and still complete the game.
Now, the overall theme and special ending may or may not do it for you. The contemplative tone faintly reminded me of the Talos Principle in a way. Your mileage may vary. At any rate you'll get to hear a few historical quotes, and might get to watch a couple instructive, philosophical (and entirely optional) videos. Note that if you get far enough in the game, the plot actually seems to make slightly more sense, but don't hold your breath.
Last detail: with the exception of one zone with audio puzzles, and a couple other specific spots with video or music, there is no soundtrack, only ambient sounds. The good thing is that it allows you to blast whatever genre of music from your own collection while you play. I found a 'Chill' playlist on Spotify to that effect and got a great experience out of it!

So, this is the first time I've actually played Magic.  I've always been interested in playing Magic, but there were a few things about card-collection driven gameplay that always turned me off.  One, it leads to uneven gameplay.  Two, it will likely have me spending lots of money on additional card pacts to try and find rare cards.  Three, even though I hadn't even tried playing the game, I figured that I'd rather play a version of Magic where the winner is determined by in-game tactics (how you use your cards) or a bit of luck (the order that the cards fly out of the deck), rather than 'the player with the best collection of cards wins.'  Somehow I convinced myself that all of this would be different if I were to buy a video game version of it...
So, completely oblivious, I started playing.  Initially I'm just having fun getting the hang of the rules, unlocking a few starter decks... and then I get ♥♥♥♥ed.  I learn to un-♥♥♥♥ myself.  I get ♥♥♥♥ed again.  Slowly, I start piecing together the 'rock, paper, scissors, lighter, squirt-gun, Legos’ style tactics the game employs.  And, through this enjoyable, yet painful, ♥♥♥♥ing and un-♥♥♥♥ing learning process, the game teaches me how important the meta-game deck selection and deck building tactics are.  This was not a point I was willing to concede for quite a while.  I had grown rather fond of a particular deck and wanted to think I could beat anyone with it, but I’m afraid that’s just not true for the starting cards.  Eventually I fell back on the 'cheaper' tactics of other elemental decks.  If my opponent was zerg-rushing, I’d try to out zerg them.  If my opponent was inhibiting all of my creatures, I’d bypass the need for creatures and just attack the player with spells.  If an opponent is killing off all of your important creatures with black magic, switch to a black magic deck so most of their spells can’t harm you, etcetera.
The game is mainly about sizing up your opponent, realizing what deck and strategy they'll try to use, and responding with an appropriate deck/counter strategy.  The gameplay elements that I had previously focused so much importance on were mainly just the aftermath.  Sure, some tactics are required during gameplay, but in my experience it rarely makes a significant difference in the outcome of a match.  There is still a large bit of luck required though.  A strong starting hand and the order in which cards are revealed can swing the outcome of a match.  That being said, most of the matches I played were against opponents with better cards in their deck, so luck could have played a bigger role.
I really enjoyed playing the campaign (player vs AI) waaaaay too much.  Like, 14 hours straight 'too much.'  The campaign, like many campaigns, seemed like a good extended tutorial.  It pits you against many opponents that attack you with a variety of strategies which keeps it fresh and challenging.  Some strategies work pretty well against multiple opponents, but eventually you’ll find something that will make you mix things up.  I’ve yet to play multiplayer to see if anything I’ve learned from the campaign will pay off…  To be honest, I’m a bit afraid of the multiplayer.  I have a feeling that it’s going to be a lot like Starcraft… there will be a lot of ‘getting ♥♥♥♥ed’ being had on my end. :)

I won't spoil anything, although I find the story in this game to be fairly interesting. You play as the character Ajay Ghale, who has traveled to the land of Kyrat on his mother's dying wish to have her ashes be placed in a place called Lakshmana. Although when you arrive, you're put straight in the middle of a civil war between a rebellious group called The Golden Path, and the king Pagan Min. (Pagan is a great character, although sadly misunderstood. He's not as bad as the game makes him out to be, you can see that by how he treats you in the game and what he talks about.)
Kyrat belongs to you, and you must take it back.
The gameplay is pretty interesting. It's sort of what you make of it, and what your playstyle is. Either it can be a gorefest, blow your way through enemy, intense shooter - or it can be a challenging stealth game where a knife, bow, and silenced pistol will become your best friend.
One thing that deserves a mention is the driving in the game. The Far Cry series has a pretty satisfying driving mechanic in the games, although this one seems to be the best in my opinion. It's a little difficult at first because it can be a bit touchy, but once you figure it out, it's a load of fun, and it makes long drives less of a pain because of how enjoyable it can be.
Gunplay is pretty solid, it's about what you'd expect from a game like this. Even though I find myself using a bow and shotgun over anything, every gun is fairly easy to pick up and work with.
The audio in this game is phenomenal. Get a decent set of speakers, or even your TV speakers, and you'll feel immersed in the game as if you're in the mountains of Kyrat yourself.

This is a beautifuly crafted survival basebuilding game.
It has its limits, and a good deal of quirks - but once you get the hang of it, it is a good game for what it tries to do.
The trick I have found is you cannot build big first and fast. Start small, expand cautiously - and make liberal use of landing privledges. Nothing wrong when knowing you can't take more in than you can handle. Expand too fast, spend too much too quick and you end up digging yourself into a hole you are not prepared for. Slow and steady wins the race, and this hammers that lesson in hard.
To me, this is the space survival management game I was looking for in other titles, and it does it in a very fair manner.
A definite reccomindation from me if you are looking for a good space survival management game.
EDIT:
Once I got enough play hours and kept growing larger and larger bases a major flaw is becomming apparent: the AI is spotty. They have done a number to help, but the core issue is a pathing problem that doesn't account the domes or connections as lines, but rather needs and a radius of search. The result is a habit to cluster, often overpopulating and draining resources much faster than desired. Its not unsolveable I think, and would hope it is patched more adequately - but aside from that issue, it does not dissuade me from enjoying the game.
It is just a hiccup to learn for now, annoying sure, but not unsolveable. It still leaves a rather astheically beautiful game that runs surprisingly well and hammers in a strong survival balancing act of how to grow and expand without overstepping your abilities. I still see this as a good reccomendation, but now with abit of caution - it is borderline punishing if you don't find a good way to grasp the AI issues, or at least until they patch them better. But to me, that's the kind of challenging addition that is almost to be expected here.

This War of Mine is a masterpiece of a game, mostly in storytelling and survival. I've played this game for nearly a good 2 years and have spent quite a lot of time on it, honestly it is one of the best games I have played. The game gets you to control a few civilians trying to survive a war in a city called Porogen, a city now where Soldiers, Rebels and Civilians are in a constant battle in order to stay alive, some will be helpful, others won't, some will ask for your help, others will help you, so on. When you start a game, you have to wait an unknown amount of days till the war ends (it's random unless you created a  custom story), you'll have to create furniture, workbenches and other items to help you survive, you will need to scavenge for supplies each night (you can stay inside if you want to) and ration food in order to get to the end of the war.
Soon, you'll come across random events and have to loot more dangerous areas, making the game harder as you go on, so you will need to use your supplies wisely in those times. Once you have made it to the end of the war, the game ends, in the ending screen you will see the epilogue of all the characters you have met, their endings will depend on how well you survive so remember to try and make the right decisions to keep them alive and happy.
That's the game in short, it's a great game and you should definitely try it out, it doesn't cost that much and the DLC that comes with the game is also very good, including the War Child DLC in where you donate money to children living in cities and towns affected by war.
I give the game 9/10, it does have it's flaws at times, but it is certainly a game that I will always remember.
You can spend hours,days without getting bored.

The first thing most people would expect after watching the trailer of Furi is a third-person action games similar to the likes of Ninja Gaiden Black, DMC, and Bayonetta, centered around mastering a deep combat system and getting high ranks by being flashy. Yet Furi is a boss rush game whose moveset is downright basic, has no ranking outside of not getting hit/knocked-out and speedkilling bosses, and has no zillion encounters to test your skills in. Rather, the game that could be compared the most to Furi would be Treasure Co.'s Alien Soldier for the Sega Genesis, a similar boss rush game which pits you against 26 bosses and features several mechanics used in Furi (parry to regain health, bullet canceling, dashing), and Treasure is even listed in the special thanks section of Furi's credits.
While your moveset may be incredibly simple, as you will be mostly shooting, slashing with one combo, dashing and parrying, all of which chargeable except the parry, Furi's strongest aspect is definitely how it can make the most out of these limited moves through its incredibly varied bosses. On top of the audio-visual presentation and the wildly differing personalities of the bosses, each boss also brings its own gimmick to the table, so no two bosses feel the same. This isn't a case of having an incredibly deep combat system and never being challenged enough to use it to its fullest extent, but a case of simple gameplay being utilized to its fullest through incredibly varied encounter design. Furi isn't the best twin-stick shooter, nor is it the best hack 'n slash, but it combines all these elements to provide an incredibly varied boss rush experience, and a damn good one at that. On top of that, the boss fights in Furi have some excellent pacing and build-up, making the fight feel like an actual fight with its ups and downs, as each fight ends with a final desperate attack you must survive until the boss stops being invincible. It's worth playing because of its variety alone, as none can say Furi feels samey.
One of Furi's biggest draws is the many speedrunning strategies for speedkilling bosses, which is a core focus of the game. Many phases of the boss fights are designed in such a way that the boss initiates a more difficult attack during the later part of his current phase while turning invincible, which you can skip by simply dealing more damage as quickly as possible and moving on to the melee phase of the current phase. With proper zoning, you can control the position of bosses in such a way that you can dash behind them when they perform a directed bullet hell attack as you effortlessly keep shooting the boss in the back while he's too busy spamming bullets in another direction you're completely safe from. Bullets can be parried back, so you can effectively keep shooting at the boss while parrying back the occassional bullet. You can also keep shooting while parrying attacks in general. During melee phases your ability to shoot is replaced with the ability to boost, which temporarily locks you in place as you boost yourself and boosts your next attack to (usually) deal so much damage that it depletes one-third of the boss's HP, but the boost effect is lost when you get hit.
On top of that, there's several other neat little tricks within the basic moveset. Charged shots can be used to interrupt attacks since bosses usually dodge charged shots when they aren't in an vulnerable position. Half-charged attacks and shots can be used to optimize your DPS. If you land a perfect parry, you can shoot the boss for a little while as he's stunned before performing a Punish attack. When you have to strike the boss to initiate the melee phase, you can strike him with the fourth and last hit of your only combo to knock him down and give you some time to boost your attack. You can charge attacks while dashing. And there's many boss-specific speedkill strategies as well.
An unfortunate consequence is that some phases of boss fights feel like they're not designed around shooting while parrying, which will become your dominant strategy. You can literally sit in a corner and keep shooting at the boss while parrying any incoming attacks until the boss dies, like in The Scale Phase 2, 4 and 5, and The Burst Phase 4, 5. Having speedkill strategies is nice, but it shouldn't trivialize the challenge completely.
While Furi may be difficult, it's easy to learn as long as you play aggressively. You don't have to wait until the boss' combo ends before you can attack, you can also try and attack him halfway through his combo to save you some time. Shooting the boss is always an option, and over time you don't need to learn bosses through trial and error since the telegraphing used for attacks is mostly identical across all bosses. The timing for parry attacks is always the same, bullets are clearly destructible and indestructible, you always have to dash through wave attacks, and so on. But it's the little variation in these basic attacks which can give a lot of personality to each boss. However, it might be difficult to come to terms with the controls.
Most people will feel like there's a input delay when dashing, but in reality that's because you only dash when you
the dash button, the reason being to accomodate the charging function for dashing by holding the button down. It's still a nonsensical decision to tie an important function such as dashing you want to use on reflex and delay it by making it an on-release function, leading to situations where even though you did respond to an attack by pressing the dash button, it didn't count because you didn't release it on time, which is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. While most wave attacks are slow, for fast attacks like the blue waves The Song ♥♥♥♥♥ out it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The implementation of the controls isn't as perfect as it should be either. It's hard to gauge whether you're actually aiming at the boss while shooting normally over long-ranges, and some attacks require dashing in a precise direction which is better executed using the right stick used for aiming and shooting, rather than the left stick which has you move while charging your dash. This also poses a problem where if you are using both sticks at the same time and dash, which input it uses for the direction of the dash can be seemingly random, as I can shoot forwards but I want to dash to the left, yet the game interprets it as dashing forward since I held my right stick forwards. This could have been simply solved by having seperate inputs for charged dashes and normal dashes which activate on-press, or simply ditching the need for a charged dash.
The story of the game excels at feeling like a personal journey, though this is done in part through unskippable walking segments, despite the presence of skippable cutscenes. People can say they tolerate it, but nobody will tell you it's necessary for the game, as it will likely do more harm than good to people's opinion of the game. They're about a few minutes long doing nothing but holding forwards, though an auto-walk button exists. It's there because the developers wanted to give weight to the story, but people wanted a boss rush game, not Gone Home.
Overall, Furi is a nice stylish boss rush game with excellent music and presentation on top of a lot of varied boss fights. The dialogue is still quite quotable and the story is still interesting, despite the forced implementation. The controls may not be as perfect as they have to be, but at least the game is somewhat built around it, there are already people who have speedrun the game without taking a single hit. It's challenging, but not impossible.
8/10

This War of Mine is a third-person survival game designed to show that war is not glorious, or good, and that soldiers are not the only ones who are fighting for their lives. It's a message we think we all know, but upon deeper consideration, we really only know war as the glorified task it is presented as being by most games and most movies. Well, This War of Mine will tear that belief down, and replace it with the brutal and perilous reality of war for the civilian population in the most simple, yet heart breaking way, as you are made responsible for the fate of a small group of characters who fell victim to the conflict.
The game itself is a 2D simulation, if you will, where you can select characters and have them perform certain tasks such as searching containers for useful items, sitting, sleeping (to recover health and tiredness), opening or unlocking doors, moving rubble, that sort of thing. The game works on a day and night cycle basis, where during the day you search the building you start in, and eat etc, and during night, you raid other points on the map to find sufficient food and resources to survive. Each point has its advantages and disadvantages depending on what kind of place they are. One place may be safe, and have loads of building parts, while the other may have loads of food and medication but be full of danger. You must calculate the risks and try, at all costs, to ensure everyone survives.
In the game, you face realistic challenges to be expected in a post-war society, such as raids, where other, desperate people steal your stuff so that they might live. You may also encounter the heartless military who have no mercy on scavengers, and are much better equipped than you. Your characters will also fall into depression from both illness, and the act of killing, no matter what the circumstances. There are also natural elements to overcome, such as the cold, and without fuel for fires, your characters will succumb to it.
The artwork in the game looks incredible, while at the same time maintaining a very black and grey colour scheme to highlight the depression and the darkness of life during the war. The music is aptly haunting as over it you hear the activities of your character but equally as heart-breaking in tragic moments such as death, despite it being so simple. There is also the distant sound of artillery and gunfire - not loud enough to distract you, but loud enough that you always know it is there - that the war has not gone, and death gets ever nearer. The atmosphere of the game is realistically scary, and draws out the true fear, anguish and depression that a war inflicts upon those whom it makes victims.
This War of Mine will take you on a journey - one which you'd never wish to embark upon in real life, yet one that many have, and many will. It will open your eyes to the struggle of survival in a time where death and destruction plague the land, and claim lives by the millions. The way this game impacts your emotions, evoking sympathy for people that you do not even know, in a war that you do not know, is truly powerful. It leaves the true idea with you that this might have been you. It shows the grim truth that "when the rich wage war, It's the poor that die". It really teaches you not to take your life for granted - to appreciate that which you have, for there came a day, for real people, where it was all taken off them. That could have happened to anyone.
War does not determine who is right. Only who is left.

'Furi' masterfully uses all its assets to enrich its environments and boss battles with deep and meaningful symbolism, pushing the message in a deeper level without cramming it down your throat. To conclude, 'Furi' has changed the way in which i view these 'furries' making me empathise with them on a much more deeper level. 10/10 would cry again.

Pros:
-Satisfying puzzles.

Cons:

[Review for both Episode 1 and 2]
One day when I was a kid, I was looking for a cheap holiday read in one of Gloucester’s 4396 discount books-that-no-other-shop-wanted stores and came across a book that was so invocative and fascinating that I simply had to have it. Creatures From Elsewhere set my mind alight with the apparent mystery of creatures unknown to science but somehow leaving their mark upon the Earth. The opening chapters centred upon Bigfoot, and Bigfoot foot like creatures. It was marvellous and thrilling stuff. Utter nonsense, but I loved it. I love Bigfoot and all his mates. From Tintin in Tibet to Bigfoot centric X-Files episodes, the whole mythos of this elusive man-ape creature is so engaging that I can’t help but adore the whole Bigfoot culture. So seeing a puzzle game about a Bigfoot mystery appear in the Steam store was a real no-brainer for me.
Jacob Jones is a kid on his way to summer camp at Camp Evil Eagle Feather. He wears a blue bear coat. Already this is a thoroughly charming game. Needless to say, there is a Bigfoot involved and a mystery. This plays out in a very lovely cardboard cut-out style environment with cute stylised character models. It reminded me a lot of Psychonauts, which is one of my favourite games ever so any resemblance, even if just in passing, is fine by me. The story is rather basic, but it makes up for it by having some wonderfully witty dialogue and laugh out loud worthy gags. There are an awful lot of horror referencing tucked away into the largely child-friendly dialogue, some jokes got surprisingly dark in nature (especially one right at the end of episode 2). There are only a handful of characters that Jacob has any real interaction with but the ones that are in place are well voice acted and come with their own little idiosyncrasies that set them apart. Little details such as the rage fuelled Coach and his bulging eyes or one of Jacob’s bunk-mates’ runny nose and chronic snot bubble problem made for some just adorable people. Then there’s the Bigfoot, the star attraction. Biggie, as he’s known, is a lovable furry lump with a friendly demeanour and a joyfully silly dog disguise. Getting the Bigfoot right was essential. Lucid games nailed him.
The meat of the game is in the puzzling. Although there is a world to explore and some folk to chat to, most of the gameplay is devoted to single screen puzzles à la the Professor Layton games on the Nintendo DS. The puzzles are an assortment of logic, sliding block and maths puzzles and will mostly offer a good brain teasing without being annoying. I came across one puzzle I found a bit confusing but that could be just as well down to the fact I’m not so great at maths puzzles. Give me a Sudoku and I’ll probably just draw pictures of hedgehogs on it and run away with my hands in the air and cackling like a maniac. Luckily, my hand wasn’t forced like that in Jacob Jones. With the exception of the maths puzzle I found the puzzle screens to be eminently satisfying and engaging. Sometimes the puzzle instructions could be a little vague on what needed to be done, but everything is presented excellently and more often than not the game of the puzzle comes to you instinctively.
A handy feature is the memo screen that lets you doodle over the screen to keep track of your puzzle progress. It’s a testament to how well made the puzzles are constructed in that at no point did I resort to doodling hedgehogs on the memo screen in frustration. If you do find yourself stuck, there is a hint system that lets you exchange soda cans (that the environmentally minded Jacob has picked up) for a nod in the right direction. Using his phone, Jacob can get either a vague hint from his friends, a more specific push from his brother or a fairly explicit direction from his uncle. It all works well and keeps the game flowing nicely.
I would have liked the environmental interaction to be a bit more developed. There isn’t really much to do in the world. It looks lovely but it serves as little more than a way to link the unconnected puzzles together. It would have been nice to have more to do than pick up soda cans and bother gophers. As basic as the movement controls are, they are still a bit wonky. The keyboard shortcuts for rotating the screen are Q and E but the keys for moving the view around are the arrow keys. This can be done with the mouse but doing both movements at the same time makes your mouse cursor pretty unreliable. The game was originally made for the touch screens on mobile devises but I would have liked more thought given to how the controls work on a PC, or at least to give an option to change the controls myself or use a control pad.
The game does lack configuration options in general. Volume, full screen on/off and resolution are the only options available. This irritated me specifically because I desperately wanted to turn off the damn depth of field which gave the screen a constant blurring around the edges that I found incredibly off-putting. The game is made with the Unreal Engine so tinkering with the .ini files to get the graphics settings you want is usually an option, but even that couldn’t remove the effects I found so obnoxious. Likewise, there was a constant gentle sway to the whole game that seemed entirely unnecessary but I found no way to turn it off and keep the damn screen still.
These are relatively minor quibbles to a game that I had a lot of fun with. I picked the episode one and two pack for a fiver on Steam and got around five hours worth of delightful puzzling. It may be short but I found it to be well worth the price for the amount of fun I had playing it. I’m now looking forward to episode three, assuming there will be one. I could serious go on for far longer talking about how charming it is. Jacob Jones and the Bigfoot Mystery has stomped its way into my heart and rekindled my love of Bigfoot. I love you Biggie.

Cons:
