There is so much to say about this game but at the same time, there isn't. This is not a game about a hero, saving the world and gracing everyone with their divine presence. This is the story of a little bar called VA-11 Hall-A or "Valhalla", its patrons, its owner and especially of one of the employees called Jill.

The player takes the roll of Jill in this story, making sure she has money for bills, things she might want to buy and to make sure she serves the right drinks to the patrons of Valhalla, which isn't as easy as it might sound considering the patrons aren't always as specific with their orders as they could be.

Speaking of the patrons, Jill has to deal with all kinds of people from Glitch City. From a smart and romantic hacker to an unseeming private detective over to a sexbot that doesn't even look old enough to stay up after midnight. Her co-worker and boss aren't any less strange as well as the bar seemed to attract those type of people.

Overall, this game has to be one of the most relaxed games I have played in a long time. That doesn't mean it is boring by any means though. As mentioned in the beginning, this is not the story of a glorious hero who defeats evil but rather the story of a normal girl who has to deal with bills, fears, weird events and blasts from the past. It's not always sunshine and rainbows for Jill and she knows that.

Music, visuals and character development are all stellar, coupled together with an incredibly interesting world and relatable moments make this a must-have for everyone that can take a step back and relax while playing a game. I surely will replay this many times as its many little quirks and characters have grown on me swiftly.

On the negative side, all I can say is that I ran into a small bug or two but nothing that a reload or restart of the game couldn't handle. Both were sound issues that happen if one was to go too swiftly through the game by smashing the spacebar. (Pro tip, don't do that. Why would you even do that?)

Fun space shooter game if you like a more arcade-ish experience.
* It's not a space simulator akin to Elite: Dangerous.
* It's not as big and complex as something like EVE.
* It's more of a dog fighting game.
Pros
* Attractive.  Graphics are really nice, and it runs good on modest hardware.
* Fun.  The game play is pretty fast paced and it can really be a hoot (most of the time).
* Easy to play, difficult to master.  It's quick to get into a game and start playing.  There's a lot of depth in the ship bonuses and modules, so although it's simple to pick up and play, it would take quite some time, effort, and research to really raise the bar on your play through your ship configurations and item acquisitions.  This is a pro though, because skill and wisdom really does shine in this title.
* Real time action.  A lot of MMO-type games use auto attack and auto-aiming abilities to overcome network delay (Star Trek Online, I'm looking at you), but this one requires you to actually be a good aim with a majority of the weapons -- they fire where you point, not what you are locked onto (missiles do auto target though).
* High quality.  It doesn't feel cheap or play cheap.  The artwork and coding in this game is superior to many other F2P titles.  Though it's produced in Russia, which might be a warning flag to some, it's on par with AAA titles and is definitely legit.
Cons
* Lag.  I get a moderate amount of server lag in NA (rubber banding specifically; so packet loss and ping spikes).  I have insanely fast internet, and I ping major urban areas sub 30.  Granted it's very brief, but it happens fairly frequently.  Open space seems the worst for this.
* Grindy.  Let me repeat.  GRINDY.  If you hate games that take a large investment of time, you probably won't care for trying to get to the higher tiers in this game; it grows exponentially harder than the lower tiers.  That said, there are often bonus weekends of +50% for everyone, and you can buy in-game subscriptions with GS (paid currency) that is strictly earned in game.  But it's not often nor easy (you gotta be an achievement hound and can really only swing the 3-day sub, so do it on the bonus weekends!).
* Lower tiers need more content.  Literally, I played the same 3-4 maps for days until I ranked up to the next tier.  Bleh.  Why not scale all the maps and enemies to be based on team rank??  I couldn't do open space until rank 6 or so.  This could cause a new player to burn out very quickly.
* Pay4Convenience, aka pay2getahead.  Let me be clear: it's not pay to win.  But since everything requires grinding (and quite a lot of it), you can bypass a majority of the grinding by simply opening the wallet.  The advantages of some of the paid ships are a little staggering in terms of the time it would take to do it in game, particularly for higher tier ships.  For low tier game play, it's really not bad at all.  That said, most things can be obtained in game if you are careful with currency and diligent in your efforts (read: not most people, since there's a lot of guesswork involved).  Some things are pay only (special ship skins, basically).
* Item gap and/or Skill Curve.  Maybe it's people leveraging their paid currency and synergy bonuses, but the game seems to go from stupid easy to WTF hard.  By rank 3-4 you end up being one shotted by players in PvP and even a lot of ships in PvE.  So you'd do good to save up and focus on your modules and weapons, because the scaling is a little brutal when the training wheels come off.
Overall, for the price (free!), it's good times.  It's worth an install and a try, you have nothing to lose afterall.  I would recommend this game for anyone who enjoys space and sci-fi shooter games.  It plays a bit like FPS games as well because of the twitch game play style, so it should appeal to people of other genres as well.
It's just a solid, well polished, shooting game.  If that appeals to you in any fashion, definitely give it a try.

There's a lot to cover so we'll dive right in;
This is one of the worst puzzle games I have ever had the displeasure of playing.
The effort is here, it is all here.  Every element for success has been tucked into the product, every bit of potential is bursting at the seems, and so it becomes the most insulting, most disappointing, most infuriating thing to see every single one of those aspects fail over, and over, and over, and over again.
It is hard to summize everything wrong with The Witness, and almost impossible to do so in a short period, so if you just want a brief summary, it is as follows; there is no original writing, the visuals are fine, there's no music, the puzzles range from fantastic to utter garbage, and the two endings I've gotten thus far are some of the most pretentious, boring crap I've sat through in a long time.   Everything the Witness does, a game like Talos Principle will do better, so save yourself time and money and buy that instead.
----------
A breakdown;
BAD PUZZLES:
The puzzles are simple in theory, difficult in practice as any good puzzle game should be.  You click a circle, draw a line, and connect that line to the 'end' of the area.  This can be anything from a straight line to an entire maze.  This works on paper, and could even work in practice, were it not for the fact that it becomes tedious within the first hour or two.
Puzzles begin to include symbols and icons that change the rules of the individual mazes, and infuriatingly, these rules are not immediately explained.  Natural puzzle progression from good games in the genre will introduce a concept, make it more difficult, expand on it, and then incorporate it into larger concepts.  The Witness tries to do something similar, but will hide the tutorials in far removed areas of the island.  You will walk by puzzles with unknown, unexplained symbols twenty, thirty, FIFTY times before finding the area that explains how they work.  This non-linearity is not a point in the game's favor, as frustration will inevitably cause players to brute-force puzzles and work out at least some aspects of them before being TAUGHT.
What is worse, and what some have mind-bogglingly listed as POSITIVE of this title, some puzzles will force you to rely entirely on the environment to solve, with no indication or hint as to what they want from you.  You may need to leave the immediate area, stand on a raised platform and notice the shadows mark out a rough path.  You may need to stand behind a specific area of a specific tree and line up the branches to show where you can't go on a maze.  You may need to line up SEVERAL branches, see if those are the branches the game wants, fail, and then try another set.  Over and over and over.  It is not so much being presented with a 100-piece jigsaw puzzle and being asked to solve it, but being presented with a 100-piece puzzle that only has 99 pieces, and being mocked when you didn't realize the last piece was being hidden under a newspaper in the corner of the room.
LAZY WRITING:
The writing and dialogue is highly interesting, highly thought-provoking, and highly engrossing as you find collectibles all over the map.  The problem is that NONE OF IT is original writing!  Every scrap of it is ripped directly from lectures, quotations and speeches made from all across human history, and while almost all of it is incredibly interesting to listen to, you can't give a point to the game for it when all of it is also accessible from Google.  The developers and designers have not even attempted to put their own spin or perspective on the issues they are putting forth, instead drowning the player in sourced quotations from folk like Einstein.
BAD PUZZLE COLLECTIBLES:
On top of the interesting collectibles in the form of small data-sticks or videos, there are also the much more boring collectibles in the form off hidden mazes.  These are puzzles that are hidden in the environment themselves, forcing you to line up a balloon-and-string, for example, to form the circle and line that you then trace down and complete.  The issue here is that they rarely are ever actually PUZZLES; the difficulty is in finding the markings in the sand or rocks, or standing in the right place to see the metal girder match up with the stone wall.  Once you find it, it takes half a second to complete, and then off you go searching for another and there are DOZENS of these in the world.
LACK OF MUSIC:
There is no music, and the only sound is that of your footsteps and the occasional ambiance.  The developers used if memory serves something like 10,000 footstep sound samples for the game, and while I adore that kind of dedication and wish it was used more, I was desperately wishing at times for some actual background music while I stared blankly at a puzzle I'd been stuck on for 20 minutes.
INSULTING FINAL LEVEL:
The longer I played, the more irritated and frustrated I became with the poor design choices.  I will admit freely to using a guide at times and, by the final 'level', almost exclusively, because I became so tired with the cheap and childish tactics that I simply couldn't bring myself to care any longer.  Not only do you have to deal with puzzles not providing you with enough information to be solved, not only do you have to deal with trying to find where you should stand before you CAN solve certain puzzles, or if this is one of those puzzles you need to be somewhere else and that's the reason you cannot complete it, but by the final area, it genuinely feels as if the developers threw their hands up and stopped trying.
Where in most puzzle game, and good games period, the final areas are a compilation of all the tests and challenges you've faced, where you have to rely on the accumulation of your knowledge from time spent with the game, the final areas of the Witness simply couldn't be bothered.  Instead of becoming more difficult, they instead resort to pathetic, childish distractions.  Instead of solving a difficult puzzle, you have to solve a moderately-difficult puzzle while your screen flashes at you in distraction.  Or while the colors invert, or while the puzzle itself spins uncontrollably and you have to fight the controls to do what you want.  Even elsewhere in the game this is present, making you feel frustrated not because you are failing a logic puzzle, but because you can't control your mouse properly even after you know the solution.
BAD ENDINGS:
And to top it all off, the endings are garbage.  Pretentious, monotonous, BORING garbage.  Without spoiling specifics or location, one ending even has the audacity to fly you in near silence through the map you have just spent 15+ hours completing, showing as it erases all your progress and resets all the puzzles and work you have done.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
If you have read through this entire review, it should be clear that nobody who loathes a game would spend this much time writing about it.  I wanted, DESPERATELY wanted to enjoy this game, and the fact I spent more than 15 hours on a single run should prove that.  But every design decision fails, the mixing of good-with-bad puzzles leaves you frustrated and without the glorious "AH-HA!" moment you reach when solving a difficult challenge, the graphics are good, the story is lazy, the soundtrack is nonexistent, and every single thing this game does, the Talos Principle (which was released over a year or more before this) does better.  It is incredibly disappointing to see so much effort and talent go into a product that, ultimately, comes out as a 4.5/10, average or slightly worse than average, title.  Even after spending only 2$, roughly, on this product in a humble-bundle, I would advise any potential buyers to steer clear and spend their money elsewhere.

I wanted to like this game. Sadly, no.
I engaged with it initially - it has an expansive vision, and the graphics were peculiar, the absence of music notable in it's attempt to make the player more mindful. Essentially, that's what the game is about: mindfulness and puzzle-solving. But I think it goes too far into the mindfulness side, and forgets the fun.
I enjoyed Braid - it's a different experience (obviously), but it had drama, and atmosphere, and something about it.
On a technical side, the game suffers from an extreme lack of necessary linearity - I found myself traipsing from one end of the isle to the other, in an attempt to find tutorial sections for the given puzzle 'types', which, after a while, becomes frustrating and distracting. Also after a while there was no 'flow' - some puzzles simply came down to guessing what the author intended - not unlike an adventure game - rather than deduction.
It has it's merits, but at the end of the day, I didn't enjoy it.

The Witness is a triumph of games as art, though I think it could have been a more cohesive and compelling piece if it had truly had no language whatsoever; the message of the game is conveyed so thoroughly by the gameplay that, to me, the supplemental quotes felt superfluous and too on the nose, artifacts of older, more comfortable art forms.  Even so, for me, The Witness succeeded in its apparent mission of inspiring awe.
Gameplay-wise, if you enjoy drawing lines on grids that fulfill certain rules, and figuring out what those rules are without explanation, The Witness is delicious.  The environmental puzzles are only okay, but the spatial reasoning rules produce some really lovely epiphanies.  And there are deeper mysteries to the game that reminded me of that scene in Westworld where Ed Harris finds a map on the inside of some poor guy's scalp--just an utterly bizarre and unexpected layer of puzzles underlying the apparent game.
There are some ways in which The Witness could be less remote and inscrutable.  After I activated all the lasers, I spent hours wandering around the island looking for another one, because I thought there'd be some dramatic indication that I'd activated the final one; if there was, I didn't see it.  Accessing the post-game content requires some very careful observation, though in its defense it follows rules the game laid out earlier.  But these are minor blemishes in an otherwise fantastic (and at times profound) experience.

At times, The Witness may seem as though it is reserved for geniuses. It does have parts that are "brick wall" difficult, where you stand, cursing at a puzzle for a long while. More importantly, it is a fun, challenging puzzle game that has a lot of content. The Witness has an incredible way of teaching you principles and lessons without any dialogue. The Witness at its surface is a puzzle game, but symbolically it represents how mankind interpits the world around him. I'll go out on a limb and say playing the Witness makes you a better person. You'll feel a sense of accomplishment upon completion of areas, and for good reason. Instead of pressuring kids to go college, we should just give them a copy of the Witness.

This is going to be an honest review - this game is worth the money.
Though the premise sounds simple - build a base on 3 different planets and survive, it really isn't. It took me about 10 attempts to get a base up and running (and surviving) on the first planet, and I've just started on the second planet and it's I'm back to square one. All my ideas of base building have been turned upside down by the second planet, it's a totally different ball game.
The game is very unforgiving - it's easy to make the mistake of thinking "this is going really well!" only to have a meteor land on your dorm while 14 colonists are sleeping. Or the one dopey engineer that decides to build that new building you've waiting what seems like forever to gather the resources for, only for a solar flare to appear and fry him like an egg.
There are some features the game perhaps lacks - research in the "lab" (new technologies are bought from the trading ships), alien attacks (though there are intuders from visiting ships), the ability to set priorities on resource distribution (unless I missed this?) to name a few, but it's well worth the money for hours of entertainment.

Disregarding a handful of problems regarding strange keyboard controls (I know it reccomends gamepad), Furi is a solid game that holds up perfectly fine despite a lack of normal enemies or standard structure.
To keep it brief, here's the good stuff:
- Bosses are well varied and interestingly designed
- Bullet hell sequences are balanced well, not too difficult, not too easy
- Most of the mechanics are responsive (parrying, slashing, shooting) and satisfying
- Fantastic music
- Low-poly aesthetic works well with the game and really shines in some scenes
- The story, while somewhat simple, is entertaining and worth seeing to its end(s)
- Suprisingly strong voice acting from several characters
- Runtime may be short (first playthrough clocked at 6hrs), but with difficulty modes, practice, alternate endings and unlockables it'll last a while
- Glowing abs
Cons:
- Dodge seems iffy on keyboard, i'd occasionally dodge in a totally different direction than intended
- Occasionally, RNG can change the timing on attacks, which ends up causing problems if you're working off of memorization/reaction
- Bosses can be extremely frustrating if you don't spend time nailing down specific behaviors
- Failure means repeating stages that end up being tedious when you're used to them
Overall, I'd say it's a 8/10 game. It tried something new and succeeded, while staying true to its style and ideals. Delivered a good story through fun gameplay. Worth the price.

I've never played a visual novel that captured the human condition as well as Va-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action. This game portrays realistic characters that feel like people you could actually meet and hold a conversation with despite their often bizarre characteristics. (which is a goal most visual novels fall shot of imo) Have you ever described a game you liked and said something along the lines of, 'oh there's this robot sex worker named Dorthey....' this is more or less semantics, but I feel like people often describe characters like this because the lack depth and pointing out their most prevalent trait can give someone a good idea of what the characters like. However, most people don't refer to their friends that way, you're more likely to say 'oh this is Dorothy, they are a robot sexworker.' You tend to name the person first because they as a whole is more important then their character trait.  Like instead of this is a robot that happens to be named Dorothy, you get the feeling of 'this is Dorthey who happens to also be a robot.' That's how I feel these characters are represented. idk if that makes sense. Some are relatable, some are not, you like some, others rub you the wrong way, but they for the most part they still feel like real people.
The drink making mechanic is pretty fun and helps break up the monotony, I do wish there were a little more to it and you had the ability to create new drinks tho.
Overall would recommend if you're into visual novels and interested in getting to know how people get on in a cyberpunk future.

Quick summary: The Witness is a great first person puzzle game with little exploration and a lot less story.
Pros:
+ The game has tons of optional content so it can be finished by practically any adult but still offers a lot of challenge to those who are willing and able.
+ The average quality of the puzzles is great.
+ There is a surprising amount of variety in the puzzles regardless of the simple basic concept (drawing lines on a grid).
+ The game doesn't use tips, manuals, guides or anything else in teaching the mechanics to the player. It uses the player's own deduction.
Cons:
- Some of the puzzles are more about eliminating impossible approaches than figuring out the possible ones.
- Due to the game challenging the player in so many ways, some people will have limitations that can make some of the puzzles feel impossible, unfair or illogical.
- At least I wasn't able to find a proper story or similar experience in the game.
More in-depth thoughts:
I strongly recommend The WItness to any puzzle fan. I also strongly recommend playing the game "in the right" way: stop to think about each puzzle you can find but if after trying to solve it, it feels impossible, move on and come back later. Solving puzzles in The Witness can be divided into three steps:
1. Find the puzzle.
2. Figure out the rules of the puzzle.
3. Solve the puzzle.
And each step can be a puzzle on its own. This means that you will be missing a lot of puzzles at first but realize it later. This means that you will find puzzles that use rules you haven't yet figured out, and it is not reasonable to try to figure them out there. This also means that you'll get those 'Heureka!' moments all the time when you realize something you had missed or misinterpreted, or something similar, earlier.
Playing The Witness made me feel that Jonathan Blow wanted to challenge himself after the huge success with Braid and set to make an excellent puzzle game with a core mechanic so simple that a child could have made it with pen and paper centuries ago. It was a delight to see how amazingly varied the puzzles ended up being with such a simple core mechanic. This is one of the only games where few video reviews did practically nothing to provide me an understanding of the gameplay. All I can say is that the grid is not the puzzle, it is nothing more than an input mechanism. The input mechnism could be writing, shooting, jumping, etc. The quality, depth and the variety of the puzzles lies in the puzzles themselves, not in the input mechanism.

One of the best games I've ever played. A pure puzzle game-- only play if you really like puzzles, in their most abstract form as well as ones that are intrinsically related to their environment. It took me 30 hours to get the first achievement. Runs even on my fairly dated laptop.
If you're willing to learn about geology and industry and all that jazz in your spare time, you can even find a surprisingly rich backstory. If you like symbolism, you're in for a treat. If you like experimenting and learning for their own sake, oh you will have fun. If you like looking up walkthroughs, do your best to abstain-- just keep trying, isolate yourself, take a walk (in-game or otherwise) and come back. Look up hints if you must. Recommended with headphones especially and with expectations absent.
If you didn't like Braid (developer's previous game), if you want regular alerts that you're on the right track, if you simply don't have the time to invest many hours in exploring and thinking about an isolated island, you won't enjoy this. Which is fair enough, more power to you.
If you're undecided, wait for it to go on sale. If you're unsure if your computer will run it but you happen to own an Xbox One or a PS4, go with one of those versions. The game's coming to iOS soon too, apparently.

All I have to add to the other positive reviews is if this game has good controller support for those without a dedicated racing rig. I can't answer for all the different pads out there but with my 360 controller the answer is a resounding YES!
The trucks are, surprisingly, quite easy to manage with a controller even with all driving assists off. Also, you don't need to muck about with too many controller settings except:
1) Map your controls accordingly (this is the only area where the game setup falls down, even choosing a 360 pad in the settings will give incorrect inputs for steering etc...),
2) Put speed sensitivity up to around 70% and put a bit of deadzone in for the analog stick, probably around 5-10% depending on your pad.
3) If the steering is too sensitive you can take the x-axis sensitivity down to 0% and have good control, this is what I am currently running it at.
Just remember, this is a sim racing game, so you do have to drive appropriately. It will take some time to get used to, but the reward is worth it when you nail it.

It's really obviously trying to do the Dark Souls formula of giving you interesting bosses with multiple mechanics that are puzzles you solve with a sword.
It's too bad it fails so completely at it.
Here, let me paint a picture:
I do the intro, the aesthetic is nice, going for a sort of hyper-anime over the top brawler sort of thing. Then the camera pulls back so it can support the useless bullet-hell thing they've shoe-horned in so they can put it on the description and claim to be "new" and "innovative", when they should just focus on doing one thing well.
I go through the prompts and hit the buttons when they tell me. I'm just supposed to know to do these moves, how? Is there some indicator or something that tells me to counter a boss technique with one of these moves? I end up just shooting a lot, then when that arbitrarily doesn't work, I dodge behind and stab him in the back. So far so samey, Dark Souls but with teleporting to make it even easier.
Then I figure out you can dodge AND charge slash at the same time. It's awkward to hold the buttons, but it just completely wrecks the boss. So I do that a few times, until he just starts blocking, then I know it's time to switch to something else. Not so much organic gameplay as stupid and arbitrary.
Then he goes Super Saiyan and starts to do his moves that actually start to hit me. Oh no! He's srs now! This is when the crap dodge mechanic REALLY starts to get to me. Before this I would get hit by things I dodged, but I didn't think too much about it, maybe I was still learning. But when turbo boss does hits and I try to dodge, the controls are so crap that I get wrecked.
Then ALL the way back to the beginning. No mid-boss checkpoints. Nothing. So I go through his attack patterns like a fancy game of Simon-says and get back to Super Saiyan. Boring as all crap, but at least the fast-paced gameplay of his final form is sort of exciting.
But no, we eventually just start zipping around the map not hitting each other. Since there's no stamina, I can just do it all day long, trying to hit him. But thanks to him being able to teleport too, we're just blinking past each other swinging our swords at nothing. This goes on for a REALLY long time. We might as well be talking about the weather as we blink around the room, like in a bad anime, for the all the damage or threat we pose to each other.
Then, no joke, he traps me in a move that doesn't allow me to blink out, then a giant red IMA HIT HERE indicator flashes up, but with a HUGE delay on it so I have plenty of time to dodge and I know exactly where he's going to hit. A better game would have just communicated that with an attack animation rather than a lazy “don't stand in the fire dummy” indicator. So I blink behind him and stab him in the back. So far, so samey. This continues for a while, I get bored and allow some hits to get in, so I try to get srs again, but my heart's not in it.
...and then it's back to the beginning for more boring repetitive grind.
So that's my experience. Boring because too easy, technical issues (e.g. dodge) are frustrating and useless just when you need them, no stakes or threat, gimmicky combat that other games do better.

I wanted to love it, I really did. I adored running around with my Digimon, leveling them up, and digivolving them. But once the novelty wore off, well. It's kind of a bad game.
The UI is clunky and unintuitive. The quests range from “walk to the other side of the map, wait come back” to “grind X until enough McGuffins drop,” with little variance. There are a lot of important items that are either poorly explained or not explained at all, which becomes burdensome when combined with a needlessly complex, disconnected series of systems for upgrades. Your item space is limited, and while you will initially get a handful of expansions in the tutorial, the rest you must pay real money.
Speaking of microtransactions, unless you shell out, it’s going to be a very long and restricting grind for you. While there’s a deceptively wide variety of Digimon to raise, space is very limited – you have three slots for active Digimon (the fourth must be bought with cash), and only ONE SLOT in your Digimon archive. How can you expand your archive? You guessed it, cash shop.
To get a chosen Digimon without spending money, you must grind for the egg drop, grind for the specific “data” items to hatch it, and if you don’t have a backup item from the cash shop (or endgame – you guessed it – loot farming), all your work may go to waste anyway as the egg shatters in your hatching attempt. Theoretically, you might get lucky and get some of these items through events, but you’re still going to have a lot of slogging ahead of you. Oh, and you’ll be fighting bots for spawns every step of the way.
If you’ve got cash to burn… I still wouldn’t really advise this game. There are plenty of other free MMOs, and plenty of good games that you’ll only have to pay for once.

I love MTG, I've played the card game for a good while now and considering its age, it's been the influence for a multitude of other card based games (Yu-Gi-Oh! and Hearthstone). However, this is a terrible game; I understand that a video game version will be unable to create quite the same feeling as playing it with friends and actual cards, but they could have done a much better job than this. If you didn’t enjoy the previous Magic the Gathering videogames, then you won’t enjoy this because it is identical to the last apart from different cards, encounters and story. They made no effort to improve or change the interface/gameplay which really needed a reboot, especially as this game now has a lot of competition from other games.
The encounters feel as though they are going on forever, pointless features that just drag the game on an on even though you already know the outcome. For example, even when I am unable to block an attack, it still waits for me to respond which is one of the many things that makes drag on for about an hour. On the opponents turn, if he plays a card, the game will not continue, unless you actually click it. This is the same for every card played by an opponent (except land). Why? Why does it make me do this? I cannot change the outcome, I am still watching what my opponent is doing, why not just show me the card then resume your turn? There is no point in waiting for me to click on it as I can read the cards abilities at ANY point in the game. There are plenty more examples, but these are the main ones that made me not enjoy the game.
I've only played single player, and have no desire whatsoever to play the multiplayer feature so that may be better, I don't know? But this game was a waste of my money considering I have several physical decks at home and a group of friends who are willing to play the actual game with me. I just feel as though the developers could have done a lot more to make this game flow much nicer and speed it up. Perhaps I was just expecting a little too much after playing so much Hearthstone, but there are so many little things this game lacked that could have made it at least bearable.

First, I want to state that I really, REALLY wanted to like this game. The theme is great, the graphics are decent, and mechanics are solid. However, there are a couple things that make this game very awkward to play and downright aggrivating at times.
The whole purpose of the game is to build a colony and try to have it survive as long as possible, which is easier said than done. At the time of writing, one of the biggest qualms I have with the game is that there's no way to set a building's construction as a priority. On top of this, there's no way to take direct control and issue orders to your colonists. During my first game, I got to the point where I needed to build an additional water extractor. I had plenty of supplies and placed one on the map and connected it. I then set to clock to 2x time and waited 10 minutes. During this time, all of the colonists continued wandering around with their thumbs up their asses. No water means no oxygen, which means everyone dies.
Which brings me to the AI. What AI?
In all seriousness, the AI is beyond broken. On multiple occasions, I've had a surplus of medics with lots of the necessary components to produce medical supplies and the workbench set to high priority, and I would sit there and watch the medics do literally everything BESIDES make medical supplies. A similar situation happened with the engineer and spares production. I'd have the spares set to high priority with lots of metal and a surplus of engineers, and they did literally nothing until the spares ran out and everything broke down.
There are also some other issues such as an awkward UI and lack of building hotkeys or rebindable keys in general. But, this is all minor streamlining stuff that can be overlooked. Incompetent AI and lack of agency are what really kills the game. I may buy the game again if they change these, and may even recommend the game later on. But I cannot recommend the game in its current state.

Planetbase is a great game. I see a lot of negative reviews for this game, and I don't understand why, so I decided to write a review of my own. I just installed this sim on Steam. After hours of playing the non-Steam version, here's what I think about the sim.
When I heard of this truck racing simulator to come out, I was instantly looking forward to it. "What, a truck racing simulator that's realistic?" I bought it on the release and I gave it a go. I was amazed. You do need to set everything up and I do recommend you to set your in-game wheel to 900 degrees first (if you have a wheel at all). But when everything is set up correctly, it's A BLAST!
Physics: The trucks have about 1000-1100hp and weight about 5000-6000kg. It depends what trucks you choose from. Some trucks are a little lighter with less hp, others are heavier with more hp. You need to brake early for the corners, because the machines are very heavy for racing machines. Corners have to be taken very slowly. And be careful with the throttle! You do need to steer the trucks with your right foot a bit, create oversteer to get them round. The physics are from the rFactor 1 engine, but they are authentic and realistic, but above all, they're FUN to drive! It's a blast, really.
Graphics: The graphics aren't bad at all and they improve with each update. Reiza is doing a very good job with the graphics. The sim looks full of life  and graphics aren't bad, especially when you think this is actually rFactor 1.
Tracks: The tracks in FTruck are mostly Brazilian and not very common for people that are not Brazilian. There are about 15 tracks in the sim with their own configurations. Most people know Interlagos though! Reiza is doing a very good job with the tracks, especially Interlagos looks almost identical to it's laser-scanned version in iRacing.
Truck slection: The following truck brands are in the sim: MAN, Mercedes, Scania, Iveco, Ford and Volkswagen.
The good:
-Tracks are very convincing, true to real and all the tracks from the real series are included.
-Graphics are well done, even with the older rF1 engine. When someone is off the track you can see dust blowing from the trucks and it's hard to see :)
-Truck physics (you can feel the heavyness of the massive machines, but on the straights they are very fast and can outrun a fast road car easily. 240 km/h is possible on some tracks that offer straights that are long enough)
-It's challenging!
-Multiplayer! It's fun when there are enough people in the server.
-Truck damage (debris falling off)
The bad:
-It's price. Sorry Reiza, you should have asked more for this wonderful simulator :) Haha (not very serious point here, but really, it is worth more)
Now let's get to the more serious points.
-AI can sometimes push you off the track. The trucks are very big and heavy, so side-by-side can sometimes get rough.
-Setting the wheel rotation to 900 degrees is a bit difficult, it should be possible to adjust in-game. (go to your FTruck installation folder, UserData, then go to your player's name, you'll see a Controller.ini file. Click and drag this to your desktop, right click and press 'Edit'. Then search for the degrees of in-game rotation which is 270 by default. Change this to 900, save the file and put it back into your profile folder from where you got it. Done!
-Menu and UI are too much rF1 inspired.
That's about it! A great price and a very unique racing simulator. This is the only realistic racing sim where you can drive the Brazilian truck racing series. Just go ahead and purchase this one :)

I have a hard time rating this one, so I'll try to list the pros and cons.
Pros: Lots of puzzles - two basic types - the obvious ones found on tablets, and then the ones found in the sky, on the ground, etc. Interesting terrain - you'll slowly gain access to all of the island as you unlock certain doors. You learn some simple rules for figuring out different puzzle types, and build on them to figure out more complex puzzles. Some of the puzzles are really complex - thankfully there is always Google.
Cons; Lots of puzzles - repetitive even and even with the obsidian pillars scattered around, you'll waste a lot of time finding some of the "environment" puzzles - and they aren't even needed to "win".  That interesting terrain gets boring when you have to trace and retrace your path over and over. (The SHIFT key to run fast is your friend) Also, I hated certain puzzle types that when you fail cause you to go back a puzzle and resolve it before you can attempt it again. (Most of the types allow you to attempt over and over without any penalty)  I didn't notice it anywhere, but without special setup/knowledge some of the puzzles are hard for people with visual or hearing problems. Oh - and those complex puzzles? I don't know how we are supposed to keep all these rules straight in our head - there isn't any in-game notebook or guide or notebook to reference. Some of the puzzles are just so baffling that I spent much of my time looking in Google to understand the puzzle, and then some more of the time just looking for the outright answer because solutions that seem good didn't work.
The storyline - I didn't get it at all while playing it - it wasn't until I got to "The End" that I went online and learned there is even more puzzle aggravation before you can learn the "true" story of why you are on this island. After my game play experience, I came away from The Witness confused and discouraged from trying again - I'm sure there are a few "failed" lessons in there that will make it to the Games Developer Conference one day.
The authors wanted a regular price of $40, which I can understand for all the work they put into this; I'm glad I read the reviews first though, and waited for the price to drop on sale before buying it. The long wait for a lower price I paid for it was quite frankly worth it, considering the sheer aggravation of this game. Comparing this game to other, simpler games (in terms of graphics and quantity of puzzles), I thought the other games were far better buys. If you want enjoyable puzzles, look elsewhere - The Witness will probably seem like a Walking Game with puzzles to you. If you enjoy beating your head against rocks and spending weeks, months even figuring out stuff on your own then by all means go for it - you'll get your money's worth.
Ultimately I have to give this a thumbs down - I didn't feel like the hours I spent on this were worth the few minutes of satisfaction earned solving puzzles. To give you my frame of reference, I have about 450+ games of all types on floppy/CD/DVD and Steam - so that's where I'm coming from; while the graphics are good, the design psychology is not so good - players need to get sufficient rewards in the right places; I've played games that made me attempt something over and over again and really the only thing I wish I could do is gift this "used" game to someone for free.

This is a game that has a pretty narrow audience (one that I happen to fall into).
The gameplay, at face value, seems kind of stilted with the puzzles being restricted to the panels and having seemingly no regard for the world they exist in, but the game quickly teaches you that this isn't true. That are several puzzles that are impossible to solve without stepping back and looking around.
For people who like difficult puzzles that are satisfinging to solve in their own right with no external reward, this is definately the game for you, but I'm serious when I say there is no external reward. The game seems to build up to the ending, but if you were expecting a great one, you'll be disapointed.
The price point is definately the worst part of this game. $40 for between 10 and 30 hours of gameplay (depending on how good you are at solving the puzzels) is definately not worth it. I urge evereyone to NOT buy this game at full price, wait for a sale.
That's the bad out of the way; onto the good:
This game is a lot like Portal in that it is FANTASTIC at teaching you everything you need to know to solve the puzzels. When it introduces new mechanics, it does so slowly, and makes sure you have actually learned it rather than just guessed the correct solution before it moves on.
The open world nature of this game is also a great new take on puzzle games that it manages to integrate pretty well. There are 4 or 5 different areas that could all be a person's "first level" because of the independance of each section. There are some areas that require you to have some prior knowledge, but if you ever come to something you don't know how to solve, you can just take a step back, and go somewhere else for a bit.
I loved this game, but it is NOT for everyone, and you need to know that before you decide to but it.
EDIT: Upon the request of TUO, I continued on with this game and reached the alternate ending. It's definately more satisfying, but my problem with this comes from the fact that anyone who care enough to play the game twice to ge the alternate ending were obviously fine with the first one. It still doesn't address the people who wanted a satisfying conclusion on their first playthrough and thus quit the game.

The Witness is pure art. It needs no story just as a painting needs no story. I would compare it to other games like this: Portal is like watching a film, The Talos Principle is like reading a book, and The Witness is like going to a concert or a gallery. It is a different kind of experience, maybe not for everyone, but it is definitely
boring, as some reviews might make you believe. I would even say that it has a story - your own, as you explore the island. Exploration in The Witness is not just walking around finding new stuff, but finding out
that stuff is there and
it works.
The puzzles are clever, often challenging and immersive. Whenever you cannot figure a puzzle out, you can bet that there is a location on the island somewhere that teaches you exactly what you need to know to solve it. On top of that, the island is full of visual easter eggs based on perspective, so apart from trying to solve it all, you keep discovering new sculptures or shadow plays.
There are audio and video recordings scattered throughout the island, that offer ancient and modern philosophical quotations or even just stuff to think about. Yeah, among the easter eggs is a lecture on easter eggs about Bach, Shakespeare and free batteries. As weird as that sounds, you
listen and you
love it.
Basically, I found that the game is actually much better, more fun and addictive than it appears in trailers or reviews. The price is high, but if you have doubts, just catch it on sale and you will not regret it.

It's a Solid, difficult game
Most of the difficulty comes from the very mechanical mechanics, there are locked jump arcs, 1 checkpoint/level, passive shields with incomplete coverage (chest but not legs or head), your damage, enemy damage, and health can all be counted in very basic integers, enemy "AI" is on the level of Mario 1, and insta-death pits are plentiful. If you want to do well you have to control Volgarr like you are operating a toy car, or crane, not like an organic human we're use to in games.
The level design is mostly excellent*, generally letting you see possible threats before it's too late**, and requiring full use of your abilities. Every enemy feels different and needs to be aproached differently and the game ensures every encounter or obstical is unique from all others.
The game does spike in difficulty beyond the first level, mainly due to spawning enemies faster, and with less forewarning (from the side of the screen, from patches of water, or from the ground as opposed to crawling up the screen).
The game has been compared to Dark Souls, as it features a similar experience of adversity --> mastery. Personally, though I love both, I find Volgarr more consistant, and faster, but if you prefer a focus on watching for tells, and learning how enemies act/react you'll enjoy DS over Volgarr's attempt at purity in execution.
*The very last alternate level though is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ it has several unreliable spawns of fast flying enemies that not only hurt you but knock you around during the toughest platforming in the game. I have lost many 0 death runs to that level, thankfully it's short.
**The game has an option to zoom out the camera, you have to toggle it in the options then hit space in game, this shoud be the default zoom, as it is just slightly larger than the enemies trigger distance, the game is unfair without it.

Volgarr is a throwback to certain challenging 16-bit platformers, namely Super Ghouls 'N Ghosts and Rastan. The graphics are a little odd- they look kind of like a SNES game with the "filtering" turned on to make the pixels look smoothed, but I actually do like them. More importantly, the mechanics are top notch. With these kind of games, controls and mechanics absolutely make or break the game. Volgarr has Rastan style swordplay (attack while moving, block with shield, etc) and Ghouls 'N Ghosts style platforming (a nice, crisp-feeling double jump) and powerups (chests upgrade your shield/armor/weapon depending on what you've got currently, allowing you to use new moves and take more hits).
Volgarr has a sword and a spear, and that's it. The game really makes it work, giving you a range of options. You can fight while moving, play defensive and trade blows with your shield, dodge roll, jump attack, downstab, throw spears, charge spear attack, throw spears in midair, throw spears into walls to make new platforms, and so on. All of this is highly intuitive and you'll find yourself doing some really cool maneuvers very naturally. I kind of amazed myself just now when I jumped into an area, threw a spear in midair to kill a wasp, downstabbed to kill a lizardman, dodge rolled past an arrow trap, and then jumped onto a spear I threw earlier to climb out of the pit before another arrow could fire.
It's important to know that Volgarr is very oldschool. That means no saving. Every time you launch the game, there isn't even a start menu, Volgarr is borne out of blood and bone and you start killing lizardmen immediately. A snowcross game mode on a racetrack with jumps and bumpy roads. And a championship with a mix of open world checkpoint races and snowcross races.
The overall experience of the game is very positive. The snowmobile is a bit difficult to control and the snowcross racemode is quite challenging but you get better as you play. Sometimes the music gets a bit repetitive but the music tracks do fit the races and improves the experience. The graphics are good but not the best. The story of Tiny Tales is as simple as it can get, but its charming nature, adorable visual style and atmosphere, plus entertainingly laid-back puzzles will captivate any hidden object game player… as long as they are not bothered by the dreadful animations.
Tiny Tales: Heart of the Forest is a typical forest critter tale: we play as a miniature human magician living in a kingdom of mice, who sets on a journey to get to the bottom of a mysterious drought while also rescuing the princess. Thanks to the soothing colour scheme, adorable graphics, and the simple nature of the story, this hidden object game sets a wonderful mood and manages to keep it to the end.
Simplicity is also a keyword in gameplay: the puzzles are straightforward, the various kinds of hidden object scenes often rely on large and recognisable items, and even the bonus collectibles are easy to spot.
Everything is set to have some laid-back fun, except for one thing. A thing that may be a deal-breaker for many: the animations are discomfortably cheap-looking and hideous, so be ready for a shock right from the opening cinematic.

Tiny Tales: Heart of the Forest
The game has a whimsical fantasy setting with vibrant hues of floral and earth tones. Hidden objects scenes are varied and offer an alternative Monaco card matching game. Navigating through the game is smooth, the objectives are clear and the mini-games, while nothing out of the ordinary, are fairly easy to solve and are intuitive. Items to be found and used often show their outlines on the device for which they will be used to help the player identify the item hidden in the world. I always play on the easiest mode, though; playing on advanced mode may not show those outlines.
Mild humour exists throughout the game, which is pleasant. When I walked into the tournament—finally—I remarked wryly to myself that it was kind of the tournament officials to wait for me to arrive to begin the games. Turns out the tournament would have had to wait for my arrival, lol (find out when you play). After a calamity that shook up everyone in the vicinity, a salesman remarks how startling that event was then immediately launches into his sales pitch!
Even the story is on the lighter side, the animal denizens are not scary—even the villains—and the Princess of the tale left the safety of the castle of her own volition before she was kidnapped (of course). The protagonist (we players) has some friendly competition for being the hero of the day, an added subplot that makes the play more enjoyable in that it lessens the stress of the situation somewhat. Not having the weight of the entire kingdom’s fate on our shoulders for once.
The scenes convey the idea of a tiny kingdom perfectly—buttons look to be the size of motorcycle tires. The game is played in first-person perspective, but in one scene, we see “ourselves” in a picture within the scene as though through a mirror. The attention to details sets this developer’s artwork apart from the madding crowd.
The bonus area for this collector’s edition includes re-viewing the movies, seeing the conceptual art, replaying hidden objects scenes and mini-games, saving music selections and wallpapers. I missed some collectibles but couldn’t find how to revisit the scenes to collect them without replaying the game. They are not noted on the transporting map nor did I see any other indication that they were present in a scene besides actually finding them.
I’d like to see a sequel (beyond the added bonus story) to this tiny kingdom and lighthearted adventure.

The older me didn’t enjoy all mini-games, the younger me got ambitious and didn’t want to skip them. And both of us would like to thank the developer for hours filled with fun!

In former times rats and mice were enemies and for a short period this seems forgotten: rats and mice as well as other beings live peacefully together. But this is more of an illusion, as Rattus strives for power himself and intends to destroy the kingdom.  A drought has plagued people for some time now and the King calls for help. In a tournament it shall be decided, who would be able to find the reason for the drought and make this world bloom again. Max wins together with an amazone but in the end it is him, who saves the princess and triumphs over Rattus.
Artwork in this game is stunning, HO scenes are varied and creative. Puzzles are not very difficult but interesting. Max has no easy way to go, especially a cat is a big obstacle to fight. And here we have another aspect: we see the cat and her world with the eyes of tiny Max, so she is huge!

This game's size is over 20Gb and it took all day to download. So when it finally finished I was saying to myself "This better be one of the best games I have ever played. And while this game is brilliant, it does have its flaws.
Pros
-The Graphics are really good
-The setting is absolutely, mind-numbingly gorgeous. Its like going on a holiday in the swiss alps, In fact when I first saw the Gaming lemon play it, I thought that was where it was set. I know I was a fool back then.
-I like the arsenal of weapons in the game. There are a reasonable amout with a good variety of types. I would prefer if there were some more though.
-I love the way this is an open world game. You can go wherever you want whenever you want, except during missions which is annoying and I will touch on that later.
- The story is ok, but not the strong point, Basically you can overthrow a psycopatic dictator called Pagan Min who I presume they are trying to make look like a communist dictator (Kim Jong Un!!!).
- I love some of the missions outside the campaign, especially the ones where I have to be stealthy. Eg, Assasination, Hostage rescue, the Paul de Pleur mission (even though that is campaign).
- You get alot of choices, some of which make you feel uncomfortable. In the campaign you have to choose between Amita or Sabal. Amita values progress and Sabal values tradition. Eventually you will have to kill one of them to secure stability within the Golden Path, or so they say. You can even choose to stay with Pagan Min in the beginning to scatter your dead mothers ashes.
- The vehicles are really fun especially the buzzer which is basically a really cheap helicopter. It does have one annoyance. More on that later.
- The sound effects are alright especially for the guns.
Cons
- CUTSCENES!!!! FFS there is no need for a cutscene in a game!!!! This is a video game not a movie. For the first half an hour it was just a big cutscene. Some people would say "Oh but you need that for a good story". Anyone who says that has never played Half life or half life 2. Yes you can have some cutscene of sorts but heres my limits. One in the begining for at most 2 minutes, One at the end for 2 minites at MOST!! This game is just riddled with them.In the begining of the game I just wanted to play and I was getting really impatient. It was incredibly annoying.
- Alot of enemies are bullet sponges.And I am NOT talking about the heavily armored machine gunners. I am talking about ordinary royal army soldiers. You shoot them about 5 or 10 times and they look like they are dead. So you focus on another guy. But wait!! the guy you though you just killed has gotten back up like a zombie. You run out of ammo. They kill you. I have lost count of the amount of times I have died this way.
-Drugs are messed up. Thanks alot Yogi and Reggie.
- The final Shangri la boss fight is absolutely horrible. I hate boss fights in general. They are so tedious and boring. But this is amonst the worst bosses I have ever had the absolute misfortune of playing. Basically you have to shoot some phoenix in the mouth and when it falls down you have to command you tiger to enter the mouth of the bird all while fending off attacks from demons and fire minotaurs and on top of that dodging the phoenixes fire balls.

Alright i've played this game for a few hours and there are a few good things and a few bad things I've experienced with my playthrough so far.
Pros:
1) Beautiful graphics and atmposphere. There a sense of "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; when you hear a meteor crash around you.
2) Gameplay seems balanced once you get used to it, after you use up your beginning supplies focus on metal and bioplastic production or you just won't make it.
Cons:
1) The AI is is to simple to handle some of the things that I want them to do. A build Queue would be great. Something I can manipulate so that my colonists know what i want built first. Where I want the resources to go first so we can continue to survive. Right now they just kind of build whatever they want in whatever order they feel is best. Which 80% of the time i disagree with. This goes for production as well.
Personal Note: I really want to like this game a lot, it has the potential to be a game you could sink hours into perfecting your martian colony or settling on pluto who knows, the possibilities are endless. I feel like there needs to be some AI work, I feel like there isn't enough depth into how the player controls their colonists to do what's right for them. You can tell them to prioritize working on certain rooms and that's about it. You know you really need spare parts but all you can do is spend outrageous prices on trade ships or wait for your engineers to feel like making spare parts in prioritized rooms, which in my experience was not that often. I had two wind turbines down, a solar panel and a crippled power storage center down before they even thought about making any spare parts for them. It was a incredibly frustrating experience.
I would recommend this game if you enjoy a sci-fi city builder. There are a lot of good things about this game, don't get me wrong. I feel like there's just a few things missing and it could be a much greater experience if you didn't suffer from the frustration of a lack of build order or production order or control over how things are built. I feel like a minimum would be incredibly handy, you can lmit a maximum number of any good but you can't make a minimum number to keep on hand.

In essence, a quasi-satirical rendering of the first four Harry Potter films, with a tiny bit of peppering from the books. Not that it's a bad thing though! The game has an "easy" feeling. The flow is great and the controls simple enough (I used a controller for this one).
Exploring Hogwarts is a superb experience, with the castle really exuding a sense of grandeur. The extra scenes give us the opportunity to leave Hogwarts and explore other locales. This not only highlights some of the most iconic scenes from the movies, but also helps break the monotony of being stuck in the castle. While playing Order of the Phoenix, for instance, I had the sense of being utterly confined in Hogwarts, completing menial tasks.
The use of the original soundtrack is thoroughly gratifying, from Hedwig's theme, to the music playing while on the Grand Staircase or the music just before the final task of the Triwizard Tournament commences.
This is the first Lego game I've ever played, and found it enjoyable enough. Exploring Hogwards is immensely satisfying but at the same time some gameplay mechanics were a bit tedious; like breaking every pot, flower, ornament, bench or chest you can find and collect studs. Of course you don't have to, if you don't want to, but then you'll just breeze through every area quite quickly. But in the end, more than 35 hours of gameplay (let's say about 20 to complete the story mode once) is a more than substantial amount of time to make it worth your time.

I was very skeptical about The Witness after reading the reviews, particularly the ones that said this game is pure puzzles, and that the only reward for completing them was more puzzles. Turns out those reviews were totally accurate, but it didn't stop me from logging 35 hours - doing puzzles.
The mechanics of the puzzles themselves are well-introduced, but that didn't stop me from pulling my hair out trying to figure out some of the solutions. Seriously, they get TOUGH at some points, and that makes it all the more rewarding.
The setting is an island that is intriguing, and the game's use of angles, sound, reflection - basically everything in the environment - is frankly brilliant. The "game within the game" is expertly put together. There isn't really any story per se, but I still felt mystery and delight at discovering new places and things within the island. That was reward enough for me to keep going.
That said, there were weird audio/video clips that I thought were super pretentious, bordering on nonsense. Maybe some people will find deeper meaning, but I didn't quite get there. I do wish there were something more rewarding throughout the game , I felt a little empty at the conclusion.
Overall, great puzzle game but you REALLY need to like puzzles. No story, no great reward, but brilliant settings and challenges. Recommend for those who enjoy clever, well-orchestrated puzzlers.
EDIT: If I'd been a little more patient and thoughtful, I would have gotten that satisfying reward I was looking for. Went back and found it, so I wanted to update my review with a slightly stronger endorsement. Great game.

The only "cons" you will find has to do with things that are not part of the core of the game, which is about solving puzzles, like not an actual story, and the end is kind of dull, but you feel reworded for the achievement.

I really liked this game. It's all about mazes and ingenuity. There's no intro and no help, but it doas a good job about teaching you by observation how everything works. You roam around an island which is somehow divided in "zones" which are accesible from the start, solving puzzles and in each zone you complete activates a laser that points into the top of a mountain, a place you will find curious about and you can go practically from the start.
Basically it's about solving mazes which have different rules generally (but not always) indicated by icons and marks on the different boards (if the board has no "marks" try to look around to see some feature in the landscape, or some shadow over the board, in time you'll get it). If you find a complex board with a new symbol, don't frustrate about it, and cretainly don't find a guide to solve it. I mean, come on... is a game about solving puzzles, searching a guide to walk it throug is like to find someone to eat the food you just ordered, and paid for it.
If you see a puzzle with rules or marks you don't understand yet, just remember where is it and go to another zone, there's always a place dedicated to teach you about the different symbols, you just have to pay attention.
I found it challenging but with a rewarding feeling when you complete it. It's suitable for all ages and good fuel to stimulate the brain, logic and observation, something that modern games are getting lack of.
I totally recommend this game, there are some hidden audios along the game with lectures or quotes from famous scientists and thinkers, but is just a candy, this game it has an universal language, through symbols and common sense. If I had a kid, this is one game I'd play with him to stimulate thinking (this game and chess).
IMPORTANT: This game is about puzzle solving, forget about a story or anything else. Also, some (very few) puzzles require you to pay attention to sound, so hearing impaired persons might need help in those cases.
Hope you enjoy this game as I did.
Have a nice day!

The Witness is a polarising game.
It's just a lot of simple line puzzles.
Lots of things are unexplained.
There's no real story.
There are some elements you might find pretentious.
But if your enjoyment of what it gives you exceeds your annoyance at what it doesn't, it can offer a truly unique and special experience.
There are really two elements here - some logic puzzles for you to solve, and an island for you to explore. The puzzles are cool, if you like puzzles. The island is beautiful and fun to discover, if you like exploring (but, as mentioned, don't expect narrative pay-off). Neither of these elements are anything special on their own.
The real magic of this game is in how it weaves the two together. It's difficult to describe without spoiling things, but I'll give it a try. You get to a puzzle panel. You try and solve it for a few minutes, but it doesn't make much sense to you. The tricks you learned earlier in the game don't seem to work.
Then you notice that you're in a beautiful garden. You just admire it for a while. You notice something slightly odd about the patterns of the flowers. They look almost look like the symbol on the panel. Suddenly it clicks. You solve the panel. The next is almost the same, but you just can't work it out. You start searching for flowers...
If this all sounds boring to you, The Witness probably isn't the game for you. But if it's just a little intriguing, you might be like me, in which case you'll play it obsessively over several days and have an experience unless any game you've played before.

Full Review:
You should heed all the promotional materials on Volgarr The Viking's store page. This game is brutal and is in no way short on ways to punish every little mistake you make. If you want a game that's very true to Capcom's Ghosts 'n Goblins/Ghouls 'n Ghosts series, look no further than Volgarr The Viking.
It's a very intricate and meticulous platformer in almost every way. Stage designs and enemy layouts are all constructed and placed for the very specific purpose of you dying over and over again. There's a heavy-handed focus on memorization, and only nigh-perfect execution will see you through the many obstacles in Volgarr's path. This game doesn't play nice, and no victory in Volgarr is ever handed out. You'll have to think your way through each enemy or boss encounter and then execute that plan with nothing short of perfection. It can be intensely satisfying to crack open the game's stages and enemy encounters.
That said, frustration is very likely to set in at times due to the game's heavy reliance on memorization and perfect execution.  The only way out of any situation is usually the one the developers set up for you to figure out. While Volgarr himself has a lot of great tools at his disposal, it never feels like you're really free to use those tools in any way you want, which is a real shame. Additionally, attempting the "Path of the Valkyrie" route through the game is almost a task too herculean in nature for most to have the patience to ever see, which is a shame since it's the only way to access the alternate stages.
Volgarr The Viking is a game made for someone wanting a very specific type of experience. Newcomers to this style of game may still find enjoyment through the frustration, but it's tuned much more for arcade junkies who don't mind a bit of repetition and tedium in their experience.

I originally picked this game up months ago and refunded it because I wasn't feeling it, but eveyone continued to talk about this game like it was the best thing since sliced bread. So I decided to pick it while it was on sale for $9.99 and give it another go. It actually caught me this time. For awhile, that is. I've seen people say that this is near perfect or something, but I can't agree with that at all. This game has some major flaws that I'm not sure anyone can ignore.
First off, the combat is tight and doesn't have a ton of variation to it, but it's fun and difficult to master, which isn't a bad thing. You have a sword and a gun as offence, and parrying attacks to get special and just blocking attacks to get health back. It starts fairly easily as this game is entirely boss fights and walking sections. I had no problem with around the first 6 bosses. Then the game gets a werid difficulty spike for 2 bosses that sucks because the bosses have stages, and if you die, you go back to the first stage. Then the 9th boss is laughably easy followed a bullet hell boss that has a long and rather unfair last phase. Dying on the final stage of a boss more than once makes this game in(furi)ating, which is probably where is got it's name from.
This game is around 5-6 hours and most of that playtime will be with 3 bosses that you'll get to the last stage of only to die and then restart the battle from scratch. I do really want to like this game more, it has an excellent soundtrack, visuals, combat is fun when it's not a bullet hell(bullet hells aren't my thing, you might feel differently), but it really has some balancing problems. I still like the game, but not as much as I thought I would. I guess I recommend it, but it seems to me that if you're more into casual or even wanting to dabble in hard games, the difficulty might prove too much even on just normal.

Furi is an overhead bullet hell/fighter game with the focus on bosses. The game uses many different mechanics to create an incredibley fun experience. Warning to those out there who don't really enjoy a challenge because this game is fairly punishing. The most challenging part is the length at which some bosses will last. They can last up to 10+ minutes and have 3-6 phases. The game is merciful enough however to give you 3 lives which can be restored by beating a phase and many opportunities to get health back.
Pros:
- The combat is extremely responsive and a lot of fun. The variety of ways you can move, shoot, and slash really makes the boss fights exilerating.
- Bosses in Furi are the main focus so they better be good. Thankfully they are done very well. Each boss is unique in appearance and offer fights that will keep you guessing. One boss might be ranged focused while the other could use only melee. I don't want to spoil any fights but each boss gets their own crazy phases and abilities that they bring to the table.
- The soundtrack. HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥THE SOUNDTRACK. Several different artists contributed to the music for the areas and bosses in Furi. The music can really bring out the energy in each fight to make it truely epic.
here's an example if you're curious
- Visually the game has a very strikingly beautiful style. It was done by the same guy who did Afro Samurai and it really shows here.
- The story can be seen as a negative for some because it isn't really explained in detail. You are left to figure it out by yourself through dialogue and context clues. Fortunatley I'm a big fan of stories like this so I see it as a plus.
- Decent replay value thanks to the speedrun mode and "Furier" difficulty. The higher difficulty level will actually change up all the bosses attacks to be different and harder to avoid, opposed to just having attacks do more damage and giving the boss more health.
Cons:
- Some visuals in the game can be quite distracting at times, such at the main character's hair or some of the facial animations. They aren't too terrible for using Unity and being made by a smaller team so it's not too bad, but can get distracting at times. Fortunatley it's an overhead fighting game so you'll rarely notice
- There are a few boss mechanics here and there that can feel unfair. There's only a few but it definitely frustrated the hell out of me a couple times.
- The most difficult topic for me is game length. The problem here is how quickly you can beat the game. I finished it in a little over 4 hours, but I've seen some people take up to 9 hours because of the challenge presented. I got the game on sale so 4 hours for $10 is acceptable, but $20 feels maybe a little high. I will say though that this game is an amazingly condensed experience and stretching out the game to be longer probably would just end up hurting it. Also, the replay value I mentioned earlier could add some play time if you cared to try it out.
Overall I found the game to be a joy to play and can't wait to see if the devs are planning on making any other games. The combat, bosses, soundtrack, visuals, and story really hold this game up above the competition and provides an experience unlike any other.
*Final Verdict: 8.5/10*

Controls are simple with boost, and one button used to trigger handbreak/fast turn/air rotation/reverse, and the use of the right stick is for avatar stunts. Performing stunts will refill the boost, even while you're driving and boosting at the same time, although stunts forces slower turning. Releasing the gas in sharp turns provides more control over movement, and I've used it in conjunction with releasing the left stick - timing is everything. The avatar can lean forward or back with the same left steering stick which affects the whole sled and wheelies are easy to do too. The game is great and supports local multiplayer to crush your friends in.
SMRF is worth picking up and playing with friends even if your not a fan of racing games in general.

I'm from Sweden so I know how big snowmobiling is! The developers Zordix are from far up North in Umeå, and their enthusiasm really shows up in the game.
I discovered this new game after coming back to play 2016 year's surprise hit Aqua Moto Racing Utopia and I'm equally impressed with this one.
Looking at some old films on Youtube from earlier popular snowmobile games, my conclusion is that this must be the best game in the snowmobile genre so far. Congratulations on such a great achievement!
The physics in this game is really advanced and the snow is well simulated. I love the controls and how the snowmobile slides sideways into each turn on the Snocross tracks.
It feels like the level of fun has been turned up one more notch compared to the jetski game. There's more speed and more freedom taking different routes. I guess that's what the subtitle "Freedom" means.
I noticed many interesting metal music scores which I never get bored listening to. The engine sounds are well done and makes you feel like you're totally there. Especially when switching to first person view.
The single player is perfectly tuned with AI that gets harder to beat for every new race. I got some of my friends to play the game with me online. For each race we're collecting points and climbing in the World rankings list. It's quite fun and different to level up in a racing game compared to an RPG. To me it feels like a totally fresh and fun approach in a racing game.
I'm now a huge fan of the Moto Racing series and I hope there will be more great games like this coming soon.

Snow Moto Racing Freedom is a really cool and solid arcade racing game much in the style of Aqua Moto Racing Utopia, a game that I like a lot since it reminds me of the old wave race series of games except with more of everything.
This game feels very different and in a great way. First, it’s on snow and it gives you the racing options to either sprint cross vast mountain landscapes or to race head-to-head in arenas full of jumps, turns and sometimes high hills to climb.
I was impressed to notice that the snow sparkles and that the weather effects range from daylight, sunset, storm, into even dark night where the snowmobiles have their headlights on. The trails that all snowmobiles make stays in the landscapes and are not removed like in other snow games I’ve played. Overall I find the sound quality superb. There are dopler effects as you get passed, the engine pitch goes up when you’re in the air and I even hear the skis in the snow.
The game is rich on features with an extensive single player career mode, time trials, freestyle, leisure, just to mention a few. I think a lot of effort has gone into all the details of the game. And to top it off this game has online play with world rankings.
My best advice to beginners:
* Try out the first person camera for a great sensation of speed and to gain more direct control on the tight racing tracks.
* In snocross, release the stick early in turns to keep on track.
* Don’t be affraid to try different routes in sprint, even if they seem crazy.
* Use the boost button to go faster!
* Charge your boost by making stunts now and then.
* Press the left front lower button to rotate the snowmobile in the air! That’s what I enjoy the most, since this game let’s you fly high in the air in every race.
I give it a high score of 9/10 – it’s that good!

We’re at a mountain top. Wind blows up snow in the air and the the two-cylinder smoke lies as a curtain behind the drivers. All equally tense. Everyone looking in the same direction with the same goal. Hearts pounding, nervousness and an enormous adrenaline onslaught. The drivers tightening their grips on the handlebars with their thumb on the gas. That’s how it’s like on the starting line, now let me tell you about the gameplay.
Ready-Set-Go! Off we go and all the tension is wiped away. I’m off to a perfect start by timing it and my controller starts to shake as I push the nitro button for extra speed. My snowmobile shakes from the speed boost as I switch to first person view for better immersion. I’m totally there, taking a crazy route noone’s ever taken, far away from the other racers. I barely miss two trees and bounce slightly on a wicked bush. I manage to release the gas, and I slide sideways past two competitors, to line up perfectly in front of the next gate.
Slowly up the hill now, trying to make a stunt with the right stick while driving to reload some nitro, slowly towards the goal on the top… curses … I’m passed, not once but twice, and I’m third in the race. If you’re like me, that’s not OK, you’ll want to stay for a long time in this world of snow and speed - to be the best!
