I can't recommend this any harder, I've found a new home in VA-11 Hall-A. I remember seeing the trailer and thought, "wow this already looks like my new favorite game, and I wasn't kidding myself. I'm trying to lower my rose-tinted glasses as I write this, because personally, I'm in love with the worlds that were created in my favorite anime like Ghost in the Shell and Bubblegum Crisis, and this game exerts a slight nostalgia for shows like these, all while creating its own unique atmosphere.
VA-11 Hall-A is unbelievably immersive, every second is so involving of the character's presence you can easily slip out of reality and into the world this game creates for you. The environments are a great backdrop for the things that happen in the game, and you spend most of your time at your job as a bartender, but man is it rewarding. You get to chat with different characters who all have their own stories, personalities and backgrounds. The dialogue itself is so well written and believable, and that contributes an entire dimension to the level of immersion VA-11 Hall-A creates.
There's a ton of commentary in the game as well, and quite a bit of cute and silly humor that's just inserted here or there. Every part of this game is a treat to the player, the developers accommodate you, welcoming you into their world where every aspect caters to your experience without feeling like the game is playing itself. This is a simulation game that you don't get to create your own character, but Jill is so lovable you can easily identify with her and find yourself assuming her role in this world.
The last thing I'm going to comment on, which is the element that first attracted me to this game is the music. It's one of the most important parts of this experience to me because it does an incredible job setting the atmosphere. You get to choose which songs play from the jukebox while working your shift, which is pretty rad because the songs are absolutely incredible. For me personally, it's instantly one of my favorite game OST's because it reminds me so much of Phantasy Star Online and that kind of synth used in those songs instantly reminds me of being in a futuristic world full of wonder. It's absolutely perfect for this game, and every song invokes some kind of feeling out of you, sparking your imagination into grasping at every element in the game.
VA-11 Hall-A is without a doubt an instant classic for me, it's everything I've wanted in a cyberpunk simulation game, and I really hope that if you enjoy the same things I do, you'll get a chance to play an hour or two at least. You won't regret it, even if you don't like the game particularly, you will walk away having experienced something unique that you may never forget.

The game is $19.99, if it was 3-4 USD I guess I would understand, but I really can't recommend it as of now.  When I first started playing I was under the impression it was an early-access title, so I excused the lack of features.  But it's not an early access game...
Pros:
Cool idea, resource management is a huge challenge and it keeps you on your toes.  Is not an easy game.
And..thats about it.
Cons:
Resource management...  If you can get past the initial rush which will kill any chance at a colony should you not build the SAME BASE every single time.  Go for the same strat and make sure you become sufficient, you have no wiggle room whatsoever.  This is not a city-builder, this is a puzzle game with "tycoon" strapped to it as the genre.
Clunky controls, no micromanagement, too restrictive.  For example, you can only build in specific locations in a certain distance from pod to pod.
Little to no variety in buildings, items, or units.
Planets are bland and boring.
Building space is a massive issue.  Maps seem at least partially procedural and there's no terraforming.  Even the smallest dip in the terrain will prevent building.  This essentially sticks you in a little valley and I have yet to find a build that lets me get to "hundreds of colonists".  A few short hours (MAYBE that much time) into your colony you will come to the point where you just sit and wait.  2-3 of the hours on my playtime were spent waiting for something to happen.
No 'helpful' graphs, meters, or sufficiency tools to help you crunch numbers.  You could do the math yourself, but most of it is just "throw a crap ton of food plots up and hope it works".  It would be nice to be able to manage things more closely so as to avoid the inevitable "everyone starved" thing.  The only output vs. usage meters there are, are for energy, water, and oxygen.  Most of the game is just throwing massive amounts of work into things until you're stable.
Little to no control over your units and what they do.  They also arent very productive (those lazy astronauts!)
It's too tediously difficult.  Not much challenge, just be quick and build the buildings in the right order.  Otherwise you WILL get stuck and have to respawn.  This is challenging so to some people it'll be fun, but to me it's not.  Not so much a con, but it's part of the game anyways.
No depth... whatsoever.  This is unfortunately a real problem with the tycoon / strategy genre.  No storyline, no fun events.. no nothing.  There's even a very poorly designed trading minigame.  Where the trader will literally fly away while you're filling his ship with goods you're selling.

I dont normally review games but I have to say I am bemused  with the negative reviews for this game and have decided to leave my opnion as some people may find it useful.
So far I can see two negatives points being made as reason for the game being poorly reviewed, one I strongly disagree with and one I agree with somewhat however feel that to give this a negative review based on these two points is extremely misleading and makes me question the motives of the reviewers as this is a very fun building / economy management sim. Any real fans of this genre will feel right at home with this and 20 - 50 hours of fun for 12 pounds is a good deal in my opnion.
Here are the points:
1) AI is garbage.
In my 20 something hours of gameplay I have experienced poor AI on one occasion. A constructor basically stopped working and would go to work on something, but then stop immediately and idle. I deleted the node he was trying to work on, and he started working again.
That is it. I have built a base with everything in it, 150 population and 80 robots. That is the only AI error I have encountered.
I think people are missing a core mechanic of the game and confusing it with AI not working. Let me explain.
When your colonists needs become severe (orange  - red), they stop working. The only thing they will do is try to fulfill that need.  Guess what, if you cant fulfill that need, they wont work again. If you have no colonists that are free to work, well you lost the game. Time to rethink your build and start over.
In one negative review (the most popular one), the reviewer explains that even though his colonist was carrying food, he was starving to death and  this means the AI is garbage.
What it really means is the reviewer does not understand the mechanics of the game let me explain. So you can only be carrying raw food which is grown in your bio sphere or in your lab. This is not ready to eat. For it to be ready to eat it needs to be delivered to your meal maker which in turn uses it to produce a meal ready for your colonists consumption. There is the possibility he may have been carrying a meal which you have imported yes. however it still needs to be carried to the meal maker for it to be consumed by a colonist.
Now remember colonists wont do any work if their needs are severe, so no matter how many meals you have or raw food, if there is no meals ready in the meal maker/s, and all your colonists are starving, well its gg.
Once you understand the mechanics you make sure you are always one step ahead. Power supply, food production, meeting needs of colonists, the golden rule is dont over expand if you havent considered the impact it will have on your economy and havent sufficently upgraded your infratructure to incorporate it.
Blaming poor AI in my opinion is because players do not understand the mechanics of the game. As stated in 22 hours I have had to restart maybe 6-8 times, however every time I learnt something which my made my next base much better. The reviewer also talks about The more colonists you get the more of a problem this is, however in my opinion this is the complete opposite. The more colonists you have the  easier it is to maintain colonist needs as if some stop working due to `their needs being sever others take over the work and you can in time fulfill the needs of all.
You may find it unrealistic that a colonist starves whilst there is raw food available, that is fair enough. But that is not poor AI, This is a core and valuable game mechanic, which is part of the games challenge.
I hope that clears this issue up for some people.
2) The game lacks depth
I agree. Right now I believe there is 40-60 hours of game play here. This will involve you building all the buildings available and creating a successful base on each of the planets available right now.
There could be so much more to what is a fantastic core game. More buildings, more resources, more needs and more events. Rival planet bases inhabiting the same planet of you. And my main suggestion once all the things I have mentioned and more have been added, a campaign.
I think this games is perfectly set up for a campaign each with diferent objectives etc. For example you get a base with a robot facility and X amount of semi conductors, however you can not recruit workers on this planet etc. (some tweaks to job roles maybe required but you get the idea).
The ideas mentioned could turn this game from a great little city builder with 40-60 hours of gameplay to a all time classic with 100s of hours.
Summary
Despite the poor reviews this is actually a highly polished and extremely cohesive and fully functioning economy/city builder simulation, which will provide you with 40-60 hours of absorbing, challenging and fun gameplay.
If you like this genre and enjoy games which are a challenge and require you to use your brain in order to progress then this really is a must buy.

Just to start, I LOVE this game. It pretty much nails the feel of building a colony on another world. I do have some bones to pick, but I'll do a quick summary of the game first.
The point of the game is to build a base on another planet or moon, gradually building larger and larger, while attracting more colonists, and eventually visitors and dangerous enemies. The building system is solid and fun to use, and the game is very intuitive. One run through the tutorial is all you'll need. In addition, this game really, really does resource conservation well, demanding very careful spending, and lots of planning to make sure you have enough for the next round of expansion.
One thing that I absolutely love is that not watching your resource almost certainly will lead to the death of your colony, as it can become a chain reaction of cascading failures in the system. You run out of power halfway through the night, which means your food stops growing, which runs you out of food, which starves your engineer to death, which means you can't build more power generation, and thus the process repeats itself until all your colonists are dead, or you start desperately shutting down non-essential buildings in an attempt to conserve energy. It's brutal, you WILL restart your colony several times, especially on the last planet (moon), and this aspect makes it a blast to play.
However.
This game is awesome, but there are only three planets. This is depressing. I fervently hope that the developers will add more planets. I especially hope to see other types of colonies, such as water world colonies, gas planet floating colonies, etc. I would also like to see things like colonist progression, such as experience, and even skills. Why can't a worker be taught how to run a spares machine or semiconductor unit? I used to work at a company that produces RAM, and those kinds of machines definitely don't need engineers to run. A technician can do that all day long, no problem. And how about an engineer learning how to more efficiently build things? Or, perhaps some more advanced structures need engineers who have more experience building things? I'm not saying these kinds of things absolutely must be in the game, it's already fun, but this kind of depth would add more to the experience.
This game has incredible potential, and I see that the developers are still making updates, so I have absolute confidence that the game will continue to expand, but right now, it IS slightly lacking in late-game content. Once you build colonies on all the planets, you've kind of run out of things to do, unless you're a completionist.
Regardless, if you like city building games and resource management games, this is definitely the game for you, and I found it well worth the price of admission.
Could be better, but it does have addictive gameplay.

Planetbase is fantastic. If I were to rate it on a scale of 'Oak Tree' to 'Fish eye', I'd have to put it somewhere around 'Cotton Garden'
First of all, the devs seem to actually be paying attention to the feedback given by their player base, and quickly implement the changes into the game accordingly. They don't scream back "Well then you're just not playing it right!", instead they say "Oh, actually that does make more sense. Thanks, we'll get onto that." (And then a day or two later it's fixed!)
Now, to be completely transparent, there are still some little annoying things that would usually rub me the wrong way - HOWEVER, with this game, I'm actually pretty confident those things will be fixed relatively quick, unlike other devs which leave you waiting months for minor updates that don't even fix the problem.
With all that aside;
The gameplay is also addictively fun. There are so many fun things to be doing;
- planning new sections of your base, such as placing the gym equipment right next to the dining facilities, because you want to force your colonists to feel guilty every time they want to eat.
- making deals with merchants who bring a variety of goods while you curse them for their inflated prices as they cash in on the fact that you really need these tomatoes.. because you just are not that good at planning ahead.
- entertaining visitors for some coin on the side
- installing and manning giant defence lasers to shoot down meteors that would otherwise crush one of your dorms, instantly killing 15 sleeping colonists
- arming your base to the teeth with guns so that bad guys get a face full of pew pew when they try and attack
- treating your people for radiation sickness because you were too lazy to activate the Red Alert - leaving them to go about their work outside without warning them of the solar flare about to hit them
- locking the air-lock so that no one can leave the building, and leaving the outside workers to scream and pound on the door as they are destroyed by aforementioned radiation, fully aware that all you would need to do is turn on the Red Alert, and no one would leave. (Ok, well, the screaming and pounding doesn't happen.. but I like to imagine it does.)
- Or, turning your entire base into a mass grave, due to the fact that you didn't think about your resources, and overworked your biologists, leaving them to starve to death, halting the production of any food whatsoever.
This game is worth price, in my opinion.

I've tried again but it is just so hard to get excited about these later Far Cry games. The story is full of awful voice acting, awful model animation, cliche villany, amateurish immersion on all fronts, and the open world environments are shockingly sterile. Mindless NPCs - animals or humans - bumble around the landscape in utterly uninteresting ways. NPC drivers in particular crash their cars at the drop of a hat. Look at a hillside from a few km away and it looks like it may be interesting, but explore it in person and it will just be an inert feature, about as entertaining as a planet from No Man's Sky, dotted with ridiculously visible bright-green (kermit green) herbs.
Far Cry 2 remains the best post-Crytek game in the series, if not the entire series. This is a careful distinction to make, because it is pretty much the same thing that you get in these more recent games (minus a plethora of gimmicks that are solely there to make trailers look cool - who the heck cares about freaking zip lines really?) The thing about Far Cry 2 was that, to save on draw distance (I assume), most zones were full of obstacles to block sight lines and keep your attention largely in the near-ground - whether they were annoyingly xbox'ish canyons, that literally funneled you where you were meant to go, or just dense foliage thickets that stopped you noticing how detail may be dropping off in the distance. Keeping the game at bite size like this helped you ignore the deficinecies of the map technology and mechanics and focus on the dangerous and satisfying combat, which could happen far more frequently because you couldn't see 1:1 just how densely situated all of the camps were.
No such luck in Far Cry 3 or 4. No, in these games you shell out AAAAAAa title fees to play a game with a world that is essentially less interactive than vanilla World of Warcraft. Am I supposed to be impressed by throwing bait to attract predators that MATERIALISE OUT OF NOTHING in an instant?
After playing the Witcher 3, your standards soar. Any game made after Witcher 3 MUST take environments of that kind of detail, OPTIMIZATION (Far Cry 3 and 4 suck at this), texture variety and interest, elemental dynamism and NPC populace. Anything less than Witcher 3 is an instant previous-gen title in my understanding of game generations. The Witcher 3 world was alive purely by dint of the technology behind it, let alone the great content they loaded it up with. This world is old-fashioned, low-tech, basic, uninteresting, unrewarding to explore, and populated by uselessly mindless NPCs. It is formulaic, using a formula that was Never going to stand up to the close inspection that a 4k screen with max draw distance was going to subject it to.
Am I supposed to get excited about climbing a bell tower? Like the radio towers in FC3? Oh look, they're really high, a computer game is simulating vertigo for me. What the actual fudgebucket.
Meet the new grass, same as the old grass. Meet the new trees, same as the old trees. Meet the new invisible walls preventing you from really exploring terrain a la Skyrim, et al, same as the old invisible walls preventing you from really exploring terrain a la Skyrim, et al.
Meet the new villain, same as the old villain. Read: Hyperbolic, charicatured, stupid looking, of ridiculous motivation and character, pointlessly violent.. This dufus was designed to make 10 year olds go "wawww" because none of them have seen the fifty computer games and two hundred movies that had an IDENTICAL villain in the past 20 years.

I'll start off by saying that, overall, I personally enjoyed this game. The puzzles are all the same idea, draw a line incorporating various elements that the game teaches you naturally over time. The game doesn't need to stop and explain, but shows you how each new element works gradually, as most areas tend to revolve around a new concept. A lot of puzzles incorporate the scenery as well, which itself has puzzles hidden within it.
Just bear in mind that that's the game. Line puzzles. If you aren't absolutely crazy about the idea of constant line puzzles, then don't even bother reading further. This is not the game for you.
Now I have 2 main problems with this game.
First, I'll be blunt, the game is pretentious. There are audio logs of prolific quotes scattered about, they mean nothing. There are perspective tricks hidden in the scenery, these are neat, but mean nothing. The game tries to be deep, but it isn't. There's a wiki cataloguing all the unexplained things in this game. The thing is, they're unexplained because it's pure nonsense. Admitadly, this isn't a huge problem, it's all quite the spectacle to behold really. I just don't think the game should get away with so much... malarky.
Now for the real issue at hand, one of the most egregious offenses of any game, it's designed to waste your time! You spend a lot of time wandering aimlessly trying to find the next set of puzzles so you can learn how to interact with their elements, and this only gets worse the further along you are. Worst of all there are puzzles that force you to go out of your way. For example, during a sequence of puzzles the floor opens up and becomes a wall. The puzzles you have to solve are now on the other side of this new wall which is now blocking the path permanently. You have to leave and go around the entire area to continue solving these puzzles! Furthermore there are puzzles that make things articially difficult, especially later on. Obscuring your vision, forcing you to go back and forth, basically not things that make the puzzles themselves harder, just waste more of your time.
Ultimately, I wouldn't even recommend it to puzzle enthusiasts at the rediculous asking price of $40. If you are into puzzles, and like to admire the scenery, you might find value in this at half off. I barely did.

A mix of positive and negative. I cannot really recommend it, and under no circumstances should you even consider this game if you have any visual or audio impairment, whether in your computer or your head. The game will require things that are physically impossible for you and not even explain that.
When it works, it works, and when it doesn't, you Google and probably find that you were wasting your time because you needed to solve some other puzzles before this one had enough information/pieces/whatever. If that sounds fun, this is for you.
Puzzles do not explain their rules, so you are stuck with trial and error to find what this puzzle wants. Except that maybe there were a series of introductory puzzles for this rule type, but you happened to walk into an advanced puzzle before a basic one and nothing explained that the rules changed. "What do you want from me?!" If that sounds fun, this is for you.
Half the puzzle is finding the puzzles. Some need a chain of other puzzles or precise placement. Some need to be activated in a long series of steps, so make sure to backtrack and see if finishing puzzles A, C, D, E, F, and K opened B.
Not friendly to visual impairments. Some things look like logic puzzles but are instead puzzles of "can you walk to the right spot and turn at the right angle to find a visual effect that just gives you the answer?" Once you have that down, you get multiple steps, like (1) find the puzzle, (2) activate it, (3) find the right angle for part a, (4) find the switch to change the puzzle's angle, (5) find the right angle for part b, (6) maybe repeat those steps for a few letters, and (7) put it together and answer (from the right spot) (from the right angle). That probably sounds fun to some folks, so this is for you. I am told it does the same for audio impairments later; I have not gotten that far.
This may be surprising for some players or developers, but there is a range of human visual function and memory. Some people cannot see some colors. If a puzzle requires color vision, the game is over for those players at that point, and they will not even see why until they Google it. Some people have literally no visual memory or ability to picture things in their heads. If a puzzle requires combining multiple visuals, that could be surmountable with screenshots. And so on with other perception difficulties.
I am going to play a bit further in search of epiphanies, but the mix of "figure out the rules, we won't tell you" and "sometimes the rule is neurologically unlikely for you to even perceive" is bad for me, like giving a game requiring pixel-perfect placement to someone with Parkinson's.

For starters: Puzzles. If you don't like them, then you're going to struggle through The Witness without a companion guide (and honestly, there really isn't much point in playing that way unless you're totally stumped, so move along in your Recommendations Queue). Love puzzles as much as I do? Liked Portal? Chances are, you'll enjoy The Witness; maybe more or less than I did--but about that, later.
The Witness has an elegantly simple premise: Solve a puzzle = Move Along Home. Solve a puzzle = Move Along Home. That's the first layer of the game; and the game teaches you how to play as you Move Along Home, steadily increasing the difficulty of puzzles, the rules of certain subsets of puzzles, all the while, tantalisingly, and teasingly, edging you on with beacons you feel, eventually, will culminate in answers. That's all there is to it. If that's enough for you, if you think you'll get your money's worth from this paragraph alone, what are you waiting for?
The second layer, without giving anything away, is all about presence, space, time, and perspective. What the first layer does is rewire how you see the world of The Witness; and, in turn, how you experience your own sense of presence, space, time, and perspective, external to the game. There are a handful of Easter eggs to this effect, reminding you... well... about yourself. Your relationships with things, within other things, without them, be they objects, people. That difficult-to-quantify substance about human nature, all of it harking back to my undergrad philosophy days and them some.
I'd say the third layer, that's a combination of the first and second, challenging how you experience your self; and your self experiencing the game; how you move about space; how you regard the time you spend (in game, out of); how you see, what you consider you see, how that changes, how your perspective has changed throughout the course of the game and your life; how a moment ago, a puzzle seemed impossible, and the next, is solved. Always the now.
All of this culminates in a unique gaming experience, philosophical, at times almost spiritual, as you delve into your own psyche (sometimes at wit's end), and the delicate strata of the developer/s, "clues; scattered all over the table like crumbs".
Will it be easy? No.
Will it be hard? No.
Will there be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t? Such is life.
Get out there and find out!

"Lost Luggage" is a mini game accessible from the main menu of Let's Explore the Airport. Most of my playtime was spent in this mini-game, so that is what I will focus on.
AVOID THIS GAME. I was with two other adults, and we all worked together to solve the puzzles in Lost Luggage. Initially, we were having fun joking around about a game that one of us had fond memories of. The game starts out wtih very little challenge. This is a facade to lower your defenses for the brutality you will encounter later.
Lost Luggage is a tile-based action/puzzle game. Up to four suitcases have to be redirected to their color-coded luggage carrier to complete each level. There are conveyor belts, switches, etc., which are manipulated by the player to change where a suitcase goes. The player has to direct the suitcases of each color to the carrier that matches it.
There are 99 levels. The difficulty changes wildly. Throughout the entire experience, even as high as level 70 or 80, there will be simple levels that can be completed in two attempts. These break up the challenge from some other difficult levels. The difficulty rarely comes from the puzzles itself. Almost all of the difficulty comes from the "action" part of the gameplay. Levels put four suitcases very close to each other, so the player has to rapidly enable and disable switches to split up the suitcases and send them where they need to go. The animations in general are clunky and unresponsive. In particular, the pusher device that moves luggage one tile off its path has an odd recovery/cooldown animation that makes it hard to hit the precise timing required in later levels.
Near-constant player interaction is required to complete many of the later levels. We called this "juggling" - manually making a switch or conveyor belt activate, to keep a suitcase going in a loop while trying to move another suitcase where it needed to go. The player needs to do this because otherwise, a suitcase can fall of the edge or fall in the wrong-colored suitcase bin, both of which fail the level and cause a level restart. With no safe areas for some suitcases, no spot you can just put them and temporarily ignore them, this is required.
It took three fully-grown adults, one of whom had prior experience with the game, around 2 hours and 20 minutes to finish all 99 levels. We were working in full co-operation. Each of us noticed strategies the others didn't. I would expect a full playthrough to take longer if you're playing by yourself. 20 minutes longer if we're being generous, at least one hour longer if we're being realistic. It started as a fun nostalgia trip. It became a maniacal suicide pact. We had to keep going. The levels were bad. We had to keep going. The action was hard. We had to keep going. The suitcases got merged on top of each other. We had to keep going.
I cannot imagine any child aged 3-8 being able to handle this garbage. We nearly gave up. The cruelest part of this whole game is the MASSIVE difficulty / unfairness spike that comes on the very last level, number 99.
Level 99. I curse it. I curse whoever created it. I curse whoever tested it and thought it was a good idea. After beating it, we tried looking up people who worked on this game, so we could harass them on Twitter, something which is generally not proposed or advocated by civilized people. That's how mad we were about Level 99. I really want to talk to the people who worked on this game. Did anyone actually play this level? How did they think it was a good idea? And what monster created it? Let me tell you about level 99.
Level 99 is one of the worst levels of any video game ever made. It takes one of the worst things about this game, and bases its entire solution on this. It is not a culmination of the game mechanics introduced in levels 1-98; rather, it is a short-circuiting around most of Lost Luggage's core values, like puzzle-solving and clever timing. Here is the structure of level 99. There are four suitcases colored red, yellow, blue, and green. This is typical, especially in the later levels. They each have matching luggage bins they need to go into. If, for example, a red suitcase falls into a blue bin, you fail the level and have to try again. The level starts with two suitcases in the middle of the screen on a path of certain destruction (falling off the level, which makes you fail). The first step to beating this level is switching the direction of the conveyor belt they hit right before they fall off. The next step is stopping four more similar fail states: two each on two luggage chutes (think "Portal"; they go in one chute and out another. But which chute they end up at, and the direction they exit, is random). You have to switch those four conveyor belts from pushing exiting luggage off the level, and instead push them back into the chute for another trip on the Random Express.
Then, I'm pretty sure there are more conveyor belts to change the direction of. If you don't, you open yourself up to more possible failures. Sorry for not being exact here, but the point is, it takes manual work to play level 99 perfectly. Each time you fail, you have to redo that manual work. At least six mouse clicks; probably more.
The rotten core of Level 99 is that even when you play perfectly, you barely have a chance. Mathematically, there's almost no hope. I got out paper and a pencil and tried to figure out the odds while my friend operated the mouse, a digital Sisyphus. Except instead of rolling a stone he was rolling a trackball. By my count, here's how it works. There are 6 baggage chutes. 4 of them can lead to the color-coded suitcase carrier. Suitcases exiting a chute cannot directly enter a carrier. Cases never come out of the chute they just entered. That means the number of outcomes for a case entering a chute depends on which of the six chutes it enters. This combines with the other attributes I mentioned to make calculating the probability of a case travelling any one path rather difficult. I also have not measured whether the game takes a stratified sample of chutes first, then the exits from the chutes, or just takes a simple random sample of possible exits. The sampling algorithm should not change the chance of winning, but it would have a dramatic effect on how long each attempt takes. The only outcomes of a chute that matter are the ones that put your suitcase in a carrier. The other outcomes all involve your suitcase going back in a chute, so it's just another attempt at getting a carrier. There are four carriers, you don't win without matching carriers to the right suitcase, all of them have to be matched, and a suitcase already being in a carrier doesn't stop another suitcase coming through the chute and landing in it, failing the level.
We can simplify this probability problem. When you put a case in a chute, there's a (1/4) chance of it ending up in the proper carrier. (3/4) of the outcomes that matter involve the case landing in the wrong-colored carrier, which causes a level fail. The other outcomes just make the player re-do these odds. Outcomes are independent. Each suitcase has a (1/4) chance of success. The chance of multiple independent events happening together is calculated by multiplying the individual chances. In our case, that is: (1/4) * (1/4) * (1/4) * (1/4) = (1/4)^4 = 1/256 = 0.00390625 ≈ .004.
But if you're smart, you can help your odds immensely. Send all the suitcases except the yellow one into the chute closest to the yellow carrier. Send the yellow suitcase into the chute closest to the red carrier. As I said earlier, cases never exit the same chute they enter. So putting the cases into chutes corresponding to outcomes you DON'T want improves the chance of success. Then it becomes (1 / [4-1] )^4 = (1/3)^4 = 1/81 = 0.01234568 ≈ .012. That's four times more likely, and puts your chances above 1 percent.

You're going to tell me that I didn't spend enough time to test the game. Well, I'm not a kid anymore and I must say that while I'm open to every new knowledge, planes and airport aren't really my field of interest.
However, Let's Explore the Airport (Junior Fiel Trips) did amaze me for its richness. Let me explain.
The aim of the software is to educate young children to everything related to an airport. You're going to find in there planes (well, outdated as the game was released in 1995), the luggage circuits, cockpit, hangars, shops, etc.. You can navigate from a location to another, though I must say that going back is sometimes very hard, as seen at the security gate for example. But to learn, you have to be aware of every area of interest, thanks to the button What is this?. With that, you'll see names with an interrogation mark. Just hovering will trigger the pronounciation of the object. And if you click on it, you'll enter the index (which is also existing on its own with the button Index).
More precisely, clicking on an object will send you in the definition page of the index. There, some highlighted words can be read aloud and lead to their own definition. The Read Aloud button will read the entire definition for kids that can't read or that are learning English.
However, it wouldn't be fun if you didn't have minigames. They're five: a trivia quizz (self-explanatory), What is this (associating a picture to a word), Lost Luggage (a puzzle game where you have to lead some luggage in the cart of the same color by changing the arrows on the conveyor belt), Find it (where a small picture is shown and you have to find in the right scene) and a coloring book (with a brush to color and a eye dropper to mix colors to obtain complex ones like green, orange, purple, etc..). Score are also kept as you can create several profiles (with the choice of the colors for each letter of the name of the player). Each game, except the coloring book, has three levels of difficulties.
As you can see, Let's Explore is really thought as an educational game. Contrary to Big Thinkers, you're not drown into overcharged graphics, even if these are clearly outdated. But as it's representative of its time, you have some areas that can be clicked on and allow a little animation to play. Kids can have fun with that. The soundtrack is nice too.
My only little problem is that everything is in English and it might be quite hard for kids that aren't native speakers, it might also be a problem for an adult, even if he's fluent in English as there are some technical texts in there. However, if it's for learning English, it can be a good way. Well maybe not with the airport, but with the two other games in the same series (farm and jungle), it could be really fun for children.
Anyway, don't worry, Let's Explore the Airport is excellent for learning how an airport work, though, you should be aware that given the age, security back then wasn't as tight as today. But aside that, I find the software interesting for non-English speakers in a course for learning the language.

First of all, and my biggest happy thing with this game: Female perspectives. Real but futuristic, quirky, sometimes even "bad", female perspectives. You're not getting male fan service with this game. Sure you could say there's a lot of games out there like that, but most are very pink sparkly magical worlds. This is a dystopian society with androids, talking dogs, and brains in jars. I'd be lying if I said there was zero - there's a lot of mention of boobs, but it's mostly casual and not invasive talk; not aimed toward's just one half of the human race's gaze.
My next favorite thing that ties in with the former, LGBTQ relationships! That are not perverted to hell and back. Do not get me wrong, I can be a pervy as they come, but this game focuses on the actual relationships without, again, worrying about a guy enjoying the lesbians. I don't want to spoil too much, but if you are LGBTQ, play this game.
Then there is just the story it's self. The game for being kind of short (I mean, you have multiple play throughs, but I finished round one in a day and even AFKed a ton) it's really involved. There's a lot of lore, companies, government, factions, and just people you have to keep track of to make sense of everything. I really appreciate this in a game because often times in visual novels I can end up... well, just clicking away to progress without paying attention to details. Missing the minute details can have an effect on the story, as most of the progression depends on your memory and slinging drinks.
The game it's self between the colorful music, the retro styled graphics, and the futuristic storyline reminds me a lot of movies from the 80's. It's hilarious, it can jerk on your heart strings a bit, it's involved, it has little fan service, and LGBTQ galore but with plenty of straight material as well. Not to mention some how - again for how short it was - there's a lot of subject material that makes you stop and think.
Definitly plan on playing to finish the rest of the story and achievements.

Valhalla is a visual novel where no one actually talks like a god damn human being. A normal human to be specific; the majority of dialogue is entirely interchangeable between the characters because they all speak like a person trying far too hard to be wacky, zany and/or quirky. They use childish insults like jerkwad, giggle incessantly at lame sexual innuendos that they repeat ad nauseum and then talk loudly about actual sexual acts to get attention. They are the people in every university anime club that has and ever will exist.
I never went back after the first meeting. Perhaps I should thank them for being so obnoxious.
I am getting off topic, the dialogue is legitimately awful for most of the game and outside of a couple of bad stereotypes that have zero depth, each character has roughly the same voice. The underage sex bot is pretty gross too and extremely unfunny and unsympathetic. Bad shock value I guess? She does have one chunk of dialogue which is vaguely insightful but it's completely undercut by everything she says and does up to that point, a complete 180 on her atrocious character design.
All of the aforementioned is unfortunate because the main thrust of the story, that of the main character Jill is actually solid and relatable. It's handled decently, although it does get a touch melodramatic and the dialogue veers off into just awful territory undercutting the emotional significance and gravitas, but it still works because it is not an issue bound to its setting.
The rest of the side stories were honestly forgettable; some had run of the mill problems and others were stupidly outlandish and a bit too anime. Again, the dialogue makes everyone unsympathetic and it's hard to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥
The actual gameplay is really fun though with the drink mixing mini-game essentially acting as a dialogue choice in a way of speaking; the right drinks keep things going and improve relationships, certain drinks at certain times can unlock unique dialogue as can getting the patron extremely drunk. It's fantastic and innovative but kind of wasted on the cast.
If you're interested in trying a unique visual novel it is worth a shot, but if the dialogue starts to grate on you just quit because it does not get any better.

The presentation is done alright, at least when it comes to visuals. The character designs are brilliant. I won't comment on the music, not to my taste, don't believe it fits with the gameplay, but I can see it is well engineered.
The set-up is pretty cool, the athmosphere of the game plays well with the combat.
This is an all bosses game, all thriller and no filler... Or that was the plan at least, but it seems the creators didn't fully comprehend why boss rush games exist. Instead of having nothing but the fights, you have these inbetween segments. Now Quiet TIme is good in games, it helps you relax after a challenge then build up tension for another. But this concept is executed godawfully in Furi. They got a wacky character to talk to you about the world, your past and future enemies and that's good enough for some build-up to the fights, but these segments over which he talks are painful to go through. From the nauseating jump cuts to the fact that you can only control the character 10% of the time, and by control i mean hold the analog in one direction while he moves at a snails pace. No sprinting dashing, or even trning another direction. This doesn't calm me down after a fight this is frustrating. WHO THOUGHT THIS WAS A GOOD IDEA? If they wanted cutscenes they should've made these segments cutscenes. This anihalates the pacing the pacing. Honestly going from boss to boss with no introduction wouldve been much better. Or maybe having some very basic platforming with weird mario galaxy like physics, since the world is so surreal.
The combat system itself is great. A lot of complexity, comprehensive utorial that doesn't hold your hand and plenty of interactions between moves hat are not explaind but have to be understood through play. The encounters themselves leave a bit to be desired. The lives system is fair and interesting but some bosses have way too many phases to go through and sometimes they completeley change the rules(not the style, the rules) during the final phases. The difficulty is all over the damn place, it feels like the bosses shold've been in another order and once you understand all the mechanics you see how much artificial difficulty the injected into this game to pad it out(see the constant running away, shields, aoe charge up and jump atacks that have no dodging window of the 2nd fight).
The battle arenas also suck, they look cool but feel terrible to play in. Because of the perspective you will often not be able to see what's goingon when there's something in the way. The game TRIES to remedy this by having glowing outlines when the characters are obscured, but this doesn't help since you won't be able to read the animations just from the silhouettes. Also you never know if you're gonna fall of the edge or not and ou cant always stay in the safe since bosses like to run along the edge of the arena.
If you're a casual gamer who prefers defensive tactics this game is gonna assault you. If you like offense and are good at executing frame perfect moves and keeping your head cool as you stand inches before your opponent this game will enrage you as the enemies will keep running away from your perfect counters, making you chase them for minutes, just so you canget comboed.
This is a great idea with terrible execution. It might look cool and the combat may look fun, but its not. Unless this game with the DLC is under 4 bucks I would advise against purchasing it. It's a very short experience that will leave you feeling sour and unfullfiled. For all you people who love challenging games, look elsewhere, this game isnt hard, just endlesly frustrating.

--Review for veterans who love the genre--
I know you were looking for THAT space station game that would finally replace Space Colony, Startopia, etc. from your game library.  This game, while passable, is NOT it.
- The COLONISTS are not an improvement from older games.  They stand around doing nothing or pick the jobs that are just not needed right now.
-  You CANNOT assign beds, to make it easier to get to work.
-  There is no fast travel to reach the farther areas of the base.  So if you plop down a cabin, which is a room that assigns colonists ther own PERSONAL bed, and then they have to work in the other side of the map.  Well then thats quite a problem. If I could asign the bed to a someone who works nearby, tha would be awesome.
- You can hire five different colonist types. Who cares what there names will be, because your going to have hundreds of them.  They do NOT improve in skill nor can you improve their equipment.  The only ones that get an upgrade are guards, you can give them a generic gun.
The INDUSTRY/ECONOMICS.   You can make robots to help run the base. Miner/Constructor/Carry bot.  Make generic "guns" to either give to your security force or sell to traders.
- You can sell any other surplus items you over produced in the base.  Its very easy to have a surplus of food.
- You CAN prioritize rooms, but not specific jobs in that room, like making specific materials you need. This forces you to specialize rooms, for example I have a small factory room at the corner of my base that can produce 4 weapons at a time.  I turn this on every time I hire guards.
-  You can also trade with passing ships but you CANNOT prioritize transporting goods to the landed trader.  So if your base is just too busy the ship cancels trading and leaves.
-  You can limit the amount of items your base can produce which will stop your colonists from expending all your resources.
-  So the fun really is in managing a 300+ person station with a bad interface and Bad AI.
Tech
No research.  You buy every new tech from the traders.  There are 8 improvements.  You will not use all 8.
Combat/conflict
Automatic lasers that shoot down meteors that get to close.  Guards man security consoles to look for intruders.  The guards can then track down these intruders and use the gun you gave them.  You can also hit the red alert button to allow colonists to go to the guard locker and grab a gun.  Which I never needed to do yet as the guards have easily destroyed every intruder.  Sadly no other items like armor or medkits.   No other enemy aside from the generic "intruder" 15 hours in.
Biggest caveat ---> There is very little control over the people, aside from "prioritize this room".  And we all know AI tend to be dumb in games like this, which is why I like the option to help it once in a while.
While pretty to look at and I got to kill 16 hours playing it, I realize, it has LITTLE OR NO REPLAYABILITY.  Once you figure out the right build order and how to stabilize there is very little challenge in the game.  The only challenge remaning is figuring out how to grow larger, population 300.  And for someone like me, I was hoping for more gameplay.  The completionist in me might just reach for the 300 just to say that I did.  But really after 15 hours, other games are more interesting/challenging/fun.
Don't get me wrong its an OK game, which can be played with one hand.  So if you have to be bedridden for a few days this game is a good fit.  But not worth the asking price.   Wait for a sale less than $10.

I really want to reccommend this game and give it praise. I've spent a lot of time playing it on my PC, and many more hours have been spent on my ps4. Until my experience with this game on PC, however, I had no idea just how amateurish Ubisoft really is. I should clarify that if it weren't for Ubisoft's abomination of online services or their track record for rushing out unpolished turds, this game would a 10/10 in my books. I wish I didn't let Ubisoft's half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥pepsi-like attitude ruin this game for me, but after completing the game (which is incredibly easy and repetitive), all that remains for entertainment is finishing up odd ends in the campaign or playing online services. Both are affected by Ubisoft's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ self, the ladder more so. Regardless, here's the good, the meh, and the terribly infuriating:
Why should you play this game? Well, the graphics are fantastic, for one. The voice acting is incredible - the emotions the actors convey really help to integrate you into the game. Speaking of in-game integration, the surround-sound headphone support is just as amazing - I can hear tigers before they come at me, I can hear bullets whistling by, and I can hear trucks pulling up filled with guards. The scenery, the open-land concept, the wing-suit and the thud of an arrow into an enemy's chest all make this a visually and all-round sensory pleasing experience of a game. The smaller details, like rustling of bushes, heavy panting from breathing, and an awesome Indian-feeling soundtrack shouldn't go unpraised, either. However, like most of Ubisoft's♥♥♥♥♥♥ they only focus on the outside, and while the outside may seem pleasing, I'm sure most gamers would agree that it's the core and substance of a game that really makes it worthy to remain in our libraries and echo chambers of praise. This game, unfortuneately, is hollow, shallow, and void of substance. Which brings me to my next section.
Why shouldn't you get your hopes up for this game? Well, it's repetative. LIke all Ubisoft games. I can't stress that enough, though I feel like I'm beating a dead horse, I'm just late to the party n my stick is strong n freshly polished. Once you turn off the looting animations (which becomes essential, unless you want to spend 3 extra seconds in the middle of combat feeling up dead bodies for statues and needles), the 'hold X to interact' becomes singed into your retinas. It doesn't help that the same action is required for disarming bombs, entering vehicles, opening chests, picking leaves, or skinning animals. But that's not all that repeats. The gameplay, the story, the missions - they're all the ♥♥♥♥ing same! "Hey, Ajay, these guys over here are against us. Go kill them!" "Hey, Ajay, you need to asssinate that guy, but this time with a different gun." "Hey, Ajay, sneak into a camp and difuse the bombs.. lol just kidding, you can just kill everyone instead" "Ajay, great, you're here, listen, we need you to assassinate a general and loot his body and make sure no one sees you doing it. Did we mention you can just kill everyone there?" "Hey, Ajay, you must make a choice for Kyrat, which way will it go? Lol anyways just kill the person you disagree with n let me know when you're done". I wish I was joking, but I'm not. The guns have no range (with regards to customization) and it's made very clear very early which 4 weapons you should have on you at all times - a shotgun for close range, a bow for explosives/hard to reach posters/ silent kills, the bushman (an assualt rifle), and a sniper, which you will proceed to use to clear out every single outpost. Ever. Money becomes something akin to scratching your♥♥♥♥♥ as its everywhere and of no significance, items become useless and a waste of time to look for, weapons become boring and unexciting as you quickly learn that nothing really works quite like the combo mentioned above, and vehicles become a last-resort when you're not high enough altitude-wise to use the wing suit (which is ♥♥♥♥ing sweet, no matter what sort of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you find in this game). I could continue ranting about terrible vehicle controls, awkward take-down intitiations, poorly-designed inventory cycling, the moot options of difficulty which have no reward system, and the unneccessary and boring-as-♥♥♥♥ skill tree, but let's move on to the real issues.
Why shouldn' you waste your money on this game? Well, for one, it'll tell Ubisoft that they're doing a good job, and they'll pat themselves on the back, and continue to rush out unpolished nuggets of poop like this - we're consumers, folks, and it's a little sad that our voice isn't as loud as it should be. By paying for games like this - not to mention pre-ordering ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like the new AC - we're not only shooting our selves in the foot but giving♥♥♥♥♥♥run companies like Ubisoft the gun, the ammunition, and the rights to our other, less-blown-apart foot. But more importantly, the glitches, the horrible, HORRIBLE online client/dumpster fire of a program called 'Uplay', and the awful online service/support should all be enough to deter you from paying for this game. Glitchy is an understatement. Now, on PS4, it seemed to run fine, so this may only be a problem with the PC port, but while running on Windows, the game constantly has problems with barriers and hit boxes, fusing your character into scenery or inbetween boxes, being blocked by NPC's, looping sounds, or delaying in-game messages. To be fair, lots of games have problems, but Far Cry 4 isn't new, and it still hasn't had any good fixes to issues like your bow stuttering and being unuseable, or your take-down icon not showing up while you're right behind an enemy. If any of that doesn't bother you, how about you take a gander with Uplay, which is exactly as it sounds: a retard asking you to play a game with them. You play? You play game? Yes. You play games. Online. Sometimes. The connection is as attrocious as it is pretentious - why on earth should I have to suffer through your stupid pepsi-like self-promotion just to play online with some friends? Isn't that what steam is for? No matter, I'll just run it on offline mode and play my game on my own time, away from an internet connection, without the need to broadcast to people that I just completed yet another stupid Ubisoft-created achievement. Shouldn't be a problem, right? Wrong. Uplay constantly forces you to update the game save data to a cloud. When it can't sign you in the first time, it brings you back to the log in screen with your password left blank, and recommends you start it in offline mode instead - without giving you a proper option to skip sign-in and just go offline. Playing with friends over a set connection was even more infuriating, though to be fair, once we got it started, it flowed more or less seamlessly - we just had to make sure our controllers, headphones, and hdmi-output cables were all connected before hand, otherwise we'd be♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck, forced to restart the game and rewatch the beginning ads for Ubisoft and NVidia - "The way games should be played".
I wish I had some little tidbit of good news, like that I have faith the team over at Ubisoft will get the message and release our shackles to Uplay, their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cousin. Or maybe that they'll update the game, fixing the glitches, adding some sort of variety to the play style. But to be perfectly honest, with Far Cry 5 coming out in May next year, this will just continue to exist as an unfinished masterpiece. It could have been great, but thanks to Ubisoft, it's just... meh (if not infuriating).

The Witness is a gaming experience like no other. It has no narrative, no other characters to interact with, no health or HUD, and very few game mechanics (you can't even jump), yet it's ability to teach, evoke emotion, and captivate you into finding every secret and solving every puzzle simply through the design of it's environment and the puzzles within it, is what defines this as one of the most intelligent and absorbing games ever made.
You cannot begin to understand the layers of intelligence and cleverness that the game's island possesses and challenges you with, and I can't describe them to you without giving away any spoilers. I can't recall any other game I've played (and I've been playing games for over 20 years) that has provided so many "oh my word that's absolute genius" moments when I've noticed yet another thing the game does that is easily overlooked and brilliantly interwoven into the island's design.
The puzzles themselves follow a simple common rule - draw an uninterrupted line from the circular start point to the half-circular end point - but the additional rules and challenges that each area of the island throws at you are enough to keep you constantly thinking, observing, and obsessing over their solutions, even when you're not playing the game itself. What's more, most of the puzzles have enough variables that you're extremely unlikely to get the solution just by guessing - although sometimes an element of trial and error is necessary to figure out if your theories are correct.
If you play this game, I strongly recommend you don't get any outside assistance. The solutions to all the puzzles and secrets are, of course, available on the net, but the feeling of satisfaction when you've finally cracked that difficult puzzle, or of wonder when you discover a secret about a seemingly innocuous area that you've walked through oblivious many times before, these are the emotions that define the game, that reward you for your perseverance, and that make it the masterpiece that it is.
Even when you think you're finished, there is more to do, more to find, more to see, and a special area of the island that provides you with it's toughest, most frustrating, most heartbeat-increasing puzzles of them all - you'll never be able to hear Grieg in the same way again.
To summarise, if you're looking for mindless entertainment with lots of explosions and the ability to swear at 13-year old kids, this is not for you. The Witness is a game that took several years to make, and it shows in every detail packed into it's game world. It's ability to combine clever puzzles, many layers of intelligence and intrigue, and a beautiful, colourful world is unmatched by anything that has come before, and probably by anything you'll ever play again.

Biggest question, is this game PAY TO WIN? As someone who has figured out most of the free mechanics I'll answer
My review will both be an recommendation and a guide for new players since there are many mechanics not apparent.
1. Like most clicking games, use an autoclicker is preferred to power through the first few time loops (this games version of resets)
2. Permanent upgrades that can carry over in time loops are gems (green currency), Blue currency, purple currency, your artifacts, your tomes, and hero equipment levels gained from chests.
3. Most of your progression your dozen or so loops is powering through the first 100 levels with mouse clicking (magic) so use all your gold to upgrade magic.
4. As you are looping, open boosted chests with keys gained from looping to upgrade your heroes, I would only summon the defender and huntress (first 2 heroes) so the permanent upgrades from chests just go to them. after about 10-20 loops, your huntress and defender will get powerful enough to auto clear the first 100 levels.
5. Skill wise, Defender should have a few points of defense to give shield to other heroes and Huntress should have a few points in rapid reload to clear faster and when she is high enough level put points in big game to auto farm arrowhead artifacts.
6. VERY IMPORTANT. If you are not going to spend money. DO NOT use your gems/green currency to buy anything, you gain quite a bit from achievements and you should save up to buy the chronosphere which costs 500 gems which you can earn eventually with achievements. The chronosphere is a decent artifact and best of all, once bought you can use the free purple currency to upgrade. This is the only gems artifact I am aware off and can be earned free.
With this setup you are set to autoclearing the first 100-200 levels with just your first 2 heroes, and be able to gain income for both blue currency and purple currencies. Blue currency drop more and more frequently the more levels you go up.
1. Once you earn blue currency consistently, friend tomes are worth it only costing 25 blue currency which can be easily earned in 1 deeper run. It gives you 24 hours to allow help from 2 other people. The game chat regularly advertizes auto clicking friend codes, and you can switch codes as many times as you want in that 24 hours.
2. Crafted artifacts from the purple currency, do not reroll if you are a free player. there are a limited amount of artifacts that you will eventually gain all of them and their stats are fixed so rerolling cant improve them.
3. The only Pay to Play option worth buying is the $1.99 to gain the enchant master for mimic chest, which is not needed but can help speed up progression. Early on only craft Keepums (+2 chest items) and you can keep the chest on time loop and open early on with a key to help upgrade your heroes. Basically with 1.99 for the month you basically unlock all the worthwhile features in the game.
Hope this review/guide helps! Ignore the other reviews saying this is Pay2Win. They simply havent figured out the game mechanics, there are quite a few mechanics you need to understand to start the ball rolling for this game, but once you understand and have an auto process going, this is one of the better clicker games out there.

This the first Visual Novel that i have ever played, and this game was an absolute treat. I think I can safely say that my countrymen's best game to come out of Venezuela is no longer Crazybus.
Here's some advice. Before the game begins, the creators said the game is best enjoyed with drinks and/or snacks. Take the advice and get yourself a drink, and take in this crazy Blade Runner-esque cyberpunk world.
The writing is just absolutely charming, excellent and never overdramatic, and the same applies to the characters that you meet. For the fantastical characters that you meet, they seem to be pretty grounded in reality. There is conflict in the game, but there is no aim to change the world like in other games. You're the little gal just trying to pay her rent on time living her life as a lowly bartender in a cyberpunk hell-hole, after all.
Outside of the mini-game you can purchase, there isn't much "gameplay" to be honest. Your objective is to serve the drinks and listen to their stories, to play the role of the bartender in a comfy bar, trying to help people cope with their problems. There are no outright dialogue choices, but rather, the drinks serve as your choices. Do you give them what they want? Intentionally double the amount of alcohol to possibly get them drunk and say something completely different? Get the drink wrong intentionally?
Mechanically it is a pretty simple game, but the writing is where this game shines, and the awesome soundtrack complements the feel and setting of the game. Speaking of writing, there is ALOT of dialogue, so if you wanted a more active role in a game, this might not be for you. As stated before, this is a laid back, chill game. So have a drink, listen to the stories, and before you know, you'll warm up to this game.
The game is now fully complete. There is an extra ending plus the prototype prologue for those wanting to come back, and a complete product for newcomers.

This War Of Mine puts you in the shoes of civilians caught in the cross fire of conflict, who are just trying to survive. Its a bog standard survival game but with a unique and never done before premise.
I was going back and forth between reccomending and not reccomending it. The positives are the game does what it sets out to do really well. The world is bleak and there are no easy choices. You will feel bad for things you did or could not do. Its not a "fun" game in the traditional sense. The survival mechanics are standard but well implemented and properly explained. Its fairly engrossing building your shelter up and going out at night to scavenge for stuff. The game above all should be played for the storytelling, atmopshere, characterization and tension. It also helps that none of the traditional survival meters are nagging or annoying you. Its okay to sleep hungry or be a bit tired or sad. But the fact your characters can never ♥♥♥♥ing stop getting sick for no ♥♥♥♥ing reason is beyond my understanding.
In terms of subject matter This War Of Mine is really good at what it does. However the never ending grimness does come at some cost. The game is relentlessly depressing and often boring, and not by accident but by pure intention. Your situation is essentially hopeless and that’s exactly the point the game is trying to make, but that makes it difficult to keep you engaged over the long term.
It doesnt help that the combat and stealth mechanics are awful. The AI can hear you and see you from a mile away making the dangerous missions all the more terrible. You dont have much room to hide and your characters speed is that of a drunk Walrus. Nor can you control how stealthy or quiet you are as there is no mode or mechanic to compensate for stealth. So you will slowly be pushing your controller while you sit in agonizing boredom and frustration.
All in all its a fun little survival game but dont expect it to hold your attention to the end because you will either quit out of boredom, frustration or just beign too damn easy.

I have been playing for a week and putting at least 6 hours time into the game per day.
After about a week I have come up with the following opinion of the game.
We'll start with the negatives first:
1. The game is all about grinding the same Pvp & Pve maps over and over again until you get a Rank 6 ship.
2. After that huge grind for a week to two weeks at 4-6 hours a day you finally get open space.
3. Once you get to open space anything and everything can and will kill you including other players at high levels.
4. You start to understand that PvP is way off balance and that open space is one big PvP map with sectors in it.
5. There is very little info on this game on the internet other than people showing off in Pvp or Tutorials that give you almost no game enhancing info that you can actually use.
6. There is almost no info on open space and the tutorials don't show you what the game is really like and leave you guessing what to do next.
7. Corporations are a joke and finding one that will accept a new player that has its own active members is harder than fitting a square block through a circle hole.
8. People offer to help with info in the game, but then give jokes and ignorant childish remarks instead with little info relevant to the game; and you may spend hours trying to find someone who will actaully give you usefull info.
9. The game offers FREE players smaller than adequate Exp [Synergy] amount and urge you to buy licenses to get the full intended amount or grind for another 2 to 3 days to level even a R3 ship to max.
10. You are normally placed into Pve matches with people who take all the kills or don't do anything at all.
11. Pvp does not really start until you have a R4 ship, until then it's mostly bots and does not count as a Pvp match.
12. Customization is a joke and is just a wrothless waste of real money.
Now the positives:
1. Graphics and game play is awesome.
2. The game interface and interaction is easy and simple to use.
3. You can play the whole entire game without paying money.
4. The missions and rewards are easy to complete for the most part and are actually worth doing and benefit you.
5. There are different ships and each type has a purpose and place.
6.  You can earn 10 Standards for completing achievements.
7. You can keep all of the ships you buy and transfer weapons and gear between certain ones as long as they are within the specific rank for the item.
8. In-Game currency is easy to get and can be saved up in great amounts.
9. There is a workshop that higher level players can use to create better ammo, weapons and ships; eventually.
10. Grouping and playing with friends is ultra easy and fun.
11. Daily rewards for logging in.
12. Being able to be mainly with one faction but still being able to have other factions ships and keep them.
13. Random polls & votes will give you Standards for participating.
14. There are choices in weapons and modules so you won't have to deal with basic ships with bland set-ups.
I recommend that you try it for yourself, all games have negatives and positives and I do not think that should stop someone from trying it out as you can play it 100% free if you wish it will just take longer to do everything.

While I do have some critique for this game, largely I have enjoyed playing with it and have enjoyed the time I spent playing it. I feel I did get my money's worth but YMMV.
The initial establishing period on a planet is the most difficult portion of each scenario, but I have found that unless you stay on top of things, everything can fall apart very quickly. Sometimes you can recover and sometimes you cannot so there is still some risk of over expanding late game.
The good:
I liked the navigational controls for moving around the map and this game absolutely scratches a number of itches for building and resource management. I like the hints provided by the game and the tutorial was informative and fairly short, yet still left a great deal of on-the-job learning of the details. I found learning how to build to be part of the fun and challenge as it was fairly quick to restart if I needed to do so. I also thing that the environments are fairly pretty and the kinetic Oomph and flash of falling meteors is rather nice.
It is timely given the current buzz over the Martian (an excellent book)
It also does do a nice job of showing how stuff can go wrong quickly if you make a misstep, but it doesn't bog down into the micromanagement details so that you also lose the bigger picture.
The Ehh:
I want more challenges in the late game. I think that it can become easier as you become established. I feel that there is a missed opportunity in the form of requests by visitors or trade ships to provide challenge to produce specific goals, or to provide scenarios which would give an established base something to do beyond maintaining the ebb and flow of resources.
The AI is its own challenge. They have little self preservation and it is hard to guide them where you would prefer they be. I would love to see an improvement to their behavior. The most critical issue I have is that often they will stand around starving or thirsty and be so distracted by this they will not build the items which would alleviate their issues. Thankfully we have bots, but I feel the AI is a shortcoming.
the Ugly
You are constrained by the terrain utterly. You cannot level mountains or tunnel under them, which means if you have not chosen wisely or underestimated the space you will need, you are trapped in a valley. If I havea  thriving base and I want to continue, I will be stopped by the terrain which is kinda sad since I wish to play more but cannot.
The challenges for "completion" are too few. I would like more! Additionally I would like more options in planets and scenarios and the expansion of the tech trees.
You cannot define that priority production goes to a specific unit in a dome, just to a dome. While later in the game you can make single purpose domes to direct production, earlier, when it is most critical and when you want it the most, you cannot. This was one of the most frustrating aspects of the game.
Despite aspects where the game falls short, it is very enjoyable to play and is a a great price point for what it is. I would hope that additional bits added in the future would expand what is a fairly solid base game.

One of the biggest pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥I have ever purchased.
The presentation is done alright, at least when it comes to visuals. The character designs are brilliant. I won't comment on the music, not to my taste, don't believe it fits with the gameplay, but I can see it is well engineered.

This is an all bosses game, all thriller and no filler... Or that was the plan at least, but it seems the creators didn't fully comprehend why boss rush games exist. Instead of having nothing but the fights, you have these inbetween segments. Now Quiet TIme is good in games, it helps you relax after a challenge then build up tension for another. But this concept is executed godawfully in Furi. They got a wacky character to talk to you about the world, your past and future enemies and that's good enough for some build-up to the fights, but these segments over which he talks are painful to go through. From the nauseating jump cuts to the fact that you can only control the character 10% of the time, and by control i mean hold the analog in one direction while he moves at a snails pace. No sprinting dashing, or even trning another direction. This doesn't calm me down after a fight this is frustrating. WHO THOUGHT THIS WAS A GOOD IDEA? If they wanted cutscenes they should've made these segments cutscenes. This anihalates the pacing the pacing. Honestly going from boss to boss with no introduction wouldve been much better. Or maybe having some very basic platforming with weird mario galaxy like physics, since the world is so surreal.
The combat system itself is great. A lot of complexity, comprehensive utorial that doesn't hold your hand and plenty of interactions between moves hat are not explaind but have to be understood through play. The encounters themselves leave a bit to be desired. The lives system is fair and interesting but some bosses have way too many phases to go through and sometimes they completeley change the rules(not the style, the rules) during the final phases. The difficulty is all over the damn place, it feels like the bosses shold've been in another order and once you understand all the mechanics you see how much artificial difficulty the injected into this game to pad it out(see the constant running away, shields, aoe charge up and jump atacks that have no dodging window of the 2nd fight).
The battle arenas also suck, they look cool but feel terrible to play in. Because of the perspective you will often not be able to see what's goingon when there's something in the way. The game TRIES to remedy this by having glowing outlines when the characters are obscured, but this doesn't help since you won't be able to read the animations just from the silhouettes. Also you never know if you're gonna fall of the edge or not and ou cant always stay in the safe since bosses like to run along the edge of the arena.
If you're a casual gamer who prefers defensive tactics this game is gonna assault you. If you like offense and are good at executing frame perfect moves and keeping your head cool as you stand inches before your opponent this game will enrage you as the enemies will keep running away from your perfect counters, making you chase them for minutes, just so you canget comboed.
This is a great idea with terrible execution. It might look cool and the combat may look fun, but its not. Unless this game with the DLC is under 4 bucks I would advise against purchasing it. It's a very short experience that will leave you feeling sour and unfullfiled. For all you people who love challenging games, look elsewhere, this game isnt hard, just endlesly frustrating.

When you finish your first session of Volgarr, one thing becomes abundantly clear : Either you're in love or you've simply wasted your money.
This game is extremely hard but manages to strike that balance between frustration and that wonderful feeling of accomplishment that only comes from punitive, hardcore games. If the level design and enemy behaviors weren't expertly handled I would've stopped playing a long time ago. Fortunately, this game is very precisely and masterfully crafted and I just can't put it down.
There is no way around it, you will have to memorize enemy patterns, attacks and level layouts in order to progress.
Getting hit means losing a power-up, just like in Super Mario Bros. While it is possible to keep trudging forward without these power-ups, it makes the game a whole lot trickier
If you manage to get through a level without getting hit, you get more Gold and a chance to play a bonus level. In this way, Volgarr forces you into Speedrunning. If you don't like old-school games where repetition and pattern mastery is obligatory, you will hate Volgarr.
Super Meat boy is the most recent example of this kind of experience; It's a game which is hard but its pacing and level length / instant respawn was crafted to make sure that you'd give it just one more try before heading to bed. Once you cleared a level, it felt abolutely amazing. The same applies to Volgarr.
At first, Volgarr evokes classics Altered Beast and Rastan; in fact, it could be argued that the first level is largely a re-telling of Rastan's first level. As the game progresses, you'll see some Mega Man, elements from Chakan : The forever man and even bits of QuackShot!
This game is obviously targeted at old-school hardcore gamers; if you fit the description, I really don't see how you can not enjoy Volgarr. It is truly a modern classic masterpiece.

Solving each puzzle is interesting, as is dealing with the more general question: what is going on here?  What am I slowly but steadily revealing or accomplishing as I solve one puzzle after another.
I can sense, or at least I anticipate,  that everything somehow fits together in some way; but so far the mystery remains, and only grows.
Even if there were no puzzles and no purpose at all, I would still enjoy the experience of simply walking the large island, discovering what is there.    In places, it is really beautiful.   And the atmosphere is, oddly, both serene and haunting at the same time.
I can't help saying it: this seems like a work produced by genius coupled with great diligence and care.   It may turn out to be my favorite video game of all time.
Will this very favorable impression remain, fade or grow?   Yet another mystery to be solved over time.
