"The Witness" is an amazing puzzle game like no other I'd played.  This is a game where you have to solve a maze without crossing any lines you've highlighted, with symbols in the maze providing extra rules that must be followed.  In a twist, the game gives you no outright instructions - only training puzzles that allow you to intuit how each symbol works.
Note:  I strongly suggest you write down how each symbol works, because you run into symbols late in the game that you learn early in the game.
I like that "The Witness" needs brainpower and not speed or reflexes for success.  There are only two puzzles that are timed in any way, and one of the puzzle is easily solved in the time alloted.  In fact, you know you have solved one of those puzzles correctly when time becomes a non-issue.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to everyone.

This is the BEST puzzle game I've ever played, handsdown. The puzzles are expertly crafted such that they're feasible, but not overly frustrating. If you feel like you can't beat a level, walk away take a tour through the BEAUTIFUL world and find another.
One of the most interesting things I found about this game is that they treat knowledge as a form of progression. There are no items (as of yet, I haven't beaten it) to solve puzzles, and it's not like you cannot progress because of something lke that. Rather, it is your own brain, your own experience, knowing the "syntax" and rules behind each symbol and format that allows you to solve the puzzle. I orginally had no idea what the "star" symbol meant, and each time I encountered one, I would have to walk away. But then I found a series of puzzles that taught you how to do it, in an intuitive yet challenging way. As soon as I knew what to do, I immediately went to solve the others that I had stopped up on.
This game will give you countless "ah-ha!" moments, as well as bend your mind in dimensions not thought possible. Absolutely worth the price. 10/10.

"VA-11 HALL-A (Pronounced "Valhalla") is a visual novel developed by Sukeban Games for PC. VA-11 HALL-A is... well.. it's.. let me refer to the Steam description: "VA-11 HALL-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action is a booze em' up about waifus, technology, and post-dystopia life." Yeah. That. VA-11 HALL-A takes place in the fictitious Glitch City, where you play as Jill; a bartender, working in a bar from which the game earns it's namesake, who is barely able to afford her rent, and therefore must do her best making drinks for her customers so she does not get evicted. That's VA-11 HALL-A in a nutshell, but the game is so much more than that simple description. Every customer that walks through the door is a real character that Jill will have a real conversation with. There are no dialogue options, and there is barely any real gameplay at all. Most of the time it comes down to making the drink the customer wants, the more accurate you are, the more money you get, and some branching story paths come down to whether you serve the right drink at the right time. The gameplay is not difficult and overall is nothing to write home about, but it is also not the reason to play this game. VA-11 HALL-A grabs your attention from the time you first turn the game on. The main menu oozes style, much like the whole game, in a way that I knew I would be hooked as soon as I heard the delightfully warm and somber song than plays over the start screen. VA-11 HALL-A is not a game you play if you're looking for a challenge. It's a game you sit down, grab a beer or a cup of coffee, and just let it unfold in front of your eyes.
The writing is wonderful. It's equally hilarious and poignant, delivering in all the ways you'd want from a visual novel. The characters, though, are the reason to play VA-11 HALL-A. Every character is written differently and perfectly. Every. Single. One. Even characters I disliked upon first meeting them, warmed up to me in ways I did not expect. Each character has different goals and reasons for being in Glitch City, and more specifically, in the bar. One of the major stand-outs of the cast, is the fan-favorite Dorothy. Dorothy is a Lilim, which are a race of humanoid robots. More importantly though, Dorothy is a sex worker, while she has the appearance of a fifteen year-old school girl. Most of the time, this kind of character exists for the sole purpose of being "fan-service," or otherwise known as the risque character whom men will fawn over. Not to completely take a shot at my fellow men, but it's no secret that if men will assuredly fawn over anything that moves. I am, however, proud to say that Dorothy does not fall into any tropes. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in media, are generally represented in two different ways: Depressed and alone or sex-loving manics. While Dorothy definitely does not shy away from her physical enjoyment of her profession from time to time, her character is handled wonderfully. She is a bubbly, cute, and warm person who just wants to make people happy. Dorothy is one of many characters handled with such class and care, that it makes me ecstatic just writing about it here. There's so much love put into them, to make them feel like real people. I could go on for hours about how much I love every character in the game, but the character are the reason for the game, and I would hate to steal that experience from anyone.
VA-11 HALL-A's is so great because it's world is presented in such a way that makes it feel so real. Remember, you're playing as Jill, a character that would go largely unnoticed in the real world, and that's the same here. Things happen in the world around the bar, and you don't do anything about it because that's just how the world works. There isn't even any closure on some of the things that happen, but that's also just how things go in real life. Not to say there isn't a happy ending, just that the overarching problems in the world of VA-11 HALL-A don't become any more clear by the end, but that's not a bad thing. VA-11 HALL-A builds a world that is not much more different then our own, but it's different enough that the game is still engaging. I actually failed my first playthrough of the game. I didn't have enough money to pay rent (Which was my own mistake), so I got the "Bad" ending. In VA-11 HALL-A, there are many endings, but if you get the bad ending, you cannot unlock the others. So, I did what any normal person would do, and started another playthrough. There is actually a New Game+, so any money you collected in your previous run gets carried over to the new one, making it much easier to get all of the secrets and also get all of the endings. But it wasn't just my own stupidity that drove me to want to play the game again. It was my love for the game and it's characters that made me want to see how their stories end. I was able to get all of the endings in my next playthrough, and I couldn't have been more happy. Jill starts every in-game day with the quote at the top of this section "Time to mix drinks and change lives." It's her motto, mostly drenched in sarcasm, but it has some truth. Jill does not have any effect on her world, but she does have a great effect on her customers. Jill does not see herself as someone who has helped people, and still helps people a ton. That's how we as humans are, or at least how we should strive to be, whether you're a bartender or not. I truly love this game. Not only is it my favorite game of 2016, it is easily one of my favorite games ever. Play it. Play it right now."

This war of mine is an impressive demonstration of how very simple gameplay mechanics can serve as a medium to tell a story of a far more serious and far more touching story than one could ever imagine a game being able to tell.

The gameplay is far from stellar, it's passable for the most part and over the years with more stories being added, the possibility to run custom stories and with DLC coming out... the passable gameplay is enough to tell impressive and lasting stories.
Its a way to provide to charity, its a way to prove to people that games can be artistic, its a way to 'enjoy' yourself for some time much in the same way the depressing feeling of something like The Walking Dead can inspire and be a good passtime. Its not 'enjoyable' per say, but it is a rewarding and satisfying experience to well, experience.
All of this making you feel part of it with the gameplay - nothing in the veins of a massive RPG that spans hundreds of hours with a great climax at the end of a tale but... the story of a father making it out of a war with their daugther, the war reporter that got stuck inside the war, just your average fellah' having to cope with surviving and knowing that danger is everywhere and not a single day can be spared!... even tho', you have to spare some days to just simply not go insane.
It difficult to explain what this 'game' can do because its a game, but also not. Its a piece of art, but one that you experience... and its also something you wish to experience, but never in a million years ever want anything near like this happen to you!

While MTG purists stick to the very expensive and uber archaic Magic Online platform, I find that the Duels of the Planeswalker series has provided a much more accessible and varied experience.  Magic 2014 is by far a huge update from past games.  The co-op modes have been included and improved, and we finally see the beginnings of a serviceable sealed play format (think Hearthstone Arena or Scrolls Judgement modes).
The UI in this installment is slick and responsive.  I love that this game streams well, too, so I will be doing more YouTube and Twitch gameplay videos for sure.  There are tons of features packed into this game.  I'd say this is the definitive version of Magic online.  Campaign/single-player is satisfying as well.  I will say I found even the initial battles challenging so this is a great tool for shaking off rust or [re]learning the MTG ropes..  It's a fantastic introduction to the "Return to Ravnica" series, too.  Excellent across the board.
At it's core, this is still fundamentally the same game.  At $10 or less, it's worth it.  You can grind to unlock all the pre-made decks, which you can tweak a bit to your liking, or you can pay to unlock the decks.  Some complain about the microtransactions due to the silly business of buying foil conversions and deck slots but these items are more for the hardcore players..  or those who are impatient.
My only complaint, if I had to say something bad, would be that the DotP: SE version is pretty poop.  They should have included more deck slots for sealed play and perhaps a token to unlock your preferred deck.  The eBook and soundtrack are cool additions but that could have been a third tier bundle, really.
I think this will be my last DotP purchase as it seems that Wizards is committed to releasing one of these every year, which sucks because it spreads the online community thin.  They seem to use this series as a glorified marketing piece but, fortunately, the replay value is very high in spite of these blatant greedy moves.  If you are looking for a definitive MTG experience, look no further!

• Resources that are dropped on the ground after recycling an object will typically remain on the ground until decay if you have a significant job queue or have anything toggled for priority.

The Witness is a gaming experience like no other. It has no narrative, no other characters to interact with, no health or HUD, and very few game mechanics (you can't even jump), yet it's ability to teach, evoke emotion, and captivate you into finding every secret and solving every puzzle simply through the design of it's environment and the puzzles within it, is what defines this as one of the most intelligent and absorbing games ever made.
You cannot begin to understand the layers of intelligence and cleverness that the game's island possesses and challenges you with, and I can't describe them to you without giving away any spoilers. I can't recall any other game I've played (and I've been playing games for over 20 years) that has provided so many "oh my word that's absolute genius" moments when I've noticed yet another thing the game does that is easily overlooked and brilliantly interwoven into the island's design.
The puzzles themselves follow a simple common rule - draw an uninterrupted line from the circular start point to the half-circular end point - but the additional rules and challenges that each area of the island throws at you are enough to keep you constantly thinking, observing, and obsessing over their solutions, even when you're not playing the game itself. What's more, most of the puzzles have enough variables that you're extremely unlikely to get the solution just by guessing - although sometimes an element of trial and error is necessary to figure out if your theories are correct.
If you play this game, I strongly recommend you don't get any outside assistance. The solutions to all the puzzles and secrets are, of course, available on the net, but the feeling of satisfaction when you've finally cracked that difficult puzzle, or of wonder when you discover a secret about a seemingly innocuous area that you've walked through oblivious many times before, these are the emotions that define the game, that reward you for your perseverance, and that make it the masterpiece that it is.
Even when you think you're finished, there is more to do, more to find, more to see, and a special area of the island that provides you with it's toughest, most frustrating, most heartbeat-increasing puzzles of them all - you'll never be able to hear Grieg in the same way again.
To summarise, if you're looking for mindless entertainment with lots of explosions and the ability to swear at 13-year old kids, this is not for you. The Witness is a game that took several years to make, and it shows in every detail packed into it's game world. It's ability to combine clever puzzles, many layers of intelligence and intrigue, and a beautiful, colourful world is unmatched by anything that has come before, and probably by anything you'll ever play again.

Are you someone that:
If you said yes to most of these, then you might find something appealing in this game.
Gameplay itself is really straightforward and simple. Every digimon has a maximum of 2 abilities. the first a low cooldown (CD) attack that does decent damage, the second is a high-hitting longer CD ability. The range of abilities (and animations/looks) are the only differences between digimon regarding abilities. There are no buffs, or status ailments in this game.
The other aspect of this game is collecting digimon and leveling them up or grinding to unlock their other forms. This is a very length process if you do not want to spend money (Or it can also be expensive).
I should note that
. However non-paying players may be able to get these through trade if they have enough in-game currency, or through special events.
Most of the starter from the shows are availble however, such as Guilmon, renamon, agumon etc. It's mainly their variations (such as DexDorugamon, Lucemon etc.) or the main antagonists ("bad guys") from these shows that might be hard to get through normal play. Fortunately sometimes even these are obtainable from other players (they buy them with money, then sell them) or through events.
As you may have read from other reviews, hatching digimon can be hair-ripping, it does require a decent amount of farming to hatch your first few eggs (Or do what I do and trade for them). Unless you have a reinforced egg, the process leading up to hatching has a chance of either failing (losing your farmed items) or destoying the egg(losing the egg as well.)
However you can mitigate the change of failure by consuming 1 hatch backup per attempt but these are EXPENSIVE (consumed every attempt, even if you succeed)!
People can opt to grow eggs beyond the required 3 to hatch and get a change of getting a larger digimon (higher stats as well) but the risk and reward is greatly increased.
My advice to new players:
When hatching, just take the L3 eggs for now and worry about getting your perfect digimon later when you can afford it, you have the option of exchanging the stats between digimon with the same starter, this includes size, augments, and evolution paths-- So just focus on getting what you want first and start enjoying it.

Basically what you see in the previews on the store page is what you get. But some bonuses that I have to add, it seems that every digimon has its own unique model, animation set, and graphical effects(smoke, lasers fire etc.) To me the game earns some plus' there.
The music is forgettable, and the sound system is overall unimpressive. Though the sounds are explicitely bad or anything, just just don't help with the immerstion. The explosions and abilities from a lot of digimon sound really basic "explosiony" and there are no english voice overs (sometimes Iheard some voiced but no idea who they belonged to or what they said since they were not english) The game rather uses text boxes and dialogue to fill in conversations.
I thought it was a little neat twist, but your parter digimon says stuff occasionally, but most of it is redundent and often tips that are annoying to look at over and over again. One funny thing is that you can customize a lot of what the digimon says yourself -- sometimes they will say something when they cast spells, or when you get an error message-- and you can change what they typically say.
Thought I would throw this topic in here, because I know plenty of people who love making their own characters...
Unfortunately there is no customization on character creation aside from picking from one of the 3-4 main cast from Digimon: Data Squads. I believe you can get one of the Digimon Adventures (1st season) main characters if you spend real money. There is some limited customization with the character clothes after creation, but it is all just generic t-shirts, jeans, shoes, gloves and nothing particularly flashy or eye-catching.
The User Interface nothing spectaular, and that most of the translation was done by someone without a fluency in english. The grammar is regularly off, plenty of mispellings, and at times random advanced words are thrown in (that some younger players might not understand the vocabulary) The descriptions and how-to's that the game throws in tend to be confusing or vague. There are just plain lacks of descriptions for some systems in the game that require personal testing or tiral and error to understand what they actually do.
This game feels like a cheaply made digimon game (sadly most do) and there are plenty of translation errors as the company does not natively speak english and their translators do a poor job. People that are likely to find this game enjoyable are those that just want to play with digimon for the novelty and for the purposes of just collecting them. Otherwise, there is little in the game that will attract players. There is nothing that requires skill, little customization, and the grinding is lengthy (Sometimes you get quest chains require you to kill the same heavily farmed monster ~80-100 times)

This game is ridiculously fun. It's claim as a Nintendo Hard game is completely true; not thinking your way through the game will result in death. Not that death requires you to not think it through, you'll just die less from thinking. Knowing and personalizing the controls is the first step in beating this; being able to have every control down will help a lot, since this game requires you to be able to deftly dodge and strike when needed. The bosses can be very puzzle like, since you need to know when to dodge, strike, or otherwise act.
Volgarr has two attacks: sword and spear. The sword will probably be used most often, but throwing the spear not only gives you a ranged attack, but can also MAKE A PLATFORM TO STAND AND JUMP FROM. That's incredible! And this isn't just a feature, you are required to use this ability to make it through the game. Alive. There are many secret areas that make you think "I know what to do, but how", as you need to figure out where to throw spears and where to jump onto those spears.
Volgarr, being a viking, is a badass. Enemies, being dangerous, can rip Volgarr's armor off to kill him. You don't have a health bar, so much as armor. You start with your shield, a buckler. THEN you upgrade to a better metal shield. THEN you get a helmet! THEN A FLAMING SWORD! Each hit you endure will take a piece of armor off, until you have no shield and thus cannot block attacks. This makes being hit a punishment, not an inconvenience, which I absolutely love.
Notes:
You can try to avoid enemies altogether to stay alive.
You can zoom out, making the graphics better and plan ahead easier.
You can set the Zoom out to Toggle which will help a LOT.
You can try to learn all the controls, I mean ALL, to look badass and flashy while also retaining armor.
Bottom Line is; I love this game and absolutely recommend it's full price. It's hard but very rewarding, in a way that games like Rastan, Dark Souls, older Zelda games, and even Super Mario World portray. If you are easily angered, however, probably don't buy this. You will die a lot before you develop a strategy.

This game... Like a combo of Ghosts'n'Goblins and Zelda 2. It takes elements from both of them, and throws them together into a golden gem. At first I found it frustrating, then infuriating, and now... Now, I find it amazing.
It runs very smoothly (important for a game reliant on precision control). Even though you have a limited number of moves, you will learn how to combo them together, and each move has several uses. Roll to dodge, move faster, or make a small hop down a ledge. Jumping combined with spear-stepping can let you climb a flat wall. Double-jump can become a major attack, and when combined with the spear throw you can take out some stronger enemies in a single combo.
A full run takes anywhere from 30 minutes to just over an hour, depending on how much you die. If you can't sit down and play the full game in one run (or simply get frustrated), you can continue along "Path C" with the warps, to any world you've previously reached.
If you are easily frustrated, this may not be the game for you. If you're a speedrunner, a completionist, or just like a good challenge, look into Volgarr. It's the type of game we haven't seen in YEARS.

Toki Tori, pode parecer um jogo infantil há principio pelo fato do personagem principal ser um pintinho. Porém o legal do jogo é a jogabilidade e a tua habilidade de pensar no que irá fazer. O jogo possui o efeito já visto em "Braid" que se baseia em se fez algo errado e viu que não conseguirá refazer, Terá a oportunidade de voltar com o efeito de camera fazendo assim com que você imagine a forma única e correta de se fazer o stage.

It took almost a year, but I finally completed everything in Toki Tori. This speaks to the type of game it is - easy to pick up and play, yet also difficult (but just enough so that it keeps you coming back, despite occasional frustration). But what type of game is it? It's an action/puzzle game, I suppose. You control a chicken-thing named Toki in a series of increasingly challenging 2D stages in which the goal is to collect eggs. As you may have guessed, collecting those eggs without dying or getting stuck is where the "puzzle" part comes in. I also have to say that the one thing which sticks with me about this game is the level design - it's just so perfect - I swear the developers must be geniuses. And although the solutions to some levels are difficult, the game features a nifty time-rewind mechanic, so it's easy to correct mistakes and (eventually) solve levels via trial-and-error. In summary, I highly recommend Toki Tori. And luckily, there is a demo available, so give it a try!

The problem with all the "newest" MTG games...has been theres no customization, you know, like in an actual card game.
They're designed for people to just pick up the game and go, and not have to put in too much thought or reason at the start, so that it doesnt feel "overbearing" to get into the game.
Building your own deck is quite the steep learning curve, but its something that teaches you very quickly what the ins and outs of the game are. When all your decks are pre built....you lose half of the point of card games.
Having said that, I feel like I wasted my money. More to the point, I feel cheated and disenfranchised. When you call your game "Magic the Gathering", there are certain good-faith expectations that are informed, such as core gameplay elements, but also axiomatic truths that are intrinsic to the format of a card game. Core among these are the ability to build your own deck. Due to these misrepresentations, I feel I'm entitled to a refund.
Even at $3.39, I regret this purchase (though I purchased the Special Edition at $6.79).
Would not buy again.

After finishing this game a few hours ago with 75 percent side missions and such, I have a few things to say.
First off, the difficulty is way too easy and scales poorly. Whether you play hard or normal, you will have an easy time with this game if you have a smidge of an understanding of FPS. The AI is incredibly dumb. You can snipe an entire fortress even if bodies are detected without anything happening, so long as you can aim. Dying isn't punishing enough. You can die as many times as you want and you'll just be spawned at the nearest base without losing any progress, unless you were in a quest. Enemies aren't threatening at all. If I see a group of 20 or 30 elite soldiers, killing them all isn't very difficult at all, even without stealthing. You can just pump yourself full of healing syringe and run around shooting everyone in the head. Do not get this game if you like difficult and interesting gameplay rather than story.
The difficulty scales poorly in that towards the end or mid game, Ajay becomes some sort of immortal god who can just walk around kill everyone and soak up all damage and walk out unscathed, provided you have decent aim. This should never happen in games. There should always be a challenge that you have to think around. Half the weapons in this game are overpowered. Once you get a decent amount of money, you can buy guns that can wipe out everyone with no effort, and when you have all the skills you get an insane amount of health and damage resistance which practically makes you invincible.
Something that FC4 does right, though, is stealth and reconnaissance. Most missions can be stealthed. The feeling of sitting on a vantage point and scouting, and then proceeding to take everyone out one by one with knife takedowns, and beat the outpost/fortress undetected is incredibly satisfying. However, the AI deals with stealth poorly. For example, upon finding a body, the AI will split up and search, which makes them very easy to pick off. They also stop searching incredibly quickly and return to an un-alerted state quite quickly. Other than that, stealth is done very well in this game. It is much more satisfying that playing loud, in my opinion, and I have completed virtually all missions and outposts quietly.
The immersion and visuals are needless to say, very pleasing. Sitting at high altitudes to just stare at Mount Everest for a bit is very peaceful and is hard to find in other games. The lighting in darker places and such is perfect, and the soundtracks and ambience to go with this is amazing. The music you hear and sound effects perfectly reflect and remind you where you are. From the dark ambient throat singing in demon caves, to the soft chiming bells in the quiet shacks of the himalayas and higher Kyrat are incredibly immersive and well done. Like FC3, during some campaign missions the music you hear fits so well and really just makes everything so much more fun. You get every emotion with sound in this game.
The narrative isn't very strong. The paths and decisions you take don't really affect the endings and you only really get any real choice towards the end. Anything before that feels rather meaningless. However, what I will say is that the characters can get really interesting. Everything you know about the 'good guys' and 'bad guys' gets very twisted towards the end and you'll be questioning everything.
The side missions are done quite well. There are at least 10 different ones you can try, and there's something for everyone. The situations are similar but always different, and always require different approaches and techniques if you stealth. The assasination and hostage rescues and bomb defuse are some of my favourites.
I'm too tired to write anything more but I do believe this game is worth getting, if you don't mind having ridiculously easy gameplay at times.

When he reaches the bottom, he just lays there while a shark observes from a distance. It knows that there's a frog to eat, and swims over. I'm still running down to Steve screaming for help, but it's already too late. The shark flies out of the water and bites Steve. "F**K! NO! STEVE!" I was alone again. All alone. On a large, lonely island. I stand there defeated, the shark watching me... Waiting for the right moment to strike. There's no point to this anymore. I've gone a whole... how long has it been? 2 hours? 10 days? 5 years? And even then, I've found nothing. I realize that I've been torturing myself this whole time... I could've stopped. I had an fPhone. I could've called it quits. I pull out the fPhone and there's no reception. I take a deep breath, and quit the game. I could've made it... but it wouldn't have been the same without Steve.
RIP STEVE 2016.

It's kind of tough to review an every year iteration of a game like this because all you really have to compare it to is itself. I definitely can appreciate the actual in-game game play improvements and a couple of the decks are pretty awesome with some cool improvements and real synergy (Jace's deck immediately comes to mind). On the downside, the initial game startup is a little less streamlined and takes longer to load, if you're playing with an older computer the graphics setting will randomly reset when you start up, and the decks can feel really long to unlock sometimes. I won't even mention the "Sealed" play because it really varies from person to person.
In the end, new or old player, if you enjoy Magic and want to get a little bit more in your week, this is a great way to do it for cheap.

Magic 2014, like all previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games, is an introduction to Magic: The Gathering. In that regard, it is spectacular, giving new players the tools needed to learn the game. It's not perfect, however, and veterans of MtG will be disappointed by the lack of deck customization and alternative play modes. It can also be a drag to unlock cards to use in the prepackaged decks. The Sealed play mode is also very weak, and generally inferior to previous Duels of the Planeswalkers' featured modes (such as Planechase in 2013). Still, if you're looking to learn Magic, there's no better way than with the Duels of the Plansewalkers series, and even those who know the game can still get at least $10 worth out of it.
At the base of the game are the various decks you can use. Each one has a different theme and playstyle, with relatively little overlap between them. These decks are pre-built, though playing with them unlocks new cards that you can use. Decks are still perfectly capable without the unlocked cards. There are 30 cards to unlock for each deck, with 1 unlocked per with with that deck; if you want to unlock every card for every deck, abandon hope of that now. Between the base game, deck packs, and expansion, there are about 20 different decks to use, giving plenty of variety and allowing for many playstyles to be utilized.
The only mode where you're allowed to build your own deck completely is the Sealed Play mode. This gives you booster packs to open and has you build a deck from the cards you find. Unfortunately, there are problems with this. Firstly, you'll likely get almost no synergy between your cards, leaving you with generic decks each time you play. Secondly, you have sealed play "slots" which, once you have a deck in them, cannot be used for another deck. The game comes with 2 slots, meaning you can only actually create your deck twice before you must buy new slots as DLC. It's a bad DLC method for a bad mode of play. Compared to the modes unique to previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games, it's weak at best.
As far as other modes, there is a campaign and a series of challenges, as well as free play and online play. The campaign puts you against AI opponents of generally increasing difficulty in mostly standard duels. There are some variations, including the last duel of the campaign, but for the most part it's simply basic battles, the kind you can play in free play at any time. The main draw of playing the campaign is that access to the various decks is unlocked at certain stages in the campaign. Challenges are a series of scenarios in which you are handed the game in a certain state and asked to win the duel before your turn is over. They're interesting, though once you do one once there's no more to gain from it. Most of them will be relatively easy for an experienced player, though the last challenge in the expansion will likely cause headaches for many of them as well. Free play duel types are basic 2-4 player free-for-alls and Two-Headed Giant, which is a 2v2 mode. I don't have much experience playing online, but it worked flawlessly when I played.
In terms of DLC, only the expansion and deck packs are really worth buying. Foil conversions give you access to shiny versions of decks, deck keys unlock the 30 cards in a deck that you unlock by playing, Sealed Slots I went over above. The deck packs add more decks (obviously!) and the expansion adds new decks, campaign missions, and challenges; if you're looking for more Magic to whet your appetite after going through the base game, those are your options.
Overall, it's a good game, especially for the price it's at. It's also worth checking out previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games to see if the decks or modes of play are more interesting to you.

EDIT: This was initially a negative review, but the devs have been steadily patching the game to address the major flaws the community has had issue with.  With the changes made thus far, I'm giving the game a qualified recommendation.
Planetbase is fun, although it lacks the depth needed for lots of replayability.  There are limited chains of production and very little base specialization.  Several reviews have compared this game to Banished, which is a fair comparision although I think Planetbase doesn't have the complexity of Banished.  It is very resource management focused and you expand your base to anticipate the increasing needs of your colonists.  Because you are a lone base on a planet, failing to meet some of these needs can be pretty catastrophic.
The colonists' AI is relatively strict, which sometimes results in seemingly counter-intuitive behavior.  This was my biggest issue with the game at launch.  But they have recently patched the game to allow for limited prioritization of behavior and building queues that can supercede the AI's default behavior.
===== From my original review =====
As an example, while playing my second colony I was in the middle of trying to build a spare parts factory when I realized I was going to need more power soon. So I put down a wind turbine plot and waited.  While waiting for either the factory or turbine to finish (because you can't control what gets built first or pause the construction of something), my other power generators degraded enough to need repairs and started causing power shortages.  The power shortages prevented my colonists from sleeping, and a tired colonist won't do jack.  Within two days, all of my power generators were failing or needing repairs, which meant even greater power shortages.  Then the water stopped flowing because of the power shortage, so I had tired and thirsty colonists just milling about inside, refusing to go outside and make the repairs that would fix all of their problems.  I gave up when the airlock shut off from power failure.
===========================
I went back to this save after the most recent patch (10/28) and was able to save my base. Although the base lost power for part of one night, this didn't cause a cascading failure of needs like it had previously.  Instead my colonists struggled through their tiredness and built that wind turbine so they could get some sleep the following night.
TLDR: Now a qualified recommendation from a previously negative review. Fun game, but with limited replay value.

The Good:  There's a real feeling of accomplishment in building a base.  Good graphics.  This game is hard, very hard, but not in an unfair way, sure random events can screw you but more often than not the fatal mistake is one you should have seen coming, everything flows logically... for the most part (see "the bad" for when it doesn't).
The Bad:  The AI is utterly useless.  People will starve to death carrying around a box of food even if standing next to an open dining table.  It seems that this problem gets worse as your base gets bigger, and you get more colonists.  The "alert" system and random disasters are coupled in a very poor way, oftentimes even with ample warning you won't be able to get your colonists to do what you need.
Ultimately, however, the fatal flaw is lack of depth.  No upgrades to equipment stations, and a production system that maxes out at two layers deep, and then only for making robots, everything else is one layer deep (bots are ore -> metal -> semiconductors -> bots, everything else is, for example ore -> metal -> spare parts).  Spare parts are a constant thorn in your side, because you can't ever stockpile them for some reason.   This game would be an amazing game if it only had more structures and a tech tree, and the colonists were not prone to random starvation or dehydration even with ample resources available.
The bottom line:  Keep an eye on this game, in three-four content patches it might be worth it.

The gameplay is SOOOO well done! The game uses the first bossfight to train you in the basics, and each boss following will have a sort of gimmick, in which it completely solidifies your ability to use certain skills, like
. I don't rate the the gameplay at 5 stars, only because the way it is structured detriments it. While its useful to have whole bossfights centred around one mechanic, and it helps you learn them, there were times when I was so frustrated by certain boss fights, who were just difficult for the sake of being difficult. Depends on who is playing, as some people like the frustration element of games like this. Personally, I was on the verge of putting it down for a while a few times, but I'm really glad I persevered.
Perfectly responsive, and there are very clear visual signals which tell the player what is about to happen - key example being the white flash and 'pwang' sound effect before the player needs to parry. There are also a very wide variety of options in bossfights (unless they are centred around a singular mechanic), as you could play it safe from far away and go for charged shots while they are charging, or you could play very aggresively and block all of their moves before they can kill you.
I should say that I used controller for the full game, so only take this part of the review seriousl if you too plan on playing with a Dualshock (using DS4Windows to make my computer think it was an Xbox gamepad) - I don't know how it runs with keyboard and mouse, but the game itself does recommend the gamepad.
The soundtrack to this game was a masterpiece, and I couldn't congratulate the developers more on it! I downloaded the entire thing to my phone and listen to it all the time. If you hate the game (you won't), you'll at least love the music and you can't deny that.
There's a distinct lack of world building in this game, and its sad. The little amount of lore there is really intrigued me, but so much of the story is left to the imagination. It needed more.
The game is stunning visually, and has clearly made a theme and distinct art style for itself. Each attack has a different visual based on what it does, and they are consistent for the whole game. The consistency helps the player learn how to deal with the boss, and get a good idea of what to expect for the first time they face the boss. My only small gripe is that the animation of the protagonist's hair is very strange, as if it has a low framerate IRL? Like, the whole game is very fluid and has a high framerate, but the hair is for some reason slow moving, and it is just weird...
As long as you don't have a potato plugged into a monitor for your computer, the game will perform just fine.

"The Sega Genesis." It's often the answer that I give when asked what my favorite game console is.  It was a great console with a lot of hidden gems and an appealing art style.  But the Genesis somehow never released a game called Volgarr the Viking.  Wait, this just in-- Volgarr is a brand new game from Crazy Viking Studios and Adult Swim Games, but it looks and feels as if it would have been right at home on the Sega Genesis. Hell, it even has a Genesis-inspired manual.
Transient
Volgarr the Viking is exactly what it should be: an assault to the senses of those willing to take the plunge into this ultra-violent romp through a minion-drenched hell.
To many that have gotten their hands on it, Volgarr has chewed them up and spit them out. The difficulty seems to be too much. The hardest thing about Volgarr is understanding one main rule that was shared with me: there is nothing unfair about Volgarr.

So, now comes the hardest part-- putting what Volgarr is into words.
Volgarr is an old-school 16-bit side-scrolling beat-'em-up in the vein of Castlevania and Golden Axe. But what sets this game apart is the extreme difficulty when it comes to figuring out what every enemy's attack pattern is. Every enemy attacks in a certain manner, and Volgarr (while only using two buttons other than the movement keys) always has a way to dispatch them.
The other beautiful thing that this game adds is how Volgarr traverses the world that he is a part of. Volgarr is a viking, not an all-powerful god. He still has to climb ropes to get to higher places, and in some cases he has to throw his spears into walls to make new platforms. This becomes one of the most satisfying things about this game, especially when those spears double up as a weapon or a way to block projectiles from above.
To add to this already epic adventure, Volgarr the Viking has a decent soundtrack. It fits the action, and the Clash of the Titans-esque world. While it isn't the best music ever heard in a game, it totally matches the action and look of the game. Just don't go in thinking that there will be epic viking chants.
Transient
So, if Volgarr the Viking sounds this great there must be something horrendously wrong with it deep down, right? No. There are some things that some gamers will have difficulty with. Problems like the extremely brutal checkpoint system. Currently, if  players die, they will find themselves all the way back at the beginning of the area of the screen they are on. This can mean losing 5-10 minutes of progress. Thankfully, players will learn something new along the way every time. This system seems crazy in a world of extreme simplicity, frequent 2-minute checkpoints, and hand-holding tutorials that never fully release players from its grasp, but players willing to stick with Volgarr will feel some of the greatest satisfaction in recent memory.
Volgarr has so much to offer for players that want to feel a deep satisfaction when completing an area, or personal task. The difficulty only adds to the dark style of the game, and everything fits perfectly into the presentation of this game. Volgarr the Viking is the type of experience that has been missing from the gaming world. Do yourself a favor and pick up the best offering from Adult Swim Games yet.
Finishing move:
I love Volgarr the Viking. Like, really love it. It brings back so many memories from my childhood gaming career. I wasn't handed anything in games. Instead, I had to bust my♥♥♥♥♥to progress all of the time, and it was a great feeling to tell all of my friends on the playground about the strategy I had used. Now I find myself talking to friends that I handed my USB NES controller to on my couch. Learning the patterns was satisfying in a way that words can't truly explain. Quick doodles were made to explain how we handle the upcoming area, and we quickly found that Volgarr, while being a single-player game, was a great game for two people to pass a controller back and forth to.
This game has lovingly stuck a spear through my heart, and is easily in top contention for game of the year.

The Myst-like atmosphere felt too solitary and pretty to look at to ever realise any of my silly fears.
By the time I had settled down and took each lesson the game gave me to heart, learning to utilize the simple tool given to me from the very start, it really threw a curveball. Now it has me paranoid about my very senses instead, expecting every little beautiful vantage point to be there for a purpose, and I'm starting to see puzzles in everything I look at.
It might cost me my sanity in the process, but I'm in too deep now to pull away. For better or worse, I am witnessing more than I ever expected. I just hope nothing is witnessing me while I'm at it. One kind of paranoia at a time is enough, thanks.

An amazing little gem of a game when you crave something different than the usual.
Keep your expectations in check - this isn't an action game by any means but, instead, an interactive novel with a tasty throw-back pixelated aesthetic. The music alone could justify the price for me, and the soundtrack consists of well-composed pieces inspired by the 80s and 90s eras of jazzy/RnB/cinematic electronic computer music.
This is NOT a dating sim (thank god). Characters are imaginative, vivid, and feel distinctly human aside from a few comical exceptions. The quality of dialogue was stunning, so I never once lost interest and the mini games enhanced the immersion further.
Most of your interaction takes place within the dialogue boxes and drink mixing interface. The story was mature, enjoyable, and well-executed despite the occasional typo. You influence the story in minor ways depending on which drink you serve to each character. The main story arc cannot be changed, but there are extra ending cutscenes to unlock, so there is not much replay value past the second playthrough. It is also worth mentioning that the cutscenes unlocked during the playthrough will play in sequence at the end of the game.
A fun little trip for players in their mid 20s who want to enjoy a neat story. Highly recommended.

I'm a long-serving, die-hard fan of Unreal Tournament, ever since UT99. A lot of reviewers claim this is a rip-off of Unreal Tournament (and even uses Unreal technology, oh the irony). They are right... sort of.
TOXIKK (which is a weird name, by the way, please change it!) is what would happen if UT2004 and UT3 had a baby. The fluid, functional, fast-paced movement of UT2004 combined with the astonishing graphics of UT3. UT3 always felt clunky and more suited for console play, and TOXIKK has rode in for the rescue, making arena shooters fun on PC again.
Enough about Unreal Tournament. Yes - they basically copied the blueprint. But when it's THIS good, who cares?
TOXIKK is immensely enjoyable, bringing all those post-millennium memories of UT, DOOM etc back. The movement is extreme and fast, bringing back wall-jumps and double-strafe-and-jump movements. The aiming mechanism is nigh-on perfect, possibly on-par with 2016 DOOM. The wide array of weapons on-hand, from flame-throwers to the unforgettable rocket launcher, creates an armoury palette every kind of player can enjoy. The graphics are simply stunning, with currently-available maps ranging from ancient jungle ruins to Chinatown! (I think... or something Chinatown-esque).
Time for the drawbacks. I've paid for the full version, so I feel I've earned the right to complain a little.
- First, the weapon-spawns provide an outline of which weapon it is (along with the name). A part of me feels they aren't clear enough, especially since every gun is essentially the same colour.
- Next, the UI could use some love. The scoreboard is very old-school, cramming data into tight rows and columns. In addition, the post-game victory/defeat screen voting panel on the right seems unnecessarily small. At this point, after a few seconds of seeing the winners and losers, can't we just use the entire screen for a much nicer map vote?
- The customisation menu is simple, but just bizarre. Using a toggle to switch between armour, helmets, colour etc. There's surely a better way to present the choices.
That's it for now. Otherwise it's a fantastic arena-shooter. I hope the developers keep working on it!

After trying this for a while I cannot recommend it to any FPS fans, as I find the design and execution to be rather disappointing.
1.The few levels are all very small and unoriginal, especially the one CTF map that was basically a big box with a couple vehicles and a pillar in the center.
2.The quickplay button tries to put you in full servers and ends up with an error message some times when you click it, requiring you to manually click it over and over again to get a match.
3. Weapons are rather lackluster, especially the melee weapon, which is just a pathetic re-imagining of Q3A's melee weapon.
4. Game defaults some pretty funky stuff, like the double-tap dodge mechanic, which you will repeatedly end up accidentally activating, until you finally find the way to turn it off is through a unintuitive slider in the key binding menu. Also, mouse acceleration is on be default. Who thought this was a good idea in a competitive FPS? (yeah I know some people actually use it, but I find them to be the exception in FPS games, not the norm)
5. Chat is hard to read and jumbled together with a bunch of useless information.
6. Bots on the servers are just terrible and only serve to feed kills to the other team.
7. Post-game screens are a jumbled mess that require you to uselessly left click to proceed through them, when all the relevant information could easily be presented in one easy-to-use panel.
I don't see anything that this game is doing that isn't already done better somewhere else. The controls are tight and easy to pick up (had a 13:1 kd/r within my first hour of playing), but that doesn't salvage it from the rest of the issues it currently has.

MagNets is an arena based game with simple problem solving. You play as bot, let's call him Mag. Since Mag has a round-head I assume he dislikes square-heads.
Gameplay Video:
Starting at a relaxing pace the game quickly ramps up the amount of enemies thrown at you and speed they get deployed. Gradually being introduced to new mechanics the basics always stay the same, cast your electromagnetic net (MagNet) around the square-heads and forge the parts collected into tools, preferably ones with rounded edges of course. Using these tools you then solve 'puzzles' contained within each arena and clearing them rewards progress to the next. After completing X amount of levels you will face boss fights and get introduced to characters you really don't want to destroy. :)
Some of the later levels became almost tower-defense like in nature requiring a balancing act of defending structures and taking down all square-heads, which was much higher paced but controls stayed responsive. Great soundtrack, interesting side-story, loveable characters and very family friendly. Cheers.

As other reviewers have commented, this game feels like it just got Greenlit.  It plays and feels like a $5 smartphone game. There are a few moments of complexity peeking through but the devs never follow up on them.
The food system for instance, allows you to grow multiple types of plants in two categories.  One category is purely food as plant or synthetic meats while the other sacrifices some food potential for building materials.  With all these varieties of food you can make different meals to add variation to the diet of your residents to avoid malnutrition.  However there is little reason to bother growing anything other than a two plant combo that gives you a complex food to meet that malnutrition need.  The other plants and the meats available are unnecessary to the game and just clutter the UI or your inventory.
With almost every other part of the game, it seems like they wanted to make a complex system of unique desires by your residents but stopped it way short to rush the release.  I suppose my feeling about the game could be summarized by the devs running low on funds and needing to capitalize on the game by an early release. For $10 on Good Old Games you can get Space Colony which is much more complex and rich game that was released over a decade ago.

Thrillville is a blast from the past to many games, in which you construct your own theme park from the third person perspective of the park manager, that's you. The game allows you to build rollercoasters, race tracks, sideshows, games and stalls. Thrillville also allows you to play your games, ride your rollercoasters, and create relationships with your visitors (even to the point of romance!). An all around incredible theme park tycoon.
The gameplay is both easy and smooth, with standard movement and interaction tools. Ride placement is done primarily through the keyboard, while building a racetrack or rollercoaster is done with both the mouse and keyboard. The game handles smoothly and effectively on even the lowest tier PCs, and I'm sure the game will handle to a playable level even on laptops.

The graphical quality of this game isn't incredible, but it looks good for the time it was developed and published. If you're complaining about this games graphical capabilities, you're probably an elitest who belongs with the Star Wars: Battlefront crowd.
The primary objective of Thrillville is to generate 'WHOA!' in order to establish and manage the best theme park possible for your visitors; you accomplish this by talking to your visitors and findign out what their needs are, and then developing the theme park accordingly.
This game is of the management genre, you can replay this game as much as you want until you personally get bored. Change up the designs, change the way you play, or purposefully build the worst theme park in existence; either way, this game is a tycoon-based title, which means it's replayability level is definitely up there.

Toki Tori is a 2D puzzle game that might look like a game parents would give their 10yo children to play, but don't be fooled by the looks of this game. As cute and adorable as the tiny chicken called Toki might be, as challenging are the puzzles and as tricky are the techniques that are required to beat the levels the further you progress through the game.
Each level comes with a predefined and limited set of equipment that you're allowed to use. Your goal is to use the equipment wisely to move around the level and collect all present eggs. This sounds easier than it is!
Toki Tori features more than 80 levels across 5 different worlds (including a Portal themed world!), each divided by normal, hard and bonus levels, so there is plenty stuff to do and once you are done you can go on and create your very own custom levels with the included and easy-to-use level designer.
If you enjoy puzzle games you will love Toki Tori as it will keep you pondering for many many hours. Buy it!

Oh this one is freaking me out more and more...
At first I thought it was silly of me to feel paranoid when I started the game. Why am I here? What are all those noises? Will those things move if I turn my back to them? Should I avoid attracting attention to my presence here? I was on edge more because of my own inclination to expect being watched or hunted, than because of the setting. The Myst-like atmosphere felt too solitary and pretty to look at to ever realise any of my silly fears.
By the time I had settled down and took each lesson the game gave me to heart, learning to utilize the simple tool given to me from the very start, it really threw a curveball. Now it has me paranoid about my very senses instead, expecting every little beautiful vantage point to be there for a purpose, and I'm starting to see puzzles in everything I look at.
It might cost me my sanity in the process, but I'm in too deep now to pull away. For better or worse, I am witnessing more than I ever expected. I just hope nothing is witnessing me while I'm at it. One kind of paranoia at a time is enough, thanks.

Don't let this game fool you into thinking it's only a gaggle of placemat-puzzles. It's a vibrant, dazzlingly gorgeous game with an intricately detailed world!
It can be very difficult - but you are given free reign of the island and can wander as you please. Stuck? Take a stroll through the cherry blossoms, or eye the beautiful crystal ocean. Go somewhere else, and explore enigmatic gardens or stately ruins.
It's much more obscure than Myst (which had journals to explain all the vagueness). Nonetheless, The Witness gives you an extra sense of achievement, not only from solving its puzzles, but from developing your own theories as to what is really going on.
There's no music, so you might wanna stick something on in the background if (like me) it helps you think!
The lack of the more traditional gameplay elements adds to the atmosphere very well. There's no tutorial, no HUD, no hand-holding. Just a fully-immersive experience. Definitely play on highest graphical settings if your computer can handle it. It's so damn pretty!

I bought this game after playing Far Cry 3, which I absolutely loved. I certainly was not disappointed after playing this game.
I think I may have seen a couple reviews saying Far Cry 4 is just a fresh coat of paint slapped onto the last installment, and I can see why they might think that. But after briefly testing out Primal I can say that I'm glad they did do a sort of revamp on the last game instead of taking it in a different direction; amazing gameplay. A badass main character. A horrible yet extremely likeable and charismatic bad-guy. They took all of the great things from their most popular game and put it into this one, and they set it in a new, beautiful location - The Himalayas. What's not to like?
That's not to say they didn't add new aspects to it. There's certainly a lot more to do, with a lot of mini-game-type aspects that riddle the map. Something else I noticed is there's a lot more decision-making possibilities than in the last game. A big part of the story is restoring the civilization of Kyrat to its non-totalitarian lifestyle - as to whether you restore it to its simple ways or push it in a 'competetive world power' direction, that's up to you.
Whether you like Ubisoft or not, they do a great job with graphics and creating breathtaking and immersive environments, and in that regard you won't find this game wanting. As a general note here, if you've enjoyed the Far Cry series up to this point, you won't want to leave this game out of your collection.

Oh man... Did you game in the 80s? Classic NES such as Ninja Gaiden and Wizards & Warriors? Do you love a game that is unapologetically tough (but not unfair)? Do you remember sinking quarters into Stryder? If the answer is yes, this game is totally for you. No save points, just check points. You die, you start the level over. Get to the boss and die? You start the level over. Quit the game? Start the game from the start. Never unfair or cheap, this game pushes you (much in the same way as Dark Souls but this isn't near the sadist/masochist relationship of that).

This game is the best kind of hard.
Every miss, counterattack or fall could have been avoided, and was telegraphed to you. The colours might just look like they wanted a synthwave aesthetic, but everything has a meaning and you can tell the properties of every bullet and beam, while still looking really sweet. This means every fight is fair. Some of them could be more fair, like some ranged-focussed bosses probably needed their patterns spread over one more health bar so you didn't have to do so many at once, but it's still possible, no, feasible to beat them without taking a hit. Barring a few rare glitches and slowdown, or camera weirdness, (it's still a Unity game) you always know what you could have done to avoid that hit.
This game is just bosses. The devs clearly noticed how the best parts of Metal Gear Rising and No More Heroes and the like were when you were duelling someone with similar powers, so they left out almost everything but that. It's not as relenless as that sounds though, there's a breather between each fight to give you some sorely needed explanation as to what's going on. More importantly, each boss is contrasted with the next in fighting style or attitude to you, usually both. If you talk to someone about this, you'll probably have a different bosses that you loved more than anything, could barely touch and walked all over.
Get this game if you love those duel bosses, a surprising subtle story, and the sweet cyber sounds of Carpenter Brut and the like.
If you are looking for a game that will test your reflexes, get your adrenaline pumping, and give you a very satisfying experience, then this is the game for you.

I stumbled upon VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action (Vallhalla) before it's release.
The artstyle and soundtrack both pretty SNES-esque IMO, got me hooked immediatley (actually it's inspired by PC-98 adventure games).  Try listening to it, while reading further:
The fact that it's a Visual Novel kept me from buying it at first, but then I realized it's not like "those" other V Novels out there. And so it became one of my favourite games out there.
It has a great story, which is told almost completly by, you guessed it, bartending. Many different characters enter the bar, and depending on what you serve them, they'll  tell you their stories, and in result you also learn about Jills ( the protagonist) story.   The stories are mostly about the problems they face in their town "Glitch  City", news or their favourite Idol. The game is about the STORIES. Not stereotypes, nudity or boobs. In fact there's even a female character that tries to hide her breastsize, and you can learn why she does so. The humour is mature and great, and especially the "sexbot" is great at sexual innuendos.
Every day, before you start to work, you can check news, boards and blogs on Jills tablet. They are "lore"heavy, a reflection of our life, or just supid/funny. (There's a newspost about a new law that wearing socks in sandals
is now illegal).
The soundtrack is a mix of many things. It sounds a lot like old game soundtracks, while still being futuristic. Other then that they have a wide range, most of them are pretty calm, which fits the game, other of them are fastpaced. Some song have an E-guitar ,a calm piano,  or heavy bass, but all have a lot of synth in them.  Everytime you start your day at the bar, or reenter after taking your break, you can switch the songs you want to hear in the musicbox. You can fill all slots with one song aswell, if you wish to do so.
I highly recommend  giving the game a try if you are interested, even if the genre of V. Novel doesn't appeal to you.  Get some snacks, a cold drink , get comfortable and  enjoy. VA-11 Hall-A has it's own charm, and the way it tells it story is just awesome.
In case you want to learn even more, check out the games website:
Go ahead, it's time to mix drinks and change lives! :)

I don't normally write reviews for games on Steam, I'm going to take a minute to write one here:
I bought this game because it's by the creator of Braid. I loved Braid. I hold Braid as one of my favorite gaming experiences of all time. It was a fantastic game, and every now and again, I go back and play it. I've bought it on every platform it's been available on, just because I want to support more people having access to the game.
This game is not Braid. It's a series of quiet puzzles that, while satisfying to solve, quickly wore on me. I got to about my tenth series of flat puzzles that could just as easily be a flash game, and then I looked up a Let's Play of the game on YouTube. To my astonishment, the flat puzzle mechanic continues to the end of the game.
This is not Braid. Do not buy it thinking it is Braid. If you like to sit and tinker with puzzles for hours and hours on end, this game will do you well. I did not, and I do not, and therefore I cannot recommend it.
As a side note: the game is gorgeous. It's a shame you spend most of it looking at ugly puzzles.

Occassionally new elements are injected, without explanation. While I do like the element of discovery and not being coddled, I did find some of the puzzles later in the game irritating, rather than challenging.  And after 6 hours of play I finally gave up.
If there was an interesting story I may have kept playing, however for the 6 hours I played is almost non existant.

The Witness is a puzzle game that makes you uninterested in solving puzzles. Most of your time will be spent trying to figure out what the mechanics of the puzzle are. The puzzles themselves are fairly trivial once you know how they work, mostly they're a chore.
There is no discernible story, just a bunch of audio recordings about having faith and believing in God. The ending is so bad it feels like a hoax.
tl;dr Looks stunning, plays horribly.
Worst exploration puzzle game if you hate the genre.

Bottom line: not worth the $20. Catch it on sale.
Having been floored by Braid, I had high hopes for this game. If you're into endless silent puzzles, prepare to be delighted, but I was truly hoping for some sort of plot, or just any sort narrative. The Witness is just a hipster art show that you need a strong fortitude to get through.
Edit: It is on sale, apparently. Still not worth it.

Open space has been balanced so pretty much whatever enemy you encounter will own you. Loads of people will then say you need light nimble craft to fly in open space, in other words, forget about using you leveled frigate there (incase you only unlocked frigates .. you're screwed).
PvAI* was pretty fun since the AI spawned in ships roughly equal to your level. It was said this was too easy and would be fun if they could lenghten the mission, so the devs did, by making you fight ships 5-6 levels above your own. Now PvAI means you'll need to team up to take down an AI ship, but since they also team up (somewhat) you're better off expecting to die. If I want to die I'll just play PvP, and just PvP does not make for a good game, at least not in this game, imo.
*PvAI = like PvP, but vs AI controlled ships, not the same as PvE

I stumbled upon VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action (Vallhalla) before it's release.
The artstyle and soundtrack both pretty SNES-esque IMO, got me hooked immediatley (actually it's inspired by PC-98 adventure games).  Try listening to it, while reading further:
The fact that it's a Visual Novel kept me from buying it at first, but then I realized it's not like "those" other V Novels out there. And so it became one of my favourite games out there.
It has a great story, which is told almost completly by, you guessed it, bartending. Many different characters enter the bar, and depending on what you serve them, they'll  tell you their stories, and in result you also learn about Jills ( the protagonist) story.   The stories are mostly about the problems they face in their town "Glitch  City", news or their favourite Idol. The game is about the STORIES. Not stereotypes, nudity or boobs. In fact there's even a female character that tries to hide her breastsize, and you can learn why she does so. The humour is mature and great, and especially the "sexbot" is great at sexual innuendos.
Every day, before you start to work, you can check news, boards and blogs on Jills tablet. They are "lore"heavy, a reflection of our life, or just supid/funny. (There's a newspost about a new law that wearing socks in sandals
is now illegal).
The soundtrack is a mix of many things. It sounds a lot like old game soundtracks, while still being futuristic. Other then that they have a wide range, most of them are pretty calm, which fits the game, other of them are fastpaced. Some song have an E-guitar ,a calm piano,  or heavy bass, but all have a lot of synth in them.  Everytime you start your day at the bar, or reenter after taking your break, you can switch the songs you want to hear in the musicbox. You can fill all slots with one song aswell, if you wish to do so.
I highly recommend  giving the game a try if you are interested, even if the genre of V. Novel doesn't appeal to you.  Get some snacks, a cold drink , get comfortable and  enjoy. VA-11 Hall-A has it's own charm, and the way it tells it story is just awesome.
In case you want to learn even more, check out the games website:

Options include fully-mappable controls, resolution from 800x600 to 1920x1080, and a variety of quality settings for graphics and effects.
As someone who'd never played a LEGO PC game before, I found gameplay to be a bit confusing and overwhelming at first.  The key is to explore, interact with and/or destroy everything you possibly can, and collect every coin (aka stud) you see, as you'll need them for purchases later.
There is no speech in the game - everything is communicated via tone of voice ("Uh?" "Uh!") and character actions.  The LEGO HP games are based upon the movies, from the Fat Lady trying to break a crystal glass with her voice to the movie soundtrack.  I have both listened to the whole series of audio books (Jim Dale is an AMAZING narrator!) and watched all of the movies, so I am pretty knowledgeable about the world of Harry Potter.  I'm really not sure that these games would be as enjoyable for someone who isn't familiar with the stories, and they are of course FULL of spoilers!
There are six chapters per "year", for a total of 24 levels to play.  Once you finish a chapter, you can replay it by going to the glowing board in The Leaky Cauldron (your home base, so to speak), and choosing it from the list.  You will NEED to replay chapters in Free Play mode in order to get all of the collectibles, as you'll need alternate characters that you won't be able to unlock until later in the game.
There is also all of Hogwarts, Diagon Alley, Nocturn Alley, and Gringotts to explore outside of the story levels.
Cutscenes can be skipped once you've seen them the first time.
Your characters will learn a variety of spells as you progress, and though you can manually switch between spells, I recommend leaving it on "pink" (Wingardium Leviosa aka levitation) at all times.  First of all, your characters will automatically used the spell you need most of the time, and it's too easy to miss things that you need to interact with if you have any other spell selected.  Leaving it on pink will
make a pink halo appear around anything you can use Leviosa on, which will save you a lot of frustration later.
A lot of characters have their own special ability, so you'll need to switch between characters often.  A few examples:  Hagrid is very strong, Hermione and Ron have pets that can interact with the environment in their own way, Harry has the invisibility cloak, goblins have keys, dark wizards are the only ones who can interact with items that have red sparkles around them, Hermione can use the time-turner, sometimes you'll need to be a Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, or Slytherin to get past certain blockades... (Hello polyjuice potion!)
- 167 character tokens (you'll have to purchase the ability to use them once you find the tokens)
- 200 gold bricks
- 50 students in peril
- True Wizard (collect a specified amount of studs in each story level, which will earn you an extra gold brick)
- 20 red bricks (allows you to purchase abilities/bonuses.  Pause the game, select
, then turn on the ones you want to use)
- 24 Hogwarts crests, each consisting of four pieces: Red (Gryffindor), Blue (Ravenclaw), Green (Slytherin), and Yellow (Hufflepuff)
- Spells to purchase at Wiseacres Wizarding Supplies (love that one that makes the person you hit turn into a human slug)
Besides being a completionist, there are several other reasons to be collecting gold bricks:
- Build special items in the basement of The Leaky Cauldron - one for each "year"
- Unlock vaults in Gringotts, which gives you access to challenge levels, which in turn earns you another gold brick
- Unlock an extra level in Borgen & Burkes (have to have collected all 200 bricks!)
The red bricks I mentioned above allow you to purchase some great abilities, such as stud multipliers, brick detectors, token detector, fall rescue (so helpful!), and more.  You can go to Wiseacres Wizarding Supplies and enter a cheat code to get these abilities if you haven't found the red brick/purchased it yet, but I personally did it all the hard way... I didn't even know how to turn the abilities on until after I finished the game. ;D
All in all, LEGO Harry Potter is a beautifully-done tribute to the world JK Rowling created, and Hogwarts was a true pleasure to explore.  There was a strong sense nostalgia with the familiar locations and the movies' music, but it was still fresh due to the way the stories needed to be adjusted to make the gameplay interesting.  I had no technical difficulties (unless you count the THREE items I cannot find to get my 100% completion, which is really a user-error), and I really had a lot of fun.  Absolutely recommended.

I haven't been glued on a chair to play a game in a while...
I like the idea colonizing other worlds  and I like strategy/micro management games. Planetbase gives that and more. Unlike other games that toss immense data and spreadsheets at player, Planetbase forces player to observe and be aware what is going on. Player must be aware of risks and issues that can struck his colony and to figure it - where is and what is the problem. Even when player achieve "stable colony" that still doesn't mean player is free to go wild.
Player do not have direct control over colonists as in most games. This feel strange at first but once you get used to it, it is better that way - controlling 300 colonist individually would be really too much. Player must understand the needs of colonists, face the issues, solve problems and prosper above all.
This is one of rare challenging games when some simple thing (i.e. selling too much unneeded resource) can kill your entire colony. Also this game has overwhelming feel "Just to make this one thing..." and you keep saying that for the last 20 made things. I really like that game loads quickly.
There is not all so nice and well. The bad things about Planetbase are:
- AI is strange (especially in crucial moments like engineer builds connector to the Solar Panel but then he ignores Solar Panel even though all needed materials are there)
- many features should be extended:
* visitors can be more gamy mechanic not just intruders or tourists
* helping ships in distress also offers huge potential
* new home made tech research could be a thing and to be specialized per planet
* possibility to have some colony speciality that can affect gameplay
* ABOVE ALL WE NEED NEW PLANETS WITH THEIR SPECIFIC CHALLENGES (lava planet? liquid methane planet? planet without solar power possibilities but almost constant wind and slowed movement outside?- can only enhance specialization idea)
- better control over prioritization
- better control over saving games
- better airlock model (new airlock that can let in or out more people)
- windowed mode
I hope game will evolve and offer new content. Even as a base game, I recommend it to everyone.

I'll probably never beat Volgar, but that's part of its appeal. It has great controls, everything feels tight and precise. The enemy types are clearly identified, green Nose-Beaks takes one hit, blue two, red three, and so on. The spear's simple/easy to use, and is necessary for traversal. The games core is its difficulty. It is very hard to get from checkpoint to checkpoint, but when you do progress the sense of achievement is genuine. The game is hard but not unfair and I keep coming back for more. I definitely recommend.
