Extremely enjoyable visual novel story with small and relaxing gameplay elements added.
I saw some people comparing this game unfavorably to Papers' Please. While there is some truth to the statement that the drink mixing and your responsibilities as a bartender aren't that expanded and meaningful as they could be, people stating that often forget that Papers' Please had barely any other interesting qualities aside of "artsy" gameplay mechanics. Those were often times irritating, frustrating and unsatisfying for me. While I still respect Papers' Please, I didn't found it wholeheartly enjoyable... especially where it lacked something called "meaningful, fun characters" and "engaging story".
Va-11 Hall-A has both of those things in spades. Putting you in the shoes of common bartender you hear stories of people stumbling upon your bar. You quickly get attached to the colorful cast of characters, each with own story arcs, motivations and sidestories. Reading is the name of the game here and the writing is remarkably excellent throughout with specific spice added that you often don't see in video game dialogue. It really makes the job done: you root for ALL characters introduced (player character included - she has problems of her own) and the world build indirectly before your eyes (you don't really see any major events yourself - you always get them via reference). There aren't any boring faces on the other side of the bar table. It's a stellar effort that elevates the title from the self-proclaimed, honest label of "Waifu Bartender" into something much more serious.
What I also like, but isn't that much prominent in the game yet still I wanted to mention, are those "our" world's hot topics that are brought up. They are constructed and presented in really respectful manner - with many points of view provided and not really forcing the player to take a side. I really like when the game considers you an adult and doesn't shove in ideology with subtlety of the skydropped steamroller.
While story takes the priority, the bartending mechanics aren't detrimental to the game and they are a engaging distraction between digesting a large swaths of text. As long as you don't expect a full-blown simulation and you are vary that Va-11 Hall-A is a visual novel first and foremost, you should be fine and enjoying yourself with those simple rules. The visuals and soundtrack are also top tier and they are great catalyst for you to help soak in this interesting and unique vibe that game provides.
The game and it's story isn't without its few lower points. While serving different drinks to the same clients may sometimes trigger a different responses, sidetracking from the core story, there aren't any straight out branching paths in the plot as much as one could imagine there would be. Ending of the game also leaves the player with more to be desired. Don't get me wrong, it's still a very good ending, although it feels a bit sudden and it doesn't address all of those loose plotpoints that are left hanging. There are additional epilogues that I not reached yet, so I could change my mind when I see them, but for now I walked away from the game wanting a bit more of it. On the last negative - while I praised the social and political commentary before, I would still point out that they may feel a bit out of place when you consider that the game is set around 60 years into future and the more "outworldy" topics could be discussed in the place of the "current" ones.
All in all, if you like a good, story driven games and you didn't considered Va-11 Hall-A yet, I'm strongly advising to do so. The main campaign can last 9-12 hours (with modest replayability options) and it's exceptionally enjoyable ride from start to finish, well worth your hard earned non-future-financial-crisis-inflated money. If you can handle the punch, you should take this shot.

VA-11 Hall-A, also known as Waifu Bartending, is something I personally wouldn't pass up on. In short, it delivers a relaxing story with a few influential factors for you to pick from, which then influence the outcome of the game. Said experience is delivered with humor, interesting dialouge and plenty of content that lives up to the price this game has. (Especially after the prolouge being added.)
Going into a more in-depth look, there definitetely is more to talk about than just that, of course.
You are playing Jill, being the Bartender of a place that is called exactly like the game, then providing the drinks that are ordered from you. In exchange for you doing your job, people will more or less enroll their backgrounds to you, chatting about their lives, work, events or other things that are going on around the city.
As you listen to the folks, you generate income, especially when serving the right drinks. Some customers may prove a bit trickier to please than others, so the player also has to make sure to remember core-features about every customer they serve.
But in the end, the most important thing to mention is:
What I am trying to say with this is, that you will find yourself serving drinks inbetween without them taking up the major part of the game. The dialouge between characters and the player is what gives this its content. It is a Visual Novel with a simulation aspect to it. If you are looking for something where working on customer's orders is most appealing, I suggest not taking this as your first choice.
That out of the way, it leaves me with another fact that has to be pointed out.
VNs usually come with a high price. I will not call out any game about this, but I feel like the content-to-price factor usually is quite imbalanced in terms of what hits the market on Steam. With VA-11 Hall-A, which costs 14,99€ without a sale going on, there is a demonstration about how a proper balance of said factor can look. It is safe to say that you get what you will be paying for, if not even more. The effort put into this seems to be far up there, which I can't say for other, more expensive VNs on the market.
But in terms of effort I don't just mean a rich dialouge or a lot of content. I mean the whole thing as a whole! Graphics, music, sound and the immersion once all these things get combined are a great influence to summarize what I mean.
A fair chunk of the story will be streamlined and also will repeat itself throughout the second playthrough. This doesn't automatically mean that replaying will be something that can be considered useless. Special or successful orders will result in you branching off into different arks of the character's background/responses, then also bringing previously unseen scenes and endings to you. Getting all of this in one playthrough is not possible without a lot of savestates either.
As the bottomline of this review I must add that I had no perfomance related issues or bugs either. No crashes, weird errors in dialouges, freezing or unforseen consequences happened for me throughout the whole experience. I am not eliminating the fact that it's bug-free by saying that, I am sure there always are glitches that lie somewhere once you try hard enough!
If you made it this far, congratulations! I hope I was able to give you some insight about what to expect from the game. Thank you for your time and enjoy the game, should you get it!

I'm someone who love Visual Novels, but it's hard to find the good ones, let alone the great ones in the flood of cheap VN that have been made in the past few years. Since Greenlight, anything can find its way on Steam, and that leaves you with a saturated market.
But forget the awful dating sims, this game is a pure gem! It's in the same spirit as Read Only Memories, and you could almost think it was done by the same studio. Va-11 Hall-A is interesting in that it doesn't make you follow a defined plot, but it put you into the shoes of a bartender. Your only input into the events of your city, Glitch City, is the conversations you have with your customers. You discover the characters, their personalities and their views at the same time that you discover about the in-game world. What's interesting in that is that necessarily, their opinions are subjective, and so you decide, as a player, what and who you want to believe and how you want to see things.
Mixing drinks is not the most exciting mechanic ever, but I like to learn about my customers and think of a drink that would suit them. I like the decisions you have to take regarding what you serve, and how this is an original way of implementing choices in a game. For example, there's a point when one of your customer is not feeling well at all and asks you something very alcoholic. You can do as they ask, or you can take into account that they're not feeling well, that it's probably not the best idea and serve them instead something they would usually order (something with sugar or ice, in this case). This is very clever.
The game tackles modern issues like artificial intelligence, class warfare, journalism and feminism with a lot of taste. It doesn't necessarily say what's wrong and what's right, but it shows you how different people feel about it and what are some of the impacts of those issues in daily life.
A mature work of excellence. With a lot of humor, that is.

A charming little visual novel-type game. Giving it a thumbs up because I played it all the way through - that took quite a while so kudos to the writing, characters and fun cyberpunk setting. The drink mixing struck me as a bit of a missed opportunity, since there are few scenarios where changing a drink actually results in a narrative divide, and the times where that does occur aren't very clear and usually fall into good/bad outcomes. But if you mostly treat it as a visual novel, it's enough that it gives you something to do, and the scenarios where a drink choice hinges on how well you payed attention to someone's preferences or habits are clever and rewarding.
One major complaint/warning, however. The gratuitous 4th wall character, which I'm assuming has to be some kind of tacky reference to something, came very close to outright ruining the game. Every time they showed up, the writing degraded to 4th grade level and otherwise interesting conversations became nonsensical and cringeworthy. If they'd appeared in one more scene, I'd probably be giving this a thumbs down - I'll be wary of any follow ups to this title for this reason alone.

This game was ported to PC with all the finesse of a rampaging hippopotamus conduting open heart surgery. The controls are a mess at times (two characters to control at the same time on the keyboard, needing to work together at times, one using WASD and one the arrow keys), none of the buttons are intuitive save basic movement, and I don't recall ever being told how to jump (it's U, or Num. 5, if you want to know). It is a console game first and foremost and it shows; there's a reason developers usually make one version of a game for the console and another for the PC. It took me most of Year 1 to get intuitive with the game controls, and I'm still not entirely sure.
It's a testament to the charming nature of this game that I'm willing to put up with all of the above. The game makes gentle fun of the movies, keeping all the good parts in and playing down the tension to create what is ultimately an adorable, feelgood game I can get lost in for hours.The game boasts the film score as a soundtrack, which adds to the magic; you can never really die in any way that detriments you; you can run around Hogwarts to your heart's content in what might be the biggest sim of the castle I've encountered; there are multiple sidequests to keep you amused; and you can never really get stuck, because at least 60% of the gameplay is good old fashioned smashing things and rebuilding them with magic.
If you're looking for a serious, challenging game, then LEGO HP is not for you. If you're looking for a fun game in which you can mess around, smash things, collect coins and generally regress to kindergarten, then I definitely recommend. I would recommend playing with a controller if you can, though, as that seems to help others.

Ill keep it short.
Planet base is one of the best base building / micro management games that I can think of in recent history. Its a slow methodical game that requires you to keep everything in balance if you want your colony to grow. The three planets each offer different variations on the same theme with different starting conditions. They each have their own environmental issues to deal with as well. For example the third planet which is a moon that has no atmosphere means you will be relying on solar power. The second planet has a dense atmosphere that light doesnt penetrate very well so its wind energy.
The game has a way of throwing you curve balls right when you don't want it to causing you to make sudden changes to what you are doing to adapt, if you fail to do so a colony that was thriving that you spent a couple of hours on can literally be rendered unsustainable within a few seconds if you don't have what you need when something bad happens such as a sudden solar flare or armed intruders enter your base and you have no armed guards to fight them and they proceed to gun down all of your workers or biologists.
Fun game, easy to get into and widdle the hours away tweaking things and watching your colonists do their thing under your iron fist.
Couple of A.I. issues in the colonists that I have noticed, just minor annoyances in their priorities as they go about doing their thing. Other then that. Solid game.
If you are interested in this kind of game set in a sci-fi/futurists setting then pick it up. I have easily gotten my money's worth out of it. Trying to finish up getting all the achievements. Good times.

WHERE DID MY WEEKEND GO? The first review I read was "Its like Banished, but in space and you build a colony" and I was sold. For the price, you can't beat it. Its worth it at the $19.99 price point if you're in to this type of game.
I thought I would only spend about 10 hours playing the game. Right now I'm at 18 hours. I can see myself playing this game about 50 hours total over its lifetime.
I'm pretty big on the idea behind $1 per hour spent on the game. With Planetbase, I played it all weekend and amassed 16 hours of play time and I'm just now getting to beating the first of three planets. I had so much fun that I'd consider going back and restarting on the basic planet at some point just for kicks.
The simulation depth is slightly shallow when it comes to being creative and customizing all the things, but I'm willing to look past that because of how much fun I'm having solving problems. I've heard complaints about people with the AI, but I've not experienced much of it. For the most part, its been pretty predictable or at the very least, semi-logical.
One legitimate complaint I have is that its moderately narrow in terms of the player's creativity (some would say "player agency"). I enjoy the solid challenge for survival that it throws at you, but once you figure it out then there's not much in the way of creative solutions, the game starts to lose its shine.
But looking past some of its flaws, I'm a simulation enthusiast and this game hits the spot. 8/10 from me.

Really fun game, not easy at all either. You have to actively anticipate the needs of your people or you will be quickly overwhelmed. That being said, the game starts bugging out when your population starts getting around 250 (my game flat out died once I got past 300). People and bots forget they can't walk outside from one end of the base to the other and all manner of nonsense starts happening in your base.
Don't try and rush build your base either, you will end up running out of spares or overextending your power grid.
Save often and if your people start dieing, move back to a save where you can correct the problem before it starts I have never been able to stabalize a base once something gets out of balance.
It can be daunting to start out, but here are some things that worked for me.
- Build the biggest oxygen processors you can and try to locate them between your food production and habitation.
- The small water producer is only there for filling in gaps where nothing else will fit, use the big one
- Start out with a medium sized bio dome and as big a lab as you can, only fill the domes as you have wokers availible initially, as you don't get much if they have to spend all their time maintaining.
- Start with wheat, then once you have a steady stream of starch, build onions exclusively
- Don't cump your power/water/batteries on one side of your base, it will end up limiting the direction that you can expand, try to cluster them in corners as you expand.
- Once you can aford to make a duplicate of the resource processor, lab, factory, etc. specialize them to only produce one type of resource per dome.
- Put two control centers in sequence in front of the airlock that leads to your starport, makes it easier for your security forces to gun down intruders before they get very far.
- once you get a stable base with around 30-50 people, STOP, to go further you need to collect all the tech you can, build the most massive structures you can past this point or the spares will end up killing you
- 4-5 driller bots per mine, they will die over time, so keep a few extra, still better than treating your people in the medbay
- Past this you just need to make sure that you have excess capacity before expanding.

I'd like to give this game a neutral review but that's not a thing.
I really wanted to like this game, but it didn't go that way.
I bought this game for the open world co-op, and it's...okay, I guess. You can't do story missions in co-op, so you'll be going around destroying outposts, fortresses and climbing belltowers. Trouble is, that doesn't take long. The outposts are tiny and often cleared in less than two minutes if you do stealth. You'll get more out of them if you go loud, but that kinda sucks if you're someone who likes being stealthy.
The fortresses are supposed to be kind of "super outposts", they're labelled as being very hard and give you the option of weakening them through story missions. We cleared all of them easily without weakening them, they're just bigger outposts.
Don't get me wrong, messing around with a friend in this game is fun, just not very challenging and you can clear the map pretty quick. There are random side objectives around the map and collectibles to find if you're into that sort of thing.
And then we get to the story. Oh boy, the story.
First of all, this is really just my preference. People like different things so hey, people who aren't me could like it.
Second of all, I did not get all the way through the story of this game. I couldn't. I'm not a masochist.
I hated almost all of the characters in Far Cry 3 (which I did play all the way through, unfortunately), and 4 is pretty similar. I found this game's story plain excruciating and hated almost every minute the main characters were on screen. Even the protagonist got sick of their s*** part way into the story.
I love story games. I'm also fine with games with no story at all, or even a mediocre story that wasn't really important, as long as the game's other aspects made up for it. I've never played a game whose characters I hated so much that I had to stop playing, until Far Cry 4.
If you don't mind them, then good for you. You'll enjoy this game a lot more than I did.
All in all, the co-op is okay. The basic gameplay elements and weapon diversity is decent. You can have some fun. The story is up to personal preference. It's a Far Cry plot, for whatever that means to you. Personally I was begging the game to let me use my RPG in cutscenes, if only to drown out what the characters were saying. Oh, and the drugged out trippy dream sequences are in this game too. If you like them then good news.
If this game was offered to you for a few dollars? Sure, go for it. Full price? Meh.
Oh, and to upgrade your small leather wallet to hold more cash you'll need to kill and skin 2 bharals, 3 monkeys, FOUR F***ING RHINOS and a wolf.
That's one quality wallet.

One major complaint/warning, however. The gratuitous 4th wall character, which I'm assuming has to be some kind of tacky reference to something, came very close to outright ruining the game. One part of the fun is making customers drunk and listening to their honest conversations. However you shouldn't make them drunk too fast or the customers just leave early and give you less money.
The main attraction of the game is the story and characters. The game is set in the year 207X. One of the main topics of this game is about technological advancements of mankind at that point in time. For example, androids and dogs have human like intelligence, society is controlled by corporations and polution forced humans to adapt. The dialog never keeps you bored and neither goes too far to make it unconfortable or exaggerated, being often relatable and sometimes very funny. However note that the dialog contains sex, violence, politics and other adult topics,
. With the story goes a very calm music that makes this game a very relaxing experience.
All in all it's a very fun and calm game. I recommended if you like visual novels.

I enjoy puzzle games and I really wanted to like this game, but there are no words to describe how mind numbingly boring this game is!  On the positive side, the game utilises an attractive Island setting filled with every variation of a slide puzzle imaginable, often working the puzzle in with the environment.  However there is no intro to the game, there is no music, and there is no commentary on our progress (a sarcastic/abusive GLaDOS or a fatherly Elohim would have been a welcome break from the monotony).  There are a few audio logs scattered throughout the game, however the drivel they contain is so unbelievably pretentious they somehow make the game even more boring.  Combine this with the fact most of the puzzles feel exactly the same and you will realise playing this game is a deeply tedious experience.

This game is a masterpiece. It's deeply complex, but not on the surface. There are layers and layers of abstraction to explore and appreciate here. The world itself is beautiful and immersive. There is a peaceful, almost meditative ambience to the place, but also an eerie undertone of loneliness and mystery. The level design is impeccable; what may seem random at first will eventually become an important and well-thought through detail. The puzzles evolve in difficulty over time, testing not only your logic but also your perception. The story is not linear and there is nothing to guide you through it. You must explore, discover and make sense of things yourself. Very few games have impacted me quite like this one (certainly Riven comes to mind, but perhaps nothing else). This game certainly isn't for everyone, but for us lucky few it doesn't get much better.

The Witness is a game about knowledge, exploration, and game theory. As you slowly discover the mechanics which govern its beautifully rendered world, you free yourself from shackles of ignorance you didn't realize you were carrying in the first place.

The Witness will repeatedly and consistently ask you, "Do you understand?" and the journey from "No I don't," to "Yes I do!" is worth every penny.

I don't often leave reviews, but at this point I really had to.  I was very excited about this game.  I absolutely adore resource management games and civ simulations.  I've played for a few hours, starting over dozens of times, trying to find that perfect build that will get my colony seed going.  I love that it's difficult and your decisions matter.
Then it happens.  Maybe an hour into a map, and the AI just gives up.  Out of my 7 starting colonists, 6 of them are hungry.  There's piles of unprocessed food in the storage building waiting to go into the processor, and no one will move it.  ONE lonely engineer will stop what he's doing, grab some veggies or meat and takes them to the machine for himself.  He eats, and then goes back to his tasks.
There is no way to schedule or rank work.  (The max build queue is kind of a joke.)  There is no way to manually assign tasks or override a colonists broken path.  A sandstorm hits, and I have a colonist that walks out side and just stands there in it for no reason.   My bots finally broke down.  One engineer walks right by, and the other is standing right next to it, but refuses to attempt repairs.  I have piles of spare parts and materials waiting to be used.
If a game doesn't have a strong AI to actually simulate well, it needs to allow for granular manual control.  This does not.  Once you've reached an equilibrium the game just stops working.  I love difficult and challenging games.  This isn't a challenge, this is an infinite loop of broken.  All in all it's a very simple game that had the promises of complexity, but failed to deliver.   I would say the AI is a joke, but there would actually have to be an AI to rate.
Do yourself a favor, give this one a pass.

The Bartending visual novel I never knew I needed. Well, tell a lie, ever since Cyber Punk Jam I have been foaming at the mouth in anticipation. The entire project oozes quality and is wrapped in one of the most brilliant OSTs in recent memory. Composed by the talented Micheal Kelly (@garoadmusic).
VA-11 Hall-A is a passion project, and this shows through every neon-soaked moment. The narrative is supported by some of the most memorable characters I have ever seen in a game. VA-11 Hall-A is not scared to tackle adult themes and social issues that run parallel to our own impending cyberpunk dystopia. The result is a compelling experiance that you feel part of. A deeply immersive, and satisfying title. A must have.

I'm not going to call VA-11 Hall-A (shortened to Va11halla for the rest of this review) a masterpiece or the greatest game of 2016, but I will say this: it's a decidingly great effort in storytelling and using the visual medium in a clever way. I can't exactly remember if I've ever played a visual novel whose branching paths and alternate stories hinged on nearly invisible choices, but I like it, in a way. There's a bit of magic in arriving at an ending and pondering just how you got there.
In Va11halla, you make drinks and you serve them to customers. That sounds pretty dull, but I promise it isn't. Your patrons are full of tales and lore, and as the game progresses, you feel yourself falling in love with them (even the hotheaded and rude ones) and wanting to continue their story. In some ways, this is a positive, but in other ways, it's a bit of a negative. Perhaps this is simply a product of my ending, but there are several loose ends that never really tie up or get answered, and I personally find it annoying at the least, aggravating at the most. I left Va11halla feeling a weird mixture of satisfaction and unsatisfaction.
In fact, if I were to give it a larger criticism, I would argue that Va11halla didn't go far enough--that is, your character sort of ends in the same place where she started, and to me, it doesn't make for the most exciting tale. Is the game about a relaxing bartending setting? Sure. But the city and it's people and it's lore--It makes you wish that the game would eventually become... "bigger". Hell, there are a handful of scenes that take place outside of the bar, feeding that delusion that we're leaving the box eventually. Alas, that is never the case in Va11halla.
What more is there to say? The writing is delightful (although sometimes some sexual dialogue can feel very grating and unrealistic), the artstyle is incredible, and the soundtrack is mesmorizing. If you're looking for a visual novel that is 100% on story and not about banging some anime chick, you're in for a treat. Just be prepared to read.

VA-11 Hall-A, or Valhalla, is a cyberpunk visual novel where you play as a bartender called Jill in the titled VA-11 Hall-A.
This is a bar in the midst of Glitch City, a dystopian city run by a megacorporation that also serves as a testing ground for human-like AIs, called Lilim. Unlike a lot of cyberpunk stories, this one isn't about some rebellion against an oppresive ruling megacorp, it's about the regular people who live i the city and their lives.
It's a very simple game: you read (no voice-acting) people talking to you about diverse subjects usually related to their lives and you serve them drinks when asked. Everyday before work you're at home, where Jill is notified of bills she has to pay or things she wants to buy not to get distracted at work the following day. Distracting her will replace the reminder and comments about drink requests from her patrons by Jill's thoughts about the thing distracting her (an item that you did not buy or unpaid bills.) Apart from this, she can browse several websites on her phone with blogs, articles and threads.
The characters have some interesting stuff to say, barring some that are just plain annoying. This is a fairly light-hearted game with serious moments so don't buy it expecting serious dystopian stuff. The bartending minigame is pretty cool and to get in good terms with your patrons you'll have to remember their drink preferences and pick whatever's right. It consists of 5 artificial ingredients + age/ice that can be mixed in different quantities in order to create one of the drinks on the menu + a secret one. Some drinks do have an ingredient marked as optional - Karmotrine, or alcohol, and getting people drunk sometimes changes their dialogue.
Overall a pretty good and light-hearted VN.

This game can be described in one word - Mediocre.
Awkward un-intuitive controls and an unpolished finish ruin what has the potential to be an awesome version of the classic card game. The controls caused me to accidentally skip attacks, skip turns, not be able to target who I wanted with spells, among many other errors. When you chat during a duel the timer keeps going but the chat window blocks up right where your cards are, so you can't continue to play but must instead chat, without being able to see your timer, and then whoops your turn's gone. I ran into people in multiplayer using this mal-formed feature offensively to eat up my valuable turn time. Some of the cards special rules are explained when you zoom in on the card, but others, like regenerate and its exact mechanic, are not.
The game would have benefited with much more thorough play testing, and a focus on making the controls slightly more userfriendly. All in all, I'm pretty underwhelmed, which is too bad, because I was so excited to pick this up before I played it.
PS -  I don't know what design genius decided that the continue button should alternate with the button that skips attacks, but I have had SO MANY frustrating moments due to accidentally clicking on skip attacks. It's ridiculous, and there's no double check, which is so unlike a real table top game of magic. It's the sort of error that builds frustration, and is at fault in the game design. Terrible.

It's nothing compared to holding actual cards in your hand, but when you can't find anyone else that is in to the card game, Magic 2014 does a good job at keeping things fresh.  Now if only they didn't release a new version for every year like they do with the blocks and just kept adding to what they've already built.  We might actually have more people interested in picking up this series.

Planetbase sucked me in like no other game.  I purchased Planetbase within the first couple days of release and spent a solid 8 hour grind immediately after purchase.  Planetbase is a very challenging space colony building simulator with a steep learning curve when it comes to resource management.  The extremely challenging gameplay got me hooked right from the start.  I began researching what I need to utilize a fully functioning base.  Why did my water run out?  What are spares for?  Why are my solar panels breaking?  There were many questions I had to solve before ascending to a fully functional space colony.  Planetbase has a very narrow margin for error, if you take a step in the wrong direction it will likely be the end of your colony.
The whole space colony survival aspect reminds me of Outpost.  I would suggest Planetbase is the BEST extraterrestrial colony builder ever made.  I can't remember the last time I've bought a game thinking “it looks cool” and then sinking a whole weekend into it.  I regret nothing, this game was beyond fantastic and for being a new release is very stable.  I did notice at one point in the game I had interior structures surrounding another, I had destroyed the structure in the middle and the colonists circled around dying trying to get the unobtainable items.  It wasn't a game breaker though I just had to wait for the items to disappear.
If you want to see my first successful base you can view it at the link below:
If this is a genre you like then look no further, Planetbase is for you!

The quick and simple explination of Planetbase is Banished on Mars.
The game is quite demanding in trying to balance resourses and base management despite what appears to be a rather simple game on the outside. In reality, you are always on the edge of colony colapse with one well placed asteroid early-mid game. (I do not yet know how it is long-term yet, I have not had a succesful colony thus far. But I will not quit!) Due to its simple nature, but demanding level of skill it can easily be an enjoyable timesink but only for those who love base/city building.
For the above reasons, it is a niche game but for those who enjoy this niche, it is a must buy.

[UPDATED] Right from the start, let me say Planetbase is a mixed bag of mostly very good with some bad mixed in. In lieu of an explanation, here comes a list:
Pros:
1) Challenging and balanced survival/builder game. Enough elements for sufficient complexity, not overwhelming
2) Beautiful  and surprisingly engrossing atmospheric game, both in concept and graphics. For a game with no storyline, you will feel attached to your colony.
3) Has a sort of "one more building" hook, similar to "one more turn" games. Each time you get your colony self-sufficient, you will have to risk failure by expanding. There is a balancing act to everything you do: new buildings mean more power, air, water consumption, which in turn means needing new staff, which in turn means...
4) If you've ever played "Banished," this is basically the space version. If you liked that, you will love this. Entails the best elements of strategy/city building games with a fun concept.
5) (Was initially a con) AI has been greatly improved and there is a much more intuitive priority system now. This point serves as a double credit since the DEVs have to be credited for promplty responding to concerns.
Cons:
1) Limited replay value: Once you have learned the nuances of the AI, the game feels a bit limited. You'll spend a lot of hours trying and failing; once you figure out how to succeed, there are not enough elements to keep you wanting more. (all other criticisms stem from this)
2) There are only 3 planets to colonize and the Devs don't seem interested in adding more. So much potential...
3) Some things that would seem essential to space colonization are missing. Things like "heaters," "bathrooms," "security checkpoints,' "radar," "vehicle construction," "marriage and children," "schools/retraining facilities" etc. could add more spice/challenge, yet not present.
Bottom line:
If you like the genre you will love this. If you're not specifically into the genre, you may still like it because it's fun.  Definitely expect around 10 hours of fresh fun. After that, it remains to be seen how much content is added.

to Mr. Hollywood.
Mr. Hollywood's mouth stops
chewing altogether and he just looks at
you as you continue.
Mr. Hollywood gets up now, along with
Ra's Al Goon.
You look back at Killer's Conscience, who
has taken on the form of a demon from
that nightmare realm between Kyrat and
the other worlds, a Rakshasa with smoke
billowing everywhere. Ra's Al Goon has
taken on the form of the evil Kalinag from
Kyrati myth and Mr. Hollywood is still in
the garb of Pagan Min, bright fuschia pink
amid a swirl of color and blood.
He responds, a guttural
roar that is ominous yet expectant.
You look back
at the two Demons now, the Rakshasa of
Novocaine.
Killer's Conscience
roars a low roar. You look at the urn, this
world where Mrs. Novocaine sees herself
dead and the reason why Mr. Hollywood
is so fixated upon ending your existence,
preventing you to continue.
You close your eyes for a moment and
hope for the best when you open them.

Killer's Conscience's
voice interrupts, as both Ra's Al Goon
and Mr. Hollywood charge at you, the
false world of Kyrat and Shangri-La
bleeding into one another when you
open your eyes.
And the Lordvessel is restored, with
herself seated at the
head of the table.
You glance at the very demons of this
mountainous, glorious country, where
the sun is cold gale and the life of its
people is the ultimate marriage of
asian culture. A dream once upon a
time of you and Novocaine perhaps...
but no longer.
You rush forward towards her, sliding
across the table with arms outstretched,
food flying everywhere, Mrs. Novocaine
reaches out for you, expectant and happy.
You take the Lordvessel in your hands as
Mrs. Novocaine looks at you from relief
to horror to outrage. You've waited for
this moment for too long, and finally, at
long last... all you can think about out is
the next true world where your Samara
Rayne can be found.

In a blink, you are gone, but
the words ring in Mrs. Novocaine's ears
as tears fill her eyes and she hits the
table in anger, planning her next revenge.

I had some fun with Far Cry: Brotherhood. Never got to be quite
and never got to really experiment with co-op, but still.
It's basically a very fun game, with the downsides mostly consisting of Ubisoft's insistence on being... Ubisoft.
Not the recycling or the collectathon aspects. I can see how people might be annoyed about those, and I think it's worth pointing out that Far Cry 4 barely qualifies as a full sequel rather than a DLC campaign on a different map (hence my insistence on calling it FC: Brotherhood), but I liked FC3 well enough, and didn't mind reprising it again (twice over even, including Blood Dragon). (Though recycling the exact same gameplay in the Shangri-La sequences was a step too far, and I hope Primal does better)
The collection was properly varied and moderately challenging, in that the collectibles weren't
just different reskins of a box you ran up to and pressed the interact button - you sometime had to think a bit and had different ways to interact with each. Collectibles also gave you useful stuff (small amounts of cash and xp per each, and bigger rewards at regular intervals) in addition to slowly increasing your progress towards 100% completion.
What I genuinely HATED was the single automatic save, the harsh limits on what you can do during main missions (as opposed to the mayhem of sandbox exploration and side-missions), and the terrible main plot (with it's ♥♥♥♥ing unskippable cutscenes, in 20-♥♥♥♥ing-14).
I don't know why Ubisoft insists upon disallowing manual saves. I know that♥♥♥♥♥♥is kinda their thing right now (for whatever reason) but it's just... terrible in every way. If I want to replay a specific moment, my only choice is to go back and replay the whole game. If I crashed near the end of a long mission (which happened more than once) I'd have to go right back to the start of the mission, back to the endless unskippable cutscenes, travel and other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I think it's even worse than the usual Ubisoft♥♥♥♥♥♥ because I'm fairly sure other games allow you to restart from a checkpoint even if you had the sheer gall to quit / crash the game before finishing a mission.
See the video I linked at the start of this review for the kind of fun♥♥♥♥♥♥you can do while free-roaming, taking over outposts and assassinating people. Way too many plot missions stopped you from doing anything interesting, forcing you to either stealth through without ever engaging, or fighting waves of enemies that knew where you are. (Also - I know that you can stealth through regardless, but having enemies become aware if someone was killed right next to them, no matter how quiet the kill, is basically a stupid violation of stealth conventions).
The plot. I'm a pretty left-wing person, and this might be the first and last time I ever bag on popular game reviews for being too PC, but the basic idea that "FC3 had a white person saving natives, while FC4 didn't, ergo FC4 is superior" is just... ♥♥♥♥ing insane. Jason may have had an obnoxious personality, but at least he had
personality. A character arc. A degree of interaction with other characters that was more than the verbal equivalent of a floating question mark above his head. He wasn't a clinically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ puppet like AJ, is what I'm saying. Compare and contrast (for instance) the interactions with Hurk:
FC3 actually had themes. It was trying to say♥♥♥♥♥♥ Perhaps it was a touch ham-handed, but at least it tried. FC4 has absolutely nothing beyond "um, have you considered that violent revolutions may be... not good? Blew your mind, amirite?" Which:
A) Is a drum the series has been beating since FC2.
B) Bioshock Infinity came out around the same time, and had the exact same theme. I wonder why one game took so much more♥♥♥♥♥♥for it than the other.
Then there's the minor stuff like NPC companions being useless, having to drive to a location to get instructions to start a mission (even though you have a radio) and then driving to the actual mission, and more annoying details. Ubisoft is really fond of creating good games and then doing their damnest to ruin them.

tl;dr: 8/10 - Game is great but ridiculously overpriced (more than 2x as much as the original) and the Sekai Project translation is horrible. Don't buy it.
The dialogue was also full of typos and mistakes, many of which I've screenshotted and uploaded to Steam mainly out of OCD. You can have a look, but they're not the kind of funny typos you can laugh at, they're just wrong. Actually,
was kind of funny, but charging $40 for a translation that is barely passable and clearly hasn't even been proofread is a little steep, don't you think?
This brings me to my next two points. Firstly, screenshots.
Sekai Project knew from the get-go that this was going to be a Steam release. The game was obviously reverse-engineered to translate the dialogue, and they even went through the trouble of adding their splash to the welcome screen and their name in the credits - there was even a typo in the credits, by the way - yet no effort was made to change the game shortcuts so that they don't overlap with the
. The screenshot key is the same as the minimize button, which would normally only amount a mild annoyance, but the problems don't end there. After taking a screenshot and maximizing your game again (only at this point will the screenshot be taken), every successive keypress of any key will take another screenshot. Even the media keys and every notch of my K70's volume wheel. Also, the Steam overlay is laggy, unresponsive, bugged and overall, simply unusable. I haven't heard complaints about this elsewhere, so I'm not counting out the fact that it may just be me, but it's true of both games. Again, at a $40 price point, I was really hoping for a functional game.
The other thing I wanted to elaborate on was the price tag, which I really haven't mentioned enough.
This
of the game costs $40 in total, and you're paying for a bugged and badly translated visual novel, and a couple of dollars worth of trading cards, if you really want to go there. On the other hand, I've seen
of the game on sale in stores for as little as ¥1700 - $14. This is, of course, likely to be above the actual production cost and Frontwing's profit margin because the retailer needs some pocket money too. When presented with this information, you really have to ask yourself if you're happy to pay what could easily be three times the original price, of which only a fraction would go to the actual producer, for this abomination of a translation? I really want to know Sekai Project's justification for marketing this title at such a ridiculous price, and why they think they're entitled to so much.
Of course, if you don't speak Japanese and would like to play the game, this is probably your only option, unfortunately. However, there is a silver lining. Koestl, the man behind the impeccable once-fan-translation of The Fruit of Grisaia for TLWiki (now officially licensed to Sekai Project), has admitted that "there are issues" and said "the hope is that [he] will be able to go back and fix it up for them later",
. In my mind, he's honestly Sekai Project's saving grace, and the only reason I hesitate to dump their releases altogether and read the novels in glorious nihongo. That being said, he's currently working on translating the other two installments of the Grisaia trilogy, and I doubt TLCing this game is very high up on his list of priorities.
If he ever gets around to it, I'd gladly recommend this game to anyone who's looking for another great VN starring the Grisaia cast we all know and love. As it stands, however, I urge you to hold off for now. Sekai Project has shown with their World End Economica release that they are willing to receive feedback and actually take action - something which cannot be said about most publishers nowadays. The original release was of poor quality, which I discussed in-depth in
, but the game has allegedly been TLCed and edited, though I've yet to confirm. Hopefully something similar will happen with Idol Magical Girl Chiruchiru ☆ Michiru. Until then, though, I really don't recommend purchasing this title.

My full review can be found here:
Disclaimer: I was provided a copy for review by the publisher.
Following the events of Part 1, a dangerous threat has appeared for Michiru and Kazuki! What could it be? Idol Magical Girl Chiru Chiru Michiru Part 2 takes on a generally more serious tone in comparison to Part 1. Don't worry - there's still plenty of laughs to be had within! The final 6 episodes sees the story wrap up nicely, though I was left curious about a few points that I'm guessing might be more explained in the main Grisaia series (I haven't played it yet).
I wouldn't suggest playing Part 2 without having done Part 1 first, but I do recommend Part 2 if you've played Part 1. You'll end up extremely confused otherwise as there are no introductions to the characters and you're just thrown in. I know this is pretty much a given, but I wanted to put it out there in case. They are a bit expensive on their own though, so you may be better off trying to get them on a sale.

Part 2 is definitely worth picking up as a continuation of part 1.
Part 2 sees a shift in tone towards more serious events, as you'd expect from a story that needs to wrap itself up in six more episodes, but it's all still interspersed with the series' trademark humour. Better still, despite the shift in tone, it manages to find the right balance between more heartfelt, serious moments and the odd shot of (relevant) humour, switching between both with near-perfect timing.
Overall, Chiru Chiru Michiru is also a great spin on the magical girl genre. You can certainly feel the energy and enthusiasm that went into making this spinoff work on the many levels it's based on. It's set up cleverly too.
Sure, it takes a rather easygoing approach to things by nature, which results in a quickly-shifting narrative where anything can happen. But despite this it ties itself together rather well, especially in its conclusion, and most importantly, remains hugely entertaining and endearing throughout.

For all those cliff hangers in the ending of part 1, it's just a rain. Casual Kazuki's joke.

If you are on your way to Valhalla... be sure you have earned your place there.
Volgarr the Viking is a game that seems to have done everything wrong. The checkpoint system - or its near absence - makes you go back to the beggining of the stage each time you die. The challenge lies mostly in fixed patterns, so running the same section over and over to master it is necessary. Air control seems lacking, making even the easiest jumps a potential death trap.  Moreover, the game is short - only 7 levels, if you count in the one awarded to a player beating the hardmode. So many flaws in one game.
You know what? It creates a perfect sidescrolling action game.
Volgarr gives you a challenge to beat the game, and does not care if it's too hard for you. Every time you die near the end of a section knowing that you have to spend next 10 minutes redoing the stage, the game gives you a choice of just quitting it. And you don't, because it has just made it personal. Every time you die to a boss you feel like you should give up - but Volgarr motivates you to just try harder and do better next time. And when you finally beat the stage - I've never played a game that gave me so much satisfaction after that. The game is never unfair. You have a level to complete, that's all. All you can do is to master the controls of the viking and learn the weaknesses of you enemies.
The graphics are great. Volgarr looks like a real badass viking, equipping more and more awesome armor and weapons at every step. The effects of his flame sword attacks are just glorious. The audio is stunning, providing you with top-class effects during combat and amazing sounds congratulating you on completing the challenges. Also, this is the only title with credit screen so good that I don't even think about skipping it at the end of the game. I won't spoil the fun, experience it for yourself.
If you seek for a nice, fair challenge, get Volgarr. If you are an old-time gamer of NES era and want to relive some of the spirit of Castlevania and Ninja Gaiten, get Volgarr. If you are tired of games that hold your hand at every second, get Volgarr. If you want to play a great game, get Volgarr.
And good luck.

THE GAME:
========
Simple realtime 4-ship-fleet vs enemy engagements. 4 types of engagements I have found so far:
1) Destroy All ships
2) Destroy <insert target name>
3) Survive
4) Escort/Rescue
Small maps. Missions are linear and increase in difficulty. Time restrictions make DPS king even if you can manage your ships to be able to defeat stronger foes. You level up as a commander to increase your ability to have more powerful ships per fleet and also level up ships to unlock weapon ports (equip slots) making them stronger. Abilities can be equipped into equip slots bringing an interesting twist to ship customization.
I have played this on Android and so far, aside from some store changes and the pricing, everything seems the same. An engaging game for casual play.
RECOMMENDATION: Purchase ONLY if on a Sale. If you already have this on Android, I don't see the value of acquiring this unless you really want it badly on PC. If they improve upon the base game (a lot of potential) then yeah, it would be worth it, but otherwise don't get this.
Why?
1) Game is Free on Android
2) $ amount you spend to get the game at full price does not equal the free DLC value plus game
3) Powerful ship variants missing from Store so likely DLC only :-( [This is no longer true; ships can be bought for in-game credits now]

Some of the negative reviews concern the AI and pathing in this game, but if you've played other colony management games in the past, these aren't really new problems, it's just how the colonists establish a list of what they're going to do next.
Ask yourself if the price of the game justifies the amount of time you're going to spend (15 hours if you just want to do everything once as quickly as possible and then put it down) and if it's worth it to you, then you should definitely buy this game. The developers are actively patching this game [as of September 2017] with new content and bug fixes although it sounds like their plans on whether or not to significantly develop the game further rely on the success of the game itself. This is definitely a game made for a small audience, and I'm super grateful to the developers for making it. You only ever have two weapons: a sword and a throwing spear. The sword can be used in a few ways and upgraded to a fire version (if you're good enough), but the real star of the show is the spear. Not only can it be used to attack enemies from afar (infinitely), but it can also be used to make platforms to stand on by throwing them at walls. And that's not just a fun gimmick... there are numerous chests out of reach through normal means until you find clever ways to throw spears and make paths to them.
That's also how much of the battles unfold. It's not really a good idea to charge ahead and hope for the best so much as learn how enemies attack and make deliberate movements in order to vanquish them. The bosses work the same way too. Believe me, you'll die plenty of times fighting them, but each death helps you learn their pattern and once you know it, you can bring them down without taking a hit. Thank goodness for unlimited lives, eh?
Just in case it isn't hard enough, there's actually a harder alternate version of each stage (with limited lives) that you can only get to by playing the previous stage near-flawlessly. And the only way to get the best ending is to do that for every stage.
If you miss the good ol' days of fair but unrelenting difficulty, pick this sucker up.

This game really is an ode to the video games of the old days, it even has something akin to wall chicken!  The game is brutally punishing, and very challenging.  But the game is so structured that everytime you die it is your fault, even if it was slipping up for just a moment.  Enemies telegraph their attacks, they are very predictable, bosses have very recognizable patterns, and so on.  You would think this would make the game too easy, but because the game punishes even the slightest of misteps, and checkpoints are far between, you may find it takes a long time to beat this game.  It is a relatively short game, but I would say it has good replay value if you're the kind of person who likes to 100% things, or if you like a challenge, as the game presents a bonus hard path if you manage to max out your power ups without losing them across multiple checkpoints.
My only beef with the game is that there is no saving.  I know it is trying to go for that old game feel, and certainly the original Super Mario didn't let you save your game, but I feel like this only detracts from the game, rather than adds to its charm.  But to each their own, the game is short enough that this isn't a serious problem, and if you managed to beat the first few levels, then you should be able to beat them relatively easily again.
EDIT:  Correction, you can skip worlds you've already completed by going left at the beginning of the level.  This pretty much resolves my only issue with the game!  Please give this excellent game a shot!

Valhalla (sorry, it's just easier to write this way) is essentially a visual novel with drink mixing replacing the typical branching choices. The action takes places in a dystopian cyberpunk world (is there any other kind?) where your character Jill works at a local watering hole, Valhalla. You will spend your day serving drinks to a cast of colorful characters and listening in on their lives and troubles in typical bartender faction.
There are hints of greater things going on in the world at large, but really, the games plot is entirely character focused. Thankfully the characters are well written and engaging, you will even be interested in what's happening with the chracters you don't like. The characters you like though, you will flat out love. The game has a lot of heart and there is tragedy mixed in with the comedy (Of which there is a lot). I really got a kick out of the game as a whole. In the couple of days that it took me to solve, I played nothing else.
The graphics go for a retro vibe, but are excellently done. They are full of detail and character and they really work well to create a sense of place and personality. The music also is really well worth mentioning as it's varied and excellent. Oh there is a new game+ once you finish too, so if you missed out on the best ending first time around (Like I did), you can restart with all your cash and items, making nailing the best ending next time around much easier.
Really highly recommended and I would love to return to this world at some stage.

The darkness parts as you regain consciousness and, with it, awareness of your surroundings. You're confined in a small, circular room with yourself locked in the center. The contraption that holds you is tight, and you ache with the tension of your uncomfortable restraints. The rain outside is pouring tumultuously; the sky itself seems to weep for your circumstances. A voice interrupts it the steady metronome of water; lighting amidst the storm. Gravelly and electronic, its idle taunting is delivered with quite the verbal slap coming from someone with such control already, but you suppose one would grow contemptuous of a man who they've got to keep killing until the end of time. You hold that thought, however, as a swift fist meets your head and your mind fades. The three-masked man shares a bit of your history with you. He calls you a weapon, and says that his ceaseless torment of you is your punishment, that this hell is your future.
The rain is parted once more with the gentle drip of a second voice. It whispers to you.
"I hear thunder, pitter-patter."
"Time to wake up"
Your restraints drop. You slump down the ramp and meet a sword--your sword. Your bunny-hooded savior has more wisdom to share, perhaps the most important words for you to remember on your journey.
"The Jailer is the key. Kill him and you'll be free."
You lurch to your feet.
REVIEW
Furi
GENRE
Action/Boss-Rush
The product of up-and-coming indie devs, The Game Bakers, and with art headed by Afro Samurai creator, Takashi Okazaki, Furi is a stylish, adrenaline-pumping reflex test of an action game. Centered entirely on boss fights (with exposition filling your quiet time), Furi's main goal was to be all killer with no filler, as it were. This can be seen straight from the get-go, as, directly after the opening cutscene, you’re launched into the first fight of the game. Though you’ve just broken out of prison, a large zoom-out shows the scope of the entire game, with multiple planets that act as a multi-layered prison on the player’s journey to freedom. The first fight is rather open-shut story-wise, but the chats you have with your lagomorph-clad companion seem to imply that there’s more to the picture than just a man fighting for his freedom. Who created this prison, and why were you imprisoned in the first place? Who is the man who freed you, and why does he say he knows the other guardians? Top priority to you, however, is probably: when’s the next fight?
Thankfully, The Game Bakers weren’t kidding with their philosophy on rapid-fire killer content. One short walk from each fight will have you swiftly on to the next in no time. Each provides a new, gruelling challenge for you to decipher and destroy along with new gimmicks and threatening new abilities. The player, while having a massive health pool of their own, has a very, very simple moveset with which to dispatch all the guardians that stand in their path. First, and most importantly, I’m going to be speaking of gameplay purely from a gamepad centric experience. I can’t vouch for how the keyboard and mouse controls, but the game itself recommends a controller, so I’ll allow that to speak for itself. Second, there are two modes of gameplay: twin-stick and close-combat. Twin-stick will almost always come first, so I’ll elaborate on that first.
In twin-stick, it would obviously be inferred that one stick moves your character whilst the other shoots projectiles. The player is given the full length of the arena to duke it out in a near-topdown perspective with their foe. Once you’ve whittled down the enemy’s health-bar far enough, you can engage them in melee-combat and destroy the other half of the bar. Dodging, parrying, and counter-attacking replace the running and shooting as you must meticulously hack-and-slash the life out of the boss. Afterwards, they lose one square of their mountainous pool and gain more lethal abilities until the bitter end--you, however, only have the same moves from beginning to end. No one boss plays the same, and some even limit your playstyle to one of the two available in their battles; a subtle way of teasing the player into mastery of the combat. Furi’s combat keeps you on your toes while teaching you what you need to learn; it’s up to the keen player to use the tools presented to them efficiently as well as learn a few secrets the game doesn’t teach you directly.
Combat is flashy and satisfying, all the while providing a challenging and rewarding gameplay experience. Hits with the sword are meaty, and though your combo is a measly four hits, you feel each one to its fullest extent. The blaster, while arguably just as effective at dispatching your foes, is sadly not as enticing. The mindless spray-and-pray gameplay that the bullet-hell sections often devolve into was not personally my cup of tea, but I do suppose either is up to player preference. The parry system is rewarding to those who take the time to learn each foe’s attacks. Timing a parry well enough will net you a blocked hit and some health back, but I should note that the basic parries are very forgiving. You could miss the attack by a solid second in some cases and still evade your punishment. Timing it at the perfect moment, however, will stun the boss and reward the seasoned player with a cinematic, brutal beatdown. That on its own would seem to be all well and good, but i do have the most nitty of picks with the perfect parries: they seem very finicky. On bosses such as The Line and The Burst, I feel like I get a perfect just about every time; with that literally happening in my most recent run against the former. On other bosses, such as The Hand or The Song, these tantalizing hits seem all but unattainable. It’s not enough of a problem to bog down the general oomph of the combat, but it’s most definitely worth a mention.
Also most definitely worth a mention, are the art design and soundtrack. True to his other works, Takashi’s signature art style is heavily prevalent in all of the character design. No one character is even REMOTELY similar to another, with perhaps the only similarity being the near-invasive amount of neon swagger that permeates the game. A particular favorite of mine would have the be the previously mentioned Hand. Cybernetic fire erupts from his weaponry and helmet, creating a downright badass and intimidating visage. The slick, 80’s-esque, cyberpunk presentation of the game pairs lovingly with the synth heavy OST,  featuring a litany of pulse-pounding and original tracks from quite the track record of artists. I spent the entire game feeling ever-so-slightly reminded of my time with Hotline Miami and was thoroughly pleased to see a personal favorite of mine, Carpenter Brut, appear alongside the other musicians present. Music is well tailored to each fight, encouraging the general flow of combat and giving a beat to the beatdown. An honorable mention goes to The Scale’s track. Its glum, dank chords emanate a feeling of dread and hostility, near-mimicking the all-consuming contempt the toxic threat exudes.
All in all, is Furi worth it’s weight in gold? As much of a copout answer it might be, I’d say that’s for the individual consumer to decide. I, personally, was enthralled by the whole experience, staying up into the wee hours of the morning to complete my first run of the game--5 AM to be precise. Upon completion of Furi difficulty, Furier and Speedrun modes are unlocked; two enticing options which provide those thirsting for more with their ever-sought succour. Overall, it depends on how much you love the nitty-gritty of fighting a boss and feeling like one. If what you’re looking for is your chance to feel like penultimate badass; Furi’s killer combat will surely be apt to scratch that itch. Just be wary, freedom comes at a price--especially when you’re killing first and asking questions never. Blood’s a dangerous currency to bargain with, though it does pair quite nicely with Furi.

Galaxy Reavers is an oddly addictive Real Time Strategy Space Battle Simulation. On the surface, it doesn’t look like it would gain too much attention, but for some reason this mobile game turned computer game is one I have been having trouble putting down. The game simply involves sending your little fleet of ships against the mean old enemy fleets and hoping against hope that you come out victorious. To aid you in your strenuous endeavor, you are able to customize the armaments of each of your warships. With luck, you are also able to control the manually fired abilities for each of the ships. You can tell your ships which enemies to target first, but sometimes…usually….most of the time; they have a mind of their own. Even if you order the entire fleet to focus firing on one specific ship, odds are their ADHD disorder suffering AI will break away from their target and take off in pursuit of the nearest enemy ship that happens to cross their path. Additionally, often times you will line up your forward firing laser cannon and start it charging just to have your Captain decide to turn the ship to fire the port side guns. This action of course means that despite all your careful plotting and planning, the main cannon almost certainly fires off harmlessly into space. It can be quite frustrating, but it does add to the realism when your pea-brained Captains think they know better and do not exactly follow your orders to the letter.
You can tell this game was originally designed to have in-app purchases on a mobile device. At present, there are two currencies in the game. One currency is gold, which you earn with every battle you win or item you sell. Another currency, which at one time likely required cash to purchase, is now relegated to being given to you in small amounts for some missions. The premium currency can be converted to gold or may be used to buy special weapons boxes.
I want to be fair and say I played the game before it was officially released and at the time, it seemed to be lacking a lot of polish. I couldn’t seem to find any way to rebind the controls or even see what keys were bound to what. One of the tool tips seemed to suggest I should be able to summon my second and third fleet to aid me in battle. Unfortunately, so far I have been unable to figure out how to do that which is a shame because I could really use more than 4 ships for the level I am currently stuck on. There are also a number of grammatical errors likely due to the game being translated from Chinese.
The gameplay of the game is fairly straight forward. You go to your fleet screen to equip and upgrade your ships however you want them. Once you have them configured how you want, you select the planet you wish to visit and the battle will begin. A quick story is told you and you get a few seconds to give your initial move orders before being cast into the fray. Once in battle, you need to keep your ships alive long enough to complete whatever mission you were assigned for that area. Typically it is just kill every other ship in the field, but sometimes you have to kill a specific one or guard an ally. The difficulty in the game can be a bit off at times. The previous mission may have tested your strength but left you mostly intact and well off for the next fight, whereas the next mission will kill you before you even blink. Another thing that really ramps up the difficulty is the mission timer. I can’t count the number of times my nearly intact fleet was mopping up what was left of the enemy ships, when the timer runs out one laser blast away from killing the last enemy. This of course means you failed the mission (even if one second later you would have been victorius). Upgrading and refitting your ships is the best way to solve this problem. Damage to your ships will be repaired slowly and automatically even if the game is not running. Alternatively, you can throw money at it and the hull breaches will magically repair themselves instantly.
Presentation wise, the game looks pretty good. You can still tell it was made for a smaller screen, but it doesn’t look bad blown up for a bigger screen. There is plenty of details going into making the ships look cool. The various hull designs and the wide variety of weapon effects make the game quite appealing to look at. The sound effects are perfectly fine for this kind of game, the soft sounds of a battle waging as the various weapons fire off and hit their targets.
So should you get it? I find the game to be very addictive. Despite each new mission being just a harder version of some previous mission type, I still want to press on and see what happens at the end of the game. Getting stuck on a mission and having to redo previous missions enough to gain the funds to upgrade my fleet would usually annoy me in most other games, but for some reason, I don’t mind doing that in this one. Once the free Cruiser DLC releases many of my frustrations in the early game should not be experienced by those who get the game after launch. Adding a Cruiser to my fleet really got me through a fair portion of the game more easily than when I just had my Chasers, now that I have added a Battleship, I am having an even better time of it. So if you are looking for a fairly casual, play a single mission now and leave it for something else for a while kind of game, Galaxy Reavers is one you should consider.

I've read at the Magic: The Gathering site that Duels of the Planeswalkers is really designed as an introduction to Magic and in that regard, I think it's highly successful. The game is excellent with its optional tooltips in teaching players how the game works and in a controlled environment. It even teases you into the card game by providing a while-supplies-last opportunity to redeem a one-time code for a six real world cards in the form of an exclusive booster pack at your local game store. And so I think, especially with the game's limitations when it comes to deckbuilding and the overall ease of the single player campaigns, new players are who will best appreciate Magic 2014.
That said, multiplayer does give Magic players who have a drought of time or people to play the game with a chance to play Magic more often even if matchmaking isn't all that speedy. And that makes Magic 2014 a decent game, one that gamers who like Magic or might like magic, but don't want to wade deep into either the real world card game or Magic online, will appreciate. And one that even more regular Magic players might like now and then when they don't have any people around to play with.

This game is tough. Thats not at all a bad thing however. If you have fond memories of Ghosts & Goblins, Super Ghouls & Ghosts, Rastan, and Castelvainia 1 then this purchase is a no brainer.  This game has an old school play style that provides loving discipline while punishing lazy or rushed players.  This is a game where understanding your enemies weakness and changing your tactics to correspond after failing is often rewarded with success.  There are few games out there that provide this experience and if you are willing to endure many deaths you will find this game is more rewarding then most modern titles.

Do you want to play a hardcore Action/Platformer? Do you want to face hordes of monsters simply to prove yourself a badass? Do you want to be a man? If the answer to all these are yes I cannot recommend this game enough. This is a throwback to everything good about the "good old days" where games were made to challenge you to the maximum. This game is challenging with great focus on detail of the system.
Volgarr the Viking is an amazing game created by Crazy Viking Studios which pushes the players to their potential. You play as the games namesake Volgarr on a quest to be a badass. This game has a great soundtrack that keeps you tense and feeling like the Viking you are. Controls are responsive and tight leaving you feeling that any death is your own mistake.  Visually this game looks great for being a throwback to the days of the arcade, which in my humble opinion is a plus, having wonderful 2d sprites which bring the game to gory life.
This game has good ability to be played again and again, which you'll likely be doing because each time you die you must go back to your last checkpoint, which can be quite a loss of progress. I'm not kidding this game is truly hard, and it will challenge you. Its simplistic controls leave the only challenge you face be the hordes of enemies who will stop at nothing to kill Volgarr and end his quest, which will likely happen more than you want it to. Luckily for our hero death is not the end for him, for each time he dies he returns to life at his last check point. Check points are a rare occurrence though, keeping you on your toes for fear of losing your progress so far.
Power ups appear in the form of armor which grants you extra health, each time you are hit however you lose that piece of equipment and ability it brought with it. The only downside is the lack of any form of storytelling, and the lack of saving which can make the challenge all the greater when you realize you'll need to beat it in one sitting. For its flaws it is truly a fantastic game that reminds people of what games use to be.
If you don't like hard games I really recommend you stay away from Volgarr, but if you’re a fan of the hard core, die repeatedly, but enjoy it all the way through then this is your game.

I don't have time for this game! A puzzle game where you get puzzled over what the hell you are suppose to do. Delicate and intricate design. I am sure it is a fun game for those who want to run around from puzzle to puzzle, and figure out what the hell each puzzle mechanic is about. I for one do not. Not my kind of game. But...I would still recommend it.

The Witness is a puzzle adventure game set in an open-world and built around solving grid-based puzzles that are spread around the landscape.
The puzzles require you to draw a line from a starting point to an end point. As you explore the island you will be introduced to new symbols that place requirements on how the line must be drawn. You will need to explore the island to find areas that ease you in to the new mechanics and symbols. There is no item collection or inventory, so progress is gated only by your knowledge of these mechanics.
Paying close attention to details in the environment is critical to progressing through the game. Most of the game is hidden in plain sight and you just need to look at things from another point of view. Highlights vs shadow, positive space vs negative space, foreground vs background, color, reflection, even sound, you will eventually change the way you look at each scene because the game makes use of it all. There are over a hundred puzzles that are hidden in the world that you will walk past dozens of times before you look at them in the right frame of mind. The observation-based puzzles are absolutely masterful and by far the best part of the game.
Another chunk of the puzzles are purely based on learning the logic of the different board symbols and mastering them. This was the part of the game that I disliked the most. I found a few of the mechanics very frustrating to work with which made progress through certain areas slow. What made things worse in comparison was that many of these sections were there only for the puzzle boards and they lacked the same relationship with the environment that most of the other puzzles had. The environment didn't play into the puzzle board, and the puzzles didn't change the environment short of enabling the next puzzle.
Thankfully when all was said and done the excellent observation-based puzzles far outweighed the puzzles that I hated. After spending hours scouring The Witness for the last of the puzzles, I've found myself doing double-takes at familiar shapes both in other games and in reality. It was worth it.

The first few hours are magical. Then the tedium sets in. And the unresolved questions: What are all these panels doing here? What's up with the statues? Where am I?
It's one thing to be vague or mysterious or suggestive. It's quite another thing to not even attempt any kind of explanation. This game was clearly a victim of its years-long development process. It is beautiful and occasionally brilliant. But only occasionally. The rest of the time it is opaque, directionless, repetitive, and--the cardinal sin for any game--boring.

TL;DR Fast, rewarding combat with cool varied, attacks and bosses. Camera struggles a little. Slightly unpolished. Overall, still really good.
A fast-paced twin-stick shooter meets old-school top-down action. Fun and frenetic, yet similarly expected, much like an old-school SNES boss fight. Personally, I really like the art-style. It's pretty much a more futuristic version of Afro Samurai. I'm almost certain the main narrator is the actor from Shogun Assassin, one of the Masters of Death, and that is freakin awesome. It may be an impersonation of that voice, either way, I dig it.
Combat works in stages. First, a wide-angle that is the main bullet-hell section. Here, you'll have a mix of up-close and bullet-hell style attacks from the enemy. They can be parried for a little health, but it also risks being hit. Once that life bar is drained, you move into a close-up section. This plays with circling inside a fixed area. Normally something I detest, but the samurai style and the flow make it work quite well. It has a circle, block, parry feel of sword fighting without being inundated in lame animations that take away control.
The bosses have repititive attacks like in older games, but they can still be taken down with reflexes given the skill. They have about 5 "life boxes", but it varies. Each box lost gets progressively harder, until their final box, which is basically a hail mary effort you need to defend. Each time you defeat both stages, wide-angle and close, your health is refilled by two boxes. Sounds bizzare, but I've found it works great.
It forces you to make a good run when damaging their life bar. While, also giving you a fair shot overall with enough health refills for success or sklil. My only real complaint so far is the camera on the close-in sections. I find that sometimes the dodging is stifled by their radius attacks, the one that turns red. Sometimes, you can't spot the safezone because of the camera, and that's frustrating. You take a hit, not because you dodged improperly, but because the safezone is out of sight of the camera.
Overall, a worthwhile experience for anyone that likes old-school grindy boss battles, they've been given a new gloss with kickass future samurai action. Definitely, a cool take on a classic formula.
