Im not sure if I can recommend this game or not. Its a great concept and is kind of fun, but leads to be boring after a short time. It can be funny and make you laugh but it can also just drag. After only 1.5 hours of playtime I am not sure I will play again until the next update. My 4 year old even got bored of it after a while. While I can certainly appreciate the open world sandbox experience, it doesnt feel like it is fully there as of yet. I'm certain there are things outside of the city to find, however its a drag if you flip your car upsidedown and are stuck out there trying to search on foot - you end up spending a very long time just walking back to find another car or even just walking to -- nowhere really. It feels empty and barron outside the city walls and there doesnt seem like there is really much to do inside the city either (except for fall down over and over).
The mechanics feel clunky as well which is another thing that was really aggrivating to me. Walk up a curb fall down, walk to a wall fall down, walk to a door fall down, walk to a car door - fall down, even walking to an object results in getting knocked to the ground. I'm not sure if this is how the physics are supposed to work or not at this point and being I never played the previous version I dont know much about the game, but constant ragdoll when trying to walk to a object or even a NPC is very annoying to me.
I saw a bunch of stuff in the videos and update news but cant seem to find them in game. Rocket Launcher?? Where is it? Fly a blimp, uh how and where?? Just thinking that the game is not very intuitive on letting players know where things are at, I mean I know there are things to find outside the walls of the city, but who wants to drive for 10 minutes somewhere, flip the car upside down then have to walk for 20 minutes though empty fields to find a freakin boat because there is no way to flip the car back upright??
Also the game needs some background music, all you hear outside of radios in the area is the frogs feet slapping against the ground as you walk. While I give it a +1 for creative thinking there some ambient music would be nice - the silent slapping of the frogs feet I feel contributes to making it feel more bland.
All in all the experience so far is OK, not great/amazing and not totally awful. I am going to recommend this game to sucker more people that skim over this review into buying the game so that maybe they will give some ideas in the forum and help make the game better.

I really do want to give this game a great review. But like everyone else, there are a few things that just bring it down. To sum up why I CAN'T recommend it...
- The devs will not be adding more content in the future (such as Banished)
- AI are a hit and miss at times. I mean they're the core of the game, so if they are performing poorly, then you're done for
- The replayibility may be dull, no random generated planets or anything
- The "challenges" may seem fun and difficult to play with (solar flares, different weather conditions per planet) but these get really old very quickly no matter how you approach them into achieving a grand colony
- The UI looks like a UI from an alpha build from the early 2000's. It needs an overhaul
- To get a good colony going, you have to set up a base almost the same way everytime
There are many more downsides which I will not mention because I wanted to address the most important aspects of the game
So to conclude, it has so much potential and so many hours of entertainment (yes I have only 9 but I can see how it is down the road). It is a great game, similar to Banished.
What may sway my decision in the future (to recommend this game) is if the above aspects of the game are improved, fixed, etc.
Don't forget about Steam's refund policy. Worse comes to worst, you can ask for a refund. I think you can have only two hours max of gameplay to request a refund. Double-check the policy.
EDIT 11/18/15: As I've played last night and the devs commented on this today, the AI has been improved a lot, however I don't think that's enough to sway my decision to recommend this. However for some people, that is a make or break, so if that applies to you, then I would now recommend it for you since the AI has been improved.

I've been wishing for a game like this for a long time. If Sim City had a love child with "The Martian", you'd get Planetbase. Pioneering a new home on a planet with a harsh environment is as difficult, as it is enjoyable. I had to restart my game several times to figure what to build and when, to help my colonists survive their first night on their new planet. Building the equipment you need to maintain a self sufficient colony is the motivating factor in this game. No real story to speak of, the game relies on a milestone system for game progression. Similar to the way Civilization games progress.
Your starting crew of 7 colonists with varying professions, and their two droids, touch down in a lander with supplies. It's up to these brave few to get the base set up with the basic needs to survive on a planet with no breathable atmosphere. Get your oxygen generator set up, then provide it with power by building solar panels to collect energy during the day (or windmills to generate power around the clock). Build an energy collector to store surplus energy for use throughout the night. Once your colonists can breath some air, Build an airlock to let your people in. Then there's more to build from there. You need to make food, make building materials, etc.
A great game with a a lot of bang for the buck!

Didn't think much of this game. Saw it on the steam store page, and the "Frag like it's 1999" motto caught my eye.
I remembered the good times of '99 when I was play Unreal Tournamed (classic), Quake 2, and the Beta version of Quake 3, that consisted only of q3dm17 (think there were 2 maps though).
Looking through the screenshots of Toxikk , they seemed a bit eye-candy, gave the impression that someone's heavy photoshop skills were involved, but I decided to give it a try nevertheless, so I hit install on the free2play version.
Game was downloaded fast, since it seems to only take up 4GB. "Something that fits in 4GB can't be that good, especially not look like in does in these screenshots", I thought.
Well, I was wrong. I started playing the game, and the minute I did, wife came to me and informed me I have to go to the store and get groceries, "We're all out of food, and it's lunchtime", she said.
"Just give me a couple of minutes to try out this game, and I'm going", I said.
Fast-forward 2 hours later, I'm still playing the game, wife's in the kitchen mumbling something about "..those god-damn groceries already..", and I'm over here just fragging like it's 1999!
Game seems to be a very good combination of the Quake-genre's high-paced action, and the Unreal Tournament-series mutators and map design. Whichever of these 2 games you've played, you should feel right at home with Toxikk.
This is the true multiplayer that quake fans expected Doom (2016) to have, and really what it should've had.
The graphics are superb, and the level (or maps, fow new-schoolers) design is absolutely marvelous. I salute the crew that put (probably) tens of hours of development into the level design alone.
Creating a free edition to this game was a nice touch. It gave us a chance to actually see what a wonderful gem this game is.
For those of us that had the luck to play these kind of games in 1999, this game is a nice reminder of a time when life was easier, and games weren't a stone-throw away, yet we all had a lot of fun.
Keep it up Reakktor Studios, you're doing a good job. This genre deserves a comeback, one whose direction isn't dictated by today's modern trends.
I could blabber on about how unexpectedly good this game is, but the above-mentioned wife started thundering in the kitchen. That's my cue to leave for the grocery store. You'll just have to try it and see for yourself.

So. This is a perfectly brilliant puzzle game, the sort of which forces you to think laterally and is all around fun. It's awesome, and guessing the puzzles together, discussing the solutions and cuddling are just perfect compliments to a wonderful game.
Also, The Witness is wickedly clever in the puzzle "language" it creates, and wicked smart in the ways it communicates the grammar of this language. Play it. Really, really, play it.

Besides that, good puzzle games are hard to come by, and this is a great one. I wouldn't say it's worth 40 dollars, but I wouldn't say it's not either, it's really going to depend on each person and how much value they feel like they got from it.
10/10

-Shield  (you start with it but you can lose it, it can parry a few hits) ;
-HammerShield  (can parry every hit, unlocks the power to charge super spears);
-Helmet  (i havent found any specific ability for this, it just grand another layer of defence);
-Flame Sword  (deals increased damage).
Overall the difficulty could feel a bit frustrating at the beginning, especially if you're used to save your game every few steps.
It's gonna be brutal, you'll die a lot, but each time you'll learn a bit more about the level and slowly you'll progress and be able to finish a level without dying.
It is really hard, like the old Rastan and Ghost'n'Goblins were, it took me roughly 1 hour to complete the first world, which is divided in 2 levels + boss.
Overall i love it, it brings me back to when i was a kid and couldn't wait to go to the Arcade and spend tons of coins to play these beautiful games. This game is just all that...a sweet jump to 20 years ago...with style!

The Witness is a puzzle adventure game set in an open-world and built around solving grid-based puzzles that are spread around the landscape.
The puzzles require you to draw a line from a starting point to an end point. As you explore the island you will be introduced to new symbols that place requirements on how the line must be drawn. You will need to explore the island to find areas that ease you in to the new mechanics and symbols. There is no item collection or inventory, so progress is gated only by your knowledge of these mechanics.
Paying close attention to details in the environment is critical to progressing through the game. Most of the game is hidden in plain sight and you just need to look at things from another point of view. Highlights vs shadow, positive space vs negative space, foreground vs background, color, reflection, even sound, you will eventually change the way you look at each scene because the game makes use of it all. There are over a hundred puzzles that are hidden in the world that you will walk past dozens of times before you look at them in the right frame of mind. The observation-based puzzles are absolutely masterful and by far the best part of the game.
Another chunk of the puzzles are purely based on learning the logic of the different board symbols and mastering them. This was the part of the game that I disliked the most. I found a few of the mechanics very frustrating to work with which made progress through certain areas slow. What made things worse in comparison was that many of these sections were there only for the puzzle boards and they lacked the same relationship with the environment that most of the other puzzles had. The environment didn't play into the puzzle board, and the puzzles didn't change the environment short of enabling the next puzzle.
Thankfully when all was said and done the excellent observation-based puzzles far outweighed the puzzles that I hated. After spending hours scouring The Witness for the last of the puzzles, I've found myself doing double-takes at familiar shapes both in other games and in reality. It was worth it.

But I did encounter a few issues. I played at my native resolution which is 2560x1080. After I finished each level, the buttons "Next" and "Replay" were cut in half, falling off the bottom edge of the screen
(I had to guess what they said). At standard 1920x1080 it looks fine.
After the first few levels I thought to myself: "this could really use some UI, at least to show me how many bombs I currently have or how many machine parts are there still left to find". And I completed the whole game thinking that. Imagine my surprise when I sat down to write this review and wanted to check something about the game's intro. Instead of starting the game, I just found some let's plays on YouTube. And what do I see there? A panel in the top left corner showing the information I wanted! I thought that maybe I missed the latest update or something, but no, that wasn't it. Turns out the panel is not displayed at 2560x1080 resolution and for me it looked
. When I then started the game at 1920x1080 it was there.
One more thing that I found annoying - there are 18 levels in each world. Every time you close the game and come back, the selection is on the first level and you have to move it to the latest one. I know it doesn't sound like much, but you select the levels with your character's avatar riding in a mine cart, and it's moving very slowly.
It sounds ok at first. The piano fits well with the steampunk theme.
But after 8 hours I was sick of it. The same thing over and over again.
You have to push boxes and barrels around, collect machine parts, blow things up and kill robots.
It's actually pretty cool, a nice casual puzzle game.
There are 3 worlds - Caves, Arctic and Castle. Each with 18 levels. That's 54 levels.
I'd expect each world to introduce a new feature or functionality, something fresh that would require new tactics.
Out of 18 levels in the Arctic world, only one (level 17) is actually making use of the ice, making the boxes slide once you push them. One level out of 18! In all the other 17 arctic levels, and all 53 across all wordls, the boxes move just by one square. That's a complete waste of the arctic setting.
Similarly, level 18 of the Arctic world introduces new enemies - those alien-looking jumping creatures. And that's the only level in the whole game you'll see them in. Doesn't make any sense!
It's a fun game, got me hooked up with that one-more-level-syndrome.
But it just feels unfinished. There is no progression. The things you do in level 1 are the same things you'll be doing in level 54.

If you're coming into it expecting the same great experience of Far Cry 3, I caution that you will be disappointed, especially on the story aspect.
Come with me as with delve into FC4's problems:
In Far Cry 3, you go on an epic adventure to save your friends. In Far Cry 4, you're the Golden Path's errand boy. I'm serious, you're going to find that the campaign basically resolves "Do this to solve that problem".
Unlike that one time in FC3, FC4 thought it was a good idea to make the story less linear by letting you make "who's side are you on" choices in the game. When you have a game that lets you choose between X or Y, it has to be well tailored to the game's narrative. FC4 does not do this and the narrative suffers. I almost didn't complete the campaign because of how tediously boring the story is.
There seems to be more of an emphasis on stealth than in the previous Far Cry game. Even though I love stealth, it does get pretty annoying when an enemy execuetes a hostage because you didn't notice them within a split second. Maybe it's just me but the enemies also feel harder to beat, meaning stealth is always the better option. This is bad because I understand that everyone likes to choose their style of play and a good number of players prefer the chaotic approach to combat.
I love and hate Ajay's "No ♥♥♥♥s given" attitude. He's so calm given his situation its hilarious, maybe because its probably how I would react too lol However it makes his character so much more boring than Jason from Far Cry 3 who was clearly out for blood to kill Hoyte and Vass because of what they did to his friends.
The game makes it very clear to you who the bad guy is at the start of the game. And then he proceeds to never show up again the game begins to reach its climax. And it's a shame too because Pagan is a great character! One of the reasons Vass was so liked was because of the tension every time he and Jason cross paths. I could go into detail to how Vass was under utilised in FC3, but then Ubisoft went to barely using the main villain at all? That is nothing but a shameful waste.
All the negativity aside there is one positive side: Gameplay. My main complaint in FC3 was there basically being no replayability, however FC4 solves that. Plenty of new activities and quests. You can retake outposts, there's always something happening like saving hostages and saving rebel fighters. All of this in a big open world and  all the great elements of what makes Far Cry's gameplay so satisfying is here.
There's a map browser that I don't remember seeing in Far Cry 3 which I really have to say is a spectacular idea. Basically players make their maps with enemies and such and so other players can take on the challenge of beating that map. Brilliant idea which is almost like never ending content for players who loves Far Cry's gameplay.
Game has gorgeous detail and it's not too power hungry, on my build at least [i3 CPU with  RX 470 GPU]. My processor struggles on Ultra but most of the time the framerate is very acceptable.

From the sound-effects to the level and enemy-design, this game wants to be Megaman so bad it hurts. It's too bad that Gunworld is completely insufferable from top to bottom. This is one of those games that's difficult for all of the wrong reasons.
Why is this game is so difficult? It's because Dwayne (Dwaine?) is on the wrong-end of the screen at all times. When playing a 2D platformer, it's important to be able to see what's ahead. This rule was established back in the 80s. When the hero of a 2D game is running, they should be in the very center of the screen. Instead, you have very little real estate, so if an enemy appears, you probably won't be able to react in time to avoid it.
Alright so let's break it down. In the City stage, Dwayne has to jump between conveyor belts. There's enough space ahead of Big D so he can see the jumps he has to make, and not much else. At one point, a large fire-spewing robot is going to spawn out of seemingly nowhere. You'll have no idea this robot is here, until you jump off of a conveyor belt, bump into the mech, and fall to your death. When you restart the stage, at least you'll know when that particular mech is going to appear, so maybe it won't kill you again. I'm hesitant to refer to this as "trial and error" game-design. It's more like you get the middle-finger at every opportunity, simply for having the gall to play this game.
At this point, I don't even have to find other aspects of this game to complain about, it's already a failure. When you're practically expected to die just to know what's ahead, then the game is an absolute mess. The worst part is that fixing this game shouldn't be a complicated process. All GunWorld really needs is a handful of improvements and it would be playable. I suppose that's how developers make hard games. They break all of the established rules just to guarantee easy deaths for the player.
I'm done discussing this pile of filth.

I picked this up initially because cute VN with a clever, small gameplay hook. Calling something waifu bartending is a pretty easy sell for me, even if it collects dust on the Steam library shelf for a few years. And hey, Linux support so that's awesome. I didn't expect much, but started to read and play through when I wanted to wind down for the night and wanted something a little more passive.
I haven't completed it yet, but I've become entranced. The story is deep and well presented. The music is outstanding. The gameplay hook of mixing drinks, while easy, provides enough consequences and puzzle solving that it keeps you involved and makes you mindful of the simple task. The easy gameplay doesn't get in the way of the story while letting you feel the main character, a young woman in a transitional period of life working a job that just pays the bills. The mundane nature of mixing drinks adds rather than subtracts from what the game is trying to tell. The job is easy for her, at least the drinks part.
The story feels deeply personal. The developers manage to craft a world outside the bar with complex political goings on, corruption and terrorism, and real fear around the streets. Yet, the characters, especially the main charcter, react to these events as normal people. They carry on, they go to work, they read a story in the news or in a forum on their phone. The events of the world are experienced in the real way we experience them, through small talk, rumors, and unreliable internet sources. With this setting, there's a powerful display of the relationships we have with technology, each other, and the helpless feeling of a surrounding chaotic world. I think everyone can relate these days.
By using chit chat in a bar, serving drinks and passively trying to understand the surrounding world, you're invested in the characters in a way not often seen in games. The motto of serving drinks and changing lives becomes the main character's way of accepting the mad and dangerous world around her, while doing what she can to make the world a better place.  It's a page turner that rather than settle me down before bed, keeps me reading on to the next section.
My only complaint would be with the jukebox system. The music is fantastic, and the soundtrack worth a purchase. However, by having the player pick tracks, and have them play mostly randomly, I think it limits what the developer could have done with the soundtrack. It would have been better if the developer had found a way to make those tracks come up in key moments, more like a Phoenix Wright game. I end up not adjusting the track settings because I don't  know if one song is better than the other, and feel I might be missing out on a lot of good music. I worry about picking tracks that might not fit the mood later on.
When all is said and done, this game has come to occupy a special place in my library. If you're looking for something a little slower pace to pass the time, any time spent mixing drinks in VA-11 Hall-A is not time wasted.

Reading some of the negative reviews, I can't help but feel that some didn't have the patience and got angry when the game didn't do what they wanted it to. If you have patience, Furi will make you a better gamer by training you to improve your reaction speed and timing. Furi is easily the most challenging, fair, and rewarding game that I have ever played. There are no items, leveling system, gear, ect. The game is essentially a boss run that places you in each level with the exact same amount of power/skills/abilities as the previous level. Your character is a constant while the bosses are a variable. There are some bosses that will take you an hour to beat because you will keep dying. Do not lose hope because your failures are still experiences which build up to teach you the correct methods to defeating each boss. Depending which boss you are fighting, they may have 4-5 lives. Each of their lives is a new stage adding layers of difficulty. In order to defeat these bosses you will need to understand when you need to parry and what rhythm is used, when you need to run, when you need to dodge, and when you need to shoot. As you progress through the 4-5 lives of each boss, the strategy that you learn is built upon, or in some cases slightly altered. I played this game for 1-2 hours per week for a live stream with no practice in between and I was able to learn how to succeed, of course I had hints from my viewers as well. As a gamer I am not very good at bullet hell shooters, my reaction speed and rhythm aren't the best, but by the time I finished beating the standard difficulty setting I was able to dodge lasers with a narrow margin of error because I had the patience to continue and not get upset when I lost. There were times when it took me over an hour to defeat a boss, after winning I was left sweaty, exhausted, and my hands were sore, but the sense of achievement made it all worth the effort. In addition to the gameplay, the soundtrack is amazing and everyone loved it. If you are a fan of the anime series Afro Samurai, then you will also appreciate the character design as it was influenced by the anime. Overall, I will continue to play fury in its newly unlocked speed run and Furrier difficulty settings to improve my skill. If you are looking for an incredibly challenging, yet fair game, Furi is a must play.

Usually I can play an MMO for hundreds of hours before getting sick of it, but after a measley 6 in DMO.. I doubt I'll get above 20.

DMO is not a great game. That doesn't mean it doesn't have things to be enjoyed about it, though. For fans of the Digimon franchise, it is incredibly easy to forgive a lot of shortcomings because of its huge library of Digimon, the familiar and colorful (and sometimes terribly designed/repetitive) maps, and the usual mmo perks of occasionally finding decent people to play with or, more times than not, just buy overpriced items from.
I enjoyed being able to play with the Digimon that aren't given so much spotlight attention, like Gazimon and his line of weird demons. I enjoyed the events and time-based rewards. I enjoyed talking with fans who enjoyed Digimon and talking is what helped pass the hours of grinding. I did not enjoy grinding by itself.
Which is what this game is all about. You thought the other assorted fantasy mmos with their 'click on the guy, kill some things, report to guy, get stuff, repeat' were bad? You have no idea until you play Digimon Online. I've played the game on and off since it's launch, but typically resort back to the account I spent some money on--because this game is free to play, pay to win--because of the time and effort invested. Kill this thing, kill that other thing...You thought Leomon had it bad in the shows? You have no idea. You will murder thousands of them and their kin for the dirtbag scientist you have to talk to all the time. You Elecmon fans will be showered in eggs, congratulations.
That brings me to another selling point/drag. There is a large selection of Digimon to obtain as 'mercenaries', or partners, and over time the library was expanded to include Armor Digivolving, the Spirit Digimon, and even some Xros stuff. Your favorite digimon is probably in the game. Hell, even the recolors get love there, as they should! On the flipside, the way the system works for the Digimon is incredibly rigged against you unless you drop some money. Digimon have levels 3-5 of sizes(all hatching requires at least level 3). Level 3 Digimon are the physically smallest and weakest, and level 5 are of course the largest and biggest. You input data you harvested from killing everything else corresponding to Digimon type, at least 3 times, but its all luck if the data works. Usually it will not work, and then it will break your egg and laugh at you. That egg and data you spent has been thrown into the dumpster and ignited. Unless you have reinforced eggs or hatching backups--which are found in the cash shop, or for a pretty penny from other users. Also, when you buy an egg in the cash shop, it is randomly assigned if it is lvl 3, lvl 4, or lvl 5--so good luck getting your Giant Guilmon. Lvl 4 Digimon are the upper-average, and not impossible to obtain the hard way, but lvl 5? Yeesh. This can cause a lot of wasted hours killing things to gather various items that end up being wasted anyway.
But, there is a bright side. There are constant events in the game. Once, updates came as quickly as every 2-3 weeks, but it tends to settle into a monthly to bi-monthly cycle these days. Items can be earned, rewarded, found--and though sometimes the events are god awful, sometimes you're showered in cash items that would otherwise be a pain to obtain. Those lvl 4 and lvl 5 digimon aren't impossible to get your paws on with those.
The quests are incredibly dull, the 'plot' is an incoherent smear of several chunks of the Digimon stories, and the multiplayer element can be ruined by item sellers and the usual assortment of various rude players. Botting is a problem and always has been.
But yet I still play the game, running around watching my cute little Gazimon beat the ever living hell out of every Leomon in the Digital World, feeling good when I unlock a new digivolution level, or find some players who actually like to communicate. I love Digimon, and so that is what I enjoy about this game. If you don't love Digimon, you will definitely find a different and superior version of this kind of game. It really makes me miss that SMT Imagine Online, for sure...

I really hate to say this, especially considering how much I enjoyed Farcry 3 -- warts and all -- but yikes, is this game ever boring. The whole experience feels like a big checklist bolted on to a half-hearted story and cardboard cutout of a main character. Things look good visually in 1440p, and gunplay feels mostly fine except for some weirdly broken hitboxes and questionable AI, but the noise to signal ratio in general is so poor that I struggled to care about any of the characters or the plight of the resistance.
The antagonist is (ironically) one of the few bright spots in the whole thing, but we see and interact with him so rarely that I frequently forgot about the tyranny of his regime and the game's central dilemma as I bounced around a vast sandbox laden with tons of fetch quest-style missions and achivement-hunting distractions. The apparently requisite dream/drug sequences in Shagri-La LOOKED amazing but were what finally led me to rage-quit the game, but that's probably for the best: at more than 20 hours in, I soaked up as much of the game's better parts as I could: the outpost liberations, fun gunplay, and tooling around the sandbox Blowing Up Bad Guys(tm) until it got old.
Unless you're way more committed to fetchy achievement grinding, frustratingly omniscient AI, and a far less compelling copy-paste of Farcry 3 than I am, I'd say give this one a pass and hope that Farcry 5 gets things back on track.

Being this is a bullet-hell game, having fast-paced gameplay is expected.  However, the games suffered from wrong pacing.  In each stage, the player will go through a few minor enemies, and then fight a boss after only 30 seconds.  After that boss is defeated, a few more minor enemies and another boss will appear again after 30 seconds.  Having bosses so close to each other each, it lessens the pleasure of defeating each one.  If the stages had the bosses spaced a lot further apart, it would have made the action much better.
One thing that could be considered a plus and a minus is the fact that your ship is auto firing the entire time.  Logic says that this is good because you do not have to think about pushing any buttons in order to attack.  However, when you are trying to avoid the enemy bullets, this will cause both shots to blend together making it harder to avoid.  The way that the player controls the firing is by occasionally using one of its special shots.  However, there are times when defense is more important then offense.  Without being able to stop shooting when you want, being able to avoid damage is more difficult than it has to be.
Speaking of which, getting hit seems to have the wrong feeling to it.  If a shot does hit your ship, there will be a slight pause in the action.  Otherwise, things keep moving as if nothing happened.  In other games like
or
, getting hit will have a clear impact on your ship if it does not destroy it.  Seeing no damage does to your ship gives the false sense of security that it is still in good condition.  When you consider that there can be dozens of enemies and bullets on screen at one time, knowing how you are doing through your ship is vital.  The only time you know that is by turning up the difficulty to hard where only one shot is needed to destroy your ship.  Considering the volume of enemies, that could be suicide.
While it is a decent amateur game, it is not one worth recommending.  This game is available at
for free.  If you are curious about the game, get it there.  After playing it, if you still it is worth paying for, do it then.

Please note that having no instructions on what to do in the game or giving the locations of the puzzles is what helps make this game amazing, it is not a flaw. The purpose is for you to explore and have those descovery moments when you finally understand something about a puzzle or the world that you previously did not.

This review will contain spoilers, see conclusion after the break at the end for spolier free rating and conclusion.
Disclaimer regarding my time spent playing: some of these puzzles were so boring or needlessly difficult that I developed an unhealthy attatchement to the IGN guide and did not continue for much longer after beating both endings. If you do not believe that I finished this game just because I did not clock in over 40 hours, check my achievements.
I feel like I absolutely need to write a review for this or else I will go insane from the amount of irrational love and hate this game gets. First, an obligatory pros/cons list:
Pros:
- Oh my sweet Lord the graphics
- Interesting mechanics for panel puzzles
- The environmental puzzles (at first)
- The keep (except the leaf crunching part)
Cons:
- The description is full of lies
- Panel puzzles become monotonous
- Sound puzzles
- Panel puzzles only become truly unique and potentially awesome in the last area of the game
- Environmental puzzles become tedious and stupid
- Difficulty curve and style is garbage
- Narrative is garbage
- Themes are garbage
- Sound puzzles again, it's time to stop
Now I'm going to clarify a few things. Firstly, why am I calling the panel mechanics interesting but the panels uninteresting at the same time? Here's the thing: no matter how many mechanics you add, they're just line puzzles. They're just line puzzles, and it becomes extremely old. They're. Just. Line. Puzzles. This is better placed on a 2D mobile game priced at $5, not a 3D console/PC game priced at $40. This is partially redeemed by graphics and environmental puzzles, but still, THEY'RE JUST LINE PUZZLES.
(Note that this is transcended in two areas: the keep and the mountain. Which is great, we get some real variety with life size hedge mazes and bridges and wrap around pillars. The question is why is one of these mechanics not seen until the last section and the other not required to be used until the last five minutes?)
Next, what's wrong with environmental puzzles? They increase variety and aren't seen in any other games, what is this "at first" crap? Let me tell you a secret: they are line puzzles. Without mechanics. The most interesting thing in the game is another line puzzle but without all the cool colors and shapes. These puzzles are extremely interesting in that they are perspective based, something not seen enough in games, but they don't have enough variety to keep it from feeling like a chore. I went through a lot before just googling "the witness do obelisks do anything", followed by another search reading "wikihow tie a noose". Needless to say, I am not 100% complete.
Next, how does the Steam page lie? Well, it advertizes over 500 puzzles "without filler". What. The puzzle count includes all the tutorial panels and all the single line control panels, which are most certainly filler. It also advertizes that it "treats your time as precious". Those tram, elevator, boat, and running speeds beg to disagree. I can't help but feel they're just screwing with us.
Next, OH MY GOD THE DIFFICULTY IS PART OF THE GAME YOU'RE JUST DUMB AND DON'T GET IT No stop. I get that this is a Metroidvania style puzzler, and that's okay. What isn't okay is stuff like the tetriminos at the entrance of quarry that looks like a tutorial panel but uses information from the marsh. You have to make it obvious when the player isn't in a purposefully accessible place. Even worse are some of the tutorials, like the jungle. Sound puzzles do not belong in your predominantly visual game, especially when they have fake difficulty or outright don't work as intended.
And finally, the narrative and themes are absolute trash. The story is basically a person beta testing a VR game about line puzzles. The narrative, however, has different ideas. You're never given this information until a poorly made live action clip after the secret ending, where it's all just dumped on you. Until then, it was hinting some sort of apocalypse or mind cleansing island thing with all the statues, monitors, and general mountain creepiness. This is shot when it ends the first time and you get some random Buddhism without answering who the witness is supposed to be, which you were thinking was like big brother or something. This is shot further when you find the ending with the environmental puzzle that frees you from the simulation, and no answers are given. I'm fine with abstract story telling, but those audio logs are not enough to make up for the confusion of the direct story. The themes are worse, with everything being extremely inconsistent and undecided. Many audio logs outright conflict, and the videos have no holistically coherent or consident information. It's just a mess.
At this point you're probably thinking: why are you recommending it even with all these glaring and frustrating problems? The puzzles. I know I'm being contradictory, but my philosophy is that if it is an enjoyable game with relative value in its genre, it is at least leaning towards good. This game barely squeezes in. If you aren't worried about price, if you are the kind of person to enjoy something as repetitive as sudoku, if you don't care about storytelling, if you only want a game that fills the category "puzzles with literally no explanation, you're on your own" and thrives in it, then this is the game for you. There is no flaw that absolutely destroys all appeal for mindless, repetitive 2D line puzzles, and that barely keeps it in the green for me. God, I hate and love this game so much. I heard that this game, Portal, and Talos are part of a 3D first person puzzle holy trinity, and I was left wanting my $20 back.
6/10, if you know what you're getting into, if you enjoy repetitive tasks like sudoku, if you have low expectations, and if it's on sale, this game will give you plenty of enjoyment. If these four conditions are not met, you will be dissapointed. If you are interested enough to see the story but not enough to pay the price on sale ($20), watch a let's play and pause to do pen and paper with a guide explaining all the symbols.

I would only suggest this game to the crowd that like challenging simulation games.
The positive(s) for me have been that the game feels like a puzzle - after trial and error it does feel rewarding.  There is constant tension because of random affects of intruders, weather, and just trying to keep up with all your colonists needs. This tension seems to feel too abusive to some reviewers but unlike other games like Banished you can't really let your guard down and enjoy the aesthetics of what you are building. the AI does need to be tweaked more even though this last patch did help)
You do have to micro manage and consider your choices. You cannot just plop structures down because it feels right - you are almost required to have experienced losses and understand the cause and how you could have affected future problems to prevent them in future builds.
The negative(s) for me are that the amount of structures you have at your disposal are limited at the moment. Besides wanting more to play with you have limited options or tools to solve certain problems. If you have a problem like morale - get a bar or multi room. Problem with food - canteen, lab, bio. It becomes formulaic quickly as a result.
I really hope for modding support in the future because I can see some cool content being built. Banished and the colonial charter mod(s) come to mind as a similar situation I can see. I think there will always be a difference between Banished and Planetbase in that the later will require constant management and choice making to simply survive where Banished evolves into an aesthetic experience the longer you play.
At the moment I would recommend this to those of you that like the Dark Souls of sims experience. I know I do ;)

I thought I would give this game a try, it looks decent and fun, it's mostly original and it's always good to see more management and base/city building games hit steam. BUT after playing this for 6 hours straight just... ugh, this game really tries to be good but the dreadful AI is just barely tolerable and really lets this game down. The learning curve isn’t that steep but with the barely fair amount resources you start out with as well as the clumsy, super inefficient AI this game is brutally hard, stack this on top of the nightmare that is balancing every single resource in this game and your left with one tedious and frustrating experience. At times this game feels pretty decent, but then suddenly you realize how much of a chore it is when you forgot to build one more power storage and boom! it's all over... everything goes to crap, again.
This game will be a major pain in your butt for your first few play throughs, I don't know how many times I restarted and reloaded a save after who knows how many failures just to learn enough to get a base -barely- going, and I did the tutorial, I learned everything I could, but nothing can prepare you for how insanely fickle the game balance is. Got no biologists left to get food cas they all died somehow? It’s over, everyone starves. No workers left or don't have any meds to heal them so they work again but need you need workers to make plastic to make the meds in the first place? well your screwed, the game will never make any progress and it will be boring a heck. Need to make one more wind turbine but can't get enough metal cas the power keep going off stopping the workers making metal? ugh, yay, you forgot to make extra power a second ago and everything comes crashing down because of it, fun. Everything in this game relies on each other for a base to work, -everything-, if you forget to make even meds it's all over, ''but that’s the whole point of the micro management and is what makes the game interesting and challenging though!'' you might be saying, yes it is, but in this game it just feels like a joke, this has happened to me in Banished before but it generally felt like my fault in that game, in this one, I just feel cheated. The fact there is no difficulty setting to be seen is very disappointing to, so if you plan on playing this game casually then lol just don't, this game is on brutal difficulty all the time, every time. Just something to keep in mind.
Last thing I’m going to go over is the AI, like everyone else that has down voted the game on the AI I also have to admit it is as dreadful as they say, it is 'barely' functional and is just so frustratingly not good at what it's supposed to be doing. Even when prioritizing room for tasks you need done badly they will roam around and go on strolls or fill up their sleep meter every 5 seconds, they seem to do everything in their power to avoid doing work to keep the base running before doing a tiny bit of work then going to fill another need cas a need bar went down alittle again, are you kidding me?! There is no way to adjust when they go to fill their needs or where they go to fill them they just go and do it when they want, I even saw a worker abandon making metal just to get afew seconds of sleep then go and eat when he really didn't need to, meaning the end of that game cas I really needed the metal to make more power. I’ve even seen workers die of hunger as others eat the last of the food cas their hunger bar went down alittle and got to the canteen first, like what!?!? there is no way to stop them from doing that either, so enjoy watching your space base of morons have no idea what they are doing. In a game where the AI is essential to the whole thing running and being fun you think the dev would have done a better job right?… it’s a shame really.
I also hope your not looking for anything graphically impressive or nice to look at either cas it’s pretty below average for me, the only anti-aliasing is FXAA im pretty sure cas it does a bad job and blurs the game pretty badly. It seems to be running on Unity 4 engine tho so you can’t expect much I guess, a real shame cas I sure wish it looked as pretty as the store pics.

Okay, I've updated my review... Again. :)
The game did have some issues when I began, but it has been vastly improved.
1) I had a resource outside, and the carrier robot just kept slaming itself against the closet wall instead of going outside and getting the resource. UPDATE: I haven't had this happen lately.
2) Resources called "Spares" are needed to fix things.  While the people have access to all the resources to build spares, they'd rather not build them, thus crippling power and eventually killing the colony. UPDATE: My colonists seem to build spares out the wazoo as long as I have the components and things are set correctly, the trick now is balancing mining and production with everything else going on.
3) Other resources are needed to build additional facilities.  In one game, I had a colonist stop at 99% completion of an iron unit needed to build a new solar collector so that the base would stop losing power near morning, no one else worked on it and eventually the base failed. UPDATE: They seem to do alot better now.
4) People were starving to death, because no one could be bothered to collect the food packs. UPDATE: This has gotten better, the trick now is balancing biologists with just enough food components that the biologists don't get overwhelmed so things dont start breaking down creating a chain reaction of death, but it is better then when I first started :)
NOTE: I've had my base saved because my last colonist was sick and in sickbay without a doctor, apparently the colonist refused to die, but it gave me enough time to get some new colonists to keep the base going :)
So overall the game has definitely improved since I began playing, it's no longer extremely frustrating, it's more of a balancing act now that I'm continuing to try and improve.  Keep up the good work!

TL;DR

Be the viking... Or die trying, a lot! Having actually finished this game I feel qualified to recommend it to anyone who likes extremely difficult platformers. Volgarr is something of an anomaly, a game that could have been made back in 1990, but works so very well today. It is not the same kind of fast paced action featured in games like Super Meat Boy, though. It is slower, more deliberate, and much more violent. Every movement must be deliberate and you will die a lot just figuring out when to jump, what the boss pattern is, etc... However, you do get unlimited lives and the most you have to backtrack is maybe 5-7 minutes after dying to a boss, if that. If this doesn't sound like fun to you, it might not be, but it feels great once you've mastered the levels and bosses, eventually being able to clear them without even getting hit once. Oh, and you do get armor pickups that enhance your abilities and you can take 2-3 hits before dying depending on your items, and can block most ranged attacks. The game is very fair, just very hard.
There is a lot more to the game than most people will ever see, as well. By completing levels perfectly (or near perfectly) you gain "lives" you can use in extra-challenging alternate levels. There are 4 or 5 of these, and when you run out of lives in them you get dropped back into the main game levels, at which point you can try to win them without getting hurt again and get back into the alternates. There are 3 different endings based on how many of these you complete.
I'll wrap up with a quick tip for anyone who buys the game and wants to actually finish it... Press left on the title screen to warp to the next level. You can keep doing  this all the way to the end game tower assuming you actually beat the boss of the level you're skipping over.
If there was one game to embrace the classic Genesis feel, this'll be it

One of the funnest games I've ever played. It's just so many good things mixed together. You got amazing and creative character and world design, really fitting and energetic music, very fun boss phases and mechanics and insanely fun combat. There are no stats or menus to worry about at all. It's just you, the enemy, and your fighting prowess. I have just started the 6th boss and am about 5 hours in and I feel this is a good time to write a review because I'm honestly in love with this game. I'll be short and sweet about how this game works.
So you and your enemy have life nodes and health bars. Your goal is to reduce the bosses nodes to zero.  If you or the enemy reduces their openents health bar to zero, the loser loses a node and the winner regains all lost health on his/her health bar. If you lost a node in a previous phase, removing a node from the boss will refill one of your nodes.  Each node for the boss introduces a new, more difficult phase than the one before it. Most bosses have around 5 bars I would say and the whole encounter take 10-15 minutes to beat if you're successful. I lost to most bosses at least twice (except the first one). It's taken me 5 hours to beat 4 bosses.
It's a difficult game but each death makes you a stronger opponent and it's incredibly rewarding when you pull off perfectly timed parrys and dodges. You have a long distanced pistol and a close quarters sword. Each has a charge attack that does more damage. You can also parry and dash. When dashing, you are invulnerable to any attack. The first 5 bosses I've encountered have all been varied in what they offer. The setting, theme and mechanics are surprisingly unique to each boss. They really tried hard on making each boss feel like a different opponent.
What makes this game so damn fun and rewarding to play is the combination of music, combat and visuals. There are no outside mechanics. The sense that your'e in complete control of the character and that every single action gets you closer to victory is the key. If you button mash, you will NEVER beat a single boss. It's honestly amongst the best games I've played, and if my friend didn't gift this game to me, I would have bought it for 20 bucks no problem. It's an amazing ride.

Mediocre game which has aged terribly.
Here's what I like:
- It's a digimon game. There's a serious lack of them.
- It's an MMO that doesn't run like♥♥♥♥♥ Yay cellshaded graphics.
- Ancient and simple design. Easy to pick up and understand.
Here's what I don't like:
- The UI is absolutely terrible and a strain on the eyes. There is a serious lack of graphical options and changes to the placement of UI elements do not persist between sessions.
- The sound is terribly loud and the music is unbearable to listen to. A lot of sound choices for certain actions in the game will give you a headache over long sessions. Not to mention a lot of it gets redundant and unamusing pretty quick.
- The game looks borderline unfinished There's a lot of unoptimized quests, localization errors, glitched, and unexplained server disconnections.
- This game makes FF14 look like Sonic meets Mario. It is slow, sluggish, and literally a "press 1 to kill" kind of game.
- Leveling at first is pretty rapid, before becoming incredibly slow. Having to level up multiple digimon separately on top of a tamer which levels around 4x slower than they do means lots of grind, lots of back tracking, and a lot of beating your head against the wall (Read Further).
- Kill stealing is a huge problem in this game. All rewards and XP as well as quest progression is given to the player who attacks first. This makes doing quests which require killing specific digimon and absolute nightmare. It literally took me 30 minutes of frustration to complete a "Kill 10 of X" quest. Sound fun?
- The Non-English speaking audiance is more than abundant in this game. Coordinating parties or finding English-speaking guilds proved to be impossible.
- Egg hatching is a joke. Do not spend any serious effort, time, or money attempting to hatch an egg. 3/5 eggs are borderline worthless. 4/5 is a minimum viable egg and I've already busted 50+ eggs trying to get 1. Of them, I only managed to get 5 to 3/5. The success rate is lower than both the break rate and the failure rate. If you're one of those people who like playing slots, maybe you'll get some amusement out of this - I certainly didn't.
What's sad is, they have had multiple years working on this. A lot of these problems are totally fixable and would improve gameplay a lot. There's a number of glaring issues with the game I didn't feel like touching on because they're simply problems with the game's initial design and instead of fixing them you may as well make a whole new game all together.
Tl;dr - 2/5. Played worse, definitelty not impressed. This game would have some potential if it got some serious developmental support, however as it is, it's impossible to recommend.

Many people have already talked about the more emotional side of this game, and I think many of their thoughts ring true. While I wouldn't go so far as some reviewers in saying this was an "emotionally difficult" game to play, I would say that it gives perspective and makes you think in ways that games usually don't. That's valuable in itself.
I think what a lot of people don't mention though is that beyond all the weighty themes, the gameplay itself is solid. It plays well, it's challenging without being overly punishing, it surprises you and keeps you on your toes, there's a definite and satisfying sense of progression. It has the quirks you would expect of a small indie title - the controls don't always work as you want them to for example, especially during combat - but they remain as quirks rather than frustrating bugs or flaws. I know others have mentioned bugs in the game, but my impression is they aren't common or game breaking as I have yet to encounter one.
I also appreciate that there is in fact an end to the game. Many games with similar approaches as this one feel content to let the game simply go on and on without end, and while that may be fine for some it's never been something I've enjoyed. I want to feel like there's a goal to the game, an end point where it all wraps up, and this game provides that.
I've really enjoyed this game thus far after putting close to 20 hours in, which was a complete playthrough and a few aborted attempts, and I can see myself putting in another playthrough or two before I decide to move on. With the full price of this game being so affordable, and sales being even cheaper, I would definitely recommend it for anyone who enjoys games with elements of base-building, strategy/stealth, and unique atmosphere.
Update: a couple weeks later and I've put in much more time than I originally expected. I've pretty much maxed out my interest in this game at this point, but it hooked me for even longer than I thought. A great game at any price, and an easy decision with the very low price of admission.

GET A CONTROLLER OR DON'T BOTHER.
I wanted that first in case it was the only thing you read. Yes, you basically need a controller to play this game. I played the first two years with just the keyboard and it was pretty much a nightmare. It's not impossible, but it is really annoying. I didn't realize how much work it was until I went and bought a controller, it became ten times easier instantly.
Also I feel as if this game was made by two different people. On the one hand a lot of the visuals and level designs are amazing. I almost cried when I first got to Hogwarts, or I glimpsed the Quidditch World Cup. But then at times the levels are just unnecessarily stupid. There is almost no help the entire game to explain to you how you are supposed to do things. 95% of the time this is fine because it is overall a pretty easy game and kind of obvious how you are supposed to play. But then some of the time the only way to complete an objective is so mind numbingly abstract that you sit at the end of a corridor for an hour trying to realize that the only way to defeat a book is to become invisible (???).
If you are a true Harry Potter fan this is pretty much a must buy even if just for getting to walk around Hogwarts. As a true dork I also loved figuring out which students were those barely mentioned characters such as Alicia Spinnett or Susan Bones. Of course true fans will also get frustrated with things like why Hermione tags along in the first task, or why Ron kind of sucks at flying a broom even though he's pretty good at it. But it's honestly worth any of the negatives to enjoy the positives.

If you enjoy puzzles for the sake of puzzles, you will absolutely love this game.  Though the premise of all of the puzzles are the same (go from point A to point B on a grid), the variations on this theme are quite extensive- though there are hundreds of the puzzles throughout the island, you won't tire of repetition.
This being said, if you need a story, or any goal to motivate you, I would recommend staying away from the game.  There is no story to be found; just disconnected, pretensious, 'philosophical' ramblings.  The game would have been better if these had been left out completely, but since it can all be skipped, it's not really detrimental to the game.
The main puzzles of this game are all possible through logic alone- I would highly recommend avoiding any walkthroughs, as being given the answers greatly cheapens the experiance of figuring it out for yourself.  That being said, the black monolith puzzles vary from "obvious" to "there is absolutely no way you will figure this out on your own."  Once you complete the main game, don't feel too bad about breaking out a walkthrough to find all of those really obscure patterns in the world...  or just skip that section entirely.
In summary, I highly recommend this game to puzzle enthusiasts, but not anybody else.  Know your own tastes, and don't try to force this game on yourself if this isn't your thing.

Mediocre game which has aged terribly.
Here's what I like:
- It's a digimon game. There's a serious lack of them.
- It's an MMO that doesn't run like♥♥♥♥♥ Yay cellshaded graphics.
- Ancient and simple design. Easy to pick up and understand.
Here's what I don't like:
- The UI is absolutely terrible and a strain on the eyes. There is a serious lack of graphical options and changes to the placement of UI elements do not persist between sessions.
- The sound is terribly loud and the music is unbearable to listen to. A lot of sound choices for certain actions in the game will give you a headache over long sessions. Not to mention a lot of it gets redundant and unamusing pretty quick.
- The game looks borderline unfinished There's a lot of unoptimized quests, localization errors, glitched, and unexplained server disconnections.
- This game makes FF14 look like Sonic meets Mario. It is slow, sluggish, and literally a "press 1 to kill" kind of game.
- Leveling at first is pretty rapid, before becoming incredibly slow. Having to level up multiple digimon separately on top of a tamer which levels around 4x slower than they do means lots of grind, lots of back tracking, and a lot of beating your head against the wall (Read Further).
- Kill stealing is a huge problem in this game. All rewards and XP as well as quest progression is given to the player who attacks first. This makes doing quests which require killing specific digimon and absolute nightmare. It literally took me 30 minutes of frustration to complete a "Kill 10 of X" quest. Sound fun?
- The Non-English speaking audiance is more than abundant in this game. Coordinating parties or finding English-speaking guilds proved to be impossible.
- Egg hatching is a joke. Do not spend any serious effort, time, or money attempting to hatch an egg. 3/5 eggs are borderline worthless. 4/5 is a minimum viable egg and I've already busted 50+ eggs trying to get 1. Of them, I only managed to get 5 to 3/5. The success rate is lower than both the break rate and the failure rate. If you're one of those people who like playing slots, maybe you'll get some amusement out of this - I certainly didn't.
What's sad is, they have had multiple years working on this. A lot of these problems are totally fixable and would improve gameplay a lot. There's a number of glaring issues with the game I didn't feel like touching on because they're simply problems with the game's initial design and instead of fixing them you may as well make a whole new game all together.
Tl;dr - 2/5. Played worse, definitelty not impressed. This game would have some potential if it got some serious developmental support, however as it is, it's impossible to recommend.

I had this one sitting in my Library for some time before i got around to play it.
And oh boy, i was in for a ride. The situation is simple - you get three people with different traits who depend on you to navigate them through the hell that is war. The days are spent inside the hideout where you improve stuff or craft new things. But to be able to do this, you have to gather materials at night by sending one of your people on a scavenging mission. Just be careful not to get him killed!
All in all, while the gameplay mechanics itself are rather simple, they are unforgiving - if you get shot, you'll probably die.
Add a depressing atmosphere and a soundtrack that really nails it down and you get yourself a powerful experience. The dread and despair of the situation comes across really well.
I recommend this game since you rarely get such an impact out of a game. This game is an experience.
Added bonus: the controls and mechanics are actually good, too!

X
, trying to figure out which magic combination the developer intended for you to use this time.
An example: Suppose you're in a clearing in a forest and you need to reach a high ledge. What do you do? Simple, just follow this easy guide and you'll be on your way!
1. Find a gray cylinder-shaped lego piece.
2. Using levitation magic, lift it up into the air.
3. The cylinder will split into five separate disks. Why wouldn't it?
4. Use these disks to form a shape, sort-of resembling a rain-cloud.
5. Levitate the pieces over that old tree next to the clearing.
6. The "cloud" will start to rain. (Why do I have to tell you this?)
7. Water will make the tree grow (Duh!). Super-fast. In the middle of the night.
8. As the tree grows, tree-pixies (or whatever) will sprout out from it. You DID see that coming, right?
9. The tree pixies will build you a ladder! Problem solved!
It's so simple you'll be kicking yourself that you didn't think of it in the first place.

I don't typically write reviews, but I recently picked up this game years later because I re-played Far Cry 3 and thought "Man I'd like more Far Cry 3!" and well, here we are.
So for those of you coming over from Far Cry 3, here are some things you'll find yourself saying aloud while playing.
"The wingsuit is the real antagonist"
"What's a stealth?"
and last but definitely not least
"Why aren't I hitting him? Oh the hitbox for the terrain was bigger than the actual model....I was shooting the invisible air that extends past it and now the entire camp knows where I am."
They added some nice new things, for example the animal handling and the larger supply of weapons. (Although if I'm honest I never found myself using anything but 1 of the 2 silenced ARs, the silenced sniper rifle (there's only one), the signature silenced pistol you start with if you bought the "Big Dong Johnson" edition, contrarily you can spend a pittance in ubisoft points to unlock Robocop's pistol from Far Cry Blood Dragon and put a silencer on it and have a burst fire silenced pistol 10 seconds into the game. And when I finally unlocked the ONLY silenced SMG I used that.
That is of course until you unlock the Signature Weapons (you'll start with 3 of you bought BFG America edition) which unlock extremely easy in this game. I think when I first finished Far Cry 3 I only had the Bushwacker, in this game I'm pretty sure I had like 6 or 7 within a couple hours. Thankfully every Signature Weapon is either a silenced death machine or directs a lead wall in the direction of your enemies so once you get those you'll probably never die to combat again.
The Ugliest of the Ugly:
Here's where the game hands you your favorite pal from Far Cry 3! The wingsuit! And then immediately punches you in the♥♥♥♥♥♥everytime you touch it. If you touch anything while using the wingsuit you will instantly die. After you pop the parachute, if you touch any vertical surface you will instantly die even if you're 2 inches off the ground. Also, the line of "vertical surface" is very gray, I've died from landing on an incline in a clearing where I pulled my chute a good 5 or 6 seconds before landing.
I can't tell you how many times I've been caught because I lined up a shot with my sniper or AR and while aiming down the site I legitimately couldn't see the corner or the cliff I was aiming around/over in the scope. Yet I still hit the invisible hitbox that stuck out a good foot from the wall/cliff. It's hard for me to say anything nice about a game in which I couldn't beat a single stage.  The difficulty in this game is right on par with Silver Surfer for the NES -- that is to say, it's next to impossible.  I get that this game is meant to emulate 80s platformers, but it did so in all the wrong ways.
One thing that bothered me greatly was the lack of checkpoints.  Every time you die, you start back at the beginning of the stage.  Unless, of course, I hadn't yet reached a checkpoint in the stage, which only compounds the difficulty issue.  Another problem is that, like many platformers of that era, the game relies on pixel-perfect jumps as a means of coaxing cheap deaths from the player.  Speaking of which, the game also tries to include the Ninja Gaiden style of wall jumping, but it doesn't feel as fluid as that game.  I find that a frequent problem in games of this type; they want to emulate Ninja Gaiden, but in the end all it does is make you wish you were playing that instead.
There's one level which effectively starts with a boss fight.  At first, the pattern to beat the boss seems simple: Get out of his way when he jumps or charges, and avoid the rocks that fall when he does this.  That's enough to keep you focused, but the game devs didn't stop there.  They also throw in these slug creatures that fall along with the rocks, so you have MORE things to avoid.  Why bother?  It's unnecessarily difficult.
As a lesser point, there are some glitches/bugs, though nothing game-breaking, as far as I can tell.  During your death animation, you can actually still shoot from side to side, which is funny even though it's pointless.
I notice the game is marked as Version 1.5; I hope there are future fixes coming that address the insane difficulty, otherwise I have to say this game is not enjoyable in the least.  Thank goodness I only picked it up for $2.99, otherwise I'd be even more upset.

Great game for starters.
It is a game with players going through many heart wrenching(not emotionally), mind breaking, hair tearing, eye poking, intense sweating and swearing on many situations. In comparisim of the difficulty between build sim games (I played), Banished, Anno 2070 and Planetbase.
Planetbase is  probably on par with Banished for me.
AI in Banished seems a little better for me. But in Planetbase, the AI system really hates me and frustrates me the most, where a Engineer/Bot constructs one building but not the other next to it. For example they choose to build the building but not the connector afterwards. Especially on startups and in a crisis where you need that particular building to be built. Workers tend to be a little inefficient due to the many things they do (mostly anything that involves hard labor). Piority tab is just something for you to click on but its up to the AI to do your bidding while you are watching them in agony. They also tend to build the things that are closest to the spacepot at start up and from the base after you got it built up.
I was also hoping that there would be some sort of a slidebar that controls the efficency of the AI Humans (by category) and Robots to do their jobs better.
What I do hope in the future for a patch or expansion (which may or may not happen)
- AI System taskbar to control the efficiency of the Humans AI and Robots.
- A piority queue system? Something lets your workers know what to build next and what not.
- Another panel for the Alert system for easy access once you build of the Control Centre.
- Tweaking of the Human AI with Negative Status, they should be working on half efficiency instead of completely dropping their task and Idelling around the base.
- Machines that uses materials should go first instead of Buildings.
- Some sort of Emergency Back up Generator to last through the day? (Or half a day depending on how much power has been stored in it.)
(There is probably more to add but this is the best I could come up after unlocking the second planet.)
In the end, Planetbase is a management game with a huge hope of luck that 'stuff does not happen' when you are just starting up your game. For example, Worker getting an injury when you got no Medbay to cure him, Random Meteor hitting onto your SolarPanel/Wind Turbine/Power Storage and situation where you really want natural wind to blow across the globe but does not do that. *Especially on the 2nd Planet which I am currently on.*
But once your base has been built up for all self-producing machines or up to Medicine/Spare Parts for your Wind Turbines and Solar Panels. You are pretty much set and have to be cautious of keeping your power management up and expand cautiously. Only time I had trouble was multiple intruders attacking my base while I was in the middle of setting some furnitures down for my Dorms. I had to back track everything to the start of the menu and towards the Security section to put on High Alert for my guards.
In other words, if you like Management games that are really hard, about the same levels of FTL and Banished. Go for this game. It takes a couple of times of trial and errors to know which to build first and hope for the best of nothing happens. If you are uncertain of it, ask a friend who has it to let you try a game or two. Though be warned that a good game can take a couple of hours to get it right to your playstyle.
Cheers to all playing as well and fingers cross on random encounters in the game.

It's... very hard for me to say whether or not I recommend this game. I certainly can't whole-heartedly.
At it's core, the witness is a beautiful exploration of the maze puzzle mechanic, and builds a system of interconnecting rules and symbols that feels syntactic. The difficulty curve is sharp but not unmanageable, and the rule represented by each symbol is presented naturally and organically, though certain rules come (much much) easier than others. Most puzzles with environmental cues are cleverly incorporated. The environment itself is stunningly beautiful and the overall game experience borders on meditative. More than anything, the puzzles require non-linear thinking; the moment when you change perspectives and look at a puzzle with new eyes, and can solve that puzzle, is an immensely satisfying epiphany.
However. The lack of hand-holding is admirable, but perhaps excessive. The fact that the entire island is available for exploration from the very beginning means that it is relatively easy to skip all but the very first "tutorial" panels and immediately become frustrated by encountering puzzles that you haven't yet found the rules for. Although it is simple enough to step back and try and find something that you are capable of, it can be difficult to differentiate between frustration over simply not having had the moment of 'epiphany' and genuinely not having the skillset to complete a puzzle.
Another well deserved complaint is that certain areas are literally impossible to complete for colorblind and/or tone deaf persons. As I am neither, I don't have much else to say about that, except that the auditory environmental cues were frustrating and unclear despite not being tone deaf.
More than anything, though, the puzzles that rely mostly or even entirely on environmental cues are overwhelmingly frustratingly opaque. For many of them, you have to position yourself nearly pixel-perfect to get the perspective required to solve a puzzle. A great number of challenge puzzles exist entirely as very subtle cues in the environment and have no apparent purpose. In fact, a great number of the puzzles in the game have no immediate feedback as to why you've solved them. The so-called "story" is similarly opaque, and is really just a series of thematically connected philosophical quotes and baffling videos found throughout the island.
Overall, I suppose that The Witness was... interesting. It was in turns frustrating and deeply satisfying. As a meta-commentary on perspective, and as a gameplay experience, I personally think it falls somewhat flat. However, I would play it again, and probably will, and I don't regret buying it. I deeply enjoyed the vast majority of the puzzles presented. If you catch it on sale and you're the type to enjoy puzzle games along the lines of The Talos Principle, give it a try I suppose.

It's a Digimon game! A. DIGIMON. GAME! As big fan of the series since childhood of course I had to try it out, which I did but... it was disappointing compared to what I expected. The game has some neat features and the graphics and music are acceptable to say the least, but I'm going to explain why I think the game is still a mess right now.
Let's start with the good things first. As I said, some of the mechanics are nice. You fight other digimons and your digimon levels up and grow stronger, and you can also get Digi-eggs of Digimons you defeat as a loot drop, which you can use to incubate that Digimon, and then you can use them in battle, all of which I think is pretty cool. The combat system is also similar to a lot of action RPGs so it's definitely something a lot of players will be familiar to - having a set of skills with cooldowns assigned to different keys etc.
However, the game has a few big problems and it's... quite apparent from the start. The quests and tutorial are very bland - basically read on how to do this, do this, complete the quest, get rewards, and repeat in an endless cycle. There is no interesting dialogue and the characters literally have no personality. Plus, the English is also a bit... atrocious. I mean, I've never made a game in my entire life but I can probably still make dialogues 100x more interesting than these series of badly translated instruction manuals. Even if you get past that, you'll also probably notice that the enemy AIs literally only has 1 attack pattern plus you don't even get to move around and interact with the environment once you're locked in a fight, which makes the fights boring very quickly.
In conclusion, I think the game has potential but right now? It's piece of crap, don't bother with it. I'll definitely come back after some months to retry this game because I want to hope, but please at least fix the English by then for my sanity's sake.

Volgarr is a pretty cool action platformer with a slower, more methodical pace than most. You can't change direction mid jump (except by double jumping), your melee attack is very short range, and your projectile locks you in place for a second unless you do it in mid-air, so you really have to commit to your attacks in this game.
It's pretty much a thinking man's action game. It rewards precise timing and execution, but it's very difficult to get out of bad situations unscathed once you get put in them. The emphasis here is more on carefully figuring out how to safely go about things and avoid getting trapped, and the game is excellently designed in this regard: there's tons of different ways to get past obstacles, the level design is really clever with a lot of attention to detail, and the game generally feels pretty fair even when it's hard (though some of the bosses do jump off the deep end into pure trial and error).
So if you want a thinking man's hack and slash platformer that doesn't leave you feeling "oh, I should have reacted to that faster" when you die, but rather "oh, I should have thought that through better", than consider Volgarr since it does a fantastic job of accomplishing that.
