The Far Cry series has a very special place in my heart.
And Far Cry 4 is an outstanding game, no doubt. But I do have some gripes with it that I will address in a second.
- Amazing gun play
- Story is great
- The antagonist follows the traditional Far Cry formula
- Open world aspects are next to flawless
- The graphics are beautiful
- There's so much to do
- The protagonist is a really flat character
- Some of the side quests are really repetetive and some time an annoyance
- Some minor bugs
- Some of the controls are a bit whacked
Now on to my personal gripes.
Far Cry 4's story.
Don't get me wrong, it's really good.
But it's not Far Cry 3 good...
The protagonist is a really flat and dull character, sure his motivation is cool and is really noble, but his lines and his personiality is just so boring and monotone it doesn't really get me feeling him.
A lot of the characters aren't memorable.
Take Vaas from Far Cry 3 for example, everything about him made you afraid, and angry, and sad, and confused all at the same time.
But here with Pagin Min and some of the other higher up antagonists in Far Cry 4 just aren't as emotional.
I remember at one point Amita was talking about how crucial it is that I take out this leader.
And I remember thinking "Uhhhh who the ♥♥♥♥ is this?"
You don't get any personal hatred for the antagonists like you did in Far Cry 3. In Far Cry 3, I genuenly HATED Buck, Vaas, Hoyt.
But with Far Cry 4, I just don't really feel as much as I really was hoping for.
In summary, if you're looking for the groundbreaking game that Far Cry 3 was, you're not going to find it here.
Don't get me wrong, its an AMAZING game.
But it's not Far Cry 3.

text:
As someone who has played countless hours of this game on Ouya, I'm SUPER excited this is finally on Steam!
Amazing Frog is a quirky-physics sandbox game. The amount of enjoyment you will get out of it will depend a lot on how much you can provide your own entertainment. There are trampolines, vehicles, cannons, trampolines, ramps, and other objects strewn throughout the world. It's a playground of items with near-limitless potential.
In the transition from Ouya they've made the world MUCH larger and removed the odd pricing scheme for level access, opting for a flat rate. I think $15 is more than fair for the amount of time you'll get out of this discovering items, screwing around with friends, and having a good time. The game doesn't bring much to the table if you're playing alone; playing with at least one other person is best.
My few disappointments are the lack of availability for weapons (there were many more readily available in the Ouya version), and that the game no longer appears to outline where the other players are on the map. On the Ouya version you would see an outline of the other players wherever they were on the map. The settings menu is SLIGHTLY confusing because when you choose "Fantastic" for graphics it appears to accept but reflects "Fast" in the menu anyway. I'd chalk that up to a glitch.
All-told, it's GREAT fun for local co-op and I'd recommend it to anyone that wants to have a great couple hours with friends just messing around.

Not a game for everyone. You have to be willing to move on and accept you can't solve a puzzle until you've gathered more information around the island.
This game will take some patience, but if you enjoy being stumped, I think this game offers a lot of really great logic puzzles that consistently build on top of each other. Some of the puzzles that depend on abstract concepts (like extracting information from environment art) can feel obtuse, especially in some cases if you are color blind.
The art and core mechanics of the game shine incredibly well. Without getting into spoiler territory, the implied story is great if you don't mind having a considerable number of loose ends. I believe the intention is to have thoughtful discussion with friends afterwards about the mechanics and the loose story.

This game is challenging, not just in that it is filled with difficult puzzles, but also in that it explores very subtle and complex thematic ideas about video games through its gameplay. If you are willing to listen closely to the things that are going on in the game (and this is pretty hard, because it almost never outright says them), then you are in for a mind-expanding experience.
Genuinely one of the most compelling games I've ever had the pleasure of playing.

There is a general dichotomy I have noticed when people talk about The Witness. There are people who adore the game, and there are people who hate it. There are people who view it as a pinnacle of the artform, and there are people who think it's pretentious garbage. Me? Personally? I find The Witness to be a brilliant game. But you might disagree.
The majority of The Witness is solving puzzles. A vast majority. They are good puzzles. They are thoroughly engaging and clever puzzles. Some of the twists on mechanics are outstanding and mindbending. Almost all the puzzles are designed in a way that make solving them impossible unless you understand the mechanics. They're the investment of the game, and they're truly fantastic. An amount of the puzzles, unfortunately, are designed in such a way that kind of throw colorblind people (in certain, specific areas) and tone deaf (or deaf people at all) people under the bus. Even if you aren't one of these, there is a possibility to get hung up because you don't pick up on what the designer wants you to pick up on, whether it be the perception of shapes, the perception of mechanics, or perception of the world. These, while often fun, put a lot of expectation on the player to perceive things like light and sound the same way as the designer, which is quite a burden for the player to bear. (Also, the ship puzzle sucks. You'll understand if you play it.)
Do you like puzzles? If you don't, do not play this game.
One thing I greatly appreciate about The Witness is how much of a learning experience it is. Many puzzles are based on rethinking mechanics you already thought you understood in completely different scenarios. In certain moments, I audibly exclaimed something like "Oh man!" at the new way I looked at things.
The other percentage of the experience consists of walking, and listening to audio tapes, and occasionally watching a video. The audio tapes are usually some thoughtful quote for you to chew on. The videos range from really interesting to... uncomfortable, honestly (four of them are neat, two of them are... just strange.) The Island itself (the location of the game) is colorful and beautiful. There are plenty of nice sights to see, and mystery to ponder, even if theres no real answer. It's a little boring, all of it, but it's pensive quiet time, and serves as a set for the secret second half of this game.
Because there's this other half to that percentage. I have a love-hate relationship with this half of the game.  Without spoiling anything, I will call them "secret puzzles". They are not necessary to complete the game, and serve (unfortunately?) no mechanical purpose other than gratification. A lot of them are easy to find, but many are so out of nowhere and convoluted that it feels more like a directionless scavenger hunt. It might be the case that these secretive puzzles are intended to bring together players outside of the game to trade secrets (a la Zelda on the NES, or PT), in which case, the game succeeded. It's likely that it's the case that these are part of a kind-of meta narrative (something that becomes evident when watching these videos in the game)And that being said, some of these secret puzzles are jaw-dropping, even if I couldn't sleuth them out on my own. They are creative and unique, evoking those "Oh man!" responses frequently. But there is still that dissonance.
The Witness is a good game. If you don't like puzzles, don't play it. If you do like puzzles, maybe play it.

Star Conflict - first impressions
TL/DR– FTP garage game, pew-pew in space with great graphics, you should definitely try Star Conflict.
If Eve & War Thunder had an arcade pwnage kid…
This is my first review of any game on Steam, and this is the first FTP game I have spent real money on. (… and not because I had to.)
Over the years I’ve played at lot of Space combat games; Eve, Elite (originally on my Spectrum48), Star Citizen, Freelancer etc so when I spotted Star Conflict on Steam FTP, I decided to give it a try… Glad I did.
The introductory tutorials show you the basics and give you some in-game resources as a reward, but as a noob, even a space vet such as myself, I was a bit lost in the first few gameplays as there is nothing to explain play styles, weapons, shiptypes, game types etc… it’s not rocket science but. Oh wait..
Anyways, I went to youtube and watched some tutorials … highly recommend this for all new players.
Apologies in advance for any errors in my explanations …
I’m not going to get into ships or combat tactics, but i did want to mention some other aspects of the game.
Gameplay & Progression (while not flying the ship)
In-game progression isn’t really explained very well so I made a few mistakes on what to spend my resources on… I’ll try and give you a basic understanding of what to expect so you can spend more wisely than I did.. If you've played WoT or WarThunder etc you'll understand the layout easily.
You have a fleet of ships, most of which need to be unlocked or purchased in sequence; you have up to 4 ships from your fleet in your ‘garage’ slots at any time (slots are also opened by progression).
Ships come in ranks 1 – 15 (plus the ‘secret’ top levels custom ships) – the rank of ships you have unlocked determines your number of slots in garage, ships available, game types available and crew abilities/bonuses.
There are multiple classes of player ships, based on 3 types on hull; interceptor, fighter and frigate.  Generally, frigates are the largest of the ships and are slow, whereas interceptors are the smallest, most manoeuvrable and quickest… (the semi capital destroyers have not yet been released)
There are 3 ‘sides’ (factions) to choose from, each has its own fleet ship tree and ship progression. You can unlock any of the ship trees regardless of which side you choose.
Whichever faction you choose will reward you with corporation vouchers which can be exchanged for weapons/equipment upgrades.
Each ship has a number of equipment slots; this allows for customisation to suit your own playstyle, and is an extremely important aspect of the game… a badly fit ship in the hands of a noob means you’re going to die, A LOT! (speaking from experience)
Completing tasks, PVE & PVP gives you credits, experience (synergy) and usually corporation vouchers.
Fit to a ship’s strengths and your playstyle… if you’ve played Eve, you will find the fitting options and tools to be basic … hover mouse over your ship for most stats, over equipment for their stats (including weapons) – AFAIK there are no direct comparison tools for fittings.
I’m not going to write much else about fittings, as although it’s not Eve, it’s still complex enough to say you’ll want to do a bit of research.
The game has obviously been though some changes, and ‘tiers’ are discussed/mentioned a lot on the forums and guides – references in-game seem to have been removed (replaced by rank), however ships, weapons and maps all  seem have legacy tiers… I’m guessing that the system used to work like the War Thunder tier system…
The results of this means that when combined with the poor inventory GUI the noob player has no idea when to upgrade stuff and will waste resources semi upgrading multiple instances of the same thing…
Weapons/equipment of a certain rank fit a range of ship ranks… e.g.  Weapon fits ranks 1-4 or 4-7… these ranges are not shown clearly anywhere on the ship…and there is crossover..
While this is not really a problem at lower ranks, beyond say rank 6 the ‘grind’ begins and you will be annoyed if you feel like you waste any resource…particularly gold.
I bought the premium scanner twice, and I still don’t have the size I want/need…(grumble) as I didn’t realise only the rank 15 premium scanner / hull fits rank 15 ships…
FTP
Early game is very much free to play and you will get a great flavour for free; if you do decide to spend and are new to the game, here are a few things for thought…
…the game is designed to encourage you to spend money; no bad thing really, if you like the game enough: buy something to support the devs.
Most of the game can be played entirely for free, however there is some epic grinding.
Grinding is just playing the game :-)
Premium ships must be bought in a rank sequence – while the ships are good, the weapons provided are basic so if you jump ranks you will be at a disadvantage until you can afford better equipment/weapons.
The level of gameplay difficulty increases significantly at ranks >4 - a noob in a premium on a rank 12 game is going to have problems.
There are incentives to reach certain ranks e.g. so you can participate in events like tournaments - premium ships allow you to jump right in.
mid ranked matches earn respectably…. As do premium ships – a tier 6 or 9 premium is a good way to earn in game resources once you’ve got a basic handle on things..for plenty of matches, make sure you're set to use any server in settings...
MMO/Social
I don’t really know too much about this aspect yet… there are corporations, I haven’t yet joined one yet so cant really comment if it adds much – but the social tools are woeful compared to Eve…
Open Space (Invasion) is relatively new to the game and it’s fun at first (difficult unless you have a fast high rank inte, or friends or both) but there’s not too much depth to it yet..
Non-consensual PVP is available outside of the safe systems – pirating is a thing.
From what I understand to have any meaningful social interaction  / squad play you need to get on TeamSpeak.
English type chat is usually responsive to questions and inoffensive (compared to LOL or DOTA2 etc.), ‘local’ seems unused.
Conclusions
The combat is fast and engaging, the graphics are very nice… seems to be plenty of gameplay opportunities…
I really like Star Conflict so far and I’ve had a lot of fun over the holidays. I installed just before Xmas and decided to spend much of my steam sale budget on this as I ended up playing it most…
If you like the gameplay the grind is bearable, and if you play it enough for free to get to the grind… treat yourself and support the game by making a purchase..
It’s not an MMO like Eve, and I don’t think it will ever be. But it is one of the most fun space pew pew games I have played… so many ‘splosions!
If you got here; thanks for reading I hope this has been of interest / useful… say hi if you see me ingame..

This is one of the few games I've happily purchased on both Steam and iOS. It's a great mix of CCG and empire-building type of game. From a CCG standpoint, you essentially play in a draft format, so every game feels fresh - you aren't just facing (or using) the same prebuilt decks over and over, which is what (for me) makes typical CCGs so boring after a while. From an empire-building standpoint, you have to manage and balance your resources, armies, defense and culture. Like the description says, it takes what is normally a 10 hour type game and turns it into a 10 minute experience. I personally like this because losing here doesn't feel like I've wasted a whole day on it ... just start another game and move on. Definitely feels a lot deeper strategically than any other CCG I've played. I recommend at least watching some YouTube videos to see if you might like this game.
The ONLY downside for me, which is kind of minor, is that once you unlock everything, there isn't anything to spend coins on, so the daily quests seem a little unnecessary at that point. Maybe there will be some more content later to spend those coins on.

Though the Singleplayer was great, Loadouts kinda killed the Multiplayer's feel as well as a few other niggles but that's for a different review. The no class feel of this game opens up real map control. Weapon's feel balanced right an over all emphasize map control. You really don't wanna let the enemy team over the Cerberous spawn too much.
Speaking of spawns, I love how in Team Assault weapon spawns are for each individual player which helps to avoid 'stealing' weapons from each other
2. THE COMBAT! It's fast. It's in your face. There's Gibs flying everywhere, explosions left right and centre and there's no remorse in this brutally fast paced shooter. As mentioned before, each weapon feels balanced just right and in the hands of a skilled player each gun has the ability to really decimate an enemy. Whether it's the balanced RoF and Damage of the Violator, the movement concealing billow of flames let out by the Dragoneer or the dealy rockets fired from the Cerberous, each gun has it's own style of gameplay and it's well worth learning how they all function
3. THE VISUALS! Really easy to identify a target without loosing environment detail. The game looks beautiful in any graphics setting and...
4. IT RUNS BLOODY WELL! I have tried this on both a gaming PC on ultra and on a  year old potato. I can get 30-50 FPS on the 6 year old potato on minimum settings in 720p and the frames stay nice and consistent
And finally..... 5. THE BASE GAME IS FREE TO PLAY SO TRY IT! GET YOUR FRIENDS TO TRY IT! FRAG LIKE IT'S 1999!

As someone who has played countless hours of this game on Ouya, I'm SUPER excited this is finally on Steam!
Amazing Frog is a quirky-physics sandbox game. The amount of enjoyment you will get out of it will depend a lot on how much you can provide your own entertainment. There are trampolines, vehicles, cannons, trampolines, ramps, and other objects strewn throughout the world. It's a playground of items with near-limitless potential.
In the transition from Ouya they've made the world MUCH larger and removed the odd pricing scheme for level access, opting for a flat rate. I think $15 is more than fair for the amount of time you'll get out of this discovering items, screwing around with friends, and having a good time. The game doesn't bring much to the table if you're playing alone; playing with at least one other person is best.
My few disappointments are the lack of availability for weapons (there were many more readily available in the Ouya version), and that the game no longer appears to outline where the other players are on the map. On the Ouya version you would see an outline of the other players wherever they were on the map. The settings menu is SLIGHTLY confusing because when you choose "Fantastic" for graphics it appears to accept but reflects "Fast" in the menu anyway. I'd chalk that up to a glitch.
All-told, it's GREAT fun for local co-op and I'd recommend it to anyone that wants to have a great couple hours with friends just messing around.

VA-11 Hall-A is a super charming VN-type game - light on gameplay, big on story. I recommend this game based on its two biggest strengths, the characters and the atmosphere. The characters are well-rounded and unique, each with their own personal stories, backgrounds, and struggles. You learn more about them as any bartender would, glimpsing details of their lives as they chat with you across a bar counter.
On that note, I found the atmosphere in VA-11 Hall-A very effective. Between the catchy, varied music and the cute retro visuals, it's easy to sit back and get lost in the story. The gameplay is very light; mixing drinks with the help of a recipe book is the main source of interaction. Sometimes you'll make drinks to order, other times you'll have a little flexibility based on the situation; this is your main method of influencing the story in lieu of a conversation system. Personally, I found this immersive - mixing drinks doesn't break up the story like a conversation system would, instead letting you get more invested into the bartender role and the world at large. If you prefer major choices in your VNs, however, you might prefer something else; the story in VA-11 Hall-A is largely linear.
Tl;dr Overall, I found VA-11 Hall-A extremely charming and well worth the price. The characters are lovely and the atmosphere is fantastic, so if you like the look of it and enjoy VNs then go ahead and grab it - you won't be sorry.

Brilliant, action-packed space shooter with micro-warp drives, lasers, rockets, shield management, cloaking devices and stealth disrupters... so many cool things. It even has free roam mode where you can travel between space stations, fight with pirates or aliens and enjoy vistas with distant cargo ships slowly cruising to its destinations [you can attack it and loot it ;)].
Core gameplay are team-based PvP battles and PvE missions. Game offers multiple categories of ships in many flavors, customized with weapons, special equipment, ammunition and of course cosmetic details of your liking.
Thing i enjoyed the most is the way how game is balanced and how every ship plays different role in the game. For every game you can prepare 3 ships and it's up to you to use this set wisely - ships counter each other in rock-paper-shotgun way yet skilled pilot can destroy stronger ship piloted by newbie. Matches are balanced by the tier of the ship so you wont be outgunned and if you want to introduce this game to your friends you can play with them - just switch back to your old, rusty starter-ship and have fun together.
Game offers shop with premium currency but there is no p2w in any form. You can buy special ships - but these are your usual ships with different looks and config of modules. And still you can earn premium currency while playing the game and purchase these ships.
You can buy ammo with extra damage output or boosters - but these cost in-game currency and ammo is often found in loot after the game - everyone have it and its up to you if you use it in PvP or save it for PvE [which is really hard if you fly solo].
Ah yes, after PvP matches winning team secures battlefield and gather loot - you can find new schematics for crafting, rare components, upgrades, ammo, usueless junk etc. Same things you can find in PvE missions and while roaming open world.
Visuals and audio are great, arcade'y feel of piloting ships is perfect and the way warp drive works should be role model for every space combat game.
Incredible stunts you can perform with your team could be scenarios for movies - sniping frigate emerges from the shadow of asteroid and vaporizes shielding frigate of enemies, soon afterward your teams interceptor decloacks behind enemy captain and launches everything he has on board resulting in quick weapon overheat and tonz of damage to the target. Unfortunately captain realizes his situation and activates shield boosters to save himself. This is suicide attack anyway so interceptor continues assault while being surrounded by captains guards and having his cloak on cooldown - hectic evasive maneuvers and shield boosters buy him some time to reload rockets, cool down weapons and perform finishing strike on fleeing captain, then engages warp drive to catapult himself to the border of the map wile enemy rockets are already locked on him and try to follow him despite increasing distance. Really, plays like that happen and you feel sweat on your back when you are in the middle of the action.
I mentioned 'stunts with team'. Yes, game has great community. Maybe because all 12yo are more into DoTA and CS:GO than space shooters, but still there are no griefers or haters in chat [in general ;)]. You get loot from the match only if you win it so its up to everyone to do his best. Many player are mature enough to play for the team and pick ship which is not typical DPS but pick support frigates or tanks instead. These roles require more skills to operate it's modules so it's natural that newbies start with DPS and avoid advanced ships.
Every time i play it i have great fun and i keep uninstalling this game to save myself from being totally absorbed by this single production ;)

Two sisters reunite for a splendid wedding, a day of love and joy. However, evil lurks around the corner as the bride to be, Lilly, is kidnapped. It’s up to her twin sister to set things right but she soon uncovers a world of corruption and evil magic.
is a shining example of what a hidden item game should be, it has an engaging story with interesting characters as well as very good gameplay. One of the earlier games of this genre that I played, I found it very enjoyable and happily played it two more times for the sake of this review.
One of the good parts of this title is the story, the game wastes no time thrusting you into the action as Lilly is kidnapped by a wild bear very earlier on. The first half of the game is spent trying to find her and meeting new characters. Things soon begin to change when you get closer to finding Lilly who has been taken to an abandoned castle. Pieces of the puzzle come together but before the mystery can be solved you become the enemy as dark magic works to keep you away from your sister. The story is told mostly in present day, however there also flashbacks to twenty-five years ago when things started and the dark magic of the Abyss began to control the chess pieces. There is also a beautiful yet tragic love story woven into everything as well as the heart warming tale of sisterly love.
The game is a traditional point and click adventure with the main focus being on hidden object scenes and puzzles. Everything is completely mouse-controlled as you interact with people and objects, you also have an inventory system to collect useful tools. The hidden object scenes are a mix of the traditional list type where you’re given a written list of items to find in the scene as well ones where the list of items are represented in pictures. I enjoyed the variety this added to the gameplay as it kept each scene fresh since you had to visit some more than once. The game also offers a mahjong mini game that you play as an alternative to the hidden object scenes. I didn’t like this feature since it sort of defeats the purpose of the game and also it forces you to play the game twice if you want to collect all of the achievements since two are connected to playing mahjong. The puzzles are not too difficult but they offer a good challenge. One of my favorites involved having to match your makeup to Lilly’s, it was a bit of silly fun and a nice break from the usual puzzles.
The game graphics are very high quality. All of the scenes are beautifully done and most objects are not too hard to see if you have bad vision. The characters move smoothly when there is animation as well and their models were very well done. The game has full voice acting and it’s very good quality helping players to stay immersed in the game. The music and sound effects are top notch, I can’t think of any complaints at all.
is a must-play for fans of hidden object games new and old. This game helped me get into this genre and it is still a great play through to this day; you also are given a cute kitten sidekick to help so that was instant plus for me. The title offers Steam achievements as well as trading cards, there also collectables in the game to find. You’re also given a bonus chapter complete that ties up the story well. It’s well worth the asking price but is often bundled or on sale so if you’re hesitating don’t miss your chance to add this to your library, you won’t be disappointed.

If there is a scale for measuring all hidden-object-point-and-click games ranging from 1 to 10, with 1 being excruciatingly boring and 10 being the most amazing game there is, this game would fall exactly onto a 5: Its the perfect blend of story and gameplay that’s interesting enough to keep you going until you finish, but also blend enough that at times you might get bored while playing and quit and go do something else for a while.
This game has all the issues you would usually associate with hidden-object games; examples include weak or no protagonist development and a predictable and unexciting storyline. But if its really story or interesting character you are looking for, then hidden-object games are probably not the best place to look for them anyways.
However, if you look past all those problems, as a hidden object game this game is actually quite enjoyable.  The puzzles were nice and fun (I thoroughly enjoyed some of them and one of them actually took me a while to crack), the artwork is aesthetically pleasing, and the animation is fluid enough to connect scenes together.
So if you like puzzles, don’t really mind playing hidden-object games over and over again and is content with a predictable story, then this game is good enough to worth buying it and playing it.
Oh also a final note on the game, if you do end up playing it, play it on expert mode, its not difficult at all and I have always found that the simple mode gives wayyyy too much hints and pretty much ruins all the fun.
p.s There are so many plot holes in the story that it’s almost comical if you actually stop and really think about it.

I like a challenge, but this is not challenging nor does it involve any strategy when a player has no chance of winning. Trying to get packs is very grindy as you get few gold (20 mostly - you pick a chest out of something like 30 chests with only a small few being 30, and one 50, with rest 20 - higher diffioculty only increases this marginally) for a card pack that cost 100 and only contains 3 cards. You get more if you win, but again the AI and constant losing. So expect a great amount of grinding. You get to choose portraits that have up to 3 pre-selected cards that have a chance to provide your choice of card as one of the cards you can buy with resources during the duel. However, this is also a grind as in order to unlock the 3 slots, you must aquire multiple portraits of the same one from card packs. It takes 3 or more to unlock so you continue to grind since each pack only gives you 3 cards. Even if the game only gives you cards you don't already have, its still a freaking grind. The portrait feature again doesn't seem useful as its only random if at all when it activates. The game has potential but could use better, more realistic AI and a better reward system for new players to get more card packs early (not asking for all cards here, just reduce the grind). The portrait system would be better if when it activated provided your card choice that didn't cost resources. However, the poor AI mechanic is what mostly ruined it for me. Yes it has multiplayer, but that is something I never do for specific reasons. If your on the fence, buy it when its on sale. If you plan to play multiplayer, you might have a better experience. I just can't recommend for the single player experience.

I waited for and followed the development of The Witness from the day of its reveal to release day. So many years of anticipation... Will it be as good as Braid? As rewarding, cute, memorable, replayable?
I think the answer is yes. With a stunningly beautiful word, puzzles often fun to solve, and a myserious story with an entertaining twist, I feel as though The Witness hit every mark dead on based on Blow's vision.
So let's talk about what *does'nt* work before talking about what *does*, because the former list is much smaller than the latter. I will also include what I feel to be a few misconceptions about the game that other people have, and I had at one point. I'll use lists as much as possible because otherwise I'd be writing a coverstory and not a review... :]
What to look out for --
Patience is a virtue, and a core mechanic of this game. In your first playthrough, expect to be stumped every so often even as a seasoned puzzle-solver.
The world includes several "trick-question" puzzles, meaning, they appear to break rules, and the solution will only be apparent after either the puzzle is solved, or extensive periods of time are spent looking for it. While this is not a flaw of puzzle design in and of itself, many people claim these puzzles are "unfair." However, to them I must explain that this is not a child's puzzle game, and the greatest satisfaction will eventually come to you once you solve the trickiest puzzles. Calling trick-question puzzles "unfair" is merely a testament to ones impatient or closed mind. (sorry)
NOTE: I do believe there is about 1 trick-question puzzle which the solution actually does physically break the rules, but it was one of the first ones I completed so I can't confirm this. If this is true then it is *bad*.
ANOTHER NOTE: *difficult* or *obscured* puzzles are not trick-question puzzles. They prove a challenge for a reason: to be a challenging or interesting puzzle. Embrace the world, if you are seasoned puzzle-solver you will work through it without too much brainache. ;]
Many puzzles will be presented in a repeated fashion, both as a way to progress through levels, and as a tutorial for each puzzle rule. While tutorials help us to understand each rule, the repetition of puzzles does get to be overwhelming in certain areas. (The swamp and the Treehouse). Some areas (such as the Sun Temple or the Greenhouse) have less repetition, and more variation in the solution of puzzles, while incorperating the rules of the area. But, every single area *does* have *much* repetition, and as a puzzle-solver, that will often unmotivate me to progress in an area. With this said, there is always an insentive to pushing through just a little farther, so it will *slightly* nullify the monotony.
Some people complain about the bits of dialogue spread around the world to be purely negative, in that they could be misleading the player into connecting them to the story (which they do not). However, while this is potentially true, the point of these dialogues are to be entertaining, refreshening, to give the player another thing to look forward to finding, and to just invoke some genuine thought into the player. No, they do not connect to the story. Should you be expecting them to or be upset that they don't? I'm inclined to say no. They give all that I mentioned above, and take away nothing from the world or experience.
Someone expecting a super rich, constantly developing story has probably not embraced or played vague games such as Dark Souls, Fez, Titan Souls, etc. as The Witness is not a world with puzzles in it, it is a world that IS a puzzle, following the vision of Blow.
However, speaking of story, there is one. And it's quite a mysterious one, to the point where I often forgot about the idea of a story while playing, and just enjoyed the world for what it was, knowing that one day the point of these vague signs the game is giving to me will be revealed in the end.
Quick negative: Two of the puzzle rules are immensely vague. The more important one is less vague, but I didn't find the tutorial adequate in teaching it to me which was really disheartening. However, I was able with enough patience to understand it and I completed each puzzle as I would any other. It wasn't quite as satisfying to figure it out though because of how confusing it was at first. I think it was the only rule that actually caused me frustration when I didn't understand it.
So, while theres still much more to say about the potential negatives of the game, I should wrap that up there. As you can see, my personal opinion sees most of the 'negatives' as misunderstood positives. I think the best way to enjoy this game is to really really bring out your patience, use all your little puzzle solving skills you know, and really just enjoy being in the amazingly precice and intricate world of The Witness.
A quick list of a few notable PROs:
-Beautiful world
-Incredibly fun environmental puzzles (Most entertaining rule)
-Polethora of varied puzzles
-**Pretty much** all puzzles will be solved with enough patience and effort. Please don't use google. NOT SATISFYING.
-Dialogue scattered around the world is calming, invocative, and gets me thinking.
-Story unfolds at the end, for those who want to know the secret behind the island.
-Puzzles generally quite satisfying yet will often provide a fun yet difficult challenge.
-Fun to solve puzzles with friends!
A few CONs not mentioned before:
-Zero zero zero progression of story until the end. Only a problem if you lose your patience though. Just think of it as the dessert after you go through eating all your veggies.
-Can be sluggish at times to navigate the world either on land or water.
-"Boat" puzzles will have you annoyingly going back and forth on the water. Not essential but annoying for completionists and motion-sick people like myself.
-Movies within the game are an unessential puzzle/ content. For completionists, this will be a nightmare as these movies will take up to several hours before presenting a puzzle to you. This is also a PRO, though, because the movies I found quite relaxing and interesting. Not for everyone.
-Taking long breaks from the game is punishing, because rules are sometimes specific and will take time to re-acclimate yourself to them. I recommend writing down the rules somewhere as you learn them. Also helpful because 2 areas of the game incorperate every puzzle rule into them. (Please don't google things... It's not worth it! This is a test of your skill and determination, not how fast can you finish your exam or find out whats at the end.)
Great indie game, interesting and complex for what you pay. Great buy if you're looking for something relaxing but still challenging enough.

This game is right on par with Portal 2 and Talos Principle and is without a doubt one of the best games released to date, not to mention the best game of 2016 (I'm 39 and gaming since 1995, obviously, this is all my opinion only).
Now, I didn't think that after the first few hours of the game, even though I was hooked badly by then. You see, it is layered. You discover those layers gradually. It takes time. I discovered the second (?) layer only 9 hours in, I think.
Narrative wise, it's, well, it's problematic. It will throw everything at you, - quotes from middle ages monks, budhists, famous scientists. It will also juxtapose profound insights by notable intellecutals with the complete new age nonsense and will let you see the truth. Except it won't. It will present everything as equal.
I have no doubt it can improve somebody's perspective on the world, but it may equally easily do the opposite. Relativity of thought is a very poisonous idea that contributes to global warming, spread of nonsensic conspiracies, beliefs in pseudosciences or extreme polytical movements, etc. And that's absolutely the only shortcoming this otherwise monumental piece of work has.
This is one of those things that people will remember after hundreds of years as a true classic and a milestone, even though the lesson it teaches is a very questionable one to say the least.

Furi is a third person action game that revolves entirely around a series of bosses as you fight for your freedom. You do not level up, upgrade weapons or gear and in fact your move set never changes. What does change is your skill at playing the game and by the end you'll have grown a lot as you face the different challenges.
What this game does well is that each fight prepares you for the next one, and each one changes up the formula each fight to teach you something new. So while your attacks stay the same your reaction time and the amount of different attacks the game throws at you to dodge and counter constantly grows. By the end you'll be needing to use everything you've learned to survive.
Though it may sound simple that you have one move set and two weapons there is a depth to the combat and once you learn advanced ways to power up your moves and read bosses you'll find faster ways to dish out damage, provided you can pull it off.
The game is tough, but fair. Each boss fight typically has 6 stages to them while you have only 3 continues before you have to restart the fight. However, parrying attacks restores health and if you beat a stage of a boss without losing all your health you gain another continue. The game rewards playing well and learning patterns.
All of this to not even mention the fantastic soundtrack which is well worth checking out and is a great compliment to the fights, with each fight and track being memorable.
It's not a perfect game but any gripe I had was very minor. When you walk through each level you have commentary from an NPC about the upcoming fight and while you can directly control your character its better to just let the game auto-walk for you. For one you can then focus on the dialogue and environment, but also Furi's movement animations outside combat can look stiff and its better left automated. In addition throughout levels or during fights sometimes the music very obviously cuts out as it switches between different versions of the song to accompany the different stages of the fight which while not game breaking is just a slight detraction on the otherwise great presentation.
This game isn't for everyone and it is quite a challenge but those who stick with it will have a memorable experience.
Pros:
+Great fights that are unique and continually add new twists
+Simple but deep combat that is easy to pick up but hard to master
+Awesome soundtrack
+Great visual style (character designs by Afro Samurai's creator Takashi Okazaki)
Cons:
-Music awkwardly switches sometimes in levels/combat
-The kickstarter didn't get fully funded :c
-There's really not many cons unless you are put off by a challenge

This game has bad graphics. I can live with that. This game has awful translations. It's usually kind of funny and not game breaking. The one thing that absolutely ruins this game is the hatching system. You want to hatch a digimon outside of the tutorial? You better be ready to cough up some real money.
Basically, in order to hatch a new digimon you have to grind on it's rookie form until it drops an egg. This can take anywhere from 10 minutes to 11 hours of grinding, or you can buy an egg in the cash shop for $7. Next you have to gather a certain kind of data (beast, bird, insect, devil, etc.). Once you have an egg you need to use DATA to increase it's 'level' by 1. An egg has to be level 3 to hatch but can be leveled up to 5 for a stronger version.
Now, to 'level' up an egg it takes a certain amount of DATA. Renamon takes 10 DATA pre try. Yes, TRY. Every time you attempt to raise an egg's level it has a chance to fail. It also has a chance to erase all progress and delete the egg. That's right, you can lose all your progress while trying to hatch an egg! Also, DATA isn't exactly easy to get. Far Cry 4 is one of those games that people often complain about when they say "Developers are too lazy to make another game, so they just take the old game and tweak it a bit, make a new map, then throw it out the door for $60 + a season pass." To that I say: You're absolutely right. This game is Far Cry 3 with a skin painted over it. Unfortunately, it is a less polished game.

When a game has a bunch of mcguffins lying around, I will spend as much time as I need to getting all of them. I have completed many collectathons and no other game has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off more than Far Cry 4. For one, the rewards for collecting every poster (150), masks of yalung (55), and journals/letters (20 a piece) are worthless. Seriously, you spend a few hours destroying all the masks in the game only to get "unlimited guns for hire tokens", which are actually useless because the game is easy. Anyways, there were 3 things preventing me from getting 100%. First off, the Royal Cargo apparently stops appearing when you take all the outposts. I only collected 2 and I'd have to reset every outpost in order to get 1 single Royal Cargo. Second, the Bushman rifle requires you to get level 10 in the arena. So I was actually very hesitent to buy this one, because Magic 2013 felt pretty much the same as 2012 except with a few more decks, some bells and whistles thrown in, and a clunkier interface. But when 2014 went on sale, I gave in and bought it though I had low expectations. I never thought I'd be pleasently surprised by how much it has -actually- improved.
Firstly, I simply cannot gush enough about the implementation of the player into the storyline. Before, you just fought all of these planeswalkers without any real reason... you really didn't  have a connection to them whatsoever, you followed -their- storyline without having one of your own. The game is a bit more immersive in that it actually includes you in the storyline. In the first duel you have with Chandra, she speaks to -you-, the player, and the information she gives decides your journey further.
The interface has cleaned up a lot: it's more streamlined and much less clunky. The menus are easier to use and cleaner. You can pick the lands you play for multi-colored cards, which is a nice addition. In battle, the phases bar look cleaner as well.
Graphics-wise, the cut-scenes were a little off. I preferred the method they've always used in the past: still figures and moving backgrounds. This time, some parts are animated and they look a little sloppy, as if they were created in the 90s. But it's not a huge deal. Some cards are animated, which is a really cool effect.
Other than that, you can expect the usual fair: new decks, new avatars, new game modes, etc. I've never felt any of the other games were comparable to the first PC Magic game, but this one I feel is the new standard.

Ever wanted to know if you'd survive a war if it started tomorrow? This game will test that thinking ability.
Unlike other survival games, here your choices matter and not just gameplay-wise but to yourself as a human. How? Simple. Would you steal food and medicine from an old couple living on the outskirts of the city and leave them to starve or are you going to risk raiding a militant warehouse where not only do you have to be stealthy and tactical to single-handedly kill the militants and get the supplies you need all the while racing against time and potentially permanent death if you get hasty?
The choice is yours and it's not only one or the other, you could have many choices at one moment or none at all in another. What kind of a person would you be to survive a war? Do you have the ability to sustain yourself till the war is over? Are you able to defend yourself from threats at night?
So many different elements in the game. All working perfectly to provide a greatly unique experience that many of us don't know. With the addition of Stories Mode and new DLC stories that the devs will be adding in the future, this game has become a tool to portray unique stories of people who have suffered war.
We have read about war experiences, watched documentaries/movies about them. Now it's time to play them and experience them at our own individual pace.

A great game about tank skirmishing in 80's-version-of-the-future-worlds. The player goes up against a giant eyeball overlord along with men from a resistance movement. Together they fight past vast amounts of enemy vehicles such as tanks, artillery, and even goddamn bombers.
The story is more or less just there so people won't complain about lack of a story, and the read-only dialogue is laughably bad at times, but the game contains a lot of fun to be had and some really unexpected twists.
Once you beat the campaign, you can test your strength in the "skirmish" mode, where you have 20 minutes to kill as many enemies, of all types, as possible, and try not to die in the process.
However, there are a few downsides to this game:
This game is one of a two-part series, and there is a Tank Universal 2 in the works. Hopefully we see some modernization in it, I would absolutely love to skirmish with real players.
Overall, I really like this game, and definately recommend it, but know that replayability is extremely limited and there is no multiplayer.

I don't recommend Circuits, but it's probably because I am not the real target audience for this game. The core of the game revolves around listening to a song and then putting the samples into place to re-create the song that is given to you. I have to give credit to the developers for slowly easing you into the difficulty by adding different mechanics throughout the game and it seems to be intending for you to get an idea of how music is created in different programs. They've even added their own music composition software, Circuits Composer, to allow for a sandbox mode to play with the samples they give you in game to create your own songs. The fact that they included this with the core game and not as an additional purchase is definitely a plus.
However, the reason I do not recommend it is because I come from a background of working in music composition and radio where I have experience working with this software already. Circuits almost functions better as teaching software for programs like Fruity Loops and Audacity. For me, Circuits was nothing more than a slog of listening a few times to determine where the samples belong and then dropping them into place which became very tedious very quickly. If you're interested in an introduction to music production through a UI that builds in difficulty, you'll eventually find yourself working in something similar to what many producers use in studios today. This is the real purpose of this game, which I do not think is well described. If you already have knowledge of how production software works, Circuits is probably not the game for you.

There's no going around murdering people as a super cyborg or traveling into space with a crew or taking down huge corporations here. Just you, Jill, Bartending, and all of the conversations, back and forths, and stories that come along with it.
This isn't a game for everyone and it is mostly a Visual Novel (Lots of reading with a little bit of "Mixology" inbetween) but if the setting and type of game interests you, I wouldn't hesitate for a moment to recommend that you buy and experience this wonderful piece of what I can only call... Life.
Oh also! The music is absolutely incredible and enhances the atmosphere by leaps and bounds.

LEGO Harry Potter: Years 1-4 is yet another LEGO game. This time riding on the first four Harry Potter movies. Released in 2010, made by Traveller's Tales, published by Warner Bros. It also came out for Xbox 360, PS3, Wii, NDS, PSP and iOS.
Out of ports the only notable ones are NDS, PSP and iOS ones. It's a different game, more like isometric exploration of small levels where you do quests for characters. While collecting studs.
Technically, this PC version is known to be a pretty badly done. Actually, this game is full of glitches on any platforms. You can google out a whole list of them. It actually might be useful to check one out, to know what to avoid.
Personally, I had no problems with this game. But I didn't try to 100% it anyway. I only once had trouble with making game recognise controller, so I had to restart PC. And it crashed once.
But there are just way too many reposts of real nasty glitches. Some can't make it start without crash. Other experienced losing a save! And many also have game freezing in Year 3 on Dark Tower level when activating one of the gargoyles that shoot fire. I didn't had trouble, but I played this stage only once. But the solution seem to indiacate that it something to do with rendering dynamic light. You either activate it off-screen or change config file of a game. Just check on guides.
As for gameplay itself, it's yet another Traveller's Tales lego game. It's like lego game, but with all stuff that lego sequels get. Be casual, have infinite lives, collect-a-thon, do simple puzzles. It's getting stale and writing Steam reviews on them is getting stale too.
Actually, well, this time is different, because Harry Potter is the franchise I am familar with and love. Read books, you see. And then 50 years later I will be sitting with my kids and explain them how awesome it was. And then I will realize that everybody read books too and Warner is still making money with more Harry Potter stuff.
Plot isn't all that changed. Lego figures still don't speak. So it's recommended to watch movies first, really. Well, okay, plot was changed a bit so there is always at least two characters to control at any time, so you can always have fun with a friend.
And actually, I like this LEGO iteration. There are almost no annoying fights with respawning enemies which is a huge plus in these earlier LEGO games. It's more puzzle focused than that. I also actually laughed a few times. The world here is much more lively, combining levels and hub around pretty nice. You can even get another "collectable" - "Student in peril". Help somebody out of sticky situation and feel good about it. No more ledge jumping, more of spell-choosing and aiming. It also felt like I was restricted from less stuff in Story Mode than in previous LEGO games, you can get more stuff the first time around with what is given to you.
Protip: To destroy the monster books, you have to come close and press Tag button for some reason.
Eh. It's nice. For me this whole Lego franchise got stale, as I tried to beat it in chronological order and beat Star Wars, two Indiana and the first Batman. But for those who didn't play much of Lego games this one will be nice. Actually, looking at it again, it is good as part of franchise too, as I realize that I had less frustration due to Lego Harry Potter having less respawning enemies. But watch out for all the glitches!

This game is not difficult to understand. It's not overly complex, even with all the iconography. However, this game is very deep! There's a lot to consider in between each turn and it's open-faced drafting system.
Each round you'll 'buy' eight cards, but from round 1's cards, your next rounds' first four cards are chosen randomly from the eight cards you just finished using in the previous round. So you need to adapt a strategy every round. Any resources you build become future discounts for you while they also become taxes against opponent, if they take a card aligned with those resources.
Some cards combo specifically with the next card you buy, and your opponent will know and see it. Do you bluff the next buy? Do you instead choose the card you think your opponent will want, or do you choose the card that gives you an edge in combat? Maybe that victory point card is too good to pass up?

AoR is deceptively simply - all you do is pick from one of four cards. Eight picks is a round, four rounds is a game. That's it. 10 minutes per game.
Behind that simplicity of gameplay is a cleverly designed, exquisitely well-balanced, damn fun little game. You can get the hand of it in 20 minutes, but appreciated the full interplay of the cards and game dynamics takes a bit longer. Still, after 10 hours I felt confident and was winning more than half my games against other players.
Part of the genius of the game is that, while you can guarantee you will draw up to 3 specific cards, in general each game will have very different start conditions and card draws. You can design a strategy around a particular horse cards, for instance (there's a nice little strategy around the Four Horsemen card that I enjoy), but if you don't luck out and pull horses in as a resource at some point, your strategy just won't work. Fortunately, that's not the end of it. If you are flexible and quick on your feet, you'll cobble together a new strategy on the fly, and can still pull out a win, even without a single horse.
The point is that you can plan a strategy, but often it goes out the window quickly and it can became a mad, seesaw contest that neither opponent is sure of until the very last card! Of course, routs are possible, but even as a intermediate player against seasoned opponents, games are often very interesting right through the last round.
There's nothing quite as a satisfying as pulling off a victory in the last round, after trailing in the first three. It happens.
There are plenty of things the game needs to develop into. Alliances are rudimentary, there is no pre-game chat forum, and no in-game chat (aside from about 8 scripted one or two-word messages). There is no way to spend money you accumulate after you have all the cards (that's about 15 hours of game play). Graphics could be improved, there are only 6 campaign missions. But all that will come if the game is a modest commercial success, I'm sure.
All in all, at $10 this is a total bargain. I'm getting far more enjoyment out of it than I did the $60 I paid for Civ VI, which I hardly played. Unlike Civ series, this game is laser-like in its design simplicity, has a well done AI opponent, is full of surprises and is just a delight to play.

This game is pretty difficult and I like it.
This game is all about combat, nothing more. In the first fight you learn everything you need for all the others, yet you need to adapt and relearn every new boss. The different attackstyles and patterns keep you on your toes and every boss needs to be mastered completely new. The athmosphere is amazing and so is the music.
But that's not the only thing you'll get. Once you beat the game you unlock Furier Difficulty, which is basically hard mode. The pattern and attacks of each boss change and you need to remaster everything you've learned so far. You need to react faster and become a better player in general. It's amazing and thrilling if you like difficult games.
But once you get good at it, I find it too forgiving. The game has a rating system that rates you depending on how fast you've beaten the boss and how many times you've been hit. "S" is the best rating, yet I got it in the Story Run in Furier Difficulty with about 150 hits, which is miserable in my opinion; it could be way lower. I was surprised when the game told me that my run was worthy of the best rank. It was literally my second run. Of course I got the worst rating in my first run, but that I got the best in the second run was very surprising. The game is very forgiving for small mistakes.
But my biggest complaint about the game is that there is no Speedrun Mode for the Furier Difficulty. I've beaten the game multiple times and wanted to play the Speedrun Mode at the very last. Thus I got very experienced in it. I thought the Speedrun Mode is the hardest thing this game has to offer, because you will battle each boss one after each other without story or anything else. I was dissapointed that the Speedrun Mode was only available in easy and not in furier. If the developer is still updating this game, then I wish for a more difficult Speedrun Mode.
In a nutshell, this game is amazingly difficult and a must play for everyone who likes hard games. But once you play it many many times and you become good at it, it starts to become too easy. I expected to recieve good ratings for a perfect run, not a mediocre one. Also the Speedrun Mode is not available in Furier Difficulty, which is really dissapointing.

Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride is a nice and cute point and click adventure game. It isn't really one of my favorite games, and I probably won't replay it, but there is nothing directly bad about it, and it certainly isn’t among any of the games I dislike. It is worth the money, and I don’t regret buying or playing it. I will recommend it for anyone that likes the old kinds of tales (fairy tales, sagas, legends, moral stories), as it gave me that kind of vibe.
I don't understand the choice of making the game in first person. The character has a backstory, voice actor, and no dialogue options. And through the game we see what she looks like. Personally I would have preferred the game in third person, but then again I almost always prefer third person. Doesn't really affect my recommendation of the game, as first or third person is more of a preference. But while I can see the appeal for shooters and games where your character is a blank slate, I don’t think it matches for an adventure game.
The story is nice and very easy to follow, but still manages to have some twists along the way, that I didn’t see coming from the start. That being said… I felt it was a bit too dramatic at times for the gameplay and puzzle solving. Being point and click and relying on puzzle solving invites for a more thoughtful and calculating approach, which doesn’t really match well with a story that presents characters with immediate danger and side characters trying to make you hurry. But most of the puzzles were fun.
As for the characters themselves. Like I said it felt very much like the old kinds of tales, so the characters aren’t really all that deep or interesting to me, BUT I don’t feel they are meant to be. The way I see it, it is a type of story where the characters are meant to be quickly identifiable, keeping the focus on the events and enchanting tale rather than the characters experiencing them.

When you have a medic going to pick up ore while people are dying instead of making medical supplies, you know there is an issue. Also, when a unit is working on a task or replenishing a certain stat, they just randomly decide to stop for no reason and go do something else. No explanation, and often with no specific direction.
Also, it seems like unit aquisition is very arbitrary and random. I understand that the game requires you to adjust the percentages for an ideal balance, but with no idea when a future colony ship is coming nor what class it might contain, it's almost impossible to properly strategize when reacting to disasters. I had a meteor slip through my laser network and hit a sleeping quarters where most of my biologists were asleep in bunks. All dead. My 85 person colony starved in 2-3 game days. I couldn't give my remaining biolgists accurate instructions to maintain food production.
Not to nitpick but the UI really needs some work and the camera system is a little wonky. I could get over some the camera issues but having to page through UI menus each time in order to set threat alerts or even find out how much of a resource I have just feels so unwieldy. A resource overlay seems like an easy fix as well as a hotkey system.
I'd really love to give this a thumbs up. I really would. This could be such a great game with a great premise.

10+ hours review
-------------
The game looks nice. It's a lightweight colony simulator. It's very easy to get into it. In fact the game is so easy that I feel that tutorial could be cut in half and it would be just cool. Beside that game is easy, it's also very enjoyable. Gameplay  servs small problems to the player that he has to resolve. Problems arise organically. (Need more food -> build farms -> need more water -> build water extractor -> need more energy -> build generator -> etc). It's really easy to hook up to 'I will just construct the next dome' routine. Basically, game is a quite common city/colony builder. So anyone that played simcity or anno games will quickly understand the game.
Game is really pleasing and so, but it has one major problem. It's really easy. Mechanics are very simple. Even most complicated supply chain is involving 5 resources types and 3 stages (manufacturing a robot), so it's not very demanding. There are couple of basic resources (metal, bioplastic, raw food). Nearly anything in the game can be created from such resources. And since there is so few basic resources types, the only sane tactic is to make mass production of them from the very begining. After than you are ploping next structures with balance of resources in mind. This is not ideal. Mostly cause at certain poin resources will be produced faster than you can spend them on next buildings.
Game has basic needs system. Basic. All colonists have the same needs for whole game. After first 30 minutes of play colonists needs don't do much. Mostly cause at that point you are just ploping next structures. Even when some kind of accident happens (meteor strikes power gen and there is no power and O2 is not produced), needs are droping so slowly that there is plenty time to react. I would be nice if needs of colonists would evolve as colony grows. For exmple, when colony has access to semiconductors colonists might want personal computers. That would greatly imporove mid-late game.
Another thing is that you can have only one base. I get that the game is called planelbase and it's about base building. But it could be interesting to have ability to create more than one base and have some specialization on them (one is a mining one and the other one grows stuff). That could be a great excuse to add vehicles. That's another issue. It's really odd that bunch of colonists would be sent to a remote planet/moon with a task of building a colony out there and they would not need to go anywher. Just stay indoors and make stuff. Some sort of exploration would be really nice. Even taking geological samples or performing experiments or something like that.
The whole game was built on good ideas. But it seems unpolished. Even the achievements feeld unpolished. withing 10h I managed to get most of them. And only 2 of remaing ones pose any kind of challenge ("Express Outpost" and "Express Colony").
There couple of events during the game tha can  occur. There can be a solar flare, sand storm, raiders and random quest. When most of them have real impact on the gameplay (solar flare will radiate colonists and it's safer to keep them indoors, sandstorm will slow them down and damage outside structures), raiders don't make much sense. It feels like this one wasn't thought out properly. They  occur really late game and when they occur you have 15+ armed guards vs 5 raiders. They will kill like 10 colonists in one part of the base but rest of the base will function just swell. It seems like a good idea to implement, but when encountered it's just not so interesting. Most annoying part is the sound of the lasors. And that would be it.
Things that could be improved right now:
UI has couple of things that could be improved:
- resource/population widget could be merged into one and this way all infromation coult stay on the screen all the time rather than switching between them.
- It's really unclear how colonization ship permits work.
- When trading ships land it would be nice to have a list of them awaiting deals (colony with 6 starport would use that)
Overall the game is really good. I most likely I will put another 10h into it. But the game could be so much better with more content in it. I would really like to see more supply-chain options, more events, more  base building options, more elaborated needs system, and much more.
If you like city/colony builders games with buy it. Don't expect level of anno. Be happy.
If not a hard fan of such games and want to spend an evening with nice game, buy it when on sale. Still nice experience.
If you are die hard call of duty player, don't buy it. Go play call of duty.

First off, before all you review reviewers go cutting my head off, this is one of my first reviews.
On to the game itself.
I think this is a fun game. However, there are a few, rather annoying issues.
Issue #1. The resource "tracking" mechanism (AI in general) needs improvment. In my experience, the colonists seem to ignore resources that are needed.
Ex. I sat for three in game days needing one metal for another Solar panel. My mine had four boxes of ore in front of it but instead of grabbing those, they would go and attempt to mine more, at which time they would then put the box of ore by the front door and go take a nap.
This leads into the next issue, the priority system.
Issue #2. Priorities don't seem to effect the colonists. The entire time I had the above mentioned issue at hand, the processing plant required to make the resources needed was the only priority building. But they continued to mine and use what they did eventually make into metal, into spares that were not required. And yes, I did turn the spare count way down.
Another example of this issue is with repairing robots and sturctures.
In a seperate base, I had a robot, broken down in front of the airlock. I had several spares on hand however nobody bothered to repair him. Later on, part of my power grid failed due to the lack of upkeep on my windmills, thus resulting in loss of power and a catastrophic shutdown of the entire base. After a desperate attempt to get power restored, everything just kind of fell apart and everyone died. All of this resulting from the colonists not repairing the robots or...anything for that matter.
Issue #3. The colonists are insanely needy. It seems like almost half the time they are off in some random room, wasting time when something really needs to get done before they all die. I mean, I don't know about you, but I wouldn't be sleeping 10 hours a day, taking my time eating, and working out to de-stress if my life was in danger and something that was going to keep me alive needed to be built time-now. It doesn't matter if you are angry because it's either angry and alive, or, hap...oh.. wait, now your dead.
Now, I'de like to turn and point out that this game is worth buying, if you haven't already. Personally, I think this game is awesome. It is pretty fun to play and well worth the money spent. If you are looking for a fun time killer and are into this style of game. I recommend it. The random occurrences, although they happen way too often in my opinion, are pretty cool. A few times I've been sitting there with no windmill, biting my nails waiting for the sandstorm to pass as I watch my power bar plumit. Or, been yelling four letter profanities after the connection to one of my buildings get nailed by a meteor. It adds that exitement that games like this usually lack.
All in all, I'de give it a solid, maybe generous, 7 out of 10.

VA-11 Hall - A, or simply Valhalla, isn't much of a video game. I normally try and avoid that statement. It is a fairly divise one when talking about video games. Thing is, I think it fits Valhalla more so than most of the games described that way. You do not have a whole lot of choices in the story. I expected decisions akin to a visual novel. Valhalla doesn't even have many of those. What Vallhalla does have though is amazing characters, brilliant world building and some excellent music.
In Valhalla you play as Jill, a down-on-her-luck bartender at VA-11 Hall-A, You make drinks and you talk to the people who show up there. The most interactive part of the game is the drink making, which is a matter of following simple instructions and dragging ingredients into a mixer. Have you dragged icons into a folder? Congrats, you are now an expert mixologist.
You don't play Valhalla for intense gameplay. You play it to hear the stories of the regulars who show up at your bar. Android sex workers, professional hackers (who are, surprisingly, not your typical cliche hackers), brains in jars, corgis. These are the people who frequent there. Jill is there to be an open ear. The writing in this game is fantastic and littered with subtle and not so subtle nods to various animes and video games of the last few decades. Thanks to the characters and their stories, the verisimilitude of this game is off the charts. It does a better job creating a realistic, liveable world than most games with a hundred times its budget. Combine that with an amazing synthpop soundtrack and you have what is a very charming game-novel-thing.
It has its flaws, one being what little gameplay there is. Another being that despite having a large cast of female characters, all of them seem to be lesbian. It feels less like trying to include a diverse cast and more like pandering and fan service. To be fair, that statement can be applied to just about every anime under the sun, of which Valhalla borrows quite a bit from. The small flaws don't get in the way of the bigger picture though. This game has won my affection. I plan on continuing to play it until I see the end of Jill's story.

Wow, what an incredible experience, to say the very least.
I've become absoloutely infatuated with this game, as this game paints both the positives and negatives of the bartending job in this cyberpunk future dystopia in which you, Jill, are a bartender at VA-11 Hall-A (AKA: Valhalla) whose remarkable traits are her down-to-earth attitude, yet professional mannerism. Your job is to tend with a series of eccentric guests who frequent the bar, who all have their own personal backstories that make learning more about them interesting.
From Cyberpunked Catgirls, to Robotic Lolita Sex Dolls, VA-11 Hall-A has it all. And you know what? It's not even done from a fetishy standpoint either. The lives these individuals lead are surprisingly unremarkable, but the game shows that everyone has a story behind them. Even you, Jill, the protagonist seem to carry some hefty baggage...
"Something about nothing" describes this game perfectly. If you enjoy games where you learn about people, learn their story through small bits and pieces, and various extraneous tidbits tipped off from the other patrons of VA-11 Hall-A, then you're in for a treat.
Seriously. Give it a go, it's a story experience worth viewing.
You'll find yourself wishing to spend more and more time.
It has replayability value, depending on drinks served you may very well find tidbits of info you didn't find before. So it's worth it to try multiple times to see what sort of reactions you can get from people.
Overall?
It gets a very solid 8.5/10

From exuberant robot sex worker Dorothy, to ex-wrestler bar owner Dana, to sisterly hacker Alma, to still-figuring-it-out-but-won't-take-your♥♥♥♥♥♥bartender protagonist Jill, to talking dogs and many more,
is a great little visual novel that crafts a memorable cast of characters and never forgets the human stories at its core in favor of its cyberpunk details. The bulk of the game is just conversations between you (as Jill) and the VA-11 Hall-A bar's patrons -- but there's joy, laughter, sadness, and even tension at events happening elsewhere as you serve drinks and hear about their lives and the dystopian mess that is Glitch City.
This is a game whose intro literally encourages you to sit back and relax, so there's a few nice touches like the super simple drink-mixing UI and being able to set the music you want in the bar every day. As opposed to visual novels with lots of branching paths, there's really just one route telling Jill's story with some variations based on which drinks you serve. I saw all the "good" ending scenes in two playthroughs (Tip:
) and then happily came back to find some of the other lines (there's a few good ones, especially when you get people a little too drunk).
There's a lot of humor and a lot of heart here, so I'd recommend
to anyone, no prior experience with the genre required. I plan on coming back for a few drinks myself, even if it's just to hear the same old stories again.

I was looking forward to picking this one up ever since seeing Jesse Cox's Fan Friday on the game. Playing it myself, I got even more impressed by the game's mechanics and variety. There's a lot of interaction between the cards that makes it work on a vastly different level from other card games out there.
Even Gwent with its 2-3 rounds per match and different rows doesn't reach Age of Rivals' complexity. However, the game remains extremely simple and intuitive despite it all. Card texts are crystal clear and after the first two rounds you'll already have the hang of the basic rules and design intentions, if not the finer strategical details. Go big on cash generation, excessive culture output or just keep the opponent down with devastating attacker cards? There are many ways to win and enough flexibility to adapt on the fly, due to it being a deck builder game. Synergies have to be planned for in advance to succeed in the later rounds, which is oddly satisfying to pull off.
It feels inviting while offering a lot of strategic considerations that could make this game successful on a competitive level. For the time being though, I'm just happy being able to play it a couple of times a day for leisure. I'm looking forward to seeing what the future holds for Age of Rivals.

I fell in love with this little game. Let me explain why.
First of all, this is no CCG. The game is pretty much a virtual board game, with some unlocks to try to keep things simple at the beggining. No in-app purcheases means that everything is unlocked very quickly, since there's no incentive for the developers to make you grind.
The game is quick yet highly complex mechanically. Expect some moments where you're left wondering what happened after some interactions of cards. And there are some mechanics that you'll only find out about by reading the in-game rulebook (which is short, but very informative). I found no bugs so far, which is fairly impressive given the mechanical depth.
Luck seems really important at first, when you're still learning about the game. As your skill improves, it becomes clear that this game is first and foremost a skill game. The implementation of randomness makes every game feel unique.
At the moment matchmaking is *very* quick (15 to 20 seconds). The hard AI is also quite competent if you'd rather play singleplayer.
