GDMO, Global for those unfamiliar with the Korean server, a very tough game. On my gameking account I have logged in at least a hundred hours and an equal amount of money into the game. If you're looking for a better story then go to Digimon Cyber Sleuth. If you are looking for more engaging fights then turn to Digimon Rumble. If you're looking for an easier learning curve then go to Digimon Heroes.
GDMO has a cut and paste story that mirrors season 5 that fizzles out when you get to File Island. Or Dark Tower Wasteland. The fights quickly become tedious through hours of grinding for the mere CHANCE of a reward. The learning curve has improved ever since the Yokohama map changed, but it still dumps you in the deep end. The RNG for hatching is broken plain and simple.
In the days that Joymax held this game it ran on pure, concentrated nostalgia. Gameking and Move Games have done much to make the game more player friendly but they are essentially rewriting the core of the game. Don't expect frequent or even good updates because you will only be disappointed.
At this point (if you have read this much) you are wondering just HOW did I say yes on reccomending this game. It has the potential. The movement sysytem would break other game engines with its complexity. The animations are fluid and colorful. The maps are vibrant and varied. The background music is catchy. The combat system, while not particularly engaging is solid. The inclusion of non-main character digimon and even those not even in any show are impressive.
This game isn't welcoming to casuals but for die-hard Digimon fans and collectionist types of gamers it is.
Just be glad the level cap no longer exists.

My review will be based in a few things:

Let's start õ/

Graphics:

7/10

They've cut a lot of the 4th year... the whole ball... NOT EVEN A CUTSCENE DDD:
Well, frustrations aside, they've made some changes from the original movie(s) just to make it "comic". Gameplay:
AI sometimes can ♥♥♥♥ you up, but is very well programed for the other parts, and if you play this game as it should be played (no exploits nor glitches) you'll have no problems with AI. Even in parts where two players need to separate in order to complete a puzzle.
AI 7/10
The controls can give you a hard time if you want to finish this game quickly... the spell selection is kinda of confusing and messy (Xbox 360 controller) but... you get usued to.
Control 7/10
The spell detection sucks... you want to cast a Leviosa on a purple thing and then you are levitating Ron. To kinda "fix" this, they've made a manual target. But still... even with the target on the purple thing, sometimes it doesn't recognizes the object's purple aura.

This is where i've spend the most time playing. There are a lot of things to collect in Hogwarts and if you want to complete 100% or not, i really recommend getting at least all character tokens. It makes you explore the whole castle and see all the other parts that were really well done and with a lot of details. 9/10

I've said that you have to complete the game twice to get 100%, well, i've completed 6 times because of the poor checkpoint system, only one save file that is easily corruptible, no cloud save, file location is "hidden" and you can't force a save... only when you get a token, get a golden brick, a red brick, save a student or finish a story sequence. Easy to learn, but hard to master, Planetbase is one of the most fun games I've played in quite a while.
It's not perfect -- sometimes your AI colonists (you do not control them diectly) will idle when they should be following orders, for example -- but the good massively outweighs the bad for me with Planetbase. Most of the problems I've found are minor, and could certainly disappear with time and patching.
Even now, though, Planetbase is eminently playable, and far more fun than I expected it to be. Perhaps its greatest design acheivement is that it never slips into that "mid-game dull spot" I remember from games like Sim City, where you've acheived enough in-game that the challenge is gone.
With Planetbase, you're always trying to keep your colonists alive, thriving, and expanding in hostile planetary environments, so you can never completely call your work finished.
I find the game fun and truly compelling, and would recommend Planetbase to anyone who might be interested.
Be sure to play the Tutorial (maybe even a couple of times). As above, the game is simple to learn, but developing solid survival strategies will come with time and play.
Oh, and get yourself a second Medic on base, as soon as you're able. You'll thank me later. :-)
Recommended.

Planetbase is a fun and addicting colony build-em-up.
You start off by being dropped onto a planet of your choosing. There are 3 to choose from at the moment, each with different difficulties. Some are more harsh with less sun and wind, so you can't produce as much energy with your solar panels and wind turbines, and some others might have frequent meteors.
Once your colonists land, you need to get to building. It's actually pretty intense because you need to get a lot of essential stuff going quite quickly. You need to build water extractors, a source of energy, oxygen generators, canteen, etc.
Your different colonists have varying specialties. Biologists tend to plants, medics heal the wounded, workers can mine for minerals, and engineers can fix things up. Apart from those basic skills, each colonist can do a few more in depth things. For example, you can grow a medicinal plant, then take it to a lab and the medic will be able to create medical supplies from it.
The UI is very easy to use, and is also accompanied with some keyboard hotkeys which keeps the game from being frustrating. You can even speed up the game, which is great. There is currently no pause button, however, it's possible the devs did this deliberately to keep the game from being too easy.
As you play, you can gain milestones. They can be as simple as surviving one night, to building a large amount of things. As you achieve these, you can unlock more harsh planets to try and survive on. It keeps an overall feeling of progression, to keep you going.
There's a lot of detail managing which I won't go into, because then this review would be pages long. Some examples are supplying enough power to all your structures, attracting new colonists by keeping your colony running smoothly, building bots to work more efficiently, creating anti-meteor turrets and more.
Overall, it's a really fun game which I feel could easily suck you in if you typically enjoy this genre. There's a lot to do, and building up your colony is very satisfying.

While I gave Duels of the Planeswalkers 2012 a thumbs down, this game I recommend if you enjoy playing MTG. While most people will buy this version because of the additional of the sealed deck format, please do not buy this thinking its going to be some amazing addition, its not.
One, the sealed'ness of the packs you receive are pre-determined by a hash of your game account and cannot be changed. Thus you get stuck with cards and whatever you get is what you get. Two, the computer has a major advantage against you in the sealed campaign, as they either do not played sealed, or they are given packs with one color in them to choose from.
Excusing the terribleness that is sealed, I'll now review the rest of the game.
For the most part the game follows the rules quite well, and its noobed up just enough to allow people who do not want to go through ever step to just let the computer do them for you. In this way, you only need to play things from your hands and attack with your creatures when prompted to do so.
The game also has a pretty nice campaign system with varying skill. But let me confirm the computer definitely cheats, does not follow deck rules, and has a rigged deck, so if you thought it would be like a regular game in that fashion you'd be wrong.
I was holding a peek in my opening hand and peeked the computer's opening hand. All land. It then proceeded to top deck every card it needed and could cast each turn for 7 turns.
Another time the computer was playing black, and I either destoryed or countered each of its opening cards for the first 9 turns until it kept drawing land after land. I then used stolen goods which would allow me to exile cards from its deck until i reached a non-land permanent that I could then play for free. Guess what? I exiled his deck, it was all lands. So his deck consisted of about 7 or 8 actual cards designed to combo you to death and all lands.
You will also find the computer is given decks like relentless rats with a perfect draw.
For actual games against the computer you will have to play custom and leave the campaign alone, however you will not be able to unlock the cards and decks to continue without playing the campaign.
The multiplayer is where its at. Unlike 2012 its actually stable, runs perfectly and allows up to 4 players to play the game simultaneously in either a free-for-all or two-headed giant format. A multiplayer sealed deck is also included, however its limited to 2 players simultaneously.
Now what makes this game different than magic online where you can choose from all the cards in the game, your decks here for the most part are pre-defined. You are given a 60 card deck with a pool 80 or more cards together with which you can configure your deck. For most of the game these cards will not be available and must be unlocked to play them by playing the campaign.
In some ways this limitation of the game allows for more skill, as you must use what is available and still strategize to win.
As someone who has been playing magic since 1993, I can say for sure this is one of the better ways to play online, its inexpensive compared to Magic Online and gives you the full magic tabletop experience unlike some of the game clients not designed by Wizards that allow you to play magic with other players online.
I recommend this for new players and for more advanced players who just want something fun to do, a way to play magic with no one else around to bust out actual magic cards.

The extent of customization options are just some unlockable cards that you can add on to the deck while removing other cards to compensate. The Sealed Play mode is kind of cool, but it leaves a lot to be desired when certain cards you may or may not get turn out to be instawin for the player who uses them. Also like other DotP installments, the online mode also only works when there's a Steam sale and people have just bought the game, it never works or connects you to other players otherwise. In its defense though, the campaign always does a good job of teaching you your deck's strengths and weaknesses, which is very helpful to new players.
It's a good game for people just getting into MTG, but for average fans and veterans it just isn't worth it.

Allow me to explain something to you about this game, its EXTREMELY unbalanced. You would be surprised at how clear cut the tiers are. Unless you play one of these select decks, you are going to lose unless by some stroke of luck you manage to pull just the right card. Its wraught with people who will blantantly admit they are there to frustrate you, and its just flat out a mean community. I have a fairly decent win/loss record yet most of these battles had to be won using these top tier decks. The main selling point of this game was Sealed Play which is by no means as good as it should be. You are given 2 slots to start with, and a select number of boosters to pull from. You can have the Computer assemble a deck for you based on your cards (which defeats the entire purpose) or you can build them yourself, however you are given extremely mediocre cards to use. The FFA mode is basically 1v1 (there are three way and four way matchups, but no one plays them) and once again, the top tier decks WILL WIN. People will reply with, "this deck beats this one if you have these certain cards" here lies another problem, you have to grind to unlock cards for premade decks to play with, or you can pay 99 cents on the store to buy the deck, and you can buy a 99 cent foil pack (which serves no purpose other than to take your money) and you can buy sealed deck slots (sealed was also a money grab) They have DLC by way of decks, and most of these decks are awfully overpowered compared to the others. As a casual player of the paper card game, this game is terrible by any standard. If you are looking to be frustrated by people, who are pretentious and rude, pick this game up, if not STAY AWAY and play the actual card game, there is a much nicer community in the actual product. Happy Gaming!

Every once in a while, a game comes along which redefines what video games can achieve; which changes the way people think about games and interactivity; or which challenge our notions of genre.
The Witness appears to be aiming for those lofty goals, but falls tragically short.
Launching players straight into the "action" (in as much as that word applies to a pure puzzle game) with neither tutorial nor menu, the Witness demonstrates both the best and worst about interactively teaching players game mechanics. There is no game with a more satisfying "Aha!" moment when you (as a player) finally grasp what is being conveyed by a puzzle mechanic. Sadly, a large part of that is because there is no clearly conveyed difficulty curve of which puzzles to try in which order -- you will find yourself facing a puzzle for which you are not yet equipped to solve multiple times.
The Witness masquerades as a straightforward puzzle game, which would build, one layer at a time, a dazzling array of challenges.  Like many great puzzle games before it, it then exhaustively explores this field until you may feel that every nook have been explored... and then you are perplexed by an unexpected, new possibility. Yet if you scratch this surface, you will find hidden layers within the game (but which sadly resolve themselves, with careful study and reasoning, to be the same elements as the surface presentation).
Everything in The Witness is present because of, and in support of, the puzzle elements of the game. Without any decision made somewhere in the game, at least one puzzle would not be solvable.
All of the above should make it the next Portal, or Tetris-- with the power to reshape the way gamers play and are challenged for years. But ultimately it feels like some critical element was missed-- with the tragic result that the game, while beautiful and engaging, has no lasting vitality.
The Witness is undoubtedly in the top 10 pure puzzle games released this year, but maybe only because there are so few contenders in that category. If you want a challenging (and frankly mind-blowing) puzzle experience which develops at your pace and you can overlook the lack of narrative, even rudimentary explanations, or a clear guide for progressing, play The Witness.
The best puzzle game i have played in quite a while. I greatly reccomend it.

I very much enjoyed The Witness.
It is a problem solving game with a very simple mechanic. And indeed, this mechanic is applied for every interaction in the game.
As you explore the island on which the game is set, you are introduced to different classes of puzzle, all of which involve drawing a line from a circle to a semi-circular end point, in accordance to some rule. At first the solutions are obvious, but as the game progresses, the rules that you have to obey increase in complexity. You may find that you need to be more observant, taking clues from the environment, or that you need to combine two sets of rules that haven't appeared on the same puzzle before. Later on in the game, you may find yourself puzzling over a particular solution for quite some time, but when you eventually do arrive at the solution, the sense of satisfaction is particularly rewarding.
The Witness does stray a little too far in the direction of being overly pompous and pretentious, as a number of reviewers have said, but I wouldn't say that this detracts from the positive aspects of the game.
There a many spoilers for The Witness on various game sites, and these will reduce the sense of accomplishment that you get from solving the problems yourself. However, unless you are incredibly patient, you may need to look a particular puzzle up. But do yourself a favour and only do this as an absolute last resort. I found many articles were about the author trying to appear clever, rather than trying to help you, and ended up spoiling a big chunk of the game. I found the IGN one was pretty careful to only give you answers that you were looking for:
There are multiple endings, (of which I have found two) that are somewhat unsatisfactory. So enjoy the journey rather than the destination. And save before you complete the game (because it resets all the puzzles).
Pros:
* Good puzzles.
* Satisfying sense of accomplishment.
* Interesting setting.
Cons:
* 'Up itself'.
* Maybe too hard - but this is a very subjective.
* Mediocre endings.

Star Conflict is a free to play third person shooter in space ships. It's not a MMO, despite the store page telling you something else.
The game is a team based arena shooter where players can group together in corperations to accomplish bigger projects.
The gameplay is smooth, fast paced and leaves alot of room for tactical play. In contrast the game is very grind heavy if you wish to fly everything it has to offer.
You buy spaceships and then pew pew either against other players or npc.
There are 3 different factions with three different ship sizes devided into nine classes. A fourth ship size will be added soon.
Each faction prefers a other style of gameplay as does each ship size or class. I'll only be going into the sizes in this review to keep it relatively short.
Interceptor:
small and very agile. Can relocate very quickly and generally can always be where it needs to be at a given time. Survivability is low.
Frigate:
large and slow. High firepower or alot of buff abilities. Survivability is high.
Fighter:
Medium sized and located between the two above mentioned in terms of speed and survivability.
Each ship has slots for modules and weapons that you can fit to tailor the ship to your needs and playstyle. The customizability is high for a arena based shooter.
The ships and modules, as well as pilot modifications are devided into 15 ranks. The higher the rank gets, the better will the ships and equipment become. It's kept simple for new players, because you will only have a small amount of modules and weapons available at the start. As you progress, more and more options will open up.
In order to progress, you'll have to level the ships by playing with them.
The gamemode you'll be playing the most is skirmish. Players in queue will be thrown into team based matches depending on their rank. (There is much more to the matchmaking, but this would be too much for the review)
The matches will have different objectives, with more opening up to you as progression comes along.
More advanced and interesting pvp modes like leagues or dreadnought will be available to you as you move up the ranks.
Four players have to tackle a mission with set goals against npc. There are nine different missions. Until rank four you'll have access to four of them. As in PVP, you'll get more content as you progress in ranks. Such as special missions against giant alien space ships with 12-15 players vs. NPC.
A set of maps connected together by warp gates where you can either pve or pvp. Unfortunately, one and the same map can exist on multiple servers. So not every player on a particular map will be able to interact with other players on that map, because he might be on a other server.
This game gets it right. No pay to win can be found here. You have your standard customization options for your ships, which can be bought for permanent use with real money or for temporary use with in game currency.
There are premium modules/weapons as well as premium ammo, but these only give you more experience and let you level faster.
Premium ships do not need repairs and earn more experience and income. They aren't stronger than their normal counter parts.
Finally, we've got the typical premium subscription, which will boost your income and experience gain.
To sum this section up, paying players will grind alot less, advance faster in the ranks, but will not have an advantage in battle.
Standard as in most shooters, mouse and keyboard. Keys are all fully bindable. Controllers and Oculus Rift are also supported.
Nice and as good as they need to be for this type of game. They won't blow your mind, but compliment the game play and also run very well on older machines. Some maps tend to be more demanding than others.
The sound is good, if you ignore the random chatter the game throws at you occaisonally.
"We're on the same target, shoot a missile" is neat, but after you've heard it thousands of times, it gets annoying. This can't be turned off.
I do recommend playing this game with good bass and surround sound speakers. The battle sounds and explosions will be awesome.
Nonetheless, they're still good with headsets or normal speakers.
If spaceships and shooters are your thing, this game is definitely worth a try. It is very grind heavy, even if you let your wallet do some speaking. Nonetheless, the grind does insure, that you don't unlock everything to fast and have nothing left to aspire to.
It's not your type of game for spending the whole day on, it's rather for having a few quick rounds of pew pew and fun and then doing something else.
Pros
-free to play done right.
-easy to get into, hard to master.
-fast paced and action loaded pvp matches with lot of tactical depth.
-good roster of ships and classes which all play differently and can be customized differently.
-nice amount of pve content for a game that whas built on pvp.
Cons
-the grind, this game has 9 currencies and the tenth soon to come. Their purpose? Increase grind and keep you hooked longer. Could also be a good thing, depends on your view.
-low player base. In some time zones, you'll have a hard time finding matches. EU and Russian are most populated.
-veteran players seal clubbing in lower ranks. Fortunately, the devs are constantely working against this issue and improving it.
-bad tutorials and explaining. The game doesn't do a good job on explaining it's mechaniks or importance of the ship roles as well as team work. As a result, some matches can become a real mess, if nobody is filling in their role or working in a team.
Credit has to be given for the out of game tutorial vids and helpful community. I strongly recommend the forums and the vids linked by OmegaFighter in the comments.
-find yourself an active corperation. The game is more enjoyable when working together.
-do not rush the ranks. You won't know how to properly fly your ships and will get your behind whooped.
-be thoughtful of your ship, its role and what modules you equip for filling that role.
-be a teamplayer. Lone wolves don't get much accomplished in matches.

First off; This game is awesome and i would recommend it to anyone who is into games that afford skill/are difficult.
I always here people whining about Dark Souls *cause it*s so difficult. I played all the Dark Souls games and i have to say that if you played those games, you know it's not just a difficult game and you just have to "Git Gud".

You see, Demon souls (Dark Souls ... etc.) are just unfair at some points in the game but Furi is challenging and Fair at the same time. I like this game because of it's combat, fights and action in general.
I'd say you should buy it when it's on sale and just try it out.

I should disclaim that for the longest time, I used to play games on easy (or whatever was the lowest difficulty for the game). Relevant to that, Furi has three difficulties: Promenade (Easy), Furi (Normal), and Furier (hard), which is unlocked by beating the game.
Heavily, heavily, HEAVILY advise playing on Furi for a first playthrough, and not Promenade. Promenade is entirely meant for people who just want to enjoy the story (and I'd say Furi has a great story, so they have the right idea including that option), but in exchange you'll miss all the fun of bosses being actually challenging. You get 2 more lives for a total of 5 (3 on Furi and Furier), you do more damage, and boss movesets and phases are much simpler - though there might be different numbers of them.
But If you like the challenge of Dark Souls, Bayonetta, Metal Gear Rising, No More Heroes, bullethells, etc, then Furi (the difficulty AND the game) is definitely for you. More on that in a bit.
I'd consider Furi to be a very good trinity of gameplay, story, and soundtrack - special emphasis on soundtrack. The music excels at getting you pumped up for boss fights, letting you relax as you move from one to the next, and setting the mood throughout the game.
Gameplay's very fluid, and there are no power-ups to collect, no abilities to learn, nothing. You are given a few things before fighting the first boss: a sword, a repeating laser pistol, and the ability to dash through or parry attacks - all you get, and all you'll need for the entire game.
As for story...without spoilers, all I can simply say is that the story caught me by surprise - normally great gameplay and soundtrack comes at an expense of story, but Furi manages to pull it off surprisngly well, and the story really struck me.
You are imprisoned. Around you, behind you, and ahead of you: a prison built to be impossible to escape, protected by numerous guardians, all seeking to send you back to your cell. Below you: a free world.
The guardians ARE quite challenging, though. There might be times when you're struck down, defeated for what might be the 20th time while they tell you to go back to your cell, and wondering how you can possibly hope to finish what you've started. Though, none of that matters, really.
What DOES matter is what you're going to do.

Circuits is beautiful game with great asthetics but falls short in terms of actual gameplay. It has a beautiful art style and great sounding music, but unfortunately the finished product is nothing short of underwhelming.
Circuits appears to be another unique puzzle game. You have to put the right pieces onto the music track in order for it to play correctly. The only guidance you have is a "Play mode" that plays the song in the correct order and you have to listen to it to get it right. I say this with a bit of hesitation because although that's what the developers may have intended, the game is just too slow-paced in order to really utilize it. It really gets boring to have to listen to a track over and over to see what area you might have gotten wrong. Most of the time, the player will find themselves randomly placing tracks, fast-forwarding to see if they got it right and then doing that over and over until they find success. This is the reason I can't recommend this game. It expects you to be super-patient as well as having an ear for music, otherwise you have to just randomly try stuff until they work.
Now don't get me wrong, this type of game does appeal to some people, I understand. However I've seen similar games with better implementations in various categories. Some may have very upbeat music with very distinct sections so that the player can actively listen out for them. Some may have different looking icons for each section. Some may have unique ways of directing the flow of music and so on. This one however, has a fixed track, fixed icons and very little track variations. For the average user I cannot recommend this game for the gameplay.
One thing I absolutely love about the game is the unique visual style. It was bright, smooth and attractive and really gave me a calming feeling whilst playing.
The sounds were pretty good, however the frustrating style of gameplay meant that I had to fast-forward which also meant that I couldn't hear the music during that.
This is not a game for everyone. It will appeal to some, but for others like me who has played games such as Auditorium and a ton of other musically inclined games, this is a weak attempt at entering that market. Pick it up on sale if this appeals to you.

Very fun game, well worth the money. I would compare it to Banished in terms of gameplay.

As others have said, once you get passed the first 30 minutes or so the game becomes much less challenging. There are goals to work towards, such as achieving a large number of colonists or unlocking lots of new technologies, but you can probably avoid collapse if you know what you are doing. If you plan poorly in the long term, you might have maintence backlogs and power outages that kill a lot of colonists, but it isn't ever really fatal to your colony (which I think is unfortunate).
The game has three scenarios and randomized maps that office some replay value. The scenarios determine what kind of energy you can generate (wind vs solar), and the map layout can force you to have long, scattered bases which are harder to maintain.
Overall, I think the game has some flaws and the difficulty curve plateaus rather quickly, but it a fun and quite beautiful game regardless. I would reccomend it for the $20.

The biggest problem I have with the simulation is the lack of control over colonists. I've run through three bases now and they have all failed early due to a cascade of non-performing colonists which I am not sure if this is due to bugs or some underlying game mechanic that is not obvious by the very limited information the game interface presents.
Eg.
- Colonists won't build new buildings but will instead mope around with malnutrition issues.
- Colonists won't tend to plants.
- Because the plants won't grow they won't produce food which also stops colonists from doing anything.
- I desperately needed to build another wind farm and the colonists refused to complete it because they wanted to repair other structures instead. This problem went on for 4 ingame days until the whole colony collapsed.
- The colonists refused to repair my robots making the robots useless and immobile.
- Even with a well stocked warehouse my colonists still refused to do any work.
I am not sure if the above issues are due to my lack of understanding but these issues will frustrate less patient players. My feeling is there needs to be a method to force an individual colonist or robot to do a specific job until it is completed. At this time as far as I can ascertain you simply cannot do that and your colony is at the mercy of the AI colonists who may or may not do what you expect them to do or simply sit idle for days at a time and inevitably die.
In summary this a brilliant but frustrating colony builder. So much of the mechanics are hidden from the player that I am unsure whether it is due to bugs or not. I give this game a 7/10 at this time.

Let me preface this by saying that I believe this (Duels of the Planeswalkers) series is an attempt by Wizards of the Coast to have the Magic franchise branch out to consumers who may otherwise never have thought they would be playing a card game, and as such should not be rated down by hardcore magic players for being too shallow or simplistic as opposed to having binders full of cards at your disposal - as that would both lose new players in the confusion and be a technical disaster.
That being said, I think the series is really coming to it's intended form in this revision, and while the yearly releases have so far been an improvement over the prior version - this finally feels like the game everyone wanted it to be.
The introduction of sealed play is one of the big reasons for this. Sealed play allows you to build a deck from a series of booster packs and has you play a VERY short campaign with them allowing you to unlock some more boosters. I do believe that they could have made the campaign in this version much longer and allowed for a larger pool of cards, but I also understand that as a new feature they likely intended to test the waters as to public reception of the feature (which I hear is mostly positive.
The game does allow multiplayer on the steam version (android version mishaps aside), and it's very good other than a few dropped games here and there.
I will note that those coming from past games used to just paying for an expansion or two along with some deck packs will see more in-game purchases in this game, which I assume they have adopted from their success in iOS on last year's Magic 2013 .
Overall I do believe this game is worth playing, and there's plenty of fun to be had, just don't expect the depth of actual play nor that of MTG Online.  And don't expect to play all the game has to offer without spending at least 20$ USD.

So, a couple things to keep in mind with this game. Number one is it is a free game, and number two it is a free game. These are two things you need to keep in mind when you go into this game, so your expectations should not be very high. Barring that in mind, I initially played this on mobile on my iPhone and seen there was a desktop version of this game. The game is the same on mobile and desktop. In fact, I think you possibly might even have some cross platform play going on. When I loaded the game on my PC and typed in the same name that I used on my iPhone it told me that name is already in use, so I had to create a second character (I didn't register it on my iPhone to my e-mail and create a password... doh).
Now actually playing the game. It's kind of like Terraria in a sense that it is a 2d side scrolling type of game. You start at level one, and collect lots of cool stuff and each time you mine something new you get bonus experience for that, so starting out the ultimate goal is to mine and collect as many unique items as possible and I thought that was pretty cool.
Mind you, I haven't gotten very far, but in the 20 minutes or so I spent playing the game I managed to do the following:
-Collect a pick axe.
-Collect a pistol.
-Meet up with real people and had conversation.
-Killed these metal flying things.
-Killed other cool monsters.
-Earned experience.
-Leveled up.
-Got killed by acid rain.
-Got killed by hunks of flying metal.
All in all, a pretty desirable first few minutes. I definitely plan to delve deeper into this game to see what it really offers. Like I said, it's a free game. It's not like we're spending extra money to play this game other than things and services we're already paid for (a working computer wit a keyboard and mouse and working internet connection), so if it turns out not being for you then at least you're not out of any money.
It'll be interesting to see what they add in this game in the future.

I don't have time to play journalist, so I'm just going to sum this up into a list of observations. As many of you might know, Crashday wasn't exactly game of the year back in it's day. It showed a lot of potential but it had even more problems, unfortunately Moonbyte hasn't fixed most of them...
Things they did fix:
+ The speed bug, you can't reverse into the world border to go faster than the speed of sound anymore.
+ Random crashes to desktop while racing, most of them.
+ Multiplayer netcode.
Things they added on top:
+ You can now change the exhaust flame color. Yay.
+ New and improved (I guess?) interface.
+ Powerups in Wrecking Matches.
Problems they didn't fix:
-
-
Soon to be fixed.
- The vehicle physics. Your car will still fall through the ground if you try to land on a ramp, a small hill. or other similar formations. It's not common, but it's common enough to be annoying.
- The auto-recovery. When you fire a missile at an enemy you better pray to god that it doesn't flip them over, otherwise there's a 90% chance they'll re-spawn right behind you. Especially problematic in the final mission.
- Random crashes in the customization menu.
- Random crashes in the map editor.
Problems they added:
- They increased difficulty the Payday 2 way, by turning AI drivers into bullet sponges able to defy the laws of physics. This in itself wouldn't be such a bad thing if it weren't for the problems I mentioned above. The final mission in particular is excruciating as it embodies pretty much everything that's wrong with Crashday.
- Framerate drops in multiplayer.

This is one of the first games that got me into PC gaming, as something this realistic and fun wasn't on consoles. Some people cannot enjoy puzzle games no matter how perfect it is. This is why a perfect game has an 87 on metacritic.
I have not heard a legitimate criticism levied at this game. Here are a few that I will go through:
-Frustrating/Too hard
You can't criticise a game for being too hard, especially puzzle games where there's no way to adjust difficulty. That's like disliking a classic novel because your reading comprehension is fifth grade. Or hating Dark Souls cause you don't want to git gud. If The Witness is too hard, go and play some easier puzzle games, read a math/logic textbook, and come back.
-No Story
The Rubicks cude, Tetris, and Sudoku don't have stories. They wouldn't be better games if they did. No story is a plus, because it doesn't distract you from the puzzles. If you want story go read a book, watch a movie, or play a game that's made with story in mind.
-No rewards for doing puzzles/Only puzzles after puzzles
If you need a reward for completing puzzles, I have news for you: you don't like puzzles. If you don't like puzzles, don't play puzzle games. Imagine if this game had the best story ever and rewarded players with an addictive score system. Wow, then people who want to experience the story or reward would have to play a game they don't like to get to those parts. What a terrible idea.

This War of Mine is a 2D plat forming game with some rogue like elements. In which the player is put into 3rd person perspective and is given control over a band of civilians trying to survive in an abandoned building. The game play and mechanics are simple yet solid, with a primary focus on resource management as the player searches for food, water, medicine, weapons and building materials to try and improve their groups situation. However, what really makes the game is the setting. Be aware this game is not for the faint of heart. The premise of the game is your little band of survivors are civilians living in the nation’s capital that by circumstance got caught up in the middle of a brutal civil war, and 11-bit Studios  handles this phenomenally. Several of my friends are veterans, and after I had them test the game for themselves their responses were a bit surprising.  Of all the thousands of main stream war games on the market, they said that This War of Mine was one of the ones that came the closest to showing the bleak reality of what life in a war zone was really like. Your enemies are not infected zombies, soulless terminators, or even elite super soldiers. They are just people; you all are just people, all just trying to survive another day. This game is real, it’s depressing, it’s raw, and it’s quite frankly hard to play. I’m a 6ft 300lb macho man, and there are moments while playing through the Little Ones DLC, that I was fighting the urge to cry. And despite being an indie 3rd person perspective side-scroller, This War of Mine captures life in war better than COD ever has.

Cumulatively, my impression of this game is that it's "alright". I wouldn't go out of my way to play it, but it's short and decently fun. However, for me it's also entirely forgettable.
There's a bunch of small technical issues that really got in the way. The controls are not entirely responsive. The dash has a delay (possibly because it starts charging the moment you press the button), which takes a while to get used to. Homin behavior on the slash attack is sometimes unreliable, albeit rarely. Aim assist on projectiles is the same. I had a lot of audio glitches, and there were awkward moments where the game just stopped for a second or two. It seems that a lot of other people liked this game, so maybe it's just not my deal.
Other than that, the art is competent, but it doesn't amaze. The animations are stiff. Some of the music is excellent, some is whatever. The plot is unimpressive. The dialogue is bad. The voice acting is par for an indie game, but nothing to write home about. Still, these issues are a grain of salt because it's an indie game. A lot of it seems to be stretching further than it can reach though.
It's hard compared to other games, however the normal difficulty isn't that hard. The difficulty overall was just right, and this was really welcome for me.

The game does very little hand holding initially. You're just thrown into game world and left to your own devices to figure out the user interface. Luckilly, not everything on UI is initially enabled, but unlocked soon after the story starts progressing. Plotwise the game uses simple trick of amnesia. Player doesn't remember anything of their past and figuring out why that is seems to be part of the deal. They do have a companion with them, who remembers their past and can explain things and how to use them as player encounters them. Here's the first problem, the game features a ton of text in form of dialoque. When the first conversation starts between the player and their companion, game grinds to halt as player reads through screen after screen of text. Certain parts of the dialoque grant player skill points that can be used to purchase and upgrade skills, so player is of course trying to maximize the skill points and tries to go through all the options. Trying to exhaust all the dialoque options means going through the dialoque tree multiple times, often re-reading same parts of the text multiple times, which I quickly found to be a chore. Or if they don't try to maximize their skill points, they might have a feeling that they're handicapping themselves somehow.
World is shown from 3rd perspective, using a fixed camera that keeps following player character as they walk around. This neatly avoids camera getting stuck in the geometry and allows designer to choose good looking vantage point. I wasn't fan of this method in old Alone in the Dark games, but in Abducted it works pretty well. Partly because the game is played with mouse and character's orientation doesn't matter. You click on the screen, that's where the character tries to go next. Steps, stairs and other levels are automatically scaled, which is very nice as it makes playing smoother. Glowing symbols are shown at locations of interest and they work as a nice visual cue.
I wasn't very happy with how terminals work. They weren't really explained anywhere, so only way I could start operating was to hack them. There's also an option to solve them, but I gave up after trying two terminals. The solving method felt like annoying trial and error, without any real mental effort, except memorization. The solving method might be explained later on in the game, but during the first hour or so, it just felt either boring or infuriating, depending on how long I tried to use it.
Soundscape of the game is pretty minimal. Low ambient noise that doesn't draw any attention to it. Special effects are used sparingly and they are nothign memorable. Player feels that they really are more or less alone in the area they're exploring.
For some reason cinematics kept crashing on my computer, so sadly I don't know how much they explain the game, the world it is set and the player character.

Furi is an indie game created by a studio called The Game Bakers, and as a fan of indie games myself, I tried this game out myself after watching some trailers that captured my desired attention. It is a remarkable challenging game, and I will explain my thoughts about what this game offered that met my expectations very well.
The qoute from the game description pretty much sums it up the whole game after playing it. You were captured, tortured, but now, it is your chance to escape by killing the Jailers. Despite the script sounding minimal, it is well-written and offers memorable qoutes that is appealing as it leaves it up to you to interpret the emotional appeals behind it. Every character you face builds part of the story as they reflect the protaganist's actions and past.
Here's an interesting thing about this game. We all know how video games work, you fight through a bunch of enemies and then face the boss. But in Furi, the bosses are your enemies. The concept is a lot similar like Shadow of The Colossus, where you fight bosses only and you have to be smart to know their attack patterns against the tough bosses. At the beginning of every fight, the camera angle starts off in an overhead view as you are equiped with a gun that is a lot like Mega Man's blaster, and a neon energy-saber sword. The combat is fast-paced, filled with hack-and-slash combos, and bullet hell sequences that keeps every fight challengingly hard. It is really difficult as well, and it requires knowledge to recognize their attack patterns in order to vanquish your toughest foes.
The entire game has several types of environments for every Jailer (boss) that fits along their character, personality, and setting. The parts where the game shines its true colors are the walking phases. After you defeat a boss, you will move on to the next one as you take a stroll across different worlds. The camera angles makes these walking phases enjoyable to watch, especially when it looks very cinematic. I would play this game again just to take several screenshots because the graphics are really pleasing to the eye and are perfectly fitting for desktop wallpapers.
This is the main reason why this game has sold me for: the music. Furi offers amazing soundtracks from artists like Carpenter Brut, Waveshaper, Scattle and more. These artists compose songs of 80's outrun and synthwave, and it's a must-have for those who are a big fan of these genres like myself. Also, if you are familiar with the Hotline Miami franchise and its OST, Furi offers more songs for your library and playlist. The Game Bakers studio uses their music superbly great for the use of crossfading and blending the sounds in certain scenes to match the intensity of the fights and walking phases. It is a different experience to listen the music comparing to just listen it regularly from a music player.
The game only has 10 levels, and it takes at least 7 hours to beat it on the recommended difficulty (more than 7 for those who are having a hard time). I would have given the game a better score if it has a few more bosses to fight. However, every boss you defeated gives you this worthwhile satisfaction and every Jailer is really tough to beat. You can try to get a better rank in practice mode, and you will get rewarded with concept artwork depending the Jailer you faced against. After the game is beaten once, you unlock a harder difficulty to play again, if you are willing to take a challenge to the extreme. Plus, a speedrun mode with a worldwide scoreboard to keep yourself busy and challenge against everyone to see who can finish the game faster in one run.
Despite how short it is, it is a fantastic and enjoyable game for an indie one and it should gotten more attention to see how beautifully crafted it was made. A fair warning though, this game is not for everyone and it is only for those who love to look for a decent challenge. Trust me, even though the fights are really tough and can really wreck your day, beating one after another leaves a great satisfiying feeling of accomplishment for vanquishing your worst opponent, like it is your worst enemy ever. I give this game an 8/10 for the awesome soundtracks, the intense fights, the crafty dialogues, the immersive environments, and the additonal replayability.

The music in this game is boring, but more importantly, it's
, which completely ruins the gameplay. You'd think the point of a game like this would be to split each song up into tracks so that you can reconstruct it on a track-by-track basis. But each "song" is just a succession of disconnected noises, so all you're doing is playing Simon Says: you listen to a sound, and then you find the same sound in your inventory and put it in the slot. Even when you have to "loop" sounds, they're still separated from everything else (and the songs have no rhythm), so this is just a matter of counting how many times the sound repeats and then punching in that number. Furthermore, because the music is all droning electronica, trying to tell the difference between some of the sounds is extremely annoying. And if you're having trouble, the only tool at your disposal is a hint button that tells you which parts you have wrong, rather than something like a mixing board that would actually help you identify the sounds, which is what the game is pretending to be about. In short, this is a trial-and-error game whose musical element is entirely superficial.

It can barely be called a "game". The puzzle aspect is almost non-existent: it's repetitive and tedious, rather than challenging. Most of the music tracks are forgettable and uninspiring, and some are just a pain to listen to. And you'll have to listen them A LOT in order to complete the level.
I like the idea of a musical puzzle, but this game simply does not deliver what it promises.

This game is amazing! I first saw Circuits on steam greenlight, and thought that the concept would be very enjoyable. The creator went above and beyond my expectations, and the full game is one of my favorites in my lirbrary so far! The music in the game is amazing, the controls are easy to use and enjoyable, the graphics are simple, but they are also beautiful at the same time!
Circuits is played by first listening a song or part of a song, then filling in parts with the short clips that are provided to you. You will fill in parts for beats, bass, piano, synths, and even some vocals parts. If you get stuck on a certain part, you can listen to individual layers (such as one layer for bass, one for synths, and one for vocals) so that you can hear each part in more detail. If you're still stuck, you can also use the hints to show what is wrong, or place one sphere in the correct spot. Once all parts are placed, you can play the song to listen to how your work has turned out!
I would suggest buying this for anyone who is interested in listening to, teaching, or creating music. I enjoy learning and teaching vocal music, and have developed a good ear for hearing and learning parts from it. When I saw this game, I though that this game was perfect for me, because I already could pick out parts easily without switching layers, and continue to play to train my ear even just a bit more! I would highly recommend this game!
EDIT: After 10.4 Hours total, multiple playthroughs, and some achievement getting, I have finally completed this game 100%, and enjoyed it very much! Please support these developers, so they can create more great things like this!

There's no shame in saying that this is simply a love letter/remake of Unreal Tournament (down to the inclusion of the UT classic UT DM map Deck 16).  A little more light and fluffy than the original, but not quite as flighty as UT2004.  Built on the Unreal engine, it very much maintains the basic physics and gameplay dynamics of the best of the UT series down to the dodging, and double jump/dodge of the later UT games.    It also runs smooth as butter.  A very comfy, easy to pick up and play twitch shooter.   I took the plunge after a bit and paid for the full version and it's well worth the $15.00, especially since old school twitch shooters are so few and far between these days.  But, the free version is a no brainer, simply a few options less than the paid.
I definitely say pick this up and play around with it and get the word out on this free gem of a game, escpecially if you are vet of the classic Unreal and Quake franchises.  This is a back to basics, beautiful, simple, fun treat.  Included are classic DM and Team DM modes, plus standard Domination (king of the hill), CTF and other familiar modes (including vehicles/mechs in some levels) from the heyday of competive solo and team FPS of the last 15 years.  Looks great, feels great, helluva lot of fun.   It's nice to occasionally  pick up an easy to play shooter that sheds all of high learning curve RPG style shooters that are the rage now days.   Play for hours or a few minutes.  Easy to learn.  A shiny new coat of paint on classic FPS format.

Normally, I wouldn't recommend games that make buyers jump through hoops and fix errors ourselves. We pay for the games, they should be playable right off the bat. However, this game is one hoop worth jumping through, especially when it's on sale. This is a treat for LEGO and Harry Potter fans. It looks like the movies, but it's a lot more fun. I've just finished Story Mode, and yes, there is a game-crashing bug in the last level of Year 3. But it can be easily fixed. (My rig is Core-i3, 8 GB RAM, Radeon HD4770, Win7 64 bit)
Here's how to fix it. (Credits to people who dedicated their time and effort to find the solution, and everyone sharing it. Thanks a lot :)
1. Find PCCONFIG.TXT file.
[XP] C:\Documents and Settings\admin.HVTS764\Application Data\WB Games\LEGO HarryPotter\
[VISTA & Win7] C:\Users\USER NAME\AppData\Roaming\WBGames\LEGO HarryPotter\
2. Back up the original file, then edit the file. Basically, turn everything graphic-related down to 0.
FileVersion 3
ScreenWidth 1024
ScreenHeight 768
WindowWidth 1016
WindowHeight 734
WindowLeft 0
WindowTop 0
ScreenRefreshRate 75
VerticalSync 0
FSAA 0
AspectRatio 0
TextureQuality 0
SoftParticles 0
ForceMultithreadedD3D 0
IgnoreVendorPresets 0
Brightness 10.000000
SFXVolume 10
MusicVolume 10
MasterVolume 10
MusicEnabled 1
MouseSensitivity 10
InvertY 0
Vibration 0
BloomEnabled 0
ExposureControlEnabled 0
DoFEnabled 0
DesiredShadowMethod 0
ShadowsEnabled 0
DesiredDynamicLightQuality 0
SpeedBlurEnabled 0
MotionBlurEnabled 0
ProcessColourEnabled 0
WaterDistortionEnabled 0
EdgeAAEnabled 0
SSAOEnabled 0
RingEffectEnabled 0
LensFilterEnabled 0
AllowVendorExtensions 0
TTAnimationMode 0
UseHires 0
UseHiresPending 0
ForceShaderModel 0
This will send the graphic back in time to Playstation 1.5 era. But it should be playable now.
3. Play the level. After finishing Year 3, quit the game and bring back the original PCCONFIG.TXT.
You should be able to start Year 4 with all the high settings again.
Enjoy :)

This was the first lego game I played and if I'm honest I have to say I wouldn't play this game on my own. However, I purchased it so I could play a game with my eldest son and in that regard it has not disappointed as it really is great fun as a coop game.
The game plays in 2D with depth and your view is from the side looking slightly down.
You control one character at a time with various characters available depending on where you are. You can switch between characters to make use of the different abilities available to each character with the computer controlling the non-player controlled characters and basically just moving them along with you.
The puzzles whilst not always logically solved (at least in my mind) are generally good fun, although a few are a bit tedious in that it seems to me its just a case of trying just about everything you can think of and the final solution simply has no logical reason why it should work behind it other than it does work. I also found some of the boss battles a bit tedious, e.g. final boss at end of level 2.
As only a casual follower of the Harry Potter films the game seems to keep close enough to the storyline for me to relate it to the film.
On the basis of playing this game I am purchasing other lego games as they come on sale with a view to playing those with my son too.

I played a fair bit of the demo of this and found a decently fun Tron-styled tank combat game. When I got around to playing the full game, I found that they took the whole Tron thing and ran with it, making about as blatant a rip-off as rip-offs go. From the plot to the obvious copy of the MCP, very little is original about this game. The walking portions are also pretty bad and only highlight the low budgetness of the game with poor animations and textures, and nothing you do while walking is very fun at all. It also proclaims to be part one of two games, and as far as I'm aware no Tank Universal 2 exists, so if you can somehow get into the story, you'll probably be left wanting.
All that aside though, the tank combat is serviceable, though I feel it really would benefit from online multiplayer. It would be a great stretch to call this a good game, as it seems to focus on the worst parts of itself, but if you can get it for cheap (I think I've seen 90% off coupons for it) and really dig tanks and Tron, it's probably worth a lark.

The large levels are nice, and the cyberpunk style works well with the music and the setting. Its like a damn Tron civil war.

After seeing seeing 5 out of 6 people have disagreed with my review, as well as how highly the game is rated on STEAM, I decided to play a bit of Game+ and see if I have missed something or to change my viewpoint.
The music, art and writing are all good and I agree that the characters do have depth.  However, I still find the "interactive" part of the game very lacking and not fully utilized. I wished if gameplay evolved and got a bit challenging as you progress in the story. I also wished if there were stronger choices and a feeling of changing one's fate by serving a different kind of drink. Sure, you can get people drunk and gives you alternative/additional dialogue but you can't deny that if the game plot branched drastically, it would've made me feel more involved with those wonderful character.
In any case, the game is still good for those like to read a linear visual novel. If the developers ever decided to create another game within the world of VA-11 HALL-A, I hope they consider to add more depth and weight to interactivity and more twists and turns to the story.

Some people cannot enjoy puzzle games no matter how perfect it is. This is why a perfect game has an 87 on metacritic.
I have not heard a legitimate criticism levied at this game. Here are a few that I will go through:
-Frustrating/Too hard
You can't criticise a game for being too hard, especially puzzle games where there's no way to adjust difficulty. That's like disliking a classic novel because your reading comprehension is fifth grade. Or hating Dark Souls cause you don't want to git gud. If The Witness is too hard, go and play some easier puzzle games, read a math/logic textbook, and come back.
-No Story

A wonderful demonstration of what Unity can do when a team with drive, artistic merit, and a good idea are behind it, Furi is a Hack and Slash Bullet Hell Boss Rush with a demented sensibility and a surprisingly melancholy story. A series of Jailors stands between you and freedom, and you must kill them all to become free. Who you are and what your freedom will mean is only revealed in bits and peices and in passing, giving the game a good sense of wonder and mystery, despite it's short run time.
The only complaint I have is that the 'True' Final boss of the game spoils a lot of the mystery that makes Furi engaging, calls to question a lot of character motivations, and locks the Final Boss behind an absolutely *bafflingly* stupid moral choice that even Bioware would have called too ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to put in.
But if you turn off the game after the credits and before the epilogue? You're left with one hell of a ride.

I could go on about how the game needs free customization for button layout and that some of the controls have unfortunate downsides (dash on button release, charged shot aiming, awkward parry/dash while shooting) or that the sound cues for when to parry actually make it harder to learn the game (because early bosses take too long to swing)... but at the end of the day, Furi is just an outstanding, cool experience that anyone who values the journey of learning something hard (and fun) should not miss. The music and artwork are fantastic and the walking cutscenes inbetween fights do a great job of setting the mood (and they don't strive to be more than just that).
Similar to a real martial artist your beginnings will be humble, you will falter at every unexpected attack while learning and internalizing the basics, and just when you think you're slowly getting good, the next boss will require you to step up your game in a different aspect of Furi's combat. Once you've done this enough times and built up enough muscle memory, those challenging early bosses will seem harmless, their attacks slow and predictable, so don't give up too early and take a break after a while, Furi takes a lot of concentration.

The boss fights in this game are amazing, but the controls and unskippable cutscenes killed a lot of the enjoyment of this game for me.
The control design and mechanics in this game is bizarre.  Parrying is satisfying but ridiculously easy, shooting is okay but a bit annoying to control, youre basically just firing in a general direction and slowly wiggling your stick to make sure you land shots.  Dodging feels absolutely terrible, which in a bullet-hell type game is extremely annoying.  The result is that melee combat is probably the highlight of this game, and everything else feels lackluster.
There are also unskippable cutscenes that last for ages and don't even show anything,  there's barely any plot in this game, just a bunch of "deep" quotes and lots of walking.  It really ruins the flow of a boss rush type game, and if you're not into the sort of techno-punk samurai aesthetic the cutscenes will probably just have you tabbing out until theyre over.
I really did want to like this game as the boss fights are quite nicely done and challenging (the Sniper boss and the Aquatic boss are probably some of my favorite boss fights in any game I've played), but there are too many frustrating aspects for me to give this game a genuine recommendation.  I'd pick this up if you've got a soft spot for this kind of aesthetic and are extremely patient.

As a music producer in training I got interested in trying this game from it's description, however while it's claiming to be a puzzle game about music production Circuits is more like a version of Simon Says where Simon is a robot that mimicks samples of bad EDM songs.
The game is basically a rather small collection of 25 levels where a timeline is set up, and you have to put in audio samples given to you in the correct spots. Not in a studio-like enviorment as the screenshots make it look like, that is for the song editor where you can make your own premade sample beats if you want, but in a clunky branching line with pre-destined spots where you are allowed to put things.
You then have to preview the song and figure out which bits fit where in the song, and maybe it's just because I have practice in the actual thing this is based on, but it seems like there is no real challenge or thought to this? All you basically do is painstakingly listen over the song in a unintuitive interface and then drag and drop the right sound clips to win. Not so much a puzzle as much as just making sure to pay attention.
This might have been able to work somewhat better if it felt rewarding to finish these songs, but honestly I really couldn't stand the songs in this game. Music taste is of course 100% subjecive so take this with a grain of salt, but all the songs I heard before I gave up out of boredom sounded like free pre-made snippets of beats, and it almost seems like the game itself doesn't like it's own soundtrack as it's perfectly fine with letting you skip the song you just constructed to get to the next level, so it makes the tedious effort to make these beats feel like a complete waste of time.
There is also something to be said about this game about audio production having somewhat bad audio mixing to it. There is no options for changing the volume in game, and the default volume of the game is sometimes so loud the music starts clipping (sounding unintentionally distorted and broken) which makes it rather unpleasant to listen to sometimes.
If you have a interest in audio production and you have never ever used production or mixing software in your life then sure, this might be an okay way to get into some of the basics of it, especially since it comes bundled with a primitive production software to make beats in as well as the game itself. However I can't recommend this to anybody who have ever interacted with the real deal, this is less the Guitar Hero equivelant of audio production and more like the Power Gig version of it.

And so goes the dramatic intro scene of
. Not knowing what I was getting myself into, I bought the game at a discounted price after seeing a very good friend play it. I remember looking at the store page and ridiculing it at first, thinking it was a 'stupid, little game'. Well in essence, it actually is that ... But it is so much fun that I told myself to review it right after completing the game. Now that I did, it is time to talk about what this game has to offer.
First, I'd like to mention that this game probably won't be for everyone. Just like certain puzzle and point & click games, this game is played by a fairly limited amount of people. Not because it is bad, but because it is a very specific genre (that not everyone will like) that is targeted at a certain audience. So please keep that in mind.
This game is specified as a HOG (hidden object game) and as its name implies, you play through the game finding hidden objects so that you can advance your adventure. You play through several scenes (or environments) and have to find objects that you can then use for certain actions, puzzles, hidden object scenes ... This pretty much sums up the gameplay and may not sound very exciting, but it's actually very satisfying. Even little and simple actions and puzzles are fun to do and solve.
The great and calm soundtrack that I hear in the background really makes it a very soothing experience. The story kept me motivated to complete the game, even though it may not have been a unique one. I just loved playing this game inbetween my more 'serious' games and I am grateful that I discovered Artifex Mundi, the creater of amazing HOG's.
+ A story that is not really unique, but still very enjoyable
+ Ok voice acting
+ Great, relaxing soundtrack
+ Really satisfying gameplay
+ Difficulty is just about right
+ Attention to detail
+ Decent length
+ Extra little chapter!
+ Overall fun and engaging experience
- /

The things that make Star Conflict different from War Thunder is the different classes and abilities and factions. I will give a brief run down on the classes and factions. There are a lot of things this game does right.  If you're new to Magic (or haven't played it years, like myself) this game does a good job of teaching the mechanics of the game in its current incarnation.  There's a lot of variety and replayability in the base game, between campaign mode, challenges and the number of decks available to play.  The Sealed Deck play is also very nice, allowing you to build a deck from a random distribution of cards.
The downsides to me are a lack of support.  If you happen to encounter the bug where you are unable to enter promo pack codes (as I did) then you can expect to spend a lot of time hunting through forums hoping for a solution to the problem.  It should be fixed as a patch, but the official solution is to muck about with local game files and hope for the best.  Another bug is present in the leaderboard.  It's full of impossible scores, which kind of defeats the purpose of having a leaderboard.  There isn't much point in having one if players can't honestly determine where they stand.
Overall, the good greatly outweighs the bad.  Highly recommend.

The Witness is not a game that everyone will appreciate, but it will strongly resonate with some people. Much like Jonathan Blow's previous game, Braid, The Witness takes a simple game mechanic and explores it as fully as possible. While the actual gameplay involved in solving The Witness' series of two-dimensional mazes differs significantly from Braid's time-manipulation in a platforming context, I feel that most fans of Blow's last game will love this one even more, while those who thought it was pretentious will think that The Witness is even more pretentious.
The game is still "just" a game, so I don't want to get anyone's hopes up too high, but from playing well over a thousand games over the last few decades, I would have to say that The Witness is one of the most noteworthy and original games that I have experienced. A large part of one's appreciation for the game will be based on what one puts into it though. If you look up any spoilers or hints, you're not really playing the game and are better off spending your time and money elsewhere.
If you play games for the story, you should pass on this one. If you play games for the gameplay or challenge (and have an analytical mindset), you should definitely give it a shot.

Playstation-Renaissance. These were the first words that came to my mind when I first saw and played Abducted. Why? It feels like a hybrid of Parasite Eve and J.U.L.I.A.: Among the stars, combining a cinematic third-person-adventure with old school point and click, including deep story, puzzles and insta-deaths. If you are interested, please read further.
This game is still in Early Access and thus I will focus on what I have seen and experienced so far in detail.
This game tries to focus on classical style and gameplay. If you can`t live and play with a directed camera, you should probably pass.
I do not want to spoil everything for you so let me start with this: A woman awakes in a strange place, figuring it might be some kind of alien spaceship and besides your name there is not much memory left. How did you get there? And why? Fortunately, you are not alone. Your arm speaks with you. Well, not exactly your arm but a gadget you seem to wear that looks half mechanical, half biological. It contains an AI that speaks with you, trying to explain your surroundings and purpose. It is obvious that something must have happened to her and to this ship. You, the player, shall unfold it.
While exploring the ship you stumble across a lot of strange or unique things and beings that own a very nice lore and description, for example morphing alien skin, blind and unmerciful tentacles and panels, growing like trees from the ground. Additionally, ARM (The name I will refer to your gadget) provides you with a huge database, filled with useful information about everything and has some interesting dialogue options to offer. It is clear right from the start that the developers try to create a strong fictional environment that sucks you up, at least if you are interested in story-driven games.
As stated before, this game tries to approach gamers with a classical style, meaning a fixed and directed camera to create a cinematic experience and movement via mouse-clicking while weaving puzzles, try-and-error-passages and even combat into the third-person-gameplay. Saying this it should be already clear that Abducted is not a game for everybody.  Moving onto pillars or downwards happens via clicking, meaning: If she can reach the spot, she will do it via climbing or jumping without forcing you to press any other inputs. She is human after all so don`t expect her to jump 2 meters upwards or run like a gepard, something you should keep in mind when there is a difficult passage to solve where some moving pillars might crush your humble body, if you were to slow.
Exploration, Puzzles and Combat are things you should expect. Look around and read a lot, find unique stuff and ask ARM about it. Puzzles I have encountered so far can be mostly solved in two different ways: Hacking or “Solving”. Choosing the Hack-Option, you are forced to play a small mini-game to overcome the “security system”. This can be tough sometimes and the further you approach ingame, the harder it gets. Option 2 uses symbols of an unknown alien language. Find the right “letters” and don`t let yourself get tricked, the system tries to mix true and false symbols. It`s not too hard but not too easy either, so expect to be fairly challenged. Combat is something that happens in real time, forcing Eve (the name I chose for her) to use a shield, a pulsar laser or even manipulation, that works a bit like telekinesis. This is not really an action game so don`t expect yourself to run around shooting and killing all the time. It rather works with making the right choice at the right time. Sometimes it might come in handy to use manipulate, who said a pillar can`t be used as a weapon?
Something special I`d like to mention here is the skill tree. Finding objects, having dialogues, solving puzzles and killing stuff earns you skill points. These can be spent to strengthen your laser, boost the duration of your shield or making more objects available for manipulation. It`s a nice idea so far that adds some depth and satisfaction, although I think that the tree is not fully balanced and done yet. This might change in future updates.
Technically there is not much to argue about. The graphics look dark and somehow otherworldly, creating mostly organic surfaces and a breathing, living atmosphere. It feels more like running through a body than a ship, adding a true creepy mood to the game. The devs used their own engine here and it works fine so far. Sure, it is not top notch graphic like in Witcher 3, but that is something I don`t need to enjoy a good game. What should be said here is that there is not much to config right now, besides the resolution and there are still some bugs left like moving through certain small objects but the shapes used for tentacles and stuff do look really nice! If you want to check some ingame footage, feel free to look at a dozen screens I took.
Low-Pitched, pumping sounds round out the atmosphere of being “abducted” but there could be more improvement to certain passages. I understand that I should get the impression of how “lonely” I am but the background would do well with a bit more noise and sound.
There is a lot of text in this game and I like it a lot. Adding a voice to ARM and Eve is not a necessity but it would add even more reliability when hearing Eves scared voice while she stumbles into her involuntary adventure.
What the game offers so far is the unfinished story mode, I already spent 3 hours into, with a catchy story and nice mixture of exploration, puzzle and (sometimes tricky) combat and a “Challenge Level”, that seems to function like a survival mode. The CL seems to be not done yet but is already worth a try. There are some bugs I found while playing and already reported, that will be squashed in future updates soon. This is an indie project and should be treated like one, keeping in mind that it only costs 9-10 $ right now.
I know, this Review is pretty much in detail. If you made it here, still reading, I am sure you are that kind of gamer who should give Abducted a try. I read the other reviews and also an answer that was written by one of the developers, focussing on how this game should be treated. It`s a classical take with modern graphics. If you came here for a generic (survival) horror like Slender and Co, you might be disappointed. If you are interested in a scary, well written fictional story, filled with lore and text, you must give Abducted a chance, it`s worth the try.
My personal verdict so far is 7,5 /10 since there is still a lot room for improvement but the current state already offers an interesting and somehow unique game.

There are no words that can do justice to the utter awesomeness and jaw-dropping(ness) that is Furi.
Let's start with gameplay.
Furi is a boss-rush, twin-stick and "sword-fighting" game that will kick you when you are down. The bosses are hard and will make you quit, but the game will pull you back in for a second, third and eventually 15th try until you finally beat it. The bosses fire projectiles, lasers and waves at you from all sides of the alloted movement space, often moving around as they do so. Your job is to fire back and use quick-dashes to damage and dodge. The bosses have multiple phases with each increasing the difficulty of the fight. At the end of most stages you initiate a close-combat sword fight with your character parrying and striking back while the boss attacks in telegraphed swings and strikes. That is the basic premise with the formula being warped and expanded with each vastly different and unique bosses with unique "worlds". One final point in gameplay is that, the controls on controller are tight as hell and well mapped for precision and speed.
Story
There isn't much I can say without spoiling the potential for you to have a mind blowing and amazing story experience. The beginning of the game leads you on with a few hints as to what is happening and your guide, "The Voice", fills you in on miscellaneous tid-bits and information about the world, you and the bosses. The story twists and turns and you begin to take on a different roll because of the things you learn. The very end of the story is truly, a masterpiece.
Music
Now, I don't usually buy a game's OST or listen to the music outside of the game that much but this soundtrack is joining my small list of two exceptions. The music in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic. Not only does it aid the story with each track moving in and out of the story threads, but it adds tention and emotion to the boss fights you are having. The tracks are motivating, moving and sometimes, even saddening. The music and sound design in general (especially sound ques) is top-notch and should be applauded.
Design
The art style is not for everyone, especially those who do not like physics-clipping, but I personally liked the artstyle. It is very refreshing and pleasing to see a game with an art style that is so new and different. This art style is simple but it goes a long way in world building.
Putting my copious amounts of praisea aside, the game is not perfect. The campaign lasts around 8 hours(however there are other modes such as speedrun that you can play as well as another difficulty level), There are difficulty spikes (though the game does ease you onto the harder and harder bosses, there will be bosses that you personally find extremely challenging), there is some imput lag in the controller when quickly switching from one button or action to another and the game MUST be played with a controller, unless you are a masochist.
In conclusion,
This game is fantastic. At 19.99 you might find it a bit pricey for an 8-hour campaign (with deaths and muck-ups) but believe me, it is well worth it, and if you find it on sale, that is even better. If you would take a stranger's internet advice, take mine and buy this wonderful, wonderful game.
