– The Edge
is an action twin-stick, bullet hell, hack n slash boss rush, the first PC debut title for The Game Bakers. You are The Stranger, a white haired, katana wielding badass. You are being tortured in a multi-dimensional prison. A mysterious figure wearing a rabbit mask, The Voice frees you. Your objective: escape. Guarding the cells of the prison; Jailers, the Guardians, handpicked fighters with one simple objective, to stop you from escaping.
has a basic story: escape the prison, kill whoever tries to stop you. The thing I loved about
was how the story was fairly straightforward, yet was intriguing enough to keep me playing. In a game that is completely about boss fights and solid gameplay, it would have been easy for the developers to ignore the writing, but they crafted an intriguing world and characters I wanted to know more about. The backstory is there, if you look and listen closely enough to The Voice’s exposition as you walk from one boss fight to the next.
writers did an incredible job of characterising each of The Guardians you fight in the story with such little scenes. In between every boss fight is a walking section where The Voice tells you about the upcoming Guardian, their history with you, their personality. These walking sections effectively tell you everything you need to know about the upcoming fight. The fights feel so much more personal when you learn about your opponent’s backstory why they are fighting you, and the way they behave during the fights. One of the most memorable quotes in the game was The Voice describing the personality of the 7th boss; The Burst.
It’s at that point I fell in love with the writing, you immediately know everything about the type of person she is in a single line of dialogue. Personally, I loved how they set the scene of each of the bosses you were about to face.
Depending on how good of a gamer you are,
can be fairly short, ranging anywhere from in between 2 hours if you know
what you’re doing (I managed a 2 hour run on my 2nd playthrough, and that was only after practicing every boss fight at least 5 times each) to 5-7 hours. It may seem fairly short, but there is a lot of replay value; a higher difficulty mode that unlocks after finishing the story, and a dedicated speedrun mode that cuts out all the walking sections in between boss fights and cutscenes, that kept me playing long after I finished the story.
is a straight out boss rush. This is a game that is nothing but 1v1 multiphase boss fights. And they are
If you’re looking for a “
difficulty” game that is nothing but intense, action packed boss fights that give you an adrenaline rush,
is the game you’re looking for.
You have very basic methods of attack, your katana for melee and your pistol for ranged. Individually none of these would be interesting, you can only do a basic 4 hit combo and a charged slash with the katana, and basic shots and a charged blast with the pistol. Put together however, and it’s more acceptable, if a little lacking in depth. Bosses vary enough that you’ll be using everything in your arsenal to take them down, most require a mix of melee and pistol, some focus heavily melee and one is entirely ranged only. Even though the mechanics remain the same throughout, all boss fights have distinct tactics that are unique to them and made every fight memorable.
Defensive options likewise are basic but effective. There’s a dodge move that’s used to avoid AOE attacks and ranged attacks, and a parry that blocks melee attacks. The parrying is particular satisfying, successful parries restore small bits of health, and parrying at the precise moment allows for a counter-attack. I’d recommend using a controller in this game, it’s not unplayable with kb/m, but some of the more intense bullet hell phases are infinitely easier with a controller.
The way the game handled failure was one the most interesting aspects. Being as hard as it is, you’ll naturally be dying a lot. You effectively have 3 lives. When your health depletes, you lose 1 life. You regain health, but so does the boss, and you have to repeat the current phase. Defeating a boss phase restores 1 of your lives. I liked this design because it was fair, at the very minimum you’ll always have 2 lives. This gives enough leeway to be fair but still tough; you’ll always have at least 1 life to learn the attack patterns of the current phase so you can adapt, but if you don’t you’re dead. In other words, you need to GIT GUD if you want to beat this game.
Games that are considered “
difficulty,” in my eyes have a requirement, and that is to be hard, but fair.
for 95% of the time, is hard but fair. Having S ranked every boss, I can safely say that there is nothing in
I would consider “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.” Every death in the game comes from mistakes that you make, not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t attack that a boss does.
had me playing over and over, even when I was getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me I still had a massive grin on my face, ready to give it another shot when I died and learn from my mistakes.
Furi’s has a gorgeous art style, it’s simple yet colourful and stylish. It’s graphics are fairly basic, but the strong art direction is the selling point. Each of the levels and boss arenas of the prison have a unique aesthetic and personality, from floating rocks high in the clouds, to sandy deserts, to snowy mountaintops.
The boss designs were one of the highlights of the game, I always felt a sense of excitement to see what the boss I would be fighting next would look like. Every boss has a distinct personality that was amplified by their character design, highly stylized and memorable.

has a great range of synthwave tunes that match perfectly to the adrenaline fuelled gameplay. The enviroments introduced throuhg these walking segments are beautiful though and sometimes even "react" to the music played.
+The story introduced in the end is pretty neat and explains pretty much every question about the protagonist. The game's focus is obviously not on the narrative, so I think it's fine that the story only picks up at the end.
+The skill curve is great. On your first try, you will struggle against bullet and movement patterns and be very cautious, but after I beat the game I noticed how easy it can be outplay their patterns and hit them with charged attacks in between their moves.
-First off, the boss order just seems wrong. The third boss is one of the most difficult bosses in the game, while the eigth one is incredibly easy for plot reasons; which is fine in general, but shouldn't be this late. The fight would have been much more impactful if it was one of the earlier ones.
-Personally, I think the game could have been a bit more difficult. It took me 3 hours to beat the game, and after the 4th boss I didn't need any second tries ( except the last boss ). Some fights just didn't seem epic or varied enough.
- The dodge is executed on button release, not on button press, which just doesnt work. It leads to the player failing a lot of dodges they have done perfectly, and the long dash is just never worth the hassle of charging it up ( I never used it once after the tutorial ). This could have been solved by a simple option that lets the player rebind the long dash to another key.
- Minor thing; If you play the game with keyboard and mouse ( as I did ) you NEED to set the target mode to "Screen" and the Movement mode to "Directional". The default options are stupidly bad ( they are kind of trying to emulate the gamepads joystick, which doesn't work at all and makes dodging confusing and nigh impossible ) and should'nt be like that. The game was however, perfectly playable without a gamepad after I changed these options.
It's a stylish game that feels great and left me wanting more, greater fights and it deserves a lot more attention.
Keep in mind that you will probably need a lot more time than 3 hours to beat it if you aren't experienced in bullet-hell games. The game also features a boss rush mode and a higher difficulty that unlocks after beating the game, which greatly changes the enemy movesets.

Planetbase is your basic city/colony building game based on a remote planet. It's similar to games like SimCity, Citys: Skylines or Banished except that it's set in outer space. You play the role of an architect who directs the colonist where and what to build in order to survive. This means supplying constant oxygen along with electricity, food, water and other basic life necessities.
I just picked up the game this afternoon (10/16/2015) and already have played almost 3 hours. I encountered no or very little frame rate problems on my mid-range system. There is a tutorial that I highly recommend you go through. It's a bit long (about 15 or 20 minutes) but well worth playing through as it gives you tips and shows you every thing you need to know to get started and to be successful.
The game's graphics are well done and the game play is smooth. There are several different types of pods (buildings) and mechanical structures (water storage, power storage). Unlike some other city building simulators you can place items inside the pods. For example, you build a "Canteen" (lunchroom) and then have to place lunch tables and water fountains inside the canteen. You can also place video boards, plants and other decorative items inside the pods. I believe this gives the game a more personal feeling as you can decorate and place items in areas where you want them, sort of like The Sims, but not quite as detailed.
The user interface is informative, easy to use and well thought out. The controls are a bit touchy and I found myself "over steering" and moving further than I wanted at times. The controls used are the same as most others in this genre, WASD for moving forward, left, back and right, and Q and E to rotate left and right. The game's mechanics are good and I encountered no glitches or bugs during my game play. The game auto saves in increments and you can manually save at any time.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys these types of game. If you buy it at a discount (currently 15% off at $16.99) it's well worth the purchase price.
Space-suit up and see how large of a colony you can build on Mars!
Here's a video showing my game play:

This is based  just on a few initial hours of play.
OVERALL: A tidy game based on a classic concept, the city builder in space.  You are in charge of settling a harsh planet with just a handful of settlers and a couple of bots. You can't control them individually; you just plan and build structures, fill them with furtniture, and they go about their business according to their various classes (worker, engineer, doctor, biologist). You need to see to your population's basic needs (air, water, food, rest, and entertainment). Buidling a landing pad gives you a link to the wider world and a way to increase your population. Perservere against random events, build your colony, and eventually, you unlock powerful superbuildings.
PROs:
Beautiful, crisp graphics. I don't have a crazy powerful rig and I can run it on highest graphics settings no problem, and it looks great.
Interesting challenge of connecting domes together into a network and managing traffic flow.
Doesn't hold your hand; if you mess up, everyone dies harshly.
Day and night cycle which isn't just cosmetic but actually has a strategic role. You generate power (which, among other things powers your O2 generator) two ways, either through solar (which only works during the day) or wind (which fluctuates unpredictably).
Solves one of the problems of city builders, which is: how do you enable players to just sandbox but also make a challenging path forward. It does this by handing out "landmarks" when your colony achieves various, increasingly challenging conditions. The landmarks then unlock new levels (harder planets to colonize).
CONS:
Don't seem to be able to customize key bindings.
The UI is limited. It would be great to be able to unlock or shrink elements. You can't display all of the information on the screen, but are forced to toggle between two panes (kind of pointless if you have a widescreen monitor).
Missing some kind of census screen or way to view your population's characteristics at once. Likewise, no ability (that I can find) to cycle through your colony's population. You can click on individual people and find out information about them but you can't go back and forth among them quickly.
I don't know if this is a flaw or just a design decision I don't agree with, but you have very limited opportunities to tell your people what to do. This means you have to be really strategic and when things go pear shaped its hard to recover. It also means sometimes you have to watch frustratedly as they don't do what you want them to.

This is a pretty borderline "yes" recommend for me. While I did genuinely enjoy this game after all was said and done, it's definitely a game that I can't see a lot of people liking. For as long as the game is (took me just shy of 20 hours), the game has very little actual plot, which is a shame because they've created a pretty interesting world that I'd like to know more happenings of. Instead, the game focuses more simply on building characters. Most of the characters are genuinely interesting, and even most of the pretty despicable characters you find yourself wanting to talk to a little more. The dialogue is pretty good, and it's entertaining to read. The game also has some decent messages about loss and relationships, and it's very nice to see a game focus so much on a LGBT relationship.
But as much as I did like interacting with most of the characters, it left me wanting more of an actual plot to help move the game forward. There's also very little reason for this to be a game, as the actual "game" portion (the mixing of the drinks) is pretty mundane and uninteresting. I didn't really like that part, and it was often a chore that slowed down progression of reading conversations.
When all is said and done, I decided I'd give it a positive recommendation. Just don't go into this game thinking it's for everyone. It does take a while to warm up, and even then, this is a very niche game.

I always have trouble when thinking about how to suggest The Witness to friends and other players; not because it's not worth your time and money, but because it's so hard to explain what makes it so special and why everyone should at least give it a try.
There's no need to lie though: one of the main obstacles with suggesting it is that, at its core, The Witness is a puzzle game; your interactions in the game are exclusively limited to puzzles.
And yet, it's so well crafted that it may be among the best puzzle games ever made to date.
In The Witness, you wake up on an island that you're free to explore, accessing the various areas through completing hundreds of so-called "line puzzles" that are scattered everywhere.
There's no tutorial. There's no pointing arrow. There's not even text, save for the subtitles of various unrelated audio logs you'll find on the island, which are mechanically (but not thematically) unrelated to what you're going through. The Island and its puzzles, via design and balancing, are everything at the same time: they're your tutorial; they're your test; they're your guidance. The whole island is your puzzle, your chest to crack open and treasure to pillage. Progress is your goal, your tool and your reward at the same time, one thin line after the other.
After a brief and enclosed area that teaches you the very basic mechanics of interacting with puzzles, the world will open its gates and start teaching you how to progress via the puzzles themselves. Each area will present you with new rules without stating them, together with easy puzzles that serve the purpose of letting YOU, the player, the guest of the island, infer the rules on your own. As you progress through the areas you will start to understand the game's language, what it tells to you, and your mind will start deconstructing a new puzzle or even rule before you even start actively thinking about it.
But where do I go in this game? What do I do? You do line puzzles. The world will let you know how. The world will let you know where to go. Without saying a word, of course. Go out and explore. Find out for yourself.
The Witness is many things: a journey, a journey inside a journey, an excellent exercise in game and level design, a maieutic process of self-teaching and inductive learning, a beautiful still piece of colorful vistas...
What The Witness isn't, is being a game for everyone. We all have videogame genres that we can't stand, and puzzle games seem to be at least disliked by a vast portion of gamers, if not even hated.
And yet, The Witness manages to reach such high moments, to have such elegance in its design and progression that if you'll ever have to try out a puzzle game to see what the fuss is all about, it's this one.
Do you know that feeling when you finally solve a problem, or a puzzle in a game, and it feels really good? That "ooooh, yes, finally... I got here all on my own! Suck it, game!" feeling?
Now imagine that feeling being distilled, purified, made into a crystal, polished and put it inside a 30 to 40 hour game for you to partake of its beauty.
The Witness is this, and more.

There are no words that can do justice to the utter awesomeness and jaw-dropping(ness) that is Furi.
Let's start with gameplay.
Furi is a boss-rush, twin-stick and "sword-fighting" game that will kick you when you are down. The bosses are hard and will make you quit, but the game will pull you back in for a second, third and eventually 15th try until you finally beat it. The bosses fire projectiles, lasers and waves at you from all sides of the alloted movement space, often moving around as they do so. Your job is to fire back and use quick-dashes to damage and dodge. The bosses have multiple phases with each increasing the difficulty of the fight. At the end of most stages you initiate a close-combat sword fight with your character parrying and striking back while the boss attacks in telegraphed swings and strikes. That is the basic premise with the formula being warped and expanded with each vastly different and unique bosses with unique "worlds". One final point in gameplay is that, the controls on controller are tight as hell and well mapped for precision and speed.
Story
There isn't much I can say without spoiling the potential for you to have a mind blowing and amazing story experience. The beginning of the game leads you on with a few hints as to what is happening and your guide, "The Voice", fills you in on miscellaneous tid-bits and information about the world, you and the bosses. The story twists and turns and you begin to take on a different roll because of the things you learn. The very end of the story is truly, a masterpiece.
Music
Now, I don't usually buy a game's OST or listen to the music outside of the game that much but this soundtrack is joining my small list of two exceptions. The music in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic. Not only does it aid the story with each track moving in and out of the story threads, but it adds tention and emotion to the boss fights you are having. The tracks are motivating, moving and sometimes, even saddening. The music and sound design in general (especially sound ques) is top-notch and should be applauded.
Design
The art style is not for everyone, especially those who do not like physics-clipping, but I personally liked the artstyle. It is very refreshing and pleasing to see a game with an art style that is so new and different. This art style is simple but it goes a long way in world building.
Putting my copious amounts of praisea aside, the game is not perfect. The campaign lasts around 8 hours(however there are other modes such as speedrun that you can play as well as another difficulty level), There are difficulty spikes (though the game does ease you onto the harder and harder bosses, there will be bosses that you personally find extremely challenging), there is some imput lag in the controller when quickly switching from one button or action to another and the game MUST be played with a controller, unless you are a masochist.
In conclusion,
This game is fantastic. At 19.99 you might find it a bit pricey for an 8-hour campaign (with deaths and muck-ups) but believe me, it is well worth it, and if you find it on sale, that is even better. If you would take a stranger's internet advice, take mine and buy this wonderful, wonderful game.

is an action twin-stick, bullet hell, hack n slash boss rush, the first PC debut title for The Game Bakers. You are The Stranger, a white haired, katana wielding badass. You are being tortured in a multi-dimensional prison. A mysterious figure wearing a rabbit mask, The Voice frees you. Your objective: escape. Guarding the cells of the prison; Jailers, the Guardians, handpicked fighters with one simple objective, to stop you from escaping.
has a basic story: escape the prison, kill whoever tries to stop you. The thing I loved about
was how the story was fairly straightforward, yet was intriguing enough to keep me playing. In a game that is completely about boss fights and solid gameplay, it would have been easy for the developers to ignore the writing, but they crafted an intriguing world and characters I wanted to know more about. The backstory is there, if you look and listen closely enough to The Voice’s exposition as you walk from one boss fight to the next.
writers did an incredible job of characterising each of The Guardians you fight in the story with such little scenes. In between every boss fight is a walking section where The Voice tells you about the upcoming Guardian, their history with you, their personality. These walking sections effectively tell you everything you need to know about the upcoming fight. The fights feel so much more personal when you learn about your opponent’s backstory why they are fighting you, and the way they behave during the fights. One of the most memorable quotes in the game was The Voice describing the personality of the 7th boss; The Burst.
It’s at that point I fell in love with the writing, you immediately know everything about the type of person she is in a single line of dialogue. Personally, I loved how they set the scene of each of the bosses you were about to face.
Depending on how good of a gamer you are,
can be fairly short, ranging anywhere from in between 2 hours if you know
what you’re doing (I managed a 2 hour run on my 2nd playthrough, and that was only after practicing every boss fight at least 5 times each) to 5-7 hours. It may seem fairly short, but there is a lot of replay value; a higher difficulty mode that unlocks after finishing the story, and a dedicated speedrun mode that cuts out all the walking sections in between boss fights and cutscenes, that kept me playing long after I finished the story.

difficulty” game that is nothing but intense, action packed boss fights that give you an adrenaline rush,
is the game you’re looking for.
You have very basic methods of attack, your katana for melee and your pistol for ranged. Individually none of these would be interesting, you can only do a basic 4 hit combo and a charged slash with the katana, and basic shots and a charged blast with the pistol. Put together however, and it’s more acceptable, if a little lacking in depth. Bosses vary enough that you’ll be using everything in your arsenal to take them down, most require a mix of melee and pistol, some focus heavily melee and one is entirely ranged only. Even though the mechanics remain the same throughout, all boss fights have distinct tactics that are unique to them and made every fight memorable.
Defensive options likewise are basic but effective. There’s a dodge move that’s used to avoid AOE attacks and ranged attacks, and a parry that blocks melee attacks. The parrying is particular satisfying, successful parries restore small bits of health, and parrying at the precise moment allows for a counter-attack. I’d recommend using a controller in this game, it’s not unplayable with kb/m, but some of the more intense bullet hell phases are infinitely easier with a controller.
The way the game handled failure was one the most interesting aspects. Being as hard as it is, you’ll naturally be dying a lot. You effectively have 3 lives. When your health depletes, you lose 1 life. You regain health, but so does the boss, and you have to repeat the current phase. Defeating a boss phase restores 1 of your lives. I liked this design because it was fair, at the very minimum you’ll always have 2 lives. This gives enough leeway to be fair but still tough; you’ll always have at least 1 life to learn the attack patterns of the current phase so you can adapt, but if you don’t you’re dead. In other words, you need to GIT GUD if you want to beat this game.
Games that are considered “
difficulty,” in my eyes have a requirement, and that is to be hard, but fair.
for 95% of the time, is hard but fair. Having S ranked every boss, I can safely say that there is nothing in
I would consider “♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.” Every death in the game comes from mistakes that you make, not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t attack that a boss does.
had me playing over and over, even when I was getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me I still had a massive grin on my face, ready to give it another shot when I died and learn from my mistakes.
Furi’s has a gorgeous art style, it’s simple yet colourful and stylish. It’s graphics are fairly basic, but the strong art direction is the selling point. Each of the levels and boss arenas of the prison have a unique aesthetic and personality, from floating rocks high in the clouds, to sandy deserts, to snowy mountaintops.
The boss designs were one of the highlights of the game, I always felt a sense of excitement to see what the boss I would be fighting next would look like. Every boss has a distinct personality that was amplified by their character design, highly stylized and memorable.
If you loved the soundtrack to
you’ll definitely love the soundtrack to this game. If you recognise the names Carpenter Brut and Scattle from the aforementioned soundtrack, you’ll know what to expect from the music.
has a great range of synthwave tunes that match perfectly to the adrenaline fuelled gameplay. The way the music dynamically changes during each of the boss phases never got old, those close quarter fights really become more intense when the beat slows, picks up when you hit that next phase, and then climaxes when you reach the final phase. All in all, this is a great game with some not so minor flaws.
+The visuals, the soundtrack and both enviromental and character design are top notch.
+The fighting gameplay is always tense and it feels great to land a good combo and to analyse the enemy.
+Contrary to what many people say, it is definetely possible to defeat the bosses on your first try ( with one exception ).
+The walking segments inbetween worked for me, but I can understand if someone didn't like them. I feel that they are    very much needed to create at least some kind of build-up for the bosses. I would have loved the narrator / guide to be more specific and really tell the player about them, he ends up saying a lot of nonsenical, way too vague things. The enviroments introduced throuhg these walking segments are beautiful though and sometimes even "react" to the music played.
+The story introduced in the end is pretty neat and explains pretty much every question about the protagonist. The game's focus is obviously not on the narrative, so I think it's fine that the story only picks up at the end.
+The skill curve is great. On your first try, you will struggle against bullet and movement patterns and be very cautious, but after I beat the game I noticed how easy it can be outplay their patterns and hit them with charged attacks in between their moves.
-First off, the boss order just seems wrong. The third boss is one of the most difficult bosses in the game, while the eigth one is incredibly easy for plot reasons; which is fine in general, but shouldn't be this late. The fight would have been much more impactful if it was one of the earlier ones.
-Personally, I think the game could have been a bit more difficult. It took me 3 hours to beat the game, and after the 4th boss I didn't need any second tries ( except the last boss ). Some fights just didn't seem epic or varied enough.
- The dodge is executed on button release, not on button press, which just doesnt work. It leads to the player failing a lot of dodges they have done perfectly, and the long dash is just never worth the hassle of charging it up ( I never used it once after the tutorial ). This could have been solved by a simple option that lets the player rebind the long dash to another key.
- Minor thing; If you play the game with keyboard and mouse ( as I did ) you NEED to set the target mode to "Screen" and the Movement mode to "Directional". The default options are stupidly bad ( they are kind of trying to emulate the gamepads joystick, which doesn't work at all and makes dodging confusing and nigh impossible ) and should'nt be like that. The game was however, perfectly playable without a gamepad after I changed these options.
It's a stylish game that feels great and left me wanting more, greater fights and it deserves a lot more attention.
Keep in mind that you will probably need a lot more time than 3 hours to beat it if you aren't experienced in bullet-hell games. The game also features a boss rush mode and a higher difficulty that unlocks after beating the game, which greatly changes the enemy movesets.

Circuits is an interesting concept of a game, and one that is well executed as well.
It is essentially a puzzle game where you have to match musical elements [a guitar chord, a drum beat] to where they appear in a song as a whole.

You also have to handle is the elements loop, and very often some elements are drowned out by others even though they still add to the song as a whole. Headphones are very recommended for this. There are 25 levels of increasing difficulty, so plenty to do, along with a separate "composer" application.
The game uses a very simple drag and drop interface. I unfortunately can't say for sure if it works with a touch screen, but from what I can say I suspect it will. The music elements and the song in each level are all of a high quality, so it does afeel as if you are interacting with music and not just some pizzle pieces.
Good game for those with a musical ear, or just those who want to improve their own.

"Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride" is just slightly different from most other Artifex Mundi casual, point and click, Hidden Object Games (HOGs).  Like just about all their others, it's got reasonable graphics, mostly tolerable voice acting, adequate story, and a forced second run-through because of mutually exclusive Achievements and lack of saves.  In this case, though, the story seems to have more of a "female" slant (revolving more around a relationship, dealing with marriage, and even 1) one puzzle with lingerie and bouquets and 2) one involving makeup).  Not a big thing, but noticeable.  Also, the "Bonus" chapter is not really optional:  you can't get all the Achievements without going through it on both runs.  Additionally, the puzzles seem just a tad more difficult to do than in the previous AM games I've played.  And, finally, this game is a bit longer than usual.  Overall, to get 100% Achievements, it took me 14.1 hours:  8.5 hours for the first run-through of the main game, 1.3 hours for the Bonus chapter, and an additional 4.3 hours for the second run-through (on Expert and doing the Domino games).  So, assuming you like HOGs and Artifex Mundi, I'd recommend the game even at list price.  Of course, getting it on sale is what I did.

Reviewing hidden object games (henceforth referred to as HOGs for convenience’s sake), especially those by prolific developer Artifex Mundi, has become a bigger and bigger challenge for me the more I play through. It’s a genre that doesn’t really need to differ dramatically from game to game (most people come to HOGs for a very specific sort of game, after all), but due to this similarity it’s hard to know what is really worth talking about as one review can typically serve as a blanket recommendation for a particular developer.
And yet I continue to review Artifex Mundi’s games because time and again I’ve been surprised at how they’ve managed to diversify their portfolio with HOGs which feel distinct from one another. Each of their games has also managed to incrementally build upon the previous one, creating a sense of continual improvement without being required to introduce any radical changes to a formula that is clearly working (if my count is correct this makes my fifth review of an Artifex Mundi game).
With this in mind, Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride is a bit of an odd one out. It’s perhaps the most forgettable Artifex Mundi game I’ve yet played (being barely edged out by the first Nightmares of the Deep), but also one of the most ambitious. The narrative for instance is the most layered and complex of any of Artifex Mundi’s games, taking place over a large timeline and even managing to catch me off guard with a few of its twists. That doesn’t make the plot any good, in fact it has largely fallen apart by the end in through a last-ditch effort to justify some of the symbolism seen throughout the game, but I can still appreciate Artifex Mundi attempting to provide a greater substance to their cliché ridden narratives and perhaps with a few more attempts will get closer to something legitimately compelling.
Grim Legends other notable contribution is your kitten companion you meet early on. Aside from being absolutely adorable she acts as a helper for certain puzzles in the game, which is a nice change from having to jury-rig random items together all the time. I was disappointed however with how rarely my feline friend actually got to do anything, typically being required to sit and be cute in the corner of the screen even when it would make sense for her to help out. I legitimately forgot numerous times she was even usable for puzzle solving because it was so infrequent a solution utilizing her actually worked. Hopefully animal companions (or whatever fits for a specific game) is a returning feature for Artifex Mundi games going forward and will be given a larger part that actually justifies their inclusion.
One of the weirdest things about Grim Legends is how it can look incredible during normal gameplay, but every cutscene is a horrendously compressed mess of muddy textures. Perhaps the difference was just closer before, but I can’t recall any of Artifex Mundi’s previous games having such jarring transitions and they became a continual blight on an otherwise extremely pretty game. On the plus side character models have almost made it out of the uncanny valley, though voice acting is still all over the place, unaided by a few grammatical errors which made it into both the spoken and written script.
I say it every time it seems as if I’m heavily criticizing an Artifex Mundi game, but it’s worth noting again that whatever my disappointment with a specific game may be, I’ve still yet to actually dislike anything they’ve put out. I can certainly point to my favorites, but unless you’re predisposed to dislike HOGs you really can’t go wrong with any of their games, Grim Legends included. I suppose then my reviews or their work is less general buying advice and more a quick rundown of where a particular game fits on the arbitrary leaderboard inside my head. In that sense this isn’t very high on the list, but what it tries and fails to do is encouraging enough to make it a worthwhile stepping stone to better things to come.

Star Conflict is space ship fighting game (I can't think of a better description) it isn't heavily focused on simulation nor is it overly arcade style. For me it hits a sweet spot in between. It combines elements for a lot of different games in order to give the player a fantastic choice for how they wish to progress in the game. There are PVP battles, PVE, space exploration, missions, special events and a persistent galactic map that corporations can fight over territories to control.
So many people have stated that the game is pay to win, which in my opinion couldn't be further from the truth. Yes you can pay for "Premium", the only advantage this gives you is you get more experience and money at the end of a battle. Your ships aren't better, your components aren't better. All paying for the game does is mean you can level faster. Even without premium though you can still level at god rate where it feels less like a grind and more that you are getting somewhere. I've played many games WoT, WoWS plus many others and I feel with Star Conflict the rate of progression is much nicer. As an added bonus if you work on levelling the ships to thei max you get an across the board experience boost that applys to everything. I've yet to play a game myself that does this.
I find it frustrating that so many people bad mouth the fact that you can pay for this game. A key point that it seems a lot of gamers forget is, games don't come for free and developers don't create something just for the enjoyment of others. A game is designed to make money, if a game doesn't make money why are the developers going to spend their time at work doing something for nothing. I could argue about this forever but that isn't what this game is about.
Star Conflict has a fantastic array of ships, modules, weapons all of which allow you to customise your ship to suit your play style and if your a team player, complement your team. There is a huge variety of ships each with their own unique role, playing a ship in the role it was intended not only makes it far more effective but as a pilot you become an integral part of your team.
There are 3 main factions in the game each with their own distinct ship style, Empire ships have small shields but great armour, Federation ships are a balance between armour and shields, Jericho are biased more towards shields. As well as the wide variety of modules available you also can further tailor your play style through your ground crew, which give your bonus's to your ships. You pick an "Implant" per level which acts like a perk, buffing certain aspects of your ship be it shields or weapons or modules. This means that you can really pick and choose which traits suit your playstyle the best and work for you.
There is so much to do in the game that after 70 hours I'm still finding more and more things to do.
The biggest drawback to this game is that it needs much more support, there is a great player base, but having more people would make this game truly epic. The devs actually seem to listen to the players and what they want. In game polls pop up periodically asking for the gamers points of view on potential features. Whats even better just for clicking you get given "GS" the in game currency you buy for money.
There are a plethora of premium ships you can buy, but you don't have to, they aren't better than the main ships. Their biggest benefit is an increased reward for playing them, nothing else.
I really like this game and would recommend to anyone to try it. Its free, give it a go and see if you like it. If you do join a corporation as soon as you can, its well worth it. Having experienced pilots around you can make a really big difference.

TOXIKK is not exactly what I was looking for, as I was hoping more for Quake 3 than Unreal Tournament, which is essentially what this game is, but it is fast-paced and fun enough that I have decided to stay, and eventually will give the dev's my money, as I only have the free version for now. I haven't touched the vehicles yet. I see a lot of people complain about them, but in the free version, the maps with vehicles are so small that they are pointless. The game shines in its deathmatch and capture the flag modes, but there is a domination-like mode that I don't care much for. In most games, you have to hold the point. In this, you just have to touch it to capture it. I didn't care much for other games' domination modes in the first place, though. There is a stealth system, similar to active camo in halo, but it only lasts for about a second, so you really need to learn how to move before you can use it effectively. It adds to the gameplay's frenetic nature, as you fly around and suddenly are being ambushed from an angle you weren't expecting. This game boasts "frag like its 1999," and it definitely delivers. The guns feel appropriately balanced and movement is free enough to allow for crazy gun battles games like the Doom remake or Call of Duty simply can't deliver. Doom and Call of Duty also can't run on potatoes. So go ahead, break out that old laptop from 2009, and download this game, if you really want to, just because you can.

After playing the previous game in the series, I was already biased against the rest of this franchise. Now I've played the second game -
- my suspicions are proved right. This really is a bad, bad little HOG, with an equally unsatisfying storyline compared to the first. You are welcome to try though, at least for the sake of some easy achievements, maybe?
Its 20 years after the events of the previous game - in which case, Dawn should be at her 40s, right? – And another scientist associated with the late Professor Ashford disappears. By now, Dawn is a world-famous paranormal detective with no small reputation. Worried that this recent disappearance might be the work of our previous nemesis, a sign of Ragnar's return, Dawn decides to investigate. From thereon begins an unnecessarily complicated tag game, with ever changing culprits. Even after all the unnecessary complications, the actual culprit is revealed to be the most obvious one. Congrats, developers! You've just managed to make people run after a series of hidden object scenes and puzzles without any decent story revelation! This wouldn't be the first time in HOG history for that anyhow, but it should be a first under Artifex Mundi label. The story inconsistency is basically humongous with this one.
Visuals and CGs are a bit improved compared to the first game, but they are more on the creepy side rather than being appealing. Also, there is some kind of both visual and gameplay inconsistency between the first and the second part of the game. Visuals are somewhat okay in the first half, with near alright animations and downright creepy in the second, with odd stopmotion-like movement breaks. It’s as if they've been prepared by completely different teams. Voice acting is often somewhat decent though – which is the only consistency we’ll be seeing in this game.
During the first half of the game, we encounter various different puzzle and HOG types, with a nearly elegant mise en scene arrangements. They sure are not revolutionary but they kinda signal that this game won’t be that bad. That signal is a lie though. As you come to the hospital part, it all becomes dull and ordinary, with the millionth really basic HOG scene without any elegance or challenge. There is nothing tricky about any of the puzzles either. Also, this second half comes with one plot dump revealed after another, completely ruining what's been left of the originally intended game pace. Oh, and there is still no explanation about this mysterious "demon hunter clan" and "wtf happened to them in the first place".
Brave Giant LTD sadly doesn’t deliver in this game either… All over, it is below average. I wonder if the last game would manage to wrap this whole mess up, or further sink the name of the franchise. Well, we’ll see that a bit later, won’t we? I sincerely recommend choosing another game from Artifex Mundi catalogue, a title that’s been developed by them rather than being only published by them.

Okay, so this is something really special for me.
Crashday has always been one of the games from my childhood that have constantly had a place on my harddrive throughout all the years and I played it at leats once a year, even if it was only to install some mods. I had tons of fantastic hours of gameplay in this game and when I found out that it's going to be remastered, I nearly choked. I never expected this but I love the fact that it happened!
About the game itself: Crashday is a game in which you race cars, fight with cars and do stunts with cars. Those are equipped with a minigun and a rocket launcher (not usable in every mode/event). The vanilla game features 12 cars, all of which have their own special capabilities, and a whole bunch of tracks/scenarios which are playable in seven game modes.
There's
, which is basically the Vehicle deathmatch in which you fight other drivers and earn points for kills/wrecks. This can be played in an FFA variant of in teams.
Then there's
, which is pretty much the same except for the fact that each player or team has to be first to reach a specific amount of kills.
should be quite self-explanatory, you fight other drivers to complete destruction, and the last car to stand wins.
There's also
in which the player has to show tricks with his vehicle, e.g. jumps, barrel rolls, flips and general destruction. The aim of this mode is to collect as many point through combos in a given time.
should not need to be explained, they work the same as in every other racing game (except for the gunplay, maybe).
is a classic mods in which a player or a team has to capture a flag and keep it while driving through a set amount of checkpoints. The first team to clear enough checkpoints wins and the flag can be taken away from another car by ramming it.
is a mode played in Death Match arenas where one player gets a bomb fixed to his car at the start of each round which has a timer that runs out before it explodes. The bomb gets passed on to other cars by ramming them. Whoever had the bomb last gets the most points each round, and the one who blows up gets nothing.
are a kind of races in which every participant gets a bomb fixed to his car which will only go off if the car's speed decreases below a certain point. The minimum required speed raises with each passed checkpoint of the race.
At last, there's
, which simply let you roam around the maps on your own without any goal.
Another unique feature about this game is its detailed track editor, which lets the player choose from a huge variety of environmental tiles and objects (expandable through the Steam workshop) and build a track, arena or scenario of their own. It's easy to use and gives a lot of room for creativity.
The career mode is quite short, which I find to be a little sad as the game has potential to hold a much bigger number events, but what's there is good, and should be challenging enough for most players.
The multiplayer mode offers everything that the single player mode offers aswell, except for the Test Drive mode, but as far as I've been experiencing it, it's great fun, aswell with friends as in public lobbies.
In my opinion, Crashday is an underrated game with a lot of potential for modding and building and every fan of Racing games should give it a try, especially if they love a good bit of destruction with it.

this will be a long review just as a heads up... If I had to put up a TLDR, it would probably be, Download the game and try it, make your own opinion about it.
Let me start off by saying I have played DMO on and off for the past couple years, I started playing this game around late 2012 or early 2013. The UI and gameplay was kind of annoying, but the longer I played it, the more it grew on me, now I am at the point where I love the way it looks and plays.
This game will not be for everyone, It is grindy, time consuming and at times, quite frustrating. If you are fine with this, Read on I suppose, otherwise I don't think you will have alot of fun with DMO, But Like I always say, what do you have to lose trying the game out? download it, and play it for a few hours on the weekend or when you are bored, Whats the worst that happens? you can just uninstall the game in the end, and you do not even have to spend money on it.
Controlls, The game is Lclick to move, Rclick to move camera, they also recently added the options to walk using WASD and you can set your focus on your digimon instead of your tamer, Hotkeys in DMO are a bit strange to me, F1-F4 are your Digimons attacks, while 1-0 are your tamers abillitys *attack target, pick up item, call Digimon, swap Digimon* but you can change them around in the settings *atleast I think you can, I never did since I got used to the keybindings*
Anyway, The community, from what I have seen people are pretty nice, I play on the Lucemon server, and most people I see do not speak english, but I've had alot of people help me out without asking for things in return so that is a plus.
Lets talk about events, DMO can have either good events, or boring events, but there is almost always an event of some sort going on so that is fun.
The cash shop, The place you spend real $$ on, you can buy anything from new tamers, *such as Tai, Mimi, etc.* exp boosters, shop stalls, Digimon, food, bag/bank/digimon storage upgrades, Digimon evolution items, teleport items and costumes that give you stat buffs. Everything in the cashshop is tradeable, so if you do not feel like spending money you can farm ingame currency and purchase the item you want from another player *some people will inflate the price immensely, but that is just how it is in mmos with trading and such*
The grind with DMO is, in my opinion, all RNG. You can be farming the same monster for a quest or an item drop for 3 hours and only have the quest 50% complete, and someone else can run in and get all of their quest items in 5 minutes with 3 copys of the summoning card you wanted. so that will be annoying.
Another thing, what everyone plays for, the Digimon. I love digimon, Always have, Always will. when you start the game you get to choose 1 of the digimon from the datasquad game,*I do not remember if there was a datasquad anime* The digimon you may pick from are Agumon, *Not tai's Agumon mind you, this one turns into Geogreymon* Lalamon, Gaomon and Falcomon.
When you start the game you only have space for a couple of new Digimon, and the tutorial quests will give you 1 or 2 new Digimon. But how do you get new digimon? you want to get a Renamon or a Impmon?, well there are 3 things you can do. you can either buy the Digiegg off of the cash shop for about $7.00 *sometimes a Digiegg will be on sale for about $2.80* Or you can find the Digimon you want in the Digitalworld, and farm it for up too 3+ hours and hope an egg drops. The last thing you can do is find someone selling either the cash eggs, or the drop eggs. In the Lucemon server, Cash eggs and go anywhere from 5T to 20T *T-Tera being the highest form of currency in DMO 1000Bit = 1Mega, and 1000Mega = 1Tera*
Hatching eggs is about the most annoying thing in the game, Unless you get ahold of a cash shop egg, be prepared to possibly lose the egg you just spent time farming for. To hatch an egg you need to inject it with Data you get from killing Digimon. *Beast digimon will drop beast data, dragon digimon will drop dragon data, so on and so forth* Digieggs you got from farming have a chance to break in the incubator everytime you inject data, You must inject data successfully 3 times in order to hatch the Digiegg, but you can succeed up to 5 times. *making your Digimon bigger and it will have more health*
A cash egg however, will always have a 100% chance to hatch, you will either get a **Digiegg lvl.3 lvl.4 or lvl.5, the level tells you how many times you can inject that egg before the 100% chance wears off. *if you get a lvl.3 egg, you can hatch it without problems, just do not try to inject more data or it may break*
I personally feel like this game shines when you are running through it with some friends or a decent guild, I convinced my buddy to play it with me when I first downloaded it and we spent about, 60 or so hours on it just having a good time, killing monsters and ignoreing the quests before he got bored with it.
I think I have been typing for too long, since I forgot what I am even typing about lol.  Anyway all in all, the game can be fun, you just have to get used to the game, like with alot of mmos the game starts to pick up in the later levels, not so much in the starting levels, but if you stick with the game, get a couple friends in on it and play it casually, *don't play it hardcore, because you will just burn yourself out with it* then I am sure you will have fun with this game.
Do I recommend this game? Yes, definitely.
Do I recommend this game to be played solo?, ehh, Try to find some people to play the game with, since solo can get boring quickly.
Sorry for the long review, and if it looks a bit messy, sorry but I am not used to reviews and such. Anyway have fun.

My favorite part is the musical portion, it's unique (at least to me) in a puzzle game to have it all reliant on sound. Nothing is more satisfying than correctly matching up the sound bits to the song, piece by piece, and playing it as a whole and hearing it match solidly to the original. The composer is fun, even with next to no knowledge on how to make music you can throw in a few random things on the track list and it'll probably sound close to decent, I haven't experimented with it too much but I look forward to it. The game itself is fairly priced, if you enjoy music based games or puzzle games, you'll feel it was well worth it, if not for the game itself but just to mess around in the composer (especially if you caught it on a sale, like I did.)

I completed this little game and all its achievements in under 5 hours.  Initially I didn't think this game would have any real replay value until I saw the Circuits Composer (which I have yet to try).  This game is well worth it's price, even its full price!
UPDATE: I just tried the Circuits Composer, and I was mildly disappointed, as I can't create new levels/circuits — only songs.  Oh well....
Two of my favorite things combine into one game: music and puzzle games.  Moreover, the devs have done it in such a special way that makes the music a serious part of the learning process.  This game, true to its word, gives valuable insight to the layering process that goes on in musical composition (and even some live performances), and quite frankly, has made me a little less shy about composing my own stuff.  It was perhaps a bit easier for me than most to solve the 25 puzzles in the game since I have a good sense of rhythm, count, and perfect pitch (try me!).  That said, while I recommend this game for anyone, I highly recommend it for anyone interested in or good at music.
My main complaint with the game though is that at times it is a bit too simplistic.  When I think of "circuits" I think of lots of complex loops and switches.  In this game there are more nodes and dead ends than loops and switches.  But don't let that discourage you from enjoying and assembling the music.
Also, if you have the game and haven't yet played through it, I challenge you to get the "Golden Ear" achievement on your first playthrough.  Reply to this review if you have succeeded.

Started off easy but interesting. Slowly got a bit more interesting, then they introduced the loops portion of the gameplay and that's where the game completely broke down from a musical puzzle to a frustrating chore.
For a musician, this game provides no real challenge or gameplay. Simply listen to each sample and figure out where it needs to go, then when you think you've solved it, just hit play and fast-forward through. There's no incentive to actually listen to the entire piece or all samples together. It's much easier and faster to figure out each "layer" (as they call it) and put in the proper samples.
You may notice that I haven't even spent a full hour on the game but that's because I finished around half the levels and then the "loop" mechanic got SO tedious that I just had to stop. It wasn't an engaging or challenging mechanic. It was just endless tedium. And the number of loops that you need to figure out has no meaning musically as there are no measures or BPM or anything. So it's a matter of figuring out how many times each sample loops audibly. And when you've heard these repeating samples over and over again, watching paint dry sounds like a much better afternoon!
So get it if it's on sale and get it if you're not a musician.

This game has so much potential but falls short. Great looking graphics and a fun concept for a game. The biggest downfalls are the PVP. There seems to be no sort of matchmaking involved. If you're new to the game you'll be dropped into battle with ships that can knock out your shields with a single round from their guns and destroy you with the second because they are two or three levels higher than you with guns and shields way more powerful than you.
The only time there is "matchmaking" is when you and a friend form a group and try to do PVP. Then you'll set there for 20 minutes waiting for the game to try and pair you against another group of the same levels. And the enemy has to have a group that matches your group, not solitary players that happen to be playing at the same time. for example, if the enemy team is made of up 5 solitary players, your group won't get put into that game. Not unless at least two of those enemy players are in a group together that matches the levels of your group.

Hey you!
Yes you. You, who remember good old times when first-person shooters like Quake 3 or Unreal Tournament ruled the world. I bet that you have fond memories of those times - playing death-match with friends, total strangers or bots all day long. You started slow but eventually you improved and rocket jumped like a king. Now fast forward to present day. You are now in mid 30s, working hard in full-time job and you don't really have time to play games anymore. But maybe you should... play a game which feels like something from 1999. A game where your body automatically remembers everything - how to aim with slow rocket launcher, how to predict and shoot grenade launcher, how to snipe those poor guys in the air or just how to run faster and jump further than normal.
Yes, you should play Toxikk - a game which brings pure old school Unreal Tournament-like experience (as opposed to Quake-like) just in new "clothes". It costs only 15E but there is also a free demo. I think that if you loved that kind of games in 1999, you will definitely like this one. I mean - you deserve this game.
Also tell your friends about it too :)

Demon Hunter 2 is a decent hidden object title, but thanks to its haphazard writing, it is also incredibly forgettable if you want to look at it as a casual adventure game.
While the hidden object genre is not exactly famous for its literary masterpieces, we rarely see a story there that is so utterly nonsense and random that it is actually amusing. Demon Hunter 2: New Chapter is such a game, where the only sense one can make of its plot is that it takes place 20 years after the previous game and that some sect tries to open a portal to the nether dimensions (or something).
The point ‘n’ click elements inherited this unpredictable nature, where sometimes even old-school adventure game logic fails to explain some puzzles. Granted, this provides some interesting challenge at least.
As for the hidden object scenes, it feels like as if two different teams created them. The first half of the game features three different kinds, but the second half seems to forget this and just sticks to traditional list-based searches.
Despite all of these, gameplay is not bad at all; sometimes it is a bit clumsy, but if we look past the writing, Demon Hunter 2 is a fun HOG to play.

The original
was a passable Hidden-Object Game, but far from the best that publisher Artifex Mundi had to offer.
builds on that foundation and comes out as a quality two-hour experience that's a solid offering even by Artifex Mundi's standards.
As is traditional for AM, difficulty is rather low, so experienced players should have no fear of ratcheting up the difficulty.  No achievement is offered for playing on a harder mode, though, so achievement-hunters might just choose to blast through quickly on the easiest setting.  It's possible, and not particularly difficult, to get every achievement in a single runthrough.
The story is constructed out of clichés, per the normal practices of the Hidden Object genre, but it's much more elaborate than the plot of the original.  Though it never has a truly astonishing moment, the twists are sufficient to keep the tale interesting this time around.
I happily recommend this game to any HO fans, and hope that
continues this process of improvement on the previous title.

is a hidden object game with lots of puzzles that serves as a direct sequel to
and continues the story of the heroine, Dawn. While the first title left me feeling rather lukewarm, this game manages to improve on some issues I had with the first installment. The best part is, while it’s a direct sequel you don’t need to play the first game to fully enjoy this one. The story of the first game is referenced in this one but you get enough of a recap to not get lost along the way.
This game takes place twenty years after Dawn’s first adventure, she is now a respected -and experienced- demon hunter. However, her past continues to haunt her as she is called in for a case that connects to her adoptive father who was slain two decades ago. Unfortunately, much like in
there isn’t much actual demon hunting in this game. However, there is a lot more action and while the story still isn’t stellar it’s certainly interesting. Someone working for a demon is out to tarnish Dawn’s reputation and she must both stop the forces of evil and also avoid jail by clearing her name. One downside to the story, however, is a lack of a bonus chapter. The game takes place twenty years after the first, there could have been some small adventure to give us as a bonus chapter.
With the improved story also comes improved gameplay. The game offers a variety of locations filled with puzzles and hidden object scenes. One thing I enjoyed was a small bit of variety with the scenes, usually you are just given a list of items to find but this game added a shadow hidden object scene and a few other variations. Sadly, these were very few and I wouldn’t have minded seeing more. None of the puzzles are too difficult, they range from easy to a decent challenge. I did not find myself frustrated at all while playing and the game gave adequate instructions if you needed help. You have an interactive map that is useful to teleporting or finding where your next action is as well as an easy-to-use inventory system.
The graphics also received an upgrade in this sequel.  The visuals are much crisper and the animations a bit better. However, the characters still have weird lip movements when they speak, I’m not sure if this is just a stylistic choice for this series or not but I find it off putting. Overall, however, things look fine. The colors are vibrant and even when the setting is dark and spooky you can see what you’re doing pretty well. The voice acting is alright, some actors were pretty bad but as a whole I didn’t find myself laughing at anything or wanting to mute the game. The music is fitting for the theme of the game but easily forgettable.
If you’re a fan of hidden object games then I do suggest adding
to your library. It’s a very solid game and an enjoyable experience. Also, if you’re playing the game on Steam there are achievements to collect, all of which are pretty simple. None require you to play the game on the highest difficulty so you can still relax and play the game while collecting said achievements. There are also Steam trading cards if that is your thing. While I wasn’t a huge fan of the first title, this installment peaked my interest in this series and I look forward to playing the third game.

I purchased this game because a friend compared combat to dark souls. It does bear a passing similarity; parry, dodge, melee and ranged attacks are core parts of the game. What did this game in for me however, is the ways in which it is unlike those games. The game is built entirely on bosses, there is no substantial content in between them, and boss fights themselves are built on phases. Beating a phase of a boss awards and additional life, something I'm already opposed to in gaming, but since there are no upgrades to health or weapons, it seems like this was the best they could come up with in terms of letting the player control their experience.
The biggest problem with this game is how it forces you into certain play styles based on which phase of the boss fight you are in. During bullet hell phases, you're not allowed to rush up and attack the bosses that stand still and shoot at you. Melee attacks do no damage in these phases. If you're not a fan of endlessly shooting oncoming projectiles while waiting out these phases, then this game is not for you. There is no way to speed up these phases other than doing damage to the boss. These phases often have two phases within one, where you are required to first shoot and dodge projectiles, once the boss's health is depleted, the camera will switch and you'll enter the melee portion of the phase. Why are these not separate? If you have a hard time with shooting, or just find it boring like I did, you aren't rewarded for slogging through these sections since you still have to beat another phase before you and the boss regain health and you move on to the next phase.
Melee combat is also unfulfilling. The combat relies on a few basic principles. You have a regular and a heavy attack, and parries. Dodging is low risk, low reward, and awards no health bonus. You would think that parrying would be the opposite, high risk and reward, since it awards a health bonus, but almost every attack has the same parry timing, so once you learn it melee bosses pose no threat whatsoever. Melee sections are easy clears since parrying is so easy and awards a generous health boost since bosses always, always attack in the same 3/4/5 hit combos. I never once used the heavy attack since it only seemed to open me up for damage from the boss, and the damage you do in return is dwarfed by your combos. You cannot stunlock bosses through good movement/attack timing. If you do enough damage they will gain some kind of poise mechanic and power straight through your attack. Even the power attacks when you land a combo aren't worth it since they award less health than parries.
I'm baffled, because this game seems to be sold on it's fast combat, but it forces you so many times to wait out stages where the boss won't let you attack or is altogether invulnerable. Rushing up and doing enough damage should be rewarded by stunning the boss out of the bullet hail phase. add a block button instead of forcing people to parry, which they can't do in bullet hell phases. I only played this game for a few hours, but I made it through four of the ten total bosses in the game, making it pathetically short.
I did not get into the furier difficulty before uninstalling, but I didn't really feel the need to. The game isn't hard in the same way that Dark Souls is often described. Furi pulls quite a few punches by not allowing you to damage bosses in certain stages and forcing you to take damage if you're not in a certain place in the arena. Furi is not a difficult game that rewards you for playing smartly, it creates artificial difficulty by bending the rules for the player and intentionally putting them in a bad situation. You can beat this game by mashing two buttons and the sticks if you give it enough time.
Not recommended.

There's no big picture or grand build up of skill.  You are powerful, incredibly so, but your power comes from how well you can see patterns and exploit timings.  Find the pattern, execute your moves, win the fight.... always.  Difficulty is a series of hanicaps. The fights really don't change... the story doesn't change.
Don't buy for the music (Hotline Miami 2 has a much better soundtrack).
Don't buy for the art (The effort is all in the character models).
Don't buy for the story (it doesn't matter and when it does... it still doesn't matter).
Also the voice is probably the most annoying part of the game.  He's needed because without him it's just a dull walk along a linear path, but his nutter-butter musings are probably as thrilling as absolute silence.

This game is so good and distills some very tight mechanics down into 9+ fights that require you to be disciplined, recognize patterns, and be quick to react. It doesn't overstay it's welcome and the first run through will require you to constantly adapt to new patterns and new ways of fighting that it almost always feels fresh.
It is so close to being that goal of "perfect" that the few minor problems that I have with the game are all the more glaring. There are 2 of the fights that seem so out of place with the rest of the game that they stick out like the proverbial sore thumb. One could have been alleviated if placed differently in the procession of fights while one is infuriating from a flow stand point rather than difficulty.
It stands out as a very precise and well tuned that it is well worth it if you enjoy difficult games that demand your attention and execution.
Highly recommend for anyone who likes the bullet hell genre and wants a challenge.

Furi is a bit of a weird game.
Its beautiful to look at. The art style, designs, music, and even writing are all fantastic. There isn't much adult language in the game, but when it is used it takes you off guard because you aren't expecting it, making its use even that much more powerful. The music is absolutely fantastic. The voice acting suits it well. The visual style just pops off the screen.
The gameplay is simple. There are times where you walk, listening to the Voice (Rabbit guy) tell you about the world, yourself, himself, and the boss to come. Then there are the boss fights, endurance matches where you are really tested. This isn't a game about "oh shoot this guy with enough bullets to win". This is a game where you, as a player, are tested. You have to pay attention to your surroundings, as it'll constantly get filled with bullets to dodge. You have to watch for patterns, to know when to strike, when to block, and when to dodge. This game demands the player THINK and REACT quickly and logically, something you don't see in many games today. Yes, the game is pretty much a series of boss battles with some walking and exposition in between, but honestly its enjoyable all the way through.
This game isn't for everyone. But i'd say give it a try. I wish there was a demo up, so people could give it a go and see how they like it. I definitely recommend it. Its challenging, beautiful, and rewarding.

The Forsaken Bride is the first installment of Grim Legends series by Artifex Mundi. The next installement of this series is Song of the Dark Swan.
Game Menu Option: Two section – Volume and Miscellaneous settings. The volume section has the following: Music and Sound. The miscellaneous section has the following: Custom Cursor, Voice Overs, Difficulty Mode and Full Screen. Wide Screen is automatically supported in the game.
Game Difficulty Modes: Three game difficulty modes – Casual, Advanced and Expert.
Cinematic/Dialogue: All cinematic scenes can be skipped if you do not want to watch them. They can be watch over again under the cutscene section the extras. There is an option for skipping the entire dialogue scene without having sit through it.
Voiceovers: Nothing much can be said about the voice overs asides from that they are well done.
Game Music/Sounds: Nothing much can be said about the music/sounds asides from that they fit well with the game.
Game Graphics: Nothing much can be said about the graphics asides from that they are nicely drawn with a painted feel to them.
Inventory Panel: There is a lock option for the inventory panel. Easy access for the items that are collected in the game.
Notebook: Two sections – Map and Objectives.
Map: The map interactive with useful indicators; map icons/markers. The legend on the map explains the function for each of the map icons. The ability to fast travel to another location and back. The map can be access two-way via through the notebook or map scrolls next to the notebook.
Hidden Object Gameplay: Fragmented items, Shadow items, Traditional Word list with some and/or no interaction required. The hidden object scenes can be replayed in the hidden object puzzle section in the extras.
Domino Gameplay: This game feature is optional for those who don’t want to go looking for items in hidden object scenes.
Puzzle Gameplay: Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve. Some puzzles has extra puzzles in them to solve (ie: Lily’s Wedding Gift Necklace) There is a skip button if the puzzle(s) becomes too tasking to solve.
Game Helper: A furry feline helper can carry out certain tasks that the players can’t complete themselves. Like retrieving items that are out of reach.
Game Ending: There is an ending for the main portion of the game. The bonus chapter portion of the game extends that ending a bit more.
Game Achievements: Most of these achievements are featured in Steam’s achievement. There are four different sets of achievements to earn. Trophies – 11 in total; Spirits – 30 in total; Elusive Objects – 28 in total and Story Achievements – 13 in total.
Game Collectables: Two sets of collectables – 30 Spirits in total and 28 Elusive Objects in total. The “x” on the two bottles, Spirits and Quill, will light up; If any area in the game that has collectables in them.
Game Concept Art/Wallpapers: 12 concept art and 12 wallpapers.
Game Soundtrack: Nine soundtracks from the game.
Game Length: There are eight chapters in the main portion of the game. The bonus chapter portion of the game mostly likely to have at least two chapters the most.
Game Trading Card/Badge: This a special feature only available in the Steam’s version of the game. The game drops three different trading cards only once and the rest of the cards: Community Market, Booster Packs and Trading. The game badge can be crafted after having all the card in the inventory then it can be upgraded four more times.

Definitely more of a "girly" title than the others of their I've played, it's still a solid point and click adventure with hidden object scenes. The staging is nice, good music, not in any way challenging puzzles (but that's expected) and a reasonable story.
This time there is a twist on the hidden object parts - if you don't fancy them you can play with dominoes instead (and you can actually flip between modes - for example using dominoes to pick up a few items you can't find or switching back to hidden object mode to find items you aren't going to be able to reach with your dominoes.
It's worth noting that the achievements include the bonus chapter in things like completing all hidden object puzzles without hints so don't expect them to pop at the end of the story. You'll also need at least two playthroughs to get the dominoes and HO achievements (as that's an either or choice). If you mix between them while you play and keep track, the game also does so you can fill in the blanks on your next playthrough. Or if you're me, completely forget and end up playing through three times.
The game did start to run decidedly slowly with big pauses by the time I hit the third run through.
As for the girly elements. Well you gain a ridiculously cute kitten as a sidekick. I mean really just insanely adorable. Would like to have seen it used more. *shifty look*  It's also definitely a romance. You will also have to solve such puzzles as  reassembling jewelry, applying makeup, flower arranging, ironing - not to mention the obligatory moments where during your life or death adventure your heroine suddenly refuses to do something because ...eww cobwebs/bugs/vermin. Such moments always make me want to kick the heroine. Luckily for the most part she remains reasonably resourceful and not overly whiny.
All in all a great example of this genre. If you like this type of game, I would highly recommend this.

Also, this is the same for the domino achievement.  In order to get these, you must play both.

A clever twist on the visual novel formula, in VA-11 HALL-A instead of simply clicking on different decisions your character can make, you get to serve drinks! And it's actually pretty fun!
The story is good and the characters likeable and memorable, but honestly the best part in my opinion is the worldbuilding. There's a reason the word cyberpunk is in the title, and the game does a great job of slowly feeding you little tidbits and details that build a surprisingly bleak, disturbing image of the future. Because sure, the everyday little adventures of genetically enhanced cat girls, cheerful android sex workers and inexplicably sentient corgis are fun enough on their own, but to me the main draw was figuring out the mysterious backstory and history of the world. Glitch City is a true dystopia, filled with all the usual trapping of the genre (like evil corporations, corrupt government, scifi elements, etc etc) and all that is kept in the background and doled out in small doses while our protagonist goes through her everyday life.
Nevertheless the story is kept lighthearted and funny most of the time. There's not much of an overreaching plot, but the characters have their own arcs that can range from the silly to the dramatic, and Jill goes through quite a lot of character development while dealing with relatable issues. At times the game even gets pretty philosophical with surprisingly deep topics, and I thought the game had some genuinely helpful advice about life.
The other aspect of the game that struck a chord with me were the lgbt+ elements, which were a very pleasant surprise since I wasn't expecting it at all! It's always resfreshing to see queer protagonists and characters treated with respect and thoughtfulness by a narrative, and VA-11 HALL-A deals with the issue with a lot of sesitivity and care, making it just a natural part of its world. This kind of good representation really makes a difference, and I'm glad this game exists for this reason alone.
In the end I had a lot of fun with this, and I definitely recommend it if you like casual dialogue-heavy games.
