There's a lot of visual novel games on Steam. Most of them aren't very good, and just seem pumped out without much care because they're a simple genre to make. VA-11 Hall-A is not one of those games at all, a lot of care went into this game.
The story takes place in Glitch City, a cyber-punk setting where crime is on the rise, the officials are corrupt, pretty much every bad thing you can think of. With this sort of backdrop there's a lot of stories you could tell, and the one the developers chose was a simpler one, which allows you a glimpse into all the others: bartending. You play as Jill Stingray, who works at the titular bar, serving alcohol to private investigators, power armored policemen, robots and journalists. Each of them has a story they're the main protagonist of, and you get a look into them through Jill's eyes. They come to the bar for various reasons, and you serve them drinks.
Gameplay-wise, this doesn't amount to much, so if you're expecting a full bartending simulator you'll probably be disappointed. Mixing drinks is very simple and every drink has a direct guide, so unless you forget the order or they give some cryptic request, as some characters do, it's unlikely you'll mess up. Ordinarily Jill will supply the name of what they want or their request as you're moving through the mixing menu, but from time to time she'll have something she wants to buy - if you don't, she'll be distracted and not do that. That's about the only incentive for having money in the game, aside from right at the end.
That leaves most of the game's appeal its writing, which I found pretty good and has some memorable lines, although mileage seems to vary there for people. There were some characters in it I didn't much care for, such as an Adam Jensen-lookalike who had the old 'hitman with morals' trope, but there were many more I did. There's enough characters that you'll probably find someone you like. Hopefully Jill is one of those characters though, as she does have her own story which gets a lot of prominence as the game goes on.
I should mention some things that might be turnoffs. Not just the hitman character, but a lot of them are references, subtle or otherwise, to other things. Most of the time it doesn't detract, and they all have character beyond that, but one character is pretty much a dead ringer for George from Seinfeld, and he's a private investigator, something I couldn't really take seriously. It also has a lot of internet humor - the fascist security force are called the White Knights, Jill uses an imageboard based off you-know-what, and one extra is basically a Twitch streamer in real life. So if you can't tolerate that sort of thing I'd stay away.
Also, one thing a lot of people don't like about the game is one character who's a robot designed to look like a ten year old girl, who also happens to be a sex worker. I didn't really have a problem with her myself, because she felt like an actual character to me, and the game doesn't throw up CGs or anything of her work, although she does mention it a lot. If you don't want to play the game because of her, that's perfectly fine, she is in it a lot. But I don't feel the game's irredeemable from her being in it.
The music in the game also bears mention, since there are over thirty songs of different tones and genres which you can put into a playlist every night. So if you find some songs you really want to hear, you can whenever you want. The playlist might be unnecessarily long, though, as it resets halfway through each day when you go on break, and even if you let every conversation scroll onto the box by itself I'm not sure you'd get to the end.
VA-11 Hall-A has a couple different endings based on whether or not you pay your bills, and serve particular drinks to certain people at the right time, but overall it's largely linear. There's a looming threat hanging over any multiplayer game, becoming more and more apparent as time goes by and digital distribution stores such as Steam offer more and more content. It is, as you know, lack of playerbase.
Lack of playerbase is a degenerative sickness of game medium. In its first phase, it brings games down to their knees and than completely destroys them. Simply, there are no well defined rules which game will suffer from it, but most affected are indie games without well oiled and highly paid PR machinery.
TOXIKK's been on my radar since I first saw their "Frag Like It's 1999!" tagline. It aims to provoke warm and fuzzy feelings in the belly of all arena shooter players who were active playing that kind of games at the end of the nineties and beginnings of 21st century. In digital years, we're talking about one of the prehistoric eras of gaming - let me remind you that kids born in 2000 are now 16 years old and may have never heard, yet played your favorite old school games.
Of course, the whole arena shooter concept has been almost beaten to death by FPS evolution. Come to think of it, we haven't seen any significant games with that ancient concept in the last few years. Loadouts, items, cover systems, iron sights, all these elements made FPS much more complicated and, unfortunately in many cases, more boring beasts. They became standards so many people these days don't really understand the concept of arena shooters.
Probably after experiencing an extremely low playerbase during their paid Early Access phase, Reakktor Studios made a brilliant decision and offered new players a chance to try their game for free. TOXIKK's FREE edition is much more than a demo - it basically keeps only several game elements behind the paywall. These are server browser, map voting, customizing your character and some maps. As such, Free Edition will suit casual players more than fine and, by buying Full Edition, you will be able to customize your gaming experience even more. Mechanics-wise, it needs to be said, there's no difference between two versions and when you shoot, you need to shoot to kill. No money deal can save your from rocket launcher fire, you know?
If we judge TOXIKK by its tagline, it's making an obvious reference to arena shooter classics such as Quake III Arena and Unreal Tournament. However, it isn't that simplified. Yes, TOXIKK does follow the rules: you spawn with simple pistol, you pick armor and weapons off the ground and they don't last beyond your death. It's fast paced and frantic, you will be missing more while backtracking than standing, shooting and hitting the target.
However, it also implements vehicles so game clearly and closely resembles Unreal Tournament 2004 which is still being loved, cherished and played around the globe. UT2004 seems like the main inspiration for the game in the terms of movement as well. Also, some ideas have mutated and presented itself in TOXIKK as its own: short-term invisibility and playing-dead abilities are definitely adding a new layer to the same ol', same ol' routine. They especially come in handy when it comes to matches that require a certain amount of strategical thinking, such as Capture The Flag.
If we talk about ideas, TOXIKK basically brings nothing new to the table. We have seen it all. However, innovation is not purpose of TOXIKK's existence. As a homage, Reakktor's game is doing wonders - all weapons have double modes and have that 'I've seen this somewhere before' feeling attached. You will be fighting in well known and classic modes such as area domination, capture the flag and deathmatch. These modes have been named differently (for example, deathmatch is Blood Lust), but the rules are still the same.
Game visual design is what really makes TOXIKK stand out - it is modern and awesome looking. However, this is double-edged sword because colorful maps and shiny weapons will sometimes impact your game performance, not in the technical, but skill field. I like to keep all the shine toned down a bit because sometimes it's rather hard to concentrate on your opponents and their movements, especially on maps that boast different neon lights and colors.
Level design is spot on. From cramped, arena style spaces to wide open levels, TOXIKK has it all. Interiors and exteriors are brilliantly modeled and designed for balance. However, only a blind person or someone who didn't play the classics will not see obvious thef... (homage!) of blueprints that most TOXIKK's maps are based on. DEKK is basically Deck 16. The Citadel is larger version of Facing Worlds and so on. But I don't really mind because good copies are more than welcomed here.
TOXIKK also boasts its own experience level and skill class system. First one is a way for person to unlock many different personalization options which let you customize your soldier's appearance. Skill Class is a concept of keeping the players of the similar rank on the same servers. However, if you want hardcore experience, Skill Class can be turned off so you will be able to join No-SC servers and be obliterated by veterans of the genre.
Skill class and EXP points can be earned via multiplayer games or solo experience which consists of contracts and skirmish games. Contracts are basically matches that have several objectives listed such as winning, finishing within certain time limit and so on.
TOXIKK's gameplay is enjoyable. As stated previously, it is fast-paced and there's no need to think - you shoot and ask questions later. It is important to mention TOXIKK does not feel like a cheap knock-off and that's the best thing about it. If UT2004 was made in 2016, it would definitely look and feel like this. There's nothing wrong with it if you're a member of niche audience. I wholeheartedly recommend you to, at least, try out Free Edition.

This game is quite enjoyable for me, being someone who has enjoyed games like Rimworld and Factorio.
Fair warning to all those that wish to play this, however: The learning curve can be a bit steep, and the game is not forgiving of failure. No power means that your people can't get in or out, or use any functions of a room (Even when it wouldn't make sense for that to happen, such as with the case of the dorms and tables in the canteen). Play it slow, and make sure you have a surplus before trying to expand, either of power or food.
Speaking of, a size two greenhouse is good early on, before you get the larger one. And wind turbines, though they can be finnicy, are immensely helpful.
A couple of things that might turn people off: You have no control over what your colonists are working on, save prioritizing a room (Not a single machine, a room), and disasters can be a bit.. Ehh, especially without being able to lock your colonists inside (gained by a building). The food system is a little obscure; you want to have a meal type other than 'basic' unless you want your colonists to all complain about being malnourished or, as happened with me, your sole medic to be complaining about that while your workforce is sporting numerous trauma injuries.
Assuming one can manage that curve without messing up, you have an interesting, if not incredibly deep, game. There are three planets, each of which is unlocked by the previous via milestones (my experience this far has been on the starting planet, so grains of salt and all that). The tutorial is decent enough for getting started, and the stat system is largely intuitive. The menus, despite being a bit clunky, are easy enough to understand, and it's easy enough to have varied enough food for the colonists to avoid issues.

Planetbase: it's like Banished in Space, but with WAY less frustrating AI. Like many players, I really enjoy games that contain the combination of basebuilding, resource management, and survival. But Banished didn't do it for me: I really tried to like the game but found the insistence of the AI to take long trips of death frustrating to no end.
Planetbase isn't like that. After 8 hours of gameplay, the AI is almost flawless, with just a few minor documented issues. Some players have had a hard time, but every problem with "my workers refuse to work" is due to a determinable cause - i.e. their required resource is out and you need to produce more first, or they're injured/sick. This leaves you free to explore the larger aspects of the game. I would definitely call one of Planetbase's biggest strengths the fact that is focuses on the bigger picture, rather than getting caught up in the micro with games such as Space Colony.
At the same time, Planetbase definitely doesn't dumb down the difficulty. There are numerous ways to die. I lost my colony and restarted a new one 6 separate times before I made it to 100 colonists, where I am on my current save. Starting off a new colony is a challenge of very limited resources, trying to get yourself to self-sustainability. And unlike other reviews, I have to disagree that the game doesn't have challenges later on. Enemies will attack your colony, and may kill a dozen people while your colonists try to defend themselves (these visitors' motivations for committing suicide on your colonists are unclear). Power utilization remains an issue (you WILL die if you run out of power), and you NEVER have enough resources. I am currently finding robot production quite interesting, as you can automate some of the simpler tasks.
There's been some other reviewers suggesting that the game doesn't have much depth or isn't replayable. So far I have found this to be far from the case. And you should feel assured that if I do play a game for an extended period of time and give it a bad review, it won't be because it was "boring", it'll be because of bad mechanics or developer support. I don't play boring games.

While streaming this I was asked for a quick description of this game, and the first thing I said was "Banished in Space."
The basis of the game is clear, you take a colony ship and build a colony. Sounds simple right? In theory it is, you supply your colonists with Oxygen, Water, Food, and Entertainment. Your Colonists have different roles, such as Worker, Engineer, Biologist, etc and each plays their part in the colony in their own way.
Where the game gets interesting is that as your colony grows, it needs more everything. More Energy, Materials, Colonists, etc. It suddenly goes from simple idea, to managing multiple spinning plates on sticks. Think you have it all under control? Not so fast! Add in natural disasters and invaders, and you have found yourself precariously low on materials, which cause other problems, and now your spinning plates can come crashing down.
However, the game never feels like you are out of control of the situation. Many problems are caused by your own doing. Grow too fast and your people starve. Forget to defend against a disaster, and suddenly you are salavaging parts of your base to recover. Even when I lost all my colonists to lack of water, I was not frustrated because it was my own fault.
The tutorial is very well done, and covers the important basics very well. They leave some advanced buildings to mystery, but the tooltips and help menus cover as much or as little as you want to read.
My favorite part of the game is that there is not only logical progression, but how things interact is logical. Additionally, you can customize the interior of your colony to specialize as much are as little as you'd like. Need more Engineers? You can adjust the percentage of Engineers you let come to your colony! You don't need any more Medics? Don't allow any to arrive on the next ship!
Add in there's techs for bigger buildings (which provide more space, power, etc), and that some tasks can be done by robots, and you've got a deep enough game to satisfy the micromanager in you.
Overall, if you are a fan of this type of game, you'd be doing yourself a favor by getting this game. For me, it is hands down one of the best colony builder games I have played.

Demon Hunter 2: New Chapter is unfortunately a below average hidden object game, with a simple (yet still almost non-coherent) story and some advanced hidden object elements. It's created by Brave Giant and is the sequel to Demon Hunter: Chronicles from Beyond. I admit I haven't played the first one, but after having finished this game, I don't feel too much inspiration for that.
As the title implies, we hunt a demon who threatens the world and that's all the story basically in this 3-3.5 hour long adventure. I understand that plots are usually not overcomplicated in hidden object games, but a bit more introduction with deeper characters would have been nice. Later on, we get the usual plot twist, but it's so crazy, it actually makes things worse. We also seem to have a talisman that can save our life in many, seemingly lethal situations, but since its use is automatic, it doesn't bring any changes regarding gameplay.
The minigames are pretty easy, which is a shame, since harder puzzles are always welcome as opposed to frustrating hidden object scenes. The latter aren't that bad: the game uses tricks to hide some of the items, but these can be frustrating sometimes (we have to wait for something to turn into the desired object). One of the better puzzles was the one at the beginning where we have to start up our helicopter, wish there were more of those. There's also an extra puzzle: there are swords scattered around (usually 1 in each of the major scenes), but all we get is an image under the achievements tab displaying a room with furnitures, ornaments and other accessories (and an achievement accordingly of course). I missed one in the hospital scene and had to start over the whole game because of that, so keep an eye out, they aren't that hard to notice.
What made the game look and feel strange for me right at the beginning was the choice of location: it's a mixture of an autumn forest and a semi-tropical setting taking place on 'Iowa Island'. Maybe it's just me, but this setting is unusual for a hidden object game, mainly because it's hard to maintain the traditional mysterious tone throughout the game with all the vivid and vibrant colors of the environment. Don't get me wrong: the scenes are beautifully drawn, but they lack that atmosphere we all (at least myself) love in HOGs. Also the character models seem very cheap, which is a common problem in these types of games (yes, I know they are primarily made for tablets), but still they are not nearly as well animated as the beautiful, interactive backgrounds.
Many people criticized the synchronization of the voice-overs and the facial animations of the characters in the first game and sadly yes, the problem still exists in the sequel too. The music is very monotonous and irritating as well, so no good points there either.
While the game plays as a run-of-the-mill hidden object game, the story and all the additional small things make it uninteresting. If you are desperately looking for a casual game you haven't played before, it could be worth a look, but there are many-many better games out there.
PROS
+ if you like the semi-tropical setting you'll like some of the locations
+ the graphics is generally good
+ some good minigames
CONS
- the atmosphere takes a hit because of the location
- very bad, tiresome story
- the music gets quicky on one's nerves
- bad synchronization
- a bit too many hidden object scenes
RATING
3.5/10
Poor writing, poor character rendering, EXTREMELY poor voice acting, too easy puzzles. Avoid it.

Twenty years ago, the last Demon Hunter, Dawn Ashmore, managed to defeat an evil entity called Ragnar, that killed her adoptive father. However, she knows that the demon will wake up one day. But when she received a desperate call from Professor Williams, a friend of Professor Ashmore, she goes straight to his manor...
If you remember the first Demon Hunter, it wasn't a catastrophe in itself if you stuck to English and if you can get past the fact that you were roaming free around after meeting Ragnar instead of having to defeat him quickly. This time, Dawn is a middle-aged woman, living alone, waiting for Ragnar to come back.  Guess what, she even has an helicopter as main way of transportation! Well, apart this strange little way to introduce the story, the rest is enough well-written to ask yourself who is really the killer and why he wants Miss Dawn dead. And finally, the final confrontation is reduced. At least, it's making sense now to be stuck in two rooms and to have less actions to do than in the first story.
The gameplay is quite the same: pick items, use them, clear hidden objects scenes (with one that I've liked as it was finding items to move), solve puzzles. You have also swords to hund but they're not in every scene. However, contrary to the first game, this one is divided in chapters, where you're visiting one location only and can't go back to what you've done previously. You have four main locations: Williams's mansion, the hospital, the docks with the mayor's yacht and the professor's cabin.  However, you have enough scenes there to enjoy the diversity. The puzzles are often easy, though some of them will require several sequences (like the helico).
A good relief for Demon Hunter 2 is that the translation was this time accurate. Finally, it was well-translated, without having to wonder if you were going to guess the item as in the first game, still not patched.
The graphics are also very good in itself and despite the dark ambiance, everything is brightful, maybe the hospital is perhaps more in a sad mood than the rest. As for the soundtrack, it was very good.
I really enjoyed this sequel, way better than the first game. I would have preferred an explanation on how Dawn managed to get a chopper and maybe a little more Ragnar action as he's still waiting for his demise, even if now, the time is shorter between the discovery and the actual "go back to your realm". You can go ahead with this one.

Demon Hunter 2 is a hidden object casual game published by Artifex Mundi. It’s a pretty good game for killing time and I like some of the puzzles in the game. You play as “Dawn Foster” who is a demon hunter and is the last remaining one in her family. While the game can be pretty easy most of the time you’re either doing find the hidden objects mini games or moving around different places looking for clues and trying to save yourself from the demon “Ragnar”. The story can be cheesy but it’s good enough to have you sit through the entire game which isn’t that long.
The graphics are your average run of the mill standard hidden object finder games’ graphics. The hand painted art is nice though and good looking. There are cringe worthy and yet hilarious character models and speaking animations (are these deliberate?). The game runs at a solid 60 FPS, there seem to be no problems in the performance as well.
The voice overs are not the best similar to the speaking animations but then again I think this is deliberate. They still do their job telling the story and interacting with other characters etc. The music, however is very good and kept me playing the game and had that mysterious feeling which is pretty well representative of a hidden object game.
The game has simple hidden object finding mini games. You go into different rooms and different places and find things which unlock other rooms and stuff. The demon tries to kill you many ways like with an RPG, car bomb etc. but you have this pendant which protects you.
There are also mini games which can be skipped but I never skipped any as these can be pretty fun to solve. Most of them are pretty easy and can be done in a minute or two. Other than the standard hidden object finding mini games you also get mini games similar to a hidden object game but instead of finding the objects you must place the objects in their appropriate place as shown in by its silhouette.
You go through many locations such as streets, houses, basements, closets, hospital, surgery room etc. All these locations are beautifully hand painted. The puzzles are pretty clever and most of the time you would know what to do with each item unlocking something else.

Furi is a bit of a weird game.
Its beautiful to look at. The art style, designs, music, and even writing are all fantastic. There isn't much adult language in the game, but when it is used it takes you off guard because you aren't expecting it, making its use even that much more powerful. The music is absolutely fantastic. The voice acting suits it well. The visual style just pops off the screen.
The gameplay is simple. There are times where you walk, listening to the Voice (Rabbit guy) tell you about the world, yourself, himself, and the boss to come. Then there are the boss fights, endurance matches where you are really tested. This isn't a game about "oh shoot this guy with enough bullets to win". This is a game where you, as a player, are tested. You have to pay attention to your surroundings, as it'll constantly get filled with bullets to dodge. You have to watch for patterns, to know when to strike, when to block, and when to dodge. This game demands the player THINK and REACT quickly and logically, something you don't see in many games today. Yes, the game is pretty much a series of boss battles with some walking and exposition in between, but honestly its enjoyable all the way through.
This game isn't for everyone. But i'd say give it a try. I wish there was a demo up, so people could give it a go and see how they like it. I definitely recommend it. Its challenging, beautiful, and rewarding.

I do not typically write reviews, but I feel that this game deserves it. At the time of writing this, I have beaten the game once on the normal difficulty (Furi difficulty).
Quick rundown is as follows:
Things I like about it
- Soundtrack varies from pensive or mysterious to intense. The music always felt like it fit perfectly. The fights had my hands sweating and my heart rate up.
- Learning the timings of each of the enemies felt somewhat similar to what I have experienced in Dark Souls games. Learning how to deal with everything was almost always rewarding. When I say almost, let me add that I don't count it as a bad quality that it wasn't always rewarding....
- The gameplay and responsiveness in general is amazing. Dang does it look cool when you get a perfect parry.
Things I don't like about it
- It can feel a bit like the gameplay is driven by quick-time events at times. Personally I don't mind the way the game handles it as it still requires you to be quick. I know some people that won't play such a game, however, so I feel it is worth mentioning.
- The whole experience is a little short if you just beat the game once. If you're someone that likes to 100% games though, have fun getting S rank on the hardest difficulty for everything!
